Short Version: I needed something to make it so my Logitech M705 mouse could use Setpoint while on the Steam Link. The mouse sensitivity without Setpoint was way too low. This did the trick and there are no latency issues.
Long Version: After trying several wifi adapters that either had terrible range or simply didn't work, I decided to snake some Cat5e from my desktop to my router. After doing this, I thought, "why not hook up the Steam Link?" A buddy of mine worked at the Valve factory in Chicago, where they assemble the Steam Link and Steam controllers, and he gave me one a while back. I didn't really use it much because my previous wifi speed was pretty bad, due to an outdated wifi adapter.
The Steam Link quickly replaced my Chromecast. No longer was I restricted to using tab-casting to view Amazon videos. I could just fire up the Steam Link and watch things on my TV just as if I was sitting in front of my monitor. I used my roommate's discarded wireless keyboard and mouse for a while, but I missed having a 5-button mouse and I didn't want to have to rebind the controls for games just to play them on the Steam Link. So, I ordered a wireless Logitech K360 keyboard and M705 "Marathon" mouse.
I quickly and easily got the keyboard and mouse unified and everything seemed great, but there was one major problem: the M705 mouse's sensitivity was very, very low compared to my Logitech G402 mouse that I use on my desktop. I didn't want to have to adjust the sensitivity in each game depending on whether I was playing on the Steam Link or at my desktop. The crux of the issue was that the M705 mouse wasn't recognized by my desktop when it was plugged into the Steam Link, meaning that I could not access Logitech's Setpoint software to change the M705's sensitivity closer to that of my desktop's G402 mouse.
After looking around the web for a solution, I stumbled upon VirtualHere. I figured that, if VirtualHere didn't work, then I would just refund it. Thankfully, I didn't need to refund VirtualHere, as it works perfectly. Now, my desktop recognizes the M705 through Steam Link and it can use Setpoint. Another great thing is that Setpoint's settings are specific to that input device, meaning that changing the sensitivity for the M705 doesn't change the sensitivity for my G402.
While it would be nice if the Steam Link intrinsically had something like VirtualHere, I'm just glad to find a solution to my dilemma. Now, my user experience on the Steam Link is the same as on my desktop and I couldn't be more pleased.
It's a shame that VirtualHere either doesn't work well or doesn't work at all with some devices, but it has worked for my needs.

TL;DR: If you are thinking about buying VirtualHere, first get the trial version.

VirtualHere is a solution to a problem that shouldn't be a problem.  When it comes to the SteamLink, I think plenty of people have got some (deservedly so) harsh criticisms about the whole thing.  It seems like Valve pushed them out the door, and then left all the broken aspects broken.  If Steam ends up putting up one of these applications for wifi for the Steamlink, I wouldn't be surprised, because the Steamlink's wifi support is abysmal.  Anyway, on to this nugget...
VirtualHere acts as a passthrough link to your PC, Steam Link tries to interpret USB controllers (though only supports the big vendor ones and of course the Steam controller).  But what if Steamlink doesn't have a driver for said USB controller?  Well it just kind of does nothing.  And that's been my frustration with the Steamlink for a while.  I'd seen the VirtualHere option in settings before, but didn't realize VirtualHere was a separate purchase software.  I was "thrilled" to find out that support for my generic USB devices was relegated to a $12 DLC (which has another $10 DLC to allow it to work with an unlimited number of devices).
VirtualHere doesn't try to interpret the USB controllers, and instead creates a virtual USB hub on your computer.  Every device that's been set to be shared across the network will be broadcasted to the linked up Steam client.  After purchasing this DLC you need to restart the Steam Link so it can install the VirtualHere package.  Also you'll need to go to the Desktop for this, because of UAC.  Then in the settings just set whatever USB controller you want to use to be shared, and then play.  One of the nice things is that it remembers what devices you tell it to share, so you don't need to stop streaming every time, just hot plug the device in (provided you've shared it before), wait a few seconds and you can use it.
Do I recommend this software?  Hell yes, I recommend this software, but begrudgingly because this should have been part of Steam from the get go.  Billions of dollars and Valve can't be bothered to properly support controllers, so they instead tell you to buy some external software to do their jobs for them?  Apparently games as a service ain't good enough reason to help the customer anymore.
It's a really awful joke that I needed to pay $12 to use my SNES controller over Steam Link.  The adapter for that controller is a DirectInput USB device, since when are DInput devices not supported?

First off, I play offline. I do not have internet at home and the likelihood of that changing is zip. Therefore, I have had limited experience with the online only aspects of gameplay and cannot really comment on them. You can probably guess my feelings about online only features in singleplayer games anyways.
I "loved" SoM, as most folks did and still think it's one of the best 3rd person sword slinging games around. With that said, SoW is NOT a worthy successor. Everything about it feels, well, gimmicky compared to the first title. It is currently wrought with glitches such as having your entire army simply disappear, giant white glow bubbles forming over characters, getting stuck in the forced orc intro cutscenes etc. The overall combat feels less fluid, more repetitive, constricting, choppy, and very formulaic i.e. being regulated to using the same stupid combos repeatedly for certain enemies over and over (*cough* Ologs.) The micro-transaction/drop system is pointless and hardly provides incentive to continue playing as Legendary tier sets are rather cheaply animated and lack in any visual variation i.e. one set might be a slightly different color but is otherwise exactly the same. Pause to reminisce upon how lovingly detailed the skins from SoM were. Additionally, with regard to end-game, all those orcs that you’ve cultivated and trained to walk in your footsteps are totally useless once promoted to Captain / Warchief etc. They just sit in your fortresses untouchable and unusable for anything beyond siege defense fodder. I really enjoyed manipulating the Nemesis system in SoM but it seems somehow dumbed down now even though I know it’s been “improved.”
While they've added some new features that expand the gameplay, I found that after the credits rolled I have had no desire to continue playing SoW, unlike SoM to which I have devoted more time than I care to admit. Maybe it's because I'm still raw about everything WB did with their false advertising and hype campaign, maybe it's because what I see in the game seems like a cheap rip-off of the first title rather than an evolution, maybe it's because as a 3D artist I can't help but notice when something's not up to par. I’m sure that as 2018 rears its veiled head Monolith will gradually improve upon SoW, hopefully working out the kinks, polishing the armor and squashing the bugs, but for the time being when all is considered, SoW gets a C- from me.

Despite quite a short campaign with a fairly abrupt ending, this game is still worth playing because of its co-operative mode.
The visual style is very dark and dreary, as if filmed from a low-end camcorder in the hands of a novice journalist documenting the exploits of an ex-mercenary and his unmedicated psychotic best friend, complete with light flaring, grainy image and mosaic censoring out headshots and nudity.
The co-op campaign is interesting enough as-is, but the game also comes in a co-operative/backstabbery multiplayer flavor called 'Fragile Alliance' where teammates rob a cache of money and compete to try to make it out with the most cash. Everyone starts out as friends and teammates, but at any moment any player could decide to betray the alliance, to try to keep his share for himself and not split it. This fact keeps the multiplayer very dynamic and tense, and you have to keep an eye over your shoulder constantly, as any of your teammates could decide to shoot you in the back, given the opportunity. The multiplayer is, in that way, just as vicious as the campaign.
The game isn't without flaws, the campaign is fairly short and ends pretty suddenly, and the story may be lacking in some departments. But it's still a solid title for people itching to play something with a friend. As opposed to the first game, this title can be played in co-op online.

Unknown Worlds has ceased development after one and a half years and a half-million dollar "reinforcement" program (read: donations for an update).  There will also be new skins for sale for $6 soon!  A terrible example of greed and lack of vision.
As a beta-tester, I can say that the game itself never got out of beta.  The balance changes that occurred consistently and without much consideration resulted in a game that was mostly unlearnable and never quite sure which side it would favor.  Additionally balance changes would alter between considering professional and casual gameplay.  Without a consistent direction the community is more insular and aggressive than the stereotypical FPS community, and while this aggression is not always outward or vulgar the players are prone to dramatic and violent changes in behaviour.  Don't do the wrong thing as a commander or player or there will be at least one person to let you have it.
Originally a bunch of designers that knew each other in college, Unknown Worlds' expansion and solidification in San Francisco to launch Natural Selection 2 was a ploy to earn enough money and acclaim to work on other projects.  Amazingly video game companies did this for the last thirty years without sacrificing the games that made them successful, but these days customers do not matter to any business, even a successful small one.  The giant game company whose name denotes a violent winter storm supported the first iterations of two of their most prominent IPs for over ten years with patches, charging once after purchase for a single expansion pack.
The Spark engine will ostensibly be re-used, but I sure won't be as a customer.

So let's talk Dust: An Elysian Tail, which actually now reminds me of An American Tail for some reason and I never noticed it till now.
But hey you want me to talk about the actual game so here we go!
First thing you should know about this wonderful game is that it was created by pretty much 1 guy who did the coding/sound/art/design with some of the music and voice talents being outsourced. Why is this important? The game is a fully featured game which is up there with AAA titles, you wouldn't even notice it was made by 1 guy.
Dust: An Elysian Tail on average should you between 12-17 hours, including going back to previous areas with upgrades to find secrets and hidden stuff.
Gameplay is a blend of action hack and slash with Metroid style level design, RPG elements let you level your character and spend stat points to upgrade hp/defense/magic attacks and weapon attacks. Some secrets involve finding friends from other games such as Super Meat Boy.
Without spoiling the story, it has a couple of twists but you might see it coming. Despite a couple problems with the story it's got some wonderful dialogue between the characters which make it comparable to a Disney movie.
In short, you should buy this game at any price, I believe it's one of best 1 man team games ever created. Game is beautiful and immersive, and the PC port is great. I hope one day it receives a sequel.

So after beating the first Kane & Lynch I can fairly say that they improved a lot of things that really bugged me. Shooting is more accurate (still a little fustrating at times especially when the bullets are not going where you aim), they added hit markers to indicate that you hit them and where. The levels are drastically better designed in this one, from the streets of Shanghai to the dirty cluttered sweat shops, everything is beautifully done giving you a sense of realism the last one lacked. The variety of weapons was definitely welcomed, there were several different kinds of pistols, machine guns, and shotguns. This game encourages you to experiment with each one to find out which compliments your playing style. They improved the cover system as well by simply giving a cover button, letting you control where and how you want to take cover, its way better but could use some tightening up.
The characters Kane & Lynch are better represented and displayed this time around, Kane is again hastily trying to rush to his own agenda (doesn't really contribute to the story beyond the point of telling us what happened to his daughter who we saved last game, and providing some assistence in fire fights), Lynch on the other hand puts on a pretty good show, I actually felt bad for the guy, he had his life together then all these bad events start to happen. There are plenty of memorable moments in this game, like when Kane & Lynch get sliced up all around thier bodies and they have to escape while running around completely naked. A lot of tense fire fights and action to keep you busy (which was one good thing about the first game), it rarely slows down to catch your breath, you always want to keep going and see what craziness is going to happen next.
For the most part this game was really good with only a couple of issues that bothered me, one was the camera, they were going for an amatuer filmed experience, its a great idea but in practice it got really annoying and bothersome, so I'm glad the developers thought of putting an option to disable it (steady cam). Its very shaky at tmes which can throw you off because the game has a lot of tense battles, you don't want the camera to assist the enemy, so I ended up turning steady cam on. Another thing thing that bothered me was again the lack of any real story, this game is a short experience (beating it took me 4.6 hours) and there is no reason to replay it unless you want the achievements for beating it on hard or extreme. So I'm confused to why they didn't try to throw some more story, whether learning more about the character's past or adding some information about the current relationships these characters have. There is really nothing here story wise which is a shame because I like this game.
Kane & Lynch 2 is a good game that I recommend giving it a shot, but since the multliplayer is dead the $10 price is pretty good, not worth $60. Playing co-op with a friend is also a great idea for a short acton packed experience.

At the center of Sol Trader is a shining gem of a game, which may currently be occluded to some players by bugs and some yet-to-be-fleshed-out features.  But understand that this is just the beginning -- I've been playing since Beta and it's absolutely unreal how many bugs / features the developer has fixed in the short amount of time I've been playing.  Seems like every day brings a new patch that makes serious improvements to the game.
That being said, I think it's definitely worth saying that Sol Trader is ALREADY FUN!!  Yes, it takes time to figure out.  At first you should expect to be lost in the mechanics of a game that is *fundamentally different* from most.  This game is about people, and most of the gameplay occurs through person-to-person interactions, so you need a drop or two of patience to enjoy this game.  In the end, it's well worth-it.  Getting to be part of a solar system whose inhabitants have been fleshed out to an insane degree and whose AI blow most games out of the water is a really, really cool feeling when it finally hits you.
Also,
.  Don't think mission rewards are high enough?  Change 'em.  Cargo capacity too low by default?  No problem.  All you need is notepad.  I've already basically got my own custom version of Sol Trader :] (heck, you can even replace the title screen!)
If you've got patience and can deal with the fact that this game is currently a bit unstable and not fully feature-complete, then don't hesitate.  Nab it and start enjoying.  If you don't want to deal with that, wait a month or two and come back.

Alan Wake is an action adventure game with horror elements that dives into the story of the character who names the game. As you arrive to Bright Falls to search for inspiration to write your next book, you quickly sense that something is wrong, as your wife is “kidnapped” by the “Darkness” that roams the town.  You later find out why this is all happening, as you try to find your wife and defeat the “Darkness”.
With outstanding views and frightening forests filled with foggy sights, Alan Wake doesn’t lack in the graphical department. The visuals in this game really help you to feel within the game, with amazing light effects and great work done on putting you in one of most atmospheric games I have played.
The sounds are really well done. Between the scary sounds you listen as you walk in the forests and the gun shots you fire, to the voiced characters and music, you actually feel immerse in the game. The ambient sounds are spot on with help to set the tone to the scenes you are playing.
The gameplay revolves around getting from place A to place B, while going with your trusty flashlight and some weapons, picking up supplies along the way. The premise is simple but effective, because it was done in an innovative manner. Besides, you sometimes get some puzzles to solve and epic moments like the concert scene. It’s fun to play this game and although there aren’t truly jump scare moments, the atmosphere really makes you dread on where’s the next enemy. There are some problems though. There aren’t many enemies to fight and sometimes you feel like you are going into the forest yet again. But somehow it’s all small things to complain about when you think of the enjoyment you got out of this game. It will take you anywhere from 15 to 20 hours to complete.
The story in this game is very solid and enjoyable, although there aren’t many twists to it. The game is split into episodic parts, which worked out tremendously well for this plot, because at the end of each episode you want to find out what’s going to happen next. The characters are well developed although some of them just seem a bit stereotypical at time. The end, although great, only really finishes in the “second” game: Alan Wake’s American Nightmare. I didn’t really like this, since the “second” game is more of an arcade experience than the first one and doesn’t focus on the story as much. Besides, splitting the story like this is not fair, since you have to buy the “second” game to really finish the original Alan Wake. The pacing of the story is well done and overall it was an incredible experience, from start to finish.
Great graphical quality, good sounds and music, along with a solid story but somewhat predictable and a very good atmospheric gameplay surrounding third person shooting make Alan Wake one of the best experiences I have had with this genre.

I'd still like to love this game... and I very nearly can. It's got a special something about it that made me come back even though I disliked a lot about it immediately after starting playing; partly this is acknowledgement that getting launch right is difficult for the big players and even harder for indie developers.
So. How is it a little bit AFTER launch, and after some TLC by the dev (as pointed out in his response to this review)?
It's pretty good. Flight is much improved, and, one or two "gamebreaking" bugs that I'd noticed (and didn't actually overtly refer to in my review as frankly I didn't want to be even more negative than I already was) have now gone away. This quick response is exactly what I would've hoped for, and makes me feel like I can change my review wholesale. Not only that, I'm going to go much more in-depth, because it's nicer to be nice than it is to be unpleasant!
So. My main thoughts, listified:
1. I like the ship mechanics. They are simple, evocative of space, and work really well. What I don't like is the background; it is half static and half mobile, and this reminds me of old Psygnosis games... but not quite in a good way. The background is too busy and calls too much attention to itself and this harms the immersion of the thing as a whole. Space shouldn't look quite this noisy & being this noisy is problematic because it draws attention to the fact that there is in fact a very limited vista! But on the other hand...
2. Very few design decisions are poor ones. The game is a little click-heavy at times but partly this is likely due to too little testing, something which is common to small development teams. Now the game is "out in the wild", it's entirely possible this is an area that can be improved on with much greater feedback RE clickflow. Not really my area but I can tell it needs improvement. I really do like the UI, however. It is pretty, functional, and relatively minimal. No bloat.
3. The writing is solid but needs work. Of course, as you can probably tell from my gargantuan block of text, writing IS my area, so I'm always going to be most critical here. But this is where mods may come in. I may even make one or two myself.
4. Story. This game is great for it. I found myself creating little stories from the conversations, which, although still shallow and to me somewhat unrewarding, do provide roleplay hooks. I can even see having fun with this game as a group. Albeit, admittedly, a highly nerdy group. Unfortunately as I said before, there's not much depth here really, but this is again something that may improve over time either with mods or with future features added by the developer, who seems very responsive to the community thus far.
5. Immersion. It's quite good for it. The sound effects are simple but work well, and the music is very, very, very pretty. I'm happy to leave it running in the background.
Conclusion: I'm changing my not recommended to a recommend, but with a caveat. This game may not be what you want. It may not quite be what you think it's going to be. But I think you'll at least get 10-20 hours of fun out of it, and I think I will too, so I can't do anything BUT recommend it. :) That said some of my original complaints do still stand: there are real issues with how career and everything else hooks together; some things do not entirely make sense to me in terms of design. But I'm now confident that either these things can be fixed in the future or otherwise are not too problematic.
I'll leave my original review below for fairness and balance.
---
"I'd like to love this game but I can't, because it doesn't work properly.
Flight mechanics are totally broken.
Career progression makes zero sense because it is utterly divorced from everything else. In fact, that's true of many game systems; things do not connect together, at all. The focus is entirely on conversations, and those are puddle-shallow. Since the conversations supposedly drive you towards goals, this is a bit of a problem, because the goals are utterly meaningless. Become president? Well... that just involves making someone like you enough to suggest you should get the job. That makes no sense whatsoever.
Missions are absurd; they often involve finding people, which could be a fun mechanic, but often just involves more tedious repetitions of the same conversations 1,000 times until you realise the person you're looking for is in fact just repeatedly circling in space, doing nothing, infinitely. Until you fail the mission. Then they land. Yay?
Essentially: this game is either not finished or it is very, very, very bad. It could be very, very, very good. It isn't yet. It probably won't be. But I still quite like the premise. Fingers crossed, I guess? But no recommend as of now." ~ 8 June, original review

1.	Detailed family tree and contacts structure.  This is very detailed with a very intricate web which can be hard to follow but leads to very enjoyable intrigue and political maneuvering.
2.	Character creation is gives you some choices that can open up benefit (or negative) chat options once the game starts.  I really like the detail and history this provides.
3.	Multiple character options to be rated against.  For example loyalty, reliability, mechanical aptitude, likeness, star ship piloting etc.  You can even be given the background of inventing items that are in the game that give you additional chat options.
Con:
1.	Skills and back story after character selection do not appear to matter other than the chat options they provide.  For example you may have invented that engine but all you can do is brag about it.  You can even be a master mechanic received accolades for repair and expansion but when it comes down to it you have to pay someone else to repair your starship.  Lastly after talking to a dozen or so people it becomes very tedious to scroll to the bottom to use the same chat option to increase influence because new ones don’t seem to be generated despite having a role at an organization.
2.	Roles and jobs are just another way to generate chat options to attempt to increase “likeness” with the NPCs.  They may say you are receiving a decent wage but you don’t get paid (just another chat options) for the role you’re in, and accepting the role doesn’t seem to give you access to anything unique or even jobs that you couldn’t get not performing that role/job.
3.	Space combat and ship piloting.  Combat is mildly amazing think of it like a very bad version of asteroids from the Atari era and you will understand.  The break doesn’t seem to break and in fact propels the ships I have played forward.  The accelerate key is slow to accelerate then all of a sudden it boosts which caused me on multiple occasions to overshoot my goal.  Pulsing the thrusters seemed to help a little but that reverse thrust is a fail and the ships I flew couldn’t turn fast enough to allow proper maneuvering.  Lastly the auto pilot is the worst aspect of flying because it’s like circling a drain or toilet every time you use it.  Even the game doesn’t know how to go in a straight line and deaccelerate.
a.	Update 6/8/2016:  Space ship auto pilot orbiting has been drastically improved since the original posting of my review.  While there is a residual of it still there it is not so extreme that it prohibits enjoyment of this part of the game.  Additionally I have noticed that the thrust seems to have been corrected in this last patch as well as the reverse / break now seems to work properly.  Combat remains unchanged at this point but it is probable that I need better gear on my ship to enhance combat effectiveness.  Space Combat and ship piloting are vastly improved and not a negative any longer for me.  I did notice one thing that is likely a bug and will more than likely be resolved in a future update and that is the auto pilot remains active forcing auto thrust after exiting from a jump through a gate.  The work around I found is to click back to manual before the load sequence completes when jumping from system to system.
Final thoughts, I like the idea of the game and the developer appears to be responsive but I will not tell you to buy or not buy this game my only goal is to share what I have learned of it so far and my personal opinion while playing the game.  I hope this helps good luck.

At first I was a bit hesitant to play this game because I don't typically like fantasy RPG themed games.  I do like games that have deep and mature narratives.  I also like games with complex combat mechanics.  I heard that this game was very good at these things, so I decided to give it a try.
The story is  very good.  It is also very complex so it is important to pay attention to the dialog.  Player choices definitely have an impact on the game world and many choices are morally ambiguous which tie-in well to the mature theme of the story.  What impressed me the most was how much impact player choice dynamically altered the game world and the direction of the story.  The game has 8 different endings based on the player's decisions.  This is also the only game that I have ever played that completely alters the main quest line depending on these choices.  This means that you will not see every main story quest, characters and locations unless you play the game through multiple times.  Many games that change the world based on choices usually do so using trickery that gives you the "illusion" of choice.  The developers of this game actually took the time to create all of the extra story content instead of using tricks and this gives the Witcher 2 a ton of replayability.
The combat system in this game is also very deep and challenging.  You will carry a steel sword to take care of humanoid opponents and you will carry a silver sword to deal with monsters.  Knowing when to switch is important to dealing proper damage to your target.  Combat also requires proper preparation so the player will need to know how and when to use magical signs, place traps, drink potions, oil swords and use bombs and other Witcher tricks to get the job done.  Simply wading into the combat only slashing away with a sword will often times get you killed.  Combat can take some time to get used to and is definitely a refreshing departure from simply auto targeting and mashing a single button.
Visuals are very impressive and it is very apparent that the developers took a lot of time in creating the environments for the game.  Music is outstanding and the score sets the tone appropriately.
One of the few downsides that I can think of is the disparity of the difficulty levels.  Normal difficulty can be daunting with the complex combat mechanics and is a bit harder than the normal difficulty level of similar games.  Easy is a nod to RPG beginners, but is so easy that you can ignore most of the combat mechanics and simply survive every encounter by using only the swords.  The only other downside that I had with the game was related to map design.  I found navigation on some of the maps to be overly complicated and I spent a lot of time simply wandering about trying to find a way to get to certain points on the map.  Other than these two small quibbles I found the game design to be very solid and entertaining.
Lots of content in this game.  My playthrough took about 40 hours doing most of the side activities, and I mostly took my time without rushing things.  Additional playthroughs would be required to see the other 7 endings and to play the other story paths leading up to those endings.  You can easily get hundreds of hours out of this game if you wanted to explore all of these options so lots of replay value as I mentioned earlier.
I highly recommend this game.  I understand that the Witcher 3 is supposed to expand to a much more open world environment and have even more non-linear story options.  After playing Witcher 2 I am looking forward to playing the upcoming sequel when it comes out.

"The Binding of Isaac" may be one of the best games ever in terms of price and the value it offers in return.
It's a totally morbid, off-the-chart twisted action game. You play as Isaac, whose mother - a religious fanatic - is listening to the voice of god which tells her to first take away all things evil from Isaac's life (including his clothes and the rest of his stuff), then to lock him up in a room, and finally to sacrifice him. Just as she's about to burst into his room with a butcher's knife, little Isaac, butt-naked and teary eyed, finds a trapdoor under a rag and jumps down... into a maze of basements, and caves and depths full of deadly monstrosities.
The core gameplay is the same - you have to clear a room of enemies in order to advance to the next room. You can run around and shoot the monsters with your tears (yes, tears; you cry at them). During his journey, little Isaac can acquire the most crazy of power-ups. He can find a rock that he cracks against his skull, thus making him cry harder and deal more damage; he can find metal knuckles and smash his teeth, so he can occasionally spit a high damage-dealing tooth with the usual tears; he can find mother's panties which increase his tear range; or wear mom's heels, which make him run faster; he can make friends with pretty flies; he can swallow pills; or he can find his dead brother Bobby's fetus, who then follows him around and cries at the enemies with Isaac.
The acquisition of any of these power-ups (or power-downs) relies on good luck. The rest is your skill. But no matter how skilled you are, know this, "The Binding of Isaac" is VERY... DAMN... HARD. It took me 24 tries just to kill Mom (only to then learns this instance of her is actually NOT the main boss).
The beauty of this game is in the fact its levels, and anything in them, is completely random-generated each time, aka 'roguelike'. This includes perma-death. There's no saves. Once you're dead, you're dead. Game over.
Even though it look very simple, "The Binding of Isaac" is a complex game. There are huge amounts of items. A variety of enemies, upgrades, special items. There are unlockable characters. 13 endings. That enough?
It should be. SO GET IT NOW!
P. S. The "Wrath of the Lamb" DLC is a must, because it adds extraordinary amount of stuff to the game.

Really mixed feelings about this one. I agree with all the negative reviews and I also agree with all the positive reviews...
Let’s first start with the Scottish developers which can be found here
who made this 9 minute memorial tribute that plays out like some sort of visual Hallmark card 'Sorry for your loss' with a sobering indigo/blue palette beach which entices you to go further and further into the dissipating waves while accompanied by a well-fitting orchestrated piano soundtrack of musical poetry.
It’s an interesting premise when a visual art/game suggests that a normal tombstone which displays a person’s name, date of birth and time of death is impersonal and lacks the power to do good that can come from reflection on a victim’s stories, wonders, struggles and achievements that a person had made before their life was snuffed out. This raises a pertinent question. Is Media portrayals of loved ones a more fitting tribute and force that can do good than the simple old granite slabs that we hide in places known as cemeteries where seldom humans dare to tread?
20,000 people lost their life to this tsunami off the Japanese coast in 2011. Contrary to popular belief this game does not depict the lives of known victims, nor does it present a solemn list of names on which to pontificate in the end. Instead from a first person perspective your lead across a serene beach following the trail of a glowing butterfly which is a Japanese symbol for the soul. These butterflies will lead you to dark silhouettes that represent lives cut short, their stories being trapped in precious items that have washed ashore. When you find the hidden butterfly trapped in the item in question, the soul moves on and you then follow another butterfly that flutters ahead to the next shadow and soul waiting to be released. Eventually you’re confronted by the myriads of butterflies and shadowy figures and their stories which the waves/deluge have covered over.
The problem is that just as a tombstone is too dry and really inadequate to properly commemorate the tumult of any human life lost, 9.03m is really no better and is pretty shallow in length, meaning and design to be a long-lasting force of good. Player’s interactions with the precious items in question seem fleeting, frivolous, flotsam. Maybe that was the motto? We have no way on Earth that currently really honours the lives lost and our personal memories of those people are a personal symphony mingling beautiful musical notes covering when things fall silent.
I really can’t fault the developer’s intentions, and I can't fault it since this was their first project. I also can't fault them since they NOW donate 100% of all profit to charities. For those that loved this game I really recommend you to take a look at a game called 'Homesick' which follows a similar premise, but carries much more depth.
I guess in final thankyou developers for the experience. How we will remember the dead in future? I guess we will just have to wait and see...

It's a unique space game based on social relationships. You can befriend people to get better deals (make sure you befriend your banker if you take a loan, it's a big difference) and even borrow ships if they like you enough. If you happen to have a rich family member and you can get on their good side you might be able to borrow a nice ship. You can get jobs, take on missions, and apparently even run for public office - my current char wants to be president, a big dream for a very modest start.
My current character was the result of an affair between two married people. His dad wants nothing to do with him, his mom is on the other end of the solar system and also wants nothing to do with him. Both of them are unreliable. The only person who gives a crap about him at the start is his half sister who lives nearby, but she's a broke factory worker with no ship or influence. So he had to take a loan to rent a starting clunker ship and another loan to buy some valuable cargo. Flying blindly into space to find a place to make a profit, he lucked onto a good trade route and soon faced the option to buy his current ship outright, or rent a bigger ship for an exhorbitant amount per day. I went with purchasing the clunker and went off to explore with my newfound rent-free freedom.
A bit rough around the edges, but it certainly has potential to be a lot of fun with post-release polish.
I don't know if I would have released it in its current state, but despite the issues I find myself strangely drawn to its gameplay. I find myself playing it even with a nasty bug I'm experiencing that makes it difficult to move around in space (due to be fixed tomorrow, according to the very responsive developer).
In short, it's unique. A rough gem.
-Update- The bug with space flight, among many others, was fixed as promised.

TL;DR: recommend with caveats.
How do I possibly rate this game?
I've played it for countless hours, and I would say that most of those hours were fun, and maybe a little addictive. So in terms of value and providing positive gameplay feedback loop, it's a success.
And it does so many things right! So many things I want! The writing is consistently competent, despite the punny character names, and the areas and the scenarios they present are generally compelling. I really love that there are no truly good or bad choices in most situations.
It's an isometric tactical RPG THAT ISN'T fantasy! Be still my heart!
And it's huge! Too huge for my taste; I'd have preferred something about half as long, but everything feels full and fleshed out, so I can't complain about that.
But there is a LOT to complain about.
Let's start off with my biggest gripe: it is impossible to play this game well without reading a guide. This permeates every bit of the game, from character creation (make one character good at charisma and leadership, but DON'T make it your social character, and for God's sake, don't EVER give another character leadership. Also, always dump luck and almost always dump strength, and you might could have a competent character) through individual scenes (oh, you want the good ending for this area where people make up and mutually coexist? Well, go ahead an reload that game from four hours of fighting ago, and disarm that bomb. Oh, you thought you couldn't do that during the cut scene?) to the goddamn pixel hunts required to find the ONE CORRECT PATH through (to me) critical quests.
And then there's the inverse bell curve of difficulty. The beginning of the game is hard, in a way I don't mind. The middle of the game is really easy, to the point where combat is a chore. Then the last third ramps things ALL THE WAY UP, and the best weapons all feel like peashooters, because the same enemies from before now have 5x the HP.
I like the moral ambiguity, but I hate that the decision points, or the impact of those decisions, are neither clear nor logical.
Sure, I'll recommend it. It's fun, if you're not averse to doing some googling for your games. But as someone who's played through Fallout 2 10+ times, I'll never return to Wasteland 2. I hope Wasteland 3 is a more focused and less opaque game.

Objectively Subjective Review of Life Is Strange
Life Is Strange calls itself a storytelling adventure full of important decisions depending on the player. I wouldn’t really agree. I believe that LIS is in fact an RPG in it literal meaning – it is a role-playing game. The difference from most of the role-playing games I have played is that you do not get into the main character. You become sort of a director of this heart-breaking butt-kicking hair-rising story.
Many people asked me, why do I like this game so much. Why do I put so much emphasis on the decisions you have to make, when they in the end do not really matter as much as probably anyone, who gave LIS the shot, expected? As I mentioned, you are a story-maker. Through the plenty of choices, you create a story. And this is actually the point – to create a good story. And the game allows you to make the story exactly to your taste.
“Ready for the mosh pit, shaka brah!”
The whole story revolves around two teenage girls, one of them – Max Caulfield is your decision-making instrument. She is the turning point, the Firelink Shrine* of your very story. Do you want her to be a cringy shy good girl, a sassy renegade, or both? This is your choice to make.
Setting wouldn’t probably be that much of a thrill – just imagine the clichés… high school full of stereotypical teenaged characters and other stuff. However, the immersive feeling of going through all the drama, revolting against the authorities, smoking pot… the game really lets you return into your school years ones again. And it is bloody good in it. And you can wipe the floor with this b*tch Victoria Chase. And friendzone Warren. And do not really smoke pot. Shame…
“You sound high, but thanks for the morning grope.”
The characters are pretty distinctive, memorable and some even lovable. Some will probably stay in your mind for a while. It is not a thousand-page novel, but I have to admit, good job creating all those jerks.
The game itself seems to me as a prostate exam. It can be either very weird and unpleasant or a hyper o*gasmic experience, depending on how much are you comfortable with the procedure. The plot design is in fact a detective/love/friendhood story (pick the one you like the most and develop it).
“Why don’t you go f*ck your selfie?”
To sum it up, LIS is a very good game that is very worth those few bucks. I don’t think I have to say anything more to persuade you.  You should have an idea about it right now…
+ good story, characters, setting, puzzles
+ okay graphics, good optimalization (30 fps on a 5-year-old 500$ notebook)
+ a ton of easter eggs, cringy humour and memorable quotes
+ first episode is for free
+ no time-limited dialogues like in Telltale series
+ you learn, who was Louis Daguerre
+ emotional experience (I was unusable like two days after finishing the ep. 5)
+ fantastic soundtrack by Jonathan Morali (Syd Matters)
- lip-sync is horrible
- could have had a much darker ending
Game time: 10 - 30 hours depending on how you like reading all the notes lying around and having a chit-chat with folks

Final grade: S*
*Dark Souls reference

This review is for episodes 1-5.  I just completed it this morning.
As an adventure game, it's one of the best games I've ever played.   While the adventure genre formula hasn't changed, the new time travel abilities really enhance the gameplay.  If you love adventure games and you're on the fence about buying this, don't hesitate, it's very well done.
Now let me talk about the content of the game.  It's based around two teenage girls and their relationship.  How one girl's desire to save her friend's life and the lives of those around her has dire consequences, when she learns she has the ability to alter time and "fix" wrongs.
The story draws you in and the acting is very well done.  However, there's a bit of cringe factor for a male playing this game.  I don't mind embodying a female character, in fact it's something I do often in games, but this is a little bit different.  A male playing a female in such a personal (feminine) adventure game feels a bit too personal to me, because of the story and content.  Stuff only females deal with.  And then there's the male character that's always hitting on you and texting you.  You just want to tell them to go away.  These things aside, it's well worth the money and it's an enjoyable story.
If you're still on the fence, stop and buy it now.  If it's on sale, that's even better.  I'll be playing the second game shortly.

In short, this game is a generic hack and slash. It doesn't even try to hide it, the levels are arena like in nature, and enemies teleport into the arena and waves. (which begs the question, why not just all attack at once?) Typically, I'm a fan of these kinds of games, I enjoy the fast paced combat that they offer and the quick thinking required, and as much as I wanted to like this game, too many things kept me from my eventual ragequit (yes, I'll admit it, I ragequit). To start with, the combat itself is fairly bland, with very few in the terms of combos or special attacks, it boils down to alternating between mashing two different buttons however you feel like it. Combos are not based on a length of time, but rather how many hits you can get it in before you get hit. This isn't so much a downside as it is a personal preference; combos are more challenging and more entertaining when there's a time limit attached to them, to keep you in the fight for as long as possible. Some of the controls feel unintuitive, such as moving the control stick in any direction to use your directional attacks rather than your standard ones (this could be just me, as by habit I move towards what I'm attacking). The camera is sloppy, it positions itself how it feels and makes you have to constantly tweak it in order to watch out for attacks from other enemies, making it feel like you're playing two games at once, one that involves mashing buttons, and the other that involves photographing group pictures. While not particularly a downside, the amount of fanservice tends to be a bit much.
In short, its not the game for me, but someone out there is bound to enjoy it.

Before I start this review, I just want to mention that the only reason I even own this is becuase I got it in the Humble Weekly Bundle.
I'm just gonna jump right in this and start on the gameplay, since the story is almost non-existent anyway.
The basic enemies are allllll the same design wise; guys in suits wearing masks. Red ones have a special little spinny attack and some of the other colored ones do different things. There's also some big fellas that are just as easy as the regular enemies. The AI is pretty stagnant too. Most of the time, they just circle around you while you combo (and by that, i mean mash the X and Y button on the gamepad) the death out of one or two of them. On occasion, one enemy will get the brilliant idea of trying to gang-up on you, but that is usually easily dodged, unless the camera is being a♥♥♥♥♥♥...which it does a lot. The bosses aren't very hard. They have 2-4 different attacks and thats it. You just run around them in a circle, dodging whatever attacks they have, and then mashing X and Y to damage them and then just rinse & repeat. This game is just bland. Obviously the draw here is the anime-sexy-schoolgirl-pantsu-whatever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but even if you were to buy this game JUST for that, you have to wait a while since alternate costumes cost a solid 100,000SP and you need SP to purchase combos or level up health/katana gauges. Then, you can mash the X and Y button in different ways to earn more SP to level up your combos until you can start saving up for the other outfits. Woo hoo. The only slightly redeeming thing about this game is that you can use the SP you earn to buy new combos...but there aren't even that many anyway, hence the "slightly" before "redeeming," if you could even call it "redeeming" to begin with.
As for the graphics, they aren't HORRIBLE or anything. I mean i've seen much worse here on Steam, graphically speaking. And usually for gameplay I didn't have hardly any issues with frame-rate drops, however the cutscenes only run at about 30fps. So not "good" graphics, but not the worst.
Another big flaw is the sound. The music is completely bland and forgettable. The noises the enemies make are so repetetive, i'd rather listen to a metronome while fighting then hear the same grunt of pain whenever you hit them every time. The big ones make a slightly deeper sounding grunt at least....
In sum; Don't buy this. It's a waste of time and money. If you were gifted this or got this in a bundle, just let it run in the background, get the card drops, and sell them for ~$0.22 on the market.
Now, if you're looking for GOOD 3rd person hack-n-slash combo-y games, then I would like to direct you to the MUCH better DMC and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance. They both have everything this game doesn't: a good story, good gameplay mechanics, cutscenes that stay over 30fps, great soundtracks, good SFX, and even better voice acting.

9.03m is technically not a game, but an interactive video. It makes aware the warning signs and effects of a tsunami to the player. 9.03m is a very deep and meaningful game, and the money from every purchase of a copy contributes to two wonderful charities which helps the victims of the Tōhoku tsunami.
9.03m is all about symbolization, in which you need to figure the situation out for yourself. The total game doesn't take too long to complete, though the story is amazingly powerful. You're on a beach, on which the tsunami previously hit. Your task is to follow the glowing butterflies which lead you to the ghost of a victim. Heading to them in the dim moonlight, you will find a possession of theirs in which you need to find a clue to inform you of their name, history, etc. The whole game is based on supporting the victims and raising awareness, and in my opinion it has succeeded in that. 9.03m is not meant to be played as a game, more as a meaningful, sad and informative story.
The game is simplistic though meaningful. Symbols are a large part of the game, creating mystery and suspense. With all it's revenue headed directly to the two charities, this game is worth the full price. An enjoyable and meaningful story.

At this point it's probably fair to say I've developed a dislike for 'walking simulators'--as a gametype, they seem to be strung together by the bare minimum of required interaction from the player, which to me seems a betrayal to the medium of video games as a whole. '9.03m' is inarguably a game of that type, asking no more of you than a depressed W key and occasional fiddling with the mouse. At first, I found the objects the game wanted me to interact with interesting, but eventually they became part of an overly sentimental narrative--childrens' toys, specifically--and I found it harder to care. In terms of actual gameplay, '9.03m' is essentially a slide show which you are holding W to navigate.
The world that's constructed within, however beautiful (and it is beautiful, in a mystical, fantasy-light type way), is ultimately incredibly linear. The game has one objective at a time it wants you to go to, and if you go anywhere else, the screen fades to black and points you back towards your objective. So that there's not even a world to interact with--just the idea of a world, and the idea of the people that might have lived within it.
Up until the end of the game, I was ready to deem '9.03m' unsuccessful--but in a strange way, it managed to make even the device of player frustration and incompetence useful in its narrative message. I won't spoil anything, because the game is incredibly short, but if you play thru the entire thing and aren't at least slightly moved, it's possible art games of this type aren't for you at all. I was beginning to think they weren't for me, but '9.03m' seems to be on the shallowest side of the 'gameplay' spectrum, yet still proved a rewarding experience. I recommend it to anyone who wants to examine the interaction between art, tragedy, and games, but with the warning that the actual 'game' is probably about twenty minutes long in total.

I'll cut to the chase and say that what ruined the game for me is: Cutscenes, cutscenes, cutscenes and cutscenes. The sheer amount of cutscenes and stale conversations in this game is staggering! For a good while during Act1 i spent maybe 1½hour walking from cutscene to cutscene with just five minutes worth of actuall gameplay inbetween. This is no game, this is an semi interactive movie with some super unoriginal elements to it.
And then there are the "minor" problems like the game not telling me anything, I agree that many games today holds your hand way to tight, but there has to be some middleground, Witcher 2 just asks you to be clairvoyant and to guess what the devs intended you to do all the time. The combat takes obvious inspiration from the Batman Arkham games but fail to deliver the same fluent combat, clumsy animations makes Geralt move as graciously as a drunk and the targeting system makes strange decisions. Yes i know, they wanted us to explore their beautiful world (it really is beautiful, I won't deny that) but running around aimlessly in a forest looking for some cocoons i could not find for an hour is not exploring, it's irritating.
In short, The Witcher 2 has way to little gameplay and when it gives you something to do the game works against you every step of the way, which makes for a very frustrating and rage-inducing experience.
The Binding Of Isaac is truly an addictive and fun experience that offers hours of fun.

I really wanted to like Wasteland 2, but in the end I feel it failed me on most counts, the first and foremost being the writing, to the point where I couldn't muster the will to finish the last mission after 81 hours in (Director's Cut).
The good?
* Squad management with all the skills and weapon types is actually fun.
* Combat is enjoyable enough.
* The setting has some gloriously bizarre moments and characters.
But all of it is undermined by shoddy execution, overall simplistic writing, lazy and uninspired artwork (honestly, Fallout Tactics looks better and put more effort into customizing character portraits) - all the things that kill immersion and suck the fun out of the game.
As far as execution goes, there're plenty things in the game that feel unfinished or unpolished. Pieces of dangling quests here and there or failure to react to you doing things in wrong order, small things like rearranging squad formation or viewing completed quests sorted in order, reused locations - all contribute to the death of a thousand cuts. Squad management fun is obliterated by the fact that your companions don't level if you leave them at the base, which effectively means that you'll be stuck with almost the same party throughout the game. So much for recruit diversity.
But what really killed the game for me was the writing. I'm honestly struggling to see the lauded brilliance here. It's a pulpy shlock, by design, sometimes funny and eccentric, but so over the top that it kills all tension and willingness to care. It doesn't know what tone it wants to set. On one hand it attempts to be grim and portray a ruthless wasteland, but most such moments go hand in hand with cartoonish grotesque hilarity. First third-to-a-half of the game is a tedious linear slog. The Prison -> Canyon -> Damonta stretch is a dreary and dull timesink with no redeeming qualities or payoff. But when it suddenly becomes somewhat more open, you are still offered only cartoon characters, clear cut black and white choices and moustache twirling villains. The choices are obvious, the outcomes are formulaic, quest chains predictable, no subtlety, no suspense, no stakes. The one moment of doing something different literally happens during the 2nd assignment, and that's that, the only trick up Wasteland's sleeve.
It probably sounds a bit too harsh and bitter. If I had an option, I would've given WL2 a mixed review. Ultimately it's a game that can be fun but is undone by its flaws, and in the end looking back all I feel is frustration and disappointment, so I can't honestly recommend it. ...The first Shadowrun Returns also left a sour taste of disappointment in my mouth. But it was followed by Dragonfall and Hong Kong - two games I love to death. Here's hoping that inXile could only go up from WL2.

This game is absolutely phenomenal! It starts out with a very dour story regarding a fanatical mother who hears the voice of god commanding her to sacrifice her son Isaac, who then flees into the basement to escape her wrath (only to encounter a variety of demonic creatures).
After the opening cinema, the player starts the game and is introduced to all of the necessary keyboard commands via a series of cave paintings in the first dungeon room. From there, trial and error will teach you the rest that you need to know. The rouge-like style game consists of a random series of procedurally created dungeon rooms, monsters, secrets, item drops, and treasure chests. The monsters and bosses are hideously gruesome things that display Edmund McMillen's fantastic diabolic art style. There are countless homages to past classics such as The Legend of Zelda, however TBOI's treatment feels very original and fresh this day in age.
If you are a fan of A) Team Meat, B) Zelda, C) gruesome artwork, D) fiendishly difficult game play, or E) all of the above, you owe it to yourself to give The Binding of Isaac a try. Very addictive game with a high replay rate.

===
Disclaimer: i played both Wasteland 2 and Wasteland 2 Director's Cut, for some reason Steam posts this review as one for both. Ya know, steam strange stuff.
===
===
- Recommended purchase
- Purchase only if on sale
- Purchase only if on heavy sale
- Avoid purchasing
===
GRAPHICS: 7.0 / 10
Made with Unity engine, graphics are average for a cRPG title. They do not shine in any particular way to be honest, just some average models and textures, good detail in environments and decent art direction. They do the job and generally are pretty good for a game of this kind.
SOUND: 7.5 / 10
Music, effects and voice acting are very good and never out of place for the setting of the game. You will not be astonished by anything in this field either, but nothing is bad either, sound direction is good enough to help the player immerse well in the game atmosphere.
GAMEPLAY: 9.0 / 10
With very deep character development, party managing, intricate dialogue trees, reputation systems with compansions and the world factions alike, tons of different loot, enemies, items and secrets to discover, you will sure have a lot to do in the Wastelands, this game does not disappoint as of variety and quality of gameplay, no sir, very high quality i say.
LONGEVITY: 9.0 / 10
It will take you a long time to discover everything in the Wastelands. Let's say around 80-90 hours if it is your first playthrough and you don't already know all the tricks. To get all the possible dialogues and situations it will require more than one playthrough and it will be worth it to do so as things can change a lot depending on what you do. Hell, there is even a secret ending, but i will leave that for you to discover!
===
- Immersive, well made and plausible post-apocalyptic world. This specific post-apocalypse world is very grim toned and leaves very few space to lighter tones of narration and contexts. You will se famine, plague and death all along, things will be cruel and unforgiving, and people will try to stab you in the back when they can. Everyone will have its own morals.
- Tons of stuff to collect. Seriously, there are really a lot of weapons, armor suits, trinkets and all sorts of misc loot to collect as you progress in the game. Remember that one man's trash is another man's fortune, in this game this principle is really true, as you will realize...
- Very deep character customization. Aspect, skills, attributes, it's all there right from the start. There are a myriad of skills to choose from and all of them are useful in some way (well, almost all of them, as you will read later...) but anyway, the character development part is just amazing, it will allow you to create exactly the type of team you want, with the specializations you want, even write their biographies and select a lot of roleplaying background elements for them, so you wikll have a really unique roleplay experience in the game.
- Varied, intelligent, challenging enemies. There are really a lot of them, and they are all different, inflicting sometimes unique statuses to your party, or having unique skills or weapons. The wasteland will throw everything at you, and you will have to be ready or die.
- Complete and deep combat system: precision attacks to weaken specific parts of the enemies, cover system, weapon proeficencies, optimal weapon ranges, weapon modification, ambushing, suppressive fire... it's all there right now. This is the real deal, the combat is just spot on. If you played XCOM then well it's half like that and the other half is from Fallout 2. And if you don't know what i'm talkin about be sure: it's damn good.
- Meaningful choices: everything will have consequences, because you are a Ranger it doesn't mean you have to follow a Lawful path, oh no. You can do quite the opposite and see how the story goes. You can just kill everyone and still complete the game, because maybe your team got mad from radiation and the straight horror of the Wasteland... or maybe not, it's up to you to decide.
- Moral system: your companions will have opinions about what you do, and will behave in different ways. Some for exaple can lose control in specific contexts and not obey you anymore, or even leave your party or become enemies if your decisions go against their principles.
===
- Some Attributes and Skills are borderline useless for almost the entire game. For example: bartering is useless because even if maxed out will give you just +10% to sell prices and 10% discount at all vendors. To max out a skill it requires really a long time and some bonuses even at max level just are not worth it. Another example is Charisma or Luck stats, which can be forfeited without major consequences and all the points be put in those stats who really matter, like Strenght or Coordination.
- At higher difficulties, the game almost mandatorily requires a min/maxed party. Min/maxed means you max out 2-3 core statistics in each character, say example Strenght, Intelligence and Speed, and so you will have characters with lots of HP, lots of action points and lots of skill points per level. You will need that to face most enemies in the lategame / endgame because the combat will be really hard. This is a problem BECAUSE since this is a Role Playing Game a player should be free to make his/her partywith focus also on diplomatic / miscellaneous skills, not just on combat. But this cannot be done at high difficulty ranks, or you WILL die.
- Vendors can be exploited: you encounter a random vendor? No problem: sell him all the stuff, kill him, get all the stuff back and the money. Realism wise, perfect. Game-balancing wise, a kick in that place.
- Random encounters ruin game balance: you are roaming the wastes with your crap assault rifles. You can go in the corner of a zone you can't access because you need to progress further in the game, but still in this zone border you will trigger random encounters from the other, higher level, zone. This means this way you can meet enemies far above your level. Well if you manage to defeat them and not become a bloody stain, you will mostly get pretty good stuff, like weapons meant for far higher game progress than you currently are at.  Happened to me some times, i found myself at early game with mid-game gear and steamrolled everything. There are no requirements of LEVEL for anything, balance wise, another kick in that place.
===

Shadow of War is a fantastic follow up to Shadow of Mordor, improving nearly every aspect of an already great game.
The things I really liked:
The combat is familiar, but deeper, and more engaging.
The orcs and ologs have a lot more variation -- different models, skins, skills, moves, strengths, weakness, personalities
The new weapon/armor sets and the unlockable skllls and skill upgrades allow for actual differences in playstyles
The story is surprisingly engaging with a few surprises along the way
The sieges feel like huge battles (most of the time) with any number of orcs and beasts engaged in combat all over the place; there's just enough chaos to make it feel like there are real stakes, but Talion is a god on the battle-field
The collectibles are worth collecting and there aren't so many that you feel like it's not worth finishing
The beast related missions are minimal and much more fun than the previous game
The emergent stories are fantastic -- getting ambushed by an orc you thought you killed, throwing a long-time foe into a pit of lava, shadow-striking across the battlefield to take out archers and then diving into a mob of dead-but-they-don't-know-it-yet enemies, having a rediculous captain talk about wanting to get a promotion in the middle of a massive melee, and so many more
A lot of the reviews I read from major gaming outlets complained about the end-game grind and the requirement to pay to avoid the grind.  I thought the end-game lasted just the right amount; I never purchased in-game currency, and never felt that the game got too grindy, I hit the level cap and finished leveling my legendary sets just as I hit the end of the story-line.
Shadow of War exceeded my high expectations for the game.  Highly recommended.

Been playing this game since it came out and am still enjoying it today. Also runs on modern systems without any issues. However, it does have its flaws:
- The AI of your main hero is ATROCIOUS. He only attacks anything if manually told to, or if he gets attacked by a melee unit (yes, he doesn't attack ranged units firing at him either.)
- Unit AI can also be pretty bad. If you tell them to go somewhere and attack anything along the way, they will do so. However, after destroying their first obstacle, they simply quit moving and wont continue until being told to.
- English voice acting is ATROCIOUS. It's like they hired a few drunks and weedheads and had them reading the script in front of a microphone
- Everytime you quit the game on a map, the entire map turns black again, even if you've already discovered everything.
- The soundtrack is buggy as hell. Sometimes it changes, sometimes it starts seconds after the corresponding event, and sometimes not at all.
- Parts of the game are extremely unbalanced. While you won't have any issues most of the time, some parts of the game require you to build SEVERAL maximum sized armies to even scratch the surface of a small handfull of enemies.
- On the other hand, you can clean out some maps on your own using only your main hero without even having to bother with base building.
- The ending of the (first) campaign is confusing, anticlimatic, and just plain weird.
- Gathering enough resources to build a proper army can easily take several hours, forcing you to use cheats or let the game run on its own to gather the required amounts.
- Game only runs in 4:3, there is no widescreen support at all (though it can be circumvented with some .ini tweaks
- You have the ability to buy things from stores and sell items to them, which is completely unnecessary as you receive everything you need from exploring and looting enemies.
- Some quest items get stuck in your inventory even long after the quest is over.
- Controls suck a bit. While you can create unit groups and give them a series of commands, it is impossible for instance to tell them to attack different targets one by one. This can be especially frustrating on maps where you only have your main hero to use.
These are all the negative aspects I could think of. Now despite all those flaws, I still strongly recommend this game for the following reasons:
+ Great blend of RPG and strategy elements. The idea of having a main hero really fits well.
+ HUGE amount of content. Large maps, tons of items, secondary heroes, and quests, quests quests.
+ Six different races to use with different advantages / disadvantages
+ Three large campaigns which will keep you entertained for several days, if not weeks.
+ Completely customizeable main hero: Light/Heavy weaponry, Bowsman, Healer, Nature/Black/Ice/Fire/Earth magic? Or a mix of those? The choice is completely yours to make. And the game supplies you with any items you would require for any of these classes.
+ Good story/universe for strategy game standards.
+ Large connected world with in-built fast travel system
If the positive part of this review got you intersted, I strongly recommend that you try out this game

My initial impression of Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae was pretty dismal. Upon starting up the game, you are given a 2-minute blurb of generic short-skirt anime-babe save-the-world mumbo jumbo, then thrown into a fight with a bunch of samurai robots in business suits. Combat initially feels jerky and stilted, and the enemy AI is less than stellar. Mere moments into the action, my expectations were rapidly hitting rock-bottom, but I decided to play on. Fortunately, the game gets its act together soon enough.
Ignoring the story entirely, MKH is actually a competent, demanding arcade beat-em-up. Each stage places you in a circular arena, in which you must take down five waves of opponents, each more difficult than the last, capped with a boss monster. While combat initially feels sluggish, and the early enemies are laughable, both problems solve themselves in short order. You eventually start to grasp the nuances of the combat system, allowing a skilled player to duck and weave in and out of combat, hammering foes with punches and sword slices, leaving the opponents a bloody wreck, all without ever giving them a chance to strike back. Later foes block and even counter your attacks, brutally punishing you if you attempt to button mash and forcing you to fight cautiously. They also don't all look like murderous C-3P0s, which helps the aesthetic tremendously.
Opponents that have been damaged enough start flashing red, signifying that they are now more vulnerable to your basic attacks and are also capable of being instantly defeated through use of your cinematic sword-sheathing magic. Slaying enemies grants you SP, which you can spend to buy upgraded skills or better durability, as well as occasionally offering up big blobs of health. All in all, MKH is goofier than it intends to be, a bit repetitive, and doesn't exactly have the most complicated system in the world, but it's still a fun bit of slice-em-up action to burn an afternoon with.

Spellforce is one of the very few RTS / RPG games to have ever been released and the series is among if not the very best of them. By todays standards graphics are quite dated and there are resolution issues with the engine, nothing which can't be remedied though.
The gameplay itself is fluid, the story is great (although voice acting is terrible), there are hundreds, if not thousands of different items as well as countless build varieties and a therefore a huge replayability. The story itseld unfolds very linear for the most part and map progression is predetermined for the most part, yet the first Spellforce entry never claimed to be open world and in fact is more open world, than many other games who claimed otherwise, as the player may decide to visit previous maps through a portal system any time they desire, where defeated enemies are still defeated, but the RTS elements are reset upon each new visit, making it a bad decision to jump maps without having completed the current one, if it does require a base to be set up.
All in all, Spellforce and it's 2 addons aged very well and can be considered a timeless classic, known by way too many people.

It's a shooter. It does that really well. It has a solid story to justify all the shooting. It has driving which I enjoyed more than GTA 5. Unlike the GTA series the game is not built around driving. Cars are there mostly to get you to your target and back again. Voice acting and cutscenes are excellent and reinforce the story. AI can be odd but is often hilarious and it doesn't detract from the shooting which is what we're here for. The graphics have the potential to be very good if higher res textures come out, which won't do the people having problems with frame rate any good because they won't be able to run them. The game is graphically very demanding and I can't say for sure why, but I think it's because there are a lot of complex effects happening at once. Example. I was driving through bayou at night in pouring rain. I stopped the car to get out and noticed all the subtle effects on the screen. Rain was hitting the hood and evaporating into mist from the engine heat. Water was also vaporizing off the engine block underneath the car and rising out in front of the headlights. Engine exhaust curled out from the twin exhausts and mixed with the vapor as it was carried by the wind. The game has excellent fog and mist effects that really make you feel like you're in a very wet, humid place. The color palette reflects that kind of location. It ain't California.

Ok so i down-voted this game, but let me explain, and also say the game can be casually fun.
This game has some interesting characters, all of which have somewhat fitting abilities.
Gameplay varies just enough from character-to-character to make it feel fresh between them.
The problem comes in some of the game modes.
Most of the game is a direct copy of TF2 in how the modes play, but with extremely tiny maps, and little to no diversity between the maps.  The maps themselfs are fitting for the setting, but the small sizes can lead to some of the intent of the characters usability being lost and degrade into every character just doing the same thing.
So here's part of the bad so far.
The characters have skin unlocks that can be earned through reward chest that appear to be earned every time a character is leveled.  These rewards change after leveling to 5 though.  I dont know if they space out more levels, or you dont earn any after that.  But either way, the skin unlocks for the characters dont vary enough to make them interesting.  It's mostly just, same thing in blue/yellow/red etc., or such a minor change that it's hard to tell what the differences are.
Another check against the game is the unlocks to get more than just the base characters.  It requires crystals (a currency form) which of course you have to either, play a PVE mode to earn, or play cash for.
All of the characters that are unlocked in this way seem to have better abilities than the ones you get unlocked at start.  So unlocked these seems to be high on the list to do, but the PVE mode in game is (and i can say this in all sincerity) the worst attempt at a PVE mode in this type of game I've ever personally seen.  The mode is so poorly done, that the only viable way to win is for players to glitch the mechanics, and this is fairly well known in the player community.  So this being the only way to earn in-game crystal currency, means you will have to pay real money if you want to unlock more characters in game.
The last item is the 'card' loadout.  This checks a plus and minus checkbox for the game in my opinion.  The cards are interesting, and you earn them randomly from chests.  Once you aquire them, you can craft them, level them up (in a way) and disenchant them if you dont like them.  This allows you to build loadouts to build your characters for one type of ability or another.  So you can customize how you play with each character.  Sounds good, but here's the minus part, they come from chests.  So if you are unlucky, and dont want to pay cash, you probably wont have a big variance in which abilities your characters have.  Another downside is, it doesnt feel super rewarding to get these cards.  Especially since they are completely random.  I've gotten cards and skins so far for locked characters, that i can't even play, that I'd have to pay cash money to unlock.  Why they didnt have the chests give items for only the characters you have unlocked is beyond me.  So if you are extremely unlucky, and you don't want to spend cash money, you could literly never get anything usable from any of the chests.  That's not rewarding for players.
Another minus is that if you are a free player, with a limited set of champions, at game start you essentially fight over them with the player selecting the one they want first getting that champion.  Leaving you with having to select another that you might not want since the pool is very small.
In the end though, the game has characters.  I'll continue to play it a bit if it keeps me interested every now and then, which is somewhat has so far, but it's charm is wearing off fast.  Too fast it feels like for a new game.
I will say this, it's worth downloading and trying free.  If you want something to play a few hours a week, and not spend a dime on, this might be something to look at.

Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days

+ Decent graphics, but nothing amazing.
+ Arsenal of weapons to use throughout the game, such as uzi's, shotguns and a variety of military grade assault rifles, along with pistols.
+ This entire game is action, with frequent shootouts and some intense cutscenes (although these are all too rare). As a result of this non-stop combat you do feel engaged in the game.
+ Various parts of the environment are destructible, and become damaged amidst the firefights Kane and Lynch are involved in.
- The story is lacklustre in comparison to Kane and Lynch: Dead Men (the original). The characters themselves feel dull and the interesting aspects of their personality are absent in this game. The story is straightforward and doesn't have any complexity to it.
- The main campaign takes about 3-4 hours. It would definitely be longer on the highest difficulty but still nowhere near long enough.
- While the constant shootouts in this game can be viewed positively, it also becomes so common  that it loses its charm.
- The new arcade mode is boring and repetitive. If you like to unlock achievements this is a grind. You join a team of AI criminals where you execute a heist to steal cash or other valuables, then shoot your way to the escape vehicle. After you become accustomed to the different maps (which are nicely thought-out I shoud add), you just repeat them over and over to gain ranks and access to different weapons. Not fun.
Overall Score: 5.0/10
