Brian Fargo really re-creates the late 90's magic here with the sequal to the original Wasteland. Most will know Brian ran Interplay studios which created and produced the Fallout 1, 2 and Tactics games. Such a shame it was sold...
This feels so much like Fallout 1 and 2. The big differences being you are managing a party of up to 6 or 7 characters not just the one. Combat is far more frequent (a little repetitive) but the game has that same post apocolyptic feel with great writing, dark humour, sarcasm and just general wittyness that I remember from Fallout 1 and 2. I feel a little sad that I missed the original Wasteland, I should really get that going somehow and play it too.
I have about 19hrs or so in Wasteland 2 and am only up to Dimonta (a place you must visit as a part of several different quests including the main). Now I know a little about what's to come as I've read teasers here and there (without spoiling the story for myself) and because of this I know that this game is huge. Just monstrous really.
I think what makes it so big is the fact that there are loads of side quests that really draw the game out and the fact that there is a lot of back tracking sometimes in order to beef up, resupply and then carry on. But regardless of this I find it a treat finding all sorts of new weapons and modifying them to get that awesome assualt rifle bypassing armour by 10-15% with a few mods.
I also love all the 80's and 90's pop culture references in there such as Cabbage Patch dolls, MAD magazines, D20 dice, trolls and many more. Those little items you stumble accross gives you a strong sense of nostalgia especially so if you grew up in those periods. I think there a real treat. I won't even go into the "toy snake" you find ha ha.
The Director's Cut is definitely where it's at. Heaps more recorded dialog and just general performance increases and polish. I wouldn't bother playing the original Wasteland 2 and I don't think you can anymore? The game is also fairly stable with one wierd CTD (nothing in my event logs either) out of that 20 hours. It runs well and for the most part looks ok. I feel like some areas are a little bland and could have used a going over but aside from that the world looks good.
Some areas feel a little empty. I know it's post apocolyptic but some more NPC's to engage with would be nice. The writing really shines when you do talk to those few NPC's that can talk. Overall the main quest story hasn't kicked in a whole lot just yet so I can't comment on it.
Anyways it's not a perfect game and this is proven in the repetitive combat. There is some advantage to finding cover and ensuring your perks and skills line up to how you want your characters to operate but it's always the same. Battle starts and you find cover and then off you go until the enemy is dead. The AI enemies are good at taking cover and trying to flank but once you've seen it a few times I think you can say you've seen it all. I've heard that there are boss fights but I am yet to reach one so I can't comment on that either.
Despite these flaws, the game isn't too bad. Give it a try if you love Brian Fargo, Interplay and the original Wasteland and Fallout series. I think you'd like it. I give it a 8 out of 10 overall.
TLDR: Good writing, a little empty with repetitive combat but reeks of pop cultural references from the 80's and 90's that will have you thinking back to those times. Overall not a bad game but not perfect either.

If you have started the game playing the standard Wasteland 2, then please stop and start again with the Director's Cut version. I know it's annoyin, it takes time, but ultimately you will appreciate that the most unfuriating user interface design problems have been fixed (still not perfect, but it's going to make the game experience most pleasurable).
Regarding the visual quality differences, honestly I can't say it really maters if like me you are playing zoomed-out because you prefer the strategic view to the close-up one.
Now, let's see the pros and cons:
Pros:
- It's a decent RPG, with an ok story
- Some nice characters
- Funny dialogs now and then
- Some interesting faction dynamics
Cons:
- It's so long, combat is so not interesting, that I ended up cheating my way by maxing out all the attributes, all my skills, max money, etc... skipping all the random encouters, and it still took forever to finish the game
- Many places where you have to search online to find the solution... because you did not see the interactable element that is 2 pixels on the screen or not highlighting because the camera position decided that it would not
- Places where you have to do things in a specific non obvious way despite descriptions hinting that other ways would work
Ultimately I think it's a decent game, but it's probably not going to stay in players memories as Fallout was, it's just not that good.

Didn't work for me - refund requested.  Wanted to play Planetside 2 over Steam Link using my XB1 controller (plugged in via USB on the Steam Link) *and* the XB1 headset (mic and earpiece).  On PC, I can have game audio through my speakers, chat audio through the earpiece, and of course chat record through the mic - I want to be able to have the same setup through Steam Link.
First off, there's a little hidden step in the VirtualHere FAQ for getting the XB1 controller functioning at all over Steam Link wired USB (after enabling controller USB sharing in the "root" Steam Link settings and then streaming) - you have to push the XBox controller button (illuminated "X" button in the center of the controller).  The Steam Link will "hang" for a few seconds while the computer gremlins do their thing, and then the controller will function.
After that, the Steam Link ambient and interface audio played through the XB1 headset earpiece (although that's not what I wanted, but that's more a fault on Steam Link for not currently having an option for telling it where you want audio to go), so there was a connection there.  In game, the audio played through my sound system as desired, and in the voice settings, the XB1 headset mic and earpiece were both detected and selected for their respective desired functions.  Unfortunately, they didn't actually work.  Doing a test record (in-game feature) produced nothing.  I switched the voice output to the speakers to make sure it wasn't just a conflict with the earpice, and still nothing.
In hindsight, I did *not* attempt to send the game audio through the earpiece, however, so there's a chance it was *just* a conflict with the mic.  In fact, I did go into the Steam Link voice settings, and tried to do a test record there (with the headset mic selected), and that didn't work either...  I did try testing with the mic mute button enabled and disabled just to be sure - no difference either way.
Final note:  In my testing, I also updated my XB1 controller through my XB1 to ensure it wasn't a firmware issue with the controller.
I'll keep an eye out for future updates, though.  Really hoping this stuff gets added to the Steam Link by default soon (as are we all)...

Natural Selection 2 is NOT as good as NS1. Saying that, it's still worth a buy when it's on sale. Be prepared to only play it multiplayer, there's absolutely no storyline or singleplayer. Furthermore, there's only about a dozen maps actively in rotation.
Saying that; NS2 could have been a million unit game. The balancing is perfect, and it's probably one of the most fun, rewarding, and entertaining games out there. Sadly, the dev team went wayyyyyyyyyyyy too gung-ho on the multiplayer competitive front, (thinking CS), so unless you're an old NS1 pro like myself, you'll find games are pubstomp after pubstomp, (what happens is all the pro's know to join 1 team, and alternate sides every round. This creates really super fast 5min games).
Don't expect there to be any additional updates; the dev team has already moved onto their next title. It's really a shame though; the team should write the book on atmospheric development on a shoestring budget, (they developed their own game engine, textures, models, etc with less than a million dollars. Trust me, this is VERY unique!). If you're looking for a balanced and unique online game, this is it. Yes, you're playing the same map, but RARELY does it get repetitive due to the hyper complex potential for the game.
At this time, the game is 24.99. I can't recommend anything more than 9.99$ for this game. Yes, I've personally dumped 200 hrs into it, but I'm an old ns1 pro. I can see a new person spending 25$, getting into a game, getting IMMEDIATELY annihilated via a pub stomp, and then chuck the game in the trash. Lack of single player (no training!), really makes this hard to get into.

This review comes from a person who prefers to try out a game's single player mode(s) to see if it is a game worth doing.
The tutorial that the game comes with takes the player through the basics of the game starting with the marines.  Your one soldier is unable to be killed but not immune to damage.  The swarming tactics one would be familiar with for alien creatures does come into play, even when it is only 1v1, and I've found myself wasting ammo on a single one of those doglike creatures as it circled me and bit me with precision.
The tutorial takes you to the other side of things after a while and is much shorter for the Aliens than it is for the marines.  True it takes you through some steps to help build your base and see some of what the base units can do, but it ends with the flyer and doesn't even touch the other two beasts, which are the assassin and the Onos.
Trying to begin a single player game is as simple as playing against bots.  However, the frustrating part comes in that the game options only allow you to choose whether the alien side has an AI commander.  Want to play as a marine or a beast?  You can forget about it.  You're forced into the seat of the Marine Commander at all times.  It is the only option since only the Alien can have the AI Commander as noted before.  Nothing whatsoever is there for automated commander for the Marines.
This game is, in my opinion, not worth the time or the effort unless you have other players willing to help you get a game going so you have a ghost of a chance learning how to truly get a feel for the Aliens in action instead of a free-build scenario that is the Sandbox.

I thought I would leave writing this review until I have completed the game. Overall the game is fun but nothing absolutely amazing.. it's one of them games you play once and never look back at again.
[NEGATIVES]:
- Throughout my whole playthrough there were consistant bugs happening and performance issues which are yet to be 'fully' dealt with, even though they have solved some issues with patches already.

While it is nowhere near as polished as Shaow of Mordor, it expands on the gameplay significantly and adds a seige aspect. Gameplay wise there's still loads of issues, such as orcs spawning randomly next to you and yet not spawning close to your fast travel spot (so quickly moving via shadowkill is essentially nerfed). Another negative aspect is micro transactions, although they are not essential and coins can be earned very slowly in game (I have bought 2 things from the store with coins earned in game). They make the game an easy P2W game if you pump cash in, but as most don't, it's still pretty fair overall in PvP.
There's a lot of RNG and there's an introduced major unfairness aspect, especially in regards to level/ vulnerabilities of captains. They could have allowed more customisation so you could build captinans the way you want, though they seem to want your captains to always be weaker with only small room for customisation, which is probably the most negative thing. Training orders allow you to upgrade your captains but still have RNG aspects which is really hit and miss and they are rare as hens teeth. I've not found a single legendary, and only 5 epics after completing the game and doing many PvP vendettas/seiges. You still cannot build your ideal army, but you can make do with the ones you find with a little investment in training them up/ pairing abilities.
The devs really needed more refinement time, but they've come up with a winner regrdless. Overall, it's still a great game.
EDIT - After playing many more seiges (which is really all you can do end game) and having to replace half my armies after the last expansion, I can confidently say that seiges are full of bugs and that they need real attention in order for end game to move to the next level. Examples are:
*Captains running randomly past cap points, forcing you to solo them
*Your captains (not often, but sometimes enemies too) running back randomly to (seemingly) the middle of nowhere after you cap points. Most apparently the last 3 points.
*Captains randomly dying for no reason.
*Invulnerable captains (not just immune/tough but actually could not be hurt at all)
*Delay between cutscenes/ cutscenes turning you around and allowing orcs to kill/KO you because of the delay/camera and lack of response to input
*The end walk into the throne room is a pet peeve! What a waste of time and why can't I run?!
And the list can go on.
Also, after reaching max (1000 rating) in one area and gaining nothing it was pretty disappointing. If only they'd put enough refinement and effort into making the game amazing from start to finish, not just doing the basics this could be one of the greats. Again, whilst I list the negatives, it's only because the game is so bloody good in most other areas that I really feel they need to put the work in! I've maxed out the majority of the game in around 200hrs. Besides grinding 1000 ratings and all legendary captains I've got nothing left to do. Very cool game, I want more!

I love this game, played it for over 100 hours (estimated) and got it on steam additionally. That's why it shows different here.
SpellForce is an "older" game and you can definitly see that, nontheless the gameplay, mechanics, story and just everything else is great! While the concept of Spintires is great (and I truely do love the idea), I cannot see how this game can be considered finished. The camera control is unusable, trailers have a habit of disappearing, and the map feature is near useless.
The camera does not have dedicated pan and tilt. Instead, you have a hotkey to 'focus' on the truck, and a similar key to focus on the trailer. To view 'first person' camera, you click on a transparent camera where the driver sits. There is no hotkey for this. If you click anywhere that isn't on a menu item or winch point or similar, the game toggles into or out of camera control, rather than only while you hold down the button. You'll be accidentally switching into camera control mode rather often when you meant to release a winch or click on a menu item.
Trailers may disappear until a game restart if you change the bed of your truck at a garage. I do not know of a way to make them re-appear without a game restart. Similarly, if you disconnect your trailer because it got stuck, I cannot figure out how to re-attach it; even when directly on top of the hitch, it constantly states I am too far away.
The map starts out nearly completely black for each map. The concept is that as you drive around, the map slowly reveals areas you've been to. However, the area that is revealed is smaller than what you can already see. As you travel down a road and spot a side-road heading off of it, the map doesn't reveal enough that you can see that side-road. While this doesn't seem like an issue, it's annoying when you're trying to turn around onto such a road and you can't see where it is because of the aforementioned camera issues. Maps therefore become a complete guessing and memorizing game, which while more realistic, doesn't actually do what a map should. Oh, and there's no minimap, so you'll be starting and stopping a lot.
All this being said, the concept of the game is great. It's a ton of fun when you get a giant truck through some deep mud or a river that you thought would be impossible to cross. Given a bit more work on the camera and map (as well as bugfixes such as with trailers), I can see myself playing this quite often. However, seeing the age of the game and that these basic things are in such a state, I can't say I'm too hopeful that it will ever reach its potential.

Spellforce is a mix of RPG and RTS. It's pretty unique for that matter. The only problem is that it fails in both departments.
The RPG aspect is as weak as can be. Your character, a rune warrior, is extremely generic. There are little customization options, however, you have a lot of skill options. Be a warrior, a hunter, any sort of mage or priest or something in between. It's up to you. You will gather items, get companions, complete quests and finish off monsters. The way in which you do that, however, is terrible. The quests are for the most part bland, the controls are an abomination and the story and voice acting are atrocious. There are SOME exceptions like South Park's "chef" (I think), but he then goes on to voice like 10 different characters -.- so they all sound the same, naturally. Gear is boring. Skills are boring. It's a game from a different era. If you're looking for that, you may find it here, however. Too bad, party based RPG gameplay is only possible on some maps in the campaign.
The RTS part is even worse. There are 6 races in the game. In the campaign you will be able to control them all eventually (I'm at race 3 right now), even simultaneously at times. Each race has different units and requires different resources. Humans require wood, stone, iron and arya, elves only wood and leny, dwarves most likely stone, iron and moonsilver, etc. etc. Humans have strong healing warriors, elves have strong ranged units, but weak melee units, etc. Sooner or later resources WILL run out and if you haven't beaten the "map" by then...well, bad luck? There is almost no autosave in the game and there aren't really missions. There are only maps and once maps have no more resources left, you might be looking at a restart. Considering the time investment for each map, that is terrible game design.
Speaking of terrible game design: Base building is functional, units are ok, but not being able to attack move is a terrible, terrible thing to do. The "maps" work in such a way that the enemy has several camps that are "inert" at the beginning. Units only spawn once you activate a monument and start building your base. That means, later in the game it definitely makes sense to just kill as many camps with your hero as you can before you "start" the mission, because the longer the game goes on, the more units will spawn. It's ridiculous really. This may also be bugged, as I once cleared out a map apart from 1 base, started building my own base and was promptly confronted with around 50 evil Orcs that murdered me...and it gets to that point on almost every map. One map has you fighting through 20 flame spitting towers with CONSTANTLY respawning units. Needless to say the game wastes a lot of time. The maps are big, and even with quick travel it takes a long time to navigate them.
That being said you can revisit every map at every point in time (but you will lose all your units and structures you currently have). I'll give them that: the game is huge. You're looking at 30 hours I guess. At least. And I'm playing on easy. My hope is that my character will slowly get to that point where he can solo solve most issues though :)
I'm hating a bit on the game. It's old, obviously. Times were different back then and you can still get enjoyment out of it, but I doubt many players will still be able to put up with all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that gets thrown your way.

LUXIS is a 3D physics-based action puzzler. I'm a big fan of Neon Space and this is like a next-generation deluxe version of it.
Each level is a maze and you're the lab rat. You can only see the local room/corridor, not the whole map, so you're exploring the level to find your way around to the final exit node. You control a glowing orb with a comet tail. It starts white but you have to move it onto different colour nodes to change its colour to unlock nodes of that colour to unlock gates to open up new passageways to find balls to move past obstacles to other colour nodes to open other gates... etc etc, you get the idea :)
My controller skills have always been poor and as expected for the first few levels my performance was awful. Pretty early on it became a case of not just controlling the orb but pushing floating balls around with it like a football, making it extra tricky. After doing this for a while I discovered that the action of simply moving the orb had become relatively easy and I found myself whizzing around the place at breakneck speed with precise cornering. I was Dumbfounded at my sudden skill (see what I did there?)
New game mechanics arrive at regular intervals, no format outstays its welcome. You want to keep playing as it becomes trickier and the obstacles (some of which chase you) ever more interesting.
Throughout all levels there are 'Glitches' to collect. They are always in out-of-the-way passages so it's possible to complete levels without collecting any. However, the game has 5 main sections and you need to collect a certain number of Glitches to progress to the next section. I would have thought most developers would try to avoid the word 'glitch' but I'm happy to report that these are the only type found in the game.
Graphics are clean and stunning, with perfect lighting. The neon colours are gorgeous and stylishly put together, it's not in-yer-face neon just to get your attention, every colour is meaningful to the puzzle of the level. There is no unnecessary small detailing, objects are crisp and sharp in keeping with the gameplay itself. The long shadows in some areas have a super WOW factor which I've never seen before.
Music is brisk and catchy but not annoying. It comes and goes rather than being permanently on. I like that. I left it on. One minor annoyance is that there's no in-game volume control.
It ramps up at a comfortable pace. At time of writing I'm on the 4th section out of 5 and both the puzzle elements and orb control are becoming quite challenging but not to the point of rage-quit... yet!
With this type of game it's important to have responsive, intuitive controls, good spacing of walls and that kind of thing - there's nothing worse than occasional lag, glitches or imprecise movement to ruin the ambiance. LUXIS delivers with lovely fluid movement and well designed levels that feel natural to play. For example, at the corners of long corridors you find strategically placed 'bouncers' which propel you to the end of the passage, saving you time. It's the little touches like this which make it a joy to play.
Windows and Mac are available and Linux is on the way (the dev told me so). Yay!
as promised Linux is now available, it runs like a charm and the cloud support is cross-platform so now I'm off to continue my game in a proper OS!
Trading cards, achievements and cloud are all included. I would like to see leaderboards added, it's the sort of game that could benefit from it.
50 levels separated into 5 main sections. The levels in the first half of the game all take less than 5 minutes from start to finish, then later on stretching towards 10 minutes. It always takes multiple attempts to complete levels though. I haven't finished yet but I'm guessing I'll get a good 10 hours out of it. There's plenty of replay value - levels have timers on them so once completed you can go back and try to beat your times. Sections also have total time taken. The overall quality is top notch so I have no hesitation in recommending it at full price.
Games of this type can sometimes become samey and tedious but LUXIS stays fresh and challenging throughout, with smooth controls and beautiful eye candy to top it all off. Love it.

180 hours later and I am ready to jump into Spellforce 2!  Spellforce is one of those games that I figured I would pick up for next to nothing and maybe dabble for an hour.  It became much, much, more than that.  I figured after going through the game and all of it's expansions on hard (took maybe ~150 hours), I'd write a review.
STORY:  7/10 - The story takes awhile to really pick up.  In the beginning, it seems like a typical corny fantasy game about a mage gone bad.  In fact, I fully expected the ending to essentially be the hero catching up to the baddie, killing him, happily ever after.  You'll be in for a surprise and the story only gets better as you go through the expansions.  I REALLY enjoyed the story on the Phoenix expansion.
GAMEPLAY:  9/10 - Really solid RTS with RPG elements mixed in.  You can go into 3rd person mode (which I don't recommend unless looking for hidden loot) and actually jump back to prior stages to complete quests, vendor some loot, etc.  The controls play out really well for having control of up to six "hero" type characters.
GRAPHICS:  8/10 - Let's be real.  The game came out in 2003 so we're not expecting much in terms of the graphics.  I gave it a higher score due to the look of the world which was generally pretty decent.  The variance in different armors and weapons are pretty cool as well for a game that old.  'Dem load screens.
SOUND:  6/10 - If I were judging the music alone... it would be a solid 9.  However, we have to consider the voice-acting which is HORRIBLE for the most part.  If I remember reading this correctly, the game was originally in German and translated to English which likely has a lot to do with it.  Both text and spoken voice are just pretty bad.  If you can look past that, the sound effects are pretty good and the music is solid.
FUN: 9/10 - I was having fun the entire time.  Nothing else to say there.
So if you're in the mood for an old-school RTS/RPG with a decent story and plenty of sequel content (as well as Spellforce 3 coming in 2017!), I'd say give it a shot!

Bought this game back in 2005, but was too young to fully understand the mechanics. Lost the key and bought it again on Steam. Now, 12 years later I finally managed to get into this great game.
Yes, it is flawed, but if you truly give the game a chance, it will win you without doubt - implying you're a fan of RTS as well as RPG games. Spellforce is an RTS game that can turn into an RPG game depending on the map and on the quest you're currently on. However, if you do not enjoy RTS games, you won't have much fun with the RPG parts either, because they're mostly secondary. While you don't need to have any RPG experience to progress in the game, knowing your way around classic RTS mechanics is crucial.
The world is really nice and it has this cringy 2000ish fantasy flair with all the ridiculous things such as misleading splash and title screens of women in revealing armor, awkward dialogues with mediocre voice acting and application of even more awkward "medieval language" and many more fantasy cliches.
The story is not outstanding or remarkable at all, but neither is it bad. The way it is presented makes the whole game pretty immersive and despite being "not that great" the story still kinda makes you want to know what happenes next. The world is well designed and there is a lot of exploring to do - RPG-style with your squad of heroes as well as RTS-style with a huge army of buffed out elite soldiers.
Speaking of the units in the RTS part of the game: What makes Spellforce really stand out is the player's ability to not only play as different races (dwarfs, humans, elves, dark elves, trolls and orcs), but also play as multiple races simultanously, which sometimes results in some really nice syngery regarding military units and recource management. The game makes is easy to buid up your base fast and spit out tons of units, which makes it clear that the RTS part is heavily focused on battle and military. This does not mean, that you can not build and prosper in peace. Sometimes that is fun too.
The RPG part of Spellforce is probably best described as a hybrid of Warcraft 3 and Diablo. A lot of clicking, enemy targeting, item drops, skilling, etc. is to be expected.
All in all I really recommend Spellforce to people who enjoyed the classic fantasy setting of games such as Gothic - BUT ONLY if you are comfortable with the RTS genre. If the conditions are met, Spellforce will become one of your favourite games. I hope you check it out and enjoy it.

Dust is a 2D action-exploration game in the famed 'Metroidvania' style, with some pretty cool elements to it. It actually reminds me a lot of "Muramasa: The Demon Blade" (if you've ever played or heard of that). As with Muramasa, the first thing you will notice are the stunning hand-drawn visuals and animation. The look of the characters and backgrounds during gameplay are quite beautiful. Additionally, the characters all have detailed animated portraits that appear on-screen during conversations. It just looks fantastic all around. The characters themselves are all pretty good, assuming you can stomach a cast full of anthropomorphic animals (and a seriously cutesy flying bunny-type-thing sidekick). The voice acting and plot are generally good as well. Gameplay consists of 2D sword combat with light platforming elements. The combat also has a few cool twists - your sidekick has projectile attacks that can be combined with a special sword technique, resulting in some spectacular combos and on-screen fireworks. It all looks and feels really cool once you get the hang of it. Eventually you will become just  ridiculously powerful, making the game very easy, but it's still good fun. As with similar games, you progress through various areas that unlock as you gain additional abilities. There's also a ton of extra stuff to do (such as side-quests), if you are into 100%-ing games or completing achievements. If you are a fan of this type of game, this one is well worth your time. Highly recommended. A-
Technical notes: I highly recommend using an Xbox360 controller for this one. Although I haven't actually tried the keyboard controls, I just can't imagine them working well enough to easily pull off the actions required by the game. Plus, these types of games just control better with gamepads anyways. Anyways, just be aware of this... you've officially been warned.

Fantastic RPG.  Even though the player is stuck with playing as Geralt for (most of) the adventure, he is presented as a complex hero, and his world is extremely detailed, leading to a realistic and believable place to explore.  Don't get me wrong, this game has a story to tell, and it doesn't aspire to do so in a complete sandbox environment.  Still, even though the world is sort of segmented depending on what chapter you're on, there is a lot to see and do, from taking missions from the neighborhood notice board to picking herbs to create crazy awesome potions to a game of dice poker or a friendly arm-wrestling match.
The visuals have already been hailed by critics as some of the best in the genre.  Still, let me take a minute to reaffirm that, as well as offer my own (slightly paradoxial) critiques: This game is beautiful, especially in regards to the fantastically detailed environment, character (and costume/prop) design, and imaginative special effects that don't jar you away from the grit of the world with stereotypical fantasy fireworks.  My only gripe is that the transition between certain animations could be smoother, but it's a minor annoyance.  The audio side fares a bit worse; while the music department delivers an epic score that matches well with the action, I found the audio mixing to be lackluster.  When going from one area to another, the music makes such an unnatural shift that took forever to ignore.  One track doesn't fade 'way to another, it just plays on top of the first for a minute, or pauses the first track mid-note and leaves an awkward silence before starting the other.  It's another arguable small gripe, but the audio team took such time to add in little details with the ambient sound (like individual bird calls!) that it just felt a little more unforgivable.  The voice acting is decent all around, although Geralt himself can be a little wonky at times.
My only other major gripe is funny.  See, I love both this game's story, and world.  I also love the difficulty, because it feels natural within context of, well, the world of the Witcher.  With that being said, a few boss battles make absolutely no sense on why/how their so difficult.  Letho's first battle in particular, which is one of those bosses where you may neither pass nor fail, was particularly infuriating.  It just seems like some of these guys have god-like priority!  Overall, though, the difficulty is fair.  The map was also an issue, but I'm sure there are mods for it.
Overall, this game is near perfect, and worth a buy.

[Quick review - Also, hooray for my first real review!]
Gameplay is fantastic, but certainly not easy even at the NORMAL difficulty. The real seller though is the fantastic "pollitical vs. mystical" storyline that leaves you wiht 16 possible endings! Insane for any game, especially when you consider its the second game in a trilogy.
[Slightly extended]
Gameplay: At first, combat certainly feels like a cliched "keep-attacking-or-die" button masher, which is why I have to highly recommend ramping up the difficulty above easy. Only then will you realise, especially in group fights, how much you'll have to rely on defence, counters and dodges, and the game will definantly profit from that.
Story: SPOILERS! An Assassin kills the King you were hired to protect. This is the beginning of an entire political meltdown that you have to fight through in order to bring this assassin to justice. It is told so brilliantly, that as a player, I went from this 'revenge/justice' mindset to genuinely mourning my decision at the end to kill the dude. That kind of twist is very rare in many of these games, and is something I havent felt since playing Spec Ops the Line.
The only weak point I can think of is very minor and occurs just after the beginning of the second chapter. The story takes a bit of a complex turn with a whole bunch of new characters and alot of talk about mystical curses. My advice - suck it up and power through - it gets alot better on the other end.
But aside from that point, its an incredible game. The Witcher 3, due for release later this year, is definantly one of my own most anticipated Games of the Year

The Director's Cut has fine-tuned many aspects of gameplay that made the original a little rough around the edges, though at times the game can still feel unpolished.
However, if you're willing to look past some initial shortcomings and allow yourself to be immersed in the story and setting of the game, you won't be disappointed.  The breadth and depth of player agency and freedom of expression is reminiscent of the mid-90s cRPGs that inXile are clearly trying to resurrect, and though they fall short of this goal at times, no other mainstream game gives you as many different tools to solve your problems as Wasteland 2.
Though I was skeptical at first, 20 hours into the game I found myself genuinely roleplaying for the first time since Fallout: New Vegas (other RPGs that managed to get me to eschew mechanical functionality for immersion: Baldur's Gate 1/2, Planescape: Torment, Fallout 1.  End of list.)
Neither is there a dearth of problems to solve with your plethora of tools.  After 55 hours of gameplay (not counting 20 hours in the pre-Director's Cut version) I finally finished my first playthrough, and even after all that time I feel like there were plenty of quests left unfinished or only incompletely solved.  Which is why I'm starting another playthrough.  See you guys at 110 hours!

This little utility saved me returning my Steam Link!
I bought the steam link on a whim, and I immediately regretted it when it arrived and I felt the poor quality of the controller. I initiated the return process and was about to box it up, when I read about Virtual Here and thought it could be my saviour. I had recently built a racing cockpit as a DIY project, incorporating a Logitech G29 wheel, PS3/PS4, surround sound etc, and now that I have a powerful PC, it would work with that too. The problem is my cockpit lives in the man-cave, and the PC at my desk, the two are at opposite ends of the house and neither are very portable. Step-in the Steam Link, Virtual Here and a couple of powerline adapters. Within 20 minutes I was gaming at solid frame rates and console-smashing graphics from my man-cave, using my G29 wheel with no physical connection to my PC besides the mains electricity.
This software is fantastic, to be honest it would really benefit from some instructions, or even a UI (the only thing I ever *saw* of VH was a small white window listing USB Hubs – of which the list was empty), but it does the job. I got stuck at first having read on the steam forum “go into the steam options > Virtual Here”, only to find this menu was missing, I later found there are two sets of options menus on the Steam Link, one being prior to connecting to the PC, and one being after (I am very new to the Steam Link! lol). Once I got my head around this, set-up was none-existent and I was on the tarmac in Project Cars in no time at all.
It’s not my place to say, but I am confident a lot of the negative reviews are people who aren’t using it correctly. Read the Steam Forum for this software for the developer’s instructions on to get up and running with it and you’ll be fine. Plus for the price of a couple of pints – what is there to lose?

A monster named Joseph Stalin once said "A single death is a tragedy; a million deaths is a statistic." Sadly, there is a cold, blunt truth in this statement. When we hear about a natural disaster or an ongoing war somewhere in the world, and read about the number of casualties on television screens, newspapers or history books, that's all we usually see: statistics. We live in an age that detachment and conformism are the norm, so it rarely bothers us enough to even think about collateral damage, if we are not a part of the collateral affected by it.
Here, all you'll ever find will be a collection of blurry scenes, scattered around a beach lot in San Francisco, painted in shades of blue and purple. Not one of the greater works of Unreal engine, surely. As we start the experience, we are asked to follow the butterflies and that's all we are going to do for the next 15 minutes, until the game ends. We walk in the beach lot, approach disappearing shades and discover phantom objects to contemplate on people that we know nothing about. We probably never will...
is not a game in the conventional manner. It is a really short, interactive art exhibition that serves as an empathy simulation. It is a tribute and a requiem for people who lost their lives in 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, aiming to humanize the victims by presenting hypothetical anecdotes from their lives, hopes and dreams. It is not a good game, neither necessarily quite successful in an artistic manner; but here with this specific project, it really is the thought that counts and nothing else. All profit made through the sales are sent to Aid for Japan and Redr charity organizations. With this ridiculously low price tag, it really is a choice of donating or not rather than buying a game.

This program solves a very specific problem for the Steam Link. Most non-Steam games added to your Steam library are not going to recognize your controller as an actual controller (it thinks it's a KB/mouse) - I'm guessing this is because the software isn't passing through the Steam API. VirtualHere can trick your PC into thinking that your controller is plugged directly into your PC. For me, that means I can use my Steam Link with my Xbox One controller to play emulators and games purchased through the Windows store (e.g. Gears of War 4, Killer Instinct). It looks like there might be some slight additional input lag with this setup, but it's minimal - this software works.
VirtualHere offers their client for free on their website, but it seems that this version doesn't actually see your Steam Link on the network- you need to purchase this version for the Steam Link to work with it.
There are quite a few negative reviews here suggesting that the software doesn't work. It shouldn't take you two hours to figure out if this software is going to work for you or not (you can see I've only got 0.3 hours on record) so I recommend doing like I did and purchasing it for yourself and quickly figuring out if it solves this particular problem for you. If it doesn't work, just get your refund.
note: I recommend launching VirtualHere from outside the Steam interface cause if you minimize Steam Big Picture on your Steam Link, you're gonna see a full screen image of the VirtualHere client which is a bit annoying.

There are a lot of negative reviews for this product virtually all of which are tied to the reviewer not understanding what this software is doing.
This is a rather specialized piece of software. Yes, it technically adds compatability for a lot of gaming devices. That is somewhat useful. But, it is not adding that functionality to your Steam Link. It is really just sending the USB traffic directly to the host machine instead of having the Steam Link send connections via other formats. This software acts as virtual USB Hub on your host machine emulating that the controllers attached to the Steam Link are actually directly attatched to the host machine itself.
As that is concerned it is incredibly useful for particular setups, and only moderately useful for the rest. I will say I noticed significant input lag for graphically intense games when running my Steam Link in the "Beautiful" setting. I assume that is because the bandwidth is saturated with the graphics data and there is not enough bandwidth to handle the USB data as well.
Where this comes in very handy for me is for emulation. I have added a number of emulated games to my host machine's Steam library and many of the emulators detect if a controller is connected and return to default keyboard commands if it is not. Because this software acts as if controllers attached to the steam link are directly attached to the host, the emulators see there is a controller and it just works.
I also use joy2key to allow me to exit the emulators gracefully with controller combinations. This is another ascpect that can only be done with a directly connected game pad because of how Steam Link chooses to send the commands to the host.
TL;DR: This is specialized software that happens to add flexability to your steam link. The price for this software is $20 cheaper than the software otherwise would cost (VirtualHere's website) though you can get a free client from them that allows bridging a single device (so a gamepad, but not a gamepad+keyboard+mouse). This software is a necessessity if you need directly connected controllers for any software you wish to run through your steam link.

is an open world crime game developed by Hangar 13 and published by 2K. As a huge fan of the previous two games (yes, even
), I was very excited for the third installment. While it is not bad, it could have been a lot better.
New Bordeaux, 1968. Lincoln Clay comes back from Vietnam to his hometown. He reunites with family, friends, and crime, only to be double-crossed by his partners and left for dead. Now he goes on a revenge-fueled rampage to kill those who wronged him while also building an empire of crime, helped by the boss of the Haitian mafia Cassandra, the boss of the Irish mob Thomas Burke, and Vito Scaletta, the main character of
.
The story is told in part with documentary-style interviews to friends of Lincoln, and the first 4 hours of the game are brilliantly paced, hugely entertaining, and with excellent dialogue. Unfortunately, with the gameplay being more open, it quickly loses focus, which is truly unfortunate. The characters are still very interesting, and you tend to know them very well by the end of the game.
This has to be one of the buggiest and weirdest looking AAA games I have ever played. On one hand, the facial animations in cutscenes are outstanding, with subtle nuances in the faces that not even
had, and the city and bayou are varied with a moltitude of districts to explore. On the other hand, the performance is very poor, there is a grey-ish filter on the screen, the transitions from cloudy/sunny and day/night are jarring, there are multiple bugs and crashes... As you can see, the bad unfortunately outweighs the good. The game is still very much playable, with some users with better performance than others, but I still think that a couple of weeks could have made this game better.
Let's start with the only bad aspect of the gameplay: the repetitiveness. You do the exact the same thing for the entire game (with a couple of exceptions): go to a district, talk to two people, kill some baddies and destroy some boxes/stores, kill an underboss, and you have conquered a racket. Rinse, and repeat. This will make or break the game: in the long run it is tiring, but playing it every once in a while isn't so bad.
The neutral/mixed thing is the lack of customization. The developer has already promised to add vehicle and character options in a later update for free, but right now I do not see the need to have them since it wouldn't affect the gameplay.
Now the good, which is REALLY good: the shooting feels very smooth and accurate and there are many weapons to choose from, being able to call a hit squad to help you is cool, calling a weapons van and a personal vehicle is fun, driving is accurate and arcadey, the map is big... I have fun playing this game, and the only really bad thing is how repetitive the missions are, and the lack of any sort of fast travel makes going from one part of the map to the other kinda boring (but not as much as in
).
The AI is... wow... sad. If you try stealth, you can quickly kill a mob boss by hiding in a corner and whistling so that one at a time they come to you to get insta-killed. Gunfights are hard only when cops swarm you, since they never drop ammunitions, thus leaving you with no bullets. There are plenty of checkpoints during missions, so you don't need to repeat over 10 minutes of a mission like in
.
The voice acting is top notch, and every actor and actress does a spectacular job. The sound effects are great as well, and the soundtrack is the best one of the year: The Animals, Elvis, Johnny Cash, Rolling Stones, every artist and song I love, and I love just driving around the world listening to great music.
The game is the longest of the franchise, and this time around the collectibles are actually worth finding: you can actually read articles and interviews of Playboy, Hot Rods, and even Communist Propaganda posters. The 55 Steam achievements also force you to play around with the mechanics.
Overall, this is a great game with fun shooting and a compelling story that is underminded by its open world and repetitive nature. Didn't think I would say that, but I prefer the linear nature of
to this. Highly recommended when it goes under 35$ or if you are a huge fan of sandbox crime games.

Breath of nostalgia, could have been the turning point in RTS and RPG gaming if W3 wasn't able to work with the idea better and developer had more money and support. Mostly lost and forgotten game but not for those who know and remember :).
One of the first RTS and RPG hybrid, but I think the FIRST one actually playable. (There are actually earlier but for me unplayable). You control your Avatar as your hero plus an army of fantasy races (Dwarves, Elves, Trolls....). Gameplay is sweet and simple but lengthy (most of the time victory on the map is assured but nevertheless will take quite some time to accomplish it). World is divided into islands (maps) and you move within them by portals. Could be actually slightly considered open world because game doesn't restrict you to actual location, but the freedom of the movement is not utilized except few quests where you have to go back to specific locations. Mostly you will move forward to new locations and never look back.
RPG system is classic. Xp gained by killed creatures and completed quests. There are actual some mathematical modifications for gaining xp, such as killing one monster too many times cause you to permanently gain less xp for that monster, but except that, it is pretty straight and simple xp system. For every level you recieve two ability points. There are primary (Heavy Combat Arts, Elemental Magic, Mind magic...) and secondary, which derives from the primary ability (Heavy Combat Arts ->> Heavy Armor or Two Handed Swords). You can select any of the abilities, making you capable of doing any type of hero you want, you can pick Black and White magic at the same time or Heavy and Light Combat Arts simultaneosly. Before upgrading secondary you need to have primary at least on the same level (You level the abilities, you pick the ability and it is on lvl 1, and then you can upgrade to 2,3....). You can pick an ability only if you have sufficient stat for that ability (Example: For Heavy Combat Arts lvl 3 you need 38 strenght). For every level you recieve 5 stat points and can be distributed freely. Leveling system that doesn't restrict you by a skill tree or a class is actually dangerous in this game. You can find yourself in the middle of the gameplay realising you screwed up and picked useless abilities and you cannot undo it. So character grinding thumbs down.
Abilities are unbalanced, cool looking magic school is actually useless. Game favors fighters! You can play a mage, but you will have harder time.
Equipment for your hero is designed the old-fashioned way. Enemies drop items, you equip them, higher lvl monsters drops higher lvl items, you know that thing... Quest rewards etc...
Game is unique (as far as I know) in the rune system. Well, you are actually the Rune Warrior. You gain runes from loot and quests, and those runes represent for example a hero. Heroes that aid you in your quest needs to be "dropped". With the army runes it is the same. For example you drop Elven rune lvl 5. Runes can be equiped and when a player finds a monument (same type as it is the rune), it can be activated and the monument can call your rune army, or rune hero. Rune monument is like a main building.
RTS system is again simple but I find it fun. You activate the monument (Elf monument with the elf rune), summon the workers, workers mine recources, you build the base, summon the troops (from the monument). Where it gets interesting is that there is 6 types of recources, and some are race specific (Elves don't mine iron for example but harvest "lenya"). Plans for individual buildings and soldiers needs to be obtained, by loot or quests. Some of them are actually missable which I find idiotic. Troops are well designed, they vary in abilities and are divided into tiers. Races are following: Human, Dwarf, Elf, Orc, Troll, Dark Elf. Playing multiplayer back in the day gave me knowledge that it is heavily unbalanced (Dark Elf and Human are the late game strongest) but I think it is unnoticable in single player. This where the game shines (take into account it is quite old).
AI is normal. The engine however doesn't do well with the RTS genre. YOU LITERALLY CAN'T MICRO. Battles are mostly A-move and waiting for the outcome.
Graphics, game design, artwork are very very good. Back in the day very few could compete. Story is average with strange outcome but it sucked me in. You can finish the original campaign pretty fast, with the expansions it may take you more. If you can overlook the flaws that haunted older games, it is definitely worth playing, considering on steam it is ridiculously expensive.

+ + + BACKUP YOUR SAVEGAME + + +
If you don't do this, you are liable to lose your progress, and with it any purchases you've made. They will not apply to your next new game.
1. On a PC, open File Explorer and find the Users folder in the root directory. Now pick the folder with your username and then Appdata and Local. (As an alternative, just enter %LOCALAPPDATA% in the address bar.)
2. In that Local folder, find FalloutShelter, and alt+click drag it to c:\games or the desktop (wherever you like) so you have a handy shortcut next time.
3. Now ctrl+click drag the FalloutShelter folder to an empty spot in the panel you're in, or to where it says Local in the address bar above. Windows will automatically number your new copy so it doesn't overwrite your previous backup.
4. If you don't want incremental backups cluttering things up, make a folder called FalloutShelterBackup, ctrl+click drag the FalloutShelter folder there instead, and confirm the overwrite.
5. Double check to be sure you haven't accidentally moved the savegame folder instead of copying it.

You may be questioning the authenticity of an RPG and RTS mixture, so I'll explain in simple terms;
RPG elements used in this game are similar to that of most others, with elves, dragons, trolls and the rest. You can choose and blend from different classes, then use points to improve your character's performance across 6 stats, making customization very flexible. The game has a large leap in difficulty after the first few levels, rewarding the educated players and punishing those who rush through it aimlessly.
The RTS (real time strategy) portion of the game makes up a vast amount of the combat. You can build camps for you and your workers, then fund an army with resources and carefully plan out assaults on enemy camps. Much like the Civilization games, it is imperative to protect your camps or you may find yourself tumbling back to the start of the stage and losing everything you've worked for.
There are some downsides, such as abusable power and mechanics that limit challenge, but for a player that wants a real tactical adventure, this is near enough the perfect game for it. I played it a lot on it's CD form, so I can honestly say that it does not get boring.

Fantastic RPG.  Even though the player is stuck with playing as Geralt for (most of) the adventure, he is presented as a complex hero, and his world is extremely detailed, leading to a realistic and believable place to explore.  Don't get me wrong, this game has a story to tell, and it doesn't aspire to do so in a complete sandbox environment.  Still, even though the world is sort of segmented depending on what chapter you're on, there is a lot to see and do, from taking missions from the neighborhood notice board to picking herbs to create crazy awesome potions to a game of dice poker or a friendly arm-wrestling match.
The visuals have already been hailed by critics as some of the best in the genre.  Still, let me take a minute to reaffirm that, as well as offer my own (slightly paradoxial) critiques: This game is beautiful, especially in regards to the fantastically detailed environment, character (and costume/prop) design, and imaginative special effects that don't jar you away from the grit of the world with stereotypical fantasy fireworks.  My only gripe is that the transition between certain animations could be smoother, but it's a minor annoyance.  The audio side fares a bit worse; while the music department delivers an epic score that matches well with the action, I found the audio mixing to be lackluster.  When going from one area to another, the music makes such an unnatural shift that took forever to ignore.  One track doesn't fade 'way to another, it just plays on top of the first for a minute, or pauses the first track mid-note and leaves an awkward silence before starting the other.  It's another arguable small gripe, but the audio team took such time to add in little details with the ambient sound (like individual bird calls!) that it just felt a little more unforgivable.  The voice acting is decent all around, although Geralt himself can be a little wonky at times.
My only other major gripe is funny.  See, I love both this game's story, and world.  I also love the difficulty, because it feels natural within context of, well, the world of the Witcher.  With that being said, a few boss battles make absolutely no sense on why/how their so difficult.  Letho's first battle in particular, which is one of those bosses where you may neither pass nor fail, was particularly infuriating.  It just seems like some of these guys have god-like priority!  Overall, though, the difficulty is fair.  The map was also an issue, but I'm sure there are mods for it.
Overall, this game is near perfect, and worth a buy.

Dust: An Elysian Tail.
What to say about that game? Is it it's time worth? Something that you should play?
Well, let's say that: It's been a long time since I played such a great game!
It's basically a 2D game in an awesome drawn graphic style that combines many game features together like a combat system, for hack'n'slash fun experience, a crafting system to collect materials and craft them together into better gear, inclusive your own inventory to store all these gears, materials and quest items.
And yes, I said quest items. There are missions you can accept and complete, optional ones and your main-story missions. The story is great and the dialogues are just amazing, especially the funny ones, which you'll meet often.
There's even a leveling system. Kill enemies, complete missions, find secrets and do other stuff to gain experience to level up and use your level points to spend on your character to get even more powerful. I also mentioned secrets... there are many of these hidden in the world and you will only be able to find some of these later in the game because there are a few helpful unlocks awaiting for you. Of course there's a map and you can travel to every level whenever you want like for example the city to accept or deliver quests or whatever you want to do there. ;)
The enemies are often tough and the combat system isn't bad with all the skills and parrying stuff you can use. The music is beautiful and the animations are perfect, no wonder  since the creator of the game is an animator.
There's a lot more to explain and to find but... why don't you just experience all these things for yourself? There is a lot to find in the world of... Dust: An Elysian Tail!
I mean, seriously... look at all these awards and review points. This game is a masterpiece of it's genre and just recommendable!
Oh, did I mention that this game was mostly done by only ONE person? In a four-year development.
Buy'n'Play it! You won't regret it! :D

How does someone begin to describe Alan Wake without nostalgia?
In a weird sort of way this series is somehow an underrated, some might even say underappreciated, classic similar to shows like Red Dwarf and, an even greater influence, Twin Peaks. There is also the undeniable influence of authors like Stephen King that is referenced all over the game, and there is the musical talent of Children of the Elder God who I was introduced to through this game. In a strange turn of events, AW is a conglomeration of pop-culture talents that all came together to form Remedy’s beloved cult-classic.
As a fan of AW that giddies at the thought of AW2 when I played Quantum Break, it saddens me that this series is another victim of copyright legality issues like Fallout 1 & 2 as well as Duke Nukem 3D.  There will always be the Xbox version available as well as the future hope of its return, but for the moment let’s reminisce about what made this game distinct while being so generic.
It’s an odd statement to state that this game is unique in some way. The horror-vibe is one of a suspenseful Stephen King book where a writer takes his writer’s block in some way into a supernatural event in suburban-rural America where only local legends thrive. Its terror is not emphasized as much as its collage of horror that shows up in cutscenes, plot-elements and other subtle little references from The Shining’s Axe to the made-up shows like “Night Springs” that will make ‘70s and ‘80s horror fans fawn over every little detail.
That’s how you should approach this game, which is a campy “Uncanny Valley” mismatch of horror that will work or not depending on what you think of the mess. The writing itself gets very repetitive and annoyingly vague like H.P. Lovecraft with the constant muttering of “The Darkness” and “The Light.” (As a writer, I also found the plot very relatable, but that’s a minority opinion.) Pulpier elements of the plot will remind you of a psychological thriller storyline, and the various Night Springs episodes are obviously a Twilight Zone spoof. It’s all unnecessary filler to the gameplay that adds some sort of charm in a jarring manner.
In a way in how the game is structured, it’s designed much like a TV serial of episodic content before there was TellTale games, which makes better usage of that idea than what Remedy would work on for Quantum Break. Out of all these types of episodic releases, I think Alan Wake’s gameplay benefited the most from this design.
When it comes to episodic games, they can either appear to be formulaic stories that rise and fall in each release much like TV episodes with little gameplay, if any, (TellTale) or they can feel like a game being broken up for little to no reason (Resident Evil: Revelations 2). AW strikes a nice balance between both extremes.
The main thing I believe helps the game keep its sense of progression often missing from games by having a great sense of linearity. Each chapter has a rise-and-fall sequence to build up tension as well as balancing the action versus the psychological thriller storyline with flashbacks, quiet-time and other means of telling the story. Central to all these chapters and the gameplay itself is using light as a weapon to weaken an enemy before they can be shot, which leads to creative level-designs such as fighting at a concert stage with fireworks and other props and intuitive weapon opportunities such as flashbangs, flares and even car high-beams. On higher difficulties and in the bonus content, however, these weapons become less viable and you mainly use them as a distraction to run to the next checkpoint light. This is the only time the game effectively uses its horror by heightening the tension, but the gameplay itself remains enjoyable.
In the main-game, combat is primarily focused on where there are a few interesting book-it-and-don’t-look-back sections where you get to play with light-weapons like flashbangs and flares. The bonus chapters are where these sections are primarily focused on and goes to show how the game could have become an effective horror experience, and the constant shifts in open-ended and focused environments keep the game from ever feeling stale or stuck in the same locations.
Now the gameplay itself isn’t perfect; enemy variety is somewhat limited by shadow-people, bigger shadow people, hordes of crows, inanimate objects and a few others; over time the gameplay itself gets to feel the same; and there are frustrating moments every now and then where if you aren’t careful you’ll have to retry sections a few times. However, I think it’s because of how great it is paced as a linear, enjoyable experience that these issues are mitigated by how varied the game itself feels to play. No two chapters feel alike, and the set-pieces really do heighten the strengths of AW.

At the risk of sounding like an old fart, I find revisiting AW to remind me of how AAA games aren’t what they used to be since the days when AW came out. For example, the PC port as well as the bonus features and content you get with this game is spectacular, and after I revisited fondly my favorite moments I can’t help but think of how few original IPs outside of Quantum Break showcase as much creative enjoyment in the development of a game as well as something to rival its charm.

Gameplay is fantastic, but certainly not easy even at the NORMAL difficulty. The real seller though is the fantastic "pollitical vs. mystical" storyline that leaves you wiht 16 possible endings! Insane for any game, especially when you consider its the second game in a trilogy.
[Slightly extended]
Gameplay: At first, combat certainly feels like a cliched "keep-attacking-or-die" button masher, which is why I have to highly recommend ramping up the difficulty above easy. Only then will you realise, especially in group fights, how much you'll have to rely on defence, counters and dodges, and the game will definantly profit from that.
Story: SPOILERS! An Assassin kills the King you were hired to protect. This is the beginning of an entire political meltdown that you have to fight through in order to bring this assassin to justice. It is told so brilliantly, that as a player, I went from this 'revenge/justice' mindset to genuinely mourning my decision at the end to kill the dude. That kind of twist is very rare in many of these games, and is something I havent felt since playing Spec Ops the Line.
The only weak point I can think of is very minor and occurs just after the beginning of the second chapter. The story takes a bit of a complex turn with a whole bunch of new characters and alot of talk about mystical curses. My advice - suck it up and power through - it gets alot better on the other end.
But aside from that point, its an incredible game. The Witcher 3, due for release later this year, is definantly one of my own most anticipated Games of the Year

Geralt of Rivia is a Witcher - a mutant monster hunter with magical powers, silver hair and so many scars that chicks probably don't dig it anymore. This sequel starts off right after the events of the first game with Geralt having saved King Foltest of Temeria from a mysterious assassin, been hired as a gloried bodyguard and then framed for said king's regicide. Geralt must clear his name, catch the true assassin and solve any well paying citizen's problem as he faces the poverty ridden, racially tense, and monster infested world.
Geralt's world is an unforgiving one filled with bickering nobles, downtrodden peasants, and racially abused "non-humans" (elves and dwarves).  CD Projekt spared no attention to detail creating believable environments to explore. You'll see townsfolk go about their daily lives chopping wood, butchering meat, and selling goods at shops. Drunks stagger outside taverns, ♥♥♥♥♥ houses are thriving businesses, hangings are common place and interacting with townsfolk and major characters is just as colorful. The “F” word gets tossed around like nobody’s business, dialogue is as hilarious as it is vulgar, and the “romance” scenes put Mass Effect’s soft-core love to shame. It is easy to get lost in the world they've created, especially one so gritty and unapologetically vile.
Anyway, the greatest draw in The Witcher 2 are the ways Geralt can affect the world through the story. There is no clear cut, black or white situation or character, more just taking sides of a conflict; comrades have ulterior motives, bandits strive to free the downtrodden, and righteous leaders can turn out to be political puppets. Everything is grey, making every decision that much harder to choose. But to that end, the Witcher 2 succeeds gloriously in making us feel invested in every choice we make.
Beside the immersive world and engaging storytelling is robust, challenging, action-packed combat that is supported by all the things RPG lovers love: deep crafting, leveling, and inventory management systems. Geralt has an arsenal of traps, bombs, potions, swords and armor that can be crafted, upgraded and modified to fit specific combat situations. Jumping head first into a battle will often get you killed, so gathering ingredients beforehand, laying traps, crafting special bombs and drinking stat boosting potions becomes a necessity. Geralt can exploit enemy weaknesses by coating his swords with various oils to boost damage or gain status effects, or protect himself by drinking potions to counteract harmful effects like poison or bleeding.
There's no get-out-of-jail-free health potions or aid available during combat and no amount of preparation guarantees victory. When Geralt is out in the wilds staring down a horde of Nekkers or the massive Kraken-like boss, the Kayran, all of the careful preparation, crafting, and sword polishing comes into play with intense, active combat. Once we got used to the sticky controls, and earned the essential upgrades from our skill tree, we were chopping up enemies, dodging, blocking, and casting Aard force pushes like we were some kind of medieval Jedi. Having our set traps, disabling bombs, and good ol' fashioned swordplay work together as a perfectly planned strategy is amazingly satisfying and exhilarating, especially knowing that one second of carelessness can quickly turn a fight.
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is probably one of the best RPGs you'll play...

If you played the original Fallout or Fallout 2, and liked them, then definitely check this out.  It feels like what Fallout 3 would have been like if Bethesda hadn't taken it FPS.  This game is really fun and has a lot of depth to it.  The story is ok, nothing amazing but solid and keeps you wanting to find out more.  Keep in mind that "fun" doesn't equal "exciting".  It's a slow paced, tactical rpg.  You'll get 50+ hours of exploration in a single playthrough, gradual character development, etc.  It's also got replay value, considering there are a few choices that you have to make that alter the game quite a bit.  There are some mechanics that I could see frustrating some players, like friendly fire chance if there's a teammate near the person who you're shooting at, weapon jam percentage, etc.  But I think it adds to the fun when you start upgrading your weapons to NOT jam so damn much.  Skill checks are a bit annoying, since you have to wait a bit for an animation with each one, and there are a LOT of them.  But it feels like they shortened the wait time in the Director's Cut (along with other improvements that were made to UI and graphics).  The graphics are solid.  Nothing special, but really feels like a polished, higher texture version of a late 90's top-down rpg.
The best part about this game, to me, is how the story just kind of develops around you.  For example, my first playthrough:  I'm trying to get my sniper out of this jail.  I'd offered to have him locked up in this settlement (fairly far into the game) while I complete a quest for the leader.  But after I complete, he refuses to let him go!  It's my sniper, so I try to take a hardline against the guy.  This sets off agro for the ENTIRE TOWN (dozens of people and soldiers to suddenly fight).  So my team's backs are agains the wall, fighting endless waves of guards.  As we're fighting, I accidentally target the town's merchant as he's fleeing (the target was red, I thought he was an enemy!) and kill him.  Sorry bro.  Keep fighting, and after 30 minutes or so I finally have murdered the entire town, but my sniper is free!  While I'm looting the corpses for ammo and such, I come across the merchant.  His ENTIRE inventory is on his body, and lootable!  I bank upgrades for all of my characters, plus armor, plus a sizeable amount of money.  Did I feel sad about murdering the town?  Hell no, they'd double crossed me.  Felt more like I'd hit the lotto!  Would do it again.
So if you need constant excitement and stimulation to enjoy a game, this won't be for you.  But if you can appreciate a well designed game that unfolds slowly but gives you a great story with random humor mixed in (the screaming goats, lol), then check this out.  I highly recommend it.

I demoed the games in this series elsewhere and decided to take a chance on them since I like the genre.
If you are like me, the first game in the series (MOAI: Build Your Dream) requires (at least for me) replaying levels over and over to go for gold which is too frustrating. I did finish MOAI 1 and enjoyed it but did not stress over gold for each level. Playing it that way was a lot of fun!
This sequel (MOAI 2) has a CASUAL difficulty mode which is just right for me. I got to enjoy the game without the frustration of a fast timer running down AND still got gold on all 40 levels plus all 38 alternates. I did replay several levels because of strategy but several levels is a LOT better than ALMOST ALL! The CASUAL difficulty does have a timer but it is a lot more generous and you still can get gold. That is a big complaint I have with some of the games in this genre that if you go for a relaxed game play, the best you can get is silver or the equivalent.
So if you like time management / strategy / building games but don't like harsh timers, give this one a whirl. I definitely recommend it over MOAI 1 although they are both great!

Shadow of War is a game that takes emotions in times of war and can carefully consider them. It challenges the characters with their own gains and goals, which allows them to define what they want and where they want to go. The main characters, Talion and Celembrimbor, are at odds since the beginning of the first game when Talion is 'possessed' by the wraith that is Celembrimbor. We see their relationship form to a single goal in the first game, to become split apart again for good in the second game. This separation in their relationship isn't just out of the blue, the game is filled with different views of the people sharing a single body. It creates cracks and eventually the union withers. 
The story leaves nothing to be desired other than the fact of what exactly happened to all the secondary characters. Though this is something that would be nice to be closed up, the DLC seems to hint that we will see the rest of the story at a later time. 
The main characters stories were wrapped up nicely with a little bow on top with our names on the tag. Talion gains the freedom he had wanted for decades and Celembrimbor although locked in an eternal struggle against Sauron finally was able to move on. Though I am not sure he is completely gone, in the end,  we see a blue wisp disappear behind Mt. Doom. A hint towards DLC or something else?
Facial sequencing for the game was something to be inspired about. Times that Talion, Idrial, or Baranor were in pain or surprised was clearly etched into their faces. 
In all it's splendor, if you are looking for a game that has fun mechanics and really drives home a hard difficulty if you are surrounded or outmatched, then pick this game up.  It has characters that really feel alive, that have their own desires and needs. It brings the story to a close with an interesting way to make the player feel the frustration that Talion must go through to continuously defend his fortresses from Sauron. Some may say that this is a cope out of ending gameplay, but I think it allows us to feel the repetition that Talion has to go through. It allows a final breather at the end of the fights because they do eventually get intense that you will be sitting at the edge of your chair hoping you don't lose your fortress. Or you are laying there screaming for one of your orcs to save you from an Olog-hai about to crush your body. Just to be revived and saunter back to the fort and try to retake it.

After the happy end of MOAI, Bright Light and the Hero are living a peaceful life until the God of the Underworld kidnapped the princess, forcing the Hero to journey through many lands to save her.
MOAI 2 is following what the previous game established but with many revamps: indeed, now, you have only 40 levels in the campaign, contrary to the 60 from MOAI. However, this number is increased as you can play at least 38 alternate levels: same "level" with different objectives AND harder.
The gameplay didn't really changed: MOAI 2 is a casual time management game, where objectives must be met in order to advance. But you have to respect the timer if you want to win the "gold star" (in other words, respecting the time) - which is changing from a timer divided in three and representing stars.
In each level, you sent workers to remove obstacles (down trees, rocks or holes), to build/upgrade/repair buildings (fields, quarries, houses, temples, markets, bridges, trees, statues), to trade with bandits or hindus, to open chests, to fish or even to cut down trees. The novelty here is a new building: the bakery that allows you to produce more food by giving a certain amount of food. About the chests, there is also a difference: golden chests have artifacts or bonus while normal chests will contain resources.
Indeed, you have five types of resources - all of them can be traded with hindus or found in chest): food (obtained by fishing or by building fields), stones (obtained by removing rocks or by building quarries), essential oil - replacing the sandalwood - (obtained by building trees), wood (obtained by cutting trees or by trading other resources at the market) and mana (obtained by praying at the temple by giving sandalwood).
However, the game includes also bonus: a wealth scales to have more wood at the market, a horn to have more produced resources, sandals to make your workers work faster, a shield to repel ghost.
Indeed, many levels has waves of ghosts attacking your buildings: you can whip them by clicking on them or build statues (Moai Statues) that will destroy them. The ghosts are of three types: blue (easy to kill and giving 5 mana), red (fast and giving 10 mana) and purple (slow but hard to kill and giving 20 mana).
Moai 2 adds also a backpack that can give advantage to the Hero: more wood, more food, more stone, more essential oil, more mana, less sick workers, faster workers, etc. etc. It will come handy for alternate levels but also for the normal levels later in the game.
However, Moai 2 perpetues the legacy of bugged achievements: you have to play the game in English if you want to unlock Steam achievements (else it will be unlocked only ingame). So, make sure to change the properties of the game to English (your Steam can stay in your language). Add to that that the achievement On Your Own was hard to unlock as you can't use any bonus unless they're stated in the objectives and that many people unlocked it differently. Indeed, some couldn't despite not using bonus or artifacts, others did with artifacts, others unlocked it only while playing normal levels when the rest had to play the alternate levels. As far as I know, for me, artifacts were used and I had to play alternate levels to see it unlocked.
Anyway, while the game isn't really getting many novelties, the bakery idea is nice, like the backpack and the reduced number of levels in normal play.
Graphics are still nice and exotic, with the Hero now living like a local, despite him being a Westerner and making new friends. The soundtrack is also good.
If Moai 2 is a good game, it's really MOAI 3 that will see many novelties. However, it's like 12 Labours of Hercules, you can easily play all games and enjoy yourself very much. Go ahead, seriously, MOAI 2 is really a good sequel.
