"MOAI: Path to Another World" is an TM* game developed by Toyman Interactive; Alawar Entertainment and published by Buka Entertainment.
*TM - Time Management
"Path to Another World" is the second game of the "MOAI" series. Other games from this series: "Build Your Dream" "Trade Mission" and "Terra Incognita."
There's actual story plus with banter between characters in-between game levels. The story itself is okay even though it isn't one of those stories that tends stick with you.
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're well done. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are two game difficult modes to choose from: Normal and Casual.
This is a time/resource management game. So there's a timer presence throughout the entire game. The time on game's timer is generous for the most parts. The levels can be finished before the time has completely run out on the timer. It's advisable to plan ahead before starting the level.
The character's rank is updated after earning certain amount of points from playing the game.
There are twenty-four different artifacts to collect. All the artifacts are stored in the backpack. The artifacts can be equipped and swapped with another.
Four different islands to visit. There forty amount level in the game. Also there are forty bonus levels. Each of these levels has certain objective that's needed to be carried out.
The resources that building structures generates has to be manually collected by the players themselves.
There a few different temporarily power ups to help producing more resources and completing task much quicker. These power ups are available later in the game for most of the levels.
There are fifty-four different achievement to be earned from the game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements before they can be obtained.
There are total of six different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I felt that this game is good, even though the story would've been better. As for the game's replay value it's low. If you're into time management game then I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

is an open world crime game developed by Hangar 13 and published by 2K. As a huge fan of the previous two games (yes, even
), I was very excited for the third installment. While it is not bad, it could have been a lot better.
New Bordeaux, 1968. Lincoln Clay comes back from Vietnam to his hometown. He reunites with family, friends, and crime, only to be double-crossed by his partners and left for dead. Now he goes on a revenge-fueled rampage to kill those who wronged him while also building an empire of crime, helped by the boss of the Haitian mafia Cassandra, the boss of the Irish mob Thomas Burke, and Vito Scaletta, the main character of
.
The story is told in part with documentary-style interviews to friends of Lincoln, and the first 4 hours of the game are brilliantly paced, hugely entertaining, and with excellent dialogue. Unfortunately, with the gameplay being more open, it quickly loses focus, which is truly unfortunate. The characters are still very interesting, and you tend to know them very well by the end of the game.
This has to be one of the buggiest and weirdest looking AAA games I have ever played. On one hand, the facial animations in cutscenes are outstanding, with subtle nuances in the faces that not even
had, and the city and bayou are varied with a moltitude of districts to explore. On the other hand, the performance is very poor, there is a grey-ish filter on the screen, the transitions from cloudy/sunny and day/night are jarring, there are multiple bugs and crashes... As you can see, the bad unfortunately outweighs the good. The game is still very much playable, with some users with better performance than others, but I still think that a couple of weeks could have made this game better.
Let's start with the only bad aspect of the gameplay: the repetitiveness. You do the exact the same thing for the entire game (with a couple of exceptions): go to a district, talk to two people, kill some baddies and destroy some boxes/stores, kill an underboss, and you have conquered a racket. Rinse, and repeat. This will make or break the game: in the long run it is tiring, but playing it every once in a while isn't so bad.
The neutral/mixed thing is the lack of customization. The developer has already promised to add vehicle and character options in a later update for free, but right now I do not see the need to have them since it wouldn't affect the gameplay.
Now the good, which is REALLY good: the shooting feels very smooth and accurate and there are many weapons to choose from, being able to call a hit squad to help you is cool, calling a weapons van and a personal vehicle is fun, driving is accurate and arcadey, the map is big... I have fun playing this game, and the only really bad thing is how repetitive the missions are, and the lack of any sort of fast travel makes going from one part of the map to the other kinda boring (but not as much as in
).
The AI is... wow... sad. If you try stealth, you can quickly kill a mob boss by hiding in a corner and whistling so that one at a time they come to you to get insta-killed. Gunfights are hard only when cops swarm you, since they never drop ammunitions, thus leaving you with no bullets. There are plenty of checkpoints during missions, so you don't need to repeat over 10 minutes of a mission like in
.
The voice acting is top notch, and every actor and actress does a spectacular job. The sound effects are great as well, and the soundtrack is the best one of the year: The Animals, Elvis, Johnny Cash, Rolling Stones, every artist and song I love, and I love just driving around the world listening to great music.
The game is the longest of the franchise, and this time around the collectibles are actually worth finding: you can actually read articles and interviews of Playboy, Hot Rods, and even Communist Propaganda posters. The 55 Steam achievements also force you to play around with the mechanics.
Overall, this is a great game with fun shooting and a compelling story that is underminded by its open world and repetitive nature. Didn't think I would say that, but I prefer the linear nature of
to this. Highly recommended when it goes under 35$ or if you are a huge fan of sandbox crime games.

This game is quite addictive!
Your mission is to be a vault overseer - this means that you have to keep the people inside (vault dwellers) safe from raiders, radscorpions, ghoulers, etc. You also have to make sure you have enough resources, such as power, water and food.
By assigning a male and a female inside a living room/barrack, you can reproduce popularity inside your vault until you hit the maximum capacity, which is 200 dwellers.
Alongside this, you have to assign the correct dwellers to the correct room by looking at what stat the room acquires and what the dweller has, this is called S.P.E.C.I.A.L stats.
S = Strength // Power generators and nuclear reactors
P = Perception // Water treatment and water purification
E = Endurance // Nuka-Cola bottler (makes both food and water)
C = Charisma // Radio studios and living quarters (radio studios make people in the wasteland know about your vault)
I = Intelligence // Medbay and science labs (these makes "Stimpaks" and "RadAway" )
A = Agility // Diner and garden (these produce food)
L = Luck // Increases chances of rush attempts succeeding
Having the correct S.P.E.C.I.A.L stat dwellers in the correct rooms makes the room finish producing resources faster.
You can also, when getting the command center, go out in the wasteland and do various missions which also gives you some items like bottlecaps or wasteland junk which you can make clothes or weapons out of.
:
Resources will slightly be used when you exit the game, pregnant women will start giving birth after around 3 hours, even if you're away. Kids will use plentyfull of resources until grown up, so if you do not have plentyfull of living areas or resources, you'll have quite a bit of problem. You can also not drag them into a room of your choice, they will roam around your vault as they see fit.
Also, some quick tips: Do not randomly place the rooms, if you have 3 rooms right next to each other, they will merge and produce more and can store more resources, 3 is the maximum merge limit. Also, if you upgrade one room, you might not be able to merge another room to it. And you should only upgrade rooms when they are merged together, it's cheaper. You should also equip all your dwellers with weapons, so they can defend themselves if neccessary. You should upgrade your vault door and assign 2 dwellers with heavy armor and the best guns in the vault entrance.

A frustrating game that is riddled with bugs and design flaws even after Directors Cut treatment. Ultimately saved only by good world building and writing.
+Entertaining dialogue, jokes and references
+Long mostly for the right reasons
+Mark Morgan music
+Interesting world
+Actually functional pathfinding 99,99% of the time
+Has decent replay value if the flaws don't bother you too much
-Awful follower AI that will try to shoot through your squad every time or run into suicide charges
-Strange difficulty spikes that are sometimes close to absurd and a few cheesy scripted battles
-Skill systems and some other design choices are practically begging for save scumming since so many things are random
-Hilariously bad in-engine cutscenes
-Voice acting varies from decent to cringeworthy. Most of the game is text only, was it really necessary to include bad voice actors?
-Dialogues can go in nonsensical order that causes contradictions
-Quests stages can be accidentally skipped leaving you wondering what was even going on in the first place
-Some quests can only be completed with one specific skill (at a fairly high level as well) and nothing else
-Clunky and buggy UI that sometimes makes navigating and moving in larger areas a complete pain since there is no quick travel even inside explored and pacified areas
-Camera position keeps resetting too close to the ground to be useful between map changes, forcing you to zoom it back to a more convenient distance again and again and again...
-Realtime elements blend poorly with the turn based combat system
-Lack of sneaking or proper ambush mechanics. Nearly all battles are best started with a sniper round in someones arm or face outside of combat
-Crummy weapon balance: most unique weapons are close to worthless etc.
-Various bugs including a repeating memory leak that butchered the framerate after a couple of hours of playing

I've played some wonderful RPG's over the years, but this is the only one that I have ever played through twice -- I've spent almost 120 hours in this world! This is in large part due to some decisions you make that will completely alter an enire 1/3rd of the game, and much of the flow that follows for another 1/3rd. Because of this, there is an unusually high replayability-factor. With one playthrough, you simply will not see the entire game.
It also has my favorite opening cinematic (only in the 'Enhanced Edition').
I didn't play the first game (it's up next on my list!), but you can import your save file from the first...which will apparently alter some dialogue & options. If you are thinking about purchasing both, while I don't feel like I missed out on anything not having played the first, I am guessing there are certain things I would have caught or, at least, "felt rewarded" in conversations due to decisions I had made in the first game if I had.
At least currently from what I have played, this is one of the best looking titles around; the environments are nicely varied, and there were many times where I just stopped to admire the scenery & attention to detail. That being said...I don't play an RPG for the graphics...I play it for the story -- and this game does not disappoint! The voice acting is wonderfully done, and the music has been getting played constantly for months now...it's a very memorable score!
Just as a note -- the game starts off quite difficult if you are not familiar with the mechanics; there is an opening 'tutorial', but you are left to figure things out pretty quickly. I almost stopped before I even got through the prologue...not because it was unreasonably difficult, but I just didn't know what did what.
With the third-and-final title coming out later this year, this would be a great time to play through the first two. I thoroughly enjoyed this one, and am looking forward to booting up the first!
Highly recommended...obviously. ;)

Wastelands 2. What to say. First off, if you like turn based games wich offer immersion, depth and an enjoyable long story then this game is for you. Wastelands has quite some really good things going for it but some flaws as well as I see it. I'll try to list them below.
Good:
- The setting. Really well done. Heck, the intro made me misty eyed and I felt my emotions responding to things happening in the game more then once. I was quite touched when a companion died for one and really came to loathe the bad guys even if they weren't bad for the sake of being bad. All the factions made sense to me and their struggles were a delight.
- Your choices and actions matter. Maybe you don't see it at once but very often you do see the results of choices later in the game, sometimes quite subtle. Well done! Actions have consequences. Quests almost always have more then one way to solve it.
- The combat system is well done even if it isn't entirely balanced and I feel some stats (speed) and weapons (assault/ sniper/ late game heavy) are better then others (luck/ charisma and melee, shotguns and hand weapons.)
- The game looks quite nice. The locations are quite varied and ussually carefully made. Some minor locations and battle scenes were slapped together or recycled though. It takes a while to fully explore a town and that's good.
- Lots of easter eggs and hidden secrets - you are rewarded for taking a good look as opposed to rushing through.
- The voice acting is really well done, adding to the immersion.
Not so good:
- Quests tend to need a string of actions to be done in exactly the same the correct order to get the optimal solution. Who cares if I order first and then put coins on the counter or vice versa in the shop? This is a source of frusteration. You also likely will look untill you are eighty or crack and shoot everyone for the solution of some quests without using the internet. Ye gods. This would have ruined the game for me more then once if the story wasn't so compelling.
- The difficulty spike half way the game is beyond silly. For a few encounters you have to fight vastly superiour enemies with hugely sub par weapons. I don't enjoy duelling a fully armored knight with a wooden sword thank you. After you find some new weapons the difficulty goes back to a much more acceptable level. This really needs a fix.
- I didn't like the first major choice and how it would doom people no matter what I did.
If you can live with three two above points I think you should grab the game, pin on your desert ranger star and start patrolling Arizona.

Pros: One of the most intense shooters out there. The "YouTube/documentary" filters(and don't complain about the "hand-held" camera style - go to Options, turn Steadicam on. You're welcome) are well-done and a memorable approach to the gritty, realistic TPS. Both new multiplayer modes are great(Undercover Cop joins Fragile Alliance in providing a unique approach to multiplayer shooter game-play). The setting of the crime-ridden, corrupt-laden Shanghai manages to be bleak without getting boring, repetitive or off-putting. Controls, shooting and cover mechanics are responsive, open enough to not feel linear yet tight enough that it always does what you want it to. This never, ever lets up, telling the story, establishing characters and keeping it all moving with twists along the way without ever, for a single second, pausing... and yet it doesn't overpower the player; it's like The Terminator in video-game form. Cons: Not only should the first one never have a sequel, but plot-wise, this does not need to exist, and completely undersells both leads; why is Kane doing another job(and don't say "money for you-know-who" - that's an excuse, and not even a good one), and in what *universe* could Lynch "settle down" like this? This is one of the shortest SP campaigns you'll ever find, and the ending is unsatisfying. Multiplayer is all but dead, the only way you'll get a match going is to find people who also want it.
My recommendation: Only the biggest fans of the TPS gritty crime story will like this, and most people will never need to give this even a first look.

“Find the butterfly.”
It's not really a game in the sense of the word, but more of a platform for remembrance. Like how an artist paints a memory, or puts emotion into an event, this game does the same thing. It shows a brief glimpse into the awareness of those lost in the Japanese Tsunami of 2011. The butterflies represent the spirits of those gone. As I've said, it's not a game. It's a small walkthrough to feel a little of the emotions of what happened. I think there should have been a little bit more in the remembrance and perhaps the exploration than what is there. The ending was beautiful, but I do feel like I'm missing something.
Maybe that's the point.
I'm not sure to give it a good or bad review. I want to give it a good one because I think this kind of thing should be encouraged , as it's a means of remembrance, which rings true for those who know and perhaps felt the sadness of what happened in Japan. It's also a way to contribute to the charities that exist to the people who survived, and who lost someone they loved. The idea is good as an art form. It just shouldn't be viewed as a game in the traditional sense of the word.

MOAI 2: Path to Another World is the most recent entry in the enjoyable time management series by Alawar Entertainment.  Not only is it a continuation of the story from the first, but includes many unique additions and improvements in game play that sets it as a worthy successor to
.
Game play is generally the same consisting of multi-tasking activities as efficiently as possible while managing resources to complete specific tasks (build, gather, etc.) in an effort to beat the clock, but with the addition of the ability to store power-ups for use at your leisure.  This small quality-of-life change makes a HUGE difference when you're trying to effectively strategize your actions.  Each level now also has a second, harder version with completely different objectives and alternate strategies to complete them.  This essentially doubles the amount of content in the game and encourages approaching each level in several different ways.  Really cool change.  You also have the ability to find and unlock (via achievements) artifacts that your character can equip to give him special bonuses.  This alone adds quite a bit of strategy to the game play as you customize bonuses to your own preference and swap them out depending on the requirements for each level.  Toss in the addition of an Easy/Expert level toggle, and the game now covers both casual and "hardcore" tastes.
The sequel offers the same high quality artwork and music with the only change being the removal of voiced narration during the interlude scenes.  While the absence is noticeable for those who've played the first, it doesn't affect the game much at all.  Oh, and we have female natives now! No longer is Bright Light the only woman on the entire island. YAY!
I normally do not gush this much over sequels, but MOAI 2 is a true improvement over the first in every way, and I LOVED the original.  With full Steam integration including trading cards, and especially achievements, there's absolutely no reason to not have this game in your library if you are a fan of time management titles.  MOAI 2 is up there with
as one of the best of its kind, and that's a huge compliment.  If you loved
, then you will absolutely enjoy MOAI 2.  Even if you haven't played the first, or any time management game for that matter, this is a great introduction to the genre.
Bottom Line: Highly recommended for fans of time management games as well as those looking to try their hand at a more than solid entry in the genre.

MOAI 2: Path to Another World is the successor to Moai: Build Your Dream (from Buka entertainment who also publish Promised Land, Rescue 1 and a slew of other family friendly games).  MOAI 2: Path to Another World is yet another delightful casual game featuring this publisher's trademark cutesy art style and family friendly content. Moai 2 is almost Identical in many respects to Moai: Build Your Dream.  Both MOAI games sport very similar game play to Promised Land, but are slightly less complex but more demanding on reflexes and quick puzzle solving.
The game runs in 1920 x 1080p full HD in full screen mode. The art style is cute and would be at home in any children's story book. The sounds are cute and atmospheric and the music is pleasant easy listening and unobtrusive.
Game play is smooth and intuitive with helpful tool tips and a quest status tracker on the lower right of the screen.
The interface is well laid out and uncluttered. Stages are well designed and start out simple progressing in complexity as the player gets deeper into the game.
Before each stage there is a scenario-setting dialogue providing a story driven element. Between stages there are storyboard pictures with story text.  Sadly MOAI 2 does not have the superb Voice Overs for the dialogue that the original title had.
Moai 2 picks up where the previous game left off.  Unfortunately the peace is broken when the Chief's daughter is kidnapped.  The player is then tasked to guide the hero through many scenarios and will meet many characters and challenges along the way.  MOAI 2 is larger than the original game in game content and could take about 40 hours or more to complete and does have replay value.
Completing quests before the timer runs out will earn the player gold status for that level. Fortunately players can select to re-play any previously completed level via an easy to use map which tracks game progress. Games are automatically saved for each registered player and can be resumed at any time.
MOAI 2: Path to Another World is only 300Mb in size and will not hog valuable hard drive space. The game is fun to play and will provide several hours of enjoyment. MOAI 2 will appeal to casual gamers of all ages and is especially suitable as a family game for younger children. Children unable to read will need adult assistance as there is a need to read mission text.
Players familiar with the first game will feel right at home in MOAI 2 as the gameplay mechanics are identical and many of the original characters are featured in this new installment.  It is however not a requirement to have played (or completed) the first game to play MOAI 2, but it would be a good idea for story continuity.
Overall this is a great budget game, offering family friendly casual gaming and will provide lots of fun and enjoyment. Those looking for something similar with more complexity should look at Promised Land.

This game is quite addictive!
Your mission is to be a vault overseer - this means that you have to keep the people inside (vault dwellers) safe from raiders, radscorpions, ghoulers, etc. You also have to make sure you have enough resources, such as power, water and food.
By assigning a male and a female inside a living room/barrack, you can reproduce popularity inside your vault until you hit the maximum capacity, which is 200 dwellers.
Alongside this, you have to assign the correct dwellers to the correct room by looking at what stat the room acquires and what the dweller has, this is called S.P.E.C.I.A.L stats.
S = Strength // Power generators and nuclear reactors
P = Perception // Water treatment and water purification
E = Endurance // Nuka-Cola bottler (makes both food and water)
C = Charisma // Radio studios and living quarters (radio studios make people in the wasteland know about your vault)
I = Intelligence // Medbay and science labs (these makes "Stimpaks" and "RadAway" )
A = Agility // Diner and garden (these produce food)
L = Luck // Increases chances of rush attempts succeeding
Having the correct S.P.E.C.I.A.L stat dwellers in the correct rooms makes the room finish producing resources faster.
You can also, when getting the command center, go out in the wasteland and do various missions which also gives you some items like bottlecaps or wasteland junk which you can make clothes or weapons out of.
:
Resources will slightly be used when you exit the game, pregnant women will start giving birth after around 3 hours, even if you're away. Kids will use plentyfull of resources until grown up, so if you do not have plentyfull of living areas or resources, you'll have quite a bit of problem. You can also not drag them into a room of your choice, they will roam around your vault as they see fit.
Also, some quick tips: Do not randomly place the rooms, if you have 3 rooms right next to each other, they will merge and produce more and can store more resources, 3 is the maximum merge limit. Also, if you upgrade one room, you might not be able to merge another room to it. And you should only upgrade rooms when they are merged together, it's cheaper. You should also equip all your dwellers with weapons, so they can defend themselves if neccessary. You should upgrade your vault door and assign 2 dwellers with heavy armor and the best guns in the vault entrance.

So I saw a lot of negative reviews on the game and I do understand where they're coming from.
BUT, to be fair this is originally a mobile game and most of the problems that are pointend out come from the fact that it is a MOBILE GAME...
To get straight to the point do I recommend?
Hell Yeah! If your a fallout fan and hungry for some extra fallout content definately go for it. Its even FREE.
And really by all means try it out cause its not a bad game at all. If you've played mobile games before you'll aprreciate that it is one of the gems in a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm that is the google play store...
For a more detailed overview, here are the Pros & Cons
Pros
-Its Fallout
-Decent vault managing content.
-Nicley polished Fallout style graphics.
-Lots of loot and equipment.
-Not a pay to win.
Cons
-Quest lines can become repetitive quick.
-No strong story line or dialogues treading in grey areas.
-Difficulty drops pretty fast.
-Can take long to perform upgrades or crafting.
Now with all of the above being said...I'd like to point out that some of the Cons are quite inevitable for a mobile game.
"-No strong story line or decision making dialouge"
For this I have to say I do agree that life or death deciding moral decisions will spice up the game a lot.
BUT, you have to take into account that this is F2P. People spend cash to get there rare equipment or dwellers.
Imagine the♥♥♥♥♥♥storm the devs will have to go through confronting angry players who had there cash items disappear to an ingame event...
(The main Fallout games can give you difficulat decisions cause you have a savegame to fall back too. Plus if you ♥♥♥♥ up you can always start a new game with out having to pay extra for anything...)
"-Can take long to perform upgrades or crafting."
ITS A MOBILE GAME... guys... people who play mobile games usually don't spend hours to play a game in one sitting. They usally play while on break, while they go home, during lunch, etc...The hours don't matter to much because they spend most of that waiting time to do what they do. Plus the game isn't a public service. The devs need money to create new content. Upgrade speed boosts are a good way for them to monetize the game.
You can hate on microtransaction all you want but, this game has one of the more reasonable microtransaction schemes I've seen in years for a mobile game... Plus for Fallout Shelter the paying is really just for time reduction. There is no PVP elements so your not missingout on anything even if you don't pay.
"-Quest lines can become repetitive quick."
"-Difficulty drops pretty fast."
These two I actually have to admit are probably the biggest flaws of this game. Even considering the fact the devs can't really throw you difficult decisions, the questlines available are very bland. Just to be fair I think the devs decided to add the quest content as an afterthought because it dind't exist at launch.
For the difficulty, it gets really easy pretty quick. The raiders/death claws/roaches become easy to repel soon enough and serve nothing much than a minor annoyance in the later game. Occasionally fires might breakout in the vault but, that is also a minor issue. Until the devs introduce some new threats and new buildings, after you build up your vault(100+ dwellers) it will get repetitive.
Thats pretty much all I have to say about this game. It has a fair share of flaws but, if your a Fallout Fan its deffinately worth checking out. It might serve as a good filler in between your long journeys in the Mohave and Capital Wasteland.

I remember hearing about Fallout Shelter shortly after it was released. Since I didn’t own a smartphone at the time, I ignored this game. Then, last year during the summer, Fallout Shelter came to PC via Bethesda’s launcher. Gaming companies have been releasing their own game launchers, like Steam, and they’re getting numerous, but I love Bethesda, so I installed it.
I played the game for a little while. It seemed like a game that contained a lot of waiting. It’s easy enough to play and the game does a great job of teaching you how to play and providing some great tips. Dwellers can act on their own, but it’s up to you to manage them. Each dweller has their own S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats, each of which is good for something. For instance, you’ll want to put your dwellers with high Strength in your power production rooms. Perception is good for water production, while Agility is good for food production. Intelligence is good for the medical room that produces Stimpaks and the science lab, which produces Radaway. Charm is good in the Living Quarters where you can breed your dwellers.
You can “rush” rooms, hurrying their production of a resources. If it goes well, you’ll get a bonus and caps, but if it fails your dwellers in the room will have to deal with an incident. Before rushing, the game will tell you the percent chance of an incident, so if you find that percentage is high, then it’s not a good idea to rush the room. The room can catch on fire, or creatures can appear such as Radroaches, Mole Rats, and Radscorpions. If your dwellers get hurt, you can given them Stimpaks. If they die, you can revive them after the incident. If not taken care of quickly enough, the incident could spread to other rooms.
In the meantime, there are chances that Raiders, Feral Ghouls, or Death Claws could invade your vault. Once they get in, it’s up to your dwellers to fend them off. These enemies always work their way from left to right on each floor, going to the next floor if not defeated in time. If you have a Mr. Handy, it will fight them, too, if it’s on the same floor or you can drag it there. Mr. Handy can also help protect your dwellers during an incident. It can be destroyed, but can repaired for 2,000 caps.
Rooms can be upgraded and expanded. Most rooms can be three room wide and it’s a good idea to make your rooms three wide. This means that 6 dwellers can fit inside. More dwellers working in a room, means it can produce quicker. You unlock rooms by getting dwellers. Once you get closer to 50-60 dwellers, you’ll be able to build new, better rooms for resource production. I have three of each, I removed the old resource rooms.
There is a limit to 200 dwellers in your vault and having that many can be a bit of a nightmare, especially if you have not yet made every room. The rooms that train dwellers S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats are really good. You can train a certain stat in each room and rotate dwellers in and out. There’s also a Barbershop for customizing your dwellers, which I’ve made, but haven’t used. Also there is a theme workshop that lets you create themes. You’ll find theme recipe pieces on quests. It looks like the themes are Brotherhood of Steel, Railroad, Institute, and Minuteman.
There are a good number of quests to do. On most quests you can have up to three dwellers, but some quests only allow one, or have other various requirements. They can be difficult so it’s a good idea to bring your best dwellers with the best gear and the max amount of Stimpacs and Radaway they can carry (25) from the Vault. You can get a variety of rewards such as weapons, outfits, pets, lunchboxes (which can contain anything), junk, and more. If you fully upgrade the Overseer’s Office, you can have three groups out on quests at once. If your dwellers die and fail a quest, you can retry for a cost, or revive them and send them back home. I have a few certain dwellers I send out on quests. Many quests take some time to reach and get back from, but you can speed this up by spending Nuka-Cola Quantum, which is a very rare resource.
Speaking of quests, there’s a Bottle and Cappy quest line and when that is completed, B&C will occasionally visit your vault, raising happiness. While they’re exploring your vault, you can click on Cappy for caps or Bottle for caps or Nuka-Cola Quantum when they’re dancing. This is so valuable that I highly suggest doing this as soon as possible.
I like this game a lot more than I thought I would. I think this is about as much fun as another Fallout game. I’ve clocked 67 hours in Steam. I’m not sure how many hours I’ve spent playing on my phone or via the Bethesda launcher. I’m often surprised that this is a free game, you don’t always expect free games to be so good. You can spend real money to make in-game purchases, but I haven’t found that to be necessary.

This game might very well have defined my childhood and forever formed what I expect of an RPG, along with classics like Divine Divinity and Neverwinter Nights. Back when patches were got from magazines and expansion packs actually meant something, this was up there for me. I still play it when I want a hit of nostalgia or when all I have with me is my laptop that can't run high-performance games. And that's on modern hardware, back in the day it was gorgeous and demanding to the point that my old PC had to rest for half an hour before I could do anything else. Good times.
I have a combined 500+ hours in this for sure and only bought it on Steam for easy availability.
Before I go to a TL;DR pros & cons list (see below), here's my opinion:
You're the classic hero, a chosen one to rid the world of an evil scourge. There's not much to it until you think about the twist: a warrior stored in a rune, an immortal and special little snowflake whose tales have survived an apocalypse. You're not a commoner witnessing an event and moving to arms, you're not a soldier rising through the ranks, not an arbitrary divine pick. You're always meant to become the hero of the story because you were a hero in wars before.
With this, you've also arrived at the hook that keeps the game rolling. You can't die, you can't exactly lose. When you fall, you resurrect at a bindstone. But that doesn't make the game easy - it takes thought and some strategy and a number of fights are an honest challenge if you're not prepared as a character or have stacked up an army to support. That said, if you like the thrill of perma-death or the prospect of immense consequences to a lost fight, this might not be for you. It's a heroic epic with you in the centre and only very few things can go horribly, game-breakingly wrong. 'twas a different era, after all.
Have some fun with it, don't take it too seriously, but enjoy the story. It's got wit, it's got snark and if you play games for their stories, you won't be disappointed.
Back in the day, gameplay was a bit buggy. As the kid I was I didn't understand what that meant, but none of the ones I encountered were game-breaking, perhaps mildy infuriating at worst. The latest versions have got rid of most of the bugs I remember and if there are any left, I haven't found them.
With that out of the way, SpellForce managed to balance RTS and RPG quite well for being one of the innovators. You had many ways to accomplish your quests, from sneaking around with your hero party to building up an army to steamroller the whole map. Of course you could easily exploit a near-infinite time window to fortify, gather resources and power-up your army to the max, but it's up to you to limit yourself for more of a challenge or if you'd rather build an epic army to impress your foes and allies alike. Minmaxers will find this game very easy, be aware of that.
Character progression was great. Your skills meant something and there wasn't a single specific progression that would eclipse all others, they all had their ways to shine. Just like you'd expect, you could be the tanky warrior going balls-deep into action or you could be a kitey wizard ranger and nuke from a distance. All viable, all great. But you can also branch out too much, wide as the ocean, deep as a puddle and so on.
Note: Melee classes have a bit of an upper hand here. They're not terribly OP, but mages do have to rely on support to shine. Once you get rune warriors, the above still stands, though.
Different races have different strengths in the RTS part of it all, but most often the game has picked what you have for you and the rare times you do get to make your own choice between, say, elves and orcs, it doesn't really matter. Mostly you'll find them all equally supportive and they all can overrun your foes if you want them to. Not much to say here, but you'll find yourself having a knack for one or the other at some point.
The RTS part was a bit cumbersome, overly shiny and maybe not quite thought-through. Its flaws notwithstanding, it's still a great asset and an integral part of the game and you can relax and have your mind off of things for a while when building a base. (SpellForce 2 got this part just right, it's far better in this aspect, but it's different enough to warrant a separate review.)
Quests.
There are a lot of them.
You'd expect to find a lot of fetch-and-kill quests, and you'd be right, but they're still... different. You often can't just take the quest, walk a few paces, pick up a thing and come back. More often than not you'll find yourself making a note in your journal to keep an eye out for a thing on your travels, at some point forget about it or get really frustrated because you just can't bloody get it. But then, just as you tossed that quest out your imaginary window, you find that thing. You're overjoyed and soonest you can, make your way back to the quest-giver five-or-more isles back. At their core, these are still simple quests. But they're packaged beautifully in story and nifty mechanics. Many of them are also linked, which is always nice.
The stuff that I have the fondest memories of is above. The story is quite dear to me, but I don't want to spoil anyone, so I won't.

This is a fantastic game that manages to be as capturing as the first installment. I'm not incredibly far into it, but I'm already finding a lot more depth than the first game had, which is a surprise. The Witcher 2 is a gorgeous RPG, with interesting game mechanics and captivating story. This episode surely marks an improvement over the previous one.
The visuals of the game are integral part of the beauty of the game. Some sources have underlined how the bloom filter is probably overused in some portions of the game; I do not share this opinion.
The combat system has been refined since the first episode, and it feels challenging overall. Potions cannot be used while in combat, and blade oils have a limited duration (around 10 minutes, plus talent or item bonuses): these limitations favor playstyles based on planning for your next encounter.
On the other hand, the combat can be frustrating for newcomers: at low levels, the character cannot parry from all directions, takes double damage from backstabs and has no vitality regeneration while in combat. This means that the first hour of the game can definitely give you the wrong impression, and even the tutorial (that features an arena event to suggest the difficulty level fitting the player's ability) will not help.
The story is definitely interesting and you can feel the consequences of the decisions that you take at the various branching points of the plot, even if not at the level of other games (e.g. Mass Effect). I will assure you that you will play the game at least twice, to explore both paths of the main plot choice of the game, that happens near the end of Chapter I. The side quests and lore are also a good complement.
The pace of the game, however, is a bit irregular. The game spans only on three Chapters, plus Prologue and Epllogue: the first chapter magnificently introduces the plot, that reaches its peak in Chapter II. Chapter III, however, feels a little rushed: the finale (ending segment of Chapter III + Epilogue) is reached too fast.
My final impression is positive, and I would recommend this game to a friend.

This game is the true successor to the old great Wasteland.  The spirtual successors are the Fallout series. This game really does harken back to the original Wasteland.
The story is fun and interesting.  The characters are also nicely fleshed out.  The game is a long epic adventure and enjoyable.  But I have a few words of advice for any players:
1.  If you're playing this game and it doesn't say "Director's cut" don't.  Delete it and get the Director's cut.  It's much better.
2.  In the very beginning, find Angela Deth in the camp and recruit her.  The game is much less frustrating if you get her on your team early.
3.  Plan out your skills/proficiencies.  I "cheated" by hacking the save files.  No I didn't cheat in any unfair way, I just cheated by reassiging my skill points.  I did this because I would assign certain weapon proficiencies to a character then decide I didn't like that weapon on that character or that character never ever used that weapon (or that I hated the way that weapon worked).  So I would have like a bunch of totally wasted skill points.  So I would go in to the save files remove those skills and put those skill points as unassigned skills.  I didn't add any extra skill points or temporarily increase a skill to get me past something and then change it back though.  It's nice btw to have someone very high in hard♥♥♥♥♥ kiss♥♥♥♥♥ and smart♥♥♥♥♥  See if any of the characters you have have the highest proficiency in one of those and rank those up.
4.  Realize the game is pretty unforgiving.  The difficulty is actually fairly high (but manageable).  There was one battle I had to give up on though, it was just ridiculous.
5.  Armor sucks.  It literally sucks.  I tried to figure it out since I couldn't understand how it worked so I eventually had to look it up.  And it's terrible.  Basically it's incredibly good IF the enemy has weapons that can't pierce that armor.  But the way the game is designed is when you get access to a certain piece of armor 90-99% of the enemies will have weapons that will penetrate that armor making that armor completely useless.  I had assumed it absorbed some damage, but it only does that if the ammo the enemy uses doesn't pierce.  So it works great if you buy armor in a later part of the game and you go back to an easy region, but you're unlikely to ever do that.
6.  You will HATE the ally NPCs and friendly fire.  Friendly fire is really easy to do even with your own characters.  So you will learn early on to position your guys and not fire when guys are possibly in the line of fire after probably nearly killing your team members.  But ally NPCs don't care.  They will fire at the enemy if you're standing right in front of the enemy and frequently will do way more damage to you than to the enemy.

I backed this game on Kickstarter and would do so again, if only to feed the hope that classic Western CRPG's might live again someday. After all, it inspired some other Kickstarter RPG's I've enjoyed, like Shadowrun: Dragonfall... But Wasteland 2 is not the messiah we were waiting for. It's a passable game that ticks all the right "old-school RPG" boxes, but it doesn't feel inspired. It doesn't feel like the game that a team of devs had been dying to make for years, as the story went. It feels by the numbers, cheap, and boring.
Wasteland 2 simply disappoints in almost every respect. The graphics are passable, and have improved significantly since the beta, but they have no art direction or style - they're just, well, ugly. The gameplay is cool at first, because it's nice to have turn-based combat and actual RPG skills back, but as you progress through the game you start to realize how unbalanced it all is. Combat is either far too easy or impossibly hard, with enemies one-shotting your fully leveled and heavily armored Rangers. Most skills are only ever used for opening different types of boxes filled with random loot that usually sucks, and since you can easily max out all skills across your party fairly early, the "hard" skillchecks just become annoying random dice-rolls with a high chance of failure, even with full skill.
And worst of all, the characters and story are amazingly bland and forgettable. There are plenty of "choices and consequences", but few of them are affected by how you built your character (only 3 skills are ever checked in dialogue - the dialogue ones), they seldom intertwine or branch out, and they're just not interesting. Most of the situations in the game are actually comical (or at least try to be). Why should we even care? It's hard to believe how many skilled and experienced writers were supposedly on board for this project, when the results are this utterly forgettable.
I enjoyed parts of Wasteland 2, just because I enjoy any oldschool RPG where you can create your own party. But in the end I felt compelled to finish it only because "Well, I've come this far..." I would not recommend the game to anyone, not even a hardcore RPG fan. Just play one of the classics again, and don't bother with Waste-of-time 2. I sure hope inXile's future RPG attempts are better.

Well well well Dust certainly turned out to be quite surprising, despite it's cartoony simple appearance Dust proves that it can be a fun and engaging experience. The initial story premise relies on piecing together the identity of the amnesiac main title character and what lead him to suffer from amnesia, honestly there's nothing hugely interesting about it. The standard story structure is followed and you meet some decent characters on the way but there's nothing hugely memorable compared to other indie titles on the market. However Dust: An Elysian Tail's biggest strength is its gameplay. Dust provides a nice hack and slash styled combat system that has RPG elements in that you can upgrade your abilities and wear specific items of clothing to increase stats further, the whole system gives depth to the game as you hunt for the best loot. Also the combat flows very naturally in thanks to the gorgeous animations that never hampers the pace of the game, allowing it to become rewarding and engaging. The only minor quibble is that it can sometimes become rather limited as you are tied with one weapon along with three magic assist abilities, as a result the game can drag especially if you're revisiting areas for a specific quest. The games presentation is stellar top to bottom with the voice acting being fairly good (Even if Dust himself can sound like he's trying too hard to be emotional at times), the background and character design's being stellar and the performance running smoothly without a hitch. Overall if you're looking for a fun action RPG to get into then Dust excels over many of its counterparts and can easily provide you with 8-10 hours of fun gameplay.

Alan Wake is a heavily story-driven third person shooter with some horror elements here and there - that's pretty much the best I can describe it in one sentence.
Visuals: nature of this world looks beautiful! Forests, Mountains, Lakes... it's really easy to get immersed into such an atmosphere.
One thing that holds Alan Wake back from being and eye candy is the texture pop-in - it's terrible, texture literally appear on your screen out of nowhere on a very short distance from you which makes it very noticeable.
Gameplay: You will shoot bad guys relatively often and the combat is good enough to keep you excited. The puzzles are rare and quite easy.
The story is Alan Wake's strongest point: it's confusing and exciting and very interesting to follow.
The story alone makes the game worth playing. Not too many games make you think about them after the end but Alan Wake does just that.

9.03m is an extremely brief walking simulator trying to make you think of the 15000 casualties of the 2011 Japan Tsunami as more than just mere numbers: it does so by letting you walk along a beach chasing a white butterfly and meeting shadows that leave meaningful items behind for you to examine.
This is an experience, not a game, and despite its extremely short length and very basic execution it does succeed in its goal .
-eerie, minimalistic soundtrack
-dreamlike atmosphere
-manages to provide at least some emotional pull
-the graphics can feel a bit too fuzzy at times
-extremely short at 15/ 20 minutes
-lacks any kind of gameplay
9.03m did manage to move me at times when I encountered certain items, it's hard to stay unaffected when certain things easily remind you of the young age or dreams of some of the victims. This is when it succeds in the goal it set for itself, when it takes a few examples out of the 15000 casualties so that you can briefly know something about them: the tragedy behind events with high death tolls is that the faces and lives of those lost are easily shadowed behind numbers and I appreciate what 9.03m tried to do hence my thumbs up.
Having said that it's short length and lack of any gameplay will surely turn some people off and I can easily concede that the message'd have been carried just as well using a video or other means. Is this brief experience worth your dollar? It's up to you to decide.

-Too much unnecessary swearing. Somebody might mind it (that's a dollar for the swear jar)

-some stereotypical side characters (Definitely not horrendous, but also not quite enjoyable, original and well-written), BUT it depends on how you look at it (I personally think, that every stereotype should represent a certain type of teenager at university, so you can have all uncomfortable topics, such as bullying, suicide etc. and high school "clichés" in one game and also some characters are more complex, the first impression can be deceiving)
-Story has its flaws, a lot of flaws (largely time-travel plot holes), however it's still a nice, interesting and "emotional" experience. For me it was mainly due to music, location, main character and overall great atmosphere. MOST IMPORTANTLY, the game is about friendship, atmosphere, characters etc. NOT about Sci-fi stuff that was there just to made it more interesting. (the whole tornado thing is just a methapor). Despite this fact, the story still seemed to me somewhat messy, rambling and the plot twists were just meh. :) I recommend you watch the DIRECTOR'S COMMENTARY which explains a lot.

They needed more time for preproduction, bigger budget, publischer, experience and lots of other stuff.
*Super subjective opinion alert*
I honestly wish it wasn't about time travel. Skip to the end of the review for tl;dr pros and cons.
I've played this game from 2003, probably over 3k hours and finished all campaigns over 30 times.
This game mixes RTS and RPG and it works, the gameplay might be slow but sometimes it really depends on the player himself. It tells of a story of a rune warrior 8 years after the convocation war which destroyed the world with only few islands remaining.
You have 6 available races in this game separated to 2 sides, Light (Humanity, Elves, Dwarves) and Dark (Orcs, Trolls, Dark Elves). Each side shares gathered resources between the 3 races. It is possible to control multiple of them at once and depending on their affiliation they might fight one another under your command. Each race has special ability, for example: elves have higher survivability in the forests, dwarves get stronger with each enemy killed, dark elves ressurect each killed enemy as a weak slave skeleton at night. There are lots of different resources used by different races: Wood, Stone, Iron, Moonsilver, Lenya, Aria and obviously Food.
The units are diverse enough and have special upgrades like new spells or better weapons. You can use different ways of movement for both heroes and units: Attack move (right click with left 'CTRL' or left Shift), send them on patrol (Right click holding left ALT) or make your units follow your hero or another one of your units (right click on that unit while holding left Shift).
The RPG part plays a big role. You need to focus on your hero a lot, if you screw up your build you will struggle a lot more, new players should probably start with heavy warrior. The RTS part also depends on your hero since he's your only source of rune energy. You need said energy to summon workers and other heroes and you lose 50% of it each time you die, of course it slowly regenerates over time.
The graphics while are old, still look good in my opinion and the music is beautiful. The voice acting could be definitely better but it's not the worst out there.
There are 3 available campaigns, free game mode (either solo or up to 3 player coop), pvp from 2 to 8 player matches with either already made heroes or heroes imported from your free game. Recently the modding community also started growing.
tl;dr
Pros:
- 6 different races with unique abilities.
- Beautiful music.
- Decently built RTS and RPG parts.
- The story is nice.
- Growing modding community.
- 3 different campaigns and coop mode.
- A lot of different gear for you and your heroes.
- Fast travel.
- A lot of different quests.
Cons:
- Voice acting could be slightly better.
- Game often crashes upon victory in pvp mode.
- Game is rather easy but it might just be me.
- Despise the fast travel, there's still a lot of running in the game.
- Multiplayer is not supported anymore so you'll need 3rd party program like tunngle for coop and pvp.

Wasteland 2 Director's Cut is an isometric CRPG where you lead a group of 4 player characters that you create (or you can take premade characters), level up, and control and up to 3 additional NPC followers that you level up and control. The story is the continuation of the original Wasteland story from the classic original game that won numerous game of the year awards when it was released back in late 1980s. Like the original Wasteland, Wasteland 2 has received numerous awards and accolades, especially in the RPG category.
The Director's Cut version of Wasteland 2 improves graphics from the original Wasteland 2 game, but even with improvements the graphics are functional but not particularly exciting. I did notice a nice increase in the number of voiced comments by NPCs that bring out more of their personalities and morality. The view is isometric and combat is turn based. You will spend most of your time in this game doing one of these things.
- Moving from place to place
- Talking to NPCs to receive and solve quests
- Fighting turn based combats, including random combats as your travel from place to place
- Digging and opening stuff
- Managing inventory
These elements combine to create a game with lots of content that will take 60-80 hours to complete if you don't skip content. That said this game does become a grind at times as combat, movement, inventory management, and talking to NPCs can become tedious at times. I found that I stopped bothering to pick up inventory items to sell because dealing with the inventory management wasn't worth the money I would get from selling it. I also found things like digging up mounds of dirt with a shovel to be a very tedious mechanic and stopped doing it and stopped opening chests that didn't promise high end items to avoid the time it took to complete these tedious activities. That said, there's a good overall story and some good side stories, and some interesting and tough combats (how tough depends on the game difficulty you select - if you play on Rookie, you probably won't be challenged by the combat). There are also lots of different ways that problems can be resolved that impact the final outcome and the ending you receive. This also provides some replayability because you can take different paths through different parts of the game.
Overall I enjoyed Wasteland 2 DC, and am recommending it. It was clearly a labor of love for the developers and I appreciate the fact that many of the original designers came back to create this sequel over 25 years later. My guess is that people who played the original Wasteland game (as I did) will enjoy this updated version of the game that continues the original story. If you never played the original game, and you're judging this game on its own merits, my guess is it will be a mixed bag that some will enjoy because it's a solid CRPG and some will not because they find parts of the game too tedious. If you generally like isometric, turn-based CRPGs, I would recommend you buy and play this game, but if you're not sure wait for it to go on sale. If you like fast paced games or more of an ARGP experience, this game may not appeal to you.

This game has a few issues, but is overall very good.
So, good first.This game is genuinely beautiful. The animation is smooth and it looks great, the backgrounds are excellent, the little environmental stuff is handled very well. There is a nice variety of scenery and weather, the whole game just looks gorgeous.
The combat is fun. The combo system works well, and when you're a rank or two above your enemies it's not so much a battle but a ballet of death.
The story is executed pretty well, the navi-like companion is decent comic relief without being annoying since she only talks in cutscenes, the voice acting is several steps above what I expect from an indie developer.
The RPG elements are decently handled, every level you gain really does feel like a step up in power. The forced balancing is new to me, but it's not a bad thing, IMO. The Zeldaish area gating is used pretty well. You can pick up the upgrades fast enough that you're really only a few hours from any area you really want to go to. There's not so much of it that I felt like I was going back to places too much.
There are also some nice cameos from other indie games, some nods to other games (Castlevania II, anyone?), and some nice secrets and hidden rooms.
Okay, the bad. The story feels a bit cliche in places, and the combat can get a bit stale. Aside from two upgrades to your super move, the combos you start the game with are the ones you finish with. I really wish the combat and combo system had gotten a little deeper.
Also, some of the sidequests are kinda annoying.
Overall, this game is worth both your time and money, if you want to play a gorgeous action rpg with a solid story and some (mostly) entertaining combat.

Wasteland 2 is an isometric RPG with turn-based combat set in a post-apocalyptic world. The story is simple enough; you as a group of new Desert Ranger recruits must set out to investigate the murder of another Desert Ranger, and continue on with the work he was trying to do.
In your travels you will meet plenty of folks out in the wastes all needing help of some form, and you are free to carve out your story as you see fit. This game excels at throwing moral dilemmas at you, often making you make some pretty tough decisions. Most of the situations you face or often many shades of grey, and you often find yourself trying to decide on what the lesser of two evils may be. I love that sort of gameplay element. There is no ‘good guy’ or ‘bad guy’, and the Wasteland world is a harsh and complicated place.
The decisions you make in your travels do have a big impact on the world around you and I love that. You will see a montage upon finishing the game reminding you of the people you met and how your decisions changed their lives or situations.  It also means this game has high re-playability, with multiple story branches to follow on further playthroughs.
Apart from that there is plenty of loot to find with all the usual weaponry at your disposal, and your Rangers have fairly diverse skill tree’s to play around with. This game can be quite tough though so unless you’re a veteran to these sorts of things I would suggest playing on normal difficulty and remember to save often.
Highly recommend to all CRPG fans.

I purchased this application to use my Logitech g25 wheel with Assetto Corsa in conjunction with the steam link. The setup was quite easy and I had the wheel working with the steam link in minutes. Everything was going smoothly up until I loaded a track and hit the accelerator.
I got massive frame drops on the stream. At first I thought it might be my connection, although I never had this issue before and everything from my pc to my link is wired. I then noticed that I would get massive lag and frame drops whenever a wheel input was detected. If I stopped using virtualhere the game would run smooth.
I then found out that apparently, the steam link’s processor can't handle the video stream as well as what virtualhere was throwing at it.
Links:
I figure all the force feedback information is enough to tip it over the edge in terms of processing power. If I turn the stream down from 1080p to 720p I can game with occasional frame stuttering and drops. I have now resorted to using my android phone as the client to connect to the virtualhere server running on my pc instead of the steam link.This setup works great.
It appears that anything more than an xbox controller and the steam link just can’t handle it. Due to this I cannot recommend the software in it’s current state. Here’s to hoping future builds will rectify the situation.

Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae can be easily written off as a Japanese fanservice filled nightmare but never fear, there are plenty of other reasons to write this game off!
In Mitsurugi you play as Misa, a high school student who is also a demon hunter of some kind, who is attempting to slay a demonic blade who has taken her friend Suzuka, when it comes to Japanese B-Movie plots, it's an alright premise if a little paper thin on the actual story and by the end you really learn nothing about Misa, Suzuka, or the sword, as the story fails to go further then just being there so you can have an excuse to hack up people.
Speaking of hacking up people lets talk about gameplay, despite what it may look like in screenshots, this is not Devil May Cry or Bayonetta, you do not have a wide array of moves and attacks, you have sword attacks that drain a meter, kicks that refill said meter, and that is about it, combos don't really exist and in the end you learn that the charge moves do more damage then you could ever need anyway and leave little reason to do much else, and your biggest problem will be fighting with the controls and camera half the time anyway.
If I had to compare this game to something else it would be the Oneechanbara series, but that is not really a complement, this game is dull, short, unimaginative, and repetitive, you fight in six levels that amount to nothing but a single, circular arena with some background changes, fighting the same dull, easy enemies over and over using the same attacks over and over and by the end you gain nothing from the plot or gameplay, even for an independent game this is nothing special, stay away.
Unless you like panty shots or something, perv.

Shadow of War set out to do what any sequel should: Take the original, and expand on what made it great. While the combat and movement still have their quirks (Talion's inconsistent targeting, for the most part), the true heart of the game still shines bright, in the Nemesis system. The variety and interactibility this time around is immense, and giving captains the ability to "learn" your tactics and shut them down makes fights much more interesting than they used to be in Shadow of Mordor. Not to mention grand, overarching plot actually had quite a bit of weight to it this time, and it all culminated in, what I found to be, a very satisfying ending.
Now, I should probably talk about the Shadow Wars, since everyone is up in arms about what a grind it is. To that I respond that, after the first round is finished, most of your orcs should be somewhere in the upper 40's-lower 50's in level, which means that they will most likely be higher level than most of the invaders. This means that you really only have to grind and level up for the first round of invasions, and the subsequent rounds can be taken on almost immediately. Plus, this phase grants the Nemesis system dozens of opportunities to introduce new orcs and ologs to you in a short span of time.
My only major gripes with this game (that aren't holdovers from the original) are that the game will assign you skill points that you are incapable of spending after you are max level, and that fights with multiple captains can get tedious with all of the grandstanding and introductions.
With that in consideration, I'd give it a solid 8/10

I wanted to like this game, I really did. In a way I actually do but I can't quite recommend it to most .  This game seeks to blend the RPG of party based RPGs withe base building and RTS tactics of RTS games. Sadly the execution did not match the lofty goals. The Warlords: Battlecry series (particularly 3) is the closest thing I can liken this game to. So does that mean if you loved Battlecry 3 you'll love this game?  Maybe. personally i would consider it a mix between Dungeon Siege and Battle Realms, with the strong points of neither.
- It is a stable and well thought out game from an aesthetic stand point.
- Relaxed pace means it is an easy game to get into and unwind with compared to most RTS games
Aaaaaaand that's all I got. To be fair it is fun at times, but I found it more of a slog than anything else.
- The voice acting lacks any energy.
- The RTS elements are disappointingly shallow.
- The RPG Elements are woefully underdone.
- The Story is a bit of a jumble.
The voice acting is bad, never mind the small number of VA's buit the all sound like Bill Murray on flu meds. No matter what they say they always sound like they're just about ready to yawn.  It's not even so bad as to be comical it's just dead.
THE RTS Elements are the next problem. You pretty much have very little information on your troops, interms of HP, Defense, Damage, etc, not unlike a Westwood style RTS but this is coupled with the abundance of mirror units. That is, while there are different factions, they are for all intents and purposes simply palette swaps. The RPG elements fare no better. In this game, the RPG happens as an aside to the RTS which more or less brings any momentum or tension back down to geriatric ward speed limits.
The Story is also a bit of a mess, rather heavy-handed but still generally tolerable thanks to the ability to skip the dreary voice acting.  You won't miss much by skipping the dialog. In the end though the game is not technically bad and it is actually a good sort of RTS game to just relax yourself with. For what it's worth, despite my complaints I still intend to play through the game and it's expacks.

Have you come looking for the best game ever? In my opinion, you've come to the right place.  This is a unique mix of RTS/RPG game, with great story, interesting characters (sometimes very cliche, can't hide that), epic battles, and... and stuff.
Elements:
+GRAPHICS - now some of you would probably say 'w8 w0t m8?' looking at the screenshots, but I played this game since it came out, and it hasn't aged a bit. It's still fun to watch your avatar stab a goblin to death, then send an Ice Bolt at another one for Crowd Control purposes, and let your follower warrior do that overhead smash for tons of damage. Units were quite diverse, and THOSE BUILDINGS... Elven and Dwarvish architecture is just so much fitting, I can't express that.
+MUSIC - I don't have a slightest idea who the main composer was, but give that man a cookie. Or Grammy. Dunno, maybe both. Music fits every map, let's say you're in a forest kind of area, it gives you a soothing tune, yet when the battle takes place, it changes to war drums etc.
+RPG ELEMENTS
++CHARACTER
You control a Rune Warrior (male/female, 26 faces each), a human bound to a rune of a powerful Circle Mage (in your case it's Rohen, the Ice Nuke guy), which grants you immortality for a price of eternal servitude, unless the owner of the rune gives it to you, granting you free will again (while retaining immortality). Some of you are probably already at 'woah woah woah what's the point of the game if I am immortal?'. I hastily answer: Immortal doesn't mean unbeatable. When your HP drops to zero, you respawn at a last activated Menhir (few of those stones are on every map), and some time passes so your army/some of the building could already be gone without you noticing. Now, abilities and attributes. Every time you level up, you gain 5 attribute and 2 ability points, BUT abilities require you to have certain attribute value each time you want to increase them, so forget those dreams about CON based fire mage if you want to max out fire magic. There are a lot of good builds, for starters I would propose a fighter (these ones are easier to play first time) with Heavy Armor, Heavy weapons, STR-CON, some DEX for accuracy purposes (gotta get dem damages up bruh). You can get up to level 30 in basic game, and 50 in addons, so you don't ruin a build by mistake (which is irreversable). Character transpones between addons.
++ABILITIES/SKILLS
Let me just explain what does each skill do
LIGHT COMBAT ARTS - light armors, daggers, small blunts, evade stuff
HEAVY COMBAT ARTS - hello, my name is Mr Tank, and this is Jackass.
RANGED COMBAT - pew, pew pew, pew pew pew pew, pew
ELEMENTAL MAGIC - fireballs, meteor strikes, rains of ice, basic nuker kit
WHITE MAGIC - heal stuff, buff stuff
MIND MAGIC -mage remover, mana upkeep
BLACK MAGIC - death magic (pure dps), necromancy, diseases
++ATTRIBUTES
Strength - hit stuff harder
Stamina - get hit longer
Dexterity - hit stuff instead of missing
Agility- dont get hit by stuff
Intelligence - mana regen
Wisdom - more mana
Charisma - better healing and mind magic
++SPELLS
You get spells from scrolls you drop/buy (mage trees), or automatically (warrior trees). They look great, sound great, feel great. 1v5? Berserk Rage and 2-shot every enemy. Enemy army approaching? Rain of Ice combined with archers. Own army below 20% hp? Mass healing, aaaaand it's all healed. RPG map too hard? Dominate that enemy to kill stuff for you
++STORY
It's linear, and you have 0 choices, but the plot keeps you interested, and DAYUM THAT TWIST.  Characters feel like they belong to the world, voice acting is top notch, there are a lot of side quests with interesting rewards. Also, much lore, very information IN EVERY DIALOGUE.
++COMPANIONS
You get up to five rune warriors as companions, but  think of them like a pair of gloves. "Oh, the new rune of a warrior, 2 STR more than current, guess who is getting replaced". They don't have dialogues, story, treat them as pawns.
+RTS ELEMENTS
++ARMY SYSTEM IN GENERAL
To summon an army, you have to reach a monument on the map. There are 6 races (3 light, 3 dark), each has a corresponding monument. Fun: if you put light race next to dark race, they are going to fight with each other, regardless of your orders, so plan army movements carefully on a map with two monuments. Now, back to the topic. Once at a monument, you can first summon workers, which gather resources, and build structures for more efficient gathering, for defense, or for recruitment. You can only build structures which plans you have found - you get those during the main plot, so you can start with like 8 structures for a race on first map, and end up with 20 later on. Same rules apply to units, you start with 2 kinds, end with like 9.
++RACES
Humans - crossbow turrets, healers, mind mages, marksmen (one of best units early game)
Elves - wooden turrets, wooden buildings, ice magic, only race in the game that can produce wood (grows trees)
Dwarves - only race without turrets. Why? Defenders. Imagine an army of heavy armored dwarves throwing hammers at you. fun? Now imagine that each kill levels up a dwarf (up to +5), increasing his health and damage
Orcs - burn stuff, smash stuff
Trolls - throw rocks at stuff, smash stuff harder
Dark Elves - death magic, necromancy
++BATTLES
Up to 80 army size per side, best tactics: put dem units in a group and press H (stop). If you dont press stop, healers will not heal, mages will not cast spells, archers will move around after every shot. H is love, H is life, H is efficient killing.
+MULTIPLAYER
You can play with friends in a group of 2 or 3, but only through Hamachi since GameSpy servers are no longer in existence, but the gameplay looks like this: 3 monuments vs 20 enemy camps, survive until you can build enough defense to safely raise an army and slowly clean a map. Sounds boring, but it isn't. I played all of the 50 multiplayer maps with friends, in 2015, IT WAS SO MUCH FUN.
Now, to summarize...
PROS:
+looks great, sounds great
+complex character development system
+epic battles on RTS maps and...
+small group adventures on RPG maps
+hours of fun
+multiplayer still working
+plot
+dialogues
CONS:
-multiplayer requires hamachi
-multiplayer map can take over an hour (which is nice), but in case of disconnecting, reconnect is impossible
-easy to ruin a character if you didn't plan it beforehand
Now, should you play Spellforce? Yup. 10/10. Best game ever.

Built my squad around a varried skill tree, heavy on dialogue choices, replete with a specialized team leader and a gameplay concept of 'leave no stone unturned'.  Should have just put all my points in initiative, speed, pistols and energy weapons.  Never had enough points in any of the dialogue skills to unlock the 'big dialogue choices' leading to unique ends to certain confrontations.  Even with a specialized team leader and a squad of middle-of-the-road-charisma-types, I was never able to recruit more than a handful of NPCs found in the world (turns out none of them are worth the effort anyway, neither for awesome stats nor interesting personalities).
Maybe I'm just not awesome enough (or Tactical RPG snob enough) but the game became simply not-fun in the second act, and I stopped playing.  It was partly the goofy factions that put me off (Mannerites) but also the difficulty curve.  We went from a gradual grade to a cliff-face in terms of the enemies I encountered, thanks to my squad's all-around average inititative and inferior weapons and armor (the best you could POSSIBLY find before starting the second act -I checked).
Wanted to like this game, but I feel the developers made it for a niche market of indie title diehard types that I just do not belong to.

Graphics: absolutely spectacular, although for a game that used to be PC exclusive, it's very annoying to change the settings around and find what's good for you(you have to use hte pre-launcher in order to change anything other than brightness). The landscapes are vivid, animations are smooth, and the gore is satisfying. The Witcher 2 is a real pleasure to look at... especially Triss ;)
Story: Pretty easy to get into, and it held me throughout playing. You don't have to have played the Witcher 1 in order to understand what's going on. The Witcher 2 has a very mature story, no happy fairytales here, and I very much appreciate that in games. Another unique aspect is that you have to actually pay attention to the story in order to figure out what you have to do, a surprisingly rare in video games. On top of that, there are a lot of important choices you can make to decide the story, which is a big plus for me.
Interface: The interfaces in this game are pretty shoddy, slow, and overall a pain to navigate, but you can eventually get used to them. The map is also next to useless, making it hard to navigate most areas.
Combat: [strikeThe Witcher 2 is very difficult even on the easy setting. That's the reason I couldn't finish the game as much as I wanted to; I don't have the time to perfect my abilities and figure out the strategies to beat the harder bosses.[/strike]The combat is pretty typical for a third person RPG just roll, hit, roll again, throw a sign out sometimes. It's fun, not too complicated, and overall quite well done. There are a lot of different abilities you can level for Geralt, and depending on what you choose it can have a large impact on how you tackle your foes.
I really enjoyed my time with The Witcher 2, the story is well above average, the combat is fun, and the graphics are amazing. The only drawback is the shoddy menus, I mean it almost feels like a bad console port. I would definitely recommmend this game if you are at all a fan of RPGs.
Edit: I decided to go back and give this game another crack... and I'm not sure what I was talking about before. On easy this game is very manageable, but you still have to pay a little attention to side quests or you'll be under geared.

is an isometric, turn-based strategy RPG set in post-apocalyptic Arizona. It follows the exploits of the Desert Rangers, a group of self-appointed peacekeepers who make it their business to settle disputes and protect the innocent from the horrors of the new world. Unfortunately, the Rangers have fallen on hard times of late, losing the trust of the common folk, and must work even harder to preserve their once glorious name.
The game is an excellent update on a classic RPG experience, placing you squarely in the harshest of settings with a more benevolent role to play than most other “post-nuclear” game experiences with an excellent and open world exploration and battle system, as well as deep character customization and a dynamic, ever-changing story and world experience.
is very open in terms of story and flow, and will almost always provide a unique experience based on your party choices, in-game decisions, interactions with certain groups, and success in handling problems for the citizens of your jurisdiction. Each game is going to be a completely different experience based on the party you choose, simply due to the access or restrictions you’ll have from the skills your party possesses.
