Great game with a robust combat system that utilises RPG mechanics very well.
The combat:
combat in this game is done in real time and does not require you to click the correct button prompted on screen a la' the witcher 1. This time combat is fluid and weighty. the use of signs is very slick too. turning a man into ice and then smashing him into tiny peices with your sword has never felt better.
Alchemy:
At first I thought "ah great a skill I will never use" but actually it's useful and adds a layer of depth to the game. wether it be buffs to the player or creating poisions it adds to the overall gameplay by giving you the oppitunity to use different tactics in combat.

I personally would recommend looking up benchmarks for your'e setup and how this games performs before buying.

Honestly, there isn't much to talk about Life is Strange and I don't mean that in a negative way. I've put this game off ever since it came out because it never really appealed to me that much. Telltale needs to step up their games, literally, because Life is Strange does Telltale better than Telltale in this genre of choice-making games.
The best part of this game are interconnected, it's narrative/story and the characters. It made this world realistic... to some capacity of course... Without spoiling anything, this game has a story that is engaging from the beginning and leave cliffhangers at the end of each episode. The choices made in the game come into play in terms of narrative and story, sure you'll still end up with the same 2 final choices and similar endings as everyone else, but it becomes evident that this is well done.
Other pros include, good soundtrack, art style, gameplay and voice acting.
The less favoured elements of the game are minor issues, like odd lip syncing or lips not moving at all, character eyes don't always look at the right places, and some questionable dialogue and actions.
I don't mean to throw Telltale Games under the bus but Life is Strange provided a whole lot more variation than most, if not all Telltale Games, with their choices. Even though some variations are minor, it makes it more realistic.

'The Smash Hit Action Game from Comic Market 84' is what the storefront would have you believe. And while the action is certainly white knuckle, with numerous combos and upgradeable skills, it's the intricately detailed and complex narrative that will have you talking about Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae long after the credits have rolled.
On the surface, it's about two teenage girls crossing swords in a battle to the death. But if you dig deep enough, you discover that the developers are actually commenting on the societal pressures that adolescent females in Japan must wade through each and every day. The struggle of Misa is one of innocence and purity versus the seductive lure of moral bankrupcy. Or perhaps....it is Suzuka the player should sympathize with. The girl that shuns forced traditions in a quest to establish her own identity.
No matter which way you look at it, this is the game that The Fullbright Company (Gone Home) wished they had created.

Mafia 3, in my honest opinion, is a letdown for fans of the series' previous games. It contains some elements from the previous games, but the game just
different. There are so many weird implementations that are unnecessary and would be too lengthy to list. Granted I only played this game for an hour before realizing that I am not a fan, but I believe those who enjoyed Mafia II will feel the same way.
The game has a very intrusive HUD (ex. the 3D GPS assistance when driving). This makes the game feel more arcadey, and takes away the immersion. Another feature that breaks immersion and changes the game feel are healthkits. Maybe this is nitpicky, but the inclusion of health kits in Mafia III just seems out of place. Why not just keep the old system of regaining health by eating/drinking at a restaurant or in your home?
Here's a short list of things I was able to notice during my brief experience of the game:
-Storyline (from what I played) is engaging, and I will certainly watch playthroughs on YouTube to find out what happens
-Open world
-Gunplay can be fun
-Vastly different (though seemingly the same) from previous games, and (imo) not for the better
-♥♥♥♥♥♥ FPS (probably just because my PC can't handle it)
-The game feels like EA tried to make a GTA clone, but failed horribly
I would honestly give this game a 4/10, because the story is engaging and it runs.
Mafia III is very different from the previous games, and I don't think the changes are for the better. But hey, I only played an hour. Everyone's opinion is different, so I encourage you to play this game if you really want to.

I really enjoyed most of the story. It was great from start, up until the end where I felt it fell pretty flat. The missions left a lot to be desired, the vast majority being Destroy X, Interrogate X, or Kill X. It is a large open world layout, but most buildings are cut and paste layouts with minor if any interior changes. The areas are very reused, with you visiting certain spots for one mission only to be sent right back afterwards, to a completely respawned area as if nothing had happened.
There is also an extreme lack of customization options. You will wear the same outfit for the entire game and it will only temporarily change a few times for story reasons. You can't customize your weapons beyond choosing which two you want to roll with (1h smg/sniper rifle by far the most effective combo) and you can't customize your cars, outside of permanent upgrades that change the performance aspect as well.
There are a few "nice" "quality of life" features, like being able to call a car to be delivered, an arms dealer for resupply, and a cash pick up, usuable virtually anywhere. I say "nice" and "quality of life" because the car delivery is really only useful once you've got the last car, the arms dealer clearly comes with the cost of being able to carry only a couple clips of ammo for your weapons, and the cash pick up ability which completely negates the games death penalty is basically a requirement as the only other way to drop your cash off is to drive to what will be bumble♥♥♥♥ egypt after the first few hours to stash it in the safe.
The combat is relatively easy, and the AI is fairly predictable and easily manipulated into coming one by one to your whistle if you go that route. The hardest part of combat comes from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments where you will have a clear shot, take it, but the enemies will be protected by some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ clipping from the objects, scenery, and terrain they are by and you won't actually hit your target.
I enjoyed most of the characters in the story, the underbosses weren't utilized very much from a story point after you recruit them though, so I didn't really care about them outside of the perks they gave me. The cutscenes and voice acting were good where applicable though. The best character in the game is easily John Donovan, mission dialogue, cutscenes, it doesn't matter. That character is ♥♥♥♥ing gold. His senate interview clips are great too.
It took me roughly 33 hours to beat the story, and that was doing just the requisite missions, and a few side missions. Although I did complete every racket available for each mission, even after hitting the cash requirement. I enjoyed the game overall and I would definitely recommend it. It isn't perfect, and could definitely have done some things differently, but it doesn't deserve the hate it is getting and deserves more than a mixed rating.

What a game. Base game plus expansions. This was truly a unique experience, but not without its own issues.
Graphics: For it's time it was probably great, and does kind of look good even today by some minor twaking and an unofficial patche which enables widescreen and HD resolution. The animation does look stiff and when interacting with characters there's nothing but body language to be seen.
Sound: Also for it's time it was probably great. Now not so much. VA was horrible to listen to. At times I just wanted to mute the sound and hide behind a pillow to avoid the VA. The music however was great, filled with atmosphere, and background sounds really added to the atmosphere as well. Making each map feeling alive, or haunted.
When fighting against enemy forces there was a clear sound of blades hitting other blades but that was about it. No unique sound for other weapon types except bows and crossbows.
UI: A little rough. Slightly confusing in the beginning, but easy to understand. Inventory management lacks features we are used to knowadays with tabs and sort functions. Each tab has its own function: Gear, Magic, Runestones/Herostones, Plans(units and buildings) and Quest items. The map shows precise locations of units and buildings. Selecting a unit to choose what to build can be a mess, but with proper management of plans this will be a breeze. The same for unit plans.
Gameplay: This is the games strongest point. Awesome combination of RTS and RPG.
* RPG: This is controlled through 3rd person view. You use the WASD keys for movement, and select spells using your mouse. Maybe even using the numbers above WASD. From this perspective you can control your summoned units and titans, open chests, complete quests etc. There are however no option for jump, but seeing as this is a RTS title it is understandable. As you level your hero you can allocate skillpoints to a skilltree, either for melee or magic.
* RTS: The easy part of the game. Select a worker, then a building and let the worker along with 4 other buddies build it. Then you can upgrade certain units with new spells or powerful gear. Each monument which has one unique for each "faction" acts as a barracks from which you can summon new units. Like most RTS games before it it too has base defense buildings. Weak on their own, but combined with certain units can be a lethal combination that can tear enemy troops apart. Eventually you can summon titans, achieve greater power for other units and with one faction even upgrade the stats of the buildings. What annoyed me is that ranged units had to move right next to enemy buildings to destroy it. Made it feel weird, especially among the magic only units.
* Maps: The maps are huge. At times it feels too huge as it takes awhile to reach the enemy camps or objective on the other side of the map. Most of the time it works fine, but other time it simply makes the game feel slow. The maps are both the games weakness and strength because of it. I found many maps often boring as most areas didn't really feel unique. Resources on some maps are scarce as it should be. Maps provides strategic places for defense as well as offense with varied terrain.
Story: I loved it at first. A lone Runewarrior tasked to prevent destruction upon the world as we know it. Help prevent the darkness to win and avoid mass exctinction. Or something along these lines. Not unique, but I liked it. It's not exactly Hollywood quality, and because of horrible VA not exactly engaging either. Cinematics looked and felt great, cutscenes was so so.
Summary
While the game has alot of content to offer, decent graphics, ok sound, almost-awesome gameplay and an OK-ish story it isn't that great in story. The gameplay felt slow many times and boring. However, I still want to recommend this game. It's unique blend of RPG and RTS is great. Giving me an unforgetable game. While it feels rough around the edges, and even feels like it lack the little extra it is well worth an investetment. If you love RTS and RPG, give it a go. It is a good game, at times even awesome, but as mentioned do have its own issues.
Rating: 6 out of 10
The negatives pulls the score down, but it still have alot of positives too, some which is hard to explain through words alone and needs to be experienced. So don't let the score scare ya. I still loved the game despite its flaws. In fact, I consider myself a fan. :)

This product does what it says.  For some reason quite a few games in my library would not work over Steam Link because of the emulation technique that Steam is using.  With VirtualHere I was able to get my Xbox Controller to work with those games; however, it does not fix the games where the Steam Controller itself is also broken due to this emulation technique since it does not show up as a device that can be shared via VirtualHere.  (Distance is one game for example where everything is seemingly broken, but it works just fine if you play it from your PC)
After some digging around on their forums I found that VirtualHere does not actually need to be run from Steam if you are using it with the Steam Link.  When the link starts streaming it handles all of that automatically and any USB devices that are set to be shared from the VirtualHere menu on the SteamLink will appear on the host PC.
On a side note, something is fishy here with the usage of the client.Where/who is this artificial barrier of seperation of the VirtualHere site version and the VirtualHere Steam version coming from?  Apparently they are identical minus some background licensing.  Do note that it seems that the version of VirtualHere from their website will not work with the SteamLink anymore.  The SteamLink is only licensed to share 3 devices.  On the VirtualHere website they offer a 3 device license and an unlimited license; however, you cannot change the server license on the Steam Link.
TL;DR;
Recommend if you have games where the controller should work, but due to the Steam Link's emulation method, it does not.  (Games where you can play them just find with a controller at the PC, but when plugging the controller into the Steam Link and trying to play remotely it doesn't respond)
Do not recommend otherwise because of the artificial paywall and some weird licensing going on.  Very weak on configuration and settings for the price.  See Controller Companion which has significantly greater customization, can be set to disabled being as In-App in Steam, has built in running on Startup, etc and its 2.99 USD.  I would also not recommend this if the Steam Controller is the device you are trying to fix via this software since it does not show up in the list of sharable devices in the Steam Link.

Great game with a robust combat system that utilises RPG mechanics very well.
The combat:
combat in this game is done in real time and does not require you to click the correct button prompted on screen a la' the witcher 1. This time combat is fluid and weighty. the use of signs is very slick too. turning a man into ice and then smashing him into tiny peices with your sword has never felt better.
Alchemy:
At first I thought "ah great a skill I will never use" but actually it's useful and adds a layer of depth to the game. wether it be buffs to the player or creating poisions it adds to the overall gameplay by giving you the oppitunity to use different tactics in combat.
The Story:

Where to begin...
OVERALL 8.5/10:
This game could have been a 9.5/10 or even a 10/10, if it weren't for MICROTRANSACTIONS.
This is a great game. Make no mistake, I LOVED IT. It satisfys the Tolkien lore well enough to be interesting, and it is an intriguing story if you remove the emotionless wall of Talion. The gameplay is a blast, and can be amazingly elegant at the most random of times. There can be a lot to do, and that is intimidating, but power through and it can pay off. If you see this on sale and are debating if you want to get it, stop debating and BUY, you will enjoy it.
PROS:
First and foremost, if you bought and enjoyed Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor, you will love Shadow of War. Everything is improved upon and there is much more content and fun to be had. The campaign is involving and interesting, keeping me, an avid Tolkien fan, on the edge of my seat at every reveal and cutscene. You will find there is a lot to do, recruiting orcs, sending them to kill eachother, or capturing castles always provides a good amount of fun. The combat is great, just as beautiful and kick♥♥♥♥♥as in Shadow of Mordor. A few new features make travelling the map less of a hassle which was a great design call. There are more custom orcs with great charecters, and new features like ambushes and revenge which can keep you on your feet at all times; as a quiet sunday stroll can turn into a battle for Mordor in about 3 nanoseconds. However, it can get tedious after a while I must admit. And you can finally customize your charecter! The gear you own will finally reflect on your person! You will find by the 4th castle the routine gets boring and there seems like there is too much to do at once. But this is a blessing as there are easily over double the gameplay hours in this game as opposed to the previous one. At around the 15-17 hour mark the game can get pretty boring, but after about 17 hours Act III kicks in and you begin to see all the pieces come together. I wont spoil anything, but if you can find a way to grind through the castles and fight your way through Mordor the payoff is huge.
CONS:
Anyway now onto why I gave it a 8.5/10. MICROTRANSACTIONS. For a game that prides itself on the customization and unique orcs designed to make you hate or love the orcs, having a system for randomly generating ghost orcs that you have no history with into the game totally ruined the game. You need to use those orcs becasue they can be at most times a lot better than the orcs you recruited doing your missions. The leveling system is a bit hectic and overwhelming, as with the gems that seem to just be an extra hassle for .10912093% damage bonuses for 5 minutes of forging. The game has not improved asthetically in any regard since Shadow of Mordor. It feels more or less like an expanssion in that same respect, as the engine doesn't seem any better, nor can it support more than 20 or so orcs at a time, which can be a real mood killer when taking a castle.

The second game is still a lot of fun despite being considerably harder than K&L: Dead Men - I was much frustrated having had to retry some scenes dosens of times (I finished K&L in 5.5 hours but K&L2 took 9, both at medium difficulty). Also, the first game had better story IMHO, but this one's is still better than any of Rainbow Six, Splinter Cell or Ghost Recon's.

Although Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days from IO Interactive has a distinct visual style, the other parts of the game never branch out in any interesting or different ways, and made worse by the shockingly brief 3-5 hour single-player campaign.
The best part of Dog Days is the visual style. The game is shot like you are looking through a handheld camera. Although you can turn on steady cam for anyone prone to motion sickness, the rest of the effects cannot be turned off. This is a welcome change. Most games allow you to turn off their effects, I appreciated that Dog Days had a vision and stuck too it with this game.
While the visual style is distinct, unfortunately the other parts of the game are not. It's a standard cover based third person shooter, the story did enough to keep me wanting to see how it played out, despite the fair amount of cliches, such as Kane talking about this being his last job, or one the characters literally saying "I'm too old for this".
The game is also incredibly short, it took me just under 4 hours to finish the single-player campaign on medium. Even though their is multiplayer, I was unable to find any ranked or player matches.
Ultimately Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days is a flawed game, the visual style is very unique, but goes to waste in a game that is not that much fun to play.

While the story is engaging several things prevented me from really enjoying witcher 2.
First off, the game was extremely unstable on my system.  I tried several of the fixes on the forums but nothing worked, just periodically the game crashed to desktop.  I experienced roughly 1-3 crashes per play session, so save often if you buy this game. My system is fairly midrange with 64 bit os 16 gb of ram and a gtx570.  It should have no issues with this game.
The games combat was riddled with problems.  First off you could defeat certain hard monsters by abusing elevation, or some monsters had a small area they would stay to, if you figured it out you can bug them out forcing them to run away and back allowing for cheap back stabs.  Boss fights while impressive, were often just pattern based and lead to just rolling out of the way at the right time. Combat was also largely trivial if you prepared yourself with potions and buffed your swords.  Some monsters you could just out damage making the fights boring
For an rpg i found gear progression to be lacking as well, if you upgraded at the beginning of each chapter you were fine.  To some that might be a joy, but by the end of the game i didn't feel powerful and i have come to expect that of rpgs.  Minor annoyance though.
Mini games of dice poker and arm wrestling seem tacked on but you should do them for the rewards.
Witcher's redeeming qualities are in it's graphical prowess and the strong story. If this game is on sale for $5 i recommend it, but at regular price i cannot.
TLDR;
Good
- the story
- graphics
- Geralt is a bamf that gets all the ladies
BAD:
- combat
- stability of game (frequent crashing to desktop)
- mini games lacked real depth
- progression of gear is shallow at best.
Full price do not recommend, sale price recommend

Its ok for a very high discount, but not really for € 10.-, let me explain why.
Its pretty uninspired and very short (3-4 hours), its one of the worst sequel of this generation, its very insulting. The story is almost non existent, many plotholes and the game is basically "OH SH*T duck shoot duck shoot". The gunplay is not that good and thats a huge problem because thats the only thing you do in this game. Enemys take way too many hits and its hard to hit them in a long distance. If they hit you, you mostly fall down and you have to get back up, in the meantime you are a very easy target and you die fairly fast in this game, especially if some guy sneaks up to you and shoots you in the back. The coversystem is also a joke, you get hit so many times anyway. The AI is actually pretty bad, some enemys just stand in the open or take in open places cover and civilians sometimes just act like nothing is going on and walk casually into your shooting sight. Some parts are so hard because the game throws so many enemys at you that you can barely survive and there are also stupid escort missions (ugh...), all this probably because to extend the game lengh, but in a bad way.
It almost seems like the devs put most of their effort into the Multiplayer that no one wanted and cared about in the first place and also into visuals, irritating mobilephone filming filter effects and the annoying as hell shaking cam and called it "immersion", but actually forgot to make the mouths of the characters move when they talk in gameplay (they did in the first one actually). It also seems like they cut allot of content and ideas out of this game because of time isssius and rushed it out of the doors, there are some huge areas where you just run through and its nothing going on there. The ending is one of the biggest middle fingers in gaming i have ever seen, when you thought the game is finally about to start, it just ends without warning and lefts you with some stupid porn music in the credits and you're like "huh? What, thats it? THATS IT?! WTF?!".
They probably thought the Multiplayer will hold this game up and thats why there was allot of focus there, but no one is playing that anymore and thats not what the original Kane and Lynch was about. It was about the two antiheroes, one a professional criminal with a dark past and one a psychopath with mental blackouts, in a cruel and tragic storyline against a powerfull criminal organisation, all inspired by movies like "Heat". But they threw everything that made the first game good out of the window (the good characters and what made them interesting, engaging storyline, different locations etc.) and desided to make one generic immersive shooter instead and reduced the gameplay just into "duck, shoot, duck, shoot" with a annoying shaking cam and ugly filter effects which just looks cool in trailers but doesn't feel good in the game.
Kane and Lynch 2 improved nothing as a sequel gameplay wise over the original and made actually some things worse and the first one wasn't actually that good in the first place, but still much better than this. Where are the teammates which i can give orders like in the first one? There is only Kane, but he doesn't seem to do much and i can't give him any orders. In the first one we had multiple teammates that can revive you with a adrenaline shot for a second chance, but you would die of an overdose if you get another injection immediately after you had one already or if your teammates dont make it to your position in time. The only downside of this is that your teammates can die too and you have to revive them in time as well, that can be really annoying if they go down in a position with allot of enemy fire, but this does mostly only happen in later levels. There was also a system where you can change weapons with your teammates and give them the ones you want. This could have been improved in the sequel, but they desided to drop all this entirely instead and if you go down, you're just dead now, no adrenaline shot, not be able to change weapons with kane and no orders. In the first one we had splitscreen co-op on PC, but they removed it in the sequel and made it console exclusive. Why?! There is no reason to remove this, i don't get it if developers do something like that, especially if it was in the first one. They also removed grenades and smoke grenades which you were be able to throw and also the ones from your enemys back as well, but now we have fire extinguisher and oil containers which we can throw and enemys can throw them too. Its a neat idea, but there is no reason to remove grenades completely anyway. In the first one we had unique locations like the streets of an american city, the bank, the prison, the tokio nightclub, the skyscraper, the streets of tokio and also havana. In the second one we got the slums of shanghai, a skyscraper with an office and the airport, thats it! It was a game that had HUGE potential because of its predecessor, but they screwed up almost across the board.

Natural Selection 2 is quite a good multiplayer shooter. It mixes elements of FPS along with RTS. The commander is in control of building and supplying the team with health packs, upgrades, and objectives, while the rest of your team makes it all come together. Its quite the thing to behold being the commander and barking orders to your team and watching them all fall in line, leading to victory. Communication is key, as well as skill from your team players. Playing the marines is quite fun, but the aliens is where the game gets really interesting. Fighting as them, or against them is where the game really shines. As a marine, you must always watch your back and listen carefully, for the aliens have the advantage of being able to hide in vents, climb on walls and ceilings, and hide pretty much wherever they can fit. Some of the more deadly evolutions of the aliens can be a pain to deal with. Seeing the infestation spead along the space station is pretty awesome. This game is something you truly must experience. The only thing i can say negative about this game is not enough people play it, which can change depending on how many of you listen to this review and buy this masterpiece.

What can I say? For it's price, this game is quite good. Especially if you picked it up during the Summer Sale, as I did.
The graphics are rather good, especially since the game is 300Mb in size or so. Unfortunately, there isn't much of a variety when it comes to enemy and level designs. Basically the levels are sealed arenas like the Bloody Palace mode in Devil May Cry games.
The soundtrack is ok, but it has only 3 songs and they get quite repetitive. After two hours I just switched the music off and went to my Metal Gear Risng and Devil May Cry soundtrack folders.
Gameplay and controls... controls are quite responsive and fast, you won't feel some sloppy reactions to your inputs. The gameplay is rather repetitve. No, you have different moves and techniques like blocking at the last moment to block a very powerful attack (similar to Royal Guard style from DMC3), different cancels, launcher attacks, dodges, but after finding a combo that is most effective for your playing style it all becomes quite repetitve.
All in all... it feels incomplete, like a tech demo. It's fun, don't get me wrong, but I would love to see these gameplay mechanics to be expanded in a more "complete" character action game.
Oh, and it can get quite difficult at times, especially on the final boss. Also, don't start at Hard mode, it exists as a NG+ type of mode, when you really need your upgraded skills.

Acts I-III are pheonomenal. The grind to get to the end of Act IV is behind a soft pay wall. With the equipment I have from finishing Act III and obtaining all the collectables, I have 10 legendaries and a +28% XP boost (from Gems and registering my email address). Ive put at about 5 hrs on Act IV and I am only level 44 from finishing the game at lvl 42 (max is 60). The grind without paying for XP boosts is UNBEARABLE.
Again, this is only to get through ACT IV. The rest of the game is pure AAA goodness. BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE. There are several small bugs in essential systems.
For example, the stealth targeting system. 90% of the time, You will attack the target that is highlighted in red. The other 10% you are at the game's mercy. Needless to say, breaching stealth to kill a grunt instead of the captain that is suceptible to stealth (and immune to everything else) is an easy way to force a player to restart a mission or (even worse) retreat, despawn that captain, and track him down on the map again (holy waste of time). This problem never pops up when there is only one target to stealth kill, but against groups, this becomes a notable time waster.
Furthermore, the parkour mechanic also works 90% of the time. I would be running on what i thought was a straight path. I would hold W + Space (PC controls mind you) and suddenly, Talion dives to the left at an 80 degree angle. Again, This breaches stealth unecessarily (as you leap down from a rooftop straight towards the ground into a group of grunts with nothing to double jump to), but it is recoverable if you aren't facing off against multiple warchiefs. The game also traps you on certain platforms. It specifically traps you on either end of the long straight stretches of rope between roof tops (not the ones you can slide down, the ones you run on).
I would give this game an 9/10 if it ended after Act II. Up to this point it is similar to its predecessor. The difference is a new skill tree, more combat and stealth options, the nemesis system (which is great until Act IV because it becomes a grind), the Drakes, the story, and the maps to play on.
I was not disappointed until Act IV. All I can say is, I wish WB would've kept their dirty ♥♥♥♥ing microtransactions out of what coudl've been and amazing game through and through.

It does what it advertises.  I needed to force my Steam Link to send XInput to my PC instead of emulating keyboard/mouse.  VirtualHere for Steam Link enabled me to do so with ease.
: For some of my games, I use FreePIE to adapt gamepad input to the keyboard/mouse controls expected by the game.  FreePIE runs as a background process, while the actual game runs in the foreground and has focus.  I found that this mode of operation does not work well by default with Steam Link, mainly due to how the Link decides when to emulate keyboard/mouse ("Desktop mode") versus when to send gamepad XInput signals.  From what I understand, the problem is that the FreePIE window needs to have focus in order for the Link to send the gamepad XInput signal, but to give focus to FreePIE, your game loses focus and you can't play until you take away focus from FreePIE again.
: VirtualHere for Steam Link solved this problem for me.  As advertised,  VirtualHere made my PC think the controller was directly plugged in, but it was really plugged into the Link.  As a result, FreePIE was then receiving the XInput signals from my controller even though my game was full-screen in the foreground.
: I originally downloaded the free VirtualHere client from the VH website, but I wasn't able to get it working.  After some digging, I found that the free client apparently only works with earlier versions of the Steam Link firmware.  My Link is running version beta 518, which requires the "VirtualHere for Steam Link" version of the client.  It's disappointing that the free VH client does not work with the latest Steam Link firmware, but I also read that the Steam version supports up to three controllers (versus the free version supporting only one), so there is some benefit to this version.  It would be helpful if the product description included some sort of note officially declaring that "VirtualHere for Steam Link" is the only VirtualHere client that will work with the latest Steam Link firmware.
:Unfortunately, RockSmith seems to have some issues with the Steam Link and VirtualHere.  VirtualHere recognizes the RockSmith guitar cable, but for some reason the PC seems to just get garbage signal from the cable.  I couldn't tune the guitar in-game or even calibrate the cable.  Also, the game audio doesn't make it to my TV for some reason.  There might be solutions to these problems, but I haven't taken the time to try and find them.  My advice is don't expect VirtualHere/Steam Link and RockSmith to work together out of the box.

There are two main reasons I love this game, one is the storyline which involved numerous characters and locations, and lots of twists and surprises. It is also long. The story itself happens over a long list of areas, and sub quests will have you going back and forth between areas all the time, and each map can take up to a couple hours if you play like me and amass as big an army as you can before you head out.
Second is the actual gameplay of each area. Quite often the overall objective is to destroy the enemy base, or to get to something behind the base, but there will be things along the way like a graveyard off to the side with ghouls that will also attack your base, or a village under siege who will give you resources if you help them. Quite often you will find things you can interact with that you have no idea about only to later find the side quest that takes you there which lead to a lot of exclamations of, "So that's what that was for!"
Sometimes though you will get areas where you have to fight with just your main hero and rune heroes and the dynamic shifts considerably. Suddenly that one powerful healing mage who can aoe heal your army  and keep them going a bit longer, takes a bit more of a backstep and changes spells to join in the action himself with his weapon. I found these segments quite fun as going from the army building action to a map where you only had your heroes made it feel very much like you were an elite force behind enemy lines.
The animation doesn't look too bad and my only gripe with the voice acting is that there is only one voice for each gender. But that is a small gripe as i can see why there is only one when there is so much dialogue throughout the story. I haven't done much multiplayer (mostly because I haven't found someone to go do it with since I don't like randoms) but what I have done has been great.
Overall, Spellforce is probably my favorite RTS because it isn't just an RTS, and it uses the blended elements really well.

I really wanted to love this game. I generally adore turn-based, squad level strategy games. This one has a lot going for it, but it has a handful of issues which are just crippling.
First, the camera controls are abyssmal. In this day and age of camera freedom in most games, having such wonky controls is a step backwards. The camera never stays put and constantly resets itself any time you do anything. It's just frustrating to have to constantly readjust the camera because it decided to snap back to some awkward position.
Second, the player character models are terrible, low quality and with pretty lousy customization options.
Third, the character skill system is just really lacking, "Toaster Repair" being the prime example. Why on earth would they make something out of place? Of all the different capabilites, I have to spend points in a niche skill in order to repair a smattering of toasters laying around for rewards that really aren't worth the expense. Why? Just take that whole thing out. It just doesn't fit and makes no sense from both a gameplay or story perspective. It's ridiculous just for the sake of being ridiculous.
The combat is fun, but can be frustrating when you're stuck in combat and can't find why.
I really wanted to like this game. I've tried and tried, but I just can't get past the camera issues. It seems even worse with the "Director's Cut."

A sequel to a 2006's generic third person cover based shooter - Kane & Lynch: Dead Men. You'd have think, that after a failure that was the first instalment of Kane & Lynch, IO Interactive would carefully analyse all the feedback and adjust to it. Sadly this isn't a case. While K&L2 no longer uses GFWL and allows to play cooperatively over the internet (finally?), it still has all the flaws of the first game. Hell - it even has few more.
Firstly, Lynch's episodes of violent psychosis? No longer present in the game! It's kind of depressing that IO basically killed the most interesting (although, certainly - not positive) aspect of Lynch.
What is also a step back, comparing to original is the music. Jesper Kyd - the composer behind music to Assassin's Creed, Hitman series and many others... no longer present in here. And sadly - a music of a new composer - Mona Mur doesn't really work. It isn't bad - it's just so easily forgettable.
Forgettable is also a word, that describes storyline of Kane & Lynch 2. After the first level, everything is based around the same idea - you trying to escape from Shanghai. It's "OMG, we have to get out of Shanghai... Lynch, let's get your girlfriend and then we go" (*level later*) "Plan failed... it's all your fault, Kane... she's dead... you've destroyed my life (blahblahblah) let's get out of Shanghai". How does it end?
Whole storyline takes around 3-5hrs to complete, which is just a terrible length for a game, where singleplayer is focal point of the game. There is a multiplayer and you can play the game in COOP. Problem is - I was never able to find anyone playing anything except COOP. And while playing a game in COOP certainly helps - it doesn't even add much replayablity (at least nowhere near as much as COOP in most of shooters).
What kills the game however is its gameplay mechanics and terrible visuals. I get the difference between aesthetics and graphics and I do understand importance of artistic vision. And to some extend I do admire it's interesting visual style. Problem is - all of the post-processing effects get in the way of gameplay. With all the intense lens-flare effects, noise, color correction etc. not only spotting enemies becomes difficult. It's hard to aim and shoot. And when you disable them - you are left with nothing but highly outdated graphics, that look like something from 2003 (although - aesthetically, Unreal Tournament 2003 still looked better than K&L2)
Shooting in K&L2 lacks impact and isn't satisfying. Combine that with a glitchy cover mechanics and you have 2 main reasons why K&L2 fails to be an enjoyable shooter. What makes the cover mechanics even worse is something what should have worked in game's favour - destructible environment. Destructible environment sounds cool, but sadly, you are the one that dies more often, because of it. And while games like BFBC2 or even Red Faction were able to make it work in their favor, in K&L2 it's just another frustrating feature.
Bottom line: Kane & Lynch 2 is a bad third person cover based shooter, that fails to provide entertaining experience. Avoid it, if you're planning on playing alone. It can be a bit of fun while playing COOP, but in that case - I recommend picking up Rainbow Six Vegas - it's at least equally as long, has higher replayablity, looks better, has better level design... hell, it even costs less!

Terms like "nice", "amazing", "awesome" or "wonderful" don't quite cover it.
This game, for me, is perfection in its genre. An extremely high quality sidescroller beat-em-up/RPG. It features very well drawn character animation in a somewhat "furry"-styled setting (people are semblances to rabbits, cats, bears mice and the like) which is a matter of taste, I, for one, don't mind it too much. The combat style, which isn't by far as annoying as I was afraid it would be, is easy to pick up and use. It allows for quick advancement through enemy encounters and doesn't slow gameplay down, which is something rarely ever seen (very very nice). The game also features a bunch of sidequests the player can take from several NPCs throughout the game (actually it's kind of necessary to do them in some cases), aswell as a lot of small secrets and puzzles. Since the player will learn different new skills through the course of the game (one even right in the final area of the game) some secrets and puzzles will only be possible to solve much later. Along with all that, there's some other incredibly  awesome gimmick. Hidden in the game are 12 caged characters from different other  Indie-titles (e.g. Super-Meatboy, Gomez from Fez, The Kid from Bastion etc.) which, when freed, will grant a permanent health bonus to the character (quite fun).
Now... don't get me started about the audio part...
...
Alright I got myself started about it, but I'll try to keep it short: the voiceover is very well made, voice actors sound believable and there's almost no dialogues that sound anywhere near "artificial" (you might sometimes be told in character that you should press this or that button to do something). There is a downside however, even though it's very well translated, except for a few minor mistakes in the german language version, there's no translated audio. Though subtitles are well readable and there's a selectable option to advance dialogue manually.
The soundtrack is awesomeness-incarnate. People who know me a bit know what a sucker for good soundtracks I am, and this game's is just top notch, from start to end.
Okay... what else to say? The game is rather funny but the story is nonetheless quite high quality aswell. There's a lot of funny references to other games, like for example, the shady merchant who seems to follow the hero around ... "Aaahh, I'll buy it at a hiiigh price!" ... (In case you don't know that's the much famed merchant from Resident Evil 4)
Anyway, I can seriously recommend this game, it's an Indie-Jewel. Suited for ages from I'd say maybe 12 upward...? Not sure to be honest there IS some undead (non bloody) and some mild spooky stuff involved anyway ;-P

I really wish I could reccomend this game, but I can't. I know lots of people harp on the game for shoving in loot boxes and having the last part of the game be so tedious in order to squeeze money out of people, but I feel there's more to it than that.
Maybe it's how any of the characters that aren't orcs are so boring, they make watching paint dry an exhilerating experience.
Maybe it's how the story tries to cram itself into the Lord of the Rings story so much, it's practicaly lore-breaking (ps, haven't watched any of the films/ read the books).
Maybe it's how frustrating the level design is and how it feels like a hassel to get from point A to point B.
Maybe it's how all the upgrades are pointless once you find the ones you want, and it's just there so you can get better loot and orcs.
Or maybe it's how you can no longer dominate an entire area of orcs, leave for an hour, and come back to see the area is still populated with your orcs.
The nemesis system is still fine in the game. In fact, it's even more interesting. Plus, the game is more challenging. However, the good things in this game can't overshadow the flaws, and I end up feeling that something just isn't right with the game.
All in all, if you want a more in-depth Nemesis system and a challenge, this game is okay. Otherwise, I can't seem to reccomend this game.

Hotline Miami is a top-down action game/shooter made to represent the retro style of the 1980's.
Complete with heart racing, fast-paced gameplay and heart pumping music, you play as an unnamed man who recieves a Rooster mask in a package and cryptic messages from his answering machine that lead him to buildings chalk-full of russian mobsters. Your goal is to clear each level of all life and return to your car as quick as you can. At first glance you'll think that this game is extremely violent, and you'd be right. But Hotline Miami does not brag about it's over-the-top violence. The story of the universe is hard to follow and all-in-all confusing, and told out of order. though that adds another psychedelic layer to an already interesting and fun concept that no other game could replicate.
Pros:
Great gameplay
Amazing OST
Great level design
Difficult (Some would think of this as a con, but I'm somone who enjoys a challenge)
Achievements
Awesome art style
A ton of replay value
Cons:
Buggy A.I. (Sometimes whip around and kill you faster than you can swing/shoot your weapon)
Confusing story
Short
All and all I'd say this game is about a 9/10 for me, and is definetly worth the asking price of $9.99, but it never hurts to save some cash. But now I have one question for you. Do you like hurting other people?

In a nutshell, this is the game that fallout 3 should have been.
If you liked the classic Fallout games then this is for you. You get the open world and story from Fallout 1 and 2 with the squad based combat from Fallout Tactics. I have 45 hours in Wasteland 2: Director's Cut. Steam doesn't allow reviews from that version of the game for some reason so that is why my time in this is so low. Anyway, onto the review.
Wasteland 2 is a solid game. There is no denying that fact. It scratches the itch of old CRPG's within the tactical genre and it does a lot well. It just does not manage to grab me in the same way other games within the genre do.
Good:
+ Solid storyline
+ Great individual character skill, perk and attribute customisation
+ Great combat
+ Interesting characters
Bad:
- Poor visual character customisation
- Very little actual "role playing" elements
- Massive variation in character build quality
The game is strongest in developing and enhancing the abilities and equipment of your squad and putting your efforts into practise during combat. The problem with this is that they're weapon types in the game that are almost not worth using. The reason for this is simply becuase they are outmatched by the stronger weapon types in the game. The same is true for the character skills in the game and this is my biggest problem with the game. You will realise around 10 hours in that some skills are worth more than others and a broad range of skills within a party is more effective than a highly specialised party. This is fine, it just takes some of the role playing out of the game when compared to Fallout 1 and 2 or other games in the genre where they're often alternative methods for completing objectives in a desired fashion. Whereas here they're instances whereby you need certain skills to simply progress forward. The same is true when you compare the damage and overall functionality of an energy weapon, heavy weapon or a handgun to an assault or sniper rifle. The game therefore artifically begins to pigeon-hole you into creating certain builds in order to make a character or the party in general to be effective.
It is almost important to note that if you haven't played a CRPG like this before then you can get truly lost and/or stuck. You may need to use a guide in order to find your way around but this is relatively minor. What I will point out though is that the game can simply gimp you for picking certain followers as I found out in the final battle. Without spoiling anything some followers of mine were rendered useless during that fight with very little foreshadowing or warning of it occuring beforehand. There also seems to be very little choice in how your characters directly handle storyline events or in side quests. You will invariably be forced into a fight at some point to complete a quest and the game rarely deviates from that formula.
Is it a bad purchase or is it worth the time to play it? I think that is more of a personal decision depending on what you have personally played. If you haven't played the classics like Fallout 1 and 2, Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment or more recent examples like Pillars of Eternity or the Shadowrun franchise then I would suggest playing them first since I would consider them better games. If you have played CRPG's before and you want something familiar but don't mind using the "optimal" weapons and skills then this is a good game for those players. Otherwise I would look elsewhere for your CRPG itch.

A bit Castlevania, a bit Devil May Cry, a bit Secret of Mana. This game takes cues from good games old and new and combines them with modern sensibilities and original design to create something great.
Beautiful visuals and memorable characters punctuate a touching story of a character with a conflicted origin, crossing both tragedy and epic heroism as the protagonist of the story, Dust, crafts his true destiny. Dust starts with little more than a vague recollection of times long past and quickly finds himself in a position to help those in need, and through his travels learns of dark deeds that have sunk the land into an oppressive sorrow, as well as his role in this situation, both past and present. Many would turn a blind eye or side with those who hold power, but there's something different about this one...
It's well worth the paltry price being asked, if you enjoy broad gamplay and exploration. A combo system that allows you to juggle entire spawns of enemies and fly around like a madman, as well as tag team attacks allowing you to amp up your signature attack and become a human lightning rod, are combined with an action RPG leveling system and metroidvania exploration. Beatiful hand painted levels beg you to explore them and find every little hidden secret, with a surprising level of detail hidden around every corner.

First let me say The Witcher 2 is an incredible game that should not be missed by any fan of the RPG genre. The goods are as follows
-Great combat that combines magic, swordplay, and crafting very effectively
-Excellent story that's well written
-Good voice acting
The cons are as follows
-Bad map system. I found myself many times getting lost and in some way either on top of the objective marker or below it. Being a long game in the first place wasting time navigating the bad map was a bit of a disappointment.
-Not enough loot to really feel rewarded from combat
-There was a lack of accomplishment upon leveling up. This is due to the fact that the leveling system never really shows you where you are in level so your leveling is out of sight and out of mind. Although this isn't a huge drawback, it does subdue the desire to reach level cap
Overall I would highly recommend this game to anyone, especially with the witcher 3: the wild hunt coming up as well as the low cost during steam sales.

Hotline Miami is a top-down action game/shooter made to represent the retro style of the 1980's.
Complete with heart racing, fast-paced gameplay and heart pumping music, you play as an unnamed man who recieves a Rooster mask in a package and cryptic messages from his answering machine that lead him to buildings chalk-full of russian mobsters. Your goal is to clear each level of all life and return to your car as quick as you can. At first glance you'll think that this game is extremely violent, and you'd be right. But Hotline Miami does not brag about it's over-the-top violence. The story of the universe is hard to follow and all-in-all confusing, and told out of order. though that adds another psychedelic layer to an already interesting and fun concept that no other game could replicate.
Pros:
Great gameplay
Amazing OST
Great level design
Difficult (Some would think of this as a con, but I'm somone who enjoys a challenge)
Achievements

Cons:
Buggy A.I. (Sometimes whip around and kill you faster than you can swing/shoot your weapon)
Confusing story
Short
All and all I'd say this game is about a 9/10 for me, and is definetly worth the asking price of $9.99, but it never hurts to save some cash. But now I have one question for you. Do you like hurting other people?

I have now completed the game and overall it was alright. It could have actually be great if developers made more focus on the main quest line and would bother to polish the PC port.
Lows:
- You need to complete majority of side missions to progress with the story.
- No hesists or robberies, just kill-kill-kill.
- All side missions are nearly identical: confront (kill or interrogate) someone or destroy stuff.
- You get good weapons way too early in the game, meaning you stick with them to the end.
- Lock breaking mechanism is overly simplified.
- Cannot skip pre-racket dialogues.
- Cannot modify cars.
- Police does not care of you speeding.
- It rains way too often.
- Night and day cycle is poorly performed - dawns and sunsets nearly blind you.
- I have not experienced any crashes or major bugs, bu there were plenty of small lags for the game of this level.
- Same price as GTA-5... that is about as much they have in common.
Highs:
+ You can actually play stealthy or go full Rembo in most of the missions.
+ Stealth gameplay is interesting, but nothing even remotely close to Hitman series.
+ Main story missions (once they get unlocked) are exciting and fun.
+ Good game if you want to have a casual session.
+ Main characters are thought through.
+ Music selection is good.
+ Cut scene visuals are good - characters actually use their facial muscles.
+ Clear ending: you are not left wondering of what happens next.

Spellforce does a good job of combining RTS with RPG.
RPG elements: First you start off with a low-level hero of your choice. You can be almost everything: form a simple sword fighting warrior to a mage using various spells to destroy his enemies.
Every class, like in almost every RPG, requires a different style of play and if you cannot decide which class you prefer you can combinate them.
From the start you always have a main quest active which guides you through the story and to the next map. But it is always worth it to leave the main path and look for some side quests which reward you with additional EXP and sometimes with a pretty neat item.
Now to the RTS elements of the game: On almost every map you face a hord of enemies your hero cannot deal with alone. So, you can summon workers at monuments of various tribes (humans, elves, orc, etc.) to gather ressources, build a base and produce units to help you in battle. Every tribe has its own buildings and units, therefore the gameplay with each tribe is slightly different.
On some maps you can summon up to 5 heros, who can be equiped with items. You can control this heros like your main character. So, instead of building up a whole base you play through the map with just a small group of heros.
If it comes to a big battle, you quickly lose track of some units (e.g. you heros). For these situations there is a bar at the top of the screen where you can see all important informations and available spells of your heros and get the current position. For different perspectives you can zoom in or out and rotate the map. There is also the possibility to control your hero individually in third-person perspective and via WASD-keys, which is nice to immerse more into the well designed world. But most of the time there is no advantage of this view.
What I really like aobut the  game: The variety of how to skill your hero is enormous. As I already mentioned: Everything is possible from a sword swinging strong warrior to a mighty spellcasting wizard. First I played the game with a combination of healer and heavy tank which worked out quite well. My second char was a complete black mage that could be easily killed in close combat, but the enemies had a hard time reaching it.
Furthermore, the design of the many different maps is well done. Each map got its own charm and it never got boring.
What I do not like about the game: Some maps are pretty hard to beat because of huge amounts of enemies that are so strong you can only kill them by luring them away from a group and kill them one by one. That takes a lot of time and can be very frustrating, because you have a constant feeling that your character is too low leveled, although you already have done every possible sidequest and gathering a good amount of EXP at an enemy spawnpoint takes ages.
Conclusion:
Spellforce is a nice combination of RPG and RTS. The urge to level my hero and to loot more and more items got me at the very first minute. Whenever I got to play with a new tribe I was curious of finding out what its advantages and disadvantages are. The story is nothing special, but it is well told. The design of the maps and units is rich in variety, so you always get something new to see. And if you bring enough time and patience to sit through a hard time completing a map, I would recommend this game.

Spellforce is a Real Time Strategy/RPG hybrid, and a great one at that. If you can get past the initial weirdness and clunkiness of the game, you are in for a wild ride.
First of all, the gameplay feels pretty unique, considering that this type of hybrid game hasn't been done too often. You get your main character who you can skill and develop in a multitude of ways, some, admittedly, more fun and effective than others, and you get the base-building portion. There are six races you play through over the course of the story, all of them fun to play as in their own way. You don't get to choose which race you play at which point in time though, the campaign is a bit rigid in that aspect. No biggie though.
While we are at the story, it's nothing too special. It's good. But the game is long.
Holy HELL is it long. I mean, you can easily spend upwards of 40-50 hours on a single campaign if you haven't played the game before, and it comes with two expansions, which are at least 30 hours long. Each.
Atmospherically speaking, the game has a lot to offer in my opinion. The maps look and feel great, and the soundtrack is AMAZING.
And then there is the so-called "Click and Fight-System". It's a really simple thing that makes so much sense and it absolute baffles me that it hasn't become a standard for RTS games. Instead of just issuing orders by clicking the unit and then clicking the enemy, you can instead click the enemy and it shows you all possible actions your friendly units can do to it. It's hard to explain without pictures, but if you play and see it, you'll know what I mean. It's efficient, it's intuitive, it's really damn smart.
The game definitely has some flaws though. It's pretty old by now so the graphics are dated, even though I personally have no problem with that. It has no widescreen support, and forcing it makes the UI weird, so my recommendation is windowed mode.
Another flaw is that the game is a bit minimalistic on giving you information and stats about enemies, units and yourself. You get a non-numbered health bar, a non-numbered mana bar, a very brief description of the spells you have, but that's pretty much it. There is no way to know how much armor ANYONE except you has, there is no way to know how much damage one unit will deal to another without trying it out, you don't know anything about the damage, range, duration, effect etc. about the spells you, a friendly unit or an enemy uses, and so on. The best you get is a number above a unit's head that shows how much damage it took.
If you can deal with that, you're pretty much set. This is a true hidden gem and worth the money. If you see it on sale, consider buying it.

Overall a great game, it plays very much like Fallout 1 and Fallout 2. I played the orginal Wasteland on an Apple IIe, and this is much better.
This game has pretty much everything to be a sucess.
Build your own party - check, Tactical combat - check, RPG elements - Check, Attractive graphics - Check, Good sound and voices - Check, Ability to customize weapons - Check, Decent inventory management - Check.
The game has an interesting mix of mission types. Some of the missions were pretty straight forward, and others turned out to be a bit difficult. At first I was not happy about having to choose which community to save and which to sacrifice, but as I played the game more I realized that it often put you in situations where you simply did not have the resources or knowledge to do everything perfectly, or pick the "best" outcome.
You are a Desert Ranger. You encounter situations, and try your best. Everybody may not like the outcome, but you are the one playing the role of peacekeeper. Do your best and carry on!
My one small complaint:
Why does there need to be a delay when using a skill? It does not add anything to the game for me to watch an "hourglass" while someone picks a lock, or disarms a trap. The only time it might be "fun" is when a party member is bleeding out, and the medic just can't stop the bleeding fast enough. That would be a pretty terrible use of the delay though.
Don't read much into the negative reviews, most stem from a recent free weekend. If it is not your type of game, I applaud you for giving it a try, but do you need to bash it?

While it may be not enough content for some, you can get a lot of playing time out of this little gem (try crossing the sea on a raft, I dare you - you haven't really played the game until you try that and fail miserably). More than anything, I made up my mind after reading the developer's responses to people posting suggestions, questions and even complaints.
The Victorian Clambake website proved a very interesting read. For such a young developer (both in age and experience concerning game development) to show that level of maturity to tackle a project is quite impressive.
Add to that the fact that he will keep on adding more content in the near future (and no, we are not talking DLCs, we are talking more content - period) and improving the game. I have rarely seen a dev react to and interact with players as much.
The game itself brought back some good old memories from my younger days when I used to play on a Commodore 64. The Caribbean Sail managed to invoke that level of imagination and joy. When I misclicked after fishing some much-needed provisions and accidently misfired my very last harpoon in the middle of the ocean on a tiny raft, I wasn't mad that the "Exit" button in the bottom should be more prominent to avoid such mishaps. Neither was I mad at myself. Instead I imagined my harpoonist mishandling the tool (just as I did with the mouse) and cursed his butter fingers. I was even thinking of a proper punishment or suggesting to the dev that we should have the option to eat crew members. (After some deliberation I decided I wouldn't want to go down that road. :P)
It was then that I realised I was really enjoying myself while playing such a minimalistic game, simply because it managed to do what so many others don't: It touched that little boy inside of me with his crazy imagination. And he will go on many more sailing trips across the ocean.

If ever there were a time to recommend Kane & Lynch 2, now would be that time.
With the sudden glut of shooters focused on characters going mad, the darkness of the average video-game player-character, and what I see as the start of unique artistic approaches to games (see: Routine, Tangiers, etc), it should be clear that this game was well before its time.
It was critically derided, despite being Spec Ops: The Line's nasty older brother. The censored headshots turn a stomach far faster than the gory over the top madness of any other game that comes to mind. The visual style is bright, eyepopping, unique, will never be seen again due to gamers not being ready for the game when it was released.
This game is worth a playthrough if you want to taste blood, smell sweat, hate yourself. That is in no way a point against it as a game -- it is uniquely visceral, and we will have a hard time seeing another game willing to go so far until the critical backlash from it is forgotten.

Hotline Miami is a top-down action game/shooter made to represent the retro style of the 1980's.
Complete with heart racing, fast-paced gameplay and heart pumping music, you play as an unnamed man who recieves a Rooster mask in a package and cryptic messages from his answering machine that lead him to buildings chalk-full of russian mobsters. Your goal is to clear each level of all life and return to your car as quick as you can. At first glance you'll think that this game is extremely violent, and you'd be right. But Hotline Miami does not brag about it's over-the-top violence. The story of the universe is hard to follow and all-in-all confusing, and told out of order. though that adds another psychedelic layer to an already interesting and fun concept that no other game could replicate.

NS2 is a tactical fps. In order for your team to do well, you have to go out and

Fallout Shelter is a click game simulator where you are the controller of a Vault-Tec Vault. At the start of the game, you are randomly assigned a number from 000 to 999. The number you receive will the vault ID and will determine the attributes of your Vault, similar to the lore in Fallout.
The goal of the game is to grow your vault and keep your population happy. To grow your population, you need to increase the space in the vault, grow more living quarters and feed them. You feed your dwellers and keep them happy by maintaining Food, Water and Power supplies. To maintain the supplies, you need to build Diners, Water Generators and Power Generators, man them and click on them to collect the resources (just like Farmville).
As your population grows, you can unlock other facilities such as the Storage Room, Medbay, Science Lab, Overseer's Office, Radio Studio, Weapon Workshop, Weight Room, Athletics Room, Armory, Classroom, Outfit Workshop, Fitness Room, Lounge Theme Workshop, Game Room, Barbershop, Nuclear Reactor, Garden, Water Purification, Nuka Cola Bottler. As you complete objectives, the game will reward you with lunchboxes which is basically a bundle of Caps, Item Cards and other equipment.
Conclusion, it's just another P2W click simulator. Best price is $150 for 1000 Nuka Cola. You can safely ignore Fallout Shelter without missing out on anything.
Note: I am surprised that Bethesda Games would fall prey to the P2W business model.
1. Simple to Pick Up
It's easy to learn and you can just pick the dwellers and hover over the respective rooms to see if it's a + or -.
1. Pay To Win
The grind currency are Bottle Caps and the cash currency is Nuka Cola. 1000 Nuka Cola for $150.
2. Click Farm Simulator
No auto collection. Remember to log in to click-farm.
3. Can't Remodel
Want to demolish a specific room? It can't be connected to 2 adjoining rooms, otherwise you're screwed.
4. Caps?
Seriously, caps to build a room. I mean, there's a limit that the imagination can stretch to.

I'll try and keep it short and simple.
Single player: The game has a more than usual initial learning curve and at first you'll hate it but once you get use to everything it's quite easy. It would be easy to just give up with it but I recommend you at least give a day or two to get familiar with how the truck mechanics work. The game is very slow paced and you'll be getting stuck in the mud a lot. Only the two 8 wheeled vehicles are any good at carrying medium to heavy loads on muddy terrain.
Game objectives are to bring lumber to saw houses. A map can have 1 or more. Optional tasks are unlocking extra vehicles, opening garages and doing fuel runs.
Multi-player: I recommend you play SP first before attempting MP for a better experience. At first I wasn't interested in trying it but it turned out to be much more fun than playing SP. The game plays the same as SP only you now have up to 3 players to help  you complete the objectives. Someone can open the garages, someone can do fuel and everyone else do lumber.
At the time of writing the game has taken a turn for the worst with a recent update. MP was very much stable before but now has a whole host of issues from truck collision problems to game crashes. Right now it's practically unplayable. This may obviously be fixed but that's yet to be known.
The lobby system is quite poor. You'll spend 15 minutes trying to find a decent game unless you already have others to play with. Connection problems are rife with games being hosted from home connections rather than dedicated servers. Lots of connection time outs and players generally being incompetent at hosting games. However, if you're lucky to enough to get a good game with good players then it's a fun experience.
I'll feel bad giving it a bad review just for the poor MP as SP alone makes it worth it.

Doing some reviews today and wanted to add my "positive" voice to this.      As has been said many times it's the spiritual successor to Fallout 1 and 2.   It retains the top down, tactical approach to gaming that old school fans of fallout remember.
But let's be fair, this isn't fallout and so judge it accordingly.
It's a modern version of the top down RPG.   Like the old D&D Goldbox games or Baulders Gate, you create a team to tackle an unknown threat to Arizona.      It does retain the open world quality and your choices on who you help do have consequences in "the end" (wink wink).
While I will recommend this game, I do acknowledge there's something of a feeling of it could or should be more.   That may have more to do with the kickstarter funds available and just how much game you can make for a given budget.
Still, as you can see by the hours spent on this game (roughly 200) there's plenty of stuff to do to get your money's worth.
One nice thing is that you do have options.    For example, hacking enemy robots to gain a numbers advantage for your team.   Or you can play your conversations Hard♥♥♥♥♥ or Smart♥♥♥♥♥      Of course witha 4+ many team, you can have enough character builds to try out all these options while still having a unique characters compared to something like Fallout 4 where you level up so much that you basically create a person with "every" option and they cease to be unique at all.
Personally I enjoy the idea of playing sides against each other and squeeking out those unique "perfect" resolutions if you're willing to try (and retry) all the options.   Based on that, I felt some pangs of dissapointment when it appeared the game design intentially forced me to choose one or the other even though "both" options were clearly visible and should have been an executible choice.
Visually it was passable.   It would definately been nice to have more unique artwork, or skipped that completely for more player face/body models.    Again it feels like going back to the 80's when the D&D games would reuse the same visual art work to represent mutliple people.      It's a minor criticism but one of those things that helps to pull you out of the experience.
All in all, if you like top down, tactical, RPG gaming with consequences for your actions, and you have 20 bucks (summer sale) give it a try.
Hopefully InXile will have pulled together enough money from this first forey to do a more expanded, enriched world with another Wasteland title.    Kind of how Fallout 2 expanded beyond Fallout 1.

While a failure of overambition, and as a result clearly rushed, it is still one of the better isometric RPG's of the past decade.
Its biggest failing, and it is one that is common in narrative RPG's which centers on an entire player created party instead of a single character, is that the story simply fails to draw you in.
You are just not given a reason to care about your characters as anything other than stat sheets, and as a result the entire world becomes less engaging.
The combat is, unfortunately, rather shallow and there is therefore entirely too much of it.
Far too many areas are riddled with things to kill, and even the overland map has an abundance of random enemy encounters.
There is a good variety of enemies, but when your tactical options are limited to shoot, move or overwatch, that does not matter as much as it should.
Various classes do get a few special attacks at later levels, but it is not enough to add any actual depth to the combat. You never find yourself wondering what the best tactical option is beyond what enemy to focus on, or if you should use explosives (aoe).
On the positive side, there is a great deal of reactivity in the various quests you uncover and the world is populated by plenty of well written characters.
Overall the writing is pretty good, the world is interesting and the art work is excellent.
While perhaps not the "real fallout 3" its kickstarter backers where hoping for, it is still a great game and definetly worth a playthrough.

The Caribbean Sail is a single developer sailing adventure that pays homage to the days of the Oregon Trail games starting in the early 1970s. You exchange your covered wagon for a newly acquired ship (or raft) of your choice. So long dusty ol’ Willamette Valley and say hello to the Bahamas!
Akin to the very early installations of the Oregon Trail series, The Caribbean Sail harkens back to the day of pixelated graphics and text adventuring mixed with well-rounded animation where it counts. You’ll start your adventure at port and asked to create a crew of your choice and name them whatever you want, which is a nice touch. What I rather enjoyed was the length at which I could name someone; the game gave me more than enough room to do full blown titles and names, which was nice. It didn’t help “Quartermaster Sam” when he got struck by lightning and met his untimely demise, but that’s another story entirely.
Once you’ve acquired your crew you’ll be tasked with selecting from various ships (some of which you must unlock) and a profession that affects both your starting wages for resources and the special ability of your captain. At the time of this review you’ll have to figure out what those abilities are on your own, but that may change with added tool-tips that let you know for better preparation. Once you’ve established that, you’ll buy your goods, maybe gamble a bit with “Liars Dice” and set sail towards Nassau!
Here we take a familiar turn, sailing the waters will take you through a multitude of challenges, some conquered by skill, some by sheer dumb luck. You’ll encounter pirates to fight, trade ships to buy/sell goods, storms to weather and reefs to cross among others. The Caribbean Sail does have a few mini games sprinkled in to spice things up, which include both fishing and fighting pirate ships aside from the dice game at the beginning. The juxtaposition of both relaxing elements like fishing and the stress of resource management (especially spears) make it an enjoyable, albeit short adventure.
When I was asked to do this review, I spent some time doing a couple of playthoughs from beginning to end (or death) before deciding; an open mind like an open sea if you will. Games like these can be difficult in this day and age; the in-between mixture of a modern title, but with retro graphics and and old world mentor. Games like these aren’t for everyone and often serve a very niche audience. That notion isn’t necessarily bad, per se, but it’s something that should be heavily considered. In the end, I enjoyed my time with the game and look forward to more adventures at sea.


Overall, The Caribbean Sail is well rounded in both nostalgia and improvements without being utterly unrecognizable to its roots. If you’re looking for a game similar to the Oregon Trail series of the 1970s, you’ll find some love in The Caribbean Sail. However, those searching for more complex management systems (food, health.ect)in the realm of Oregon Trail II during the mid-1990s…well, you won’t find it here. While basic, The Caribbean Sail does what it does well and that’s what I think is the most important. In talking with the developer there are known areas of potential improvement but as it stands now the game does well on its own.
