"Kane & Lynch 2 is definitely worth playing, as it's unique in a way where brutality, violence and misery of the protoganists crosses the line over perhaps any video game out there. IO Interactive is not afraid to step over it. A tip: Play it coop-compaign with a buddy, it is something you will not, I repeat not forget".
As you may be aware Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days is the sequel to the infamous Kane and Lynch: Dead Men, a mediocre cover shooter by IO Interactive(Hitman<3), notorious for being so bad it got Jeff Gerstmann fired. Really, it's not THAT bad. I mean it's pretty bad but I'm pretty sure I like it better than the first Uncharted at least. And anyways it came pretty close to having an interesting narrative. It starred two awful, irredeemable people(and not in the Booker DeWitt way where they're still cool and doesn't afraid of anything), one of whom has an estranged daughter. Like a lot AAA games this generation with a focus on story, it kinda fell short of its potential. 2, though, is something special. It feels like a singular artistic vision rather than a design-by-committee Frankenstein.
Dog Days takes place several years after Dead Men. Lynch is now living in Shanghai with a woman named Xiu, and works for one of the local crime syndicates. He calls in Kane to help with an arms deal. The game follows the two for 48 hours starting when Kane arrives. The very first level involves Lynch taking Kane along on a small errand to "send a message" to someone who's apparently been talking too much. Things get out of hand, the man in question leads them on a chase, the girl he's with ends up taking a bullet. The man then slices his own throat. This seems bizarre now but it will become obvious why he did it in retrospect.
- The Michael Mann Connection: (Director; Heat, Public Enemies, Collateral):
Now Dead Men took a lot of notes from Michael Mann movies, particularly Heat and Collateral, and did its damnedest to imitate that style to a tee. Honestly it does a pretty great job at it, with the club section and the Tokyo streets level in particular evoking iconic scenes with skill. Dog Days follows in these footsteps, but in its own way. For the past ten years or so, Mann has been shooting on digital instead of film, and using hand-held camerawork more often than not. K&L2 takes this and cranks that mother up, making a kind of grainy found-footage look.
That said, while Dog Days may model itself after latter-day Mann's aesthetic, it has much more in common with his 90's classic Heat. The mondo rad DeNiro/Pacino joint is about two men who can't conform to a normal way of life. They seek the thrill of The Score at the expense of everything else, including their loved ones(notice how Pacino's scene with the mother at a crime scene is more emotionally powerful and wrenching than anything to do with his family). Kane and Lynch are two men trying to reconcile the fact that their only verb is kill.
Contains probably the best quote from a video game I've ever played.
GLAIZER: So how you like Shaghai, Kane?
KANE: It's ♥♥♥♥ed. I hate it.
Kane and Lynch 2 especially has some of the best atmosphere and use of style I've seen in a shooter. Shanghai looks beautiful, yet gritty underworld, this seedy urban nightmare I find really intoxicating.
Verdict:
A real underrated title. I like its solid/no frills shooting and the visuals/atmosphere is one of the best this gen. Voice acting is top notch. A unique game overlooked due to poor reviews and media journalism, give this a go, you'll be doing me a huge favor!

An almost perfect sandbox game, based on the Source Engine (HL²), allows some pretty crazy things to do: spawn objects and NPCs, glue objects together, give them rocket exhausts, drive vehicles, etc etc. The Workshop is simply a way to put a lot more things in the game than the base game had, the only limitation is your imagination.

Fallout Shelter is a click game simulator where you are the controller of a Vault-Tec Vault. At the start of the game, you are randomly assigned a number from 000 to 999. The number you receive will the vault ID and will determine the attributes of your Vault, similar to the lore in Fallout.
The goal of the game is to grow your vault and keep your population happy. To grow your population, you need to increase the space in the vault, grow more living quarters and feed them. You feed your dwellers and keep them happy by maintaining Food, Water and Power supplies. To maintain the supplies, you need to build Diners, Water Generators and Power Generators, man them and click on them to collect the resources (just like Farmville).
As your population grows, you can unlock other facilities such as the Storage Room, Medbay, Science Lab, Overseer's Office, Radio Studio, Weapon Workshop, Weight Room, Athletics Room, Armory, Classroom, Outfit Workshop, Fitness Room, Lounge Theme Workshop, Game Room, Barbershop, Nuclear Reactor, Garden, Water Purification, Nuka Cola Bottler. As you complete objectives, the game will reward you with lunchboxes which is basically a bundle of Caps, Item Cards and other equipment.
Conclusion, it's just another P2W click simulator. Best price is $150 for 1000 Nuka Cola. You can safely ignore Fallout Shelter without missing out on anything.
Note: I am surprised that Bethesda Games would fall prey to the P2W business model.
1. Simple to Pick Up
It's easy to learn and you can just pick the dwellers and hover over the respective rooms to see if it's a + or -.
1. Pay To Win
The grind currency are Bottle Caps and the cash currency is Nuka Cola. 1000 Nuka Cola for $150.
2. Click Farm Simulator
No auto collection. Remember to log in to click-farm.
3. Can't Remodel
Want to demolish a specific room? It can't be connected to 2 adjoining rooms, otherwise you're screwed.
4. Caps?
Seriously, caps to build a room. I mean, there's a limit that the imagination can stretch to.

Okay, this one is kind of weird. But rather fun and addictive. Best way I can think to describe it is if you took Diablo, added in your standard party based format from RPGs, then blended it with a RTS game. That's not exact. But it might give an idea. Sometimes you're controlling your character (maybe) via  3rd person camera and standard wasd movement controls. More often you're using an isometric top down view and clicking on where you want your character(s) to move to or what you want them to attack. And other times you're building a base camp, fortifying it against attackers, and then building an attack force like you're playing your favorite real time stratagy game.
The storyline so far is rather interesting. The controls are intuitive. If you've played any RTS games you're going to master the controls easily. And while the stratagies aren't very complex, mostly you're just building up a good sized attack force and steam rolling everything in your way, that's kind of true for most RTS games. There's very few in the genre where a stratagy beyond "create 30 of X type of unit then blitz the enemy" is needed.

Fallout 1 / 2 are my favourite games of all time. I was very hyped about W2 Kickstarter, but realistically didn't expect another masterpiece. So no, the negative review is not due high expectations, and not because not-like-in-Fallout, I understand it's a different game.
Beta was fun. For a beta. inXile were adding and changing stuff, so I was pretty exited about future release at that point. After the game come out I was actually enjoying it, forgiving obvious mistakes. After the news about 'Game of the Year' version (that later became 'Director's Cut', but who cares?) I decided to put aside the game for a while to wait the better version. Director's Cut was a step forward, but not enough. After 40 hours all the cons overwhelmed the pros and the game fell in the uncanny valley for me.
I finished only first part of the game, don't want to waste more time finishing the second part, since you can figure out the plot in first 4-5 hours.
These are just my thoughts of the game, are they pros of cons decide for yourself.
- Level design and camera controls are miserable.
- A lot of time you'll spend just running around badly designed levels.
- RPG system is ok for me, however a lot of people fairly complain about it, it's just I'm not so much hardcore about it.
- Plot is generic copy of Wasteland 1 plot.
- Skillchecks take awfully long time.
- Too much dull filler content.
- Art direction is bad. I mean there's not much of art direction in this game, it's just a mess (Director's Cut looks better, but still meh). Some portraits look ok, you can find couple of levels that look ok, but that's it. I would forgive if it would be gameplay-oriented graphics, but no, in this game graphics actually hurts gameplay. Pieces of Andrée Wallin look good, but you can find them in his online portfolio.
- The game is generally unbalanced, but I'm ok with that in a single-player game.
- A lot of people complain about bugs. I didn't encounter anything game-breaking. After all, it's easier to fix bugs than gameplay issues.
- Some dialogues are fun, but most of the dialogues are just NPCs repeating the same info. Imagine reading the wiki-style lore over and over again.
- My English is bad, so I can't say anything about writing quality.
- Only one town in the first part was somehow interesting.
- Even Wasteland 1 world felt more alive. This world is filled with random loot and stuff to shoot at.
- Combat is fun for 10-15 hours.
- Music is good. If you are into ambient with industrial tones, you can buy it on Bandcamp, no need to buy the whole game for it. Now I'm trying to disassociate soundtrack with memories of the game because they spoil it.
- Radio transmissions definitely add interesting vibe. Probably my favourite part of this game.
- Exploring the map gives mixed feelings. At one hand you can receive new radio transmissions and even some fun cache (no spoils), but overall, there's not much to explore.
- You can wear a backpack.
- GUI and inventory icons look nice for me. But do you care?
- You can find fun items like waterchip or 'Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?' book. Obviously, it's a shameless fun-service.
- Controller support is mediocre. Mostly because it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to avoid all these mine fields.
- Mines. Mines everywhere.
- Perks and traits (or how they call it in W2?) are not very inspiring. I remember one perk was interesting, but they nerfed it the first patch for Director's Cut.
- The game is vile at times, reminding B-movies.
I really feel how much effort and personality the team put into the game, but they ended up with a fan-made mod quality product.
The game is fun for 10-20 hours. After that time if you find yourself bored, drop it, it will not get better. If not the word 'Wasteland' in the title I would definitely drop the game after that time. Developers did the worst mistake you can do while making a video-game: they chose quantity over quality.
At least it's turn-based, not another FPS RPG.

Double Fine’s Broken Age may have been one of the early success stories for the Kickstarter-backed projects, but it didn’t live up to the expectations of a long-starved fan of the point-and-click adventure games such as myself. Admittedly, that wasn’t entirely its fault: it’s a good game with a great production value for its budget, but it doesn’t exactly stand tall among the all-time greats of the genre, either. Not an instant classic, but very charming, it offers an intriguing coming-of-age story, memorable characters, excellent writing, art and sound design, but the second act is sort of a drag.

(+) a heart-warming, disarmingly whimsical but fundamentally mature coming-of-age story divided into two acts and two distinct, seemingly unconnected subplots, each involving the game’s teenage protagonists, the boy Shay and the girl Vella, who try break the cycle and escape their allotted fates in both sci-fi and fantasy worlds
(+) a diverse cast of quirky characters to meet and interact with, including the overprotective ship computer Mom, cult leader and compulsive hoarder Father Lightbeard, cowardly hipster lumberjack Curtis, mysterious Marek, even an over-sensitive living tree and talking cutlery
(+) Tim Schafer’s writing strikes the perfect balance between adolescent humour and mature themes, with many a dirty and puerile quip, joke and gag sprinkled throughout the both intriguing and charming storyline
(+) full voice-acted, featuring such household names as Elijah Wood (Shay), Jack Black (Father Lightbeard) and Wil Wheaton (Curtis), with Masasa Moyo as Vella, the veteran Jennifer Hale as Mom and some other frequent Double Fine’s collaborators like Richard Horvitz, Nick Jameson or Nicki Rapp voicing the secondary characters
(+) the art direction resembling a 2D animated children’s storybook by the team under Lee Petty, based primarily on the digital water-colour paintings by LucasArts’ alumni Nathan Stapley with some initial concept arts by the masterful Peter Chan and Scott Campbell, brings the fantastical worlds and characters to life with vibrant colours and unique, aesthetically pleasing visual style
(+) the music composed by Peter McConnell, a mainstay of Double Fine’s games, performed by wind and string ensembles and the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, evokes a sense of wonder, a thrill of discovery and a high of unchecked tomfoolery
(+) both the sci-fi and fantasy settings are chuck-full of distinct locations to visit, characters to interact with, objects to manipulate and puzzles to solve, which encourages you to probe into every nook and cranny to get the full experience
(+) you can switch back and forth between Shay and Vella at any time, which makes for a welcome change of pace or a breather if you’re stuck on a particularly daunting puzzle with one of them, but isn’t exactly necessary because they can’t interact with each other like e.g. the three playable characters in
(+) the point-and-click controls utilizing primarily the two mouse buttons are simple enough to remember and operate even for a pre-schooler
(+) the clever puzzles require some deductive skills and abstract thinking, though, and a few of them a lot of patience (
), especially because the game leaves you pretty much to your own devices to figure out the solutions (which is fine by me)
(+) a hidden retro mode for nostalgia hipsters and blurry pixel art enthusiast alike ;-)
(+) full language support for English and German, with UI and subtitles in French, Italian, Spanish and Russian
(+) an episodic, but very extensive documentary by 2 Player Productions available on
is a nice bonus and gives a fascinating insight into the nitty-gritty of the entire development process
(+) a very good production value and a good value for money, considering its budget (the over 3,3 mln USD in Kickstarter backers’ pledges plus the revenue invested from the sales of Act 1 on Steam and the studio's own money redirected to finish the project)
(−) the second act is somewhat underwhelming: despite delivering an ultimately satisfying conclusion to the story, it basically rethreads the established locations and characters, requires a lot of backtracking and involves a noticeable spike in difficulty in comparison to the previous
(−) the annoying trial-and-error puzzles,
(−) not enough hand holding for novices (many objectives are pretty self-explanatory but there’s no hint system to help you out, no journal nor check-lists to keep track of your progress)
(−) occasional voiceover skipping
(−) the controls and menus have an evident touchscreen feel to them, which I don’t appreciate in my PC games
(−) no concept art gallery, a feature I’ve come to expect in Double Fine’s games
(−) the autosave feature stopped working properly once I loaded the game from a manual save and then an annoying pop-up kept asking me if I wanted to use this or that save spot for an autosave every time I loaded a game

When I say that the role-playing is W2's greatest feature, some might translate it as the story or mechanics are very shallow. That is a gross misunderstanding, so I feel the need to explain this praise in-depth.
The most remarkable aspect is not that there are so many options; it's that the developers trust you with all of them. The level of care put here can be seen when the game accounts for almost every action/consequence, and the team's flavor-text of cheeky, sardonic humor simply adds to the experience.
If that's too confusing, then know only this:
What may seem like the game leaving too much to the player it feels more like a father adding the rocket sound-effects and shaking of the cardboard box for his child. (Or in a less emotional context, the Dungeon Master who believes in the "Never say no" rule.)
The game provides as many solutions as possible. Whether it is handling factions with negotiations, violence or some other means. To making the best out of your team with their strengths and weaknesses. To wandering off from the main-quest at any point. (You can even end the game early.) To even how to bypass obstacles like doors, safes, or terminals. The result is that the game respects that you can handle it. And with the Director's Cut, this experience only has gotten better.
Quirks, a deceptively simple feature, does so much to characterize your cast by making in-game benefits and downsides. (And unlike in Fallout 1/2, you have four main-characters, so you can roll with the negative effects.) The UI for using skills is now simplified to a right-mouse click if you have your whole team selected. Precision strikes offer more tactical options in battle, and make your character's growth feel better when you can utilize them in the end-game with better odds.
All of these extra details will make creating squads just as much fun as playing the game itself. If you care only for min-maxing characters, however, then I think you're missing the point of the system.
Although there is no wrong way to build a character, there are several missteps you can make to make a bad team if you don't read your character sheets for the details. So a few pointers might be helpful.
If you know this info before going in, then I think the stats' screen will be less intimidating for newcomers and a friendly welcome mat in time.  While the story may not warrant replay value for more context, the content itself is worth replaying, even if you've seen the Wasteland once before--but in another time and space.
While many people too often criticize W2 for not being more like Fallout, there is a unique problem with the similarities between the Fallout universe and Wasteland timeline. Addressing the problem of "Who's on first" doesn't matter but what W2 doesn't take it into consideration is its identity problem.
W2 acts like the original in the 1990s wasn't scrapped and that Fallout never happened. Except it did, and it results in a feeling that you've seen everything already if you have played Fallout 1/2 (or New Vegas).
For example, many names come off as the Mad-Libs for Fallout staples:
-The DESERT RANGERS are a militaristic, militia-based army in Arizona that has territorial expansion in mind as they claim the Wastelands as a unified force.
-The Rangers took over the Citadel base of the GUARDIANS OF THE OLD WORLD, a xenophobic group that claims ownership over pre-war tech like power-armor.
-The MAD MONKS revere Titans (nuclear warheads) as religious beings/forces of power.
-Synths, Roboscorpions, Super Mutants, Mutant animals, a "not-New-Vegas" L.A and other not-Fallout staples appear in this game.
It's weird to call this issue out, but the first half of the game relies on these similar faces that I think many people might not stick around for L.A. where groups like the God's Militia, the Mannerites, Hollywood, and the Children's Citadel come in. This is one of the only few writing problems I have with W2.
As for the main-questline, it suffers from reusing the same objectives (attach repeater units, get kitty litter, get super kitty litter and two more repeaters). The means to fulfill these objectives, however, are different.
Lastly, when it comes to the writing the only bad aspect is its sexual content. Sometimes it is really, really cringe worthy (more so than Borderlands and New Vegas), and sometimes it can be really ill-timed. (Ex. Sleeping with show-girls in a brothel with murdered women in the other room.) I don't have a problem with the content as it's optional--I simply wished they hired a show-girl or porn-star to better handle it. Sex should be sexy.
All of these complaints, however, pale in comparison to the worst offender some might find: The combat.
For all its complexities, I rather enjoy the system for what it offers, and it kept me engaged for the first 35 hours (before Hollywood). However, by that time I was either expecting the game to end and/or add more. Unfortunately, it doesn't and I had to lull in the final ten hours to my ending.
To offset its tediousness, enemy variety keeps it fresh just to the end without RNG encounters. What I think needed more effort are the weapon mods, an ability to distracts enemies' attacks to one player,  and control over NPCs in battle. These aspects feel very unrefined to the rest of the game, and they are the only other faults to be found.

If you can accept a little bloated content and dull edges, then you can enjoy an IBM computer classic made in modern times.

Hotline Miami is no doubt one of the best indie games on Steam. Simple as that. It's very fast-paced, very bloody and violent, and requires fast reflexes and high amounts of practice and skill to master and get the sought-after A+.
This game has style and personality. It has this unique retro 16-bit look to it. I've never seen anything like it in any other game. It's also very violent, and brutally challanging. You will die so much in this game, you'll press R even before you even die! I do it all the time. If you use any sort of slicer weapon like a knife or katana, you'll even see the guts of your enemies on the floor. Freaking GUTS. This game censors nothing, and even made me go "Wow. That's messed up." Gameplay is a massive strength of this game. There's a huge selection of masks that add different buffs like faster movement, starting out with a gun or melee weapon, and my favorite: one hit punches. An even bigger strength of this game is the soundtrack. The soundtrack of this game is fantastic. It's one of the best I know of. It's this unique 80s disco electro dubstep kind of music, and it's incredible, and has your adrenaline pulsing through your body at times. Chapter 8, the cutscenes between chapters, and the chapter completion screen music are my personal favorites. The 16-bit graphics are well done. It's always nice for a game to have 16-bit graphics that are actually good.
There are a very small amount of negatives to this game. One notable one, that is mainly a technical/compatibility issue with the game is that it doesn't scale well on 4K screens. You have to run the game at 720p or something like that to get the game to even fit properly on the screen. This was a issue on my brother's laptop. Luckily, I have a 1080p monitor so it wasn't a problem for me at all. That's the main one I can think of. The story is also weak, which I don't care about, as this game didn't need one. It's mainly trying to be weird and make you go insane than having any meaning to it.
Hotline Miami is a fantastic indie game. It has style, brutality, and must be bought by any one that loves a good challange.

This game is like 137 MB, and you can tell.  Assets are reused all the time, and there's like five stages total.
And none of that is a bad thing.  Minimalism helps this game.
Controls are tight and combos are short, requiring chaining multiple types of combos into each other.  The bosses are all fun, and its a game that's actually very happy to be difficult.  None of it is cheap deaths.  Everything is avoidable and survivable.
So yes, it can be beaten in like two hours, but getting everything aside from the expensive costumes takes longer, all of it allowing you to do new tricks with a simple, but effective combo system based around switching quickly between attack types.  I just finished hard mode, and there's two more above that still for me to conquer.
This game knows what it wants to be; short, fun, and difficult.  The price tag reflects that, and it's a steal when on sale.

The Binding of Isaac is a rogue-like dungeon crawl game of which you control a little scared boy, called Isaac, through a labyrinth of freakish monsters and other horrors.
First of all, the game criticizes the Christian religion is an unfair way and has many references The Bible. The title of the game itself, The Binding of Isaac, is a reference. The game doesn't "force" you the references necessarily but if you're sensitive to this matter, then you might want to skip. Also, the game is heavy on violence and  presents some other gruesome features that you may not like.
In the game, you're a little boy. Isaac, who needs to travel through the basement facing freakish mutants. Your main weapon is: your tears. You shoot tears and navigate through many randomly generated rooms. Along the way you're going to need to rely on many items to assist you on your descent through the basement. The game is chuck-FULL of items that have different functions, many of them are unique and fun to use. There are various enemies and are hard to beat, even more the bosses.
Good luck reaching the bottom of the floor. After that, good luck unlocking the rest of the items and the other characters. Because of the randomly generated levels, the game has a high replay value. I suggest you also pick up the expansion pack: Wrath of the Lamb which is has ton of new content and makes the game more visceral!
Concluding, for 5 euros or your regional equivalent, this game is completley worth it bearing in mind the concept of the game. I recommend it!

I've been looking at the reviews for Mafia III, and after playing it for 10 hours straight, I think most people have been missing the one point that the Mafia series captures: Realism.
Realism is a common theme in the Mafia series, stemming from the first game (which shows the Driver sandbox consisting of linear missions and a Free Ride mode) depicting the Mafia's staying power in the depression years, Mafia II with the Mafia at its apex before the drug trade would see it slowly decay, and finally with Mafia III as we see one (two if we count the black mob) family wiped out due to paranoia.
...despite the story being written like a Spaghetti Western; but not the intro stuff surprisingly.
What I'm trying to say, is that the Mafia series is GTA's counterpart: Where GTA likes to parody crime and society, Mafia tries to capture society as it was in those time periods as well as the crimes that were commited during those times.
Which should explain the reason why the game is padded out with rackets: taking out a family with a massive empire takes TIME!!!
TIME!!!
TIME!!!
(Imagine the ringing of a bell with that).
Every Mafia game has flaws with it, that I understand. Hell, Mafia II was kinda incomplete when it was released (Free ride mode, along with a couple of areas, never made it to the final game). I will not♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game for that. Not even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI, or the repetition.
It's the Protaginost.
Once he gets shot in the head, he just becomes typical "Revenge Hero," which you can find in every single Spaghetti Western ever.
A shame really, cause this game is surprisingly good for what it is and with 2K Czech's closure.

Wasteland 2 can be seen as the spiritual successor to Fallout, as it's viewpoint, combat, and general feel is much closer to that than the original Wasteland. The combat is somewhat similar to the original Fallouts, although much more focused on in this game. Instead of controlling a single character with companions being completely AI, the game allows you to control each character on their turn. This adds more of a turn-based strategy feel in the combat; it's more about positioning and tactics than straight up firepower and ability to withstand said firepower. Fallout Tactics holds a similar, albeit clunkier, playstyle. The different skills are pretty good for the most part, although some weapon types do stand out as more useful.
The freedom in this game seems scant at first, as you are immediately forced into the Desert Rangers and sent off on a mission, but diverges almost right away with multiple choices as to where to go first, who to help, etc. Only one time limit is imposed, and this time limit simply alters the game rather than ending it outright like in the first Fallout. Folks who prefer the darker side of life also have the option to go rogue in one of two ways, but I'll leave those up for you to discover. It's not completely open world, but more a sequence of maps linked by an overworld map.
The graphics get the job done, but they're by no means stunning. Running in the Unity engine, the optimization is okay. The general aesthetic is certainly good, but it doesn't quite jump out at me like Fallout 1 and 2, or even Wasteland 1. The primary complaint would be the character models, they're not too distracting, but they aren't exactly the fluffiest sheep in the barn. To say it bluntly, the character models are bad, and at times don't even match the portrait of the character in question.
Fans of its forebears will find it pretty enjoyable, and certainly a worthy successor, and anyone who needs that CRPG itch scratched will be plenty happy with it. Those who like fast, action-packed games will have to look elsewhere.

This review is divided into two, first as the game itself, the second part will be relevant to you if you are a LotR fan
The combat is varied, the nemesis system as been incredibly improved compared to the first game, your orc army now plays a more dominant role in the story, they have added very well placed random events for them, which makes them something more than an obstacle in your way to conquer the Dark Land.
While combat mechanics and character habilities has been improved, little more is left to say about the gameplay, the movement of Talion is infuriating at times, jumping off ledges or climbing walls in the most inapropiate of moments, trying to dominate capitans, while in battle, can be very frustating sinse the game doesn't have a lock-on option.
Anyway, the game has vast areas full of orcs to kill and treasures, navigating through areas is much more compelling now, since are a number of ways to make your way through very fast, instead of having to wait until Talion finally can make Celebrimbor run for him, the game let's you use you Focus for that purpose.
The map is full of secondary quests and missions that, if you are not paying attention, distracts you from the main story for hours, very fun in that aspect.
While I dont want to spoil anything about the story, I have to say that is more convoluted that I've had expected, little makes sense and plays a secondary part in this game. more on this in the second section
In terms of graphics, while I honestly don't see much diference with the first game, the graphics options and configurations are very well presented to the player. The game looks very good, with breath taking landscapes, but is not something that breaks the mold.
Character design is shalow, no much development on their personalities, very predictable and obvious at times, but is not bad, just meh.
As for the dificulty, it started very balanced, for the first 4 or 5 hours of the game, the enemies present a good challenge, after that period, Talion is a complete unstopable killing machine, destroying everything on his way across the land, the only challenges are the orc war-chiefs that are inmune to everything. After level 15 or 20, to conquer fortresses becomes a walk in the park.
While the first game portrayed some characters in situations that weren't described in J.R.R. Tolkiens original works, the story was pretty much tied up in terms of the timeline, characters and events of the original books, the story in this game takes everything that the first game did right in terms of keeping a minimal coherency, and abuses and distorts the story that we enjoy and love; moving events from the second age to the third, making pure evil characters good, messing with rules carved into stone that you can't just manipulate to your will without introducing plot holes into the lore.
Let me be clear, this doesn't affect my take on the game, which I think is great, what I'm saying, is that if you are going to make a game, and put Middle-Earth in the title, try to be, at the very least, respectful with that title, or maybe we are talking about other Middle-Earth altogether.
The first 10  missions gave me the vibes of the first game, while I knew that was a made up story, it fitted into the original work, this game completely ignores the lore instead.
As a final note, I didn't buy this game thinking that it was going to be a narrative masterpiece, and neither should you.

Allright first, the story of this game is really awesome. You are Geralt of Rivia. A professional monster slayer that slay monsters for golds. But because of the circumstances you become the personal bodyguard of Temerian King. But because of being too close to the king, like a dog and his master, you are being accused with a crime that you never commit. And here we go the quest to clear your name, or you want to pursue other cause rather than just clearing your name? That's your call
This is a game where choices are really impactful in overall your gaming experience. Your experience will be different from the others depend on what you choose in the game. Even the side quests if you do them in different order, the result conseuqence would be dramatically different too. And the result is not instantly occur after the choice you made. You have to continue your progress to see the how the event unfold to see consequences of your previous choice. So you may think carefully about what would it become before choose rather than just load before the choice and know every consequence it will made.
I have to mention too, this game has moral ambiguity, nothing is really good and nothing is really evil. There are no best option with everyone win and peace come to the land with people become loving and understanding each other. Only choices with the good thing and bad thing of their consequences. This game will question how is your moral stand. Just like a real world where people relatively have different standard of what is right and what is wrong. The gameplay now, well it has some learning curve and dying is not uncommon in this game. A flawed follow up to Kane & Lynch: Dead Men that covers much the same ground.
Rating 4/10
Great art style, setting and characters in a story that doesn't go anywhere. Its greatest strength is the style; similar to lo-fi handheld shaky cam. The setting of Shanghai is also well realised, showing the seedy underbelly with bustling streets and markets however in later levels it reverts to overused locations such as warehouses and docks.
It also suffers the same problems as Kane and Lynch: Dead Men, great characters but stale and awkward gameplay. Simple mechanics such as getting into cover can be tricky and the aiming is clumsy at times. There also aren't any real variants on the gameplay, often narrow alleyways where it's a repetitive game of whack a mole, popping in and out of cover until it's safe to proceed.
The recent Spec Ops had an interesting story to make up for it's lack of gameplay, Kane and Lynch Dog Days has two great disaster-prone characters but not a great story.
It's also so short the first time I completed it I thought it was the end of Act 1 only to realise it was the end of the game, and incredibly short single player campaign that ends suddenly.  Multiplayer isn't much better as it died a month or so after release and now it's impossible to find other players.
There are far better 3rd person shooters out there now such as Kane and Lynch: Dead Men, Max Payne 3 and Spec Ops which all do it better. Worth picking up for the art style alone but don't expect much from the game.

Witcher 2 is just brilliant and I highly recommend it!
I must admit, it wasn't until very late 2012 when I heard of The Witcher games. I intially pegged it as a game to play "at some stage" and gave it no more thought than that. During mid 2013 I saw Witcher 1 + 2 on special @ 75% off decided I would add it to my collection and give it a try.
The first game was pretty good, and after I finished it late 2013 I jumped right into Witcher 2. What a great decision that was! I love everything about this game!
I'll choose one facet of it, and comment on it. The story... the story is great. It had me until the closing scene's and then some. In fact, I think it will have me until Witcher 3! It gives you just enough throughout the first and second chapters to confuse you, and at the same time have you wanting more. The third chapter then brings it all together and sets the tone for your first step into Witcher 3. Personally, I can't wait, especially in regards to the impact my various decisions have on the game. This is one of the first games where I have felt that my decisions really did have an impact on where the story was being directed - that in and of itself is gold!
Everything else; the music, the characters (loved Triss Merigold's character in this one... not so much in the first game but the direction feels more to my Witchers sense), the voice acting, the crafting, the various GUI's (there are a few issues though... why can I not jump from my inventory to journal?)... heck even the way the game pauses with the bushes and trees still moving but everything else frozen is fantastic.
I won't kid myself though, there were a few annoyances and oversights but in I feel they are too small to bother outlining.
Pro's:
- Story and decision appeal
- Multiple story paths
- Sound
- Characters
- Combat
Con's:
- Controls felt delayed sometimes
- Potions felt somewhat useless... perhaps I would use them more on Dark (I was playing on Hard for first playthrough)
- Mutagens. Good concept but poorly executed. In the end I forgot to put them into my talents because I was trying to wait for certain Mutagens. How about an upgrade path, rather than once and never again?
In my books, 9.5/10

(Note: this review is covering the whole game, no spoilers!)
A coming of age/sci-fi mystery story about two young girls in small town Oregon, covering a broad range of topics, from drugs to cyber-bullying to the long-term effects of manipulating the space-time continuum.  In terms of gameplay, it's a point & click adventure with a heavy focus on "choices matter."  (How much your choices
is open to debate, but I personally feel like this game at least moves the concept forward compared to past games.)
The story is intriguing, and the choices you're asked to make are often conflicted.  They did a good job of setting things up so that it wasn't immediately obvious which choice was "best" in every case. Some choices are obviously "good" or obviously "illegal," but it can be hard to tell which option will work out for the best in the end.
The individual charcaters are deep and well defined.  You get to know them as the story unfolds, and there are few cardboard cut-outs among them.
Although the overall story is quite good, I found that the actual dialogue got tedious in certain parts.  (She's SO happy!  She's SO sorry!  She's SO SO over it!)  I guess that's just her character, and it's hardly a dealbreaker or anything.
Probably, yes.  As Adventure games go, it's a solid entry in the genre.
You've heard good things about it (all true.)  You like adventure games and/or time travel stories.

I think I'm spoiled by modern day rts games and rpg games, because by comparison this game isn't very good.  I remember beating the order of dawn's campaign years ago and I remember the game being better than it actually is.  I got halfway through the first campaign before I gave up.  Here's a few of my problems.
Translation errors: namely some of the written dialog was in a language I didn't read, like german or swedish or something
BAD voice actors.  There were a few good ones, but they were few and far between.  The main character's voice was probably the worst of all.  I just turned it off sound after a while.
Upgrading units in the store doesn't upgrade units you've already purchased.  And this game has multiple powerful upgrades which you get later on, so you wind up with a bunch of underpowered units.
Turrets.  ♥♥♥♥ turrets.  There are a lot of the things in the game and you can only MELEE them down, even units with ranged attacks.  There are no siege units.  And you have to manually and REPEATEDLY  order your units to punch the towers to death because they frequently bug out and start attacking nothing.  An associated problem, there are a limited number of units which can attack a building at a time (thanks to the melee thing) so while the towers are killing your units you have a maybe six or seven of units  out of an army of almost a hundred attacking.
And the heroes... o lawd the heroes.  These units don't do anything half the time,letting monsters walk right by and attack your workers.  The other half of the time they'll walk right up to boss enemies and get themselves killed,  instead of using their powerful spells and staying at ranged.  They only autocast a few spells, and not the important spells like Heal so you have to manually instruct them to save your army every. single. time.
A lot of the missions seemed poorly designed, being really difficult one moment only to be followed by an easy level.  I think part of the problem was the transfer between factions was the culprit for this, because the level gives you the usual amount of enemies but only lets you use first-tier units to fight against it.  The designers usually give you access to the last faction's entire tech tree late in the mission (in the form of a Monument to spawn units) to help with this problem.  But by the point that those monuments become available its usually too late to matter, because your army needs to be sufficiently large to hold off attacks on your base AND clear the monument AND defend your resource gatherers, which means your army is probably large enough to just win.
Another problem... you know what, I give up.  I have no clue how I managed to beat this game when I was young, but I don't have the patience now.

Great game, no pay to win aspect. But... this game isn't all about skill, the progression system is pretty definitely supporting the more experienced. (
) It takes a bit of time to unlock all the towers, but the addition of arenas and rankings made getting medals easier than before. Every week you get a guaranteed 1k medals if you played at least one game, if you played actively it can scale up to 2k or more. The arenas also help getting medals if you're good, you basically stake the selected value and the winner takes all.
Now of course most towers will have most of the potential unlocked by the time 3 line of upgrades are unlocked and that is relatively cheap compared to fully maxing out (all 4 lines). Here's a good example, the regular monkey is the best started tower in the game, but only if you have the 3rd line of upgrades unlocked, of course it is also the cheapest tower, since in the late game even upgraded to 4th line upgrade it is very bad. It costs around 30 medals to unlock the 3rd line and you get 5 or 7 medals every game that you win (depending on how many lives you had at the time of winning).
The games are relatively fast (5-10min), but sometimes can take up much longer, so they could be compared to the lenght of hearthstone matches. The game is very simple to get into, but has a lot of strategical depth, since when you are in game, nothing is relying on luck, all of it is skill. Oh and (just like a deck builder) you can only pick 3 towers that you take into the battlefield, with an optional 4th one (in regular mode you can roll it for 1 energy
The game is a lot of fun when you unlock some towers, I have played it very long on the phone and it was very easy to sync my progress with the pc. I truly recommend this game to anyone who likes strategy without RNG.

The prized "Nemisis system" is utter trash. I've spent literally hours tracking down orcs that I want to recruit, using training orders on them and leveling them up just to have them betray me for no discernable reason. They then become "iron willed" meaning I can't recruit them back in. Shaming them is supposed to have a chance to remove this trait. Again, on a regular basis, these iron willed orcs I've shamed (and nerfed, removing all their former good traits) all the way down to level 1, to the point where the slightest breeze would kill them. Even so, tiptoeing around their vulnerabilities to keep them alive and shaming them further never removed the trait, until eventually a sideways look from a ghul or a stray fire would do them in. These were just orcs I had found. I'd be furious if they were from a loot box I was dumb enough to pay for.
On the note of betrayal, the Blood Brother system is an utter annoyance. It was cool the first time. Its a good idea, but executed really, REALLY poorly. I can't express how many I've lost to this stupid system.
If you aren't familiar, this means if you kill their brother, they will immediately seek to avenge their death and if they are in the vicinity, they will attack you. This sounds fun in theory, when you have an orc you've turned to your side decide that he has a blood brother on the opposite side, it gets very old, VERY fast. And they seem to come out of nowhere as well.
I had an orc I had killed "cheat death" and come back to attack me in my fort. Apparently him cheating death formed a bond between him and one of my orcs. Since it was in my fort, the other orcs rushed over to help kill him. This included his blood brother who was all gung-ho about bashing his skull in for me, but the second I grabbed him to recruit rather than kill so as to not♥♥♥♥♥♥him off, he took it as an offence and turned on me.
Turning over to the combat side of things, the smooth flowing fights of jumping over enemies countering attacks, using the environment and special abilities to your advantage is a lot of fun when you're facing 20 or 30 grunts and a few captains at a time, BUT:
When you get into the large scale, massive seige battles, that all goes out the window. The combat system was not meant for massive battles in any way, and it quickly turns into trying to find a spot in the middle of 40 enemy orcs to stand still and not get hit for 3 seconds to keep your orcs from bleeding out while you have 10 enemy captians trying to skewer you. Strengths and weaknesses? pah. There's 6 warchiefs attacking, each of which have 3 bodyguards. At that point, there's no planning, it's just hit whoever is closest to you and hope it does damage.
While the chances of your fort being captured by taking all the points is unlikely, the chances of you getting your face clubbed in by a captian with the "no chance" trait while you were trying to save Shag the Shrak-Eater for the 15th time is inevitable. Thus losing the fort, and apparently most of your warchiefs and bodyguards you had worked so hard to recruit and train.
Losing orcs wouldn't be as big of a deal if finding ones you liked wasn't so hard. Between training orders, and there only being very limited bonus traits, finding decently powered ones isn't all that hard. But 95% of the orc captains all have their tribe's default mismatched captian armor. It gets really boring after a while. Even the new Slaughter tribe DLC that was just released is boring. It basically just looks like feral tribe's armor with more blood and bits of random metal tied to it. Dont buy it. The remaining 5% of captians that spawn are REALLY cool looking. Wow. WOW. Where to start. Let me just say, this game is absolutely AMAZING. I don't usually write reviews, but I simply had to for this gem of a game.
1. The graphics
The backgrounds are beautifully drawn, even when I was first in Shay's spaceship I was mesmerized by the amount of detail in the design of the ship. I could even see the brush strokes which gave a really cool tecture to the walls. They have a childlike feel to them, and each place is so unique and imaginatively structured. There never seemed to be an end to the creativity!
2. Character design
Each character in this game has such a unique personality and design. I absolutely love the talking animations, even though they get repetitive (should they not? I mean, characters talk a lot) I don't mind at all. Once in a while when Shay or Vella picks a certain dialogue option you get a different talk animation than the usual, and I think that's so cool!
3. The puzzles
I see a lot of negative reviews solely based on the puzzles, and I do have to say, they are very difficult. Coming from a person who doesn't play a lot of puzzle/brain type games, I did have to use a guide to figure them out. However, that doesn't mean they're impossible. I'm 100% positive a large amount of people could figure them out with no help. I didn't mind using a guide, it didn't give or take away from the game experience for me.
4. Soundtrack
There's not much I can describe about the music, as everyone has their own opinion of what music they like. However, in my opinion the soundtrack was beautifully composed, with very lovely themes and dramatic tones when needed. It made the scenery and graphics so much more pleasant!
5. Voice acting
There is way more than you originally expect to this game. Twists, turns, and a lovely blending of the two story paths that perfectly ties together the ending. I'm not a very thourough game purchaser, and I tend to just skim over descriptions of everything I buy. (Not a very good choice, I know, but its given me some fun surprises in the past.) Fortunately not reading this game's description while I bought it on a whim when I had a gift card and found it on sale, left me the fun part of figuring out the voice actors of each character.
Shay immediately became my favorite, because Elijah Wood, come on! I enjoyed his acting in Over the Garden Wall, and I was so excited when I learned he is expanding his repitoire. I have a bad habit of skipping dialogue in games like these, because I have a short attention span, and it just gets boring, y'know? But with this game, I sat through every single dialogue option (except for the repeats, of course) and
It's not much to put in my review, but for me personally, that was a huge plus.
All in all, I hope I've convinced whoever's reading this review to purchase this game and give it a try. You'll come away in a good mood, eagerly awaiting the next masterpiece of Double Fine Productions in the coming years.

Let me start off by saying that I'm not a point & click fanatic. I didnt like Grim Fandango or Dropsy but was really surprised by Kathy Rain. I love the Walking Dead series (if they're considered Point & Click games). That being said, I went into Broken Age with an open mind.
==============Pros=================
Graphics - Right from the main menu I was captivated by the games art style. Vibrant colours with an interesting art style.
Characters - The characters and humor were great. Most of the characters were extremely memorable and made the dialogue side of the game very entertaining.
Voice acting - Voice acting was strong and added a lot to the story and as mentioned, great characters.
Setting/Story - The story and setting felt unique and intruiging, although I didn't finish it for reasons I will explain.
Riddles - I felt the riddle puzzles were the strongest of them and really boosted the gameplay.
==============Cons ================
Gameplay - My main problem with this game is it's gameplay. Some of the puzzles are tedious and because of its fantasy setting, trying to use logic in a fantasy world can be difficult because the logics of the world dont make sense and just guessing is probably the best option.
Level Design - Some of the levels are quite large and you need to backtrack often while trying to figure out puzzles, there is a fast travel in each section but sometimes you have to walk to have the exit in view and it can take an annoying ammount of time.
===========Conclusion===============
If you really enjoy point & clicks maybe you should check this out but I can't reccomend this game when I felt the gameplay was a bit flawed. I wanted to finished for the story but the gameplay became monotonous and I'm dissapointed I couldn't finish this one.

Here's the tale of Koth the Painted.
I'm on stage 7 of Shadow Wars, just lost Nurnen so now I'm trying to get rid of any weak orcs. I see that I have some scrawny level 17 assassin who throws spears, so screw it, I order him to infiltrate a level 40-something captain to pose as his bodyguard and betray said captain (expecting Koth to die). Now he has to prove himself to the level 40-something captain by winning a duel in the fight pits. He gets put up against a level 45 Epic Olog. Great, this'll be over in a second, right?
Nope. The Olog is Enraged, swinging at Koth nonstop, but Koth just keeps dodging and throwing spears at the p*ssed off Olog, sometimes jabbing at him with the spears. Then he wins? What? A common, scrawny level 17 assassin just destroyed this Epic level 45 Olog who was Enraged through the whole fight. Koth gained 22 levels from the fight. He's now level 39 and I gave him a Legendary upgrade which I got from a Mithral chest (I earned the required gold in four days.)
Shadow of War is my best game of the year. It's not perfect, but it's the most fun I've had in a game in a long time. The Nemesis system keeps things fresh and I've met many memorable captains. The story is great, too, and the game has many missions, collectibles and skills to earn. I did feel that the game wasn't really designed for the sieges though, since I've lost many captains due to the really bad targetting. When there's too many enemies in one area at once you end up draining other orcs instead of reviving your captain. Act 1, 2 and 3 are great, but act 4 almost made me leave a negative review. You shouldn't have to grind the same four missions a bunch of times just to get the true ending, and it doesn't help that when act 4 starts the attackers will be high levels, while most of your captains will be low levels. The loot boxes are another problem, they just shouldn't be in a single player game, but I admit that I enjoy earning gold through community challenges, and I enjoy spending that gold on the occassional chest.
Anyway, don't let the loot boxes and grindy endgame put you off of getting Shadow of War. There's so much more to this game and to be honest, they barely effect the game. Everything is doable without the lootboxes, and the grindy endgame does add more playtime.

Once they had -90% sale i couldn't help but buy this game owing to much positive reception it had had in the past. After playing 2 episodes , I can definitely recommend this game to anyone, even those who are unfamiliar to the horror genre as this game is not a generic horror game per se which nowadays flood the market, being notororiously popular for their jumpscares and cheap thrills, but a unique atmospheric and psychological horror game which has amazing writing and voice acting.
Although the visuals might seem dated in certain places this game is a must buy for those who are interested in compelling and interesting piece of excellent narative.

If you are in dilemma just like how i was, you needn't be, i suggest you to get this game for the amazing story it tells.
For those who are easily frightened i suggest playing in easy mode as only in higher difficulties you would be forced to reserve ammunition and run away from your enemies, in easy you can face them head on.
In an age where games focus on only elements like gameplay and graphics, games like Alan Wake, which uses those elements effectively to spin a wonderful tale, are certainly a needle in a hackstack and makes me wonder when more games like this will take the center stage in the current gaming industry which seems like a cesspool of redundant shooters, recycled garbage and eye candies.

I have split my review into categories and I will say what I liked and what I disliked to create the most holistic review that will either convince you to buy the game or make you save your money. No spoilers that will affect your gameplay - read with confidence.
1. Graphics/performance
2. Story
3. Length of the game/Map size
4. Gameplay/missions
5. Characters/Enemies AI
6. Skills
7. Weapons/Shooting
8. Movement
9. Sound/Music
10. Overall thoughts
1. Performance is quite good I must say. I had constant 60 fps with few fps down during fast paced moments eg. shooting, explosions and so on. I played 2k with everything maxed out on my i7 3820, 16 ram, and gtx 1080.
Now as far as graphics goes, this is where I am actually torn apart. The graphics looks extremely dated, but at the same time they kind of giving you that unique feel of America 60s, almost like watching Goodfellas film. The Bayou is very atmospheric. It’s really, really hard to place graphics in this game, as I never experienced anything like that. The environment I would say is slightly "underdeveloped" in my opinion, very little details for example instead of mirrors in the game; you have some sort of reflection that updates every couple seconds (???) Is it really that hard to create a proper mirror in the game? Even silly 2004 shooters already had it. Environmental damage is also very basic for example shooting an apple will result of apple disappearing rather than explode into pieces.
2. Story is a bit different from what I expected and I am sure many of you as well. Instead of rising through mafia ranks, we taking on personal vendetta and getting mob family down, starting from lieutenants, then officers, capos and so on. But this idea really worked well I must say. Story is told from couple perspectives with narrative video every time you complete a major story mission. I really liked that.
3. That’s a quite good chunk of a length right here guys. At this point it took me 23 hours to complete enite game. I did all story missions and only couple optional. I think for completionist it would produce 30-35 hours. So if you are die hard Mafia fan, 30-35 hours is what you get out of it. The map size is decent as well. Its definitely bigger than both Mafias and what I also noticed is that every area is utilized for missions unlike GTA 5 where you have a massive map and only 40% of area where actually something going on.
4. Like I said earlier, entire map is utilized for quests; however there is little variety to the gameplay element. 80% of all missions are go there, shoot bunch of people and interrogate or kill the guy. We have some novelty missions such as infiltrating mansion, old theme park, some car chases and that’s it really. I really miss some prison escape kind of mission in this game like in Mafia 2. Some places you visiting twice; I think 2k should put a little more heart here. For most of the time you have freedom when it comes to approaching missions, you can do it guns blazing or stealthy with silencer gun. Nothing to do after you beat the game. You can carry on with outstanding side missions or you might wiretap entire city.
5. Characters are very memorable. We have already been teased in prerelease trailer return of Vito Scaletta as one of the three mobs you will be able to recruit to fight along your side. Great voice acting, different personalities, that’s a great work here. Enemies you face are mobs of main antagonist and police if you get naughty. Police is very relentless and will put you down no matter the cost, acting often as a cannon fodder. Not much care here, they going to put you down, trust me. Now AI enemies are a bit random. They can hide behind obstacles or they might as well run full retard onto you. I think nothing to complain here.
6. We have skill tree here actually. And your skill tree is...your mobs you recruit. Each mob will provide bonuses to different aspects for example improved defenses, health, carrying extra ammo, faster cars, calling reinforcements and so on. You can choose which skill tree is more appealing to your gameplay style and the only way of leveling those skills would be assigning your mobs to the district you take over. The more districts you assign to the specific mob, the more skills you will get from him. But you may decide to go equally across the board. That’s your call here. I think it’s quite interesting way of presenting skills in this game, that’s something really unique. Well done.
7. Massive variety of weapons. Handguns, smgs, rocket launchers, heavy guns, sniper rifles, grenades, molotovs, silencers and so on. The downside here is limit to only 2 weapons that you can carry. Handgun and either shotgun, smg, heavy gun, sniper or rocket launcher. I think due to variety, there should be a bit more that 2 slots. 3-4 would be reasonable. Shooting is fun and enjoyable. Combat in general is fun. Takedowns are brutal and satisfying, never gets old.
8. Character movement is quite good, we can’t jump, but we can jump through obstacles, crouch and hide, blind shooting is enabled as well as hip fire. I was huge fan of hip fire back in the day, but today games are successfully wean me away from this habit.
9. Music is very atmospheric. Not as much as Mafia 1 but I enjoyed it. We have 3 radio stations with Elvis and other stars from 60s to listen to.
10. Overall, Mafia 3 is a good product. If you are Mafia fan, go get it. If you new to Mafia, go get it as well. Its an enjoyable experience, very sandboxish feel to it. I am Mafia veteran, I played all of them and each of those games are different in my opinion. 2k did well overall. I hope guys this review helped you to somewhat get an image of the game and if you have any questions, feel free to post them.

It's a shame Alan Wake is longer available for retail or online purchase, due to "expiring music liscenses" (Thanks capitalism!) It's easily in the same class as any other Remedy title, and honestly, it's probably in a class above. What would be an inferior third-person shooter to their previous series, the Max Payne games, is instead a thrilling tale of cinematic suspense and character development. I am sorry I never looked into the series before now. It features great pacing, quality voice acting, passably good driving sections, and if nothing else, really satisfyingly loud gun sounds.The facial animations haven't aged well these past years, but that's hardly a major shortcoming.
You take the role of the titular character, a crime fiction writer from NYC with possibly the worst case of writer's block on record. Wake has come to Bright Falls, Washington with his photographer wife Alice on vacation, in an attempt to clear his head, but within hours finds his wife missing, his car wrecked, the cabin he was to stay in vanished without a trace and a week's time gone by with no memory of such to speak of. What's worse, a malign force now stalks him through the night, wielding the shadows themselves as its weapon.
The light is your friend in Alan Wake, and there is precious little of it to go around. As in Left 4 Dead and many other games, light sources often mark your path, and many of them not only function as checkpoints but quickly replenish your otherwise painfully slow to regenerate health. Your enemies are shielded by darkness itself, and only your trusty flashlight can strip their defense before you go for the kill, using the sorts of guns you'd find lying around a rural community: police revolvers, hunting shotguns and rifles. Also at your disposal are two kinds of flares and flashbangs, with one kind of flare being fired from a flare gun and acting in essence as a grenade launcher.
Mechancally, the game is fairly formulaic: You move from checkpoint to checkpoint, blasting bad guys and pushing the occasional switch or button to open a door or something that might as well be a door. But your enemies are dangerous enough, and the characters believable enough, that you forget you are going through the motions of an oughts-era console shooter- and yes, I know it orignally released in 2010. The episodic format of the game greatly helps with the pacing, and it has some really great twists, especially in the bonus episodes: however you think the plot might turn out when you begin, it will likely defy your expectations. It also ends up being a lot harder then it intially feels, even on the easiest difficulty you will have a lot of near misses and scrapes, and this I recommend for a first play through- Alan Wake actually suffers from some balancing problems and it's a little to easy to get completely overwhelmed in the blink of an eye and ruthlessly beat to death. The dodge move is essentially broken, largely working only when it wants to, and your sprint duration is extremely limited, ensuring that you will rarely have the opportunity to avoid a fight. On the other hand, you are often given more supplies then you think you need- this is because you actually need all of it, so don't be afraid to use a flashbang or flare whenever you are cornered, as you are likely to find more.
If you did not have the good fortune to get this game before it was pulled from the Steam store, I highly encourage you to dig up a used Xbox 360 copy or secondhand key if you can find one, as it is definately worth your time.

Spellforce is a hybrid RTS with strong RPG components.  It's good but has its flaws.
Good: Long campaign well worth the money; innovative mix of RTS and RPG; some nice touches in combat interface (eg select an enemy and icons show up under your heroes indicating which spells you can throw at target); a big world worth exploring; decent scenery; excellent music.
Not so good: Storyline a bit boring; voice-acting somewhat weak; RTS component a little weak - overly complex resource management (six resources?), big battles hard to micro properly (this is no Starcraft . . .); as far as it goes as an RPG - very limited/no real choices.  RPG heroes not well-balanced vs the RTS army (on some maps it can be easier to NOT trigger the base-building part and clear out some enemy bases with the heroes, as enemy spawn rate increases once you claim a base).
I would still recommend it for the novelty value of a reasonably-done RPG/RTS hybrid.

This game is fun. Real fun. But it expects a lot out of you, and if you aren't willing to make that investment, then this game just isn't for you.
First off, the game has a massive learning curve, and most of the active community left is people who will be significantly higher up the curve than you are. Secondly, the game was developed through a bond between the community and the developer, which means you need to participate in the community to really get enjoyment out of it. A bad server can completely ruin your experience, though they are avoidable to a degree. First and foremost is to make sure you do not become one of the players who makes a server bad. If you have a mic, use it, and if you don't, try to use team chat as much as possible. And when you do this, remember to be friendly, especially to your commander, as they have the most stressful job.
The second thing to do is research. Get to know all the mechanics of the game as well as basic strategies and a good group to play with. This last one is very important. There are a few methods commonly used. The first is to just find a server that is well run and become a regular on it. Good servers usually have talkative people who show up around the same time, as well as server mods that ease the balancing and management capabilities. You can find group to play with as well, such as a clan or or just a more casual gathering. With this method you tend to learn just how good each player is, and these groups can self balance when they play together. The other method is pick up games, which are a community run system for playing in a more competitive style. This last method is probably the most rewarding, and sees few completely onesided games, but most of the players are veteran players, so waiting until you have a solid grasp of the game is highly reccomended. Finding a good place to play is a necessity, as when everyone is friendly and having a good time, it doesn't matter so much if every match is a landslide, and that will keep you at it until you become good enough to hold your own in a fight. The community is ultimately what makes this game at its best, and at its worst. Learn to avoid the worse parts of the community, and make sure that you yourself do not become one of the contributors to that part of the community.
Lastly, you should make sure you also have the proper hardware for this game. I mentioned earlier the importance of using a mic, and if you are considering getting into this game, then invest in a decent mic as well. Also on the subject of hardware, this game doesn't put much load on your gpu, but does have a massive cpu load, and it may be a good idea to beef up your cpu for this game. You will typically see fps drops toward the end of the game as the cpu needs to handle more and more things happening. It shouldn't be hard to find guides out there specifically for diagnosing what any limiting factors on performance are, as well as figuring out what hardware is reccomended for adequate performance. The only thing worse than finding out you can't play the game unless you upgrade hardware is being one of the people who diagnosed the problem wrong and upgraded a different component than they actually needed.
This is a game you can put hundreds, or even thousands of hours into, but then again, it is also a game you kind of need to put that much into to get the fullest experience out of it. I wholeheartedly reccomend it, but I also recognize that not everyone wants to or is able to put that kind of investment into it. For those of you who are willing and able, you will most certainly get your money's worth out of this game. There isn't much else like it, and out of the few other fps/rts games, it clearly stands out for its polish, atmosphere, and community.

A Japanese arena style beat em' up game with heavy. Art-wise, it's fine. Liked the animations, the designs of the enemies have this neat robot theme, and the girls are cute even with the ecchi. Backgrounds and arenas are nothing to write home about. A big circle for the arena, backgrounds change but aren't that impressive.
The story barely exists, your friend has an evil sword and you want to save her. Done, whatever, moving on.
Controls are finicky, playing this game on a mouse and keyboard is impossible. It's designed for a controller and nothing but. The tutorial and interface are also a problem, they tell you to hit certain attacks without button prompts.
All that aside, when you do have a controller and know how things work, things get fun. The system allows for a lot of insane combos and bouncing around. You can block, but it's actually better not to since it kills the flow. Bosses are insanely hard and become a lot of fun if that sort of challenge doesn't aggrevate you. Enemies start off from peons you step on to to behemoths that pose a fair challenge in their own right. Difficulty spikes up quickly enough to keep things interesting.
For me, the buy was worth it based on the art and gameplay. It doesn't price itself too high so it's worth it if you like these sorts of games. Getting it on sale is fine, but you can't argue with an asking price of $15 for this level of challenge.

One of the first strategy games I started playing as a kid and loved.
The Spellforce universe holds a lot of potential and the Platinum Edition adds two expansions, the Breath of Winter and Shadow of the Phoenix.
The story is good for a real time strategy game, it follows the path of a rune warrior and his struggles to free the shattered lands of Eo and free himself from his bond with the Circle.
The gameplay is unique, I love it so much that I have played the Order of Dawn for years and seeing this edition on Steam was another reason to replay it. The base building was so refreshing in this game, using Rune monuments as the center for recruitment of armies and workers. Aside from the monuments dedicated to the humans, elves, dwarves, orcs, trolls and dark elves, there are also monuments for heroes that you can customize.
The way the six nations play out is simply amazing, each nations gathers resources in its own way and have different uses, for example, the humans and dwarves can double their iron income but the elves don’t even have a building for it, they counter this disadvantage with having the ability to build foresters that can rebuild forests and maintain a almost infinite supply of wood. These base building and army recruitment details really enhance the experience for RTS fans.
The customization of your characters and heroes’ weapons and skills also add to this, there are also a huge variety of weapons, armor and spells to choose from as you go through the game. The way you play the game really rewards you with different situations, I prefer the warrior gameplay but after playing as a mage I did find it more of a challenge to get through the game. To add to this, there’s also a fantastic soundtrack included and beautiful graphics for its age.
As for downsides, I didn’t find many aside from a few bugs but nothing game breaking.
I really hope that this mix of RTS/RPG returns in the future, anyone who likes fantasy real time strategy games will definitely enjoy this game, I personally count it as one of my favorite strategy games. It’s well worth its price even if you're not that into the RTS genre.

You play as Misa a Blade Templar given the task of protecting the Demon Blade. Suzuka a close friend of yours has gotten her hands on the Demon Blade and is being corrupted by the powers it holds. The swrod manafests enemies and bosses through Suzuka's life force. So what do you do in turn? Fight your way through countless enemies and bosses in between stages.
There are 5 stages and 6 bosses. Between waves 1 - 5 of a stage you fight the indifferent mobs and at stage 6 you take on the boss. A lot of people complain about the difficulty which I do believe is there, for a while atleast. Once you get the patterns of the bosses down it gets easier. Similar to Dark Souls (don't kill me please) mixed with Ninja Gaiden. Really the hardest part of the game for me is the mobs at the higher difficulties. Even when you get their patterns down the sheer number of them at times can throw me off. Of coarse I plan to change that as I only have 10 hours in and am planning on getting all the emotes, backgrounds, badges, cards, and acheivements for the game.
The mechanics are pretty solid for me. I don't have much experience with this genre so I can't go in further details other than I find them very enjoyable. Fluid for the most part and plenty of defensive options that that are hard for me to get down and pat (i.e counter, flourish, just guard).
Story very linear but that doesn't matter to much with this kind of game. Cute girls, hard bosses, fluid combat, high combos. What's not to like about this game? How ever I have to say even if people like the Hack and Slash nature of the game it is VERY linear. You are set in an arena with changing back grounds after every boss fight. Enemy moddles are mostly the same but I don't mind that. For $2.50 or even the full price I would highly recommend this game, as I am enjoying it imensly. MIsa + Suzuka for life <3

The puzzles in act 2 are atrocious. I'm going to spoil them, because I hate talking in ambiguity. And you should skip these puzzles anyway, because they require unreasonable leaps in logic, and are a waste of your time.
1. Snake puzzle. Unlike what the game makes you expect from previous encounters with the snake, you need to let a snake constrict your character for almost an entire minute with no input, and ignore your character gasping and hinting to free himself. The hint was that your character got a lot of hugs when he was young. I wish I was kidding.
2. Knot puzzle. The descriptions of each knot and the method to untie them require some VERY creative imagination. Look up a walkthrough, and look at the diagram that represents: untie the snakes. What the ♥♥♥♥ even IS that. You can't skip the lengthy dialogue here either if you make a misstep, because it also skips showing you what the new knot looks like, wasting you even more time. But the biggest offender is in relation to this.
3. Fish in a tree. So after teaching the player that trial and error solutions AREN'T the answer, thanks to the tedious knot puzzle... They suddenly throw us a puzzle ONLY solvable through trial and error. I was looking around for nearly an hour for anyone who could help with a good 'tree joke'. Nope. You just fling bad joke after bad joke until the right one appears in dialogue and you happen to guess it (it's not funny, and there's no way to tell it's even the right one until the punchline.)
4. Robot wiring. After setting up the expectation that you can play each character in its entirety per act before starting the other, suddenly the game expects you, with no indication, to switch characters to get omniscient information they could not otherwise have in order to progress.
5. Hose puzzle. Instead of standing on a high platform and swinging the hose over to yourself before cutting it, like any rational person would do... You need to raise a low platform, climb to the top of a hose... And cut it while you're still on it and FALL all the way down, breaking your♥♥♥♥♥on a hard surface. That's the solution.
Old point and clicks were even more obnoxious, and these are the monkey island devs after all, but it's something you'd think would be fixed by now, right? And worse, Act 1, although too easy, had none of these problems, so it was a curveball that suddenly these terrible mechanics started showing up with no indication.
