Spellforce is a game which combines Role-playing elements with real-time strategy. One hand you have a certain character which represents you and on the other hand you can control an army of up to 80 soldiers which you have recruited using resources gathered from the map. The player creates a character at the beginning of the game. This character can acquire skills and spells and gain experience from completed quests and vanquished enemies. Items can be bought from shops, looted from enemies or found in chests in the different maps which can then be used to kit out the player character according to the skills the character possesses. The player also acquires runes which lets the player summon additional characters to assist on some maps and as well as let the player summon in workers which constructs buildings and harvest resources. During the game you also pick up recipes and blueprints which will allow you to create new units and construct new buildings.
The scope of the game is vast. The main campaign may require more than 50 hours to complete if you intend to pursue side quests. You have the ability to summon armies composed of six different races (Humans, Elves, Dwarves, Orcs, Trolls and Dark elves) which each have 9 different units at their disposal. Each race has its own buildings and require different resources. The game features a story line with many side-quests available.
Sadly, the game suffers from a myriad of issues. By trying to be too much the game fails at almost everything. First, the game looks extremely dated. The graphics which might have been impressive in 2006 look really hideous today. Other contemporary games such as Warcraft 3 have fared much better. The gameplay is a mess. The ambitious design to combine RTS and RPG elements have resulted in a situation where neither of the systems are particularly satisfying. The RPG part has perhaps been fleshed out more but it never really feels rewarding. The strategy side is a total mess. Your only tactic is essentially to mass powerful units and try to send them toward the enemy in some fashion. Most units if not directly controlled will charge to attack the nearest enemy they can see which causes them to run into enemy encampments and chaos ensues. Trying to micro-control your units in combat is almost futile and if your attack fails, you might just as well just get a new troop of units and try again.
Combat is unsatisfying. You can see how much damage you do to enemies and how much they do to you but you are never given the information how much health, mana, skills, spells or speed they might possess. The lack of information makes it hard to determine how effective units are, Your recruitable units are also very similar. Each race has a basic melee unit, basic archer, magic user. Then more effective melee user and archer and so on. The magic users with their different spells are the most varied. Every other unit just feels like their models got changed and nothing else.
Your enemies will never build structures or gather resources. Instead they are spread out across in the map in pre-build encampments. As long as their buildings stand, new units will get spawned in which will attack your camp. By razing their buildings the spawn points disappear. It's a simple solution but also rather boring. The difficulty of the maps are mostly based on how fast new units spawn and attack. Whenever spawning isn't used the map is usually littered with non-consequential enemies which you have to grind through.
The game is very slow. Your units and character run at predetermined speeds and often you have to run great distances and criss-cross over a map to finish off all objectives which, frankly, takes ages. Building up your base also takes time and you always have to build the base from scratch on new maps. Acquiring the required resources to produce the necessary units is also a slow process and often I found myself stepping away from the computer and doing chores instead of playing the game. The slow running speeds combined with the dull base-building artificially prolongs the length of the game. By the end I was bored out of my skull, frustrated from assorted bugs and barely managed to muster enough effort complete the main campaign.
I can only with good conscience recommend this game to rpg/rts fans who have a lot of free time on their hands and don't mind lackluster mechanics. Anyone else should avoid Spellforce. Spellforce was purchased based on incorrect teenage nostalgia and a heavily reduced price.

This addition to the Middle Earth series is a great step-up from its predecessor - from the improved nemesis system to the larger world size there is surely a lot to do. As a first note, I HIGHLY suggest you play on the nemesis difficulty for a greater experience mainly because theres more strategy involved; not only that but it will help the extend your experience. For me personally, on this difficulty, it took me 55 hours to complete act 3. This included me having 100 percent for every storyline and collection of the memories, door parts and artifacts. The true ending however, is held behind act 4's shadow wars - a grindy fortress defense and reclaimation. I myself being at stage 8 out of 10 with 80 hours on record, so theres a little perspective for you. With regards to microtransactions they are completely optional and it isnt necessary to fork out money in order to complete act 4 or just the game in general. You have the option to get gold through doing daily challenges though, so that way you can still open non-silver crates without having to spend real currency.
Please consider this game if you dont mind: a lackluster story that makes up for it with great combat and the much better nemsis system; the fact that it is pretty irrelevant with LoTR canon; how microtransactions have been implimented into a singleplayer game; grinding out quite a bit to get to the true ending; that theres little replayabilty.
From my experience so far, and with plenty of more hours to go, I will easily give this game a 7/10.
You Should Definitely buy this game!

This game is so enjoyable to just sit back and play. Platforming, some puzzles, and lots of secrets. Looks great, plays great, sounds great. It's just great!

Beautiful artwork and animation, an intriguing story and world, well-constructed puzzles that are neither too difficult nor too easy to solve on your own. They're a little silly, but not obtuse, and there's a lot of cute hidden things you can do. Takes the classic point and click game mechanics and executes it wonderfully.
The animation is so good, I could easily see this be a well-animated TV series or something.
The bad:
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic when it does it well. It doesn't always do it well though. During action sequences though, everything feels a little floaty, a little slow, the feeling of panic and danger isn't there too much, especially during the last part of the game. I find this a little ironic considering Shay's plot, but hey.
The voice acting fluctuates between good and lacking a certain oomph during the times that it's needed.
All in all, a very enjoyable game that's worth your time if you enjoy adventure games. :)

Broken Age has been sitting in my library for a while now. I didn't know a lot about the game other than it was a point and click kickstarter funded game that has two acts. I would always read that the first act was great, but the game fell apart during the second act.
In my opinion, these criticisms have merit. The first act was entertaining and kept my interest. Switching between Shay's story and Vella's story was fun, and although the game's events seemed so outlandish, I desperately wanted to know what would happen next. The environments were are different, too. It just made me question everything more. I don't know if this happened to a lot of people, but I saw the big reveal at the end of Act 1 coming from a mile away. It was the only logical conclusion in my mind. Nevertheless, I was disappointed that the areas in Act 2 were more or less the same ones from Act 1 (and they didn't even include everything from Act 1 also, so there are even fewer areas to explore). The big baddies didn't do much for me either. I didn't feel the sense of urgency or intimidation from them. They were just like, "hey we're here and we are better than you so let's be even more better". That was a let down. Also, that ending! I mean come on! All this build up for Shay and Vella to finally speak to each other, and that's all you give me!
Regarding the gameplay, I found this game to be in line with the difficulty of most point and click games out there. Some of the solutions are like duh while some others are more like, since when was it even possible to do this? I didn't appreciate the fact that the Act 1 stories could be played side by side or separately while the Act 2 stories required you to play them side by side. I thought it made for good puzzles, but I felt there should have been a heads up to the player beforehand. Maybe a basic puzzle that lets the player know that hey, from now on there will puzzles in one story that requires you to interact with things from the other. The way they did it was sneaky and makes me go, "oh alright so we're doing this now then, thanks for the heads up"?
I still recommend this game to people because it's a decent title in the genre, and I think Shay and Vella make for great protagonists.
There are no jump scares that I can remember.

Broken Age is a point-and-click story telling game of 2 kids named Vella and Shay. You play the game through the perspectives of each child. At the beginning of the story, Vella is set to be the sacrifice for the Maiden's Feast while Shay is the "space child". Since the game came out a long time ago, I think it's fine to note down what I feel is great and what is bad. The game was moving along fine until the big reveal Mogg Cthora reveal, which was quite good because I was following another train of thought. You will find a lot of tropes in the game varied in some way or another. Like the Big Bad Wolf.
Gameplay-wise, all you have to do is move your mouse over objects and click on them. If there are people, you simply finish the conversation to get the progress. Point and click in iteself is neither good nor bad. Most of the game involves solving puzzles. You go around pointing and clicking on things, like the Deponia games, where the solutions start off simple and logical at the beginning and then absurd and illogical near the end. It is linear gameplay as there's only 1 path to your objective, you must do exactly what the game is programmed to do. There is only 1 pathway for the game to progress.
Conclusion, it's okay and the big reveal did make me feel that it was interesting. However, after the big reveal, the game's storytelling kind of slides downwards. The ending is really kind of a Deus Ex Machina feel.
1. Story Telling, Up to A Point
Luckily for me, I didn't read up on Broken Age before playing the game so the surprises were quite interesting. However, after the surprise, the absurdity began to make me go, "Huh?!".
2. Depth of Thought
The style of liar's storytelling was really good. Everything looked bland, boring and predictable until the big reveal and then, "That was pretty good". They even mentioned how they did the storytelling after the Mog Cthora reveal.
3. Artwork is Pretty
Very simple and aesthetically pleasing. While it is probably targetted at a younger audience, I still appreciate it.
4. Adult References
The talking tree.
1. Absurdly Illogical and Difficult Puzzles
Ticklish Star Weaver? Waiting for the Snake to tire out?
2. Ending
WTF? A terminator reference and then that's it? That's kind of disappointing.
1. Explore more and Delve Deeper Into the Different Lands
Sugar Bunting, Meriloft and Shellmound. You could have made a tiny town to explore and run about instead of just 1 scene. You could have created Sugar Bunting the city and made houses that looked that cakes, pies, tarts and flans. The streets could be paved with gold.... flakes. Meriloft could be a real cloud town with more people. If I were to hazard a guess, 25-50 NPCs would make the town look good. Each town would have 5-10 important characters to interact with.
2. Clues
The 25-50 NPCs add to the feel of bustle and they could serve a function by gossiping about clues to solve the game.

Castle of Illusion is a reimagining of the Sega Genesis game of the same name, and is such a complete overhaul that it feels entirely new. You play as Mickey Mouse on a quest to save his girlfriend, Minnie, from the cluches of Misrabel the Witch in her Castle of Illusion. Although the entire game takes place in this castle, the "illusion" aspect allows for a lot of variety in the levels, including a forest level, a candy-themed level, a level where Mickey is the size of an actual mouse, and more.
The platforming is tight, and there are even short 3D sections to break up the action which flow so well with the 2D areas that it feels like a natural addition. I'm also happy to say that the absurdly difficult platforming section found in the second area of the first level is now entirely optional, so there's no need for alarm if you fall. Speaking of which, since this is based on a game from the 90's, it can be deceptively difficult in its later half which might put off some players, but stick with it and you can get past it.
All in all, it's a fantastic remake and also a wonderful game in its own right. It's easily one of Disney's best games that isn't called Kingdom Hearts.

You will often find, among gamers and critics alike, diverse opinions that state the positives and negatives of various games, with things such as "the game is good" or "the game was too short" or "the controls suck."
This is not the case with Dust: An Elysian Tail.  I have been a gamer my entire life, ostracized as a child in school by the very people now addicted to Call of Duties and Madden NFLs.  I have watched the evolution of gaming from the 8-and-16-bit era of Mario and Sonic, the evolution of PC gaming from text based RPGs to DragonAge and Skyrim.
Of all the games I have played, from casual Runescape to the intensely cerebral Europa Universalis, from the flashy twitch gaming of Smash Brothers to the thought-out fights of Guild Wars.  "Dust: An Elysian Tail" is by far one of the most defining creations in the Gaming Industry.  What makes it more spectacular and amazing is the story of a single man hand-drawing and developing the game from scratch over years, of an indie developer given a chance on Xbox Arcade.
Dead Dodrill has brought to us a game that, in collaboration with secondary writer Alex Kain, and composers Alexander Brandon and HypderDuck Soundworks, defines everything we love about gaming.  He brings us back to the core elements of a video game.
I can say, without a doubt in my mind, that Dust: An Elysian Tail is, by far, the greatest representation of Video Games as an Artform.  If there ever any confusion or concern if games could be consider Art, Dead Dodrill has proved us otherwise.
No amount of praise I could give would satisfy my love for this game.  For 17 years, Blizzard Entertainment's Starcraft franchise has held a special place in my heart as my favorite game of all time.  Upon completion of this artistic masterwork, I can say that this has changed.
Dean Dodrill, Alexander Brandon, and everyone else that not only made this game possible, but brought it to the attention of the general public.  I thank you, and I heartily reccommend this game for anyone.

What can I say...
That were wasted 7 bucks.
Bought this game on friend's recommendation. Also Steam reviews were really good. Never again.
First thing what struck me is that the game presents itself like a person with severe speech disorder. You need a mediator to understand what it asks from you. Practically for every mission, even simplest ones, you going to need to Google. Because stuff is a lot, it's complex and nothing is explained.

Tutorials cover some basics but that's completely different stuff.
For example - first missions are about observation of certain site from correct altitude.
All quest conditions are met - nothing happens. I had to Google to find some good fella on Youtube who has explained that I simply need to click on landing pod and press button "Report" in the context menu...
Second - gameplay is undbearably boring and repetitive. The term is "grind".
Yeah, some of the stuff is pretty complex and when you do it for the first time it's kinda exciting. First ballistic hit, first orbital launch, first Moon slingshot.
But when you do it 30th time... 60th time? Opening first node in tech tree requires like several missions. Second tier - about 10. Third - about 30. And due to tech limitations they gonna be identical. Launch, correct trajectory, land. Nothing changes around and nothing to look at...
I don't usually complain about lack of an eyecandies in games but... Moon? Yeah, you jump higher, but it's just empty surface with pixels of different color. Have you seen Macdoodle's Galacticraft Moon? Way better, though it's just Minecraft blocks.
Also two pence about "realism". Why do you even need complex kinetics and gravitational interactions if you defy simple logic.
First. Your "space program" is all reversed. First - unmanned remotely controlled flights and only then piloted ones.
Second. ICBR can hit spot with 2 meters precision on the other side of the Earth. But to do that trajectory and thrust are calculated and plotted long before rocket reaches launchpad. In KSP I can't even see where I need to go before I adrift about 30 km above Kerbin. Term "flight simulation" rings a bell?
Third. Rocket on the launchpad stands on its nozzles. That's... really off. And then falls and explodes? Is that what comes for humor in this game?
TLDR. If you like games like farm simulators, where you, IRL year after IRL year, do the same stuff. If you like to play LEGO. If you've got patience to build a ship model from matches or a casle from cards, this game could please you. Otherwise  - waste of time and money.

Oh what could have been.  Anyone who starts playing this game is immediately going to enoy it.  It's fun, fast paced, and you even get to care about the little characters you have in your vault.  With that said, it's a freemium game, and although there's nothing inherently wrong with that the point of problem is that with most freemium games they don't want you to lose out on anything, they just want you to spend money.  So here are the main problems I have with this game because... well, there's absolutely nothing to lose except time.
Cons (rather than do the positives, which are numerous because of the joy that Fallout brings to so many fans, here are the negative aspects that make the game totally bland within one week)
- Never lose a character - someone die?  no problem, just give 'caps' that are so numerous you'll never have to worry about risking someone
- Missions - your characters train so fast that missions are ridiculously easy, never having to worry about not making it back
- Family unit - It's a free-for-all when it comes to making babies.  Trust me, you'll start out worrying about the right people making babies so you don't confuse blood lines, etc., and it's pointless.  No penalties for anyone at anytime making babies with whoever they want.  This could have had a "Sims" feel to it and at first I thought it was going to but it doesn't.  It's just, 'hey, need a kid, throw any two together, no worries'.
- Weapons - Good weapons are easy to come by, no work required to get them.
- Bottle & Cappy - these little idiots NEVER STOP showing up, it's every 3 minutes it seems which is so annoying
- Stranger - the Stranger shows up, and at least you have to find him, but he also shows up every 1 minute it seems and it's pointless to keep worrying about him, he just becomes annoying
- Can't attack other vaults - this could have been a great aspect to the game if they included it... but they didn't, so enjoy clicking on your factories every minute and going on a mission every few hours because... well... that's about all you get to do.
I've played for 87 hours, and at first it was a lot of fun to build up my little vault, but it's just in the way now.  I actually sit down to my computer and think about the game and then kind of dread having to do all the little mundane things.  In fact the only reason I've continued is that I hope updates are released or something to make the game more fun for a computer gamer, but alas this game is a tablet/phone intended freemium game, so the game that I want isn't going to be released or 'updated' any time soon.  Oh well... I've got board games to make anyway.

It's been a while since I played a simulation game. The first vault I built I expanded too quickly (too many inhabitants and too many rooms) and it is suffering for it (not enough weapons to fend off intruders and constant issues with power, water, food, the 3 resources you should have plenty of or your vault will fall apart). And money as well. My second vault fares much better, and leaves me actually time to go questing and exploring at a regular basis.
I have not had any issues with "save" of the shelters thusfar, as I read that some experienced in the reviews of this game (although it appears linked after investing rl money in the game, which I have not). I'm also glad to see that after being away for 8+ hrs I didn't return to the vault finding all my dwellers dead, I feared a bit for that, but even though time does not come to a halt upon logging out (babies are actually ready to be born by then, or children grew up, both taking a bit of time) I can start collecting all the resources. So that's pretty cool.
I enjoy the micromanagement (keep tabs on every inhabitant and keep them happy, have enough resources, enough medpacks, weapons, ... ) and the diversity of things to do. There are various ways to earn money (caps) in this game : collect resources, explore, quest, catch the intruder in the brown outfit (not easy, he announces himself with a sound and another sound when he disappears). The caps I received for his capture varies. The most I ever received was 4800ish caps. Which is very welcome in my first vault as an unexpected attack of rodents wiped out almost my entire vault, meaning I had to resurrect them all (the price of ressurection goes up with their level). And this is best done asap, as any surviving inhabitants will get very unhappy very fast (they don't like bodies in their vicinity, and can't say I blame them).
I suggest not to leave the game running when going for a stroll or doing something else meanwhile as things tend to get out of hand then, such as low on the main resources or an attack (and when you don't monitor those, casualties tend to fall unless your habitants are well armed I suppose). You can save and go to the main menu, or save and exit. Talking about saving, I tend to save now and then, not that you can load the game from the last saving point, but force of habit.
I'm playing the game for a few days now, and see myself doing so for a while longer.
Time Manipulation in a nutshell.

This review is coming from a big fan of Mafia 2. I played Mafia 1 also but only once. I was really grabbed by the 2nd game in the series - the setting, the music, the story, the graphics even. All was very well done and with a thought.
Playing Mafia 3 is a disappointment.
-The graphics are horrendous - they are like from a game from 10 years ago - there is a muddy filter applied on your screen. Whoever thought this is ok for 2016 is a challenged person. Thank God there is a custom graphics mod that makes the game look acceptable. If you decide to play this game, look for it: "Nyclix's official colour correction reshade". The thing that it cannot fix though is the draw distance. Stuff at a relatively near distance are a lot blurred. The day/night cycling is a joke too. It is like hitting a dark shadow wall when it becomes night.
-The story as a concept sounds great and there are various cut scenes that are created professionally. However, playing through the story gets boring quick - for every district you have to do one and the same thing - go steal something at place A. Interrogate an informant at place B. After that you face the disctrict boss at one of the same places - A or B. That's about it.
-Most of the Playboy pictures are the same from Mafia 2 :D There are some new collectibles with naked girls but they are drawn.
-Speaking of collectibles - there is no achievement(s) for it. That's a real let down for an achievement hunter and this could have squeezed lots of extra hours of gameplay for some people.
+The music is good as the previous (if you like such type of music), but they did not compose it so it is hard to mess that up.
+A big plus of Mafia 3, especially compared to Mafia 2, is the gameplay length. However, this comes at the expense of quaility. At the time of writing I have played nearly 20 hours and I am not sure that I am nearing the end yet. The previous game could be completed easily in below 10 hours.
Conclusion
Devs nowadays are trying too hard to make new game part of a successful series and they end up making it too different and with less features than the previous. There are lot of examples for this and Mafia 3 has become part of that group.
Anyway, if you are a Mafia fan I would suggest first playing a few missions through alternative means and if you like it - buy the game then.

Currently got 18~ hours and counting - Trying to unlock everything.
First things first - It's an Arena Hack n Slash. Don't expect fancy castles to run through, or a big universe to discover. It is an Arena Hack n Slash after all.
Second - Use a controller. I havn't tried with a keyboard, and don't intend to, but a controller works perfectly. The controls are pretty easy to figure out, and the reactions are smooth. If there's problems you can always rebind the controls to fit, and you can also check the tutorial and the upgrade shop for what abilities are binded to what.
You're playing as a Japanese school girl who is trying to stop her classmate from turning evil due to a possessed sword. The story is not exactly huge - it's basicly just that; You're trying to stop your classmate from turning evil. So the story is not the huge selling point.
There's a couple of different enemies, and as you go through the levels, newer and stronger appears.
You can initially choose 3 difficulties - the AI gets stronger and more aggressive as the difficulty goes up. Once you've completed the initial 3 difficulties (or rather, you just need to win on hard) you unlock Very Hard, which you need to beat to unlock Inferno (from what I've heard atleast - I'm only on Very Hard so far). This means that you'll have to figure your way through the various difficulties by understanding each enemy's mechanics and how to counter them.
There's an upgrade shop in which you can spend points, earned throughout the game by killing enemies, to learn new skills or/and upgrade your current ones to do more damage, have a longer range, consume less energy (Katana Gauge in this game, which is acquired by either using attacks that doesn't require the sword, or by using "Zenshin" which is the withdrawal of the sword to finish bleeding enemies).
The game also has the mechanic of "bleeding" - in which the enemies becomes more vulnerable, and can take extra damage from "Zenshin", which is a type of finisher, that, actually, also serves as a healing ability if enough attacks are executed.
There's also the ability to Guard, Perfect Guard (+ counter) and Flourish.
Guard is, well, where you hold the parry button. You can guard most attacks, but regular guard can also be broken if enough hits are taken in a row.
Perfect Guard is when you parry on the timing of when an attack will hit you - You can Perfect Guard anything (though sometimes you'll be hit by several things in a row, which means you might not be able to perfect guard the next attack in time). You can, if upgraded / bought, use a counter after perfect guarding to deal back some damage.
Flourish.... The strongest ability in the game, but incredibly hard to learn aswell. It's like perfect guard, however, you have to be even better in the timing. The difference between Flourish and Perfect Guard is (except you have to "buy" Flourish) is that Flourish is an attack - not a parry. Flourish essentially uses the attack of the enemy, where right before said attack actually hits you, to counter attack with an incredibly power attack. This skill is most probably essential to get down and learn if it's of the interest to beat Very Hard / Inferno.
The game is fairly short per difficulty, but the next difficulties takes more and more time because you have to go through more and more enemies.
To make it short:
Pros:
- A smooth Arena Hack n Slash (comboing is pretty easy)
- Easy to learn, difficult to master (I suck at using Flourish)
- Nice artstyle, which is also appealing.
- Unlockables
- Entertaining if interested in Japanese, and hack and slash.
- Controller recommended (I find this to be a Pro, as I prefer when these types of games needs to be used with a controller - Keyboard / Mouse just doesn't fit hack and slash).
- Japanese school girl (Pantsu!)
- Various mechanics (especially Bleed, Perfect Guard, Flourish)
Cons:
- Repetitive (Most people don't like repetitive game, though I enjoy this game atleast)
- Short / Underdeveloped story (this games selling point is the actual gameplay for an Arena Hack n Slash, not the story).
I recommend it, with a score of probably 8/10 in the Hack n Slash genre.

Tried the free weekend which wasn't actually the Directors Cut. Even that version is a pretty good game. It suffers from poor inventory management which is extremely tedious, you have a stash but it's far too small to be of much use. As the game has an encumbrance mechanic and you need to gather a lot of items to ensure you get all the ammo you need it's easy to become overencumbered. The tutorial tips aren't frequent or prominent enough to explain the mechanics as you go. For instance there's an Ambush/Overwatch option but it's weak. Given that ammo is hard to come by and it's possible to run out you can't afford to take lots of shots that you don't need to. However if you have several characters setup for an Ambush as soon as an enemy comes around the corner they all fire at once using up a lot of ammo if the first shot kills it (rather than fire one at a time as they would in other games). I found myself relying on walkthroughs and guides an awful lot to understand where I was supposed to go and what I needed to do because the save game mechanic is a pain. The UI is not that great throughout the game but when you save regularly (and you should as mistakes are costly) you end up with a lot of old game saves you don't need. There's no tickbox so you can easily delete them though you have to highlight each on in turn, choose delete and then confirm. Again that's tedious. What I can't say is which features are improved in the Directors Cut but it appears to be well regarded so I imagine you'd find a lot of issues have been fixed. I suggest you find a comparison review to see what the practical upgrades are. I'd certainly be happy to buy the DC version so I can complete it at some point but I suspect it's still going to be quite slow to play through. It's important to note that it's played in real time until combat starts. If you like the Shadowrun games you'll like this.

Just finished the game and christ am I disappointed.
I've poured nearly 100 hours into this game for what I thought would be the gaming equivalent of going on an expensive dinner date and making passionate love all night to a beautiful woman, when in reality what I experienced was getting molested by a tramp in a back alley behind M&S.
I love LotR, as I'm sure most people here do. Playing this game has made me rewatch the whole saga.
First of all, I loved this game. It felt just like the last one, but better. Things had been made bigger, there were more quests, the nemesis system had been expanded to cover armies and fortresses, the inclusion of armor and weapons. It all was going so great.
Then I got to the Shadow Wars in Act IV. It was clear that the people who made this thought "We're barely going to scratch 12 hours average play time on this thing if we don't add some repetitve, mind-numbingly boring defense sequence to it". And that's exactly what we got. I built this amazing army, the likes of which could rival the Dark Lord of Mordor himself. Now I must defend it. 6 stages later, I start to think that this is a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. But I'm sure it'll all be worth it. The game is going great. I'm at level 60, and recruiting stronger, more powerful orcs into my army. I can't wait to see how mighty my orcs become after all this.
Oh, there's a cutscene and that's the end. Nevermind.
I should have listened to my friend when he said the ending made him hate it. Because now I feel the exact same way.
+ Like the first game but with a bit more
+ Little touches that make your experience feel unique
+ Armor and weapons (although it could have been done better)
- The Shadow Wars
- Microtransactions/Lootboxes
- Interesting characters that just disappear half-way through the story.
Also, I don't know if it was just my experience, but the nemesis system didn't seem nearly as robust as it did in the last game. I rarely saw orcs come back from the dead. Whereas in Shadow of Mordor, I had orcs coming back all the time and mocking me. That made my experience really personal and enjoyable. There was a lack of that this time.
Play it if you like LotR. If you don't, don't play this. You'll be pulling your hair out halfway through it.

There are simply too many good things to say about this game.
The story is compelling, the characters find an immediate place in your heart, and their interactions across two intertwined plot lines create an amazing and dynamic playstyle. Every character is flawlessly voiced by a cast which was clearly selected with great care. The art style is so beautiful, it sends you into the realm of children's rhymes and fairy tales. This is a relaxing game which can be categorised as an idle game since it does not really require any interaction from your end. The mountain - whose God you are supposed to be - will slowly start growing its own plants and trees, items will soon fall on top of it and as time passes by there will be seasonal changes. I do not know if it has any "endings" - there are some achievements that certainly require you to leave the game on for hundreds of hours.
But that is the point. You start it and you leave it on. It has a relaxing music (very short ambient tracks played periodically) which really calms you while other applications are running (for instance, you are working on a finance report). Some keyboard buttons will generate music as well as strange weather phenomena and by applying a certain combination you can even create a meteorite that will eventually destroy your "tamagochi" (unless you press some buttons in quick succession). This annihilation sequence has a particularly haunting piece of music quite similar to the one in 2001 Space Odyssey.
I do not usually play such simulation-like software but I decided to give it a try after finding out it was published by Double Fine Productions, the very company that was responsible for games such as Brütal Legend. You can give it a go if you like trying out new things but let's make one thing clear: getting all the achievements will be very time-consuming.

If you let the bad press about the completely skippable loot boxes turn you away from this game, you'll be missing out on a very good and unique experience that isn't likely to be featured in another game until, perhaps, a sequel to this one is made.

In terms of gameplay second part of the adventures of the iconic characters - a complete failure. A few hours of dull, repetitive shootings, coupled with stupid opponents AI and without any hint of a coherent cooperation between the players. But there are two things that don't allow to call K&L2 a complete crap - the atmosphere and style. These two findings make incredible - flavored with poor gameplay and converted the seemingly simple story into the art-house drama, full of tragedy, pain and revenge.
Its A very fun game to mess around with, I recommend it to anyone who wants to be creative and silly.

What makes this game fun is that you can play around with angles and see how a small change in the magnitude or angle of your vector can completely change the path of the ball. Isn't mathematics great?
You can also try to get the high score by bouncing the ball against the walls as many times as you can while still completing the objective which is a fun "side goal" while you are playing.
The game becomes more difficult as you progress through the levels, but you can make a level has hard as you want it to be, depending if you want to get a sick high score or not. Even on the more difficult levels, it is still challenging in a pleasant way.
Speaking of pleasant, the music was pleasant, calm and didn't annoy me. A bit of calm background music while you are casually playing with your ball is always good.
The game shows effort has been put into it and I haven't experienced any bugs. The game has some fun mechanics, such as getting points for bouncing against the wall, breaking cracked blocks and cob webs which allow you to re-aim your ball.
Perhaps in the future, more game mechanics could be added. A level editor would be nice too, so people can make their own levels and release them on the Steam Workshop.

Bought this game on friend's recommendation. Also Steam reviews were really good. Never again.
First thing what struck me is that the game presents itself like a person with severe speech disorder. You need a mediator to understand what it asks from you. Practically for every mission, even simplest ones, you going to need to Google. Because stuff is a lot, it's complex and nothing is explained.

Tutorials cover some basics but that's completely different stuff.
For example - first missions are about observation of certain site from correct altitude.
All quest conditions are met - nothing happens. I had to Google to find some good fella on Youtube who has explained that I simply need to click on landing pod and press button "Report" in the context menu...
Second - gameplay is undbearably boring and repetitive. The term is "grind".
Yeah, some of the stuff is pretty complex and when you do it for the first time it's kinda exciting. First ballistic hit, first orbital launch, first Moon slingshot.
But when you do it 30th time... 60th time? Opening first node in tech tree requires like several missions. Second tier - about 10. Third - about 30. And due to tech limitations they gonna be identical. Launch, correct trajectory, land. Nothing changes around and nothing to look at...
I don't usually complain about lack of an eyecandies in games but... Moon? Yeah, you jump higher, but it's just empty surface with pixels of different color. Have you seen Macdoodle's Galacticraft Moon? Way better, though it's just Minecraft blocks.
Also two pence about "realism". Why do you even need complex kinetics and gravitational interactions if you defy simple logic.
First. Your "space program" is all reversed. First - unmanned remotely controlled flights and only then piloted ones.
Second. ICBR can hit spot with 2 meters precision on the other side of the Earth. But to do that trajectory and thrust are calculated and plotted long before rocket reaches launchpad. In KSP I can't even see where I need to go before I adrift about 30 km above Kerbin. Term "flight simulation" rings a bell?
Third. Rocket on the launchpad stands on its nozzles. That's... really off. And then falls and explodes? Is that what comes for humor in this game?
TLDR. If you like games like farm simulators, where you, IRL year after IRL year, do the same stuff. If you like to play LEGO. If you've got patience to build a ship model from matches or a casle from cards, this game could please you. Otherwise  - waste of time and money.

A true gem of a game with clear work and effort into it, that I can say I had more fun with then any game this year. The artwork is fantastic - the voice acting and lip syncing works really well too, and the enviroments are really fun to explore and treck across. Its not a necessary long game though - you could probably beat it in two sittings if you have the time to kill. But thats okay, because what length it does have it has much quality in. This game has loads of memorable, loveable characters, espically your nimbat friend, Fidget (Shes so darn cute.)
The combat was where things started to fall apart slightly. For the most part, I found myself spinning around the battle with the arial dust storm while using Fidget's fire attacks, and while thats great and flashy, it gets really tiring after a while. Dust's ground combos are meh, and I feel as if he should be able to cover his back somehow. Theres no progression in our tailed friend's attacks, so the attacks do start feeling dull after you have done the same move multiple times over. Nethertheless, while its improvable for sure, the combat does okay for the game!
There are tons of sidequests, and I myself didn't have the patience to complete them all, but if your looking to lengthen the game, they are there. This isn't a game high in replayability, but its one with characters you might just want to go and see from time to time. Did I mention the music is great? Cause it is.
The story is fine but its not the most amazing of them all. Its filled with cliche's and doesn't progress much, and your hit the most hard with story aspects near the end of the game. There is room for improvments but it carrys the game just fine, and despite not being the best, is filled with charm to the max. Its a charming tale for sure, not the best you've ever read, but motivating enough to keep you driven.

my first impression was the incredibly appealing intro animation. the narrator does his job perfectly and we are introduced to Isaac and his Mom.
then the game begins.
if you know what a rogue-like is, this is a great example of it. level almost always has a dedicated number of rooms, but the layout/enemies/drops are highly randomized, creating a unique gaming experience every single run. now we hear that often, but in this game, it is especially true. we have such a simplistic foundation for a game, but it is a definitely deep and highly thought-out game.
prepare to get frustrated. beating the boss for my first time took me at least 20 hours of play time. it took another 10 hours to beat it again. what's fun about this, the game is evolving, since you're always unlocking new items/enemies/dungeons by achieving certain goals. and it gets increasingly harder to do it, although you are provided with tools to achieve victory, if you know what you're doing.
there is an element of luck here, of course, i thought so too. but actually you can learn to do a lot of things that increase your chances of coming into the very best of items. it's not only the skill of dodging projectiles, it's also knowledge of where to go, how to act and what risks to take. and there's a lot to learn for a newcomer here.
to sum up - i'm writing this with only 30+ hours of play time, that's 4-5 days for me. sounds like a lot, but i'm not remotely bored of it yet. and i will be heading back to the basement.
there is always a new journey to be experienced.

This game is often called a GTA clone, but I’d rather call it a clone of The Godfather game from 2006. Of course, that game was heavily inspired by (read: ripped off) GTA, but the point is that the gameplay loop of Mafia III is almost identical* to the gameplay loop of The Godfather. And I think by examining what makes The Godfather good (maybe not great, but I enjoyed it quite a bit), we can see why Mafia III fails.
In both games, you’re an up-and-coming mobster. Both games have a strong story – extra points to M3 for having an original one, not propped up by a classic movie. (The opening cutscenes in M3 are some of the best I’ve seen in any game, and the gameworld is beautifully constructed. BTW if you “don’t like politics in your games,” this one’s not for you, go watch paint dry or something.) In both games, the primary gameplay consists of hopping from racket to racket, extorting them and adding their income to your empire.
The main problem with M3, as I see it, is that it doesn’t move past this at all. In The G-Father, you’d bust up a storefront, rough up the owner, then there was a little minigame where you’d try to get as much income as you could out of the racket boss without crossing the line, losing his loyalty altogether. It was a brilliant way to break up the monotony of the loop, flavor the gameplay, and add challenge and variability to your earned income. In Mafia 3, you kill the guards, press one key to take-down the racket boss, then press another to recruit him.
Another point of comparison: empire growth. Mafia 3 has a ‘meh’ system wherein you take the rackets in a region, kill the lower mob dudes, then the slightly higher mob dudes, then the region is yours. In The Godfather, it’s basically the same idea, except all of your actions take place in the context of the five families. So when you start taking Barzini rackets, the Barzinis react with aggression! What a concept! In M3, all your enemies just passively wait for you to come kill them.
Which brings us to an even more basic level of gameplay where Mafia 3 fails to excite: combat. M3’s shooting is solid, and taking out a bunch of guys is definitely fun. But there’s nothing more to it than that. In The Godpappy, they had these great contextual kills. You would take out a guy’s guards, shoot the gun out of his hand, then grab him by the collar and toss him off a bridge or into a furnace. They were challenging to set up, and satisfying when they paid off. In M3, you press a key to stab the guy in one of four ways.
So in general, M3 falls flat because it can’t move past its boring, old, hackneyed mechanics to make something interesting. It sets you up to think you’re going to play this exciting game about a young black man seizing power in an environment that doesn’t want him to have any, but then it collapses under the weight of both its expectations and the sheer boredom of the gameplay loop. It’s especially frustrating because the game does so many things so well that it makes you wonder why so many things are so uninspired.
With all that said, this is not a bad game by any stretch of the imagination. If you’re into games with strong environment and story, and you don’t mind a little grind, you will probably get a lot out of this game.
This is already pretty long, so I’m going to end here. Thanks for reading 

So, after spending $60 for this game I would say that it is not something that I wish I bought. The game itself was okay. Graphics and performance left something to be desired. Story line was fantastic and I loved the way they moved through it they way they did, no spoilers. However, the missions themselves were all repetative. Basically do the same thing over and over to get the district under your control and then go kill the boss. You can try to be stealthy to add some flare to the game but it does not give you anything if you do. So you may as well go in there guns blazing because you will most likely survive it. There was little to no customizing your character, Lincoln Clay. Mafia 2 at least offered something to the effect of changing your characters clothes, I assumed this would have been added upon. The only way you can get upgrades on your vehicles is through unlocking them by giving your liutenants rackets and upping their income. But there is no changing the color or wheels or plates or such in the like. Side missions pretty much did not exist in my opinion. There were missions that were "optional" but they all played a part to the overal storyline. The only real side missions were the missions you run as favors for your guys but even then it is pretty much either go here and kill or go here and steal then bring back. Way to simple for that. I expected much more from the game for all the hype that was driven from the previews and I can safely say that I am disappointed. This game is really played for the story I would say. In the end you can chose how it ends essentially 1 of 3 ways. Which were all pretty satisfying actually. I will end it there. If you enjoyed the game, good on you. I would still recommend Mafia 2 over this.

An action game, with survival horror elements, that plays out like a psychological thriller tv show.
Exellent devotion to the style, superb writing and atmosphere thick enough that it actually makes you fearful when the lights go out. Sometimes I'll find myself nervous when wandering through even a slightly dimmed hallway during the day time. If this game were a T.V. show it would be the soul reason I watch the lightbox.
The gameplay makes it even more interesting, forcing you to watch the axe murders creep towards you while you desperately cling to the ever dimming flash light and hold your triggerfinger for just the right moment. It's great, and the game loves to give you moments of pure release after an hour long build-up. Well paced, and tense as a killer on jury duty.
Even if you know the story front to back, it's worth playing just for the atmosphere it emits. You can see the enemies coming from a mile away, and you'll still panic when they get close.
It's unfortunate that it won't be up for purchase later, due to some licensing agreement for the music that plays at the end of each chapter, but after putting a few hours into the game, I can see that the TV show style remedy went for would simply not work without it. They devoted their entire game to the theme, and they wouldn't have it any other way.
They sold their souls to the devil to fulfill the directors vision, and to their credit... It was quite the vision.

[May contain spoilers!] Mafia III is an open world crime game set in the year 1968. You play as Lincoln Clay, a Vietnam war veteran out for revenge for the killing and betrayal of his family. I don't write many reviews but I felt like I needed to let people know what's up with this game, without talking about graphics.
Seeing as this game is "open-world", I should open with that. I believe that a succesful open world game should have at least 100 hours worth of content excluding collectibles. This means that there should be an abundance of side missions, activities such as drinking, mini games such as poker or darts, races with time trials, customization such as clothing stores and barbers and many, many more. Mafia III does
have
of these features, making the world feel redundant and not open at all. Sure, there are gatherings of NPCs who converse with one another, street performers, drunkards and sometimes ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (which you can't interact with), but in all honesty? They are just there to make the world
like it's alive. To
a "thriving, open world." This is a game where you're given access to fast cars, but also a game where there aren't any races(!) That's like a gun without bullets! There are some racist aspects of the world, like when police officers look at you just because you're black, but I didn't once see any police officers harassing black people, as they showed in the trailers. Racism is still a very controversial aspect of this game, as the main derogatory racist terms are used very often and are often emphasized. It's quite shocking sometimes.
The devs called the world of New Bordeaux the "main" character. Although as far as I can tell, this "main character" absolutely has
.
I played through the campaign and all of the side missions in 38 hours, taking my time and not rushing. I played stealthily a lot of the time, which probably made the game longer. That is terrible for the price I paid! 38 hours to FINISH an "open world" game? With all of the side content excluding collectibles? I probably spent 38 hours playing
in GTA 5. What a joke!
Mafia III is a gritty and bloody tale of revenge and pain, with some heavy racism thrown in the mix. It's honestly an enticing story and definitely its strongest suit. I feel that the story was very well orchestrated as a documentary (quite unique) but that there was also quite some "filler" in between. The story is probably the best part about this game, as it is with all Mafia games, but don't go in expecting Mafia II.
Sal Marcano is the main antagonist. Throughout the whole game, he is made out to be the most relentless, baddest mother-♥♥♥♥er in the game and YOU are supposed to feel as if killing him is the penultimate goal.
He's only really a "ruthless mob boss"
. The only time you ever see Sal Marcano kill anyone is in the intro, when the black mob is betrayed. For the REST of the game he is sat inside a single room, making phone calls, talking to his son and drinking whiskey. That's not what you expected, is it? The trailers didn't show that, did they? You thought he'd be out gunning ♥♥♥♥ers down with a thompson alongside his son because he's supposed to be the bad guy. Supposed to be.
The facial expressions and tonality of his voice elaborate on the emotions he is feeling (great voice acting!) but sitting down throughout the whole game, waiting for Lincoln to come to you and not taking any PHYSICAL action? Sure sounds like
all-right. He has influence over other people, but not once does he exit his room to hunt down Lincoln himself. Instead, relying on everyone else around him. I thought people were supposed to be
of this man? Not his minions? I thought this man was supposed to scare
? This man hides away at the top of his Casino, drinking whiskey. Good depiction of his influence as a mob boss -- bad depiction of himself as a man of action.
-
Rememeber in the trailer where it showed you can fight people in the arena and kill members of the KKK? Those are only
mission, and are not the main parts!
The arena is a very small part of another level,  made only to progress said level. There are 3 targets, with the same AI. You can "woo" the crowd or "insult" the crowd, but this does
- it is useless as an addition to the game, made only to fuel the hype.
The members of the Klan in the single mission about the Klan are not even your main targets, and again, is a useless addition, simply made to add content to the game and fuel the racial controversy further.
I honestly felt very misled by the trailers. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when I learned what these parts really were:
The main missions are very, very repetitive. You have to take down district underbosses in order to take down the district lieutenants/capos. To do this, you have to go through the ordeal of smashing valuables, killing people, stealing money, disrupting events and interrogating informers. It gets very tedious because they literally COPY and PASTE these missions to every other district whilst changing the
of what it is! For example: "disrupt the meeting" in Downtown becomes "disrupt the orgy" in the French Ward. Honestly, the repetition got to me at one point and made me want to play solely to reach the end. I wasn't excited to kill Sal Marcano anymore. I just wanted the game to be over.
The gunplay in this game is VERY satisfying, but the stealth mechanics in this game are the barest of bare. The AI are incredibly stupid when it comes to stealth - even on "hard" difficulty which doesn't seem to change anything apart from adding health to the AI (which still felt♥♥♥♥♥♥easy). Their vision cones are terrible and their "logic" just isn't there. There were multiple instances where I should have been seen. But alas, this is not a stealth game. It takes almost half a game to acquire a gun with a suppressor though, and even then, it's a "favour" from one of your 3 underbosses!
Burke, Vito, and Cassandra are who you will assign districts to. They will reward you with perks, "markers" (which buy services such as shutting off the phones), upgrades and weapons. Something I should warn you about is:
Depending on who you assigned a district to, that upgrade is linked to them. So I ended up finishing the game with upgraded health from Vito, no upgraded bomb ammo from Burke (because of the amount of districts I
give to him), and a fully upgraded car but no races to use the car in!
Not being able to have all the perks or upgrades is VERY stupid!!
The side missions don't even work properly. They bugged out and wouldn't let me finish them, so I couldn't even receive "max earn" (income) from the underbosses -- "Steal the boat" - the boat doesn't spawn. "Steal the truck" - the truck doesn't spawn. Even on the third and final stage of any of these side missions, the objective pops up, but the map marker doesn't, making them feel redundant and making you feel stupid.
This game is littered with bugs. From falling through floors to being detected through walls to collision on objects that shouldn't have collision on them to FLYING through the air in a car because you hit a BUMP... I'm not joking!

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings improves virtually every aspect of the first game in a major way. The graphics are a major leap forward for the franchise. The game's visual prowess is also a result of outstanding artistic design. That said, there are some weird graphical bugs on occasion, but they are not enough to pull the player out of the story. The story has many layers and weaves a compelling narrative as a result of your actions and strong writing (most of the time, some things come off as immature in my opinion). The combat system is engaging as a function of the various ways you can approach various encounters: Should you drink potions to boost your stats, use overwhelming force from you sword and secondary weapons, or rely on magic to gain the upper hand? Those who like thinking tactically before entering a fray will find a great deal to like. However, death can come swift to new players as my roommate who is new to the action/rpg genera can attest. Bumping the game difficulty down to easy should help ease people into the experience if they rather focus on enjoying the story as opposed to being challenged by the game’s difficulty.
If you have not played the first game, I imagine the story may be difficult to follow at times. That said, the game does a good job of fleshing out its characters and provides ample reading for those interested in understanding the intricacies of the game’s plot and the politics amongst the various warring factions. Sometimes things are referred to in this game during the course of a conversation that will leave the uninitiated scratching their head, but that's just a guess.
Overall this is one of the best action/rpgs I have played in the past few years and whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a strong narrative in their games.

I fell in love with Natural-Selection 1 when it first came out, played hundreds and hundreds of hours until finally, NS2 came out. The alpha and beta releases seemed interesting but you could barely play them because of the horrible performance. Thankfully, the game has been optimized since then and it runs decently these days (Obviously still not the best optimization when it comes to newer games.) That aside, it's one of the few games that successfully blends in RTS and FPS gameplay where you need a commander to build structures, order your field players around the map and eventually win the game. I've never fully enjoyed multiplayer games where you can go around solo and kill everything by yourself. Surely that's possible in NS2 as well if your opposing team doesn't know how to work together. Teamplay is the key word here, it basically forces you and your teammates to work together in order to win the game.
I've bought this game so many times it's ridiculous. Pre-ordered it three times, bought several copies after the release and even got the humble bundle package a couple of times just so it could get more active players.
Community is friendly and mods are keeping the game alive and kicking, whether you want different models or some UI tweaks, it's all available in the steam workshop.
Overall, it's a multiplayer game where teamwork is absolutely required. Don't like that? Then the game is not for you. However, if that concept seems like it could keep you entertained, then don't hesitate to buy. Highly recommended!

I recommend this game with some very strong reservations.
I downloaded and played this game during the free play period.  The game is definitely dated - they don't make games like this anymore.  This is both a good thing and a bad thing.  The game had a good story (from what I could see) with consequences for taking action in one direction over another.  None of this modern “follow the yellow brick road and if you die you pick up where you left off,” and “don't forget to mash the buttons in the correct order” crap.  This game will punish you for making poor decisions.  Don't invest in certain talents?  You will fail missions.
The game also chooses to use an isometric design for how you view the world.  This makes it awkward to control the camera, and often times puts you in positions where your character can see further than you can because of the angle of the camera changes as you zoom in or zoom out.  It made controlling the characters difficult at times.
Like many others who wrote reviews, I played the game and sought to purchase the game while it was on sale, only to be notified that I already owned the game.  Now that the free play is over, so is the sale price.  I guess that means that it is time to wait until it is on sale again.

As someone who thoroughly enjoyed Shadow of Mordor, I think that Shadow of War takes steps in the right direction.  Compared to SOM, SOW feels less restrictive in how it plays, meaning movement feels more free and free-running is actually fun.  Swordplay can be challenging, due to the different classes of Uruk having the player adapt to what they are fighting (Assassins, Tricksters, Savages, etc.).  This prevents the player from just pressing right-click/space and has them develop strategies in order to efficiently combat their foes.  So far, I've noticed only a couple of glitches that don't happen very often. One, that happened once, was when I started the game and was in Minis Ithil, when i vaulted over a bench.  Now, vaulting over a bench might not sound bad, except when the bench was against the wall, causing me to fall through the earth.  This only happened once so it didn't really effect my experience.  The other, more prominent glitch was when I was walking across these high-hanging wire things (I honestly have no idea what they are), and Talion came to a stop when I got to the end of these wires, as if something was blocking him.  This happened maybe 6 times throughout my playtime but I countered it by just jumping off.
This is where some spoilers might appear, so I'll try to be careful.  But as far as story goes, it really had me going at some points.  There are a couple twists that surprised me, one towards the middle of the game, and one big one towards the end
.  The story in this game is much more deep in my opinion than SOM, and does a great job intertwining the Nemesis System within the main story.  With this game I was feeling a bit "completionisty" so I decided to find all the memories, artifacts, etc. which there is quite a lot of.  The ithildin collecting is interesting because it's a good way for newer players to earn their first legendary armor set.  Now, unlike most people who gave this game a negative score, I actually completed Shadow Wars.  Yes, I do believe it's a bit drawn out and it can be really really really difficult, but I think it does a good job portraying
in that it is supposed to take place over the course of decades.  I also think it's a good way to earn that last bit of XP to get to lvl 60, as well as get lvl 60 Uruks.
This is a little off topic but I'd first like to share my personal experiences with Shadow Wars...
I'd first want to say PLEASE TONE DOWN THE "NO CHANCE" PERK.  I've lost many fortresses due to this perk, then I'd have to fight the new warchiefs to disable defences, then assemble my ranks, then recapture it, taking another hour of gametime away.  Yes I know, Shadow Wars is meant to be challenging, but No Chance really got my goat on this one.
I suppose that could be a negative trait of this game, some captain perks appear more often then they should.
I think that online so far is doing okay.  Right now, defence ratings and assualt ratings being used for matchmaking is a good idea and that it doesn't result in a one-sided battle.  I also really like the idea that you can raid your own fortress and see how well your defenses hold up.  The downside to online is that some people somehow have lvl 65 Uruks, which isn't possible without cheats, so I'd get on that before it becomes unfair for other players.

Dust is, in a word, amazing. Simply outstanding. It has been a long time since I've played such a remarkable platformer. It caters to every aspect of what makes up a good game. The visuals are sharp and beautiful, complemented by the grand, fantastical soundtrack, which both work in tandem to create these big, lush environments that perfectly match the tone of the well-crafted story. It's a classic tale, to be sure, but it still succeeds in taking the familiar and making it unique, clever, and memorable. The cast is colorful and lively, resulting in natural interactions that really help to establish the world around the characters. The humor is genuine and witty, the intense moments are properly gripping, and the two never clash. Every event has its time in the spotlight and gets its due attention. And when the climactic parts take the stage, they truly steal the show. It was at these highs that I felt the most astounded.
But, of course, there's the gameplay. The wonderful, flowing, visceral mechanics that really complete this epic. The eponymous hero, Dust, controls like the warrior you've always dreamed of. He's agile, acrobatic, and swings his sword with ferocity and grace. The controls are intuitive, combat always feels rich and rewarding, and I never felt a cheap death or a fight unfair. If anything, the fiends in this world never stood a chance. There's nothing more satisfying than cutting through hordes of enemies, launching them to the heavens, and sending them into oblivion with the combined power of sword and sorcery. You really feel the gravity of every power, ability, and upgrade you get, and it's great to backtrack and rediscover new places in secrets in old maps. And even better when you're clever enough to discover them early! The game never lets you down or leaves you bored, or wanting more than it can deliver. It's fun, challenging, and cinematic. Dust is worth every cent and second invested in this epic tale.

Broken Age is a classic point-and-click adventure in three acts.  You play as the characters Vela and Shay who come from very different worlds yet find their lives entangled.  You are able to traverse different scenes and interact with the people and things you find in each.  The cursor helpfully changes to note something that you can interact with.  In addition, when hovering an item you also get a contextual clue that your action is at least an option, if not always the right one.  There is a vast expanse of spoken dialog covering a wide range of actions you might take.  It is nice to find as you will often try using your limited items on everything you encounter.  The humor is light, but effective.  You may recognize some celebrity voice actors who took part in it.  Overall, a fine game for say, $5-$10.  Each act can be finished in a sitting and there isn't much replay value (even though there are achievements that might try to convince you otherwise).

This game is a Real Shiny Jewel.
Most of the "old-school & rough KSP veterans" are going to shoot me down but I must say that... mods will make this Real Shiny Jewel even more fabulous.
With the base game you will probably struggle with orbital mechanics at its finest, looking for questionable hard interplanetary transfers, gravital wells snorkeling, slinghots manoeuvres planning; maximizing fuel efficency while considering Oberth effect; make a marble statue of Tsiolkovsky in your garden while your spaceship miserably burn like on Eve's (Venus) upper atmosphere and so on. Landing on the MÜN and on Minmus are maybe the first two truly engaging rookie's challenges, shortly after the displacement of a more-or-less healty ship on LKO (Low Kerbin Orbit, that's Low Earth Orbit - LEO - equivalent).
In the other hand, with mods you can do the same things as above - with better accuracy & more tuneup - and a lot of other things, i.e. make your orbital space stations quite a bit more productive adding "3D parts printing" on board.
I cannot recommend this game enough. Just buy it, with or without discount price. Don't lift a white flag when you fail for the 100th time. Don't give up. Study. Ask 4 help. Watch online video tutorials. When you finally tame the horse, a new adventure can begin.
There's no hand holding in this game. Only a failure after another failure. And for each failure, the knowledge; and inside the knowledge, the beauty.
The only thing that IMHO must be pointed out is that instead of adding new content, Squad \ Take Two Interactive seems to favour the "golden the pill" philosophy. And so they craft localization-oriented works that are undoubtedly helpful to catch more users from around the world, but simple aren't useful as, for example, embed "Kerbal Engineer Redux" mod's features inside of the core game itself.
Not to mention the additional highly suggested mod Mechjeb, a "noob and less noob swiss knife" that, even if the original author (Cybutek) was hired by Squad team, is still an outer utility instead of became a perfectly integrated set of functionalities that extend and improve the original game mechanics.
To summarize all of this, if you're a nerd or a geek that loves space, and preferably math, grab this game now!

K&L2 is a cover shooter with a very good single-player/two player story mode and novel themed multiplayer modes. Its story mode is very tightly written and well-voiced, and it took me through gunfight to gunfight at a very quick pace. MP is more straightforward, but is more involved than other shooters' MP modes. All are co-op/team based to an extent, but they all boil down to earning the highest score at the other criminals' (your teammates) expense.
The shooting feels appropriate, the cover shooting system is quite good (for a cover shooter) and moves at a very frantic pace. It's almost always easier to survive by moving over cover to get closer or to flank. The guns are interesting if not punchy, firing blindly from behind cover is possible, and fire extinguishers and gas cans provide meaty explosions when thrown and shot. Solid, if not innovat
K&L2 is exceedingly stylish, and it received too much undeserved negativity for its divisive art design. I love the hell out of it.

This game has a lot to hate.
First of all, the setting is... well, other reviewers are correct - it is quite literally a Tumblr simulator. You play as a whiny emo hipster who's studying in an artsy hipster art school trying to become an artsy hipster photographer. You have a polaroid, with which you seemingly take tons of pictures, yet you whine about how those cool rich kids get the best equipment - and never stop to think just how much money you spend on polaroid cartridges. You're interacting with other artsy emo whining pretentious hipsters, you're constantly whining about how lonely you are, how everyone hates you, how everyone misunderstands you, how you have no place in this world, whine, whine, whine. The dialogue is sooooo cringey and choke full of "cool" language it's far beyond the "old guys trying to be hip" - it's literally a non-stop facepalm.
Then there's the game mechanics. And i'm not talking about this game being a walking simulator - i knew what i was getting into, and it is, in fact, a walking simulator. What i'm talking about is the illusion of choice this game creates. The truth is, you don't. The game stops you from rewinding time at arbitrary moments, and quite a few times it pushes you into a cutscene just when you were going to rewind and make another decision. And the choices you make end up being meaningless - the story changes only slightly. Yeah, you can save Kate, or she can die. Either way, the story would continue as before, and there won't be any profound impact on the story whichever choice you make. Well, thank god there were no quick-time events.
Music deserves a separate mention. It sucks. You're playing as a whiny artsy emo hipster, and you're listening to whiny artsy emo hipster music. And you'll be listening to that crap throughout the whole damn game. The main theme is actually pretty decent, but the rest of it is the kind of pretentious acoustic guitar-laced crap you'd hear in a hipster anti-cafe. Even the supposedly "punk" Chloe listens to artsy emo hipster punk music, not _actual_ punk music. It creates the emo whiny artsy hipster atmosphere, but by god do i not want this atmosphere anywhere near me.
Finally, the characters are garbage. There are a bunch of pretentious hipster crybabies, your run-off-the-mill "mean ♥♥♥♥♥es who somehow have good hearts deep down inside", then there's Chloe (who is the only character worth anything in this game), and then there a bunch of token bad guys (who somehow end up being whiny crybabies as well) and a villain. The villain is lame and it's not really explained how did he do what he did, why he did it, what are his motivations (beyond the artsy hipster emo "capturing the moment" schtick) - nothing. It's a standard movie psychopath - not the "No Country For Old Men" kind of villain, but more of a cheap Hollywood blockbuster "turns out he was a Hydra agent all along!" kind of villain.
You're probably wondering why am i giving this game a positive score, when i just unloaded a ton of♥♥♥♥♥♥on its head? Well, however bad the above stuff is, the game does have its redeeming qualities.
First of all, it's beautiful. The art style is fantastic, and the slightly cartoonish depiction of the world works very well to create a laid-back small town atmosphere. Aside from the characters and the whole "art scene" crap, the setting is actually brilliant. The huge storm is, well, it's a sight onto itself.
The game mechanics, however few there are (it's a walking simulator, after all) are kind of innovative and cool. While it sometimes gets really tiring to trace through exact "good" options, it's mostly enjoyable and engaging.
The voice acting is great. I mean, dialogue sucks, but the actual voice acting is great and really enjoyable. Motion capture and animation is mostly pretty good as well.
The plot... If i were to summarize it, I would say it's "Butterfly Effect: The Game". Remember that movie with Ashton Kutcher? This is game is basically that, with a few bells and whistles on top. I loved that movie (even though everyone hated it for some reason), and i loved it in game format.
Overall, i can recommend this game. For all its faults, i still greatly enjoyed it.
