[May contain spoilers!] Mafia III is an open world crime game set in the year 1968. You play as Lincoln Clay, a Vietnam war veteran out for revenge for the killing and betrayal of his family. I don't write many reviews but I felt like I needed to let people know what's up with this game, without talking about graphics.
Seeing as this game is "open-world", I should open with that. I believe that a succesful open world game should have at least 100 hours worth of content excluding collectibles. This means that there should be an abundance of side missions, activities such as drinking, mini games such as poker or darts, races with time trials, customization such as clothing stores and barbers and many, many more. Mafia III does
have
of these features, making the world feel redundant and not open at all. Sure, there are gatherings of NPCs who converse with one another, street performers, drunkards and sometimes ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (which you can't interact with), but in all honesty? They are just there to make the world
like it's alive. To
a "thriving, open world." This is a game where you're given access to fast cars, but also a game where there aren't any races(!) That's like a gun without bullets! There are some racist aspects of the world, like when police officers look at you just because you're black, but I didn't once see any police officers harassing black people, as they showed in the trailers. Racism is still a very controversial aspect of this game, as the main derogatory racist terms are used very often and are often emphasized. It's quite shocking sometimes.
The devs called the world of New Bordeaux the "main" character. Although as far as I can tell, this "main character" absolutely has
.
I played through the campaign and all of the side missions in 38 hours, taking my time and not rushing. I played stealthily a lot of the time, which probably made the game longer. That is terrible for the price I paid! 38 hours to FINISH an "open world" game? With all of the side content excluding collectibles? I probably spent 38 hours playing
in GTA 5. What a joke!
Mafia III is a gritty and bloody tale of revenge and pain, with some heavy racism thrown in the mix. It's honestly an enticing story and definitely its strongest suit. I feel that the story was very well orchestrated as a documentary (quite unique) but that there was also quite some "filler" in between. The story is probably the best part about this game, as it is with all Mafia games, but don't go in expecting Mafia II.
Sal Marcano is the main antagonist. Throughout the whole game, he is made out to be the most relentless, baddest mother-♥♥♥♥er in the game and YOU are supposed to feel as if killing him is the penultimate goal.
He's only really a "ruthless mob boss"
. The only time you ever see Sal Marcano kill anyone is in the intro, when the black mob is betrayed. For the REST of the game he is sat inside a single room, making phone calls, talking to his son and drinking whiskey. That's not what you expected, is it? The trailers didn't show that, did they? You thought he'd be out gunning ♥♥♥♥ers down with a thompson alongside his son because he's supposed to be the bad guy. Supposed to be.
The facial expressions and tonality of his voice elaborate on the emotions he is feeling (great voice acting!) but sitting down throughout the whole game, waiting for Lincoln to come to you and not taking any PHYSICAL action? Sure sounds like
all-right. He has influence over other people, but not once does he exit his room to hunt down Lincoln himself. Instead, relying on everyone else around him. I thought people were supposed to be
of this man? Not his minions? I thought this man was supposed to scare
? This man hides away at the top of his Casino, drinking whiskey. Good depiction of his influence as a mob boss -- bad depiction of himself as a man of action.
-
Rememeber in the trailer where it showed you can fight people in the arena and kill members of the KKK? Those are only
mission, and are not the main parts!
The arena is a very small part of another level,  made only to progress said level. There are 3 targets, with the same AI. You can "woo" the crowd or "insult" the crowd, but this does
- it is useless as an addition to the game, made only to fuel the hype.
The members of the Klan in the single mission about the Klan are not even your main targets, and again, is a useless addition, simply made to add content to the game and fuel the racial controversy further.
I honestly felt very misled by the trailers. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when I learned what these parts really were:
The main missions are very, very repetitive. You have to take down district underbosses in order to take down the district lieutenants/capos. To do this, you have to go through the ordeal of smashing valuables, killing people, stealing money, disrupting events and interrogating informers. It gets very tedious because they literally COPY and PASTE these missions to every other district whilst changing the
of what it is! For example: "disrupt the meeting" in Downtown becomes "disrupt the orgy" in the French Ward. Honestly, the repetition got to me at one point and made me want to play solely to reach the end. I wasn't excited to kill Sal Marcano anymore. I just wanted the game to be over.
The gunplay in this game is VERY satisfying, but the stealth mechanics in this game are the barest of bare. The AI are incredibly stupid when it comes to stealth - even on "hard" difficulty which doesn't seem to change anything apart from adding health to the AI (which still felt♥♥♥♥♥♥easy). Their vision cones are terrible and their "logic" just isn't there. There were multiple instances where I should have been seen. But alas, this is not a stealth game. It takes almost half a game to acquire a gun with a suppressor though, and even then, it's a "favour" from one of your 3 underbosses!
Burke, Vito, and Cassandra are who you will assign districts to. They will reward you with perks, "markers" (which buy services such as shutting off the phones), upgrades and weapons. Something I should warn you about is:
Depending on who you assigned a district to, that upgrade is linked to them. So I ended up finishing the game with upgraded health from Vito, no upgraded bomb ammo from Burke (because of the amount of districts I
give to him), and a fully upgraded car but no races to use the car in!
Not being able to have all the perks or upgrades is VERY stupid!!

"Steal the truck" - the truck doesn't spawn. Even on the third and final stage of any of these side missions, the objective pops up, but the map marker doesn't, making them feel redundant and making you feel stupid.
This game is littered with bugs. From falling through floors to being detected through walls to collision on objects that shouldn't have collision on them to FLYING through the air in a car because you hit a BUMP... I'm not joking!

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings improves virtually every aspect of the first game in a major way. The graphics are a major leap forward for the franchise. The game's visual prowess is also a result of outstanding artistic design. That said, there are some weird graphical bugs on occasion, but they are not enough to pull the player out of the story. The story has many layers and weaves a compelling narrative as a result of your actions and strong writing (most of the time, some things come off as immature in my opinion). The combat system is engaging as a function of the various ways you can approach various encounters: Should you drink potions to boost your stats, use overwhelming force from you sword and secondary weapons, or rely on magic to gain the upper hand? Those who like thinking tactically before entering a fray will find a great deal to like. However, death can come swift to new players as my roommate who is new to the action/rpg genera can attest. Bumping the game difficulty down to easy should help ease people into the experience if they rather focus on enjoying the story as opposed to being challenged by the game’s difficulty.
If you have not played the first game, I imagine the story may be difficult to follow at times. That said, the game does a good job of fleshing out its characters and provides ample reading for those interested in understanding the intricacies of the game’s plot and the politics amongst the various warring factions. Sometimes things are referred to in this game during the course of a conversation that will leave the uninitiated scratching their head, but that's just a guess.
Overall this is one of the best action/rpgs I have played in the past few years and whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a strong narrative in their games.

Now, i wouldn't say that this is directly a bad GAME, but a truly horrible interpretation of a Mafia-game. There is almost nothing resembling it's predecessors, it's a disgrace to the loved series. It has no "mafia feel", the era is poorly captivated, the streets look dead, and is nothing near what was expected from it. This - for me - was supposed to be the revival of the Mafia-series, the one that i've been a fan of ever since i layed my hands upon Mafia I. It disappointed me from the Mafia perspective in ever single way, i've uttered myself to play game for as long as i have, but no more. I've gotten an insight in what this game is trying to be, that's enough. I will be leaving out the technical quirks the game has, since there's a billion other reviews for that.
Hangar 13 made this game into a grindfest with a very uninteresting plot which featured next to nothing compelling. The plot (briefly summarized) is about a man named Lincoln, a Vietnam veteran coming home (they could've hit homerun with this story even though it's very generic). He finds himself lacking stuff to do and feels overall useless, so he joins a gang (I honestly don't remember the name of the gang, but it's the Italian counterpart of the Black mafia). He meet's up with the leader and they plot a heist, the italian's end up betraying him and the black mafia. Resulting in them all dying except Lincoln whom is now pumped with bloodlust and revenge. Sounds generic? Well, it unfortuantley is.
The game itself is okay, the gameplay is okay, very generic and all in all just completely O.K. nothing revolutionary. Never the less, the place where the game really shines is in it's cutscenes, oh my god are they good. They are infact revolutionary, i have never seen better. They have an immense attention to details in the characters face, and it's surroundings featuring some insane graphics in the cutscenes, but this is unfortunatley the only place the game really shows it's features to me. It's like two different worlds, there's the low polygon, poorly made player controlled world. Then there's the highly detailed cut-scene world. How did you possibly go so wrong Hangar 13? I feel I'm bored out of my mind with the same missions on repeat in each of the 9 districts the game is divided in, and it turns into this agonistic behaviour where the one grind tries to be better and stronger than the other grind. There's NO variation what so ever. Sure, you might be into this kind of thing where there's an openworld grind, but this is no storydriven game at all.
I find myself disheartened, uncompelled, disappointed and lost in faith for this game and it's future franchise (?). I hope so very dearly that the devs will find themselves wise enough to play through all the games, then come to the conclusion that they made a grave mistake in releasing this game as it is. May they create a new game that mends my sore eyes after playing this. May Mafia 4 be a better one than this. If not, the franchise will die and my faith in 2K will be lost.

What may appear to be a shallow and lazy hack and slash type action game really isn't as bad as it might seem. At its core it shows a lot of premise, with fighting mechanics requiring precise timing to perform counters, dodging, blocking and looking for openings to counter attack. When your in the rhythm, it is rather enjoyable.
There are two main types of attack, fists and blade. Using your fists builds up your blade meter, whereas using your blade attacks slowly drains it, however you deal more damage that way. As you continue to do damage, you'll build up charge in your blade, when unleashed it will do further damage to bleeding enemies and recharge your health meter. Finally there is a "holy"attack, hold down the third attack button and it will slowly charge, tap the modifier button however and it'll surge blade power into it, making it come charge instantly for each time pressed. In the heat of battle, this will help with crowd control.
The biggest downside to the combat is how repetitive it is to smash the same two attack buttons over and over again, doing 20+ hit combos on a base level bad guy. This element of grinding in an action game is not exactly the most exciting way to progress.
The other major problem is the game feels incredibly incomplete. Animations don't transition well between different movements, they just happen immediately and it looks a little jarring. Secondly the level design is non existant, you are in one arena running around killing the same types of enemies over and over.
The ultimate downside is there is a solid foundation to expand this into a solid side scrolling beat-em-up, but no real budget allowance to make it happen. As an action game that feels like a sloppy Ninja Gaiden, I don't think it would fare too well. Make it a beat-em-up not unlike Final Fight however, it could do quite well.
Visually it's pretty basic, but crisp. A lot of time went into the main characer's model which is always good for an action game, but everything else is pretty lacking. Sorely lacking really.
In the end it's a cheap wave after wave action game that is insipidly bare bones, with some potential to become something rather good. It just needs a story, level design, more enemies, more music, finished animation sequeneces....well and entire game to be honest.
It's fun though.

I played the original Wasteland as a kid, and it still remains one of my favorite games of all time.  I've been considering buying this game, but was a little worried that a "reboot" wouldn't live up to my nostalgaic expectations.
For the most part, I think this game did very well, both in catering to old-timers like me, as well as provide content and gameplay for everyone. A few pros and cons:
Pros -- Respectful of the old game without replaying everything; the relocating of the HQ was nice touch, for example.  I wonder if new players felt lost at all with all the references to the old game? It seemed like it was well-written to avoid such confusion, but I'm biased.  (Am I the only one who got misty-eyed over Ace's death?) There's some fun humor throughout, such as the E.T. cartridges north of HQ and the descriptions of the overgrown vegetables.  The mix of puzzling and fighting for missions was good, and the sharing of equipment between characters seemed to be about as good as any game could ever hope for.  I liked the combat controls -- a good mix of real-time and turn-based mechanics.  Interesting locations, great graphics, satisfying combat, fun characterization.
Cons -- The controls for moving seemed really awkward.  For example, trying to see objects in tight rooms (like Ryan's pen in the East Field) was a pain, and the "fog of war" seemed stingy.  It was sometimes hard to see where you could and could not go. This complaint plus the suddenness of saving Ralphy in the Rail Nomad camp made that quest aggravating -- couldn't find Ralphy right away, and then he drowned as I was trying to figure out how to save him. Not really fair for just entering the camp. The swearing was a little off-putting as well, not only in how it seemed "canned" and unnatural, but also in how it seemed to not quite fit in with the tone of the game.  So, in short -- awkward viewing controls, high difficulty (even on "easy"), counter-intuitive puzzling, and clunky potty mouth.
With a choice only between recommending or not recommending this game, I give it a mild thumbs up. On a scale of 1 to 10, I would have chosen "6" .....

With the base game you will probably struggle with orbital mechanics at its finest, looking for questionable hard interplanetary transfers, gravital wells snorkeling, slinghots manoeuvres planning; maximizing fuel efficency while considering Oberth effect; make a marble statue of Tsiolkovsky in your garden while your spaceship miserably burn like on Eve's (Venus) upper atmosphere and so on. There's no hand holding in this game. Only a failure after another failure. And for each failure, the knowledge; and inside the knowledge, the beauty.
The only thing that IMHO must be pointed out is that instead of adding new content, Squad \ Take Two Interactive seems to favour the "golden the pill" philosophy. And so they craft localization-oriented works that are undoubtedly helpful to catch more users from around the world, but simple aren't useful as, for example, embed "Kerbal Engineer Redux" mod's features inside of the core game itself.
Not to mention the additional highly suggested mod Mechjeb, a "noob and less noob swiss knife" that, even if the original author (Cybutek) was hired by Squad team, is still an outer utility instead of became a perfectly integrated set of functionalities that extend and improve the original game mechanics.
To summarize all of this, if you're a nerd or a geek that loves space, and preferably math, grab this game now!

This is a decent remake of the classic 2D platformer, with occasional 3D segments thrown in at random, but it has issues with running at a decent framerate. It's very happy to cap itself at 30fps for seemingly no reason. It was initially capped at 30 intentionally, as it was on console, but a patch was supposed to fix it to cap at 60.
It has a slight feeling of being unfinished, or perhaps just overly simplified for children. Many segments are optional challenges in a stage which reward you with a collectible upon completion; but if you fall in a pit that would’ve killed you in a normal stage you merely respawn near their entrance. Some of them are mandatory to attempt but will let you progress immediately upon your first failure so the speedrunning trick is to “die” on purpose.
A lot of these segments look like you were supposed to clear them before progressing in a stage, given the changes that have taken place in the main stage upon your return to it.
You now need a certain amount of collectibles to progress through the game. This was somewhat a factor in the 8-bit versions since I think you could technically miss 2 of the rainbow gems & needed all 7 to unlock the final stage. I’m fairly sure the 16-bit original was entirely linear.
Collectible hunting works more like a Banjo Kazooie kind of platformer here, since there’s hundreds of clear gems to collect, but it’s never hard to find enough gems in levels to carry on. It wouldn’t surprise me if the developers were aiming for a sort of Banjo Kazooie feel since they even brought Grant Kirkhope in to compose the remake’s soundtrack.
The original 16-bit soundtrack is also included as an option but doesn't fit some of the redesigned levels that are far longer than some of these music tracks were intended to play for. The first stage's apple chase is a particular example.
I see no good reason that the 16-bit version couldn't have been included as it was with PS3 pre-orders or at least sold on Sega's crappy emulator hub thing, even if it had to be at a higher price than the other games on it. Sega clearly worked something out with Disney both to make this remake and to release the original on PS3.
I'll at least grant that this remake has far fewer issues than Capcom/Wayforward's Ducktales Remastered does on pretty much every format. I've never had this remake crash on me but I've had Ducktales Remastered crash a bunch of times on PS3 & I hear the PC port is even less stable.
If you're looking for a retro Disney-platformer remaster then you might want to consider this game during a sale.

A game made almost entirely by one guy and it comes out looking and playing as if it were at least made by a small team. The visuals are very well done, very crisp and clean without a harshness to be had. Sprites man, they'll always look good.
The gameplay is solid, with very very responsive controls which make what the combat is feel pretty damn nice. What the combat is however, is best described as a torrent of complete destruction. You'll be erupting giant fire storms from the ground while you zoom around the sky at a hundred miles an hour. It's pretty satisfying and in some cases skillful... for awhile.
The game's main flaw is lack of variety. What you get within the first hour or so of gameplay is more or less what you have at the end of it all. Very few power-ups, with the only ones you do get being primarily keys that allow you to move in ways you couldn't before, to access new areas. Only one of which really has any impact on combat, and only loosely. The game could have benefitted from some sort of combat enhancing power-ups, that give you new things to do.
The above is only an enhanced problem due to the game being surprisingly long. I 100% the game and I have about 16 hours logged. I was expecting more like 8 or 9. So while it's great for the content, the game's repetitious nature can wear on itself.
That being said however, it is one flaw of an otherwise marvelous game. The gameplay for what it is, is very enjoyable. The story is... predictable and standard but that for me was refreshing. Also refreshing was how childish the game was in it's narrative and humor. I really did feel like I was playing a children's game that was trying to have a grown-up story about war and internal strife. It was pleasant.
As far as sound aspects go, the game is a wonder. Sound effects are clean, voice acting is surprisingly well-done, albeit a bit hit or miss depending on the character. And the music, oh man, it's so good. Do yourself a favor and look up "Dust an Elysian Tail OST Cirromon Caverns" (Track 4, not the vintage one.) That soundtrack is probably in my top 10 favorite pieces of music from video games now.
One man, a voice cast and apparently an awesome OST from HyperDuckMusic. That's all it took to make a game which I would call an absolute success. Fun, enjoyable and while a bit long and repetitive, is certainly worth picking up. If for no other reason than just to support a man's 4 year work on it.

text:
First off, this is not really a game, more of a walking simulator. If that is your thing, continue, otherwise turn back now. The graphics are mediocre, the gameplay is nonexistent, the main game play mechanic is in-universe save scumming, so that is unique and interesting. The fandom lauds the game for it's amazing story, and I would be fully willing to forgive all the aforementioned sins if the story was good, but it's not. Frankly the fact that this game is as popular as it is can only be attributed to a failure of the educational system to teach critical thinking.
The game handholds you to an offensive degree: if you make a "mistake," or a choice that they didn't write a plot branch for, which is the vast majority of them, Max hits you with a "MAYBE I SHOULD REWIND TIME TO UNDO THAT," and doesn't let you proceed until you rewind time and do it right. This ends up being the case for almost every choice in the game that doesn't lead to one of the two approved endings.
The music is awful, and I'm a fan of bad hipster music. The songs are entirely uninspired, there is practically nothing composed for the game itself. It's like they mugged some dude in a flannel in downtown Portland and used the music on his phone as their soundtrack.
The voice acting is slightly below average all around, except for the voice actress of Chloe, who does a pretty good job.
There are some short puzzle sections, but those are like 10 minutes of the game.
I will spend the rest of the review criticising the writing, as there is almost nothing else in the game worth talking about. Also SPOILER ALERT, though it isn't like that matters as the end of the game is similar the end of Mass Effect 3, but with two choices instead of three.
We need to consider the writing for three areas of the game: the characters, the dialogue in individual scenes, and the overall plot.
1. The Dialogue:
It is unbearable. Even accounting for the fact that the writers are middle aged french dudes, it is still terrible. There is very little soul, the characters all talk like parodies of what they were intended to be, and it is completely jarring to the point of ruining any ability to get engaged with the more serious aspects of the story. The dialogue predominantly consists of the cast of characters rapidly switching between spewing internet slang from 2007 at each other and trying to comfort each other while they cry about asinine issues. Some people are willing to forgive it for this, but it pushed my suspension of disbelief to the point of breaking and I could no longer get invested in the plot. The dialogue writing is a crippling blow to the game's ability to deliver its message. The writers also have an out of place gun fetish, you get impressively bad lines like "I believe in gun control. I believe I should control the gun. It's the men who need to be checked."
Other favorite lines include:
"I just vaped some dank OG bud, so I can barely see you..."
"Ready for the mosh pit, shaka brah."
There is a uniquely tasteless stand out line where one character requests that you help her commit suicide by "Turning the morphine up to 11." This tearfully delivered reference to Spinal Tap completely shattered the otherwise extremely somber mood of the scene. Many of the characters also try to deliver something which could accidentally be composed into some sort of a political commentary, but the presentation and substance are so vapid that it doesn't merit analysis. It just feels out of place.
2. The Plot as a Whole:
It's lazy and plays entirely off bouncing stereotypes off each other to see what happens. It can be neatly divided into a few self contained events that are meant to offer a facsimile of your actions having consequences, but again, the whole story leads up to the mass effect ending where you are offered a choice between the same two outcomes regardless of how you did in the rest of the game. The game also has plot holes that you could drive a cruise ship through: where Max gets her powers from is never discussed beyond a bit of trivial "wow why can I do this" lines Max thinks to herself early on. It is bizarre that no one asks these questions, and frustrating that the writers neglected to try and answer it. Many characters make choices so stupid that the only possible explanation is that they needed to do stupid stuff to forward the plot. The plot itself is basically a Twin Peaks fanfic, a fact is further established by a main character's license plates reading TWN PKS. It does however fail to capture any of the character writing or drama that made Twin Peaks so revolutionary for its time, so don't hold your breath.
3. The Characters:
Every character is a stereotype masquerading as a complex character. Every character has one driving conflict that dominates their decision making process. It is completely predictable and uninspired. There was nothing that made me consider why the people feel the way they do, as every emotional conflict can be explained in whole with something like "she's mad because her dad died," or something generic like that. These characters are also bad people. Many of the main characters are in very unhealthy relationships that get presented as mature and strong, even though they are not. Most of the main characters are selfish and irresponsible, in particular the main characters. This wouldn't be of much concern as having deeply flawed characters is the trappings of an interesting story, but they completely fail to actually cause people to learn from their flaws. There is one scene that encapsulates this very neatly where Chloe shoots a gun at a car, it ricochets and hits her, and she screams "STUPID GUN," only to have Max rewind time and stop her, causing her to not learn at all from her mistakes. The writers abuse the time rewind mechanic as a get out of jail free card for every character and it effectively halts all character evolution, which makes the story boring. This aspect of the writing is problematic only because the prevailing mindset by the community regarding Chloe and Max is one that idolizes them and their relationship, rather than criticising their deep and unavoidable character flaws. The writers also sort of offer them as a role model, which is very much not how it should be. The characters pander hard to social outcasts and basically work to justify and enable antisocial behavior. As a final aside, I feel obligated to note that none of the characters have any self awareness what so ever, and it is extremely grating to see these nearly adult people acting like middle schoolers without at least examining their own actions.
Overall:
This is an empty game with a story that always ends with you negating 14-19 hours of gameplay. The story offers writing that is wholly inferior to other story rich games such as Witcher 3 or Transistor, and mystery that pales in comparison to things like Kentucky Route Zero or even Firewatch. Every aspect of this game has been done better elsewhere, and the total package is unique, but underwhelming.

When I first started to play Binding of Isaac, I noticed immediately that somewhere along development, it must of had some inspirational support from the dungeons design in from the 1st Legend of Zelda game of 1996.
That aside, I was very sceptical about this game when I saw other people play it. I felt like they made it seem more fun than it really is, but after it was for sale for under £3 I jumped to the chance to play it myself, along with the Wrath of the Lamb DLC. This game is tremendously addictive, if it wasn't for the sombre music throughout the game, I would play it more often, however it does give the game the perfect feel that it needs.
To play the game you use the WSDA keys to move and the Directional buttons to attack with tear projectiles. You collect keys, bombs and money to buy items from a store, or if you're lucky enough to come across an arcade to gamble your coins.  As you progress you will kill various monsters that are somewhat difficult to defeat, but once you have faced off against them enough times you'll get the rhythm of it. While passing through the different rooms in the dungeon, you'll come across different doors with all kinds of loot you can pick up to either enhance your combat skills, some kind of passive item to help you along the way, or a one use item every now and then that'll really come in handy in tight situations. You'll mostly find the good items in the golden rooms, but most of the time you need a key to open one, so make sure you keep an eye on what you spend and waste, but there is always a chance you'll find a secret room of some kind with more loot or another item to help you beat the dungeon.
There is at least one boss in each dungeon floor, like the enemies, they are somewhat difficult to defeat, but there all different and do require you to think if you want to defeat them.  Once you defeat said boss it'll give you another item to help you out, and maybe some hearts to replenish your health. Once you have cleared a area you can progress even deeper, and I promise you it does get way more difficult. I would say more but some parts are really enjoyable and it is worth your time if you like a classic arcade feel to your video game.
Give it a try yourself, what have you got to lose. Thank you for reading!

Fallout Shelter is compelling and addicting. It draws you in and it doesn't want to let go of your attention. It is cute, has a lot of attention to detail and it is fun. It is also devious, manipulative and abusive.
The game uses a combination of various banal gameplay mechanics:
These four mechanics are combined so that the game forces you to compulsively check it out regularly for short moments, but if you want to move the story via quests, you must wait hours or even days. These long timers can be skipped by paying real money in what is one of the worst gaming invention of the last years.
There are other considerations for the player: How to lay out the shelter, how to breed and train dwellers, what quests to tackle in which order. These are all hidden behind the layer of the aforementioned juggling of timers, clicking to harvest and looking for hidden objects.
Fallout Shelter not only preys on the weaknesses of the human mind with a devious mix of banal, casual and meaningless gameplay, not only it adopts a business model that goes against fun and fairness, it also represents abuse of the name of an old game series that used to stand for clever writing, branching quests, meaningful choices and consequences and a lot of possible ways to play through the game.
Fallout Shelter is a compelling and addictive abomination.

It's subpar! I'm not gonna lie.
I myself have a lot of problems with a lot of games. This isn't a game I really can hate. It's just good brawling fun. The control scheme for keyboards is terrible, though, I'll admit. You use arrow keys, or WASD, and like, J, K, L, I, O, right shift, enter for the menu, left shift for something, spacebar for this sword thing, uh. Yeah, just use your DualShock 3 or whatever, if you're gonna buy it.
That said, while the controls are quite unwieldy for the keyboard warrior, it's not unplayable. It just feels awkward, is all, could have been better.
The camera is controlled via Q, E and C, which centers the camera behind you.
The controls are just so... strange, well, I can't help but mention them, and have them take up, like, this entire review. Oh well.
The graphics -are- quite lovely. At least, when it comes to your female schoolgirl katana-wielding character, who is, funnily enough, not just some moe, airheaded stereotype. When it comes to the graphics for everything else, well! Don't expect that much. Enemies are passable, environments, passable, etc. The textures aren't terrible, or pixelated, just bland and honestly not much to look at.
I mean, honestly, this is just a fun little distraction that you'll have fun with for as many hours as it takes to beat, then you'll likely never touch it again. Does that sound fair, for $10? I'm not sure. Personally, I'd just wait for it to get on sale, then pick it up.
So, it's not a terrible game, by any means. I don't want to say it's good, but, yeah, it is good. I kinda like it. And for 250mb of HDD space, well, I'm impressed they fit in as much as they did.
Bottom line? Pick it up on sale, and have fun with a fun game that is expressly for chilling out, and having fun. It's not a game to be taken seriously.

God...where to start with this game.
Well how about at the beginning...
In Shadow of War you continue Talion's quest from the previous game, starting out with him and Celebrimbor forging a new ring of power free from Sauron's power. Video games have been getting worse and worse, first is was pre-ordering, then it was DAY ONE DLC (which if you don't know was essentially the game you SHOULD have gotten, but ripped out and sold to you separately), then it was microtransactions, now it is microtransactions AND day one DLC in a full $60 GAME.
It's even more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥now, we have these apologist running around saying "Oh.... game development....oh..it costs more now....ohh.... games won't exist if they don't do this..." Do us all a favor and dounce yourself in oil and go light yourself on fire, because you are a moron, and the world does not need you in it. The game pretty much consists of you trying to do what you did in the first place after you clear the tutorial area (if you're not bored to tear of the grind by then), turning orcs to your side to somehow and in some way have them help you clear the area of the Orc's warlords. Except now the dominating the orcs applies only to captains and their interactions with each other. THE ORCS pretty much make this game, as the main character Tailon is a boring, watered-downed version of Aragorn pretty much. The orc's are probably the BEST part of the game, some are generic but there are some with unique personalities that really make them special, like there's a lute-playing orc that will literally sing whenever you have a confrontation with him, or a orc with the title "Black-Blade" which literally all he talks about is his black blade. Each orc also has his own special ups and downs like they may have a fiery weapon that deals fire damage, or a weakness to stealth attacks, them sorta things. The orcs REALLY stole the show in this one as the rival system is expanded, now you can get ambushed or even randomly find one of YOUR orcs who got his butt kicked by the hands of your rival (that you need to help). Also as a new feature you can have an orc as a bodyguard who you handpick, the bodyguard can be summoned with a small group of troops to help you fight, and btw you might wanna be cautious as the bodyguard CAN be killed, so pick wisely. Also there is a bit of online play where you can attack another person’s stronghold and deal with their orcs and defenses (expand more on this later) This part is literally about 10% of the game.
About 10% of the game is cutscene's, which are BUETIFULL to look at btw, the graphics in the cutscenes are amazing to say the least. The graphics in the game are nice too, the textures on the orcs and characters in game are very nicely detailed and flow fairly well. Another game that's pretty yet has no substance to it.
The other 20% of the game is menus, this game is literally a management-sim game as much as ANYTHING else pertaining to the gameplay. As you clear the first tower area, you can gain it as a stronghold, in which you can then assign your own warlord and captains to it as well as upgrade it with even more captains. Why are you doing this, well other players may attack your fort (not in real time btw) and you can make it more annoying for them to do so.
This game's a tragedy in motion... I WANTED to like this game guys, really, I did. The fighting is good, with a nice mix-up of bow and sword combat and some of the captains are actually hard as balls to deal with... but there's just not enough of it to justify a $60 WITH microtransactions.

My opinion of this game is (letter grade and explanation):
* F / Unfair game mechanics
* F / Poorly implemented "random events" system
* C- / Game progress is much slower than ideal, leading to too much waiting
* F / Game forces you you pay for in-game currency if you want to progress

Now before you conclude "oh this guy just don't like this type of game..." I actually do. I think the visual style of the game is beautiful and I'm a huge fan of slow-paced clicker games. This game was in fact free to try, but it leaves you with the feeling that someone is constantly nagging you about buying in-game currency to be able to do basic things. The difference between this game and what I would have wanted/expected is like the difference between:
1) Standing in line and...
2) Standing in line with 100 toddlers that are screaming.
If you know what nagging, uneasy feeling I am talking about then stay away from this horrible game. The game did not have a sense of urgent post-apocalyptic building-a-city-from-nothing. It was like struggling to find ways to actually play the game that the developers had not thought to charge for.
This is the end of the review. The following is more specific details about why I am about to delete this game.
Firstly, I don't like Bethesda. I won't go into why, but I think they do more damage than good for the gaming community. I ran across this game several times and said "no" to it because of the developer. Nonetheless, I gave it a try due to the visual style and I have a friend that said it was "an okay game." I'm not about to read every how-to before playing it, and understand my first attempt will probably not be ideal, but the game has serious issues.
Today I was playing, trying to do the questing as well as explore and keep my shelter slowly growing and dwellers leveling up. The problem I ran into is that the fires/roaches just continue to randomly spawn, even when your not rushing, causing your dwellers, who only some of which are armed, to constantly have health issues, causing your healing "Stimpak" to be in short supply. If you then run into the situation where you have an power emergency, you end up having to stack a ton of people into the reactor room and then "rush" it. The more you fail, the longer it takes and the worse your percentage is to "rush" again.
I found that when it says "33% chance" to fail, that actually means 90% chance to fail, and it never changes. I'm not saying that the percentages are slightly off, I'm saying I think it is stuck on 90% fail rate no matter how low the displayed percentage is. I've failed at 30-40% far too many times for this to be an actual percentage. Keep in mine 33% means you should fail about 1/3 of the time. not 9/10, which I was experiencing.
In addition to the "Stimpak" issue, dweller death causes the same issue, because you need to revive them, which costs caps, which are always in short supply and are even more in short supply if your dwellers start to die and therefore cannot assist with the gaining of caps.
Hopefully even players that have played this game can understand my frustration by this point.

Castle of Illusion is a great platformer game with Mickey Mouse as it's main character. You have to collect the rainbow gems in order to save Minnie from an evil witch and for doing so, you need to go through many worlds and kill their bosses to collect them.
The game soundtrack is composed by the awesome Grant Kirkhope, the same pesron that did the OST for Banjo-Kazooie, Banjo-Tooie, Donkey Kong 64, Yooka-Laylee, etc... so well, obviously the music is fantastic! The graphics are using a lovely Disney style for them. As for the story, it was a little on the basic Disney side... but it wasn't bad at all.
As for the gameplay, well it's good, there's just a few issues. The platforming is nice and the levels are interesting, but there's a few bad design ideas. First of all, in a game where you have gather collectibles, there shouldn't be parts where you are forced into a further part of the level and unable to go back. It makes having to restart the game really often when you want to gather all the gems on a certain level and it's truly annoying.
Then there's the controls... I've played with a keyboard, I know the game is meant for controller, but still... In a certain level where you have to jump from cookies and I have no clue if this happens with a controller too, but it's just so wonky! I've had to retry this level multiple times because somehow, whenever I got close to the border of those cookies, I would try and jump and get stuck in an invisible wall as if it was meant to make it impossible to fall by jumping from cookie to cookie (they're over a deadly milkshake pool). But well, sometimes the barrier would work and sometimes it wouldn't, so if you weren't ready for it to work this time or whatever, you pretty much jump to your death every time.
Then there's the feeling the last parts were rushed... The progression felt nice up to the last world or two, which felt really rushed to be honest. That and many unfair mechanics in the game... and some parts where you'd have to jump way down only to end up on a monster and die (just why?).
Lastly, I don't think game with optional speedrun modes should have waiting included in their timing. I figured this the hard way when I tried to speed through the levels to find out that I had to wait for ropes to swing to my location no matter how fast I had gotten there...
Other than that, the game is great and I suppose it will be easy to jump over it's flaws. If you're a perfectionist or an achievement hunter, the game should take you a good six hours to find all the collectibles and unlock everything, as well as finishing the game.
But sadly, if you're just going through the game like a normal person and doing the strict minimum, I don't think the game would last much longer than 1 H... maybe 2H... It's mostly time consuming to do all the speedrun mode and collect everything, but the levels themselves are really short!

Mafia III, the follow up to the legendary Mafia and Mafia II video games. I was very hyped for this game and was anticipating an epic game much like Grand Theft Auto V. However, there are a few things that make gameplay a less enjoyable experience.
Let me start off by saying the story is excellent, and while I haven't played through the entire game yet, I will hopefully change this review by the end of all the DLCs and updates. The story is very engaging and unique. There are also plenty of elements that reinforce the notion of racism during this period: such as when police respond slower and the dispatcher uses words like "maybe" in poorer, black neighborhoods.
However, story aside, the game is hard to love when the physics and graphics are sub-par. While the game does look pretty at times, there are some glaring details I cannot forgive. The first thing you'll notice is that the graphics are wonky at times. The lighting and reflections and wonky and the chrome on the cars looks more like matte plastic with a metallic paint. Sometimes the immediate world also darkens and lightens as if the developers wanted to emulate clouds obscuring the sun intermittently but it comes across as jarring. At night New Bordeaux looks very beautiful though. I think the developer added too many post-process effects that take away from the performance, this should be looked into but I think the only way to fix this is to redo the entire game engine.
As mentioned the physics and overall feel of the game is lacking. Driving feels like the cars are driving with ice wheels. While yes, older American cars had wonky and floaty suspensions, and the game allows them to leans as such, the wheels are like they are made of ice and the cars feel lighter than they look. The physical damage on cars is also dissapointing as I was looking up to GTA V and taking cues from older movies where the sheet metal cars would actually tear themselves apart after a collision. Colliding with people also seems like an unfinished feature. I feel the devs would have had a better time if they used Natural Motion as the people are more like lamp posts with animations coming in late. Sometimes the AI driven cars have erratic driving that is pretty annoying to deal with: they would be spinning around in an 'S' shape right in front of me and would clip through other cars until they are right in front of me, where the game engine decides that they should have collision again.
Another point of contention is general gameplay. I'm currently in the stage where I'm running introductory jobs for Cassandra, Vito, and Burke. But all of these characters have had the same type of missions to regain control of their respective territories: go there, bop that guy until the big boss guy gets anfry and shows his face, go back to the same large wardehouse place you bopped one guy to get the big guy, finished. As stated, I haven't finished the main story yet, but I hope the missions are not going to be monogamous for the rest of the crew again.
Tldr; well told story, everything else is sub-par. Get this game on sale or a few years down the line.

DISCLAIMER: I didn't get the memo. I only have the original WASTELAND 2.
WASTELAND 2 is a post-apocalyptic game with gameplay elements inspired by the first Fallout games. It's centered around the Desert Rangers, pretty much an untrustworthy police force that still tries to do their job and attempt to surpass their rivals, the Red Skorpions, and solve the mystery of the ranger, Ace's death.
This game is not the prettiest, it has okay textures and pretty much the same environment, but inXile pulls a Nintendo and thought laterally with withered technology. Although the environments can seem kinda repetitive, it's a desert with bits of vibrant colors and life that makes every area unique.
In terms of story, everybody has some story to tell. The Desert Rangers are the law, constantly trying to help everyone out despite their history. The Red Skorpions are scavengers that tend to do things better than the Rangers, the citizens of Highpool are a big water supply with a dead mayor and hatred for the rangers, and many, many, many more. And if you think it's just some linear solve-a-mystery story, you're wrong. You're the Desert Rangers and you have a job to do. There's even a part where you have to help one of two areas and hear the area you didn't choose quickly go downhill. There's side-quests in dem darn hills and there be plenty. The only real complaint I have is that the quests can be quite vague. And I got pretty stumped on one quest only to find out there's a specific stat for the quest, and that's the ever-so-helpful skill of rapairing
Difficulty wise, this game can kick your a$# if you're not ready. Guns jam, stats are expensive, and even having a conversation will be tough without certain stats. The combat is turn-based with every character moving around a grid and performing actions with a set of AP (Action Points), every tile you go to takes one AP, attacking takes AP, healing takes AP, even things like reloading and crouching take AP. The game requires plenty of strategy and that strategy isn't just, "Don't take cover by explosives, unload, repeat," and it can make quick work of your team, in other words this game is hard for anyone with a basic, or even no strategy.
Overall, this game is tough if you do something without thinking, and it will make sure you know it, but it will still help you out by making the game in a way that takes you by the ear and puts you back in the right direction like how your mother used to.
WASTELAND 2 gets an 8/10, and I reccomend it to those who want a test of the brain, and strategy, over.

I started playing this game a little over a week ago and I have 10.5 hours of playtime. 8/15 achievements, almost zero gameplay tutorials viewed.
My opinion of this game is (letter grade and explanation):
* F / Unfair game mechanics
* F / Poorly implemented "random events" system
* C- / Game progress is much slower than ideal, leading to too much waiting
* F / Game forces you you pay for in-game currency if you want to progress
* C+ / Many game mechanics are poorly explained, leading to a lot of wasted time/resources as part of a "learning process"
* A+ / Visual style of game and 3-D effect
* A- / Load screen menus and intro sillyness
* D- / Mouse usability within gameplay (being able to click what you want to click)
WOULD NOT RECOMMEND (not even worth being free / you would have to pay me to play this)
Now before you conclude "oh this guy just don't like this type of game..." I actually do. I think the visual style of the game is beautiful and I'm a huge fan of slow-paced clicker games. This game was in fact free to try, but it leaves you with the feeling that someone is constantly nagging you about buying in-game currency to be able to do basic things. The difference between this game and what I would have wanted/expected is like the difference between:
1) Standing in line and...
2) Standing in line with 100 toddlers that are screaming.
If you know what nagging, uneasy feeling I am talking about then stay away from this horrible game. The game did not have a sense of urgent post-apocalyptic building-a-city-from-nothing. It was like struggling to find ways to actually play the game that the developers had not thought to charge for.
This is the end of the review. The following is more specific details about why I am about to delete this game.
Firstly, I don't like Bethesda. I won't go into why, but I think they do more damage than good for the gaming community. I ran across this game several times and said "no" to it because of the developer. Nonetheless, I gave it a try due to the visual style and I have a friend that said it was "an okay game." I'm not about to read every how-to before playing it, and understand my first attempt will probably not be ideal, but the game has serious issues.
Today I was playing, trying to do the questing as well as explore and keep my shelter slowly growing and dwellers leveling up. The problem I ran into is that the fires/roaches just continue to randomly spawn, even when your not rushing, causing your dwellers, who only some of which are armed, to constantly have health issues, causing your healing "Stimpak" to be in short supply. If you then run into the situation where you have an power emergency, you end up having to stack a ton of people into the reactor room and then "rush" it. The more you fail, the longer it takes and the worse your percentage is to "rush" again.
I found that when it says "33% chance" to fail, that actually means 90% chance to fail, and it never changes. I'm not saying that the percentages are slightly off, I'm saying I think it is stuck on 90% fail rate no matter how low the displayed percentage is. I've failed at 30-40% far too many times for this to be an actual percentage. Keep in mine 33% means you should fail about 1/3 of the time. not 9/10, which I was experiencing.
In addition to the "Stimpak" issue, dweller death causes the same issue, because you need to revive them, which costs caps, which are always in short supply and are even more in short supply if your dwellers start to die and therefore cannot assist with the gaining of caps.
Hopefully even players that have played this game can understand my frustration by this point.

I'm not going to copy and paste the "About this game" section from the actual store page, so go there if you want to know how it works and what it really is about.

This depends on which one of the 3 gamemodes you are playing so I'm going to base this for each one of them:
In this gamemode you don't have to worry about anything other than having fun. You choose what you want to do and you have so many things you CAN do. To list some:
You get the point.
In this mode, funding is not a problem. Your goal is to get every single research node and after that it turns into Sandbox.
It does not have contracts like Career.
Here, as it says in the "About" section you have to plan your funding, the contracts and limit the money use as much as possible to become the best space agency on Kerbin!
Everything matters and mining is eventually going to be the money making machine. In my save I have ended up with as many as 14 asteroids in orbit around the home planet being mined and then burned up in the atmosphere when their ore is depleted.
It has thousands of mods on websites such as SpaceDock, Curse and the forum.
Also, I've noticed that some of the negative reviews are based of the fact that KSP does not have workshop support and downloading mods is painfully awful. To that I have to say NO!
An amazing person from the community going by the name "pjf" created the amazing CKAN (Comprehensive Kerbal Archive Network)
back in 2014!!
This has a pretty simple interface, support for every single KSP version and support for hundreds of mods. (of course, it doesn't always have the mod you want but it does a hell of a job in helping with updating the ones that are really important to you)
I honestly can't understand the people that are leaving reviews (many with small amounts of hours) saying the mod support is bad when for 3 years there's been a god damned mod manager.
The only problem with the mod manager is that it doesn't really integrate with steam (you can make it integrate but I didn't bother) so it won't track your hours spent playing the game. [That's
why I have a very small amount]
There are 2 building spaces :
Short for Vehicle Assembly Building, this is the place where you build your rockets.
Short for Spaceplane Hangar, it's the place where you build your airplanes and your spaceplanes.
The problem with them is that they have sort of werid controls but after you get used to them they are no problem at all. It is going to be annoying at the beginning if you are trying to make complicated vehicles but eventually it becomes muscle memory.
You probably noticed I've been pretty much only praising this game I do have this one issue with it.
The missions get really repetitive by the middle of your progress because you've been doing similar missions constantly. What I would recommend for the devs to add in order to fix this is the following : Make it so that contracts ask for things to be delivered to orbit around a certain planet or maybe for something to only be placed in a sub orbital trajectory and for extra cash you need to land your rocket. The twist is that you get the payload as a subassembly so you don't need to build it yourself and you won't have control over it after it's delivered. Maybe also some mining and delivering contracts to pre-built space stations that will unload after the mission is complete.
The game gives you absolute control over what you do and how you innovate your rockets/SSTO's.
The different modes give it a dynamic but science and sandbox are just about the same thing only with limitations.
Career is fun but should be worked on more.
Mod support is great even without workshop support due to the CKAN mod manager.
The game has you in the Kerbol System that contains 1 Star, 7 Planets and 9 Moons (if I counted correctly).

This game has something going for it.  The gameplay is better than I would have hoped for, being simple and straight foreward.  Survival is my favorite so far, because shooting dinosaurs is all I need.  What's better, is that it feels like a game where you can actually play by yourself.  If you're not stupid while playing alone, you can actually kick♥♥♥♥♥and handle things very well, which is something that has been missing even in some of my favorite games.  I've played a few rounds of multiplayer, and found...a few glitches.  Not intolerable, but general fixes needed.
There are some bad points although:  Some of the higher up weapons seem rather useless, such as the bow, or the laser carbine.  Their damage output is rather meek, being worse than some medium grade weapons.  Some animations can be rather clunky, making reloads look awkward and attacking raptors look really lazy.  The vehicle physics aren't something to brag about, but I really, REALLY hate the fact that you have to move the camera to turn.  It just grinds my gears.  There was a glitch one time while I was online, where a flying dinosaur was stuck above the skybox until we returned back to home base.  I like the fact that akimbo weapons are included, but it's limited to a seperate weapon.  I would really like to see a sort of "Gunzerker" akimbo, where you can dual wield anything regardless of all circumstances, but only for the support class (considering they are tanks.)  If you have a perk to have two of the same weapon (eg. two pistol weapons) and are using a controller, you can't swap the the second pistol.  It will automatically swap to your other gun.
All in all, a game with potential: 6.75/10

Me personally, I think that there are just some situations in which renewing licenses and keeping that game "alive" just for the sake of I don't know what is really not worth it. Remedy also stated today, that they can't just remove the tracks from the game, reason was "large variety of engineering, resources etc.". Now, it's also been stated that they are looking to renew them, but they don't have timeframe, which in most of the cases means that no, they're not going to renew it.
Alan Wake is 7 years old, there's been just plenty and plenty and plenty of opportunities to get it almost for free (today is that day too). I believe lot of you will remember 2013 and awesome Humble Bundle where it was for 1 dollar. Also, who knows how many copies was sold this year, and for what price, and then there is that major question if it is really worth to take care of new licenses, if Alan Wake is still able to bring some income and revenue. Who knows right?
Now, I don't really want this "review" to be review yet. Thing is that I did not complete the game in time of this writing yet, I was close to the end of the game but still, there is no way I want to provide any word look into the Alan Wake game yet. Once I finish the whole game, I will write review for it, and edit it under this first article. Reason is, that I want to have opportunity to have review of Alan Wake, here at Steam, in my profile, because once it is gone from Steam Store, you can't obviously review it. I made same mistake with Metro series.
I do have a lot of personal stories with Alan Wake, which I keep for myself this time and lot of times, eras and dates are related to Alan Wake that also with the quality of the game itself makes it one of the best games I have ever played and it helped climb this game on the TOP10 of mine.
Also I do have near identical coat as the Alan is wearing during the game, it is basically same, I just don't have those elbow patches in black, but in grey color. Otherwise it is 100% identical and I feel so awesome when I'm wearing that :D
I also want to say to those people who have the game, don't sleep on it.
Those people who don't own the game yet, Alan Wake is pretty much worth actual retail price and I'm not even joking. This game is really one of few that is definitely worth full retail price of 30 euros/dollars so today, when you'll have opportunity to grab it in 90% discount for 3/4 dollars, holy sh*t go for it without thinking. That'll be one of the best buys you've done for the past couple of months.
Last thing, that is on my mind, is big shoutout to Remedy. In this case, that they did notice us, that game is going to be removed, not like others who just simple don't give a flying f*ck and remove it without even saying words. So, thanks for that and for the headsup.

Except for the microtransactions (and the rigorous grind in the late game) it is an overall pretty good experience. The game flows well, there are more abilities than the first game (which increases the "badass-factor"), new enemy types, sieges and of course better graphics.
I had a few minor technical issues that caused a CTD once or twice. It was easily fixable by changing a couple of settings though. I had no issues running this game smoothly in 1080P@120FPS without any stuttering at all, apart from the CTD's (bear in mind that I have a GTX 1080TI)
The sound design in the game reminds me a lot of Shadow of Mordor, which is to be expected. There are nothing that stands out as bad sound design and neither does anything stand out as great sound design.
The new enemy types includes a completely new kind of orc, the "Olog-Hai" and a drake, which essentially is a dragon. Also there are new tribes that the different captains and warchiefs belong to. These different tribes gives the captains different abilities depending on the tribe. I.E a captain of the Machine Tribe has a hook that he can use to pull your character towards you.
Then there are sieges. These sieges are pretty fun, but the best thing, IMO, is the preparation for the sieges. The forts are controlled by an overlord, who has up to six warchiefs under him. Each of these warchiefs gives the fort you are laying siege to an upgrade. A couple of upgrades include siege beasts (catapults on graugs), spiked walls so that the attacking army cannot climb up the walls and a pack of caragors that protects the fortress. In total there are 21 different upgrades, but you can only have 7 active at a time. These upgrades can be disabled by killing the warchief in charge of the upgrade.
The skill tree has also seen a major overhaul with lots of new skills, for example "Bird of Prey" which allows you to use your bow mid-air while you are falling.
Lastly you can now get gear dropped from the captains you kill. You can get new armor, swords, daggers, bows etc, which gives you different abilities (if the gear is epic or legendary that is)
So final verdict; definetely a good game, more fun and more variety in the fighting than the first. Close to be a must-have game in my opinion. There are two things holding it back: the microtransactions and the late game grind. The micro-transactions isnt intruding (until the grind begins), but for me personally it is a matter of principle. The grinding gets to a point where you either have to invest an enormous amount of time into the game or use the in-game market to get better captains and warchiefs.

This is a game for all ages, but it's probably more relatable for teenagers and kids.
Some of the puzzles are really straightforward, others require some good thinking. A few of them are just plain tedious. I personally felt stumped
and needed to look up how to get through certain parts of the game. The mechanics of the final puzzle are really annoying and don't seem to make that much sense in terms of its purpose.
While most of the puzzles are fun, the progression of the plot feels slow. After Act 1, it's like waiting for something super exciting to happen but ultimately being let down. The ending of the game feels rather anti-climatic (there's actually hardly a climax to begin with). It's more like a cliffhanger and leaves a lot of questions still unanswered, with some potential plot holes.
Otherwise it's a pretty decent game, with great graphics. I recommend waiting for a sale, which seems to happen often, because I don't personally think it's worth the full twenty.

Wow. Oh, wow. You guys probably know by now that I overuse the word "masterpiece". Usually when I say that, I usually just mean it's good. When I  say "masterpiece" for this game, I mean it could hang in an art gallery and be remembered for ages.
Alright, let's just put something out on the table.
It should be known that this game was recommended to me by a group of my friends. They went on and on about the art, the characters, the story, the plot-twists. The closest we got to gameplay was how there was a really hard puzzle.
I kinda get why, though. The gameplay has difficulty spikes and lot of them.
Sometimes you'll know just what to do! Other times... Well, not so much.
But, I told myself NUMEROUS times that I was here for the story, which is amazing, but I'll get to that later. The gameplay to me was a big part, but it took a back seat for the art and story.
What I liked the most, as far as the gameplay goes, were the dialogue options.
Broken Age is very linear and that reflects on it's dialogue options, which isn't a bad thing.
The game let me ask questions, get answers, and let me wonder if they were telling the truth.
I've read a decent amount of reviews and everyone said it felt like you HAD to hear what everyone had to say, just so you could know where to get to next.
Well, that WOULD be a problem for me if the character weren't so gosh-dang interesting!
Alright, it's occurring to me that I'm just talking story, story, story, so I might as well just get to that part already. All you need to know about the gameplay is that it's pretty good, often hard, never punishing, and you might need a walkthrough, but it's totally worth it, just for the story.
Wow. I don't even know how to start this.
I don't want to spoil anything, I might write a "spoiler-filled" review, but for now, let me try and recommend this, without giving away anything. Basically, I'm going to vaguely describe stuff? I don't know. Here it goes.
The main story line is interesting, but a bit short. You're always interested in the main characters and are constantly wanting to see what they do next.
The worlds are also interesting, but it's sometimes hard to see what kind of theme the developers are going for. It almost reminded me of a Studio Ghibli film in the sense that I had no idea HOW I was doing what I was doing, but I knew WHY I was doing it, which was justification enough for me.
The characters are the most developed characters I've ever seen in a video game.
The writing is spectacular and flows really well.
Also, the jokes are fantastic.
There we go! I didn't spoil anything! Yay! That was way harder than it should have been!

DISCALIMER: I'M RECOMMENDING THIS GAME FOR DEVELOPERS TO INSPECT AND LEARN FROM, NOT FOR THE CONSUMER TO PLAY.
Dysfunctional Systems is a perfect example of how even though you might have a great idea for a game/VN, despite how well you're sure it'll sell, the actual execution behind producing the game is just as important as the quality of your idea for it.
DysSys had a lot of potential, really a lot going for it. The development idea of the universae was suppsed to be a trilogy, similar World End Economica (a VN series you should buy over this, since yunno it's actually finished).
However, although the Kickstarter raised what could have been enough money to last the development of the game, the developers suffered from poor money and management decisions, which ended up causing all thier capital to dwindle away.
So although the characters were well-written, dialouge was witty and interesting, the universe felt very well fleshed out with room to grow, and great soundtrack to boot, no one got to experience where this story actually went.
However, failures can hold great lessons to learn from.
If you're looking for a VN to play, STEER CLEAR.
If you're an aspiring developer, espcially one for VNs, I recommend picking this up to check out how well a story can be written with giving the user some choice over some decisions that hold weight, without killing yourself on producing a million and one endings.
I also recommend reading into the story behind the development of this game to learn the mistakes that wer made in the mangment of the team when producing this game as well.
And as I said above, if you want to deal with the heartbreak of falling in love with a dead series, be my guest.

This game continues the legacy of some of the best point-and-click adventure games in the history of gaming, without resorting to copying past successes or trying to be too different. It is worthy to stand in the Hall of Fame of adventure games.
The game hints at it´s historical roots and inspirations with references to Monkey Island, Soylent Green, Dr. Strangelove, Dark City and perhaps Silent Running and Indiana Jones and The Fate of Atlantis.
The female protagonist was extremely well-written, being heroic and clever without resorting to masculine fiction hero stereotypes of being buff or a Data-like know-it-all. The writing of the male protagonist also avoided clichés and wasn't shoved into either masculine or feminine qualities. First and foremost, both protagonists portrayed human qualities - not genders.
The story world was original which is hard to achieve in a world saturated by clichéd storylines. The game was sufficiently difficult and we only got stuck about three times, having to refer to a walkthrough after "trying pretty much everything"; usually the reason was that we´d missed a room or a change in the environment. There was definitely a back for the buck, us spending about three days completing the story.
The story ending could've been more elaborate, but the concept art in the game's end credits hinted satisfactorily on what followed. Excellent game worth every buck.

Dysfunctional Systems is an interesting little VN that raises a lot of questions about the world it's set in and the philosophy of its characters and writers, then cuts out early, leaving you with no answers.
Cyrus and Winter are fairly interesting characters, agents of some sort of mysterious, dimension-hopping organisation which tries to bring "order" and reduce "chaos" in the multiverse at large. Why they do this and how they define these concepts is... not really something that comes up. Again, a possible sequel or continuation might have explored more of this, but as it is, you're very much left to fill in the gaps. Perhaps their organisation are well-intentioned extremists who are meddling in things they don't understand? Perhaps there's some sort of primordial chaos, synonymous with evil, that they work to counteract? Winter's dialogue sometimes betrays her possibly dystopian upbringing, but again, it's all up to you to interpret.
Regardless, Winter and Cyrus appear on a slightly dieselpunk-looking planet, where some sort of international crisis is heating into a potential WMD incident. Winter, who is idealistic, thinks there's a peaceful solution. Cyrus, who is less so, thinks this sounds like the kind of problem an assassination can solve. Again, it's not clear whose side the writers are on, and it might never be without some sort of follow-up- is Winter naive or is Cyrus reckless? The player is given a considerable choice tree to navigate through to try and steer the situation, allowing the devs to add in 11 achievements- honestly more than any reasonable, non-completionist person could earn naturally by playing the game.
Unfortunately, the game then commits the cardinal sin of choice path systems by

As a set-up to a future project, this ending certainly has potential, but without it, there are too many unanswered questions.
My recommendation is entirely conditional on there being some sort of sequel or follow-up, and maybe there being a pretty dramatic discount. It's a visually pretty and seemingly well-written introduction to a franchise that has yet to materialise.

Man, Hotline Miami. How I wish I had played such an amazing game earlier. This violent beauty has been out since late 2012 and sadly I finally first picked it up during the Steam Summer Sale. And now, 33 hours later, I finished it getting every achievement, ready for Hotline Miami 2, which I also bought in the Sale. Hotline Miami is the perfect mix of strategy and brute force to get to your goal. In each level, you are presented with a building full of enemies. You must kill everyone on that floor to progress, and you beat the chapter by killing everyone on every floor. There are a wide range of weapons for both you - Jacket - and the enemy - Russians. Golf Clubs, Shotguns, SMGs, Bats, Knives, Shurikens, just to name a few. Hell, you can even throw scissors at an enemy and it'll kill them.
Hotline Miami's combat is something I truely love, and is not easy to replicate. The player cannot withstand hundreds upon hundreds of bullets
video game characters (I'm looking at you, Heavy Weapons Guy.). One shot by a gun, one swing of a bat and you need to restart. Even though you are given checkpoints on every floor, this doesn't stop you from dying any less. My 'r' key has been used significantly more since I started needing it every time I die. Damn shotguns. Now, as you would expect from many modern shooters, shooting isn't all there is to Hotline Miami. Here are some of the things you have during combat:
Now, every good game comes with it's flaws, it isn't easy to find a game with nothing bad about it, and HM is no exception. The problem is, the flaws in HM are either minor or common, so there is little use listing or complaining about them. Instead, I'd like to say this: Hotline Miami isn't a perfect game, but if you're into it's gameplay, music and style, it damn sure comes close to one. You have to decide what is good and bad about it yourself.
Hotline Miami is one of my favourite games of all time, without question. However, it isn't for everyone. If you aren't into extreme violence, hidden plot, actually needing to focus and/or spending a lot of time to complete a game, I wouldn't recommend this to you. Otherwise, knock yourself out, this truely is a well made title.

A game of Micky rescuing his beloved, Minnie. who is taken by the evil witch, Mizrabel.
This kind of story is familiar and well known if you have seen these Disney cartoons during childhood.
There are five worlds, and each has three stages with the last one being a stage boss fight. Plus the final confrontation with Mizrabel. So, the whole is not so long. playtime to finish is within three, more or less than an hour, without trying to grab all collectibles. Despite its shortness. every world is quite well designed no matter the foreground and the background, with the fantastic orchestra music playing.
As a platform game, it is mild, but because of its variety of design and settings, you won't feel much tedious, only becoming a bit difficult and challenging after entering the fourth world. Beware when Micky jumps and lands. Though the control is not complicated with basic movements, jumping and throwing consumable weapons, still it is better to use controllers to play. if not  supported, you can have some app like Joytokey to make your controller available.
In short, the whole game is enjoyable and relaxing. Playing as Micky, hearing Micky's and Minnie's hilarious voice and Mizrabel's witchlike evilish laughing, definitely recommend it.

If you read this and think "hmm, that kinda sounds like me" then don't make my mistake.  Give this game a pass.
Otherwise, you are free from whatever condition I seem to have and you can enjoy this game like the rest of the world apparently does.
