Alright, well, as you already know, Remedy is forced to take down Alan Wake from Steam, Xbox Store, GOG and other digital platforms due to expiring music licenses. Some may say it's stupid and some may say it's understandable. Me personally, I think that there are just some situations in which renewing licenses and keeping that game "alive" just for the sake of I don't know what is really not worth it. Remedy also stated today, that they can't just remove the tracks from the game, reason was "large variety of engineering, resources etc.". Now, it's also been stated that they are looking to renew them, but they don't have timeframe, which in most of the cases means that no, they're not going to renew it.
Alan Wake is 7 years old, there's been just plenty and plenty and plenty of opportunities to get it almost for free (today is that day too). I believe lot of you will remember 2013 and awesome Humble Bundle where it was for 1 dollar. Also, who knows how many copies was sold this year, and for what price, and then there is that major question if it is really worth to take care of new licenses, if Alan Wake is still able to bring some income and revenue. Who knows right?
Now, I don't really want this "review" to be review yet. Thing is that I did not complete the game in time of this writing yet, I was close to the end of the game but still, there is no way I want to provide any word look into the Alan Wake game yet. Once I finish the whole game, I will write review for it, and edit it under this first article. Reason is, that I want to have opportunity to have review of Alan Wake, here at Steam, in my profile, because once it is gone from Steam Store, you can't obviously review it. I made same mistake with Metro series.
I do have a lot of personal stories with Alan Wake, which I keep for myself this time and lot of times, eras and dates are related to Alan Wake that also with the quality of the game itself makes it one of the best games I have ever played and it helped climb this game on the TOP10 of mine.
Also I do have near identical coat as the Alan is wearing during the game, it is basically same, I just don't have those elbow patches in black, but in grey color. Otherwise it is 100% identical and I feel so awesome when I'm wearing that :D
I also want to say to those people who have the game, don't sleep on it.
Those people who don't own the game yet, Alan Wake is pretty much worth actual retail price and I'm not even joking. This game is really one of few that is definitely worth full retail price of 30 euros/dollars so today, when you'll have opportunity to grab it in 90% discount for 3/4 dollars, holy sh*t go for it without thinking. That'll be one of the best buys you've done for the past couple of months.
Last thing, that is on my mind, is big shoutout to Remedy. In this case, that they did notice us, that game is going to be removed, not like others who just simple don't give a flying f*ck and remove it without even saying words. So, thanks for that and for the headsup.
Also note that American Nightmare will not be removed from Steam.

I have NO idea what all the hate was about. Yes, the game ran only in 30 fps for the first 2 days after release, but for the first time, that didn't even annoy me that much. After the patch it runs in 45-50 fps in my 1070 (highest setting with some annoying options off) and there are no slowdowns at all. It jumps to 30 in the cutscenes but that's it.
Graphics are a little outdated but fit the dark and gritty atmosphere of the game. The bad textures people showed off on youtube and posted pictures of on the forums were recorded in the lowest setting. The game has a graphic tool that starts up before the game and it doesn't work properly (at least before the patch). I set everything to max before my first run and the options didn't make it into the game. In-game, everything was still on low and I had to crank it up again in the ingame options.

+ Great main story, aims to be 'realistic' and this works just fine.
+ Great, believable characters. Historical events are tied in.
++ Awesome music, sound effects and voice acting
+ a few 'wow' effects in turns of storytelling
- really bad enemy AI that occasionally kills the atmosphere
- boring side missions (drive across the whole map, get that, kill x, drive back across the whole map, rinse and repeat)
- the customization and upgrade system sometimes unlocks skills, weapons or items  and you have no idea what exactly caused the unlocking.
- shooting out of the car doesn't work properly due to some auto-aim system that always puts the reticle on the hood of the car.
- a few random bugs/glitches like invisible cars, invisible people,... happended like 3 or 4 times during the whole playthrough.
not worth it.

I was VERY excited for Mafia 3. Mafia 2 was easily one of the best games I've ever played so I wanted the third one something fierce. When it finally arrived and I put some time into it, I found that it wasn't Mafia III. It was Mafia II with grinding added and customization taken away.
A couple of the best parts of Mafia 2 was the ability to store vehicles in a garage, customize all of your vehicles with different paints or rims and performance upgrades that would a lot of the time add a hood scoop/supercharger, and tons of different cool (sometimes not so cool) outfits for Vito to wear. Lincoln gets to wear one outfit the entire game, you can choose from 9 pre-determined vehicles that never change color, a performance upgrade applies to all vehicles and only sometimes adds a scoop/supercharger. Why they thought taking such awesome parts out was a good idea, I'll never know. Another thing is that Mafia 2 had a lot of little scripted/random encounters that really added to the world. You could wander around and see all kinds of things. Like early on in Mafia II there's a guy trying to fix his car while his wife nags at him. He threatens to hit her but doesn't actually do it and just wanders off leaving his wife to fend for herself so you, as Vito, step in and fix the car. I once pulled out of a garage in Mafia 2, got hit by some guy in a station wagon. The cops pull up, make him get out of the car. As one cop is putting cuffs on him, the guy tries to run and they shot him. Mafia 3 has nothing like that that I've seen so far after 30 hours of gameplay.
Optimization is garbage, although it was pretty bad with Mafia II as well. With a i7 4790k oc'd to 4.6GHz, a Strix 980Ti OC, 32GB of DDR3 1600hz RAM, my processor is at 64C, my GPU is at 82C, and I'm playing in 4k at near "ultra". Textures look okay at best, lot of ghosting, lighting engine is just God awful (some interiors are pitch black, some are blinding, light comes and goes as it pleases), sometimes textures look smudged, pop in is terrible, and they did the cheap tactic of making far off movement go at like 5fps. The game has crashed a few times with no indication of why, just an immediate CTD.
Dialogue is recycled a LOT. It's very apparent at a particular jazz club you go to later in the game. NPCs kept saying, "I thought I was a honky tonk guy but this music is starting to grow on me." 15-20 different NPCs saying the same thing got real annoying, real fast. Not all dialogue is bad, however, something are pretty cool.
The AI all got dropped on their heads when they were babies. I once took out almost an entire stronghold by hiding behind a 3 foot tall wall and whistling for bad guys. There was a literal pile of bodies right behind me that anyone taller than a 3 year old could see, but these guys just kept coming. You can have bodies sitting in plain view for bad guy NPCs to see and they'll just be like, "Oh damn, my buddies are dead! Better go check it out on my own!" They WILL try to flank you, so that's a nice touch, but when you can nearly chain melee kill them all, there's a problem. You can stealth kill an NPC within 2 feet of another or (in the animation) step out from behind cover, but as long as his back is to you or you left cover because of the animation, it's cool, you're safe
Now some good points so I don't look like I'm whining too much. The story is awesome. I'm really digging what's being told and HOW it's being told. The interviews and "footage" of Donovan in front of a committee are super cool. A lot of the locales are pretty interesting though there are some that are super boring (did you need to copy paste entire buildings/layouts?). Facial animations are pretty solid, some of the best I've seen so far and character design is pretty great. There's a pretty good selection of cars if you don't mind, you know, never getting to keep any of them except the 9 pre-determined cars. Driving feels good, pretty much the same as in Mafia 2. Lot of people complain about it, but I think they're probably just garbage drivers. Some of the animations are just awesome. Some NPCs will flip you off right before dying, which is cool. When it rains, the streets don't automatically become wet, you can actually see the individual rain drops slowing soaking the asphalt/concrete. All in all, this feels like the B grade GTA5.
If you're a huge fan of Mafia 2, this may not be the next Mafia game for you. If you can treat it like its own separate thing, it's an awesome game. If you have a toaster for a computer, don't even bother. Right now, I'm going to finish out the game and then probably never touch it again until I get word that enough updates/DLC have been dropped to make this game what it rightfully should be. But I have a feeling that's not going to happen.

I cautiously recommend Broken Age, in part because it is so often on sale at such low prices that there is little harm in giving it a shot.  Despite the game's audiovisual strengths and occasional bouts of cleverness, it is a thin -- if stretched -- shadow of the classic adventure game it was promised to be.
Let me begin with describing a key divergence between almost all contemporary adventure games and the games that I deem to be classics from the 1990s.  In my view, many contemporary adventure games rival, and perhaps even exceed, the classics in audiovisuals, story-telling, and length.  The area in which they consistently fall short is puzzle design, and I include my own Primordia in that criticism.  Contemporary adventures tend to have four very basic puzzle types: (1) use inventory item A on inventory item B; (2) use inventory item A on hotspot B (which might include an NPC to whom you give the item); (3) examine object A and tell NPC B about object A; and (4) interact with standalone puzzle, such as Tower of Hanoi, Pipe Dream, Simon, etc.  The best classics included these puzzle varieties, but they also had a large number of environmental puzzles, which required the player to understand the way in which items, NPCs, and environment interact.  Off the top of my head, examples of this include passing the lasers in Space Quest IV, finding the Sword Master in Monkey Island, and winning the spitting contest in Monkey Island 2.
Broken Age has almost none of these "classic" puzzles until the latter portion of the second half of the game.  Most of its puzzles are very rudimentary variants of the four kinds described above.  The overwhelming majority of the puzzles, particularly in the first half, are so simple that they are either instantly soluble or soluble only by brute force because failure involves missing a dialogue option or overlooking a hotspot, not failing to understand the mechanics of a puzzle sufficiently to deduce its solution.  As best I can recall, all of these puzzles had a single solution, and amusing "gratuitous" interactions are fairly limited.
The game is relatively long compared to classic adventures, but its length arises almost entirely from extremely long-winded (if often amusing) cut scenes and dialogues and copious backtracking among the same relatively small number of locations.  The quantity of dialogue struck me as also out of sync with classic adventures, which tended to tell their simpler stories through gameplay rather than exposition.  Regarding the backtracking, my problem is less that the entire game occupies so little space and more that so much time is spent walking between distant rooms.  Indeed, I thought it was both clever storytelling and clever salvaging of a mostly expended budget that the second half of the game involves the same locations, but each one is somewhat changed.
Two final notes about the game.  First, I thought the game did a pretty good job of expressing the two protagonists' characters (hyper-competent girl and hyper-sheltered boy) through the puzzles they undertook.  Second, more negatively, there seems to be a disconnect between the game's children's-cartoon-like aesthetic and its laborious pacing and long dialogues, which proved intolerable to my kids when we played together.  (By contrast, they loved Loom, Sam & Max, Monkey Island, Primordia, etc.)  Moreover, while the first half of the game is so basic and so amenable to brute force that a young child can manage it, the second half of the game includes logic puzzles that are far beyond a child's abilities or patience.  It's an odd mix, one that seems to have been born of pressure from the game's Kickstarter backers during its production.
I guess my bottom line is that I would view this as an inferior version of Grim Fandango: similar in its focus on dialogue and story-telling, similar in its audiovisual ambitions, but shorter, blander, and far less compelling.  As noted, the main cost to playing this game is your time, since it is often available for a couple dollars, so I am comfortable suggesting that people at least try it.

I would say this game is worth playing. On occasion an update will cause problems, but while they are sometimes annoying and sometimes not, they're rarely enough trouble to make the game even dissapointing to play. In comparison to the very first tech demo ever released for it, it is MILES better. The first ever tech demo had all sorts of bugs, like the transmission randomly becoming unresponsive, on occasion random game crashes, sometimes hilarious graphical errors with the trucks (although that last one could have been the graphics card I used to have as well), etc. But now, the game is a lot more stable, the user interface makes a lot more sense, the game runs a bit smoother and the ground deforms even better than it already did in that first tech demo, etc. However, this game still does come with it's share of issues. Number one, multiplayer can randomly disconnect sometimes with no reason. Number two, steering wheels have been having the most issues lately. The previous update had a bug where the split pedals function incorrectly worked due to a programming error, and they fixed that...only to now cause ANOTHER problem where the game is still trying to control the clutch pedal in manual mode at the same time as recieving input from the wheel, which causes the clutch to rapidly engage and disengage when you hit the gas and therefore can't be played with a steering wheel shifter for now. The worst part is that they are SOOOOOO SLOOOOWWW to update this game too! You can't have a game with nice physics and graphics if your player can't control the darn thing in the first place!
Overall, though, I still like this game a lot. Aside from these flaws, the gameplay is still enough to keep me drawn in and everything looks absolutely gorgeous! If you are into offroad simulation, then what are you waiting for? Come join the fun!

Some immersion-breaking issues and an ending that doesn't do the game justice keep this game at the level of a short but very entertaining adventure game with high production value (especially the stellar music!) and an interesting  (albeit somewhat rushed) storyline. But ABSOLUTELY AWESOME music.
Very much recommended if you just want to play through a nice fluffy relatively short adventure game with original graphics and story.
It doesn't offer any mind-bending puzzles, you'll rarely have more than about 5 objects in your inventory, and the controller neatly shows you every interactive location. So it's not hard. Not at all, actually, to the point where a seasoned adventure gamer may find herself longing for puzzles where the first hunch wasn't indeed the full solution. But hey... At least it's newbie friendly :)
And it is soooooo lovely! Also: Vella. The Duke Nukem of fluffy female family-friendly cuddly super-thin adventure game protagonists. Don't get on her bad side - she'll f*kn have you for breakfast.
Biggest faults are a number of minor, but noticeably immersion-breaking continuity errors. E.g. object descriptions assuming you haven't yet found room X, that don't change even after you find room X. Or the protagonist being rewarded some item for no reason whatsoever (obviously a solution to an undiscovered puzzle).
Also, obvious hints are obvious in that "let's just SPELL IT ALL OUT in capitalized hints in the DIALOG lines"-way.
And what's with Marek's voice acting? It's atrocious. Especially compared to all that other very good voicing. I'd like to know how that got through.

The story really is the selling point, since the combat isn't challenging even on the hardest difficulty. If you like the exploration aspect of Metroidvanias and voice-acted storytelling, you'd probably like this game. Otherwise, you can give it a pass.

I played about two thirds of the game and decided I had enough. I don't mind dying and playing the same section again and again, but I do mind that the game punishes me after I died one too many time and reverts to the begining of a level, a good 10 minutes lost (and quite a few checkpoints).
Pros
+ Many aspects of the game are well designed and are highly polished. Graphics, maps (excluding checkpoints / save system), music, narration - are all very professional.
+ Who knew playing as Mickey Mouse can be fun for an adult? It definitely is for large parts of the game.
Cons
- Save system and checkpoints are very poorly done. The biggest issue is the one I described above. In addition, if you exit the game and then start it again, you can't resume from the last checkpoint. You're just dropped in the main hall of the castle and you need to figure out which room you visited last. At least the game remembers which parts were completed.
- Controls. So so bad... specifically platforming on the Z-axis is very difficult with a D-pad. It would have been much easier with classic FPS-like keyboard+mouse controls.
- When you die in boss fights, you have to listen to the same narration again and again, and again. Luckily it's possible to turn off narration, which I temporarily did in boss fights.
If you don't mind seeing later parts of the game (spoiler alert),
is the part that I couldn't cross because of the terrible controls. And
is how far back the game decided to drop me for failing to pass.
Both links are part of an edited walkthough, so are more compressed compared to how long it actually takes in practice (at least to a player of my modest skills). Just watch the section between these two links and think if it makes any sense to punish the player and force him/her to replay the whole thing instead of just starting again from the last checkpoint.
Considering the poor the level design and frustrating controls are, I just cannot recommend this game, regardless of cost.

These are the questions presented to you at the beginning of Hotline Maimi, and ones that you will ponder thoughtout the duration of the game.
Hotline Miami is a difficult 2D top-down action video game where you play as a man called "Jacket" whom is ordered to slaughter russian mobsters via anonymous phone calls.
At the beginning of every level you may choose a mask and depending on the mask you choose you get certain bonuses from it, OR some of the masks can make the game extra challenging. (For example: Tony (Tiger mask) gives you the Fists of Fury which gives you faster executions as well as killing blows from fists. This mask disallows you from picking up weapons in the 2nd game.)
This is an ultraviolence type of game, meaning there is a lot of blood, gore, and mutilation, and although this game is very pixelated it's still brutal.
Hotline Miami also has one of the BEST soundtracks from a video game that I've ever heard. The soundtrack makes you feel pumped and excited and in some cases makes you play better oddly enough.
The game is very worth it and the story that lies within the game is worth concentrating on, especially if you plan on playing the 2nd game.
The game also comes with another characters point of view, "Biker" whom is also receiving these strange phone calls. He is Jacket's rival in the game.
All in all, this game is definitely worth playing. Now go get your murder spree on ya bloody lunatic.

Amazing game. Beautiful tied-in story. Multiple ways to play. Multiple ways to go about the story. Takes a bit of getting used to the controls but once you have it, it makes sense.
I apprecieated how it wasn't a "hack n' slash" game 24/7. At times, it worked. However, combat is diverse and your ways to approach a situation varry. You may kill the troll, loot his corpse and make a vest out of his entrails. Or you can find his wife, he will then be a source of comedic relief when ever you pass by, and even come to your call if you need him. But really, its up to you.
There are no "Good Guys" and "Bad Guys". There are simply a bunch of awful people and a bunch of seemingly less awful people and really, you get to choose who is what. Thats the nice thing about the game; there's no simplicity to the story. No "do this", "do that", "now kill the the big guy". You get your choice in the story (like a "choose your adventure" book), and it unfolds around you and your choices.
There is a heavy emphasis on the story (it sometimes tests your knowledge on it), so if you want to go kill a bunch of zombies, or something like that, and that's it, you should probably look elsewhere. There may be a plenty of "zombies" to kill here but if you enjoy getting pulled into the events, the sotry, the lore of a game, you haven't need to look further.
And that's what I have to say. Well made game. Enjoy.

Issac arms himself with various weapons, including belongings of his parents, rosary beads, antidepressants, depressants, and cancer. I don't understand why people are complaining so much about this game. I think it's awesome! It has some downsides, of course, but they're minor. I recommend playing it on hard difficulty and simulation driving.
My PC meets the exact recommended specs. If you DO want to play this game on PC you have to use a controller to really enjoy it. I use a 360 controller for driving and mouse/keyboard for shooting. Do consider the fact that I bought this game from the store on DVD after the 60 fps patch was released. So far I've had zero problems with fps or performance/crash issues.
The driving is awesome, especially on simulation. The cars are heavy and you can feel this in the handling.
Combat is also awesome and a lot of fun. The taunts are funny as hell. I love the parts where the npcs throw molotovs on themselves if they get shot before they can get a good throw in.
The game recreates the 1960s quite nicely. The city, the buildings, the cars, especially the music. However, I've always been a fan of "Vietnam War music". 1960s cars are really fun to drive. The racism and overall atmosphere of being a black man in that time really hits you. I fell in love with the main character from the first few missions.
The first negative aspect about this game would be the outside camera while driving. I prefer it to be at a higher angle, but maybe it's just me. The second one is the variation in lighting when clouds go overhead. The variation is a bit too high and seems unnatural. Also, the car graphics in the city could be a bit better, but maybe it's because of my graphics settings.
In conclusion, this is a solid game with an excellent story, excellent gameplay and tons of fun! I give it a 9/10. Would definitely recommend.

I picked up & played Broken Age without knowing the history, and from that point of view, I was satisfied with what I got.  It's a fun point & click adventure with flaws, yes, but still a worthwhile experience overall.
In judging this type of game, I think there are three points to consider.  The first are the puzzles judged just as puzzles, and here I'd give a passing grade.  It is notable how the difficulty curves up in a way I haven't often seen in this genre.  Items are reused and there's a clear aim to go beyond "put the thing on the thing"-type obstacles.  At the same time, some of these were the ones I found the most frustrating, like trying to navigate the hexipal through the ship or that infuriating knot problem.  Also, in the later stages there are puzzles where you'll need to switch character to get the information you need.  While you can argue that the characters in-game know the information, this type of knowledge gathering does break immersion, at least for me.
The second question is how well the puzzles inform the story.  There are some strengths here.  The ease of Shen's puzzles in Act One tie in thematically to his story arc.  The gradual rise in difficulty matches the raising stakes of the plot.  In Act One, the obstacles you face help to illustrate the nature of the world you are in.  Particularly good is the way that you retread areas later, seeing the influence of your previous puzzle-solving, how the NPCs have reacted in your absence, and getting a generally different perspective.
Finally, there is the story side itself, including all non-puzzle elements.  This I think is generally good.  The voice acting is superb, the art style works, the NPCs are all interesting and there are many moments of humour.   The biggest problem is unfortunately the ending, which to me felt a little rushed and incomplete.  I understand why things ended where they did, especially from a gameplay perspective, but I think it's telling that an end credits montage was needed to wrap things up.
But despite the occaisional flaw, I did enjoy Broken Age, and I at least feel I got value for my money.

SoW proves that bigger does not always mean better, but what hurts this game even more is the arcadey direction Monolith choose. Poison or frost novas, double jumps, super speed, orc's corpses exploding after you kill them, etc. - it's just too much. I, for one, preferred the more coherent, grim and down-to-earth approach that SoM took which made me feel like I'm actually in Middle-Earth (albeit after a very slight suspension of disbelief). With SoW, there wasn't a single moment I felt like this is Tolkien's universe, that I'm actually playing a Lord of the Rings game.
The highlight and focus of SoW is fortress sieging, during which an army of your orc followers and the enemy orcs from the region clash and fight, accompanied by siege beasts (graugs with catapults strapped to their back, which guess what, can be cutomized to fire either poison, fire or cursed rocks), and whatever else you/them bring to battle. In essence, you're supposed to capture vicotry points (at least 3) in order to unlock the stronghold's boss. Now, victory points are basically small, arbitrary circles on the ground into which the whole action is funneled - orcs swarm one little area in the entire fortress and that's it, you kill them, you move to the next one. It's not a grand scale battle over the enitre fortress. It's rush point A, capture, rush point B, capture, etc., unlock the boss fight. Pretty underwhelming to say the least.
The fighting also somewhat loses its focus, with customizable skills that you can switch and activate on the fly for various builds. Let's say you want a poison build, so you get yourself some nice poison-enhancing gear, choose poison skills and you're set. The build I went for was a versatile one (to account for orcs' immunities), with the main thing being that once I counter someone, they're knocked to the ground immediately, and then I cannot be interrupted while finishing them off. Anybody attempting to stop the finisher gets countered, knocked to the ground, finished off. I played on the highest difficulty setting, where orcs can kill you in ~3 hits, so obviously this was a golden strategy for me. Sadly, it very quickly became super repetitive and sucked the fun out of combat. But was bar none the most effective approach to combat.
As for the story - forgetabble and unispired with moments that surely got Tolkien roll in his grave.
Overall, a game less focused than SoM, but with improved Nemesis System, packed with meaningless stuff just for the sake of being able to say 'IT'S BIGGER', without the LotR feel. IMHO, SoM is a better game.

Broken Age looks great. I really wanted to stress that first, because if there's something that Double Fine were always good at - it's the visual style. And Broken Age looks, animations, sounds and all the rest of audiovisual things, are amazing. They were also always good at making an interesting charming spin on some serious topics and weird cultural and temporal mixes of different ages and styles and it works great in Broken Age. The setup is pretty simple - two seemingly unrelated characters are stuck in situations they wish to control. Vella, living in a strange fairy tail-ish world is about to be sacrificed to some horrible monster in a festive way with no one around even considering fighting back instead and fully embracing the grim tradition. Shay is stuck on a spaceship controlled by a computer called Mom, who cares about his safety so much, none of the things, meant to simulate real space missions, matter or present any danger whatsoever. And both get a chance to change the situation.
And it all works amazingly and charmingly well in Act 1. But, you see, this is where I need to mention that the game was released in 2 acts - one was released in 2014. And after that a whole year and a half passed until the second act was released. And despite the fact that the story was seemingly designed from the start and a lot of things implied in Act 1 were already thought out to reveals in Act 2, what actually happens in the second act often happens in detriment to the first act. While Act 1 isn't a particularly demanding adventure game (then again - I never liked them for puzzles anyway), it was a really fun and exciting ride from start to finish. Act 2 right off the bat makes strange reveals that barely make any sense and then proceed to make the story and events being less and less interesting and creative. And by the end of Act 2 we're stuck re-doing really boring and tedious puzzle over and over again to just get it over with. Until the game abruptly ends with no real satisfying conclusion.
It's not really a game that's very VERY worth checking out, but it's certainly charming and interesting. Just feels rushed in the end and not that well designed as a complete experience.

Yes, microtransactions are bad and we all hate it, but giving this game a negative review as a whole is like amputating your leg because you've stubbed your toe. To be honest, MCs aren't even as invasive as I'd thought, if you play only singleplayer you won't even have to deal with them.
The game itself is amazing, it improves on every single aspect I could have wished for being a big fan of the first game. I bought it on sale for 35 bucks and it was completely worth the money, hell it's probably even worth its full price. Storywise, I haven't finished it yet, and even though so far it was great I'll limit myself to the gameplay commentary.
The skill system is deep, you get different that you can personalize, there are 5 maps that are roughly the same size as the 2 zones of the first game, the combat system is a bit refined, the game on "nemesis" difficulty is finally challenging (Shadow of Mordor was a joke, haven't died once), the collectibles are great, the story is great, the graphics are great AND YOU CAN FLY ON MADAFAKKING DRAKES.
Now, if it wasn't for some very rare, minor bugs in the controls (you might get stuck somewhere for a while or Talion will just jump where you didn't ask him to), the fact that no matter what armor you're wearing the cutscenes always set back your default outfit and the fact that an orc captain can cheat death after being beheaded, this game would be almost perfect.
If you loved the first game, this one is everything you could have wished for.

I finally finished the story. I don't know what's wrong with all the people that say that it sucks, I personally found it pretty great. Not perfect mind you, but overall it's just what I expected, a huge improvment on the predecessor, way more epic and with everything a LOTR fan could ask for.

Hotline Miami is a difficult 2D top-down action video game where you play as a man called "Jacket" whom is ordered to slaughter russian mobsters via anonymous phone calls.
At the beginning of every level you may choose a mask and depending on the mask you choose you get certain bonuses from it, OR some of the masks can make the game extra challenging. This is an ultraviolence type of game, meaning there is a lot of blood, gore, and mutilation, and although this game is very pixelated it's still brutal.
Hotline Miami also has one of the BEST soundtracks from a video game that I've ever heard. The soundtrack makes you feel pumped and excited and in some cases makes you play better oddly enough.
The game is very worth it and the story that lies within the game is worth concentrating on, especially if you plan on playing the 2nd game.
The game also comes with another characters point of view, "Biker" whom is also receiving these strange phone calls. He is Jacket's rival in the game.
All in all, this game is definitely worth playing. Now go get your murder spree on ya bloody lunatic.

Was quite hyped after finding it being funded on Kickstarter, and tested it for about 8 hours during the free week-end.
Saying I am disappointed would be an understatement. While I can clearly see the developper's intention into making it a good game, it really fails to deliver any kind of 'fun', and the realism they tried to input either fails or is pointless. I won't go in length about it because there are already some pretty good detailed review on it but here are some example:
- weapon's jamming occurs way too frequently, had one or two every two combat, if you're trying to be realistic, ok, but that level of jamming is just neither fun nor 'realistic'
- a lot of the early combats are just plain autistic, while I understand that you are 'just a rookie', having only a 20% or less chance to hit an immobile target at less than 10 meters makes you feel like you are playing with elementary schoolers
- the weapons ammo type and usage are just totally wrong for a lot of them. I know that I can't expect full milsim realism here, but having the M2 which is a real life .50 cal heavy machine gun used only on vehicles or tripod being lifted by a normal random joe just because he has the 'heavy weapon skill' and having it fire 5.56 rounds is just wrong. And the game actually makes the M60 SUPERIOR to it which is just plain stupid.
- rocket launchers are all single use. Okay.
- max range is 46 meters for the best sniper in the game, yup
- bringing me to the line of sight which is... weird. Sometimes you can't see just inside a room just 1 meter away from you with doors wide opened because you're not actually inside, and sometimes a full room with a lot of corridors (that you shouldn't be able to see in) is just wholly diplayed
- the AI for some ennemies is way too developped. It is understandable that human / intelligent ennemies will try to spread out in CQC in order to have the maximum malus on all of your team, but this kind of behavior isn't suitable for dumb animals. It only feels like the devs only coded one AI pattern and went 'yup, that's ok, apply on everybody'.
- a lot of RPGs integrate a 'taking my time to do that' option (particularly for shooting things when you are still undetected), this one doesn't for some mysterious reason, making you fire as dumbly outside a combat as you would during a combat
- some skills are kinda dumb, I mean ramming into a door shouldn't require a skill
- no synergy between skills (because safe cracking and lockpicking are as different as computer hacking and firing a heavy weapon right?)
- no (apparent?) synergy between skills and abilities, while I'm not sure about this one it's definitely not effective enough to be noticeable, therefor the point still stands, it's almost as if you could have two left hands and be a master at lockpicking because you levelled up the skill and are way better than the guy with average lockpicking skills but can do art with his pinkies while blindfolded
- graphics are ugly, seriously this game was released in 2014 but I felt like playing The fall (last days of gaia) back in 2004, I'm not asking for Far Cry tier graphiscs, but those could've been largely improved
- apparently it's still possible to have really bad camera angles in 2014 on a PC game (bad to the point that you might miss an item / interaction)
- weird feeling of "freedom", I've grown accustomed to Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim and this game made me feel like I'm not "that free" to do stuff, the levels and quests are way too much straight-forward and the secondary quests are boring (you did that on the main quest? good now repeat that at least 3 times again in other uninteresting locations)
- strange choices for voice acting, some voices play nicely, some others are just plain weird, and while I understand why not every single character is voiced, I can't really understand why the voiced ones aren't fully voiced (about 10 to 30% of their lines are)
- the atmosphere is ok, but the drama is overwhelming. On the main quest, you have to chose between saving location X or location Y, you can't do both. That's ok, a bit early in the game (you get into that part within 1 hour of gameplay or less), but ok. What is not okay is to remind you CONSTANTLY while you're doing everything to save X that Y is being overwhelmed / killed / whatever. Now the good things about the game. The storyline is pretty well done, although there could be more rewarding side missions. With all of that said, and I probably could have added more to both pros and cons, it isn't a bad game. Is it worth more than $20? No way. That's the most I'd pay for it. But it is a game worth buying. Just get it when there's a deal for it.

Miturugi Kamui Hikake is a speedy 3d arena based hack and slash, in which players sword fight through waves of enemies and bosses in a small circular arena with a fully realized combat engine.
The combat in MKH is extremely well executed. Combos are fairly freestyle, but there's a slight delay before you can block or dodge cancel attacks, and dodging and blocking requires a higher degree of precision and timing than many other games of the genre, so it most definitely takes  skill  and finesse to master. Many of the unlockable moves and areial attacks are also quite fun, and skilled players who can master parrying and flourishing will be able to unleash impressive destruction on the games swarms of eneimies.
There are a few issues however. The game sometimes becomes a bit repetitive when it throws the same set of enemies at you several times before mixing things up, making a few waves feel a bit like filler. Buying new moves can sometimes be a liability, as their inputs are often simply attack + any direction, which can be awkward when running around attacking enemies since you'll  have to carefully come to a halt each time if you don't want to accidentally use an unsafe special. I found it easier just to avoid purchasing certain moves. Some may also find being confined to an arena degrades the feeling of adventure and variety found in similar 3d action games. These issues do hold the game back a bit, but they are easily eclipsed by the numerous enjoyable sword fighting moments.
If you enjoy the sword fighting engine and don't mind the lack of an adventure feel, than there's a lot to love here. The game offers plenty of unlockable difficulty modes for players willing to explore it (I personally recommend starting on hard and working your way up), with the last ones being very real challenges. I recommend trying out the demo on Playism to see if the combat clicks with you, because if it does it will be fairly easy to ignore the games relatively few flaws and focus on the excellent combat.

My specs: Windows 10 with 8GB RAM and an AMD Radeon RX 480 graphics card.
There is a lot to be said about the final chapter of this trilogy, and while not all of it is good, I still definitely recommend the game. Let's get the BAD out of the way so that we can focus on the GOOD.
First, every time I entered the game I was warned that I only had 4GB of RAM, and that the game recommended six... *looks at my specs mentioned above, then back at warning* :\ Yep, I'm pretty sure that EIGHT gigs is not the same as FOUR, but I digress... This did not seem to affect my gameplay.
GLITCHES: I only saw two actual game glitches. One was where a character mysteriously appeared OUTSIDE of the compound where I'd been fighting his crew, and the other was that the bat signal indicated a quest item being over the WRONG building. Not bad, as far as glitches go!
TECHNICAL DIFFICULTIES: They are many, and could be game-breaking if you are not comfortable with adjusting some files. I had no troubles in the beginning, but then the problems started: Lagging, crashing, and even completely shutting down my computer with zero warning. *cries* Lagging I can deal with. Crashing I can deal with. Shutting off my computer over and over again? WHYYYYY??? It started happening so often that despite how much I was enjoying the game, I was beginning to think that I'd have to stop playing...
... and then I found the Master Fixes for BATMAN ARKHAM KNIGHT thread here at Steam, and my hope was rekindled. It turns out a couple of files corrupt over time, and all I had to do was delete one file and one folder, then verify the integrity of the game cache (very easy on both points), and voilà -- WORKING GAME! *cue angels singing*
GRAPHICS: If you don't have a new enough graphics card, the game won't even start for you. The plus side of the high-spec card is that the graphics are amazing. From the smallest dust particle to the sweeping bridges and skyscrapers, Gotham City truly feels alive. Every crack in the sidewalk, every fierce tattoo, each choppy wave, an craggy wrinkle tells a story that makes you want to know MORE. The people may not be as attractive as in previous installments, but they are more realistic, and they truly have character. The devs have introduced a photo mode, where you can pause the game and do a nearly 360-degree rotation to get just the perfect shot... Just use the Steam shortcut you set up (F12 default) to take screens, and it removes the ugly interface when you take the shot.
THE GADGETS: We do have a couple of new gadgets to play this time around: A voice synthesizer which allows us an extra layer of tactics by giving orders to assailants, plus the Batmobile, which I'll come back to in a bit. The gadgets are by and large underutilized and not really explained, bringing back my recommendation to play the games in the order in which they were released: Asylum, City, Origin, Knight. Not only will these previous installments give you a feel for the story, combat, gameplay, and general useful knowledge, but you'll get to play some GREAT games!
THE INTERFACE: Most of the controls are the same as what we're accustomed to, though they had to do some tweaking in order to include...
THE BATMOBILE! What a great addition to the series! Not only can you zoom around Gotham City like a boss, you can destroy half the city as you go~! I had great fun running down criminals (literally... Muwahaha), blowing up cars, knocking down trees, fences, support pillars... you get the idea. *evil grin* In addition to a new form of transportation, we have a great many quests, riddles, and fights to win using the Batmobile, which is not only a car, but a BATTLEmoblie! At the touch of a button we can transform it to a highly-maneuverable tank in order to kick all ♥♥♥... We can even do Batmobile-assisted takedowns with Wayne's patented non-lethal rounds. "It's like being punched in the chest by an angry gorilla!"
Many of the Batmobile quests are optional, but you will need to develop some proficiency in driving it, as eventually you'll have to use it to progress in the story.
COMBAT: As usual for the series, combat starts off deceptively easy, then amps up in difficulty as you progress. We have the new Fear Multi-takedown ability, which enables you to take out up to six enemies within seconds... provided that you can come upon the group by surprise. There are also points in the story where you can play two characters at once, and during this time you can do multi-character takedowns. Those are great fun, let me tell you! ;D
We have some new attacks that we can do whilst gliding, plus the items mentioned above, but nothing really game-changing about the combat. We've got our guys with riot shields, cattle prods, brutes, guns... and a few little extra things that I'll let you discover for yourselves.
THE STORY: When the game started, I felt that the side missions were much more engrossing than the main storyline. I went through the game knowing not only exactly who our mystery assailant was, but why we were being attacked... Absolutely positive right up to the moment of the unmasking, and then... Everything changed. That which had been mildly interesting was suddenly fascinating. My mental shift was profound, as far as such things go, and it pulled me into the story in ways I had never considered. Although one aspect of the story I had totally nailed, there were several real surprises throughout, something which I really cherish. A good story is something that I truly appreciate, but you have a good story with great gameplay, and I'm in heaven!
THE ENDING/THE RIDDLES (Still no spoilers!): You must secure a certain number of criminals in order to view the final sequence of the game. You do not have to 100% the game to see the ending, BUT, to get the FULL ending, you have to defeat The Riddler, and THAT means solving, saving, maneuvering, finding, and destroying a total of 243 riddles, people, courses, trophies, and destructible items.
The riddles are the one thing I won't be doing 100% on this time around, though I did get 100% on the rest of the content.
If, like me, you don't plan to solve every single riddle in order to secure the post-Riddler portion of the ending, then NEVER FEAR, YOUTUBE IS HERE! Although some may feel that it's not really important to see that extra tidbit of story, one little sentence during this scene completely changed how I felt about the ending of the game. I'm not gonna add a link, since that's just too tempting to click, and I want this to be spoiler-free.
THE BOTTOM LINE: Batman: Arkham Knight is flawed. The devs have no plans to fix that which is broken, but you CAN fix the problems yourself! If you're a fan of the series and can problem-solve enough to follow the instructions in the Master Fixes for BATMAN ARKHAM KNIGHT thread, then it is ABSOLUTELY worth your trouble. I enjoyed this title immensely, despite the frustrations with the technical difficulties. I would even start the game over again right this minute if it weren't for the fact that I have so many other games that I want to play.
IN CLOSING: I loved this game, and if it weren't for the technical problems that I encountered, it would be my favorite of the series. As it stands, I rank them as follows: Arkham City, Arkham Knight, Arkham Asylum, and then Arkham Origins. Definitely a MUST-play!

Definitely buy this game, but make sure you play with a pack of tissues at your side. (or at least something to help you get over the emotional shock and destructionit will inflict on you)
This game is one of the best games I've ever had the honour to play.
The graphics are beautiful (not the best, but still beautiful), the soundtrack is so amazing that I actually have it saved as a playlist on my Spotify, and the concept is so incredibley simple but yet so well carried out. The art style is also superb.
The best thing about it, though, is the storyline and how much you're drawn into the game with what seems like no escape. As the game goes on, you become more and more attached and involved in Max's life-you actually start to sympathise with her, laugh with her, even cry with her, which can be a difficult thing to achieve for a video game protagonist. I actually ended up crying at the end of episode 2, and physically gasped at my screen more than once as the game went on. I fell in love with max, because she's relatable, and believable as a character-and her relationship with Chloe is refelctive of real life relationships and true platonic
love.
The only big flaw I can give it is that episode 1 and the first half of episode 2 seemed a little slow to me. It took me re-starting the game multiple times, because I got bored of the first episode and forgot what happened when I wanted to try again months later, for me to really become invested in the story to the point of wanting to actively play the game again once I'd left my current session.

Duck Game is another incredible game brought to us by those fine♥♥♥♥♥folks at Adult Swim Games. They have been on a hot streak with their publishing lately. Bringing us Jazzpunk, Volgarr, Super House of Dead Ninjas, and several others. Seems someone over there has an eye for talent. Duck Game originally came to the now defunct Ouya in 2014, which makes me sad to think that this game was locked up over there until now.
A 2-4 player online brawler with guns, made by the developer Landon Podbielski. It has a great pixel art style and a perfectly matched sound track to go with it.
The gameplay is fairly simple. Pick up weapons, slay the enemy ducks, and maybe quack a few times. It's a lot of fun, plus there's hats! Well, some of the hats are heads but it's all good.
Lot's of hectic times to be had across 50 levels with plenty of fun weapons to use. There's a gun with the barrel turned around. I shot myself with it. I laughed. Get some friends together and check out Duck Game!

The quirky graphical art style screams Fallout in a very goofy Fallout kinda way.  This game will run in the background if you log out (quests, explorers, etc. still continue).  But, gone are the days of a random fire or deathclaw attack happening when you're gone, only to find out when you log back in and find your entire vault dead.  Great boredom filler with a Fallout touch.

Dust An Elysian Tail is not the best Metroidvania game out there. In fact, it's pretty disappointing.
The voice acting of your companion is horrible; it's cheesy and the character looks like it was taken straight out of a cartoon. Same goes for the rest of the characters. It looks like half of them were based on Disney characters. The voice acting of the rest of the cast is acceptable, thankfully.
There's also too much dialog and there are too many pauses.
The combat isn't fun or challenging, the game just overwhelms you with enemies. Especially near the end of the game. Taking them down literally takes minutes.
It's frustrating when you want to leave an area quickly but get blocked by a random invisible border that only disappears if enemies are too far away, or defeated.
And last but no least: the map system. It works, but doesn't make any sense. It could've been integrated so much better.
Ok, on to the good stuff... The graphics are pretty. It has sidequests. It has loot and 'secrets' (some of these can't be called secrets). And it's lengthy (although I don't consider that a plus personally).
I guess my hopes were too high. I expected Dust to be great game, thanks to all the positive reviews, but instead got a mediocre game.
It shows that you can't trust anyone but yourself when it comes to playing games. Give it a try, it might surprise you, but don't say I didn't warn you.

Bite Size Review - Alan Wake
The Good:
- Manuscript Collectibles add more story (but kind of also spoil it before you  experience it)
- Story and Setting are Unique
- Radio DJ Voice acting is just Fantastic
- Night Springs TV show in the game is great and cheesy
- Weapons, when you've removed the darkness from enemies, feel powerful
- The atmosphere in this game is the best thing about it
The Bad:
- Removing darkness from enemies gets old fast (essentially make them not "bullet sponges" but "flashlight sponges")
- Over shoulder camera doesn't feel right, and in fights often leads to enemies sneaking up behind you (feels cheap)
- Gun play feels loose since you can only aim were your flashlight is and there is no crosshair
- It feels like every 10 minutes they take all of your weapons away - you would not think this would be a big deal but seriously they do this at least 10 times within the game, and it starts to feel goofy
- The story does not end well, very few answers and ends with a cliffhanger
- This game has momentum/animation priorities that make movement and gun play frustrating in spots were it matters most
The Verdict:
I kept putting playing this game off for a few years since I bought it, having heard so many good things about it. I will say this, the atmosphere in this game is fantastic. You play as Alan Wake, a struggling writer going on vacation in the middle of nowhere in some USA mountain town. They capture the feeling of being in a small town and lost in the woods really well, and the lighting and effects in these areas with your flashlight are great. I feel like the combat and camera controls in this game kind of ruin it for me a little bit. The game is still playable but by the end of the game I was not enjoying the combat and just wanted to finish the story.
My biggest issue with the game is that it has animation priority like other games such as Dark Souls or Lost Planet etc. What this means is that when you are controlling Alan and telling him to move or aim his gun and fire, there is a delay, due to him beginning to move his body or him raising his gun to his shoulder. Now this does not sound like a bid deal, but enemies swarm you quite fast, and without the ability to move or fire your gun immediately like in other shooters I ended up dying a few times and it was sometimes frustrating. Now I did get used to this over time but while I was playing this I couldn't help but think how good Max Payne 1 and 2 were with their combat systems.
Overall I would still recommend this game to people who like an OK story (that is not really resolved) and great atmosphere. I would definitely buy it on sale though.

Autism is a disorder of neural development characterized by impaired social interaction and verbal and non-verbal communication, and by restricted, repetitive or stereotyped behavior. The diagnostic criteria require that symptoms become apparent before a child is three years old.[2] Autism affects information processing in the brain by altering how nerve cells and their synapses connect and organize; how this occurs is not well understood.[3] It is one of three recognized disorders in the autism spectrum (ASDs), the other two being Asperger syndrome, which lacks delays in cognitive development and language, and pervasive developmental disorder, not otherwise specified (commonly abbreviated as PDD-NOS), which is diagnosed when the full set of criteria for autism or Asperger syndrome are not met.[4]

Autism has a strong genetic basis, although the genetics of autism are complex and it is unclear whether ASD is explained more by rare mutations, or by rare combinations of common genetic variants.[5] In rare cases, autism is strongly associated with agents that cause birth defects.[6] Controversies surround other proposed environmental causes, such as heavy metals, pesticides or childhood vaccines;[7] the vaccine hypotheses are biologically implausible and lack convincing scientific evidence.[8] The prevalence of autism is about 1–2 per 1,000 people worldwide, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) report 20 per 1,000 children in the United States are diagnosed with ASD as of 2012 (up from 11 per 1,000 in 2008).[7][9][10] The number of people diagnosed with autism has been increasing dramatically since the 1980s, partly due to changes in diagnostic practice and government-subsidized financial incentives for named diagnoses;[10] the question of whether actual prevalence has increased is unresolved.[11]

Parents usually notice signs in the first two years of their child's life.[12] The signs usually develop gradually, but some autistic children first develop more normally and then regress.[13] Early behavioral, cognitive, or speech interventions can help autistic children gain self-care, social, and communication skills.[12] Although there is no known cure,[12] there have been reported cases of children who recovered.[14] Not many children with autism live independently after reaching adulthood, though some become successful.[15] An autistic culture has developed, with some individuals seeking a cure and others believing autism should be accepted as a difference and not treated as a disorder.[16]

This is a great game for turn-based RPG fans.  There is a ton of reading to do, as is required of the genre, but it nevertheless enables you to be a part of the story in ways that simple actions cannot.
The character building seems to be a weakness in this game, primarily because the player will want to "do everything," but spreading around Skill Points makes that desire very challenging.  Personally, I got frustrated when I couldn't "do everything," such as be a "Hard A s s," because I couldn't budget the Skill Points for it, but then that opportunity was over.  Not a game changer in the grand scheme of things, but again... I like to "do everything."
The combat system for Wasteland 2 is about 50 times better than something like Shadowrun.  The percentage chances for hitting and missing in Wasteland 2 actually make some sense, and you will be properly rewarded or penalized for combat decisions you make.  Games in the same genre as Wasteland 2, like Shadowrun, have these super-frustrating "random number generation" combat systems where you will miss your targets so much so (even with 92% "success chance") that you will yell at the freaking video game developers when things are abundantly unfair or unpredictable.  Thus, Wasteland 2 is much more strategic and fun when you have a fairly certain understanding of the risks of your decisions.  Wasteland 2 is much more fair (whether you die or live) in the combat system than other games in the genre, and thus makes you want to play it longer and care more about the story and your characters, comparatively speaking.
The other things I love about the combat system in Wasteland 2 are the abilities to (1) sort of "sneak attack" a bad guy (say, with your sniper) and get the fight started before they are ready, and (2) duck behind cover and increase your chances of survival (very similar to the XCOM combat system).  Given the fairness and strategic impacts of Wasteland 2's combat system, those alone have given me the ability to recommend this game to any fan of the genre.  (I do no recommend playing Shadowrun, which breaks my heart to say.)
Really, XCOM and Wasteland will be your two primary turn-based, isometric RPGs that you will be playing on your computer for a long time to come.

Just beat it. While I love Mafia 1 despite its reliance on tired tropes and mob story cliches, I have to give Mafia 3 the edge as my favorite in the series. The antagonists were fantastic, as were the supporting characters and protagonist, and I really appreciated the novel narrative presentation framing device. The only thing I miss were the quieter moments from Mafia 1, like when you walk your future wife home, and the player's slow decent into a life of crime. Instead, you're relentlessly focused on dismantling a criminal empire.
It's a shame the game shipped with more technical issues than most open-world games, and it's a pity that you can't customize the experience (eg: disable the UI or stop tutorial pop-ups). Hopefully these issues will be addressed in the near future. The worst part of the game is having to repeat missions to progress the story which can at times disrupt the momentum. Playing through a brewery or luxury bath house map loses its impact the second time round, especially when the objectives remain nearly identical. The side missions are often uninspired (ala Mafia 2 - a drive truck from this side of the map to the other), and player communication could be better: there are confusing objective markers that remain active even when it's not possible for the player to complete them.
Even with these flaws, it's a much better game than Mafia 2, a sequel which benefited from an 8 year development cycle and having Rockstar coming in and rescuing their game. The driving mechanics, the setting and world building, story, soundtrack (both original and licensed) and the gunplay are far and away the best in the series. Even with the filler content I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it. It has the two best scripted missions in the series (one that really makes me want to see Hangar 13 tackle a Bioshock game). For me, it plays like a 3rd person Far Cry 2, which is a great thing. You can approach a racket through subterfuge by strapping C4 to a hot rod and bailing at the last minute, inflitrate using stealth and a Voodoo doll to reach your objective unnoticed, or enjoy some seriously slick 3rd person combat. Even though the missions could use some editing, I had a really great time!

I really like this game but I do have a few problems with it.
The game has beautiful artwork, a great soundtrack and really good voice acting. I also liked the plot twist at the end of the first act and I found the characters to be really likeable. I also enjoyed the world setting in Broken Age with it's mix of both fantasy and sci-fi components. It has good gameplay and the general plot is very interesting. Plus it made me laugh a few times which is always good. It's easy to see that a lot of love and care went into these games and very thankful for it.
The puzzles are a bit of a of a hit or miss for me. Some are really easy and others (like the wire and knot puzzles) were insanely annoying and hard to figure out and I found that a lot of people (including myself) had to resort to a guide to just understand what you needed to do in these situations.
Another problem I have is that that the second act and the ending fell a bit flat for me since it felt a bit rushed compared to the first act. In general I enjoyed the first act more than the second.
Despite my few  issues with the game I highly recommend you give it a go since it really is a good game. There is a lot of good things to enjoy about it and I will definitely be playing it again in the future.

This is a painful review to make because on the one hand, the game's story is really interesting and somewhat engaging like a typical Visual Novel would but without having to resort to overused tropes and makes it clear that it has it's own identity from the get go.
But on the other hand, there's no following story because the dev team ♥♥♥♥ed up hard and tried to be a fully functional studio like Telltale Games is by comparison and produce several titles following after this. The sad truth is, there was no form of planning or meetings being held consistently. The studio filed bankruptcy some time after this title was released. The management was abyssmal, to say the least...
Onto the game, it has a very good soundtrack, one I still enjoy hearing to this day, the art style is nice to look at even if bleak at times for dramatic effect (well used and impactful I might add) and the dialogue is quite mature, despite being very one sided for a pretty good chunk of it, it doesn't feel draggingly long like in other games and is actually well written enough if you are into untraditional VNs. The included encyclopedia like feature is however not useful for most of the story aside from it's introduction. It is wasted effort and could have been made much more relevant if they bothered with it a little more than to just add an entry every now and then for plot purposes, which is to it's detriment. The amount of work put into the encyclopedic portion of the game is respectable but ultimately laughable if you take out the important bits that relates to the plot which, again, were used to introduce the player to its function/presence.
"Should you play this game in my opinion?" is the last question left to be answered; as of right now, no.
The end is a cliff hanger into the next volume that will never come. If, by some miracle, this gets a reboot/revival by the original creator and owner of the copyright and is actively working on developing the sequel, then I will revise my judgement of this first game and give it a recommendation, but unless things start moving again for the development of just chapter 2, stay away from this and save some money for an actually finished game.

Summary: Buy on Sale, Fun to Play, Decent Graphics, Loot box issue was blown out of proportion.
Combat is 10/10 . I have been playing on the highest difficulty and loving it. Brutally fun to smash and decapitate orcs. If nothing else, killing orcs is a reason to buy.
Story is 8/10. Yes, the voice actor for Talion seems to only have 2 emotions, anger and Dull. But, I personally found the obvious breaking of the lore kind of fun. This game acknowledges that it operates next to the actual Lord of the Rings story and world, but cannot ever be canon.
Music is 10/10. All the tracks fit perfectly for me and were not overly invasive or annoying. I turned the volume a bit low but enjoyed them as background music to my dismemberment of orcs.
Loot Boxes : This issue really annoyed me. Mainly becuase it seemed like people who did not even play the game for more than 10 minutes saw the word loot box and vomitted in the review section. After playing this game for a decent amount of time, the loot boxes have had little affect on my gameplay.
You earn the in game currency of mirian very easily. This lets you buy 2 different loot boxes. One gives you 2 orcs (one epic) and a training order to boost them with followers, fire weapons, a mount. The other gives you two weapons, (one rare or epic, sometimes but rarely legendary).
By simply saving up my mirian as I played through the game, I hit the last part of the game, Shadow Wars, with over 100k of mirian. I continue to easily get about 30k mirian (playing missions, killing orcs, sieging and defending forts) which lets me buy orc loot boxes 20 at a time.
As a result, I had over 100 orcs to stock my forts with and attack forts with. Each fort requires 6 orcs if you buy all the slots. With only 5 forts, I essentially had second and third string back ups if an orc died. And I was constantly getting more.
Another complaint that I saw from others, was the possibility of your orcs dying on online conquest when you are attacking. Your orcs have a bleed out timer when they go down. I am not sure about the exact length, but it feels to be at least 30 seconds, which is plenty of time with Talion mobility to go and revive them.
I did not spend or even feel a need to spend a real dollar on this game. You can even complete daily and weekly challenges to earn gold (the currency that is bought with cash) so that over time you can buy the higher tier loot boxes. These loot boxes give you slightly better orcs, but I have found it unnecessary for having only legendary orcs for attack or defense of forts. You will be carrying the game, since you are the actual player.
----End summary----
10/10 combat and music
8/10 story that does break the lore of Tolkien
Loot boxes are not a fiend or even an issue, the game is mainly single player.
Buy on sale for sure

Would I recommend this game?  The answer is actually "maybe" because I don't know if it's my low-end system that's preventing me from fully enjoying this game.  I do like some aspects, but others, such as camera movement, are rather irritating for me.  Would the camera move faster if I had a better computer?  I guess I won't know until I can ungrade in the distant future.
Other things that bothered me a bit were during character creation.  I couldn't see my character portrait very well but that may be because I don't have a real videocard.  It's a minor issue, so I ignored it.  What bothered me a bit more was that each character is assigned 12 skill points, yet all skills cost 2 points each.  Erm...just divide everything by 2 and you get the actual number of skill points and costs.  Why design it this way?
Also, I have no idea if it's just my anxiety problems, but running into characters that have serious attitude problems, and there were many, is kinda aggravating.  Though, in this environment I can understand how real people would be on edge.  But if I was also in this environment I'd personally not want to help so many crabby people.  It brings out my inner crabbyness.  And so did the first few hours of this game.  lol?
Eh, I may still buy it when it's on sale again in the future.  I would like to explore this little world, on my own time, not rushed during a free 2-day weekend.
Edit: I wanted to add one more thing.  I can't yet talk about what I really like about the game because I'd need to play to end game.  Sorry that this "review" is mainly about what I didn't like.  If I ever own it I'll be sure to edit this again.

I tend to love grid-based RPG's. Wasteland 2, however, is just not very fun.

I actually played the a few minutes of the first episode on a dude's PS3, I looked really stylish and the colors really popped everything out, but I didn't play enough to get to what the game was about, heard a lot of people praising it the last 2 years and got it on sale so I could really judge the game by myself, I went in mostly blind, I knew what the final choice would be since by now it has been spoiled multiple times to me.
The game is a "choose your own dialog" kind of game, that is: you can choose between 2-4 different dialog options and it'll change how the story is told but not the outcome of it, tell tale style. Right from the start of the game your character(Max) also obtains the power to rewind time and it becomes a player's way to remake choices recently made, a great idea somewhat well executed, from a gameplay standpoint you won't be using it a whole lot apart from a few scenarios throughout the 4 first episodes and a in a brilliant way on the last one.
unfortunately that's all for gameplay, the game is more of an interactive movie.
The amount of work put by the designers on this game is amazing, there is a lot of detail everywhere, bits of story information and world building everywhere, it's really fun just to hang around and look for graffiti, billboards and other kind of stuff to check the drawing styles, I'm not sure the name, or even if the style has a name but it ranges from cartoon doodles to photos with a ton of editing so it looks kind of abstract, although I don't recommend the game for other factors the designers aren't one of them, if the game looks pretty to you I'd say go for it, you won't be disappointed since there is not much to do in it besides press buttons sometimes and look at stuff.
The most memorable music is the opening and closing episodes ones and they aren't even composed for the game, they appeal more to the melodramatic teens but I would be lying if I said it didn't fit with the rest f the game for better or for worst. Ambient sound design is great but nothing to be remembered, that said episode 5 has some really great sounds design near the end of the game when everything is tripping out.
I might have been only applauding the game so far but that's because not a single other area of the game shows as much work as the story part, the game is about characters and their relationship, how you and your choices influence how others react to you, and it only show on few cases, I hated Chloe since she only causes trouble and never acts like a normal human being, but the game sticks you to her and make you the "bestest" of friends even if you only responded negatively to her throughout all of it, the only case where I saw the game do what it was supposed to was with Kate, making things work or not with her makes a big difference and actually impacts on story even if just for one or two areas.
The rewind time ability isn't explained so the devs could make the rules bend as it was fit for the story, sometimes you can use it, sometimes not, other times it just works completely different from the norm, consistency is not it's best when coming to settle a believable world.
Everyone is written like a one trick pony, not a single character in the game has a fleshed out personality, they are buried so deep in their tropes with exception of Warren who is the only sane and normal character in the whole story and SPOILER ALEART
, the lines and movement of teen character is cringy, not to be surprised when you ask for old french men to describe the youth.
The interesting plotline only comes at the ending of episode 4, when things really get going and it actually felt really fun to play, they try new stuff for the gameplay with a stealth ,rewind time/combat segments and the game really shines when on those moments, they're really fun but it's not worth 6 hours to get to them.
Now here comes the hard part, I was expecting a well put together story, I'd say I have a really high standard coming to story telling and the game does not do it for me, hardly even steps out of the safe zone and when it does it doesn't last more then 30 minutes, that said if you enjoy teen drama(and mind you, I do too, that's why I finished the game, otherwise it would be unbearable) I'd say give it a shot, worst case scenario you at least appreciate all the effort put on by the designers, but do NOT pay the full price for it, not worth it.

Definitely one of my most favourite games. It may not have the best dialogue or voice acting and the controls are admittedly a little clunky, but what it does, it excels in.
So let's focus on what it is: a action adventure survival horror within a TV series trapping. Sounds bloated but it's done impressively well.
Action adventure: COLLECTIBLES BABY. If you are the sort of person to waste hours of your life collecting every single collectible and unlocking every achievement, BOY is this a treat for you. Not one, not two, not three, not four, but FIVE collectibles to hunt down obsessively and ruin all sense of pacing of the story. But while one of them is a collectible for the sake of collecting, the other four help to supplement the story and build the world in which Alan lives. Definitely worth collecting if you want to fully know the story.
Survivor horror: HOO BOY were there times when you're chilling with your flashlight and revolver and suddenly you're ambushed by four lumberjacks. Or you're heading over to the control room real casual like, and the door burst opens and this tracksuit wearing emaciated youth (a Tenenbaum?!) swings two knives wildly at you. Many scream swears to be had, but shock quickly changes into glee as your character gracefully dips and weaves under scythe, axe and knife before pausing to flash a torch in their face and following up with a double tap of the shotgun. It's a simple combat mechanic (the enemies are invincible until their shadows are fully dispersed by your flashlight, whereupon said double tapping may commence) but the game's audio, graphics and super-smooth bullet time dodging makes combat tense, exciting and surprisingly challenging/frustrating if you're swamped. When the screen suddenly slows down and you hear garbled speech and a high-pitched noise, you better start mashing the dodge button and try not to hyperventilate.
TV series: man the story is good. Genuinely interesting, and the cutscenes are done very cinematically. What I love the most is that the game really pays homage to all the horror/thriller movies/TV shows that influenced it. There are tropes and tropes galores, and many references to thriller/horror movies like The Shining and Twilight Zone. There is something unsettling yet fascinating about the story, world and environment in Alan Wake, and all the references really help to build this up.
So yeah buy the game, play it. Not only is it fun, has a lot of thrills, but it has some really good music (Poets of the Fall). Fighting off hordes of shadow people and dodging in slow motion with rock music pumping behind you ? Definitely cooler than it sounds haha

Natural Selection 2 is a multiplayer based game where 2 teams (Aliens and Marines) must battle it out to best your opponent by evolving the way you play, literally evolving... that’s an actual mechanic... but not like the, it takes millions of years to grow feet because, well you already have them.
How does the multiplayer, well, play?
It is actually quite a nice blend of strategy and first person carnage, each team has a commander, it’s up to the commander to distribute orders for both buildings and troops and also upgrade their soldiers to be the best they can be in a battle. Now this does take a bit of skill, a dash of map knowledge and a whole heaping of luck, to get a good team of experienced players that is. Sounds a bit intimidating doesn't it, stop being such a baby, there’s a very instructive tutorial you can play through before you jump into the action for both Alien and Marine commanders and also their infantry counterparts.
Speaking of the infantry, they're pretty fun to play as also, at first the gameplay will feel a bit hectic, the map is bigger than your usual CoD map and there are a lot of different angles and vents the Alien horde can come at you from but once you gain a bit of map knowledge and you learn the ropes a little you'll be murdering hundreds and hundreds of Aliens that for all we know might just be expressing their need for a cuddle or a wingman to go to the club with... I dunno.
The alien infantry isn't that bad either, with a wide variety of Aliens to choose from you'll be spoiled for choice when it comes to evolving you little alien demon. You can either stay as the stock Skulk, a vicious and acrobatic killer with a deadly bite attack and low damage ranged assault that can mark your enemies for your teammates. Or maybe the supportive Gorge who acts as the team medic and can also build great walls of erm... unknown body fluids to block pathways to objectives or to shoehorn your enemy into an ambush... Tactics!
Whatever you choose to play you can have a ruddy good time blasting holes in aliens using a variety of weapons and gadgets such as jetpacks and mech suits with big ol' guns on them or on the flips side you could turn into a flying alien or that invisible one or even better the massive rhino/triceratops that makes me cry on the inside.
To sum it up, Aliens, Space soldiers, Big guns, Big aliens, decent controls, great gameplay, small learning curve as long as you put the time in and most of all overall fun, fun, fun.
