This is a great game to blow off some steam.  It's a 3D brawler, with an endless chain of combos.
The enemies just sort of "sit there" while you wail on them, but the bosses provide a decent challenge.  It's important to be able to dodge out of the way - you're not a damage sponge, but you're very agile.  If you start to get hit, then you'll be the one getting combo-hit unless you can counter or dodge.
There are no levels - it's just one arena with waves of enemies, and you survive until you die.  Fortunately, you can save, as well as continue from the last checkpoint.
There's also an upgrade system, where you spent the points you receive from fallen enemies.  I recommend unlocking all of the skills before you start increasing their effectiveness, because it will make chaining combos together much easier.

Having gone back to play this again quite a while after its release, it still holds up really well, though now I can see it isn't quite the miraculous perfection I initally thought it was.
The characters arn't the worst thing in the world though Dust's voice is a bit cheesier than I remember and Fidget, while annoying still, remains amusing to listen to throughout, a combination of self aware and just plain silly.

The combat remains as entertaining as it was when I tried it initally. Fast, precise and absurdly combo heavy, though not especially difficult. There isn't really any longterm investment unless you're a hoarder like me and just want items. Then you quickly realise that collecting items is the only reason you still play this. I honestly had no other reason.
The most optimal way to get into this game is if you play in short bursts. Log in now and then and check on your vault dwellers exploring in the wasteland, do that quest which took your dwellers many hours to get to. When that's over check out and come back later. Otherwise it's just an interactive screensaver I suppose, which can be fine too.
Quests are 'meh'. They're just an excuse to get to see a different location to your vault, but they're not too different visually or even interesting. Combat in quests is awkward as well, you just wait a very long time until your vault dwellers finally attack the targeted enemy. I've read that the attack speed can be increased by upgrading certain stats, but till you get to that point you're spending a lot of time waiting for your people to finally do something. Dialog options, which rarely come up, aren't that interesting either.
It works okay as a mobile port, but dragging and dropping vault dwellers to different rooms feels off. Sometimes you have to hover them over a room above the room where you want to place them to. This gets annoying if you quickly want to move a lot of people to help in combat during an attack. It also seems that its possible to edit save files in order to cheat.
While it is a free game, the lack of any compelling reasons for long term investment kindof defeats the purpose of what I think its its designed for: to keep you coming back every time and eventually spend money. There's not too much to get from this experience considering the combat is so dull, which is one of the main reasons why you'd want to get good gear. The other reason why you'd want gear is for your vault dwellers to perform slightly better in their act of standing around all day to give you resources to tap on. That's it.
If you've played the mobile version then you know what to expect here. Only gripe I can think of is carrying over saves from said mobile accounts, other then that, a solid f2p game

Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos is a well-written Visual Novel with a solid plot and gorgeus artwork/soundtrack. Unfortunately, it's incomplete: the game was intended to be episodic and, for that reason, it ends on a cliffhanger. Sadly, the development team dropped the "Dysfunctional Systems" project and we won't see it's sequels. That being said, I still think this episode alone is worth it. I just can't fully recommend it (and it pains me) because the plot will never be complete. Otherwise, I would,
If you like a good sci-fi tale and enjoy visual novels with real substance, this is one you might consider trying anyway.

I started the game, and after a while, nicely designed menu showed up. My mouse pointer was hovering above the "New Game" button, but I waited for the song, and hell was it amazing. With newly built up excitement, I pressed the button, and have been thrown straight into the story. I was curious what codex was so I opened it up, and "no records found" popped up on me. Nice touch, I thought, I closed it, and started with the story, I couldn't stop untill I got through it, it was written very well, and took me around two and half an hour to get through and the end showed something like "profiles", that will  enable next parts to access my choices from previous parts.
All in all, this was the second most awesome Visual Novel I've ever played, the first being Katawa Shoujo. (Don't judge me guys!)

Alas, this Visual Novel with most likely never been finished, as the stuido shut down, but I will do my part in this review.
Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel that has you playing through the perspective of a young mediator in training. Mediators are people from a highly advanced civilization that use technology to go to other realitys and such, changing things as they see fit, and nudging the other civilizations in a way that would be benificial to the home-reality.
The story was fun to play through, decisions felt impactful and the dialogue was very compelling. The soundtrack for this game is also stellar, never seemed out of place. I would recommend getting this on the inevitable steam sale to lesson the cost just a mite, but definately worth it if you need something short to chill and be immersed for a short while.

This game is dull.  You stand in a circle and mow down an endless stream of repetitive mooks.  Then a big tank of a boss shows up, who is difficult not because his attacks are unpredictable or hard to avoid, but because he takes about a thousand hits to kill.
Then you stand in a different-looking circle, and do it all over again.
Keyboard control is unpleasant; use a controller.  The camera is not your friend.  A few available upgrades are not particularly exciting.
What strategy there is revolves around keeping your sword meter full, because your stronger attacks consume it.  It's possible to refill the sword meter by isolating an enemy and beating on him with your weak attacks that refill the meter, but quicker to just put some distance between you and your enemies (Dash and Evade moves make this easy,) use a special move that refills your sword meter, then run right back into the fray.  That's the game.
This game feels like an early demo of a better game: something thrown together just to show off the combat engine, while the developers are still working on the enemies and stages.  Too bad it was deemed done as-is.

It's a fun game. Really fun in my opinion. It's a stylish arena hack and slash game. If you're a fan of stuff like anime, you'll probably think the combat is awesome. You slash up enemies with your sword at hyper-fast speeds and as you sheathe your sword, they all fall down, instantly dead. It's pretty cool.
The graphics aren't anything mind-blowing, but it looks pretty good and gets the job done. Honestly, it could have been all stick figure people and the game would hold up just as well. The real strength of the game is in mastering the combat. The main character, Misa, and her nemesis, Suzuka, both look well animated. Many reviews/comments seem extremely focused on the fact that you get glimpses of panties, but the combat is so fast paced that I've never really noticed. The enemies all look kinda bland, besides the bosses. They are mostly just robot businessmen (I guess...) with a few different colored suits. I suppose the giant robot enemies look kinda cool, too.

At first glance, the game's pretty short. On normal difficulty, it takes maybe 30 or 40 minutes to beat. It's designed for repeated playthroughs, though. You'll need to replay it multiple times to unlock all the upgrades. The flow of combat is very different between Normal and Very Hard (I still haven't beaten the last level of Very Hard, atm). I beat normal barely ever using the Flourish technique, but on Very Hard, I'm not sure it would even be possible to play without using it. Flourishes are extremely powerful, but require absolute precision to pull off. At the time of writing this, I've played for around 15 hours, and it's still a 50/50 chance that I'll get the timing right on my Flourishes. On Very Hard, a missed Flourish usually means death.
Another extender of playtime is going for the longest combos you can get. I've probably spent more than half of my time playing trying to achieve the highest combo I can get. At the time of writing this, my highest combo is 2059 (check out my screenshots, I was really proud of that run).
As for difficulty, there's probably a difficulty level suited for everyone. I started on Normal and it wasn't too challenging. You can pretty much just spam attacks and block or evade to get through Normal. On Hard, you'll have to start mixing up your strategies. You'll need to use Lai Strikes, Heavenly techniques, counters, and the occasional Flourish. Very Hard is as named. You'll really need to start using the advanced moves like counters and Flourishes. You'll also need to be really quick on your feet with dodging and blocking. I've been on the last level of Very Hard for around 3 hours. I now see that 'Game Over' screen every time I close my eyes, lol. As I understand it, there's one more difficulty level after Very Hard, which I haven't yet unlocked. I'd imagine that it's incredibly unforgiving. I haven't tried Easy, but I'd say skip it, unless you are really struggling with Normal.
There's not much going on story-wise. You play as a demon slaying schoolgirl for some reason. Another demon-slaying girl who was pals with your character got possessed by a demon when she got an evil sword from ebay or something. Now you gotta kill her. It would be cool if the story had been fleshed out more, but again, the game's biggest strength is it's gameplay.
One last thing - I'd recommend playing with a controller. I'm sure there are a few people out there who are great at this with the keyboard, but it really seems best-suited to a controller.

Overall this is a mostly enjoyable game, I would recommend playing the first free chapter and if your curiosity about the mystery outweighs your urge to punch all the characters in the face buy the rest of the game, otherwise it is probably best to leave it there.
I like story driven games, I like mystery, I like real world settings with a super natural twist, I like point and click games and this game has all of those along with innumerable glowingly positive reviews. I was so convinced I would love this game I bought the whole series before playing the free first episode. I did enjoy this game and I am going to recommend it but I was not as enamoured as most other people seem to be.
This game has a great story with plenty of twists and turns, a nice visual style and effective background music that really conjures up the sense of a relaxing autumn afternoon. The time travel abilities make for nice simple puzzle elements. I also really enjoyed the optional part of the game to use your time travel powers to capture the photo opportunities.
So onto what I didn't like about the game. The first one that struck me was the controls. As the game starts up it warns you that the game is enhanced by using a controller. Messages like this always set off massive alarm bells that the game is a half arsed port from a console. Overall the port is not too bad. However when I got to the first place where I needed to interact with a object I was presented with the floating name of the object, then when I moved the camera to look at the object it changed to an icon of a mouse with the left button highlighted beneath the word “look”. This seems pretty self evident that I needed to left click to look at the object but nothing happened. After a couple more confused clicks I realised I need to click and then drag to the word “look”. I got used to this quickly but periodically it would fail to work and I would just end up looking away from the object and cursing the UX designer thought that was a good idea.
The biggest problem I had with the game was the characterisation. I am fortunate in that I don't have to interact with young people but are they really this selfish, petty and narcissistic? The language used was not convincing to me, it sounded like they were just crowbarring in modern slang words resulting in it sounding hella forced and unnatural, sad face. I'm prepared to admit that it that is me who is out of touch but it does really stop you engaging with a character when each time they speak you think of Steve Buscemi saying, “How do you do fellow kids?”
The other big problem I had was the lack of control. I'm increasingly coming to the conclusion that, in the same way that horror movies say they're based on a true story as a cheap way to make them more scary, games use statements about how your decision matter as a cheap way to make the story more engaging. The game continually makes a big deal about how important you decisions are but they are really not. A few key events pan out differently but regardless of what you do you still have a straight choice between the good ending and the evil ending. Some of the decisions seem pretty arbitrary and don't give you the option you would actually want to choose. For example at one point you have to pick who you are going to wildly accuse of wrong doing, but there is no option for calmly and unbiasedly explaining all the evidence you have found. And this is just considering the places where you do get a say in the decision. There are numerous stupid things you character does that you have no control over. Sometimes she even says that she can't possibly do a thing, if the writers are including that line then they must be acknowledging that it is a logical thing that many of the players would want to do. In the last chapter in particular I felt very railroaded to the conclusion with little input.
Other people have praised the game for the emotions it invoked and I must admit there was one part where it penetrated my cold cynical heart but for the most part I was disengaged. This was partly due to the time travel as each time something bad happened I would shrug it off assuming I would travel back and fix the timeline so it never happened. The other reason is as I mentioned before the characterisation. The last game I played before this was Tales from the Borderlands and that was much more effective an provoking emotions because I found the characters were infinitely more believable... as they were hanging off a spaceship they made out of a mobile home above an alien planet on the way to get a component for a robot to fight a giant monster.
One last thing to mention is the music. I praised the atmospheric background music but it is occasionally interrupted with some quite jarringly bad songs.

TL;DR: 8.75/10, great combat, dorky dialogue, fun setting, food for thought.
As a non-horror fan, my first impressions when I played back in 2013 were not so good: combat can be a bit wonky at first, and the main character is a famous author but his writing is absolutely atrocious (e.g. he uses the phrase "a gruesome slushie" to describe blood on snow). But to be honest, a big part of my problem was that the game was simply too
. I was constantly being overwhelmed by waves of axe-wielding enemies and eventually just quit.
Well, I'm better at games now and understand a few things that I didn't before-- all things that this game relies on heavily. First of all, resource management. In many segments, the game gives you barely enough ammo to get through, if that, so you have to ration it out carefully. (Sometimes you are also just better off running away from a fight, which is not an approach I'm used to in other games I've played.)
Second, visual and especially audio feedback.
really shines with this aspect. There is no minimap, and enemies don't have obvious health meters and such, but you always know what's coming up and what state the enemies are in ("armor" and health) based on the visual and sound design. The evil growls, the ringing blades and the thumping sledgehammers are damn frightening too-- but the powerful sounds of your own weapons give you a strong feeling of fighting back effectively. Actually the best past is the use of flashlights, flare guns and the like to weaken enemies so that guns will actually hurt them-- it takes a
sometimes, but you can see and hear how the bad guys suffer under the light. All in all, a really solid and immersive combat experience. Bloody (!) difficult at times, but great stuff.
The story is an enjoyable mishmash of
and Stephen King: crazy convoluted and sometimes a bit excessively quirky (yes, it has its equivalent of the Log Lady), but ultimately a fun ride. Some aspects even stuck with me for quite a while, like the
aspect of the overall plot. And then there's the Anderson farm, which edges out the Konstantin Brayko fight in
as the greatest rock-themed 3rd-person set piece in video game history. Respect.

I simply bought the digital version because I 1.) wanted to have it for easier accessing to downloading DLC and have access to the Steam overlay, and 2.) wanted to support CDProjekt RED, even if it was only $10 more.  This game was much more than I was expecting it to be, since nobody seemed to give a rat's tail about the first Witcher game.  It had its cult following, but it was highly considered a "love it or hate it" type of game.  This game broke graphical boundaries at the time of release, and also broke barriers in storytelling.  There is so much to be done - you can't possibly finish this game in under 90 hours even if you tried your darndest(assuming you do as much as the game lets you).  Ramping up the difficulty proves to increase the time further, as you have to prepare much more often for your battles.  It's an adrenaline rush of a game that blurs the lines of right and wrong in a way not many, if any, have done before.  I am incredibly excited for the third installment that seems to be receiving the media attention the whole series has deserved all along.  But as for this game, it is HIGHLY recommended for any gamers looking for a mature, uncut and well-thought-out RPG that will bring out your true self based on the decisions it presents throughout the story.  Well done, CDProjekt RED!  Love it!

Beneath everything I'm about to say, there is still a solid game. However, the flaws seriously detract from the game's enjoyability and replayability.
As far as narratives go, Alan Wake is unlike other games. The story is actually coherent and strong with most the plot threads tied up at the end. The cutscenes feel like a movie.
Unfortunatley, the game is technically unimpressive, even for 2010. The voice acting is all over the place, the animations are poor, and the facial animations are downright disturbing. Remember that Alan Wake was released in the same year as Mass Effect 2 and Assassins Creed: Brotherhood.
The next problem is that survival horror is based on resource scarcity and isolation, but Alan Wake has neither. Ammo is everywhere. I consistently had too many batteries and bullets. There was never a tense moment of combat because I had too many supplies. Boxes full of unlimited ammo are left everywhere. So if the combat in this horror game isn't scary, that leaves the isolated setting. Unfortunatley, Alan Wake fails here as well because for the first 3 chapters Alan narrates everything he sees. The player is never alone, its like a podcast is constantly playing in the background. Additionally, the camera always snaps directly onto enemies when they appear, defeating any chance of a jump scare or rising tension.
The combat is not very good despite being the star of the game. There's a tiny handful of weapons and a smaller number of enemy types. You can only fight the same enemies with the same weapons for so long before it gets horribly boring. Alan Wake is 8 hours long and the vast majority of your time is spent in the gun play. Enemies only use melee weapons, sometimes thrown. Since Alan has a gun, all he has to do is prioritize based on size and distance. Even on Nightmare difficulty, the combat is tedious. Additionally, some areas have traps. Unfortunatley, these traps glow like the sun and often have no enemies to guard them. Poor combat variety all around for a combat oriented game.
The next problem is that although there's a good story buried here, 2/6 chapters are entirely Red Herrings that do not serve to move the plot along, but do serve to extend the game. Alan Wake is about 8 hours long, but it feels like 12. The pacing is horrifically slow due entirely to lengthy hiking missions and endless combat that fails to frighten. Additionally, the story itself suffers from the game's premise. In the game you collect scraps of paper that foretell the future in graphic detail. The problem is this means you'll never be surprised, especially since the most revealing papers are collected mid-way through the quest. It ruins the pacing and suspense when you already know what's going to happen next.
It surprised me how something with so much promise could be shrouded by the darkness of mechanical failure.

I like this game, I really do. But there are tons of reviews on here about the game play so I'll set that aside for now, and instead talk about the people behind the game.
When this went on it's free weekend the devs listened to feedback on steam. They very quickly realized there was a problem! The intention was to have the director's cut available for the free weekend but due to some things on how steam works it automatically defaulted to the normal version. They contacted steam trying to get it fixed, meanwhile the community had found a work around. When they heard about this work around they contacted Valve and asked if they were ok with them advising the work around to let us play the intended version of the game. Valve said sure, and the devs posted how to access the Diractor's Cut for free during the free weekend so we could all enjoy it.
My point here is they noticed a problem, and quickly began looking for ways to correct it. On top of that they listened to the community and used a simple fix that had found. They handled the situation quickly and effectively when it would have been simple to ignore or say "it's unfortunately a problem with how Steam does the free weekends".
I unfortunately can't buy the game right now, but as soon as I can I will be. Hopefully I will have the spare cash when the summer sale rolls around.

The Pros: This game is dripping with atmosphere and has some amazing writing. The core gameplay mechanics are solid, and it ultimately delivers on exactly what it promises.
The Cons: The 'annoyance factor' is pretty high. The game is filled with things that aren't prohibitively terrible, but just make you sigh and roll your eyes constantly. The weapon jamming mechanic adds nothing to gameplay and exists solely to be a pain in the butt from time to time, the camera often gets stuck behind things and makes seeing certain interactive objects very difficult, the game does not automatically reload weapons after battle, combat often feels kinda slow-paced and janky, etc, etc.
Like I said, the issues with the game are not dealbreakers, but there are a lot of things here which just seem downright bad from a design perspective - many of which would have been fine ten or fifteen years ago, which is the era of gaming Wasteland 2 takes a lot of its cues from - but are just not acceptable by modern sandards.  It's still a really good game and again, I'd recommend it just for the atmosphere alone - they NAILED that aspect in particular just about perfectly. But it feels like they could have done better.

I don't like to leave reviews for games due to changes in the way i game and having an odd love-hate relationship to this game makes it that much harder. I love this game for almost all that it is and how far Squad has taken it.
Physics
The physics are nice, aircraft are easy to make once you take the time to learn the balance system, and the rockets (when done right) are satisfying to watch take off and sucsessfully make it to orbit.
Orbits and the Planets
Speaking of orbiting, the system that they gave you to plan out your next trajectory is easy to get used to. Pull an arrow in the dirrection you want to take your orbit, and it will make a predicted line of wherre your rocket will end up. The planets are similar to our solar system but there are differences here and there compared to ours. There are biomes on each planet for you to use for science, exploring, and all types mischief when you get there.
Modes
The modes in the game are what you would probably expect from a "science, space, and exploration" game. There is a career for when you want to challenge yourself on not only to build a rocket to get to the moon (or Mun rather) but also within a set budget. I don't play this one often due to my ability to actually recover my rockets. There is a science oreintated mode which is like career but doesn't hold you to a certain budget. As long as you can get a good research rocket where they can study a thing, science will pay for it. Lastly a sand box mode. It is one of the most satisfying sandbox modes that I have ever played. Messing around with every part in the game, and pushing the game engine to see what will work and what won't is great. I have nothing to critisize here.
Mods
I haven't used many but that is due to my fear of accidently breaking my game. My internet is slow and I don't want to wait to play the game when I have a hankering for it. However, the mods I used were great, the modding community is astonishing at what they do and there will never be an end to my interest in this gamedue to it.
The Hate
The hate part of my relationship with this game is that Take Two Interactive has bought Squad and it has stopped what was content updates what felt like every-other-month to what it is now. Don't get me wrong it isn't a deal-breaker for me and with nearly 200 hours into this game I'm going to continue playing, but as soon as Take Two starts pushing what it wants into the game I can't recomend this game any more. Other than that there are a few quirks that are inherent to the game-play I don't like. The Science mode doesn't have a known weighted system in game to tell you what is worth more to go after. It is understandable but it is irritating when you don't play for a bit and forget what is worth what. The career mode, for mem is to harsh when it somes to what an item is worth. It feels like everything should be dropped by a little but that is just me. Finally, there is no resemblence of a intuitive/muscle memory way to play this game unless you are willing to put in more time into this game than others. Recenlty I went on a PS2 gaming binge and I completed a few of my favorites. A month later and everything that I commited to muscle memory was pointless. The game was nearly the same, maybe a minor tweak in localization here or something small, but everything I tried to do was up in flames.
Summary
Overall it is a good game and I recommend it. Just watch out when Take Two starts pushing things into it.

Beneath everything I'm about to say, there is still a solid game. However, the flaws seriously detract from the game's enjoyability and replayability.
As far as narratives go, Alan Wake is unlike other games. The story is actually coherent and strong with most the plot threads tied up at the end. The cutscenes feel like a movie.
Unfortunatley, the game is technically unimpressive, even for 2010. The voice acting is all over the place, the animations are poor, and the facial animations are downright disturbing. Remember that Alan Wake was released in the same year as Mass Effect 2 and Assassins Creed: Brotherhood.
The next problem is that survival horror is based on resource scarcity and isolation, but Alan Wake has neither. Ammo is everywhere. I consistently had too many batteries and bullets. There was never a tense moment of combat because I had too many supplies. Boxes full of unlimited ammo are left everywhere. So if the combat in this horror game isn't scary, that leaves the isolated setting. Unfortunatley, Alan Wake fails here as well because for the first 3 chapters Alan narrates everything he sees. The player is never alone, its like a podcast is constantly playing in the background. Additionally, the camera always snaps directly onto enemies when they appear, defeating any chance of a jump scare or rising tension.
The combat is not very good despite being the star of the game. There's a tiny handful of weapons and a smaller number of enemy types. You can only fight the same enemies with the same weapons for so long before it gets horribly boring. Alan Wake is 8 hours long and the vast majority of your time is spent in the gun play. Enemies only use melee weapons, sometimes thrown. Since Alan has a gun, all he has to do is prioritize based on size and distance. Even on Nightmare difficulty, the combat is tedious. Additionally, some areas have traps. Unfortunatley, these traps glow like the sun and often have no enemies to guard them. Poor combat variety all around for a combat oriented game.
The next problem is that although there's a good story buried here, 2/6 chapters are entirely Red Herrings that do not serve to move the plot along, but do serve to extend the game. Alan Wake is about 8 hours long, but it feels like 12. The pacing is horrifically slow due entirely to lengthy hiking missions and endless combat that fails to frighten. Additionally, the story itself suffers from the game's premise. In the game you collect scraps of paper that foretell the future in graphic detail. The problem is this means you'll never be surprised, especially since the most revealing papers are collected mid-way through the quest. It ruins the pacing and suspense when you already know what's going to happen next.
It surprised me how something with so much promise could be shrouded by the darkness of mechanical failure.

Alan Wake is a story driven third person horror game. Its premise is that you, Alan Wake are suffering from writers block and have gone on vacation to a cabin in the woods. From there things get sinister as you battle the darkness in the story that unfolds. The gameplay is great, the atmosphere is superb, and the story is quite engaging. I would definitly reccomend this game.
Without giving anything away the story is setup in as tv mystery, with several differnt episodes. Its engaging and engrossing as the story unravels until the end. That said, there are two "special episodes" after the end that continue the story that felt off as the major climax of the story had already been reached. While its great to have more content it really did not feel necessary. That put, the story is quite engaging and is one of the greatest parts of this game.
The game does an amazing job on levels and enviroments. Most of the missons are at night as the darkness plays a major role in the game. Enemies are shadowy figures and they are only defeated with the use of light. The game greatly creates a sense of isolation and the unknown as the light serves a bastions of safe haven from the unrelenting forces of darkness.
It perfectly fits the storys mystery as you try to unreval the mystery.
This light and dark continues into the gameplay as well. Lights provide safe havens and your flashlight is as important as your gun. The enemies are weak to light, so you have to aim at them with your flashlight to make them vulnerable then finish them off with your gun. Its definitly unique and quite enjoyable.
Its a single player story driven game so theres not much replayablity, but if your a completionist there are manuscript pages hidden in every level. There really well written and they forshadows things to come in the story.
This is a great game that is quite unique, and I would definitly reccomend it

Don't pay attention to the hours played I currently have attached to my Steam account as of the time of this reviewing - I own the physical copy of the game and bought it on opening day.  I simply bought the digital version because I 1.) wanted to have it for easier accessing to downloading DLC and have access to the Steam overlay, and 2.) wanted to support CDProjekt RED, even if it was only $10 more.  This game was much more than I was expecting it to be, since nobody seemed to give a rat's tail about the first Witcher game.  It had its cult following, but it was highly considered a "love it or hate it" type of game.  This game broke graphical boundaries at the time of release, and also broke barriers in storytelling.  There is so much to be done - you can't possibly finish this game in under 90 hours even if you tried your darndest(assuming you do as much as the game lets you).  Ramping up the difficulty proves to increase the time further, as you have to prepare much more often for your battles.  It's an adrenaline rush of a game that blurs the lines of right and wrong in a way not many, if any, have done before.  I am incredibly excited for the third installment that seems to be receiving the media attention the whole series has deserved all along.  But as for this game, it is HIGHLY recommended for any gamers looking for a mature, uncut and well-thought-out RPG that will bring out your true self based on the decisions it presents throughout the story.  Well done, CDProjekt RED!  Love it!

Visual novels are not for everyone, and that is fair. Even fans of the genre can admit that some of them are boring and disinteresting. That said,
is one of the best visual novels I have “played” to date. Instead of relying on cartoon drawings of “waifus” in underwear to keep your interest, it actually has a very interesting and well-told story. (But don't worry, there are still some cartoon drawings of "waifus" in underwear). The artwork is high quality and the soundtrack is one my personal favorites in the realm of video games. In fact, it’s one of my favorite music albums in general, but I also like that genre of music a lot. Anyway, if you like a good sci-fi tale, and enjoy visual novels with real substance, this is one you probably want to consider trying.
Unfortunately, the game was intended to be episodic and it does end on a cliffhanger; and at this time it seems unlikely the development team is going to be able to produce more installments. Such is life. There is still a very interesting and self-contained story within the game that I think most sci-fi fans will find interesting. You can just ignore the epilogue and still enjoy the primary narrative. If you think you would like this game, but only don’t want to try it because of the open ending, then that is your choice. But I think you will be missing out.
The universe created and the primary storyline are both products of premiere sci-fi writing. I was enthralled the entire time. The soundtrack is comprised of amazing songs, and each one perfectly captures the emotion of the game at the time it is played. The art style is mostly traditional and nothing overtly special, but it also is pleasantly not overloaded with stereotypical anime cringe and unnecessary sexuality. It is a nice, well-produced visual novel that can be taken seriously.
isn’t for everyone, but I think it will appeal to fans of good sci-fi and fans of the standard visual novel paradigm. Yes, it is unfortunate that we (probably) won’t get any more installments set in this universe, but this visual novel is still very highly enjoyable. Some things will be left unanswered, but that happens all the time in storytelling.
And, honestly, if you can find it for a good price, I would recommend it for the soundtrack alone. I know music tastes are highly subjective, but damn do I love these tunes.

Dysfunctional Systems Episode 1: Learning to Manage Chaos is a Western-made visual novel from Dischan Media available on Steam it features features two distinct endings, unlock able bonus art, an animated opening video, and a jukebox of in-game music.
I stand on a neutral ground for this visual novel. Meaning yes i do recommend it but to a certain extent. (Go to the bottom for reason of standing on a neutral ground)
Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel series featuring Winter Harrison, a student mediator from a utopian world. Learning to Manage Chaos is the first entry in the series.
What is a mediator? A mediator is someone who travels to chaotic worlds, attempting to resolve the issues plaguing them. The first entry in the series follows Winter's second mediation, where she shadows the experienced and aloof mediator: Cyrus Addington.
Character sprites are used in the standard visual novel style, but sometimes characters are integrated into the backgrounds which really brought the images to life. I loved the detailed background work. The color palette was extremely "muted" which suited the world they are on, gloomy and dark.
The music in Dysfunctional Systems is beautiful, especially ‘Terminus’, the theme track. Sound effects are well used too overall really a good job of fitting into the Visual Novel's environment.
Dysfunctional Systems Episode 1: Learning to Manage Chaos is in an episodic format providing episode by episode is satisfying, while still leaving you wanting more. Unfortunately this isn’t the case with Dysfunctional Systems Episode 1: Learning to Manage Chaos, which serves as little more than a teaser for a story that could be potentially interesting. Meaning if you do get this there will be no continuation of Episode 2 because it is confirmed by Dischan Media there will not be Episode 2 at all. [I honestly wish there is Episode 2 because I liked it overall]
Yes I do recommend this Visual Novel but be warned there will not be an episode 2 forever[as off now] so take this visual novel as just something to be read when you have nothing to do.

Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos is one of the sad cases where an early entry shows very promising result, yet does not come to fruition.  It’s very short, and in essence only an introductory episode of a longer tale.  Yet it’s one of the better but less known visual novels currently on Steam.
Now, to answer the question whether this vn worth $5 it’s asking… Maybe, maybe not.  I got it half price ($2.5) as it is on sale now.  Consider other ways I could have spent $2.5 to $5, I’d say it’s definitely worthwhile to give this vn a try.  The art style is excellent, and is quite more creative and cinematic than some budget vn where majority of the scenes are just a background image and two character sprites.  Music is atmospheric; it doesn’t stand in the way though does its job well to enhance the mood at key moments.
Many may be concerned about reading only a starting excerpt of a story where the rest of chapters are confirmed canceled.  I had similar issues when I learned about the fate of the studio and this franchise… but don’t let that discourage you.  The current “episode” mostly is self-contained.  While it definitely points to continuation, I think the central plot is independent and doesn’t prevent readers to enjoy it just by itself.
That being said, the only complain I really have is about the structure of this vn.  For this episode, there are at least two distinct endings (one is arguably a “better” ending than the other).  There is no way in the game to actually check how many endings there are and if they’ve been reached.  It is also not clear which of these two endings are “true” ending, and how they matter to the rest of the tale… mainly, I presume, due to unfortunate fact of the franchise’s cancellation.
Final verdict: Add this game to your watchlist and buy it when it’s on any kind of discount.  Even though there is no sequel episodes, the story of Learning to Manage Chaos is quite entertaining, and along with the good art and bgm, it’s a 2-hour experience worth having.

Game idea is excellent (free offroad trucking) but unfortunately Spintires fails use all available potential of that idea. I don't count any value for multiplayer which based on comments seems to have issues. Game developer should be Oovee but in reality they should be concidered as publisher. Game's real developer is just 1 guy. And this creates the issue - slow progress in development. And it also makes future of game very unsure - Oovee have already tried "kill" the game in December with sloppy updates they tried do by themselves and failed (as they used older beta versions which they pushed as "official" versions. But because game had issues they had to hire real developer again in begining of this year which have brought some changes and improvements to game.
Currently game only "real" goal is haul lumber to sawmill using Soviet times trucks in 6 different maps and you can freely decide what trucks (based on what is offered for you in the map) you use and which routes you drive.
At the begining this was good and nice idea but when played game longer and seen how development goes game becomes boring.
There have been updates (some better some worse) since launch of the game but this game is not definately finished (even it's not said it should be concidered more like beta). During lifespan of game it have received 1 new map, 1 repainted truck and some trailers. And capacities of trailers have been reduced (e.g. tanker trailer capacity have been reduced from 4000 to 3200) and at the same time trucks won't be refueled in garages more than 200 litres (even if truck fuel tank would be 270L, 350L or bigger.
Pros:
- Potential idea
- Freedom in maps
- Day cycle
(- hopefully weather changes would come too)
Cons:
- Lack of objectives what to do
- Slow, unsure and non-linear development
- Terrain where trucks sink like Titanic even if you use "big" roads and fallen trees are like concrate bars - not possible move them using crane and your truck can get stuck to them
- Not official mapping and modding tools (from Steam workshop implementation talked but...)
- Lack of dev support in Steam forums (they don't care as they just stay in Oovee's official forum which is highly cencored if people talk anything negative from game)
- Legacy mode needs be used if you want play game using "unofficial" maps and trucks
- User cannot self define controller's buttons (have to use predefined setup)
Final conclusions:
I would not suggest game at this point and definately do not pay full price! Only if you get this from discount around 10e or below then concider but even then think twice.
At least as long as there's no official mod support and map tools game is not worth.

This is a pretty decent game that feels quite a bit like DMC, especially when playing as Vergil.

This game throws you into what is basically the bloody palace mode of DMC except the story is interwoven into it. The action is fairly decent and some of the attacks are pretty satisfying. The game is also quite hard even on normal, each enemy and boss will require a slightly different approach. You'll die repeatedly on the bosses if you don't adjust your play style accordingly.
There's unlockables and decent amount of upgrades to get as well so you'll most definitely be making use of the new game+ feature if you want to experience the combat system in its entirety.
The anction flows well and makes you feel good for keeping up a string of combos without taking a hit.
It's a game with a decent amount of passion and effort put into it however, do note that it honestly feels like a small piece of what could be a big game.
If you're just looking for some decent action and a game that you can come back to every now and then for some enjoyable combat this isn't a bad choice for 10 bucks, if it's on sale then stop reading this and get it, you certainly won't regret it as long as you know what you're getting into which is once again essentially the bloody palace mode of a DMC game with Vergil as the character.
Personally I hope to see this developer grow and possibly make something grander next time.

Dust: An Elysian Tale (urgh, I mean "Tail") is a relatively solid Metroidvania-inspired action-RPG that had a LOT of potential, but was held back by a few questionable design choices. The art design for the characters was lackluster; most of the sprites and character portraits looked like they were drawn by a high-school student. The controls are just a little too imprecise for some of the platforming challenges. The writing lacks any sense of direction and never decides if it wants to be funny or serious. The characterization is flat, the voice-acting is iffy, and the plot is literally one of the worst I've ever seen in a video game.
Yet, for all its flaws, I still sunk almost 20 hours into this game. Why? Because it's Fun As Hell (tm). The platforming is almost solid, first of all. Yes, the controls are a bit loose, but that was never a deal-breaker for me. The most important thing, though, is the combat. Simply put, fights in this game -feel- good, especially later in the game. As the game progresses and you level up, you start seeing damage being done in the triple- and even quadruple-digits and, as any fan of Final Fantasy will tell you, seeing a ton of bouncing numbers on screen just feels good.
So, is the gameplay enough to save this game? I think it is. But not for full price. Dust is not a $15 game. If you have any interest in platformers, button-mashers, or Metroidvania, pick this game up....when it goes on sale.

I've logged quite a bit of play time on this game, and I still find it enjoyable. It's a simple game but can be difficult the more you play it and the less lucky you are. The story is not a big factor in this game, yet there is a little back story. You play as Isaac (or another character once you unlock them) and you have to shoot weird looking monsters with your tears (an effective way to kill monsters so I've heard!). As you progress the more difficult it becomes and at the end of every "floor" you have to face a challenging boss. Everything in this game is randomized, from bosses to floor layouts and from items and mob drops to enimies and mini-bosses. This game has a perma-death feature meaning once you die, that's it and you have to start from the begining again. But don't let that be a deciding factor as the more you play and the further you get, the more items and new bosses you unlock and the more difficult the game will become, naturally. Items will be a big deciding factor if your "run" is successful or not, and remember once you die you lose the items you had until you collect them again in a later run. A full run, once you have unlocked all the bosses, can take between 30-50 minutes (on average) depending on how good your items are. This simple game that lacks in story and graphics makes up for it big time in challenging and rewarding gameplay and it definately deserves a spot on my favourites list. Since I've played this game a lot and watched a lot of videos on it don't be afraid to give me a shout if you need help understanding something. Also if you want to learn the basics, either add me on skype and give me a call, or watch a video on youtube (there's too much to explain to just type, it would be 10x longer than this review!!). Anyway enjoy your venture through an abandoned basement, into a cave and finally into your mothers womb (Did I mention this game was a little ♥♥♥♥ed up?)

I don't think I liked anything about this game.
-The UI is not done very well. For example in character creaton a simple +/- to add or remove skills would be perfect...
-The graphics look bad.
-Group pathfinding is bad. For example 3 party members will walk one way and 1 will walk another way entirely.
-Combat is very simplistic. There just isn't enough variety in what you can do in combat.
-Interacting with the environment is frustrating at times. If you drop an item you have to move your characters to pick the item up again because they are standing on it. The game also requires a lot of camera spinning to access certain things. It's just a lot of needless tedium.
-The camera angle (and camera in general) is annoying. It is right above the group until you zoom in which gives you a better angle but worse FOV. The camera also demands a lot of micromanagement.
-The conversation system is not very good. Some NPC's have bloated conversations with very little useful or interesting information. Other NPC's (numerous) have no text at all other than "go away" or something similar.
-Inventory management and looting is not done very well.
-Map travel reminds me of the old Final Fantasy games. It worked in those games but in this one it just seems like a huge shortcut. The game is called Wasteland. I want to exlore the wasteland...not just go to pre-determined points of interest.
-Character creation was greatly limited. I did think it was pretty cool that you could choose some aspects like the religion of the character or the brand of cigarettes that they smoke. I was surprised to see how few stock avatar images they had and the fact that I could not do simple things like change hair color.
Honestly I am surprised at how many people enjoy this game. If you enjoy complex isometric style RPG games like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Fallout, Avernum, Pillars of Eternity...etc...you will probably find this game lacking a lot of depth.

This is an astonishingly strong offering for a one-person team. It's less of a souls-like and more of a straight-up demake of Dark Souls, boiling it down into its most basic elements, with mice added in for flavor.
The core elements of gameplay (skill-based combat, soft-capped stat-raising, equipment load, risk-vs-reward) are all center-stage and all feel great. Other elements (such as item-based lore, massive open world, complex NPC interactions) have been cut or minimized, and in some places the game feels a bit too pared-back because of it.
The story in particular feels bare, although the overall atmosphere is intimate and oppressive enough to compensate for that.
Similarly, encountering new enemies, new traps, new weapons, and new areas all feel great, even if there aren't a ton of those things overall.
Ultimately, with the game being as short as it is (about 5 - 7 hours) it straddles the sweet spot between "this was just starting to get good" and "this was a perfectly bite-sized experience". Certain plot points come up, but are never fully fleshed out. The varied routes to the game's conclusion are mostly the same route with a few different flourishes. Implications about the broader world are made but not addressed. The whole thing practically begs for a feature-length sequel, although it's unclear if one is forthcoming.
I would recommend this to a soulsborne purist without hesitation. For someone that likes the Souls games more for their lore than their gameplay, DarkMaus is either tantalizing with possiblity or a hopeless tease. For someone without any Soulslike experience, if you like highly techical games that reward you for careful play and good planning, and if you like to figure out how to play games as you play them, you'll enjoy this. If you like games that are easy or dialog-heavy or have AAA production values,you may want to look elsewhere.
At full price, this is a reasonable buy, but on sale it's a steal. There's a lot of love put into this game, and it'll last you a solid few play sessions.
Just bear in mind: there's no way to respec your stats, so pick either Strength or Skill for your primary weapon. Don't dump points into both.

You are a rat (not an insult) and you wake up on the beach for reasons unknown. Your goal is to progress and avoid becoming DeadMaus. Most inhabitants of this seemingly decayed world are hostile, but you will encounter one or two potential allies, assuming that you don't kill them for their cheese. The further you progress, the clearer the fate of the world and its people (?) becomes; your path is illuminated more with each step you take. The plot has a distinct 'B' feel to it; it's certainly not a selling point, but gets the job of giving the player a why and how done.
With an art style like DarkMaus', it's easy to get disoriented. Areas look very similar and colourless, and while it appears neat most of the time, it makes it hard for the player to navigate their surroundings. Luckily, we were blessed with a clean, helpful map to sort that out, so it's not a real problem.
As you explore the nooks and crannies of the world, you come across lots and lots of marrow, which is a fancier word for EXP. You spend this to increase your stats, upping your health/stamina, equip load, weapon skills et.c. You find more than enough of it, assuming that you explore properly, which means that your ratman can use plenty of different weapons for whatever situation you get yourself into. This does have a negative impact on replayability, however, as each run gets fairly samey.
Combat is rather simple, but enjoyable. Offensively, you make use of light & heavy melee attacks and ranged weapons (bows/fire spells). There are also a few other melee moves you can learn, for example a shield bash and dash attack. Defensively, you can employ your shield or rely on dodging. I found that dodging isn't very effective against smaller enemies, whereas blocking doesn't do much against larger foes; it's a case where you'll want to adjust your style to trump the opponent in front of you. Killing things is very entertaining because of this, but also due to the difficulty present.
You die very fast. A lot of rooms are like mouse traps; you go in, it springs and unless you act quickly, you are killed almost instantly. The first enemy you encounter kills you in two 2-hit combos. Pair this with scarce healing items and you've got some potentially nasty scenarios in front of you. No, you don't have healing items or spells that replenish at campfires; you only get the occasional rare morsel drop, which are also fed to NPC companions to keep them on their feet, further enhancing the rarity of the item.
A deal-breaker to some will be the amount of content. My first playthrough took about 5-6 hours of active play time with quite a lot of deaths and 100 % exploration. As mentioned earlier, the replayability is also lacking, which isn't a good thing.
It's hard to recommend this at full price, but that doesn't mean that I don't suggest you get it. DarkMaus may not be long or especially worth replaying, but it is definitely a good experience your first time through. Thus, my verdict is as follows: pick it up on sale. For 5€ or less it's a solid purchase.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

While the original Kane and Lynch may be remembered for its review controversy, for me, it was a title that really tried to do something fresh and unique in a lot of ways. Kane and Lynch: Dead Men had main characters that were difficult to like, but by the end of the dark and compelling story to save Kane’s family, players felt a bit of Stockholm Syndrome for the duo. The co-op, while offline only, offered a unique perspective for both players, something we rarely see in the age of co-op clone characters. The sequel has arrived and our anti-heroes are back again, this time across the world in Shanghai with Lynch’s story as the focus. But can Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days recapture the same fresh feeling of the first game?
The story of Dog Days has Kane meeting up with his old pal Lynch who promises a job with plenty of riches. Upon Kane’s arrival a simple task for the two turns sour and inadvertently starts a gang war. Soon you realize that your deal is going south as your contact is attacked in an intense highway assault and you make a desperate attempt to escape with all your lives. It wasn’t long after this I lost what was going on, the overall purpose of what the duo was doing.
Despite some great voice acting and plenty of memorable lines - I had completely forgot the purpose of what I was doing midway through the title. “Why am I shooting these army guys again?” I asked my co-op partner. It had something to do with a big Chinese mob boss and not dieing, but beyond that everything is a bit of chaos. Perhaps this is what IO Interactive was going for, as the main character this time is Lynch, who’s not exactly mentally stable. There’s plenty of times Lynch voices over to himself, trying to use psychological tricks to calm his nerves - no doubt from some sort of therapy sessions.
The graphical style and display are going to be the most memorable and controversial piece to this game, the shaky YouTube style camera is either going to be a complete turn off or something people really like. At moments the grainy and over saturated look of the game world makes it look eerily realistic. The neon glow of lights bouncing off reflective surfaces, the distant city line of Shanghai, and the dark alleys all can trick your eye in an almost photo realistic moment. Other times poor textures in certain areas, stiff character animation and improper lip syncing totally break the immersion.
Shortly into my first mission I almost felt nauseous from the camera movement - but it passed. The shaky camera is only really bad while running and once you get used to it, it provides some useful info on enemy position and adds to the immersive effect. Thankfully if you can’t get over it you can disable it, though it’s still there to some degree.
IO Interactive really wanted to have the feeling of intense and gritty shoot outs. They wanted your palms sweaty and your grip tightening on your controller through every twist and turn. To some degree, this holds true. There were times the firefights were memorable, with exploding objects and cover flying everywhere as bullets rained down on Kane and Lynch. The atmosphere is further enhanced by Asian inspired pop music blasting from in game radios and intercoms, giving it an almost John Woo movie feel in certain situations.
Sadly the intensity is broken once you realize the firefights break down into duck, pop up wait for guy to peak his head out of cover, and shoot mechanic. This style of combat is rinse and repeat for most of the game with save for a few battles. Which is sad, because some of the key moments like a helicopter attack on and in an office building and a mission where you need to cover Lynch’s girlfriend in an apartment building across the street are really fun. The level after Kane and Lynch are tortured is one that will be forever burned into my retinas. I just wish there was more of these moments.

Kane and Lynch 2 does make a huge improvement in terms of co-op options over it’s predecessor. Full online play and local play is supported and there’s options for matchmaking too. And while the single player is fun, like all good co-op games, playing this with a friend is much more satisfying. You can really tell that K&L 2 was designed from the ground up for co-op play; level layouts are well crafted into separate paths for cover and flanking maneuvers and there’s a nice balance of weapons to choose from for both close and long range giving players defined roles. One thing that sadly appears to be missing is some of the crazier elements of Lynch from the first game - instance where the players actually see different things. As far as we could tell they weren’t as prominent as the cops/civilians bank scene from the first game.

Co-Op makes the game a bit easier as well. While in the single player game if you get shot you’ll get knocked down and have a chance to get up, a second subsequent knock down will kill you. In co-op this second knockdown is actually revivable by your co-op partner. This can help in some of the trickier situations when the game is throwing what seems like hundreds of guys your way only to be killed by the last group and having to do it all over again. While the checkpoint system seems ok, it never seems to be quite enough, and starting a co-op game will lose any single player checkpoint progress - so you’ll need to restart back at a chapter beginning.

It’s these little nagging issues that constantly remind you that perhaps Kane and Lynch 2 wasn’t quite ready. I hit numerous technical bugs as well - mostly while playing as a guest co-op player over Xbox Live. Cut scenes were missing characters, character animations got stuck, audio cut out on me completely, and the game even crashed at one point. Strangely while playing solo or as the host these seemed almost non existent.

If you don’t want to play Fragile Alliance online there’s a new Arcade mode where you can use all AI guys and try to get the highest score possible. This mode is surprisingly addictive, though, it does get a bit long in the tooth by the 9th or 10th round. The game will up the difficulty with every round and you can keep going until you run out of your 3 lives.
So does Kane and Lynch 2 deliver that fresh feeling of the first game? Sadly I don’t think it does. While IO did a great job of fixing the cover and shooting mechanic, adding online co-op, and deepening the addictive multiplayer modes - it seems the rest of the game suffered as a result. With two characters as memorable and unique as Kane and Lynch, I was sad to see the story - which took only 5 hours to complete - a bit lacking. Don’t get me wrong, Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days isn’t a bad game, it’s just not a great one.

The Co-Op Experience: Team up online or offline through the story in co-op with a friend. Play as Kane or Lynch and work together with a revival mechanic. Online play allows 8 players to rob a bank together in a Fragile Alliance that can turn co-op into competitive.
Co-Op Score: 3.5 out of 5
General Score: 3 out of 5

看这款游戏的中文测评比较少，上来写个测评供汉语玩家参考。
优点：
1. 美术
2. 音乐
3. 人设
4. 第一章情节
游戏画风很独特，美术设计上可以感觉制作组下了不少心思，那些毛线编织的小家伙让我印象深刻，更不用说整座飞船都有很多以毛线为原理的科学设备。游戏音乐听起来很舒服，开着放很久也不腻。人设上我喜欢女主人公vella，独特、大胆、聪明，还有些小幽默，为了达成目标很执着，相比之下肖恩就有点逊色了，不过考虑到他的成长环境，这也是很合理的设定，玩游戏时能感觉到这个半大男孩的善良和勇气（虽然有点幼稚啦）。第一章情节停的非常巧妙，跟游戏刚开始的界面时候一样。章末未完的剧情揭开了一个特别大的矛盾冲突，让我对第二章非常非常期待，内心深处设想了各种场面各种大戏。
缺点：
1. 核心玩法没意思
2. 谜题不合理
3. 情节急转直下令人失望
核心玩法枯燥其实并不是大问题，大部分点击型游戏都容易这样。这时候就必须——必须！有个好故事来为游戏增色，我刚开始看了游戏的介绍，被吸引住了，感觉故事开头特别有意思，于是花钱买下来玩。结果好失望啊，第二章成功摧毁了第一章吸引人的概念，并将故事引到一个老套无聊还不合理的设定上，感觉不像一个人写的，水平差距好大。游戏里面的谜题也不得不吐个槽，没什么逻辑性，通常需要试来试去，在重复的操作中我的耐心消耗没了，画面看起来腻了，音乐听起来也有些刺耳了。读了一下简介里引用的ign评论，感觉打分的人只玩了第一章啊！他要是玩完了就不那么想了。
如果很想玩，可以等等打折，不建议全价入。

Within the name itself, Dark Maus is indicative of an ever-increasing problem for Souls-Like games by setting expectations of a beloved classic on the sincerest form of flattery, imitation. The problem is not only that the game is given demands by its fanbase that can never be met; the far greater problem is whatever innovations or interpretations the designer has made to create a different experience are only going to upset fans who don’t agree with the changes. It’s a Catch-22 situation where the creator is damned to stay the course or damned to deviate to make a name for itself.
Perhaps this is why in the wake of games like Hyper Light Drifter, Dead Cells and even, to a lesser extent, Titan Souls, have succeeded in taking the elements that people cherish about the SoulsBorne games and making an identity of its own. This is perhaps the natural course to establish a new genre much like the rogue-lite genre that has slowly eroded the name of rogue-likes into the components of Rogue into new experiences. Dark Maus, however, when considered on its own is plagued with poor choices for challenge that attempts to mask its problems by basking in the shadows of a game that has always bordered the line of fairness.
If there is one quality that sets Dark Maus apart it’s rather the way it handles its atmosphere in terms of gameplay to create an experience the SoulsBorne games have yet to match. Instead of utilizing the health system like the Estus Flask to limit the number of mistakes the player can make before the next checkpoint, DM uses the torch to instill urgency against the player’s restraint to run into the literal unknown. People who felt disappointed in the torch-mechanic of DS2 will probably fall in love with the game for this quality alone as it does add a layer of atmosphere and the fear of exploration, even when you know the layouts with time.
Unfortunately, this system also points out a major problem, the health system. Arguably one of the most important features to get right, DM relies on the limited quantities earned by killing enemies that it affects the rest of the experience. Traps, ambushes, boss-battles, etc. all are depreciated of their enjoyment because every failure that results in healing yourself means more time spent finding new resources for future obstacles. This aspect of grinding to earn back the ability to make up for a mistake is also made worse by the “entities” of DM which appear designed to unfairly kill you and waste any rations that you use.
These entities do not obey the same rules as other enemies as they can pass through the walls as well as attack from unseen corners, and the instant-deaths from these enemies makes them reek of the “It’s Dark Souls” mentality plagued by its name. This is ultimately something I despise about these games that tout they are hard but fair when they promote undeniably unfair obstacles meant to kill you. Combined with the health system and the game’s other unique mechanic, the ghosts, it feels like the game sets up these deaths to make the system more viable rather than letting it be a way to help struggling players.
On paper, spawning ghosts of your previous failures to support you in overcoming the obstacles ahead is a rather an intuitive means of optional difficulty that the player can either exploit or rely on if the game becomes too demanding. On every death, a ghost of your character will replay the previous actions you made and follow the route as you fight off the enemies with additional support; these ghosts have limited health and will only follow you as far as they made it. If you engage enemies in instances where you died, the ghosts will assist you and not vanish until the end of the battle. This is a system that does have its merits in assisting the player as an option that feels at home in these games.
In practice, however, encounters with various enemies beyond being plausible make this system a crutch the game relies on to a fault. It would be easy to dismiss this criticism as “Git Gud” where this a lengthy adventure that makes the game’s difficulty circumvented by exploring a less frustrating area to make the player stronger. DM is quite a more linear experience with not as much time nor opportunities to become overpowered that breaks the game, so the challenge is always high and it’s always punishing, which is by no means a bad thing to do. The problem, however, is when you design encounters to become even more difficult the result is eventually going to favor the player with the greater numbers or greater assistance to overcome the odds.
To DM’s credit, there are small tricks to benefit the top-down SoulsBorne experience that keeps most of the game from being unfair. Bosses or sub-bosses have a translucent stamina bar over them that shows when they’re vulnerable to attacks during their recovery period. If this system was implemented in a Souls game, it would undoubtedly break the game; in DM, it avoids the issue with vague telegraphing of attacks that still requires the player’s skill to read the enemy as well as the challenge of focusing on a fading bar rather than the dark imprints of the enemy. With the various amounts of weapons and classes to choose, the combat is rather impressively polished being a minimalistic version of Dark Souls with its diversity being gated more towards the end-game or for the player to experiment with their builds for NG+.
Lastly, the story itself, follows the source material verbatim. You play as a lone mouse washed up on the shores of a land becoming corrupted due to some dark force that you can either overcome or give in to the temptations of power by committing atrocities with the small number of NPCs you come across the journey. There are no item-descriptions nor a whole lot of environmental storytelling, so the narrative feels as minimalistic for a Souls game even if the lore is something you find enjoyable to piece together in these types of games.
This is the reoccurring issue that slowly sours the whole experience the farther the comparisons are drawn. It’s a shame that is ultimately the feeling I am left with because however great are the ideas behind its mechanics, innovations and deviations to the SoulsBorne demands there is always a caveat that follows its greatness and a distinct feeling of measuring up to another game.
Like the ghosts’ mechanic, the shadows casted in following the SoulsBorne path to success is the visage of glory that would be better to take the path less traveled to make all the difference in the world. This is a lesson that should be extended to all titles suffering the same problem with Souls-Likes as well as Rogue-Likes/Lites that stay within accepted conventions without understanding how to learn from them. Perhaps if Dark Maus had focused more on its innovations and how to incorporate them more so into the experience it made we could have had something that could stand on its own merits rather than embodying the fading soul of Soulsborne and bearing the curse of its name.

Great fighting game.
Pros:
1. Good character art. You will especially notice it during the cutscenes, just how good the character art is. There may or may not exist better today, but it's still beautiful in my eyes.
2. Good graphics. Pretty much the same as above, except this one is meant for the environment, enemies etc. The background graphics is ALMOST as good as the character art. The enemies are well made too, albeit kind of out of place for a story like this one, or maybe that's just me.
3. Cool moves and attacks. Some of them are really worth upgrading to full lvl not only in terms of dmg, but also to make them even cooler.
4. Bosses are insanely hard even on normal difficulty and that's where the game really shines in my opinion.
5. The camera is great during boss fights.
6. Pantsu.
Cons:
1. The game is fought in "waves" with the 5th one (or was it 6th?) being a boss. That in itself is good and all, but what I dislike are the waves themselves. The enemies in the waves seem mostly brain dead (except for one or two who actually take skill to defeat). In short, you can pretty much just spam attacks on them and you will be fine.
2. The maps / levels are fought on a platform and thus offers very little space. I'd rather it have a bigger map and where you have to MOVE from point A to point B just to give a simple answer to an alternative.
3. The camera during "waves" is just...Awful beyond words. It's so awful that you... Just kill the waves quickly 'kay?
4. Like I kind of said at no. 1, the game feels repetitive during waves and unless you want to practice or want to try out a new skill you bought, you really just want to eliminate the waves quickly.
Conclusion:
It's a great fighting game, albeit a very short one (I completed it in about 4h but I didn't buy all the upgrades either) but it is worth the money. DURING a -50% or at least -25% sale. I give it 7/10.
TL;DR if you like pantsu, fighting games and anime styled games, then... BUY THIS♥♥♥♥♥♥

It's a shame to read about the localization issue causing so many bad reviews, because this really is a gem of a game. I think it's unique in that pursuing your given objectives/missions is often just as fun as tinkering with spacecraft designs and sending your brave Kerbalnauts to the sun and other such nonsense.
Be warned that this is not by any means a casual game; you WILL be learning about the challanges of navigating space with realistic limitations on what you can and can't do (ie fixed supplies of fuel and power, needing to account for inertia, gravity, and air resistence when planning flights, etc). You WILL spend lots of time tuning your spacecraft and learning how best to fly them, and you WILL feel frustration when they blow up on the launch pad or in the atmosphere. However, if you have the patience to stick it out, you'll get tremendous satisfaction from putting your own little space station into orbit, or sending unmanned satillites of your own design to the far reaches of the solar system. Further to this, you'll most certainly gain a much better appreciation for some of the real-world challenges involved in space flight and exploration.
Overall, if you're a space enthusiast and/or enjoy tinkering with real/virtual aircraft and/or enjoy simulators in general, you should definitely give this a closer look; there's nothing else quite like it!

So, it's been about a week since I finished this, so I can probably review this without getting much of a biased view now.
Life is Strange is an episodic story game that tells the life of Max Caulfield, a senior student who discovers that she has the power to turn back time. As one might expect, there are the usual problems that a high school student might experience, but there are also several deep underlying issues that that the game addresses.
I was surprised to find that a game studio was brave enough to talk about these kinds of issues, and do it flawlessly as well.
To those who are turned off by the "teenage drama" that ensues, I would like to point out that they too probably had a time like such in their lives.
One thing that was evident to me on finishing the game is the game's own episodic quality. Whilst it does use the method well, I think it may have been better to release the entire thing in one batch. The feelings that one might get depend quite a lot into how much you are engrossed in the story, and how much you find yourself attached to the characters. Unfortunately playing the game with a few weeks worth of in-between time does not help the game in this case.

The visuals are excellent. The artstyle is less like those of computer graphics, and more in line with the work that an artist might paint. This is due to the fact that the textures in the game are all
. As one might expect, this game is a treat for the eye.
The music is amazing. What's more amazing is that most of the soundtrack is a collection from various artists. Any yet, it works. The music cues are timed perfectly with the scenes, and they exemplify the moods in thos scene. This game is a perfect example of how music, even when without dialogue, can be enough to define the mood of a story.
To nitpick, the controls and personality of the various characters can be iffy at times.
But in the storytelling point of view, this is not much of an issue.
The dialogue can also be cringy at times. I, for one, didn't find this too bad, but many people in the community apparently did.
As for the story, it needs no praise. It will speak for itself.
I recommend this game to
, even those who may not really like story games. I guarantee, this game is an experience you will never forget. Life, you will see, surely is strange.
