"Mun or Bust", was translated into "To be a real man, you need to launch to Mun". Now the translation is finally corrected into "We won't stop until we get to Mun".
The new translation is phonetically appealing. "To be a real man, you need to launch to Mun" comes from a Chinese saying "Bu dao \chang cheng\ fei hao han". Since "Mun", as the counterpart of "chang cheng (two syllables)" in the old saying, only has one syllable, it sounds so weird to replace "chang cheng" with "Mun". The new translation, "Bu dao Mun, Bu ba xiu", has three syllables in both the former and latter half of the sentence, making it sounds much better.
Besides, the new translation is more accurate. Original text "Mun or Bust" indicates "If we plan to go to Mun, then we will stick to that, otherwise we just don't start at all". The indication is similar to "We won't stop until we get to Mun". The old translation lacks the perseverance part, the "until" part.
As a native Chinese speaker, I really appreciate the corrections of misogynist and bigotry translations in simplified Chinese version. Even as a male scientist, I sense the persistent discouragement that blocks females from having a science or engineering career. Social stereotyping plays a rather crucial role in such discouragement, especially in regions like China. Through my whole education, I heard classmates, parents and even teachers talked to those girls and told them that they were bad at math and science even though no solid scientific evidence had ever supported the hypothesis that males and females differ in these fields.
Kerbal is a game that draws whoever has an astronaut dream. Boys and girls, males and females. I may not know the feeling that a girl suddenly finds out even in a game, a place she shouldn't be discriminated by her sex, she is excluded to be an astronaut. But I do know the feeling when I realized that no Asian superheroes existed and all princes charmings were white as a boy. That feeling is sadness, confusion, depression and anger. It took me years to re-believe that I, as an Asian, can save the day.
Therefore, I would never let any single girl feels the way that I felt. And thank you, the Kerbal team, for making this happen.

NS2 is a fast-paced action FPS, heavily reliant on team-work, strategy & twitch reactions. It's a unique blend of FPS with real-time strategy elements. It pits two teams (Aliens VS Marines) against each-other in online matches. Graphics are very nice, performance is ok - the custom made engine (Spark) does seem to be quite CPU demanding, yet a comprehensive options menu allow for various tweaking. Gameplay is awesome, sound assets are okay.
It's good fun, competitive, but also newbie friendly. Has a great community that are steadily active (so you'll always be able to find a game). It's essentially a game about map / resource control, upgrading / evolution tech research & using various weapons / skills & abilities - it's pretty sweet.
As a huge fan of both the original HL1 mod & the indie dev team, I must admit I wasn't too impressed with the initial release due to bugs, performance issues, lack of content & balancing issues - yet true to their word UWE rolled out (& continue to do so) patches / updates & free content, fully addressing my intial concerns. I fully respect UWE approch to the development process where they where open to community suggestions & really made an effort to involve players with the process even from pre-order. If not even pioneering the technique of early-access / beta release with ongoing development.
This is a must play for any action FPS fan!

I downloaded the game over the free-to-play weekend, and I'm hooked.  It reminds me of why I used to love playing computer RPGs, particularly turn-based games like XCOM and Fallout 1 & 2.  The writing is funny and quirky, and there are just an incredible amount of easter eggs that reference the developers' obvious love for sci-fi, fantasy, pen and paper role playing games and late 20th century pop culture.  Just about every item, including the massive amount of different junk items, has a tongue-in-cheek description if you take a moment to click on them.
Some people seem to be complaining about the combat system, but it's pretty standard for any good turn based tactical game.  I like the fact that you can position your team around a skirmish utilizing high ground and obstacles for cover.  It's a nice, nostalgic change of pace from the real time combat that basically every game utilizes now.
I haven't gotten terribly far into the story, but it appears that every decision you make ripples outwards and affects how the rest of your play experience goes.  Feel like desecrating graves, shooting dogs and leaving a smoking trail of destruction behind your every move?  You're free to do so if that's what amuses you.  Your skill at picking locks not too great?  Blow open the door with some dynamite, kick it in, or just blast it open with a shotgun.  If you can't disable a trap, just have a tank open the crate and soak up the damage.  There are multiple ways to solve just about any problem you encounter.  I love that feature.  In most games, I feel like I'm missing out if I can't open every locked or secret door in the dungeon.
I probably wouldn't have stumbled across this game if it weren't for the free preview weekend, and I'm so glad it was featured.  It's not 100% perfect, but I'd give it a solid 8/10.

The First half of this game is adventure perfection. It was a return to the greats, the best point and click I had played since Grim Fandango. I didn't think it was easy, but at the same time never had to use a walkthrough for any part as the puzzles were logical in their world.
Then came the second half. It had me scratching my head on at least two occasions, and I found the level of abstraction between the puzzles and their solution was getting close to the original Monkey island, which is a massive step back in adventure gaming.
The story also feels lacklustre in the second half. The first half is really interesting, almost metaphysical. You could apply religion, meaning of life, all kind of cool back stories to explain what is going and who the characters are. There was a lot of symbolism and interpretation.
The second part knocked all of that on the head and became a simple good guys vs bad guys narrative. Not bad, but... nothing original.
So first half 10/10
Second half 4/10
All together a worthy game with lovely graphics and great fantasy setting. Just be prepared for a disappointing second half!

The problem with episodic content is that they release them in chunks, episodes, or seasons. So I have two problems.
1."My Problem"- I don't like that form of business. If a game has episodic content, they should put it under early access until all of the content is released. Also *Note: I am NOT saying that games with this kind of content (I.E: "Life is Strange" and "The Walking Dead") are bad games. But even if a game like that is something I would be interested in, I would probably wait until all of it was released before I buy it.
2."The Reason"- With episodic content, there is so many things that could go wrong. Writers quit, Budget cuts, or the whole project could be changed halfway through. And while some games like Life is Strange represent the episodic games that can handle these problems, Dysfunctional Systems represents the ones who couldn't even make it past episode one.
Now...I'm torn. I don't know if I should be mad at it or sympthize with it. I wanted so much more, but I was given a piece of a great story that will never be finished.

I have never played the original Genesis game so I'm reviewing this remake on its own merits. Castle of Illusion is a platformer starring everyone’s favorite circular eared rodent, Mickey Mouse. The Evil Queen/Witch from Snow White (The game gives her another name but it’s totally her, right down to her saying she wants to be the fairest of them all.) kidnaps Minnie and tries to pull a page from Grunty’s book by stealing Minnie’s youth and spirit so it’s up to Mickey to venture through the Queen’s castle to save her.
The game is a real solid platformer, and while it’s not hard and pretty forgiving, it’s still got a lot of charm and its fun. The game looks really nice, what with its vibrant locales and cartoony charm. The level design is quite neat and Mickey will have to traverse through a candyland, a library, an ancient underground temple, and the castle itself for example. At the end of each area is a boss fight and these tend to be fun enough, though funny enough I had much more trouble with some of the early game bosses than the later ones. One problem the game has is that it is quite short, it feels like they could have had more levels. You see Mickey has to collect seven gems to get to the Queen’s throne but there’s not an area for all the gems, so you miss out on like two whole areas. Also some of the hit detecting can feel wonky at times, but not enough to be a real problem.
I bought the game recently because Sega is pulling the game from digital distribution at the end of the week. It’s a shame because this game is good, so be sure to grab it here or on Humble Bundle and Bundle Stars while its on sale for like $2 before the game is gone for good.

Alright, since I have over 3,100 hours in the game now, I guess it is my Kerbic responsibility to review the game.
As you can probably guess from the fact that I've spend that much time playing, I think Kerbal Space Program is an amazing game. There's really nothing else like it in the entire gaming world. The marketing for the game makes it look like a business simulation, but that's not the interesting thing about the game. It's a rocket design simulation. You have to design rockets that can leave the atmosphere, and then rockets that can orbit Kerbin (your home world), and then rockets you send to the two moons of Kerbin. After that, there are 6 planets to visit, some with their own moons. It's a space flight adventure!
It's kind of like a Legos set, actually. You start out with a limited number of engines, fuel tanks and crew capsules (in Career mode), and you try to use these parts to create a rocket that can get out of the atmosphere, or even into orbit. Then as you advance and do amazing things in space, you get access to more engines, fuel tanks, capsules, probes and science experiments. By the end of the tech tree, you can build a spaceplane that can get into orbit in one stage (if you're good). That's a fun challenge all by itself, because rockets cost money. It's awesome if you can recover the whole rocket and use it again. Just ask Elon Musk.
All of the physics for launch and space flight are based on real physics. After you get good at this game, you will literally understand orbital dynamics better than anyone in the world did in 1950. It's very engrossing to try to orbit Kerbin, then try to send a probe to one of Kerbin's moons, then at some point send probes to other planets. Then your challenge is to orbit Kerbals (the denizens of Kerbin), and send them to the moons, and to the other planets. It's a fantastically complex game that can be difficult at the start, and much more difficult later. But you learn with each launch, whether it succeeds or fails. The sense of accomplishment when you have sent a Kerbal to one of the outer planets is fantastic, because there's no guarantee here. This is not an adventure game where you just have to beat one boss, and maybe get a little lucky, to proceed to the next challenge. There is no way to get lucky and end up in the orbit of Jool, or one of its moons. You have to understand the process, and the mechanics of how these things work. That's what's rewarding.
I don't want to give the impression that the game is mathematical, per se. It's more conceptual. There will be instances where you might have to do simple calculations to figure out if your rocket can get to its destination, but even then, there are a ton of mods to help you calculate all that stuff. Believe me, I am no math wiz, and I love the game.
Besides that, it has kind of an informal, goofy presentation. The Kerbals all look kind of like minions. They are sort of dorky little morons, some of whom are cowards, who are mostly along for the ride (until you have to go EVA, which is yet another interesting challenge.) It makes the game fun, whereas with lesser developers, the game could seem too cerebral and technical. Hey, nobody likes to see Jebediah dive into the ground at 400 mph because you screwed up your rocket. But... that's probably going to happen. Don't feel bad. He gave his life for science. And he'll probably respawn anyway (depending on difficulty settings).
So if you are the kind of player that just likes to play one level after another, while everything you do is basically the same and you can brute-force your way to success, this isn't the game for you. To get beyond orbit, you have to understand something about how the game universe works, and the further you go, the more you have to understand (But that's ANOTHER great thing about the game: since it's all based on real physics, if you understand how things work in the game, you have a really good idea of how they actually work in real spaceflight.) If you like games that actually make you feel like you've learned something and accomplished something with your learning, this is the game for you. Like I said, I've never played another game remotely like it.
(You may have noticed that lately there have been some bad reviews, but if you look, you'll see that almost all of these are because they are unhappy with the Chinese translation, which came out recently. So if you're Chinese and easily bothered by translation issues, I guess you might not like the game. Actually you'll probably love the game anyway, but I guess some people don't.)
Signed, RocketBlam (look me up on the Kerbal forums), who returned a Kerbal from the surface of Eve - the hardest thing to do in the game. Twice.

TL;DR: Tedious button-mashy fodder battles on the same level, followed by hard boss fights where you can beat them with luck even if you lack the skill.
Why so: Not a particularly good brawler. The main characters may look nice and I'd expect them to have been the main selling point, but the gameplay itself is lacking.
The stages are all set on circular arenas with only the arena texture, the models surrounding the arena and the enemy waves varying. There aren't many different enemy times outside palette switched ones - cyborg(?) men in suits, large cyborgs, some cyborgs wielding a huge blade and some armored knight-lookalike. Sure, at least the two first have palette switches that denote different attacks, but the enemies are sorely lacking in variety. The phases before the level end boss are in general pushovers and I've managed to clear them (on normal difficulty) pretty well just mashing two buttons (sword slash and sword sheathing).
Killed enemies earn the player skill points which can be used to purchase new skills and upgrade old ones - not that there are all that many of them. I'd think Streets of Rage had more different moves than Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae has.
Whereas the fodders are way too easy, the bosses are in comparison very hard. Prepare to die by their hand several times - until you figure out that maxing out the sword sheathing and the special counter skill allows you to beat the enemies just by retrying the battle until you've managed to time your counters to enemy attacks the necessary 3-5 times to kill off the opponent. I still have trouble beating even the first two bosses, yet I've managed to complete the game (on normal difficulty).
On hard difficulty, the fodders become challenging as well and even the first level can cause trouble.

I liked Mafia III. I tried very hard not to let performance issues color my experience. I adored the soundtrack, the presentation, the style. It's all very lovely and the city is expansive with pretty vistas and manages to almost look like a painting in motion. I wasn't bothered by waiting two days for a 60fps patch. But Mafia III is a mess. I can't keep 60fps at 2560x1440 on an overclocked GTX 1080 which is just ridiculous. The game is gorgeous in its way but nothing that could justify this. On top of that, it crashes at random. There's an alarming number of bugs. All of that I could have overlooked.
But there's just not enough gameplay. The degree to which I've been doing the same stuff just in different locations makes The Division look like a paragon of variety. It's not bad mechanics, sneaking and shooting feels fine, but its not intrinsically rewarding enough to prop up how little there is to do. When a game isn't just broken but broken AND boring, I can't in good conscience recommend it, even though I don't regret picking up the game. It's interesting and there's good moments; but unless you're invested in experiencing the setting, what Mafia III offers won't be enough for most people.

I've loved the Mafia games ever since the first one was out. Mafia 2 came along and I personally thought it probably couldn't get any better than this and then I heard of the Mafia 3 launch. I tried to not look into it and be surprised for my first run through and decide for myself what I think. I'll list my pro's and con's below:
PRO's
- It's another Mafia game?
- The story is quite good, have completed it and can say it is a very interesting story line
- The music in the games make it a lot more enjoyable when you go around shooting people or just driving around
- Now that the FPS issue is fixed, it doesn't look bad as in graphic wise (but the weird lighting bug needs to be addressed)
- Has tried to keep some of the things that made the previous Mafia games a big success
Now for the Con's....
CON's
- I like grinding games as much of the next person, but after the tutorial missions that's all you seem to ever do. You could take a break i guess to go explore more of the city but I like to get the story missions done so it gives me time to go back and finish off on either side missions or just enjoy roaming around
- The driving is a little weird at times, once you start putting mods onto cars, driving on keyboard can become a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I'd recommend either driving with a controller or play walking simulator with Lincon as some cars when modded can become uncontrollable
- The big issues for me with the game was the weird texture bugs appearing. The first one was a big flash of light, almost like a nuke had gone off somewhere. The other is a weird square box would appear at the edge of the screen and it was like opening a hole to another world! Needless to say when i went towards this weird box object it would crash my game! :(
So in conclusion...
Should you buy this game? - If you are someone who doesn't mind grinding for endless hours just like the Mad Max game, then I recommend you wait for the price to drop or for it to be in a steam sale as the price for it now is too high for the quality you will receive.
What could be done to improve the game? - The problem is that it tried to keep too much of Mafia 2 in but left out all of the good parts, like how the cops would pull you over for speeding, the fact you could change your outfit and not stay in the same one the entire game (except for special missions which required you to change) The ability to have a house to store cars you want instead of requesting them. It's taken everything that made Mafia 2 fun and stripped it down to something new whilst trying to keep the same feel as that old game but have not be able to pull it off. In my opinion i think they need to go back to basic, add a few of the features I mentioned above and keep working at fixing these graphical issues to make it a proper Mafia game!
People can argue if I wanted to store cars and change outfits that I should go and play GTA 5 for that and you are right but the thing I will ask is, would you feel like a Mafia boss if you didn't have a place to go back to, to see what you have accomplished whilst taking control of your city, to change outfits as you see fit when you go out to rule your city, to drive a car of your choosing from your garage to drive around protecting your city from competition? I can tell you that this game didn't make me feel anything close to a Mafia boss and for that reason I give it a thumbs down!

Hotline Miami may seem like a great game, but ultimately boils down to multiple compounding elements that can cause it to become quite frustrating.
Pros:
Soundtrack
Cons:
After say 1-2 hours, the novelty of the setting and the ultraviolence quickly wear off. There's almost no story to the game (at least not enough of one to keep me playing through the frustration of the game itself). The lack of story information coupled with repetitive killing tasks with no goal in sight leaves the player essentially working towards nothing. At 3 hours in, there's nothing keeping my interest in this game. If this is the way the story is meant to be told, it's entirely lost on me.
The AI in the game seems to act in one of two ways:
It either seems to notice you IMMEDIATELY and tries to kill you with brutal pinpoint accuracy
OR
It is extremely incompetent and does nothing.
Even in tiny rooms with multiple enemies, one may hear gunshots and bolt immediately to the struggle while the other AI within the room will sit there and not move until you enter the room.
More often than not, one of the AI who does react to a gunfight will find you and shoot you from extreme distances (majority of the time off screen). In addition to this, they will often shoot through multiple layers of glass, which are poorly distinguished from regular walls. Certain AI will seem like they will have no shot on you, but you move an inch and they will do a 180 and IMMEDIATELY kill you while you're not even in the room or making any noise. Other AI you will be able to line up a shot with no trouble and they will have no idea what hit them.
The door physics are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The doors can be used to knock enemies to the ground, and with a certain mask, they will kill enemies. The only problem is, the doors will act wildly if you move into a sweet spot by the door, and they will flail back and forth. This is great unless you are using the door for a choke point and choose not to use the door-kill mask. Say you're using a melee weapon on the other side of the door, and the enemies get knocked down by the door as they try to go through it (based on the way they move and other factors). Now you have multiple downed enemies who you must deliberately kill one by one, with more blows and time required than a regular melee swing kill. Same thing applies if you're using a firearm and they go down in the doorway due to botched physics. You cannot shoot the enemies while they are on the floor. Couple this situation with the fact that you have more enemies coming at you, and you're likely to get overrun by the enemies randomly getting up from the floor while dealing with the ones charging you from multiple directions.
Another tactic the game uses is introducing new enemies such as dogs and a big black guy. They don't come into play for a few levels, and this is a good tactic for acclimating players to the game without overwhelming them. The one way they ♥♥♥♥ this up however, is by changing the way the regular basic enemy behaves. At a certain point in the game, the regular enemies will be downed and bloody, but will sometimes continue to try to drag themselves away. It doesn't happen all the time, but you must finish these enemies off, just like the ones who have been knocked down and require you to finish them. This requires a neck snap, which could potentially leave you vulnerable in the meantime. Why the hell you can't finish him with the baseball bat / gun in your hands is ♥♥♥♥ing beyond me. For example, when you knock an enemy over, you can finish them with your bat. But bloody and crawling REQUIRES a neck snap. This makes zero sense.  To introduce the basic enemy, but change the way he works for no reason half way through the game is just ♥♥♥♥ing stupid.
Don't get me started on the fact that the enemy when knocked down, takes more swings to kill than a standing one.
The icing on the cake is the hitboxes. The carbine/rifle type weapon often will go through enemies if not aimed dead center on your enemy.
Overall, the game seems cool at first but turns into a tedious♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I DO NOT recommend you buy this game unless it's dirt cheap or you're a masochist who enjoys badly planned and developed games.

Broken Age invites you in with sheer cleverness and charm. The plot is surprising and intriguing, the characters are likable and sometimes lovable, and the settings are original and rich. The visuals are beautifully hand-drawn and finished to look simultaneously fuzzy and smooth, and the music (written by the composer of Hearthstone's music) is compelling. The puzzles are simple enough but deep enough to be clever, and while for a few of the puzzles you might need a walkthrough to completely connect the dots, most of the puzzles in the first half can be completed with attentiveness and critical thinking.
The core gameplay at times feels uninteresting. While the individual lines of dialogue are voiced well, the dialogue system is non-linear which sounds like a good idea but makes conversation seem detatched and unnatural. Because NPCs offer hints, you feel obligated to sift through every uninteresting filler line of dialogue they have to offer just to find what's important. Similarly, in many of the areas you will need to poke at every interactive detail to exhaust every clue from them.
It abruptly says goodbye after hours of convoluted problem solving that is completed with a walkthrough or incredible leaps of logic, and recycles the same places you've been before in a way that stretches them beyond novelty and makes them become dull.
What results is a game that begins too perfectly to not recommend but ends too disappointingly to recommend. If you are willing to take the great with the frustrating, buy this game when it goes on sale (I got it for $5.50 CAD and got more than what I paid for). If you need a game that not only sets up well but ends satisfyingly, this is not that.

Know by this point, I'd had someone else go down before this, and I had experienced the urgency of recovering a teammate before they died. The thing is, my sniper was the only one who could have saved the other teammate.

Fortunately, the game threw some puzzles my way, and that took my mind off my sniper's untimely demise. More good news, I got a replacement sniper. She was a bit temperamental, but she was a better sniper than my other one. Her death was only a memory, and didn't affect me much.

And that was all on the easiest difficulty.

As of writing this review I have 5 hours played on the game after trying it on a free weekend.
I'll get right to the point. I do not reccomend getting this game. Why? The audio doesn't work properly. After roughly 5-10 minutes of play a large part of the sound effects, such as weapons, explosions, etc, simply drops, making me feel like I am playing the game with no sound. For me, at least, games like this with no combat sound get old fast, as was the case here. It's possible to get them back by restarting the game, but they will still disappear again.
I did spend some time tinkering with the audio settings, as well as using Google, but I could find no solution.
That said, the rest of what I have seen so far seems fun. The game offers some choice on how you wish to proceed and which tasks to complete. I can only assume that these choices matter, but I haven't gotten that far.
The combat itself has challenged me in these first few hours, and I have found myself getting bashed by the AI. The game is also somewhat unforgiving if you make mistakes and you can easily have your whole squad perma-killed if you are not paying attention.
I have to say that I love this part of the game. It's a shame that the experience is ruined due to the lack of audio.
Even though this may well be a pretty good game, I simply cannot reccomend a game without sound effects. If audio isn't something you use anyway, I haven't seen any other downsides to the game after my five hours of play.

The binding of Isaac is truly something special. It is a game that constantly rewards curiosity and determination. The randomly generated nature of the game means every new playthrough can bring something unexpected. The gameplay is challenging and will often have you on the edge of your seat.
All of this makes the game fantastic on the surface, but its whats hidden underneath The Binding of Isaac that truly makes it incredible. Strewn throughout the game is symbolism, imagery and concepts that the game never shoves in your face, but constantly hints themselves to you, making you think and wonder, making you try to decipher the messages it contains. I cannot think of another game which has achieved such an outstanding use of video games as a story telling medium. Without cutscenes (save for short 5-10 second snippets) text or dialogue, The Binding of Isaac tells a deep, thoughtful tale, and throws numerous messages out, and the game does not care if you ever notice them. Its a masterpiece of game design, and a wonderful example of what makes this medium so unique from any other.

DarkMaus is a top down fantasy RPG that is not particularly interesting on its own merits. I've seen it often compared to the Souls series, yet in my experience this was not the case. Story and worldbuilding are barebones, combat is not satisfying, some design choices are questionable, and the content amount is poor. It only took me five hours to complete this game even without the usage of the Death Echo function, which will be explained later. This review will contain spoilers on what little story there is, so be warned.
The beginning of DarkMaus has the player crash land on the shores of an unknown region. You gain consciousness and begin exploring inland, eventually encountering a friendly NPC you escort to a nearby town. From there, your motive story-wise to continue on is non-existent. Talking to the other NPCs around town only gives you miniscule scraps of information, and not nearly enough to give a reason as to why you're doing what you are. Regardless, you continue on and encounter a giant cat, who tells you to go to the castle. Why do you need to go to the castle, and why should you care? ... I don't know. You trudge through some other side areas, and encounter another NPC who gives you a sentence or two of exposition, and the main villian is just now introduced. Mind you, this is roughly half way into the game, if not a little more. Later, you enter the castle and kill the corrupted king; who's suddenly revealed to be the father of the NPC you found in the beginning in a dire attempt at an emotional plot twist, I assume. You then go on to battle the final boss, kill him, and get an extremely abrupt "The End" screen. No ending sequence or credits, only a display of your statistics and the option to start New Game +.
While story is not pivotal to any game, I at least expected some amount of atmosphere seeing as this game takes inspiration from Dark Souls, but I was mistaken. Despite some of the spotty writing of the Souls series, it at least gives the player clear motives as to what their character is doing and how it affects the world around them. There is not even a hint of this within DarkMaus, you're going along with everything that's happening ... because you want to? Because you've got nothing else better to do? Because the main villian tainted the only town's cheese reserves?
Story and character motives aside, the gameplay sadly does not make up for it. Instead of Souls, you have Marrow, which only serves as experience to level up. Movement is somewhat clunky and difficult to control in some cases. In combat, you have a quick weak attack, a strong slower attack, an evasive dash, and some other techniques you gain over time such as running attacks or a shield bash. There's also a decent weapon variety of swords, spears, and ranged weapons. While it sounds similar to Dark Souls in theory, it does not play alike much at all. There is little to no weight behind your attacks, and using pyromancies and bows can prove to be painful against some enemies due to the lock on's finicky nature and the alternative of free aim relying on the unruly movement. Enemy variety isn't particularly great, and most of them can be defeated with the same strategies. There are boss enemies as well, however they were not very challenging and are all similar in the way that they're big enemies that move slow with a lot of health and very little attack variety.
A mechanic called "Death Echo" exists, allowing you to summon equippable ghost NPCs only after you get killed. The idea of this sounds like it would have made the game far too easy, in turn causing me to disable it entirely so I cannot comment on how well it may or may not work. Even with this off, I cleared the game without much difficulty and ended it with 68 deaths in total.
Enemy placement in some areas is frustrating to say the least. Often times you'll get hit by off screen projectiles from multiple different angles, leading to a quick and frustrating death. One segment contains enemies who are able to use shuriken that can ricochet off of walls. Sounds managable enough, until you realize that there are about fifteen of them all in the same room or hallway, and that once a projectile is done bouncing, it gets lodged into the wall which causes you to take even more damage if you happen to touch it. This, combined with the uncomfortable movement and aiming system, led to most of my deaths.
There are other instances of some design choices I disliked as well. One of them being an NPC that claims to be a merchant, yet you cannot trade with them at all. What was the point of having them mention they're a merchant, then? Some sections imitate Souls style invasions, with a powerful NPC appearing during inconvenient situations. While this isn't a terrible idea, I cannot say I enjoyed getting sandwiched in tight areas by normal enemies, and then an extremely swift and damaging NPC invader coming from behind. Did I mention that getting killed by an NPC invader causes you to instantly lose all of your Marrow and caps your health at 50% for about 10 minutes? Also, the world is not interconnected much at all. This is an aspect most people liked about Dark Souls, so if you're playing this and expecting a similar layout, then prepare to be disappointed. For the most part, a majority of the map is lengthy vertical areas that lead to even more lengthy vertical areas. There are some slight branching paths, but these usually only contain Marrow bonuses or other minor items.
The game is very short and there is not much to do. As mentioned previously, it only took me five hours to complete on my first try, without the aid of a guide or the built in Death Echo function. You can play New Game+ which ups the difficulty and adds some other slight modifiers, but unless you enjoyed the base game enough to want to do it again, then I don't see a reason to play it. Melee weapons function too similarly to warrant another playthrough, and there aren't many other playstyle options to try out.
I cannot recommend this game. Not because it's different from Dark Souls, but because it tries to imitate the same style yet fails. It also isn't particularly engaging on its own as a dark fantasy RPG, leading me to give it a thumbs down.

I honestly wasn’t expecting much out of a Visual Novel from Steam; it’s just that, more often than not, the things put up for distribution are busts. I mean, I’ve got some experiences – both good and bad – with them and it’s just that they don’t really have a good batting average.
That said, I’m really glad I picked this one up off the 2015 Summer Sale (my only purchase, interestingly enough). At 50% off, it was still a bit high (a bad habit of mine regarding buying games, given how high Steam slashes the prices sometimes) but the reviews were really good and I was just… drawn in by the imagery. I really loved the opening sequence and watched it more than a few times just to really let it sink in, despite it not having any sort of direct dramatic impact. I don’t know, I guess the presentation was good, and I just got this vibe out of it that got me hooked; I really felt for the girl, and what she went through, and that’s still on me up to now.
It didn’t take me long to ace the game’s achievements, given how they’re basically for clearing the different endings and options during the main decision branch of the episode. It took a few tries to get them right, but it wasn’t like I was making guesses and brute forcing it; I think it did a good job because I already had a clue on what to say to elicit a certain response, as if I was making the argument myself and letting what’s natural flow.
I’m going to be straight up: There’s nothing special here. Rather, not in the writing, not in the animation, not in the music, not in the art – all of which were pretty good, though, to be fair to the ones behind it all. What I really took from this was the vibe, and I don’t know any better way to say or explain it. I stand by my statement of it not having anything particularly special, but also concede the fact that they really did everything well.
I agreed, I felt, it evoked some thoughts, and I’m overall inspired to do better. I’m not kidding, mind you. It just had this vibe to it that made you go through it, hooked, and tell its story well enough to convince you to re-evaluate some things – rather, that’s what it got me to do. I briefly considered being a diplomat, or a mediator as they’re called there, because of how honest and something (I really can’t find a word for the feeling!) it came across.
I’d actually give it 10/10, as short as it is. Or, actually, maybe 9/10 because of how short it is. It’s disappointing, really, that it’s just one decision branch and kinda just a prologue; I hate it when visual novels do that, but I’m just really impressed with this that I feel satisfied with what I just went through. I do want a sequel, though.
P.S. Where can I buy that soundtrack? Really good soundtrack.

It's a shame to read about the localization issue causing so many bad reviews, because this really is a gem of a game. I think it's unique in that pursuing your given objectives/missions is often just as fun as tinkering with spacecraft designs and sending your brave Kerbalnauts to the sun and other such nonsense.
Be warned that this is not by any means a casual game; you WILL be learning about the challanges of navigating space with realistic limitations on what you can and can't do (ie fixed supplies of fuel and power, needing to account for inertia, gravity, and air resistence when planning flights, etc). You WILL spend lots of time tuning your spacecraft and learning how best to fly them, and you WILL feel frustration when they blow up on the launch pad or in the atmosphere. However, if you have the patience to stick it out, you'll get tremendous satisfaction from putting your own little space station into orbit, or sending unmanned satillites of your own design to the far reaches of the solar system. Further to this, you'll most certainly gain a much better appreciation for some of the real-world challenges involved in space flight and exploration.
Overall, if you're a space enthusiast and/or enjoy tinkering with real/virtual aircraft and/or enjoy simulators in general, you should definitely give this a closer look; there's nothing else quite like it!

"Mun or Bust", was translated into "To be a real man, you need to launch to Mun". Now the translation is finally corrected into "We won't stop until we get to Mun".
The new translation is phonetically appealing. "To be a real man, you need to launch to Mun" comes from a Chinese saying "Bu dao \chang cheng\ fei hao han". Since "Mun", as the counterpart of "chang cheng (two syllables)" in the old saying, only has one syllable, it sounds so weird to replace "chang cheng" with "Mun". The new translation, "Bu dao Mun, Bu ba xiu", has three syllables in both the former and latter half of the sentence, making it sounds much better.
Besides, the new translation is more accurate. Original text "Mun or Bust" indicates "If we plan to go to Mun, then we will stick to that, otherwise we just don't start at all". The indication is similar to "We won't stop until we get to Mun". The old translation lacks the perseverance part, the "until" part.
As a native Chinese speaker, I really appreciate the corrections of misogynist and bigotry translations in simplified Chinese version. Even as a male scientist, I sense the persistent discouragement that blocks females from having a science or engineering career. Social stereotyping plays a rather crucial role in such discouragement, especially in regions like China. Through my whole education, I heard classmates, parents and even teachers talked to those girls and told them that they were bad at math and science even though no solid scientific evidence had ever supported the hypothesis that males and females differ in these fields.
Kerbal is a game that draws whoever has an astronaut dream. Boys and girls, males and females. I may not know the feeling that a girl suddenly finds out even in a game, a place she shouldn't be discriminated by her sex, she is excluded to be an astronaut. But I do know the feeling when I realized that no Asian superheroes existed and all princes charmings were white as a boy. That feeling is sadness, confusion, depression and anger. It took me years to re-believe that I, as an Asian, can save the day.
Therefore, I would never let any single girl feels the way that I felt. And thank you, the Kerbal team, for making this happen.

Spintires is a rather unique driving game that feels more like a puzzle at times. You're in the middle of the Russian wilderness: forests, rocks, muds, rivers to be crossed and more. Your task is to collect logs from specific locations and deliver them to one or more destinations, using a variety of russian trucks with different sizes, loading limits and offroad capabilities. Choose your accessories, carefully plan the trail you're going to follow and get going.
+The core gameplay, assuming that you're into this kind of game, is well made. Trailing through mud, rocks, water and slopes is rightfully hard and the engine will realistically deform the terrain based on the weight of your vehicle and its tires. I don't think there's any other game in commerce that really makes you experience hardcore, slow-paced offroad driving, especially with trucks.
+The maps, while only 6 by default, are all varied, rather large and each offer several hours worth of gameplay. They're good for both exploration and log delivery, and don't disappoint.
+The driving model and the game's peculiar virtual gearbox make for a very unique playing experience that doesn't feel like any other. This game is about driving trucks (up to large, very large ones) through the dirt, and you'll do exactly that. Sometimes the amount of precision required to get through some sections makes Spintires feel more like a strategy/puzzle game than a pure driving experience, and that's what makes it so one of a kind.
+The modding community is what makes this game really make a quantum leap for those that fell in love with the gameplay but felt limited or bored by the few trucks available and even fewer maps. On the Steam workshop you can find tons and tons of new vehicles to add to your garage, a good portion of which are well made, designed and functional, while external sites will supply you with a huge amount of new maps to play in, which feature both classic hauling map and pure exploration scenarios, to be enjoyed in a lighter, nimbler vehicle like the ones you can download from the aforementioned Workshop. With all these additions, Spintires' longevity is potentially infinite, or at the very least very high, for players that enjoy it.
+This thing has multiplayer with lobbies, and it even works! And by "works" i mean both that the system itself works decently and that you can find some lobbies at almost every time of the day. Playing a map with other people can be quite fun, wether you're logging together and helping each other out through a hard trail or simply exploring the map with a lightweight vehicle. In any case, it's a welcome bonus, and if nothing else saves you from the sometimes depressing loneliness of the single player gameplay (there is literally nobody else on earth in this game. Except birds). To make things easier, you can download and instantly install any modded truck the lobby owner chose, to avoid crashing or other unpleasant issues. You have, however, to already own the chosen map beforehand since those aren't included in the Steam Workshop, unless of course it's a standard scenario.
-Very, very, VERY niche game, clearly. It takes a non conventional taste to find this game anything but boring, i realize that. Most people will think slowly crawling your way through mud with trucks is anything but interesting, others will get bored rather fast and even more will probably overlook this game for its relatively high price and unusual gameplay. You either love Spintires or find it uninteresting at most, sadly.
-Adding a bunch of mods can obviously create some instability and a bunch of glitches, but as long as you remember to quit to menu before shutting the game down it shouldn't cause big issues.
-While the graphics are polished, feature good effects and a convincing day-night cycle and run quite smoothly, they are nothing too fancy, while quite impressive for what's basically an indie game. Gotta give both the developers and some of the modders credit for the highly detailed vehicle models, though.
-The camera can give you some headaches. The default view is a weird, but functional, decentered third person view with the truck on the right side of the screen. This gives you good overall view, especially on your wheels (which is quite crucial at multiple points) and cargo, if there's any, but any turn to the right can be painfully difficult due to the truck obstructing your own view, and trying to turn the camera to get a better view can be complicated. There's also an alternate "first person" view that is from either the vehicle's roof or the inside of the cabin, depending on who created the truck (default vehicles only feature the roof camera), which is great to get a more precise frontal lookout but severely limits your cone of view and the overview on your vehicle, obviously.
Summarizing, you'll know if you should buy this game from the moment you'll see some gameplay of it. If it interests you, it's probably what you were looking for, wether you knew it or not. I didn't know i wanted a game like this myself when it first came out, yet as of now I play it very often, simply because I feel it offers something new and unique, that no other game has managed to copy yet. If you're not fully convinced about buying this game, you probably shouldn't, in brutal honesty. You get what you pay for, with no warranties of future support since a new version of Spintires with more maps and vehicles and a general polish is scheduled for release soon. Time will tell wether the modding community will abandon the original game.

Mafia III…where to begin…
Let’s begin with Mafia and Mafia II…both great games.
Mafia was a masterpiece of storytelling and world creation…atmosphere and player involvement. It was different. It was Mafia!
Mafia II was pretty darned good…hard to follow such a striking first game but did pretty well IMO; equally good story telling, characters and setting. Thoroughly enjoyable and immersive! Who can forget driving a drunken Joe and Eddie home from burying a corpse with Dean singing Return to Me on the radio and everyone singing along!
If I had a complaint with Mafia II it was that such a great world was pretty sterile off the beaten track…could have done with more to do…more interaction…more hidden missions if you entered a shop or abandoned building…just a bit more imagination in creating a bit more non linear entertainment. Lots of people commented this.

So!... easy peasy lemon squeezy right? Mafia 3… you set it in Vegas in the 60s or something like that…continue the great Mafia theme… the guns, the fast cars, the loose women, the story driven immersive gameplay and add a bit more non-linear content a bit more exploration. You maintain the car customization, the choice of clothes…the music… you add….you add a bit more…you make a classic…
Well, no…you hand the franchise off and say “kill it!”
The devs cut all the customization…all the clothes…any hope of exploration. You create a huge sterile world and fill it with…dun dun dun! A quest for fuses! You cut the Mafia down to supporting actor…you make the star… racism!…yeah! Political correctness front and bloody centre…YAWN! If I see one more review praising this dirge for “tackling issues” I’m gonna puke. It doesn’t even work at doing this by the way. The eponymous hero of our PC tale is only half AA and runs around being handled by a white guy and ends up well entrenched in just the sort of stereotypical lifestyle that you’d have aspirations to avoid coming from a minority background.
The point is you don’t make a Mafia game about something other than the Mafia! It’s not big…it’s not clever it’s not surprising…it’s just pants!
No real story telling here either…Cut scenes are not story telling! Cut scenes are not a substitute for gameplay! If it needs narration then it has failed to tell the story...this is true of all cinema and all gameplay. In Mafia and Mafia II…you were the story…you were the evolution…you lived it you played it. Here you watch the story as it’s handed out to you and then you play the gaps…terrible!
OMG! The repetition! I have finished the game and I can honestly say it’s 50 hours of rinse and repeat the same couple of missions over and over and over and over and…
Even the Playboy collection is repeated in good part from Mafia II…the same girls!! Did they think we wouldn’t notice?!!
Graphics are hardly better than Mafia II!…textures are from ages past. I’m a firm believer in story first and graphics later. I could forgive the view in the rear view mirror if I was living the Mafia life…but it just appals when you aren’t…

I won’t even go near the 30fps cap at launch…I can’t… I choke up and want to eviscerate my console buying friends…
Couple of patches later and things have improved somewhat…but even a Titan X (Maxwell) clocked at 1400MHz just runs 60fps at 1440p max settings….could this be the new Crysis…just without the visuals or story?
In summary…this would have been a good 20 hour game if it was called “bored on the bayou”.
Good points?...I guess the music is still good and some of the gunplay reminds you of Mafia.
Who does this to a game? How does this happen? It’s so obvious how this should have moved forward it’s hard not to wonder at the mental acuity of Hangar 13 or the lack of s**ts given at 2K over the legacy of the first two chapters of this series…
*Sigh*
Buy on sale when it’s seriously fallen in price…

It's a fun, short overhead Souls-like. For the most part, it's not as hard or complex as some folks make it out to be (yes, you can easily beat the game with just one weapon and one tactic if you so choose), but there's a fair amount of variety in weapons and gear, and combat should be a good fit for Soulsborne veterans. The environmental hazards make up the greatest challenge, and the level designs are spot on, with creative problems that resolve themselves nicely. The bosses generally offer a pretty good challenge, with perhaps the exception of one that I assumed should have given the biggest challenge (although I guess Gwyn should have dispossessed me of that notion long ago).
My biggest gripe is the absolutely idiotic helper NPC AI, which seems intent on murdering itself by ignoring enemies and dashing right into your attacks (friendly fire was NOT necessary). They (or I should say more specifically, HE) also tend to just block hallways at inopportune times, refusing to budge despite dangers coming from all directions. Their pathing is also insane, as they will often run back and forth across a doorway rather than simply pass through it to get to you, colliding with environmental hazards all the while. I guess that's an additional challenge?
Overall, it's a solid package and I wish it was longer, which is a good sign. Any Soulsborne fan looking for a nice distraction until DS3's next DLC or Nioh should give this a try.

A surprisingly good indie title. I was expecting it to be very technically flawed, bad programming and options. However, this game nails it in terms of quality compared to my expectations. Controls are fluent, combat is perfectly paced, the progression is straightforward. You can acquire all the moves very quickly, and upgrade by earning points during combat. I like how there are no complicated menus or RPG systems, it's all about the combat. You kill enemy, earn points, use points to upgrade. Furthermore, the game is very much pick-up-and-play. It may have a miniscule moves list, but the long combos and fast animations make for some satisfying brawler action. For a game that's 286 MB, the graphics aren't too shabby. The ability to save anytime, anywhere and return to the action without going through cumbersome menus or loading screens is commendable. This game distils hack and slash to its most core mechanics, adds its own little power-up twist so that it isn't a direct clone of other games, and puts you right in the action. It's literally all combat, there's no clutter at all. If you value simplicity as well as challenging difficulty - a game that relies solely on mechanics rather than fancy visuals or a story, this game is for you.
HOWEVER, this is all assuming you can overlook the extremely difficult boss fights, where your timing has to be perfect and your health is so small and you do so little damage to the boss. If you just want to style, stick with DmC. If you don't mind frustrating boss fights, then this might be OK.

I'm one of original kickstarter backers and this game is... not good. Mighty Number 9 is often mentioned as example of KS disaster, but for me this game is equally bad.
We got the final game separated into 2 chapters. They are both different beasts, and are bad because of different things.
Chapter 1 is very short and doesn't have challenging puzzles. Except for one, which is only challenging because you might have lost item necessary to solve it. The story of girl in this chpter is acceptable, but the story of a boy is boring and wastes everyones time. Ending of first chapter actually sets up something potentially interesting...
Only to be squashed by chapter 2. The boy is still as useless as in first chapter, and the girl gets all important story bits. And the story just... ends without anything happening. Really. There was no reason for having 2 playable characters, there's no real climax, there's only wasted time and feel of completing hollow experience.
The puzzles in chapter 2 are harder than chapter 1. But they are not hard because they require thinking. Instead the game relies on multi-step trial and error puzzles, that reset each time you do any mistake. That leads to increased play time, but also is just a frustration to overcome. They even made it so you have to go trough the same animations again once you fail.
There's ability to switch characters, but since they can't communicate or share items, or have anything in common there's no reason to ever switch characters. Or so you would think. But in second chapter the game tries to fix it by making unsolvable puzzles on both sides. The game will ask you for codes and such, and you will not find the codes. You'll get stuck, and finally change into another character. Only to find out the code written on the wall in second section. Then you can input the code where needed. When your character will be asked how he knew the code he will say "intuition". It's terrible way to create puzzles. It's not like Zero Escape where it made sense to get solutions from other parts of the story. Here it's only to make some sort of justification for character switching.
The music is forgetable. I have no memories of it. I have played the game quite a bit of time ago, and I cannot remember single song. Meanwhile I still can remember music from old Lucasarts games, even though I haven't played them in years.
The game has quite distinct art style. I could wager there's no second game that looks like this one. That said, I'm not fan of the way the game looks. Arguably that's the best part of the game, but it won't be to everyone's liking. If you look at screenshots and trailers and think it's pretty then you'll like the art. Meanwhile I would preffer something more resembling old Lucasart adventures OR Vanillaware games. Broken Age, despite obvious high quality artists being employed, has a feel of cheap mobile game. That's a lot of money wasted for bad final effect.
Finally there's controlls. In other adventure games you usually had multiple options to do something with items. Broken Age simplifies the process by making everything happen with left mouse button click. There's nothing wrong with that on basic level, but unfortunatelly the way it has been done makes the game feel like Android port. The menu is quite irritating to use with mouse and would probably work better on tablets.
I cannot suggest this game unless it's bought below 5$ or as part of some bundle. There's a lot of better adventure games available. For classic feel you can play Deponia series(or really anything from the developer). For basic and simple adventures you could play Little Acre, which also is short, but at least leaves positive feelings and tells interesting story. Or play Machinarium. Or anything that is not this.

As many who have reviewed this product already know, the residents of an LGBT nursing facility near Seattle were required to work on the Alan Wake project to maintain their rent-discount status.  Despite what many detractors have claimed, these special needs individuals have produced a marvelous take on the traditional third-person shooter.
For example, physicality: the main character, reflecting the shared experience of his disabled creators, finds walking moderately difficult and running extremely difficult.  Tired of playing games where the main characters are plausibly or normally athletic?  Then Alan Wake is the game for you: the main character is barely capable of jogging for a handful of seconds, and never once is forced to "sprint," even in life-threatening situations.  The title character is also unaware of his own physical condition--the developers offered a special-needs perspective on all aspects of Wake's physicality, refusing to provide information on how Wake's body was reacting, e.g. the so-called "stamina bar" that wrongfully permeates so many games involving "running" and "jumping."
While Wake can recover health by standing near lamp posts like a downtown indigent, he refuses to otherize the elderly and/or special-needs individuals like the development team by being capable of a melee attack.  Just as Wake has difficulty walking and jogging through a small stretch of lightly treed city parks (called "forests" in the game), Wake is unable to punch, kick, climb a fence, or extract more than four batteries from an eight-pack.  Long guns provide him with difficulty and confusion, ergo the developers' wise decision to mimic their own experience by preventing Wake from carrying more than one at any given time, and by using story events to frequently strip Wake of any ammunition.  High time preference individuals will enjoy this mandated exclusion of foresightedness, almost as much as they will enjoy Wake's portrayal of flyover Americans as incompetent fools.  Some reviewers have suggested the Hillary Clinton presidential campaign had an effect on this aspect of the storyline, but such claims are ridiculous, given that Wake was showing how stupid manual laborers of European descent were long before the past American political contest began.
Needless to say, people who live in small towns are dark and dangerous people, tribal and mystical, and need to have their errors rubbed in their faces by cosmopolitan geriatrics from Manhattan, like Alan Wake.  The game developers referred to nearly five real-life authors in the story text, prioritizing Steven King but throwing in several others a single time each so that their desire to base the character around Steven King was not obvious at all.  The residents of the aforementioned nursing facility no doubt had several paperbacks to choose from on the bookshelf in the activities room, and Steven King must have figured prominently.  Postmodernists rejoice: Wake remains essentially plotless, with fewer explanations and consistencies offered than the television program "Lost," and the developers showed themselves unwilling to conform to coherency or offer resolutions of any of their many, many vague suggestions!  Those who have always felt threatened by an "ending," a "theme," or any kind of "consistency" will love this self-affirming rorschach.
People who have long been offended by the athletic, capable video game character since the Mario Brothers' high-jumping era have no more reason to be offended when they play Alan Wake, about a confused geriatric shuffling through the woods.  Wake's weakly stumble and tittering mewl (when he is struck by the toxically-masculine flyover folk who serve as the game's enemies) are a welcome break from games about action heroes who might cause people to aspire to improve themselves, and Wake's pathological whining about his writer's block will help him identify with jobless millenials, sexual herbivores, and others who were once unfairly called "lazy failures."

So, this is a tough one... This game is quite short, if you're not the sort to keep playing a game over and over to master it. If you don't like doing that, stay away from this game. Don't like repetition, stay away from this game! This game is highly repetitive and short to boot. With that said, let's move on...
This game doesn't teach you♥♥♥♥♥♥.. Literally. There is a tutorial, but there are no button prompts. You have to find out quite some important mechanics in the game. There's just guard, canceling of animations, oh and what button does what. Gotta find the padbindings for that. Got no pad? That's another reason not to play this game. Oh, and don't forget, keep a long string of hits, without being hit. That's the only time you drop your combo. Oh and why would you do this? Because an attack that hits red glowing enemies gets stronger if you can pull that off. Never mind you get more orbs to spend on upgrades.
This game is also quite tough on ya. Expect to die before you figure out how to beat a boss. Let's say I lost count at the final boss. Though 10 or 20 should be around expected. And other bosses? The first boss is easily figured out, after that, they are tough. Then there are the normal mobs. Helmet wearing suits sounds about right. In normal, the game first spawns the enemies to let you learn how they kind of work. Then it throws in enemies you've already fought. It tries to make it harder by combining enemies, so now you know what's going on.
Which is fine. The game is about honing your skill in it. Even if it is this simple, that actually works for me. Yes, this is for those that like a challenge in a way. Figure out the bosses' pattern and adapt to it. Figure out how to make them bleed(incidentally, another unexplained mechanic...).
What does work is how solidly the game controls. Once you do manage to discover how the game works, you tend to dodge, attack, guard or dodge, weaving in and out of trouble while slicing up the bad guys. It feels surprisingly good, for a game like this. The camera doesn't quite co-operate in moshpits, but it does well with boss fights. Speaking of...
The entire game is arena based fight after arena based fight. That's all there is. Boss fights, like I said, are very welcome, considering how tough some of them can be.
However, I don't feel like I can truly recommend this game. This is worth probably 2,50 or so, not the current asking price(8,49 as of the time of writing- afterwards, it's 9,99) It's too high of a price to be worth getting the game. Wait for a sale and snag it. Not now though, the game is too short for that and too repetitive.

In my opinion, The Witcher 2: Assassin of Kings is not as good as its predecessor, but there's no way you should avoid it if you enjoyed the first game.
Although it was considerably shorter than the first game (16 hours on my account), this may be to do with the fact that it seemed to be more linear that the first, with you having to follow a stricter path when exploring the world.
However, they are my only negative points on The Witcher 2. On the whole it was a highly enjoyable experience, with beautiful visuals and an in-depth story with will have any fan of the series wanting to play for "just one more hour".  The decisions make throughout the campaign make you really connect with the character of Geralt as well as moulding a personality and morality for him as you chose to spare/take a life, help/abandon someone in need and even take on various romantic endeavors.
If you haven't played the first game, I strongly advise it before playing this one as it is a direct sequel which carries over your saved game, meaning the decisions you make in the first game impact the story of the second. Although if you don't want to take advantage of this, it creates a default story for you, even though the original game is relatively cheap so there's no reason not to. The -upcoming- Witcher 3: Wild Hunt will also use this feature meaning that the story of your own, personal Geralt will conclude with you knowing you have made every decision up to that point.

Broken Age is a very odd and interesting point & click game. It has some faults, but overall kept me entertained.
The main story is actually 2 stories between 2 main characters, Shay and Vella. You swap back and forth between them to form one intertwined plot. The point and click basics are here: inventory, talking to people, combining items, etc. The graphic style is wonderful hand drawn art. It’s consistently charming and they really did a good job on this. Voice acting includes a number of celebrities and is very good. Each character has their own personality and I never forgot who a character was.
The puzzles in here are pretty good but sometimes the solution can be a bit “out there”. Going through some extra patience, I was able to complete the game without using a guide EXCEPT for figuring out I needed to switch to the other character to continue. I thought the game would do it automatically when you hit a certain point.
I agree with most reviews saying the first half of the game is better than the second half. I was really captured by the story. Kept asking myself “what is going on?” in a curious way. The second half slows down with a lot of backtracking and stranger puzzles to solve.
One change to the interface I would make is a smaller cursor “area of selection”. Meaning, how close I need to be to something to highlight it. If two things were close together you’d have to closely see if you’re interacting (highlighting) with one or the other. This could also be fixed by a more defined highlight effect on the object.
The last section of the game where you must frequently switch back and forth between Shay and Vella can be annoying and is based on some trial and error.
The ending is a letdown. I feel like more could have been done with it considering the storyline.
+60fps
+Beautiful hand drawn art style
+Voice acting is top notch
+Story is unique and interesting
+Music
+Unique characters
+Cursor area of selection (see explanation above)
+Puzzle solutions can be strange and unintuitive
+Story and gameplay drops off in the second half
+Disappointing ending
Above average.

Alan Wake is a psychothriller game based on supernatural powers. It shows how powerful darkness really is. The game is set in a rural town called Bright Falls in Washington state, USA. Alan Wake is a professional writer from New York City who decides to go on a vacation in a small town. However, his vacation turns into a nightmare as he is attacked by possessed beings known as the Taken. Wake’s wife is apparently kidnapped from their cabin located in a nearby lake, encouraging Wake to look for her in the wilderness. The game is spread across six episodes that feel like a TV show.
As Alan Wake looks for his wife, manuscript pages are scattered in each episode. The manuscript pages flesh out the story of the suspense Mr. Wake is going through, although he does not remember writing it. There are many strange plot twists such as crazy things happening shortly after reading about them in his manuscript pages. Wake is a disturbed man and this sets up effective storytelling.
The gameplay is mainly in the night when darkness rears its ugly head. There are a few daytime scenes, but it is best that there no more daytime scenes. Otherwise, too many daytime scenes would have taken away the moody feel of the game. There are many scary encounters with the Taken, who are armed with knives and other projectiles ready to kill Wake. You can evade these possessed humans by running from their attacks, creating a cool cinematic dodge. Every time you enter a new store or turn a corner you feel anxious about who or what will come after you. The Taken are vulnerable to light, so that is when your flashlight, flares, and flashbang grenades come into play.
Aiming at the Taken is required, but shooting at them without aiming a flashlight at them to remove their strength of darkness is a waste of valuable ammo. As soon as you take away their darkness, you can shoot them with your conventional weapons like a revolver, shotgun, or hunting rifle. Ammo is not very plentiful, so it is important to use your ammo wisely. You can choose to run away from them so that you can reach the next safe haven, a place where strong light is projected onto the ground. The Taken do not dare enter the light for fear that they will be killed.
When the Taken are not attacking you there are possessed objects such as barrels, cranes, bulldozers, etc. These possessed objects seem to be from the famous movie Poltergeist. You must use Wake’s flashlight or flares to disintegrate possessed objects, as they are vulnerable to light and cannot be shot. I found it quite scary to see a bulldozer suddenly turn on and chase me while no one was inside driving and a few Taken were attacking. This is when your battle skills are tested to see how good you are with your flashlight, flares, and flashbang grenades. Your flashlight loses battery power and must be recharged. The limited battery power adds to the suspense of having to insert a new battery while the Taken and/or possessed objects are threatening to kill you. It is also quite unsettling when flocks of ravens suddenly descend upon you from the sky and the only way to eliminate them is by using light sources. The only problem I have with the combat with the Taken is that it may feel a little repetitive when heading toward the end of the story in episode 6.
The graphics of Alan Wake are still neat on the PC. Bright Falls looks gorgeous in the day during rare daytime scenes. The night looks detailed enough when looking at an abandoned farm that looks decrepit. The graphics make this small town look authentically rural. I found a few graphical glitches in some indoor settings, but they are rare and superficial.
After completing the main story, you can choose to play the DLCs, including The Signal and The Writer. The DLCs are definitely worth playing since they expand on the main story. The Signal and The Writer both feel even creepier and more bizarre than the main story. It was particularly scary when suddenly, not one, but two monster trucks were chasing me in The Signal DLC with no one inside either monster truck.
I highly recommend Alan Wake for its well written horror story that translates into spooky atmosphere for the gameplay. It is a creepy game that does not let up and keeps the combat tight and intense until the very end for the main game as well as for the DLCs. I firmly believe that the DLCs, although short, are worth playing and retain the creepy atmosphere.
My Score: 8.5/10

I promised myself not to write a single word about this game, until that whole hype wave and lootbox scandals will calm down a bit. So I focused on playing other new games and completing old ones, which was left behind for some reason. But now, after I am done almost with everything, I was interested in, I felt myself coming back to Shadow of War just to make it 100%. Why? Simply because I enjoyed it a lot and I wanted to have more.
First, I need to say, that I am not a fan of Shadow of Mordor. I was literally annoyed by the mechanics of the game and this whole Nemesis system. I never felt like I was enjoying the game, because the whole gameplay seemed repetitive for me and every time I started to play I always ended surrounded with tons of enemies with almost no chance to escape. So, I dropped that game, then a bit later I gave this game another chance and still nothing -  it was still  boring, dull and quite difficult.
When I heard about the sequel, I couldn't care less, but on the same time I was really hoping that they will improve this game for the better. So yeah, no surprise, I pre-ordered it. But there was a one minor little detail I forgot about. It was 2017. Probably, the most disturbing year for the gamers and game developers as well. Year, when a massive bloody lootbox war has started. Could I ever imagine, that millions of players all over the world, will speak about pay-to-win system in a single player game, instead of discussing gameplay, graphics, LOTR universe references and, the most important, all time favourite topic - optimization issues? No. Never. But this happened.
Microtransactions are a plague, I totally agree with that. And the whole gamer community should never keep quiet about such thing. Star Wars Battlefront 2 and NFS: Payback are perfect examples what the public unrest can do. But on the other hand, we should remember, that in this case, we have a single player game. And all the purchases are completely optional. I think it's pretty much obvious, what I'm saying right now, but still, I must say, that I finished the whole game without even spending a dime on anything and I never felt myself underpowered or uncomfortable.
The whole story continues right at that place where you left off in a previous game, what I really liked that they made a quick recap of what happened in the first game, which was completely fine for me, as I never finished the original game. Right after that, game throws you into an action and you begin to hack and slash orcs, learning new mechanics and improved Nemesis system. They simply added tons of new features and cool stuff, comparing to the first game and I guess, its the best part of all this story. Literally, the best word to describe everything what's going on in Shadow of War is a "complete improvement". Yeah, that's it. Take an original game and imagine everything 10 times better plus bunch of new features - parkour mechanics, fighting, nemesis system, riding on a beasts, climbing on the back of craugs to stump 'em down, hiring bodyguards for the harder battles, conquering towers and a lot more. Speaking of story, I enjoyed it as well, it has its plot twists, betrayal lines, strong and unique characters and of course, Nazguls!
I would also like to state that the whole map is divided into regions, every region is unique and has different types of landscapes - mountains, snowy mountains, green nature, burning grounds, a big volcano with lava rivers region, etc. They all look just simply amazing and gorgeous, the graphic is really beautiful and they are also quite big to explore.

So, my dear friends, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:
+ Love action hack and slash games
+ Looking for a good exploring RPG game
+ Wanna enjoy a graphically great game based on LoTR universe
+ Interested in a rich story game, full of twists and detalized characters
+ Are a fan of the first game and eager to see a completely full improvement to your favourite game.
Avoid this game if you:
- Feel like you better listen to some reviews on Metacritic/IGN/PCGamer, etc. moaning about microtransactions in single player game instead of trying it by yourself
- Dont want to grind a lot to watch a true ending in game, the same trick has already been played in Batman Arkham Knight before. However, it's not worth it, was a bit disappointing for me.
Enjoy!
