I was thoroughly impressed by the mechanics, the nemesis system, the varied and amusing dialogue with the different Orc commanders. I think this is probably THE best action RPG game of 2017. However... as with all things that you come to love... the desire for more is always there. I would absolutely love to see large expansion packs of this game, like conquering more territories in exotic places like Harad or the Easterling areas, possible conflicts with the denizens of Middle Earth, etc. I would have really loved to see more story or quests as well. The world can feel empty when there aren't any unique things left.
Graphics: 8/10
Graphically, the game is impressive, the visuals are fantastic and everything looks wonderful. From the far away out of map areas, to the sky and waters, everything is so detailed and very well done. It's really cool to get to see Mordor or Minas Morgul so close.
Sound: 9/10
The sound of the game is pretty good, various unique sounds from the terrain to the creatures, orcs and monsters. The music has a lord of the rings feel to it and compliments the adventure! Their are some dialogue repeats, but... when you are killing a 1000 orc commanders in your time on this game... your bound to hear something familiar.
Mechanics 6/10
I feel the mechanics are still a little... rugged, in the way that they do not feel polished. Mistakes are common simply because the character or AI mess up due to their mechanics. Jumping around, climbing and running around needs some tinkering. AI commanders engaging in fights against each other tend to taunt or just wait... whereas fighting against the player, they are blood thirsty as hell!
Combat 10/10
The combat in this game is VERY fun, it's very well done and will leave you feeling like a bad♥♥♥♥♥warlord when you've chopped like 100 Orcs to pieces or get that 200 hit streak. Archery is smooth, quick and can be very useful (never really tried hammer throwing all that much, seemed a waste, gimme a Javelin bruh). Mounted combat is pretty cool, it's not as mobile as it should be though... the glaive is powerful but eh... I prefer riding the dragon.... oh yeah.. YOU CAN RIDE A DRAGON and burn things or eat people... or just fly around and admire the landscape [Warning... Daenarys does not come with the dragon ;( ]
Story/Quests 10/10
Now this stuff... this is probably one of the best stories in a game I've been too. It's a mixture of sorrow, betrayal, vengeance, comedy and just saaaaaallllllty rage (DAMN THAT B**Z). If you think of the Quality of Metal Gear Solid stories... and mix in Lord of the Rings... you get Shadow of War. I wont spoil the story, but I can say this: Don't Eat Cake.
Conclusion: Buy it... ignore the BS negative reviewers crying about in-game store or cash shopping... ignore it... I haven't spent a single penny on this game (neither have others) but many of us have enjoyed it thoroughly. If you want an engaging, deep storyline with fun combat and interesting lore, try this game.

Spintires - an all-terrain off-road simulator - has great potential and it is always nice to see an indie developer making something different, something exciting. While not many maps and vehicles are available the already existing ones give you enough challenge to spend dozens of hours with the game.
The concept of Spintires is very simple: every map has a location for the lumber you need to deliver elsewhere. This location along with the drop-off point is shown on your map. They are, of course, quite far from each other (usually positioned at opposite ends of the map. The terrain is usually difficult to navigate on so you need to carefully plan where you'd like to go and which vehicle you'd like to take. Additionally, the game does not reveal the map for you - certain "cloaking" areas are placed and in order to get rid of them you need to approach their epicenter.
Navigation requires you to pay attention. Naturally, the best is to play with a friend as in coop mode you can not only deliver more lumber at once but help each other if stuck in the mud.  Respawning is possible but only in casual mode: real challenge begins only for hardcore gamers! Near garages certain extensions can be installed - utility assets are available for repair work and you can install a tank for the fuel to have long-lasting petrol available.
I like the complexity of the game and having translations in many languages is always a plus for me. The game looks nice - especially the water and mud effects look great during interactions with your vehicles. The only downside is the missing sound effects for your friend - you simply do not hear the engine of their car but only your own. And you cannot see their tracks in the mud which would be nice if you go on separate ways only to meet up later on because of the objective.
Overall, I am really satisfied with this game. It has potential and while rumor has it the relationship between publisher and developer is not exactly great with regular updates this game can be even greater!

This is going to be tough... :(
As someone who has played and beaten now all three Mafia games, It's been somewhat odd to see how the series has changed over time. In 1, it was a superb story-driven game that also happened to have a large open map that you basically couldn't do anything in. 2 was the same way, except the story wasn't as good and they threw in collectibles and stores to give its open world some bare bones. 3... is more open world, but like it's predecessors does not seem to know how the difference between making an open world and making it interesting enough to want to explore on your own time. All three Mafia games fail at this.
But that's also what I was expecting. So why did I bother with this game if I already believed it was going to have some trouble on the gameplay front? Well, despite my issues with Mafia 2, neither it nor Mafia 1 really failed in story, and it was that I was looking for when I decided to pick up Mafia 3. Especially so when it was revealed that things would be quite different this time around.
The setting is "New Bordeaux" (A sorta stand-in for New Orleans) in 1968, one of the most tumultuous years in history. Between uprisings and protest movements all over the world, the height of the Vietnam War, and numerous political assassinations, it was quite a mess. And the player character, Lincoln Clay, very much is a product of all of that turmoil: a black Vietnam vet returned home to find himself caught up in a huge mess when he returns home since, prior to going to Vietnam, he was part of the Black Mob. As it happens, he was a volunteer rather than a draftee, and ended up being good enough at his job that he ended up first in the special forces, and then was brought into the Phoenix Program: the infamous counter-insurgency/assassination system run by the CIA that crippled the NVA/Vietcong. It means that when Clay returns home, not only is he probably suffering from PTSD from all that, he soon finds himself using what he learned in the Phoenix Program in a war at home against a new enemy: the Italian Mafia under the Marcano family.
As a protagonist, I have somewhat mixed feelings about Clay. On one hand, his character fits right into the setting of the game and his motivations for what he does make alot of sense. On the other hand, it felt like you don't really get to see him develop very much throughout the course of the game.
But... that problem isn't exclusive to him. In fact, not recieving as much attention and detail as it deserves is something that I can say about not just Lincoln Clay, but this entire game.
Why? Because the quality is inconsistent. In major scenes, and especially early on, the storytelling and cinematics are some of the best I have seen in a long time. Voice acting and motion-capture are damn good. The world building is excellent, and, though obviously I wasn't alive in 1968, it feels like they captured the setting very well. Ok, the racism is a bit thick and I wasn't exactly surprised when the game's equivalent of the KKK showed up, but for the most part, it's well done...
...But then things start to unravel. There are dialogue scenes (of lesser importance) where you end up seeing two stiff unmoving characters just talking to eachother without any of the life that made other scenes so good. Despite being in such a diverse city on the surface, it feels like more could be done to make the city feel even more alive and interesting. And then there is the gameplay... which starts as a well-designed experience I'd come to expect from the previous Mafia games before moving into repetitive open world activities and less frequent story missions of the same style as what is seen early on in Mafia 3.
In other words... Mafia 3 feels like an unfinished game, or one that was rushed out before it was finished. No, there isn't a lack of stuff to do: It took me 30 hours to beat the game. But the amount of that time spent doing the repetitive process of killing some people, breaking up illegal activities, and then taking down higher ranked people after luring them out padded out the game's length. The game's AI is pretty terrible, glitches are in abundance, and uneven performance all add to the picture of a game that was released before it should have been.
If this game had been given more development time to add more life to the world, more variety to the missions, and to clean up all the technical problems... Mafia 3 would probably be an amazing game. But it didn't get that time, and so what we have instead is something that shows all the laid groundwork for something great, but not enough built upon those foundations to ensure its success.
And that feels even worse than a game that is just bad, because you can tell that at least somebody making Mafia 3 knew what they were doing. But... the final result squandered those efforts. :(
So... what happens now? Well, as usual for "AAA" games these days, there is a ♥♥♥♥ing season pass and promise for more content. Is there hope that they will fix the game's problems and make it truly great, or are they just going to make us pay for stuff that they should have put into the game originally? If it's the former, I'm disappointed. If it's the latter, I hope both the devs and the publisher go to hell.
Either way, it does not change the fact that they released a flawed product that, until they fix at least the technical issues, is not one I can seriously recommend. And that makes me sad because... I want to. I want to say that this game has great storytelling, an interesting setting, and is a refreshing change from the earlier Mafia games. But despite all of that being true... there's just too many other issues that blacken what should be a game I should be telling everyone to play and enjoy.
*sigh*
Welp, time to go back to my usual boring routine until another promising game shows up that, like this and Mankind Divided before it, will probably disappoint as much as it entertains, and so make that disappointment all the worse. ;_;

Few games indie games give me as much to think about as DarkMaus. It's an interesting mixed bag of goodies that both delight and frustrate you with every bite.
At its most basic, DarkMaus is top-down Dark Souls with a minimalist aesthetic reminiscent of Limbo. It's visually humble and charming, and combat adheres to the same rules that made Dark Souls a success. It's slow paced, dangerous and cerebral, forcing you to carefully consider and commit to actions. Using the shadows as blind spots keeps exploration tense as you turn every corner, and the game teases and rewards observant players with clever little reveals. DarkMaus felt more like my first playthrough of Souls than any other imitator has before it.
Thay said, the game is full of small but frustrating issues. Bosses were underwhelming. The final boss, one of the most powerful beings in existence, would be a pushover if it weren't for his adds. The UI could use work. Scrolling through your inventory is a chore, and why on earth is the B button - which functions as 'cancel' in every other menu - the 'confirm' button in the level-up screen?
The art design has the unfortunate side-effect of making areas feel indistinct and hard to remember, forcing the inclusion of a map. This leads to a lot of glancing back and forth as you try to backtrack to that alternate path you bypassed. I also noticed a few fairly severe and random frame drops and freezes.
The game's greatest sin, however, is the Death Echo system, DarkMaus' unique feature. The ability to bring multiple ally ghosts with you raises a lot of balancing concerns that failed to be addressed. Individual enemies become trivial when you can team up on them, so the game balances this by filling rooms with multiple enemies and projectiles which can be insufferably irritating when solo. Ally ghosts will damage you with AOE fire spells and run ahead to aggro large groups of enemies you weren't intending/ready to fight. They often become more of a hassle than they're worth.
But for all these issues, DarkMaus impresses in something else. The level design is intricate, varied, and hides lots of secrets in its pockets. There's a deep roster of weapons (19) for a 5-6 hour experience. Enemy AI is surprisingly reactive to you. I had enemies react to being repeatedly parried by abandoning that attack, leaping backwards when I pulled out a ranged weapon, and turtling when I relied on counter attacks. And there seems to be 2-3 different ways you can play out the NPC quests, giving a sense of agency I didn't expect to have in a game like this.
Ultimately, if you like Souls, DarkMaus is worth a try. There's enough here to bring me back for another run, and that earns a recommendation from me.

In "Castle of Illusion" you - Mickey Mouse - save your girlfriend Minnie from the evil and ugly witch Mizrabel. So your goal is as basic as it gets.
You wander through various worlds inside the Castle of Illusion (like a giant library, a magical forest or a toy world) in order to collect seven gems that will make a bridge to the witch and Minnie.
This is a 2013 reboot of the 1990 Sega Genesis classic of the same name (which I like btw).
How does it hold up, as a game in general and as a reboot?
As a game in general it is pretty good. It is mostly a 2D platformer with 3D graphics, which means that you mostly jump and run from left to right or the other way round. In special parts of the game you have use all key arrows in order to jump on platforms around you or just to run to every corner of a room or bigger platform (like in boss fights).
You need to end three acts of a level and collect diamonds and other items as well as you can (certain amounts of diamonds are needed to get access to future levels).
You defeat enemies by jumping on them or by throwing stuff at them.
So as you can see it is pretty basic and it can be fun for adult players as well as for children. The gameplay also is basic and easy to learn.
However, prepare yourself for a few frustrating moments, especially for quite tricky jumping parts (a good example: the milk shake river and cookies or the final boss fight) and for cutscenes that cannot be skipped (not even the long end credits).
As a reboot it is alright, not something like the "Ducktales" reboot that amazed and entertained me very much but it is still noticeable that the SEGA team put some work and love for details into this. This also goes for the soundtrack and the lovely voice acting (like when Mickey comments the levels from time to time).
All in all I would call "Castle of Illusion" alright. Not quite awesome - and some flaws really could have been avoided - but good enough to try out. It's definitely something for Disney/Mickey fans.

Essentially, this game is a mix of Dark Souls, Limbo, and The Secret of NIMH, and by that I mean it has a dark minimalist aesthetic where everything wants to kill you and you play as a mouse.
While it obviously borrows from Dark Souls with its combat, death mechanic, and levelling system, it does have a few tweaks and perks that set it apart, if only a little. As well as losing your experience after dying, you also spawn shadows of yourself to help you reclaim your lost points. Normally they simply retrace your steps and only attack nearby enemies, but you can customize some abilities that allow you to have them follow you around until they die. There are also plenty of other combat abilities such as a shield bash or a heavy spin attack using skill points built up from reaching a certain character level or by discovering new areas and defeating bosses.
This might all sound well and good, but there are some issues with the combat and the RPG elements. For the most part, enemies have a pretty predictable pattern of blocking whenever you attempt to attack them, so you simply have to bait them into attacking you, either dodging or blocking, and then hitting them every so often.
For those looking for more of a challenge, you'll wind up disappointed that enemies simply get heavier weapons, armor, more health, and more combat abilities shared with the player that are largely unbalanced. The most basic ability being the dash attack, while simple and not terribly effective when used by the player, can be outright murder when used by an enemy simply because there's basically no reasonable tell in enemy animation, so you'll end up just eating damage by the end-game and relying on beefing yourself up with heavier equipment, effectively killing character variety.
Besides the gameplay, there is a pretty glaring issue with the graphics, specifically the framerate. For seemingly no reason, the framerate can take a massive dive regardless of setting. You could be fighting four mice with three of your own shadows and their funky graphical effects and the game will run pretty smooth, but then you'll sit down at a campfire and have the game nearly fall apart, sometimes even locking up for a few seconds. It's completely inconsistent, but common nonetheless, so it can definitely get in the way of the gameplay if you're in combat, or just trying to sight-see and enjoy the environments.
Despite all of these issues I have with the game, it was still a pretty fun adventure with great presentation, and I'd say it's a pretty impressive project for only three people. There is a NG+ after beating the game, but with how small the game is, I'd say you're better off starting a new file to try out different builds.
Great product overall, wish it was a bit more scary.

It’s not the worst game out there, and it is certainly possible to get some fun out of it, but with its lack of content and options it is probably a harder seller for most people out there.
The bad:
-Practically non-existent story.
-Mediocre gameplay at best, weird attacks that don’t work as fluid as you’d want, bad block and counter system etc.
-Unspectacular unlocks. A few costumes, no additional characters, throwaway abilities and letdown upgrades.
-Very repetitive. Hit almost identical enemies all day long.
-Bad AI. Enemies behave strange and are often dumb beyond belief.
-Very small space to actually move around, limited to only small circles that you fight on.
-Lack of graphic and resolution options. Most resolution selections are missing, making it awkward if you happen to not find your native one.
The good:
-Rather small file size.
-Graphics aren’t really all that great, but they are appealing enough to look at.
-It can be pretty fun to hack and slash around at the enemies, even though it can get old fast.
-Bosses are decently fun, even if they are rather weirdly and simply designed.
-Good for short play-sessions.
In general, this is a game that is hard to recommend to anyone. It is nice to have Japanese indie titles coming out on Steam, and for some people supporting that might be enough. For everyone else, with the lack of proper options, replay value, as well as having barely any content, there is probably not enough here if you don’t mind a very simple game that is mostly only good for a short burst of dumb (and sadly unpolished) fun.
EDIT: I usually try to stay away from writing my own opinion about something like this, but there have been too many people writing me and defending the game that I have to add a little bit of my more detailed personal opinion about how people treat such games. After playing for a few more hours, I can't imagine why people would defend this game. Even for the low price they are asking, you are practically getting a hack n' slash with terrible and imprecise gameplay, no variety in combat nor enemies, no story and annoying cutscene, bad graphics, bugs, and just no quality or content whatsoever. Not to forget that it's basically 2 hours long at best. Forgetting all of that, every time I check what people have good to say about it they just write something like "dude those pantsu" and think that makes it right. If that's the way people think nowadays, and they will let a game with no content and terrible quality slide and even defend it just because it has a main character in a miniskirt, then I am sorry for anyone that is stepping to such low levels. Come on guys. That’s just pitiful and sickening. Let's look for quality over cheap sexualization and similar gimmicks that producers try to sell a game with.

This is getting immediately compared to DMC, when it's probably closer to the Onechanbara games: simplistic aesthetic, enclosed battle space and a battle system that, while possessing some speed and flair, lacks a certain finesse. And, well, sword-wielding females making up the main cast. MKH merely lacks them wearing all but a bikini and a ten gallon.
For a doujin title, its rather respectable. Again: for a doujin title. The interface has a bit of tack to it and, as I said, the battle system doesnt feel as tight as it could have been. You are tasked with fighting things before fighting things and then fighting maybe other things before getting a boss fight. Who you fight. My main gripe with said fighting was how easy it is to trigger annoying, weak, inappropriate and, most importantly, slow to recover attacks without meaning to do so. I feel like that could have been easily avoided by having them only activate with another independent button -- a lock-on, for example.
The difficulty isnt to be sniffed at either, bosses in particular will be quick to whittle away if you dont wise up quick enough and its surprisingly easy to get stunlocked by mere mobs (another negative trait shared with the Onechanbara series). With no means to cheese enemies via a ranged attack or super mode featuring health regen the latter battles on higher difficulties can become a test of mettle more than anything.
Its a good little slasher and a fine example of what can come out of Comiket, just dont go in expecting a perfectly polished experience.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game really suprised me. I came into this game expecting a crappy version of MGR, but instead I got the beautiful lovechild of MGR, God Hand and DMC. A warning: I'd only recommend this game if you're a fan of at least two of these titles. If you don't know how to cancel or use i-frames, this game is liable to eat you up and♥♥♥♥♥♥you out, especially on anything above normal. If you can already pull this stuff off in other games, you'll find a fantastic, deep combat system. For example: enemy got you stuck in a combo? Cancel your hitstun into a sweep, then cancel the sweep into a dodge. Lovely.
The unique aspect of this game is called "Zanshin". After dealing enough damage to an enemy, you can sheath your sword to gain health and blade meter, which you need to use your sword attacks. In addition, enemies who have taken enough damage to become "bloodied" will take a burst of damage. While it sounds simple, it's an engaging move, and sheathing your sword to make 10 enemies burst into a rain of gore is immensely satisfying.
In conclusion, like I said, if you're a fan of stylish beat-em-ups and aren't afraid of a challenge, I would 100% recommend this game. If you're after cheap fanservice and panty shots, probably better to go elsewhere.

This game is definitely for any hack n slash fans of Devil may Cry, Bayonetta and Metal gear rising: Revengeance. It offers a simple control scheme, but once you invest some points into the skills in the upgrade menu, you'll find that the game has some in-depth mechanics that are well implemented. Like all hack n slash games, you control one character, in this case Misa, against hordes of enemies in a small arena with no obstacles and no obstructions in the way. That's quite perfect for this kind of game, as you wanna make sure you have full awareness of all enemies around you and combo them to your heart's content. Like every game in existence, there are pros and cons to this game:
Pros:
- Great control scheme that feels good, nothing convoluted
- A ''Zandatsu" feature well implemented that can tip the battle to your favor
- Plenty of action to be held in this game!
- Uh, hot chicks with swords
- Nice visuals and fluid swordsplay
- Good variety of skills that flow well into one another
Cons;
- very limited enemy archetypes, offers very little imagination
- Very short game, but then again it's to be expected when it's only about 300mbs
- The timing on the ''Flourish'' and '' Counter'' moves feel very awkward
- No camera lock-on feature?
- Roll hurtbox is funky
- Next to no unlockable content to unlock, other than costumes I believe
Personal input:
Since I play just about every hack n slash I can think of, this game is a defnite buy for any fan of the genre. It's hack n slash to its purest, with quite possibly the shortest story i've seen in a long time. It does have its faults, with no lock-on feature which to me is quite crucial in a hack n slash, but it doesn't hinder the pure adrenaline rush this game provides. As it stands with its current price, I'd say wait till a 50% sale comes up for it, but if you do buy it as is, then know you're getting your money's worth in the action, not so much for the story nor content.

The sad irony of Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos, is it comes so very close to standing alone but in a last minute effort, fully commits to setting up more episodes we’re all but certain never to see.
Let’s back up for a moment though. Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel following Winter and Cyrus, who play the part of mediators: peace keepers of sorts to the different distant worlds surrounding their own. It’s their job to step in when things become too extreme, and ensure a world doesn’t destroy itself in acts of war.
Learning to Manage Chaos then, is Winter training to learn how exactly someone is capable of keeping a world in check, especially in times of extreme turmoil. If anything though, this is more the story of Winter growing as a person than a mediator, her naivety and innocence being tested as she’s thrown into situations where there is no right decision and not everyone is going to come out alive.
It’s not uncommon for authors to craft ignorant protagonists or side characters so as to have an easy stepping off point for relaying important details to the reader, which characters should likely already know, but Dysfunctional System manages to very rarely fall into that trap of artificial stupidity. Winter feels authentic in her cluelessness about the larger world, being only fourteen but having her heart in the right place. Her actions and ways of thinking are often flawed, but her internal indecision and discomfort of wrestling between what she believes is right and what she’s being told is logical feel very relatable and sincere. She’s been living a life in a pristine society, where the concept of war is difficult to even imagine, so being flung into a far less peaceful and sustainable world comes at more than a small shock.
Cyrus, her mentor, is the counterpoint to Winter’s pleas for peaceful discussion and her fear at wandering into a world she doesn’t understand. He’s calculating and experienced, but also cold and seemingly worn down by the things he’s had to do for the sake of keeping worlds alive. His discussions with Winter are often full of frustration, but the glimpses of understanding that poke through give him the feeling of more than just an old, mean-spirited teacher. He’s smart and recognizes that Winter isn’t prepared for the role of a mediator, but he wants to ensure she gains the experience needed, which even if uncomfortable isn’t anything like what she’ll eventually have to face.
Most of Learning to Manage Chaos takes place between only these two characters, and the back and forth between them is surprisingly compelling. Their dialogues can get heated, but developer Dischan Media does a fantastic job leveraging this between brief moments of humor (such as Winter trying her first bear) to create a very personal, relatable feeling to every interaction. The core plot holds no great weight in all of this, being a tool to spark conversation but without much depth in and of itself, but it’s a short outing that manages a great amount of character development before then closing in a scene that while not perfectly finite, feels complete.
But then the screen comes back and here is where Dysfunctional Systems unfortunately suffers as at the time the first episode was being developed it was still believed future episodes were on the way. The fact is that development has been put on perpetual hiatus, dying after internal troubles caused the project to fall through and any hope of seeing the series completed along with it. This wouldn’t factor in nearly as heavily to Learning to Manage Chaos if it wasn’t for the extended epilogue that comes after the credits. It’s a series of exchanges which don’t exactly propel the plot forward, but leave it in an awkward state of uncompleted development. It disrupts the finality the episode originally ends with, and itself feels rather unpolished, with an abundance of useless dialogue and very limited artwork (most of the epilogue takes place in a sort of text only terminal)
So there’s the clincher. Dysfunctional Systems is an engaging visual novel, with a wonderful art style and a brilliant score, but it’s a story you have to commit at the start to being left hanging with. It’s hard for me to say then if I recommend giving it a chance. I’m caught between my enjoyment of what it is, and disappointment at what it will never become. It’s a weird place to find a game, and it’s not a judgement call I’d be able to make for anyone else.

Overall, the game is rather fun and pleasant and the levels can really vary in difficulty. Some I found were much harder than others, but none of them were to the point of impossibile as I was able to beat all 40 levels of the game in around 1 hour or so. Aside from the gameplay, the art is pretty nice, especially the nice color scheme. I also really enjoyed the soothing music for this game, even if it didn't match my frustration at times. Lastly, if you are an 100% achievement hunter, the achievements to this game will almost all unlock simply through playing and beating the game.
Overall, nice and fun little game with a cool mechanic that will keep you entertaining for some time. Plus it is only $1 to begin with.

This game is surprisingly good. It looked great when I saw it a few years ago in PC Gamer (alongside Prison architect I think?) and it looked quite good. So, when the Summer Sale 2016 presented me with a bundle of this game and Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number for only £3.74 ($4.91), I grabbed it immediately. So what do I think?
The game is very good. The controls are a dream to work with. There's no momentum on your character (or very little momentum), which made it feel very concise and meant you could execute people with precision and do it perfectly. They compliment the gameplay and style of game extremely well, and it all manages to meld together very nicely and very tightly. Unfortunately, this precision can lead to a lot of difficulty, as it also extends to enemies and the environment, meaning that (if you want to play like me) you can get stuck behind walls and get caught out by doors, ending up with you shooting a wall or door which totally collapses your plan on taking everybody out. This can lead to a lot of satisfaction, however, as it leads you and forces you to make up a new plan on the fly and it forces you to improvise.
The graphics are beautiful. The game is, obviously, a SNES-N64 era top down shooter (at least in graphics anyway), and it uses to its advantage in so many ways. The stage sways ever so slightly, making the player feel uneasy and unready for everything, which makes it hugely gratifying when you actually pull something off. The background is constantly changing colour too, which adds to the uneasy feeling. The gore, good god the gore is unbelievable. The amount of gore is an exceptional reminder to the player that not only are they killing people, but that the player actually managed to pull that off and kill so many people, spewing blood and guts everywhere which is amazingly gratifying.
Honestly, this game is amazing. It actually surprised me too, as it is very well written with some genuinely freaky "what the ♥♥♥♥" moments in it, and I can say that it was well worth my money. Do try and get it on sale, however, as it is reasonably repetitive and is punishingly, rage-inducingly difficult.

Good Plot, Addictive Gameplay, and Fantastic Atmosphere are the three things that most describe this game. Hotline Miami follows the actions of a silent protaganist (known only as "Jacket") who is being blackmailed into commiting mass murders by an unknown group of callers. The actual gameplay consists of a top-down shooter and beat 'em up style game, with multiple weapons and masks (the latter of which grant the player special abilities that they can utilize in combat) at the players disposal. Despite being fairly challenging, it makes for fun and often exciting gameplay. One of the most notable aspects of the game is the way that it really nails that kind of "80's action movie" feel. The way the world (characters, buildings, ect.) looks all add together for a nice atmosphere. It's also packed full of great songs that really match the mood of the game. My only complaint was that, if you really get into it, the game can be finished fairly quickly. However, that doesn't really affect my opinion of the game too much as it is alltogether just too good to have something so little upset me. I give the game an overall rating of 9.5/10, and would definetly recommend it to anyone who's looking for a challenging, violent, and action packed game.

This is going to be tough... :(
As someone who has played and beaten now all three Mafia games, It's been somewhat odd to see how the series has changed over time. In 1, it was a superb story-driven game that also happened to have a large open map that you basically couldn't do anything in. 2 was the same way, except the story wasn't as good and they threw in collectibles and stores to give its open world some bare bones. 3... is more open world, but like it's predecessors does not seem to know how the difference between making an open world and making it interesting enough to want to explore on your own time. All three Mafia games fail at this.
But that's also what I was expecting. So why did I bother with this game if I already believed it was going to have some trouble on the gameplay front? Well, despite my issues with Mafia 2, neither it nor Mafia 1 really failed in story, and it was that I was looking for when I decided to pick up Mafia 3. Especially so when it was revealed that things would be quite different this time around.
The setting is "New Bordeaux" (A sorta stand-in for New Orleans) in 1968, one of the most tumultuous years in history. Between uprisings and protest movements all over the world, the height of the Vietnam War, and numerous political assassinations, it was quite a mess. And the player character, Lincoln Clay, very much is a product of all of that turmoil: a black Vietnam vet returned home to find himself caught up in a huge mess when he returns home since, prior to going to Vietnam, he was part of the Black Mob. As it happens, he was a volunteer rather than a draftee, and ended up being good enough at his job that he ended up first in the special forces, and then was brought into the Phoenix Program: the infamous counter-insurgency/assassination system run by the CIA that crippled the NVA/Vietcong. It means that when Clay returns home, not only is he probably suffering from PTSD from all that, he soon finds himself using what he learned in the Phoenix Program in a war at home against a new enemy: the Italian Mafia under the Marcano family.
As a protagonist, I have somewhat mixed feelings about Clay. On one hand, his character fits right into the setting of the game and his motivations for what he does make alot of sense. On the other hand, it felt like you don't really get to see him develop very much throughout the course of the game.
But... that problem isn't exclusive to him. In fact, not recieving as much attention and detail as it deserves is something that I can say about not just Lincoln Clay, but this entire game.
Why? Because the quality is inconsistent. In major scenes, and especially early on, the storytelling and cinematics are some of the best I have seen in a long time. Voice acting and motion-capture are damn good. The world building is excellent, and, though obviously I wasn't alive in 1968, it feels like they captured the setting very well. Ok, the racism is a bit thick and I wasn't exactly surprised when the game's equivalent of the KKK showed up, but for the most part, it's well done...
...But then things start to unravel. There are dialogue scenes (of lesser importance) where you end up seeing two stiff unmoving characters just talking to eachother without any of the life that made other scenes so good. Despite being in such a diverse city on the surface, it feels like more could be done to make the city feel even more alive and interesting. And then there is the gameplay... which starts as a well-designed experience I'd come to expect from the previous Mafia games before moving into repetitive open world activities and less frequent story missions of the same style as what is seen early on in Mafia 3.
In other words... Mafia 3 feels like an unfinished game, or one that was rushed out before it was finished. No, there isn't a lack of stuff to do: It took me 30 hours to beat the game. But the amount of that time spent doing the repetitive process of killing some people, breaking up illegal activities, and then taking down higher ranked people after luring them out padded out the game's length. The game's AI is pretty terrible, glitches are in abundance, and uneven performance all add to the picture of a game that was released before it should have been.
If this game had been given more development time to add more life to the world, more variety to the missions, and to clean up all the technical problems... Mafia 3 would probably be an amazing game. But it didn't get that time, and so what we have instead is something that shows all the laid groundwork for something great, but not enough built upon those foundations to ensure its success.
And that feels even worse than a game that is just bad, because you can tell that at least somebody making Mafia 3 knew what they were doing. But... the final result squandered those efforts. :(
So... what happens now? Well, as usual for "AAA" games these days, there is a ♥♥♥♥ing season pass and promise for more content. Is there hope that they will fix the game's problems and make it truly great, or are they just going to make us pay for stuff that they should have put into the game originally? If it's the former, I'm disappointed. If it's the latter, I hope both the devs and the publisher go to hell.
Either way, it does not change the fact that they released a flawed product that, until they fix at least the technical issues, is not one I can seriously recommend. And that makes me sad because... I want to. I want to say that this game has great storytelling, an interesting setting, and is a refreshing change from the earlier Mafia games. But despite all of that being true... there's just too many other issues that blacken what should be a game I should be telling everyone to play and enjoy.
*sigh*
Welp, time to go back to my usual boring routine until another promising game shows up that, like this and Mankind Divided before it, will probably disappoint as much as it entertains, and so make that disappointment all the worse. ;_;

As a long time gamer, I had the dubious distinction of owning and completing this on both the Master System and Mega Drive versions (couldn't do it now - age gets us all!) and so was curious as to what level of remastering/reimagining this is and I was pleased to find a genuinely entertaining new game heavily inspired by the old.  Everything that was great about the original, the locations, the sense of whimsy had been successfully carried across to this new version along with a fully orchestral soundtrack and a friendly sounding narrator adding the level of Disney gloss that just wasn't possible in the cartridge era.  As much as I enjoyed this game however, there is a feeling of sadness when you realise that the developers where planning to do similar remakes of a lot of Sega properties from that era including Streets of Rage and Golden Axe which will alas never be as Sega shuttered ther studio.  Still, if your looking for a pleasantly challenging old-school platformer with a modern look, this could be ideal.

I quite like Spintires but I can not recommend it.
Going back some time, the first moment I saw of this game I rushed to a google search and looked for reviews. I have been dying for some 4x4 action for years.  I was bitterly disappointed to see it getting scores of 4/10.
Anyway not long ago I found the demo. I kept getting the little Land Rover stuck, but then discovered I could switch to the huge 8x8 or whatever it was. When the sale came I bought it.
Within only a couple of hours I realised I'd made a mistake. Getting bogged down all the time, because you can't initially jump straight into a power motor with 8 wheels. In fact I have not seen that vehicle in about 8 hours play.
I persisted though in trying because when I wasn't bogged down I was having a such a great time. It's proper non-racing 4x4 fun, which is exactly what I want.
The problem then became progress was so slow.  Every single time you turn your vehicle over, get bogged down you are right back at the start. I am in the little Land Rover again at the start of the map I was last playing. It has another issue. It is so fragile one bump will do up to half the damage it can take. Literally you'll be travelling at maybe 5mph and slide into a rock or go over a tiny crest into a rock. Damage! Once full damage is done the vehicle is useless. Add this making me have to set off from the starting position again. It's then twenty-fifty goes just clearing the cloaking to see the map. It's annoying being sent back to the garage.  Then having to drive along the same road, maybe this time not getting as far as last time. Over and over.
That's the issue really. Spintires gets annoying. It's not so much rage quit. It's more disbelief-wtf-no-more-patience-left quit. It rightly deserves its afor-mentioned 4/10 scores.

This is going to be a longer than usual review than I usually do, but I'll summarize this game now before I dig into that: Acceptable.
General: My biggest complaint about this game is that it falls under "You get what you pay for", much like Earth Defense Force, Shoot Many Robots, and other cheap knockoff games.
Story: Now, Dust has a lot riding behind it. This is perhaps root of most of the game's problems plot-wise, because a lot of the lore in the game is barely touched. It also ends with a questionable cliff hanger, again bringing up more questions behind it. As far as the actual story is concerned, it's paced up until a given point and hinted on deeply until you reach said point - Inwhich vague, general background details are (optionally) given to the player. The story is average here, certainly not bad. The dubbing in many cases, as well as character expressions, isn't as pleasing as one would expect - Though it is /slightly/ bareable.
Gameplay: Takes some getting used to, the combat system is easy to master. In fact, it's easily abused - Especially on normal difficulty. This game combines platforming and combat, but is more focused as a fast-paced side-scrolling beat-em-up. There exists stage hazards which also must be avoided. The leveling system is also very generous, but balanced so that one get too far ahead too early.
Overall: The game scores a 8/10. I have a second issue with this game: It's way too damn easy if played with a sharp mind. I should not be killing the final boss 3 times over only to get hit by him 5 times. When you posses attacks which can deal 1,500 damage per tick on a boss with 60,000, and it area of effect is that of pretty much the whole screen, I can't help but feel my breif back-and-forth sidequesting may have been a bit excessive towards the game's progression - An issue which falls in alignment with my first, this is expected.

Mafia 3: Now I was excited for this game and I mean really exited, but I feel Mafia 3 took a step back why I don't know but I feel the game was not ready for release.
Bugs: Well there are so many bugs in this game that it would be impossible to name them all.
Graphics: The textures well it just doesn't feel like they took the time with them, it just looks like they quickly made a object and slapped it in the game. The textures don't blend in like they are ment to in games. As for the sky well its so bad, I could not believe what I was seeing the dynamic weather made the changes so bad from rain to cloud to sunny that it made it look like we had a eclipse or had a 3 day night cycles in 30 seconds. Alot more can be done for graphics. For Graphics I would rate this 4/10.
Sound: Now the music on this game is so good it feels like it doesn't belong in this game because compared to everything else its one of the best features on this game, alot of time went into it that it disappoints me that they didn't spend as much time on other features. (Feels like they haven't). For sound I would rate this 10/10
Game play: The game play started really good then went to average really quickly to the point it felt like they gave up on it, only one way of killing like cut the throat stab the chest done like it would of been good if they added more to that to make you look forward to the next one. The missions are the same every district nothing new, its like a copy paste job on the missions and this disappoints me, no time and no effort was put into it and I feel was a lazy way to get it done quicker. The good thing about the missions is there is not limit on how to approach the mission and its good. The driving is ok apart from some bugs that sometimes makes it a pain to drive sometimes but the mechanics are there just needs abit of tweaking here and there. The AI look I understand that they are just AI but I feel they play a big part in this game and they are just stupid like really, really stupid if you kill one they run towards you like whats with that if I saw someone kill someone my first thought would not to run towards the killer come on and I love the fact that they can run to a phone and call the cops but I think that the AI can be given more of a personality they all act like they are all being mind controlled they all have the same reactions nothing different. Stealth is a great feature to this game the fact you can do missions without it ending up in a massive firefight that ends up being a 10 against one situation. The customization in this game is something that should be in the game now not added at a later date why they did it this way I don't no but it needs to be added asap. Alot of stuff is missing. More can be done in aspects of game play. For game play I would rate this 6/10.
Good Points:
1. Story. Even if more needs doing there is still alot there.
2. Soundtrack. One of the best sound tracks to date.
3. Story line. It has a good story line just feel they should add to it and not rushed it.
4. Map. Not limited to where you can go truly an open world and its a good size.
5. Dialog. If as much effort was put into the game itself would be one of the best games of 2016.
6. Mission approach. You can choose how you enter a mission with no limits.
Bad Points:
1. Bugs. There are so many bugs that it has confused me on how the game got released.
2. Graphics. The textures and the sky aer so bad that so much work needs doing on it
3. AI. The AI are so stupid that they all have the same personality more also need to be done on this.
4. Customization. There is close to no customization at all in this game.
5. Mission endings. They are all the same nothing different needs some work.
Overall - The game itself is a good game but again feel it was rushed, alot of work still needs alot of work done but I don't regret buying the game, it's alot of fun to play take away the bugs, glitches and the graphics problems then this game has alot of going for itself and as long as the devs do keep to what they have planned then this game will turn out really good. Should you buy the game yes even with all the problems I have had (still having) so much fun on this game. The game is not not bad. I would give the overall score of 6/10.
More will be added as I play more of the game. But I do recommend buying it as its alot of fun.

A blatant copycat from a much more famous series titled 'Devil May Cry'. No. I'm not joking. Slap a girl in it, give her different attack animations and change the enemies and you get yourself Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae.
Have I discouraged you yet? Well... don't be.
To start off this review, the menu is... a little different. You get to look at the protagonist named Misa on your right and... she looks hot, alright. Furthermore, the main menu is also where you get to change her costume, though you unlock those costumes later on in the game. Oh, and on an unrelated note, you can view the changes in graphics by looking at Misa as you change the settings, which is pretty neat.
The controls are pretty nimble. They're very responsive, but you are unable to customize your controls to your liking. You can only choose to play this game with default controls or play it like how you would in Devil May Cry (no surprise there, since the game bears so many resemblance to Devil May Cry that IT JUST LOOKS LIKE A MODDED GAME OF DEVIL MAY CRY FOR <censored>'S SAKE).
The gameplay feels repetitive as you are showered with enemies for you to kick, punch and slash your wave through multiple waves before meeting a boss in each chapter, though as you progress to later chapters, you will fight deadlier enemies. Using your katana drains the katana gauge, and if depleted, you won't be able to use the katana unless you fill it up again by dealing melee attacks or killing an enemy. Health pickups can only be dropped once you kill a boss and your overall health stays the same amount with no chance of regeneration, even before starting a new chapter after completing the previous chapter (I seem to like this feature a lot, though it does make my teeth grit in frustration as I progress to a new chapter with only a considerable amount of health left). And as you progress to the game, the game awards you with SPs which you can use to unlock costumes or upgrade your character, as well as learning new skills.
My verdict tells me that this game is a slight breath of fresh air if you're looking to play Devil May Cry as a female (assuming you got bored of playing as Dante) and if you're pessimistic enough or if you're a DMC fanboy/fangirl,  you will be disappointed with the game as it doesn't feel like the game is any different than Devil May Cry itself. However, if you can put all the blatant similarities aside, this game is genuinely fun and if you're a fan of hack-and-slash games (or Japanese girls, if you have that fetish), get it now while the game still offers a sale.
Rather, just get it anyway. It's bloody cheap. You don't really need to wait for a sale unless you're in a tight budget.

Alan Wake holds a special place in my heart between absolute nostalgia and the perfect rendition of a Stephen King type video game done right. I've heard about this game previously, probably since it's first trailer from E3 way back, and I've always wanted to play it ever since. Though since I never owned an Xbox console in my life until more recent years, I thought I would never get to play this game. That is until I was introduced to Steam and all the amazing games that were on this platform. Well, with that sort of intro out of the way. Let's dive into my review of Alan Wake.
Alan Wake is a game where you take control of famous author and writer, Alan Wake, as he tries to find his wife after her strange disappearance. The game starts in a dream sequence, essentially the tutorial of the game's mechanics and what to expect in your journey. And what a journey it is! The gameplay is rather simple. Press LT to shine your flash light on an enemy or object, RT to shoot said enemy, RB to dodge and sprint, and A to jump. You can of course move around with the left analog stick, change weapons with the D-pad and move the camera with the right analog stick but that's about it in terms of button commands. You start the adventure in the dream sequence learning the gameplay at a good pace, you shouldn't have a problem learning the mechanics in this short prelude before the game starts.
After the dream, Alan wakes up on a ferry with his wife, Alice, on it's way to Bright Falls, a little vacation town where nothing is truly as it seems, and all might not be as 'bright' as the name suggests. The game is slow to start, divulging you into the world and meeting characters that will play a part in the overarching story as it unfolds chapter by chapter. After Alan and Alice get to their little getaway cottage and start to get settled in, the power goes out and Alice is kidnapped by a dark presence, thus begins the journey of Alan Wake. This game does very well in putting you in the shoes of Alan in this psychological thriller where nothing is really as it seems. One moment you're rushing through the forest, picking up pages to an unwritten book by Alan Wake, and searching for any clues you can find to lead you to where Alice is. The next you're rocking it on stage with your agent, Barry Wheeler, while CHILDREN OF THE ELDER GOOOOOOOD plays in the background while you're tearing up enemies in the most energizing part of the game.
There's a lot of variety in the game's theme. It goes from thriller, to horror, to somewhat silly. For example, you're running through the forest and you happen upon a graveyard. Enemies come out of nowhere and one just shouts "The graveyard shift has been known to cause cancer". This little part in the game honestly caught me offguard with how random it is, but I appreciate the humor where they can get away with it, for the most part this is a very serious story and game, but when the developers and writers had a chance to slip something in, an easter egg, little joke here and there, it's definitely appreciated and makes you appreciate the game the more you play.
I of course have a few gripes with the game, some things aren't as polished as they should be, or I feel like they should've added a few extra controls in Alan's arsenal. I know, he's supposed to be a normal guy just looking for his wife... but is that really an excuse for him not being able to grab ledges? That being said, I also wish the optimisation of the PC port was a bit better, it's not bad, but it seems if you don't have a power house PC, higher resolutions, even 1080p drops framerate substantially, but dropping resolution isn't that big of an issue honestly. Aside from gripes here and there, this game is beyond worth it, I can't recommend it enough, the story and pacing is fantastic, the gameplay is fun and fluid, the characters are well written, and the Stephen King inspired atmosphere should be reason enough to play this game.

It's actually been quite a while since I finished Alan Wake.  I'm not sure why I didn't write a review as soon as I'd finished it, like I normally do.   I think it came down to the fact that it
a) disturbed me
b) irritated me
c) fascinated me
in equal measure.  I'll tackle them one by one.
Horror games aren't in short supply right now.  They never have been, really.  Since the very first "Alone in the Dark", or even "7th Guest",  I've had a bit of a love/hate relationship with them.  I like a good jump scare as much as the next player, but I've come to expect more: Atmosphere, music, a sense of foreboding.  Some of the best horror games I've played had huge sections where there was nothing in them, but my brain was expecting something so I had a constant level of fear.
Alan Wake can be taken one of two ways (like many of the old Twilight Zones), either the protagonist is mad as a box of frogs, or that evil spirits are taking over the world.  Let me leave that with you for a moment.
Most games don't really go into exploring that option, other than a bit of throwaway "Is this really happening?" dialog/text at the beginning. For them it's straight up: Demons from Hell, dripping blood, dismembered corpses and all the usual self-inflicted horror from christianity or whatever other religion or mythology the game draws on, and no hint of "well, perhaps this is all just cos you had a few too many coffees and got stressed about the Anderson presentation. What you need is a lie down".
Alan Wake, on the other hand constantly hammers. it. home. over. and. over.   you're running through the woods, shooting everything to kingdom come.  Then you reach some nice sanity, and start to think "uhh.. what am I doing!?".. then the batshit mental stuff gets going, and you're thrown back into hades.  Then you run across someone who's all "Um, you look a bit flustered, want a glass of water?", and just as they go for the water, their head is bitten off by a giant bat... or something....  The constant keeping-you-off-kilter plays so heavily on me, that after a while, I started to get a bit uncomfortable thinking "am I really shooting innocent people here?  Should I be avoiding the enemies? Will the game reveal 'you slaughtered a town of innocents in your paranoid delusion?'".
Mixed in with that sense of unease, is a distinct sense of irritation.  The game could have been so much more.    Essentially, it's a series of huge maps which seem open-world, but are cunningly crafted to be linear.  Think of a bead necklace.. A series of bloaty areas you can have a fight in, connected together with choke points, bridges, tunnels, and other things that force you down a single path.      Set in the mountains near a series of lakes, and the sea, those big open areas are lushly forested, with paths, roads, and people.  There's logging equipment here and there, ranger stations, firewatch towers, and all sorts to explore as you run away from satan's litte helpers...
But the main problem is that in those big areas, the fights are with the SAME FOUR GUYS OVER AND OVER. It goes like this:
* You're running through the forest
* You hear a sound and see a flash of light
* Four guys are running towards you
* You kill them
* Goto the beginning
That's how most of the game plays.  The reason that irritates is because that samey stuff is the fluff that separates all the REALLY GOOD sections.  There was one bit where I heard a massive CRASH, followed by massive crunching sounds and screaming... Then ran into the building to find something had bitten a hole in the building and made off with everyone in it.. Amazing sound stage, brilliant plot moment... and then the four-guys-running-at-you started.  sigh.
Lastly, the game fascinated me.  Told as it was, it could easily have been adapted from a hitchcock movie, or similar.  It was shot cinematically, and the voice acting, sounds, music and modelling is superb.  I don't mean good, I mean su-flipping-perb.   The characters, the location, the things the protagonist went through left me with some deep questions about what happened, was it all real, and what happened next; All of which are the hallmark of a good supernatural thriller.
So, apart from the extremely samey enemy modelling, and the "four-guys-rushing-you" thing, the game had a LOT of brilliant moments, truly hollywood-like thrill moments.    I'd give it an 80% if I could, but cos this is Steam, it gets a solid thumbs-up!

Wow, this game is really well-designed.
To be honest, I didn't expect much at first. I just liked the atmosphere and the soulslike approach the designer made to the topdown twinstick action game genre. I grabbed the game on summer sale and after having played it for the first 1 1/2 hours I must say that the designer did a great job in shaping this little gem. Of course you immediately recognise that the game is a low-budget title, but apart from that, the game does everything right.
Transferring spooky atmosphere on mouse protagonists and animal scenery/feral wildlife probably was a tough job, but from the start the player feels some sort of claustrophobia in his torchlit circle, because you might never know what is around the next corner. Upgrading your attributes, skills, spells and items is crucial to advance. This is done by investing bone marrow you gather from slain enemies and by resting at campfires like you do in DS titles. The simplisic Hud and Inventory design is awesome and the gamepad controls are also well-implemented. The music and background noises add to the whole experience.
Some additions would have been nice like a narrator or synch for the animals (at least the mouses) but it's understandable that these contents were cut keeping in mind that this game was mainly made by one person.
I strongly recommend buying it now, but still for its full price, this game will please you.
P.S.: You will die alot, so this game might be more for patient and thoughtful players like me than the Rambo player that is in search of a twinstick action game, so beware!

I honestly can't figure out the massive positive buzz around this game. Reading some of the 'quotes' from Games reviews sites I can't help but wonder if those reviewers actually played the game, or were simply paid to write something extremely positive completely out of sync with the actual game.
Flexibility, depth? Really, where? Having the option between 3 skills and some dynamite to open a safe merely means you have 3 similar skills separated for no obvious reason. And a game mechanic that allows opening a safe by tossing a stick of dynamite at it isn't deep or flexible, it's flawed and oversimplified. C4, plastic explosives, shaped charges, really too much to ask?
Perhaps it seems a bit odd that I start off with such an example, but ultimately 90% of the game is just that: utilizing one skill or another. Lock picking, safe cracking and trap disarming outside of combat, and the various weapon skills during combat.
One of the biggest gripes I have with the game really. The multitude of pointless and weirdly chosen skills, needlessly segregated (lock picking AND safe cracking, individual weapon classes), with no synergy between them or with the main attributes. The attribute and skill system is so extremely poorly designed that your 10 STR character won't be able to kick open a simple wooden fence (which is even described as being shoddily built), because he lacks the Brute Force skill. That's right, a skill. Dear developers, ever heard the term 'brute force approach'? It's not a skill, it's not something that needs to be learned. Seriously. Well alright, have your 10 STR wield a big freakin' axe and chop down that small wooden fence... No can do, the axe is ineffective against that shoddily built fence. Just like any other weapon, except explosvies.
Your 1 STR character with some points in the Brute Force skill however, might be able to kick down the door. Might I say, because the developers also chose to implement some arbitrarily chosen difficulty level to each of such skill checks. The skill rank is still prevelant however, with no connection to attributes. So even if you do decide to give your 10 STR some ranks of Brute Force, yuour 1 STR char with higher rank will still have a better chance to succeed. The ridiculousness of the difficulty settings is perfectly demonstrated in a certain town which you will end up in some time into the game: A large stone wall inside a building can easily be kicked down (as the animation for Brute Force is always the same, just like all other animations for skill usage. Extremely boring, and most of the time character aren't even close enough to actually touch the objects. They're just doing something in thin air), but two shoddily built wooden fence outside are near impossible. As mentioned before you can't destroy them with an axe, or a shotgun either. You also can't jump over it, or climb over it (movements in Wasteland 2 are extremely limited, just like pretty much everything else).
So attributes and skills are detached, there's no synergy. The attributes themselves provide very limited benefits, and basically the only things that matter are Action Points (AP) and Combat Initiative (CI). Coordinations would be the equivalent of dexterity in other RPG games I imagine, and maxing this stat to 10 will give you a measly 10% bonus to Chance to Hit. While min 1 gives you 1%. So no penalties for extremely low stats. Developers decided to separate each weapon 'class' into a different skill, Assault rifles, Sniper Rifles, Pistols, to name a few. Want a sniper? No need to actually put any points in Coordination, the only thing that matters is the Sniper Rifle skill. But of course that character won't be able to hit a damned thing with an Assault Rifle or Pistol when he/she lacks the skill points. Horrible design choice, and completely illogical.
Attributes won't play any role outside of combat, and your INT 1 character will have exactly the same things to say as your INT 8 or INT 10 character. CHA doesn't play a role in conversations either, but of course we do have some weirdly choses skills like Smart♥♥♥♥♥ Kiss♥♥♥♥♥and Hard♥♥♥♥♥for some extra choices during conversation. Simplicity is key, and developers certainly don't seem to want the players to have to try and/or think so of course these♥♥♥♥♥dialogue options will be visible and even provide you the information what rank in the skill you need. You can also switch character in the middle of conversation, for example to another which has this particular♥♥♥♥♥skill. These 'skills' really should have been character traits optionably selected during character creation.
It would seem I am ranting on about attributes and skills, but in my opinion they're key in a good RPG game. Create a game that responds strongly to the attributes and skills of a particular character and you have a game where you can actually role play a particular type, and replay the game with a completely different one and getting different responses, results, options. There's nothing of the sort in Wasteland 2.
Your actions have consequences? Please. I'm getting a bit tired of games (and reviewers) advertising this when all you get is some different slide show ending with narrative at the end of the game. During the game there are virtually no consequences outside of the narrow context, the situation, you happen to find yourself in right there and then.
Consequences would be running out of fresh water when you opt to save Ag Center, and thus subsequentially have to deal with issues related to that. Similarly, running out of food when you go to Highpool. But what's to be expected in a game where you can top up your canteens with fresh water from an oasis in a heavily irradiated zone? Hilarious. Water does not play any role at all in this game and I really have no idea why the developers didn't just drop it completely. Personally I would have preferred a much more significant impact, but I fear that would simply be too much to ask.
The Tiered progress on weapons, and weapon mechanics themselves, are another utter fail decision. Tiered progression means you will have blunt weapons (like a lead pipe) with higher Armor Penetration than a rifle for example. Right, makes perfect sense. Weapon damage is another one, where one 5.56 mm caliber Assault Rifle will do a lot more damage than another only because of that arbitrary Tier statistic. Weapon choices per Tier are basically limited to a lower AP usage, lower damage version and higher AP usage, higher damage version. Higher Tier means higher Armor Penetration, a flat number that is compared to the flat Armor Class number of the target. The game doesn't update appearances based on armor equiped, so it's entirely possible to run into a bare chested generic cannibal with Armor Class 10, meaning some very heavy (and expensive) Armor. With me already raises the question how a cannibal trying to survive out in the wastes even managed to obtain such an armor really... Mechanics are as simplified as this: If Armor Penetration is equal to or exceeds Armor Class the weapon does the normal range of damage. When Penetration is lower, damage is reduced based on following calculation: (Pen / Class) * 100%.
The Director's Cut added some perks (based on skills only, nothing on attributes) and one for Assault Rifles is called 'Hollow Point' which hilariously adds +1 Armor Penetration. It's these details that just show how very littly thought and effort the developers put into this game. It's all bland, illogical and inconsequential.
Combat itself is extremely boring and repetitive with barely any tactical options/variations. The Good -

Clunky, Fiddley Diddley, (almost impossibly fiddley - diddly actually) Controls that become impossible to navigate in the later stages.
Visually Incomprehensable "Combat" Scenes that require large amounts of Key Mashing to get through.

What can one say about a game which you've played for almost 5 years (since beta), with thousands of hours, and you're still not bored with? Quite a lot actually, so here it goes:
(First of all, you might see a lot uf us Steam users talk about "thousands of hours", while the played counter only shows a couple of hours. That's because most of us copy the game folder somewhere else, mod it, and play that one, so Steam can't log the played time correctly. In other words, I have 150 hours of playing this game just to test the new versions, or starting it by accident).
The Bad (let's get this over with quickly):
- the tutorial is a must, but it still won't help you in the long run. The base game can be fun to play, but you will instantly need a mod, such as Kerban Engineer, to give you some badly needed information.
- there is no "easy" mode. You will be bombarded with a lot of information. Just going through the options screens is enough to make you dizzy. They've tried to keep it simple, but we've constantly asked for more and more. So get ready to learn a bit. Even youtube tutorials can sometimes be a bit confusing. Yeah, it can get that complicated. But this is a Nasa simulator, not a 2 button survival game. Don't let the cute Kerbals fool you. These Minions are a mean bunch.
The Good (vanilla game):
- If I were to nominate the best educational game ever made, this would be it. This game has the ability to teach you A LOT about space exploration.
- If I were to nominate the best sandbox game ever made, this would be it. There is so much stuff to do, even in the vanilla game. The amount of effort that you have to put in to achieve some things is monumental. The career mode is more of a tutorial, designed to stop the game from overwhelming a newbie. You're going out there, in space, which has no limit. This game literally has no limit in your options and career evolution.
- Performance and stability have steadily increased to the point where the vanilla game has become a very solid base. Now hold on to your hats...
The Awesome (mods):
- Wow boy, where to begin? If you want any real rocket, you've got it. Want the real solar system? You've got it. Want real physics? Got it. Want to script your own bloody autopilot? You've got that as well. You want to make the game difficult and realistic? How much difficult do you actually want? Seriously, there are no words to describe the passion of the modders in this community. And the game is really easy to mod, unlike Skyrim. Just play the game. Want someting? Google it. You will find a mod which does what you want, and more.
- And it all fits. While some mods are essential for any type of gameplay, others just change the game focus completely, from construction, bases and colonisation, to exploring far away stars with futuristic engines. Or you can tone it down and make your own Soyuz and be happy with reaching a realistic orbit.
So if I were to rate this game, based on an average "first impression", it might be a 6/10. Spend enough time learning and customizing it, and it will become the best game you've ever bought.

I've played some really bad games in my day, but this... my god how this game takes the cake. I originally played Life Is Strange on PS4 when it was completely free, episodes and all, on PS Plus. I thought it would be fun, at the time I knew nothing of it so it would've been a fresh game to play. So I downloaded the game, and all the episodes and played it... and how much of a mistake that was. I'm not going to talk about the game as a whole but simply summarising it. The music is this "Indie" genre of music, I have no clue to why anyone would remotely like it, but for me, it's absolutely terrible on my ears. In my full playthrough of the game, I muted the music the first I heard it, I couldn't stand more than a minute of it. I understand music is highly subjective, but the music choice for this game, although fitting for its theme, is nothing more than agony when I listen to it. The gameplay is barebones, for a narrative-driven game, it's usually standard to have less gameplay and more cutscenes and dialogue, but just walking around collecting items, taking photos, and talking to soulless NPCs isn't fun at all. The story is nothing more than a bore. It has nothing that keeps me playing the game at all, it's only comprised of boring plot points and plot twists someone can see from a mile away. The Characters are nothing interesting, all of them I hated and wanted nothing to do with. All the characters in Life Is Strange are as soulless as a corpse; they have nothing interesting to say. Not once did I care for a character, ever. The game as a whole is nothing but horrible, even at the start of the game, it was just nothing but a slog to get through. After the first 10 minutes of gameplay, I decided to get an easy platinum and get all the achievements in the game, after all, it was free and I didn't really have much to do anyway. But, the hours spent getting the platinum wasn't worth it, at all. When I finally got to the ending, I didn't care what happened, so I chose the ending where Cloe dies and it was all over. Thank. God. That leads me to the ending, nothing matters in the story at all, sure at the time they do, but it's all reversed after picking an ending. Heh, so much for the choices mattering huh? Well, that's it. I'm sure there are other games worse than Life Is Strange, but from what I played, this is the absolute worst game I had the displeasure of playing. For the love of god do NOT get this game, you'll save yourself from wasting hours of your life playing this. For my wasted hours of playing Life Is Strange, I give it a 0/10. Sure, it could be way over the top of a game rating, but for me, it fits just fine, even the prequel, Life Is Strange: Before The Storm, seems like it would also be deserving of such a low rating.  I have no clue of how this game is so well liked. I hope it's ironic, but there are some people who genuinely like playing bad games and enjoying them, so more power to'em. But hey, for all I know it could be a masterpiece, but, even for all the money in the world, I will never touch this game, nor any game related to it what so ever.

8/10: Violent, twitchy mayhem brought on by cryptic phone calls and madness, built on a foundation filled with nationalist conspiracies and dripping with flourescent, 80's era vibrancy.
Right from the start, things in Hotline Miami are surreal and disorienting. Animal-masked entities speak in riddles and prophecy, while strange calls compel one to venture to the provided addresses and provide the Russian gangsters there with a whole lot of ultraviolence.
What ensues is a game of hectic murder sprees interspersed with a sense of descent into delusion. Different animal masks grant different bonuses, allowing a subtly different experience depending on the level. Switching between weapons and executions, trying to keep the kill combo going in order to maximize the points you get in the end, results in a game where death is a regularity and success is gauged by how quickly and creatively you can manage to wipe out a floors worth of people.
The only way to get an idea of what's causing all of this is to find the letter tiles scattered among the letters and decode the puzzle. Thankfully, the game lets you know if the level contains an unlockable mask or tile, and the puzzle letters glow if they are placed in the right slot, so anyone can eventually figure it out.
All in all, an action packed rampage with an uneasy, late 80's vibe, Hotline Miami is great fun for anyone who is fond of the Rampage challenges found in the original two Grand Theft Auto games.
