Alright, there are a ton of great things about this game, truly a ton, but it does have a few flaws.
Overall, I'd say it's excellent 9/10. I would recommend it, especially to people who enjoy tactical thinking, who like LotR, or who want to play a challenging combat game with a cool story.
I'm going to try to avoid spoilers, but the game is relatively lengthy. Expect playtime to be 2 to 3 times that of the original.
There are multiple 'acts' in this game, which each take a fair bit of time, and change the overall scope of things.
In the start, things are a bit muddled. They spring a lot at you at once, and introduce some of the game's quirky gimmicks pretty early. You've lost some of your previous power due to misfortune, and have to fight your way back into shape in this part. Overall, the first act ends up being a decent story, and the gameplay is fun, though more challenging than the original. 8/10
Act II is just friggin glorious. The game really comes into its own here, bringing out the best experience by far in the franchise. Act II is 10/10 outstanding in terms of narrative, art, gameplay, everything. This part alone is worth buying the game for.
Act III is relatively brief by comparison, though also really cool. How do you feel about necromancy? I like it. 9.5/10
Act IV is challenging, and the gameplay is great, but it gets a bit grueling. In order to beat it and finish the game you have to successfully defend 4 different fortresses 5 times each. So yeah, 20 sieges. If you mess up and die, then you lose your fortress, and have to besiege it to retake it, which takes a lot longer. A siege defense that you win really decisively can be over in 20 minutes. One that goes a bit bad goes for more like 40 minutes. If you screw up, and have to retake your fortress, it's more like a 2-hour long affair of freeing your captured captains, recruiting new stronger ones, disabling some defences of the fort, and fighting your way to the final boss.
All of this is excellent gameplay, and it is fun, but... 20... back to back.... with virtually no story progress in between... it just seems a bit gruelling by the end of it. I feel like this was a missed opportunity. If they'd broken it up with just a couple of side missions with other characters, and added in a cut scene every few sieges, it would make it less of an ordeal. It sometimes felt more like a grind than like organic growth. 7.5/10
Alright, now some generalities.
In the original, only if things went really bad did you need to run away. In this one, the enemies are stronger relative to you, so you'll have to approach situations with greater caution, and if you get jumped or ambushed, you might need to occassionally bug out entirely. You'll need to pay attention to opponents weaknesses, and their AI's have a cool aspect of adapting to the techniques you use on the fly, so they get more challenging as the fight progresses. Every single captain can end up feeling like an epic boss battle. In some casses they'll have weaknesses that can be exploited to make it pretty easy, but only if you learned what they were from intelligence sources and think about how to exploit them. Some fights will be hard no matter what.
The gameplay is awesome. Truly, it is. It's the pinnacle of animation based combat systems, and there are a lot of tactical options for you to explore and exploit. The original had a bit more rhythm to the combat, whereas this one is a bit more frenetic and desperate, perhaps even 'visceral' is the right word.
The end-game options are also pretty epic. While the original failed to provide much use for converting captains beyond a few specific missions, this one requires you to form armies made up of large numbers of captains to siege and defend fortresses in the end-game.
The humor is great. Your foes and allies alike have fantastic personality.
I feel like a few aspects could have been better with how they reward you, or don't. I believe that games should reward players for doing things that are fun. This game could do a bit better on that front. This missions are fantastic, but the in-game currency.... ends up being kind of dumb. You need some for weapon upgrades, and a fair chunk for siege upgrades early on in the siege process. But, once you have those, there's nothing to spend it on in the actual game part of the game. You amass tens of thousands of miriam, and the only place you can do anything with them is the immersion breaking shop.
Granted, using a game's currency to buy weapons and mercenaries isn't unrealistic, but as I said, it's immersion breaking, unnecessary, and just feels poorly implemented. I view it as a minor flaw.
They have a cash shop as part of it too, but needless to say, it's unnecessary, and I'd strongly advise against using it for a dozen reasons.
The point is, large parts of Shadow of War are unique, fantastic, and definitely worth experiencing.
It's a large game that takes a long time to fully conquer, but I'd strongly recommend it.
It has some minor flaws that might bother some people more than others, but it's a great game, and the sieges are among the most intense gameplay out there. You've sometimes got 15 allied captains, a dozen enemy captains, and hundreds of lesser foes and beasts on the field, and it just feels epic. A battle on that scale is larger than you can control, you just have to insert yourself in the right spots to steer it in the right direction.

This game might very well be my game of the year! An expansion on every aspect of the first game, adding nearly everything I had hoped for form the first- the ability to wear armor, use new weapons, smarter enemies, more varied areas to explore, and the ability to make orc friends and a giant♥♥♥♥♥orc army. I beat the first game twice- once on PS4 and another time on PC.
I loved the first but sometimes it just became a button-spamming hack-n-slash. There were little RPG elements to help draw you in other than the fantastic Nemesis system which created unique enemies. You basically kicked♥♥♥♥♥until you got enough XP to become god-tier powerful and soon you couldn't die. There were only two environments- green area and grey area. The areas were fun and beautiful but did not feel too different other than the color scheme and the occasional tree in the green area.
In this one, though.. you can earn awesome looking weapons and armor, each with special magical abilities; enemies can learn your attacks and learn to counter your spamy moves mid-battle; maps all have interesting twists- whether it takes place in a city, underground, or by a crumbling coast and strange forest, they are all fairly different; and, of course, you can build massive armies.
One time, I walked into strange cave and found an orc- not so strange. What was strange, though, was that he yelled at me, whipped out two crossbows and fired a volley into me. He then threw them to the side, tackled me, and then proceeded to beat the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me with his massive fists. As I lie there, dying, he lifts his axe for the killing blow when a sword swipes from off the screen and pierces the orc's ribs, instantly killing him. WTF. Then, this little soldier came popping out saying he was happy to have repaid my good work. Who the hell was this guy? Then I remembered about an hour or two before, I had saved this Gondorian sergeant from a pack of orcs chasing him through the streets. He remembered me and saved my life.
Just now, I sent two of my orc captains to ambush an orc who was ambushing another orc I hated. The three of us hopped out of the shadows and started the fight. When things got hairy, I called my buddy orc into battle only for him to be held hostage by an orc I had♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about an hour ago for ruining his drinks. That fat drunk then joined the fight, making it an even 3v3. I killed one of the orcs, my captains killed the drunk, but the orc I hated ran away. When I caught up to him, he threw a smoke bomb at the ground and disappeared. The fact this little story can happen so spontaneously- making friends with orcs, ambushing enemies, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s popping in for revenge- makes this game so magical. Finally a game where your stories are actually unique. No one else has to deal with the orcs I deal with on a daily basis. It is such a one of a kind experience. I highly recommend it.
Also, if you do get it, play it on the Nemesis difficulty- the normal difficulty might be a bit too easy if you're coming straight from the first game and you have some practice.

EDIT: I was very excited to play this game, hoping that Hanger 13 would manage to replicate the authentic settings of Mafia 2.
Firstly, some of the trailers are particularly misleading. For example, at no point do you ever get to see the Underbosses in action. The entire game they are combined to interiors or only communicated to via phonecalls.
Alongside this, unlike the previous games, the police have received a major downgrade. Police no longer notice speeding or running red lights. On top of this they no longer have a measured response to crimes. If you were to accidentally rear end another car within site of a police officer, he won't try to fine you as in Mafia 2 but will try to kill you.
The game however does have an interesting storytelling method, splitting up the narrative between present day and showing interviews with key characters but in the future documentary style. This was commendable and kept things a little bit interesting. Story wise however the plot was fairly weak. The game quickly descends from what I thought it would be about (Building up The Black Mob in the south) to a very generic revenge/punisher type story. There are vague connotations of a moral crisis towards the end, however by this stage you simply don't care enough about the game/characters to care enough. The only people that really mattered were Vito Scalleta (due to Mafia 2) and John Donovan (Who likely should have his own spinoff game).
I must say though, the game does have an amazing soundtrack but despite this there are simply too many amaterish flaws for me to be able to recommend this game. Numerous glitches, crash to desktop, multiple copies of characters appearing in scenes, graphics/physics glitches, the sky highlight a troubled development or at least lack of testing. Many aspects of the game show poor game design, from the poor UI, repetitive missions, a journal that requires you to go through each entry in order and lazy implementation of features. Gun shops and a parking garage have been removed in favour of a button that you can press that lets you summon a helper to retrieve any vehicle you own immediately. You have your own personal weapon shop in a van that will appear within 4 seconds also. I just don't understand why? This lead to me not caring about vehicles and weapons as I could summon them at will, losing a car or damaging it doesn't matter as you can summon a replacement immediately for free.
There are a huge amount of collectibles in this game in the form of Playboy Magazines, Vargas Paintings, Album Covers, Hot Rod Magazines and Fuses. However, I didn't realise until too late that there basically isn't any point in collecting them. Having done so, there is neither an achievement to highlight you've done so nor is there any in game benefit to doing so (apart from the fuses which are required for hacking). I personally just don't understand why they wouldn't at the very least put an achievement for such a thing.
Lincoln Clay's backstory I also felt was weakly used. As in Mafia 2 he is a military veteren, this time from the Vietnam war. However, the game at no point really capatalises on this, missing potential to highlight how damaging war can be on the individual. At certain points it would've made sense to make the use of flashbacks or hallucinations to show and sympathise with PTSD and I kept expecting this to come up in vain.
I could go on, there are simply so many issues with this game that I cannot recommend picking it up. Sure, borrow it off a friend but at this current time unless something dramatic happens I cannot recommend it.
p.s. I have played for quite a few hours mainly as I'm a bit of a completionist. I also wasted a lot of time collecting those fuses.

Why is this game so cheap? Why is the game play so visually smooth? Why is the combat so neat? Why is it only 7 out of 10?
In short. The game is a great smooth addition to monoliths market. However, in short the game is repetitive and the story and environment isn't captivating enough to maintain an audience. Why do people never finish the storyline in most cases or reach end game. Yes the loot box cash shop style marketing is toxic but ultimately the game ends up failing on its sales pitch. It designed a dynamic interesting Nemesis system that ultimately ends up being repetitive and boring. Most players tap out after the first 3-4 maps. The storyline also brings you to a world of characters which you ultimately don't draw the strongest relationship to. As an undead human you are akin to being an outside where you belong no where and hold no deep relationships with anyone.
Leaving this game I found myself feeling unsettled. It was clearly a AAA clean game with great elements and yet I feel like there was nothing that really jumped out at me. The Nemesis system was definitely fun for awhile though it's neat seeing the orc interactions but ultimately it just turns into a babbling talk fest of scripted NPC dialog.

Didn't know much about this game going in, and I enjoyed it, although I'm on the fence about whether or not it was fully worth the price tag. (I paid $8.something, on sale from $10). Depends on if you're a fan of the genre more than anything I think.
Personally I like supporting indie devs and am willing to try something different, but this game is pretty much cookie-cutter in every way.
Combat is entertaining enough on normal and above and gets better with upgrades; easy is pretty painless once you learn the enemy rotations and can dodge effectively. If you're not good at this style of game, start on easy, buy some upgrades, and upon completion of the game you can go through again on a harder difficulty while keeping skills. New Game +, more or less.
It took me just under an hour to complete the 5 stages on easy, so it's hard not to view this game as more of a tech demo than full game, but it does have replay value if you care about unlocking the extra costumes and maxing out upgrades.
Highly recommend controller, camera is not controlled with mouse-look and I find it unintuitive with KB/Mouse.
Graphics are simple but get the job done, not much enemy varience and the limited FOV bothers me, but again, it works.
I also enjoyed the background music. Only 5 different tracks (one for each stage), but it was fun slicing up enemies to it.
Final words. For $8, I'm not upset and I've enjoyed a couple hours of play. Probably won't bother for completion of everything, but at that price it's cheaper than going to the movies. I'd say there's enough value to warrant a purchase unless you don't find slicing up waves of enemies to be appealing. Just don't go in expecting a Devil May Cry or Bayonetta caliber game. It's not. No exploration, just fighting.

Pros:
Thoughtful, weighty combat
Eerie, atmospheric music
Interesting use of light and line of sight as a gameplay mechanic
Well designed bosses and general enemies
Doesn't hold your hand - allows you to discover mechanics and preferred playstyles for yourself
Cons:
Simplistic art style
Awkward controls
Frequent crashes
Friendly AI often bugs out, sometimes with frustrating consequences
Possible to miss important items early on, making the game much more difficult
DarkMaus is an interesting, generally well made top down RPG which takes clear inspiration from Dark Souls, though it has enough unique and interesting mechanics to hold the player's attention. It may not be as long as a Souls game, but this means that it doesn't outstay its welcome and, overall, is a very good experience for the pricetag.
However, there are a few isues I have with the game and, given the fact that the dev is known to respond to feedback, I feel that they should be pointed out.
A lot of people, including Dark Souls veterans, seem to find this game too difficult in all the wrong ways. I disagree. I feel that a lot of the negative reviews for this game came out of the fact that the players missed a near-essential item that allows for friendly ghosts to spawn and help you in combat. There are three of these items (that I know of) in the game and, without them, the game would have been much harder. These items are found in areas you have no reason to go back to - if you don't find them, then you are going to be at a disadvantage for the rest of the game.
Friendly AI is appalling. I am referring specifically to an NPC who will accompany you later in the game (but also to the ghosts to a lesser degree). He will walk into spikes, get stuck in doorways, blunder into traps, agro onto enemies we have no chance of defeating, and, on one occasion, he couldn't get through a doorway, on the other side of which there was an archer. He blocked the entire passage, so I couldn't get through to kill the archer. He wouldn't de-agro from the archer, no matter what I did. I had to go around the long way ariund (emphasis on long) and kill the archer from behind, by which point my ally had died and required a precious healing item in order to be revived.
One more problem I have is rather contradictory to the common concensus - I believe that there are too many healing items. By the end of the game I was sitting on a large stockpile of morsels and I was able to cheese the final boss by killing his three minions and then simply mashing quick attack while eating them. I never even needed to use medium or large morsels in the entire game - the number of small morsels I had was a great plenty. This was also taking into account how many morsels Destrian devoured in order to get through the fortress of traps which, as it turns out, he never needed to go through in the first place. It just wasn't properly explained what I was supposed to do when I rescued him. I had assumed that he would unlock a door in the fortress for me but this wasn't the case.
Weapon balance seems a little bit strange - it appears to me that if you aren't using a katana and shield as well as having some skill at pyromancy then you are just doing it wrong. Maybe it's just my personal preferred playstyle, but I can't imagine playing without a shield, a quick sweeping attack provided by the katana, and the ability to throw shield-ignoring fireballs if necessary.
Regardless of these issues, I believe DarkMaus is a fantastic game and it is well worth the price. If you are a Souls fan, you would be doing yourself a disservice if you did not play it.

Dark Souls significantly harder cousin.
The game plays like a 2d top-down Dark Souls Clone that mantains enough of its own unique characters and gameplay to stand out.
The game has charm, though that being said it is mercilessly hard to the point that it takes away from full enjoyment of the game.
To counter this you have "Ghosts" that appear to assist you whenever you die (up to a maximum of tokens in the game you find).  The Ghosts fight just as you do and follow your most recent path and actions independantly unless you invest in abilities to have them join you as assistants.
The game uses "Marrow" instead of "Souls" to upgrade your character, though expect to lose them frequently so spend asap.
The Games Camera is prone to shifting as you enter new areas or rooms which can disorient the player or in my case actually make me nauseous once.
The game does carry one serious flaw ripped directly from Dark Souls and turned into nothing more than padding that nearly lead me to give it a negative review.
Hunters.  Yes, Hunters.  Evil Ghosts that hunt you down like red Phantoms eager to kill you and rob you instantly of everything you've worked for while also slicing your maximum hp in half for a minimum of 10-20 minutes.
While the reward for killing one is a substantial increase in Marrow.  The sudden inconvenient appearance of these overpowered and crippling enemies that rob you of ALL your Marrow regardless of how you die including via other enemies gives the game artificial and inconveneint padding to extend playtime as you hobble around crippled waiting for your hp to return to its potential max.
I wound up spending half the game walking around in circles praying I wouldn't be invaded by another random hunter before my HP returned so I could continue playing.
Were this in some way optional or avoidable it would be of no concern to me, but it isn't.
Overall a wonderful Game for those who enjoy challenge and masochistic level design with good gameplay dashed in for spice.
For its price it is a good game but do NOT buy this game if you seek a casual fun experience.   7/10

I would certainly have considered Neutral if the option were available, but I went from Loving this to Hating and Resenting it. This COULD have been a classic if they had kept it as a Short Horror story but they just couldn't do that apparently.  I will keep this review Short and Sweet
The Good -
First and Formost this is Not a Call Of Duty clone  HOOOORAAAYYYYY!!!!!

Dont listen to blind Fallout 1-2 fanboys who tell you its a good game, its not! You will be bored and annoyed to death in 1st 30 minutes, and most likely rage quit this abomination before you hit 60 minutes! It feels like boring table\board game which poorly imitates video game. Conventionalities of gameplay (when you have to pretend that something unrealistic and simplified is actually happening), overcomplicated UI, clunky turn-based combat and lack of tutorial of how to use it all, reminds me why i never liked Fallout 1-2. It just does not feel like video game,  This game feels like it came from mid 90th, in a bad meaning of this word, since it brings up back everything that was wrong in 90th, but back in 80th it was  acceptable since tech was not that good to show everything the way devs really wanted to, but nowadays it just feels cheap and lazy, even in 90th it already did.
Some crazy Fallout 1-2 purists and board RPG nerds may enjoy this, but i dont - when i play video games i want to go way beyond board game limitations, i want to see more realistic and real time gameplay, i want to have immersive expirience where i can forget its a video game and feel like its something real (i can do it in games like SOMA, Splinter Cell Chaos Theory, Chronicles of Riddick, Thief, FInal Fantays 7 despite its blocky graphics and lack of voiceover, even recent XCOM feels more immersive than this, despite its turn based just like this game) .
if i would want to play board game i would play a board game, not a board game that pretends to be video game.
Also, dont get me wrong, sometimes board style of game and turn based combat could be good - look at recent XCOM games  for example, they managed to keep old school core mechanics, yet simplified UI, made good tutorial, even made gamepad controls and good graphics, and in general Firaxis made XCOM feel more like video game and it was enjoyable expirience. Usually im against simplifications, but this genre really needs it, because without simplification of UI and controls it just clunky, overloaded trainwreck. Broken age is a game with a great set up with little to no pay-off. If the game had carried the awesome aspects of Act 1 into  Act 2 I wouldn't be so disappointed.
First we can talk a bit about Act 1 before I highlight some issues with the overall game. Act 1 is a great level of storytelling, put into beautiful and creative environments. I honestly couldn't stop playing throughout Act 1 just to see what would happen next. Vella and shay's stories both had me wondering how they could possibly be connected and what this world was like. The puzzles were also creative and mostly made logical sense.
Unfortunately as other reviews have said, this falls apart in Act 2. Act 2 feels rushed and unimaginative at best. Very few of the actual plot points are answered adequately, if they are answered at all. Most of them are answered in a very short dialogue with Marek, in which he vaguely hints about the reasons for their actions. This seems like Double Fine came up with the initial concept, then just slapped the first idea for an ending on it and called it a day. This however is only a minor flaw in comparsion to the puzzles within Act 2.
The puzzles in Act 2 are riduculous, obtuse and lazy. It is almost impossible to solve the puzzles without having some sort of guide to show you what you need to do. Many puzzles in Act 2 give 0 hints on what you need to do and don't seem to have any reason behind them. I was only able to complete the game by using a guide and even then I thought they were frustrating and dumb. The puzzles also seem to go against or have no basis in the characters motivations. Often it doesn't seem like the characters have any reason or understanding of why they are doing these actions or the goal they are trying to accomplish. This just gets worse as you near the ending of the game.
The last section of the game make no sense in terms of the plot or in the way you accomplish puzzles. You need to get both characters to do independant actions that they would seemingly have no actual reason to do. It doesn't help that part of these actions is distracting the competant characters so that your characters can complete the game.
If the game had an actual ending that left the player satisfied rather then frustrated, this could have been a great game. Unfortunatly because of what seems like a phoned in ending it takes what could have been a 5 star game to 2 to 2.5.
If you can get this game for really cheap and you are really into point and click adventure games, then its an alright buy. however, at the current full price of $27.99 CDN I can not recommend it.

Dysfunctional Systems is a graphic novel game that tells its story and involves the gamer in a story that plays out via text and images.
You are Winter Harrison, a 14-year-old girl from a utopian world who serves as an interplanar mediator.  She finds herself in Sule, a world entering into conflict that she and her mentor, Cyrus, must help resolve.
If you're new to graphic novel games, the pacing is slow and story-driven.  As these games go, Dysfunctional Systems' episode 1 is a short, simple introduction to the story that, though somewhat involving in its events, leaves the player left short-changed on any real development of character or story.
Even so, if you have the money to spare on something you know is incomplete, this game is a small treat that can, in some ways, make up for its brevity.
While this episode has a promising start to something that could be interesting, it seems unclear whether or not there will be additional episodes following this one.
Options can be accessed before the game begins, allowing you control of game settings.  Music and sound volume are controlled separately and can be muted altogether.
The game plays out over text boxes.  Text speed, textbox opacity and color, and the ability to skip text are all available options, giving gamers control over the pace of the game.
Dysfunctional Systems is captioned completely from beginning to end and the story plays out in text, which does not advance until the gamer decides to do so.
Captions include the speaker's name and quotes for directly spoken text.  Narrated text is provided without quotes and a name, so I assume it's the main character (Winter) thinking or addressing the gamer directly.
The game's captions are very true to spoken word, so any deaf/hoh who do not frequently use English to communicate may find it tedious at times.
Dysfunctional Systems is a single player game; no communication/chatting options available.

In Fallout Shelter you play the Overseer of a Fallout vault. It is a casual F2P game with waiting mechanics. In theory it uses the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t design philosophy in existence. And yet it is very pleasant and enjoyable:
- It is full of character - visually and thematically everything is tied to the Fallout universe in an excellent way
- It does something similar to X-COM - you have vault dwellers with their attributes, looks, outfits, weapons. These things make each dweller somehow unique. You will develop empathic connection to your dwellers. You will know them. You will feel remorse if they die permanently. This is immensely cool
- It is completely playable without spending cash
- Unlike other F2P games, this one is not completely “in your face” about spending money, it does not have the feeling about “this is all about money”. It is fair and does not feel unethically exploitative of the player
Fallout Shelter a good case study if you want to understand what people find in ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile or facebook games without subjecting yourself to torture.
If you are not cool with the waiting mechanics, now the really cool stuff - no DRM. This means on PC you can disable your internet connection and change your clock. So the game thinks time have passed. No more waiting mechanics. On one of my playthroughs I played 5 months worth of gameplay in 5 days and it was ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.

Good Plot, Addictive Gameplay, and Fantastic Atmosphere are the three things that most describe this game. Hotline Miami follows the actions of a silent protaganist (known only as "Jacket") who is being blackmailed into commiting mass murders by an unknown group of callers. The actual gameplay consists of a top-down shooter and beat 'em up style game, with multiple weapons and masks (the latter of which grant the player special abilities that they can utilize in combat) at the players disposal. Despite being fairly challenging, it makes for fun and often exciting gameplay. One of the most notable aspects of the game is the way that it really nails that kind of "80's action movie" feel. The way the world (characters, buildings, ect.) looks all add together for a nice atmosphere. It's also packed full of great songs that really match the mood of the game. My only complaint was that, if you really get into it, the game can be finished fairly quickly. However, that doesn't really affect my opinion of the game too much as it is alltogether just too good to have something so little upset me. I give the game an overall rating of 9.5/10, and would definetly recommend it to anyone who's looking for a challenging, violent, and action packed game.

8/10: Violent, twitchy mayhem brought on by cryptic phone calls and madness, built on a foundation filled with nationalist conspiracies and dripping with flourescent, 80's era vibrancy.
Right from the start, things in Hotline Miami are surreal and disorienting. Animal-masked entities speak in riddles and prophecy, while strange calls compel one to venture to the provided addresses and provide the Russian gangsters there with a whole lot of ultraviolence.
What ensues is a game of hectic murder sprees interspersed with a sense of descent into delusion. Different animal masks grant different bonuses, allowing a subtly different experience depending on the level. Switching between weapons and executions, trying to keep the kill combo going in order to maximize the points you get in the end, results in a game where death is a regularity and success is gauged by how quickly and creatively you can manage to wipe out a floors worth of people.
The only way to get an idea of what's causing all of this is to find the letter tiles scattered among the letters and decode the puzzle. Thankfully, the game lets you know if the level contains an unlockable mask or tile, and the puzzle letters glow if they are placed in the right slot, so anyone can eventually figure it out.
All in all, an action packed rampage with an uneasy, late 80's vibe, Hotline Miami is great fun for anyone who is fond of the Rampage challenges found in the original two Grand Theft Auto games.

Ok so I'm going to give it a thumbs up because there are many things good about the game... but there are also a few bad things that the careful reader must be mindful of when purchasing this game.
Positives:
The atmosphere is created very nicely by the dark and light tones.  It really gives you a good sense that the world is in despair and chaos.
This is a game that rewards you for skillfully mastering the level.  You cannot simply bulldoze your enemies or just walk through levels hoping for the best.
The enemies have their own strengths and weaknesses for you to figure out and you must use the best weapon or combo against them.  For example I was able to beat a certain creature by only using a curved blade for its fast attacks and moving around in a circle close to the body of an enemy to avoid their attacks.
Which brings me to my next positive point that all battles are interesting and different outcomes can and will happen even if you have to do it over again and again.
This game was inspired by dark souls and was well designed to test you at every step of the way.
Negatives:
This game was inspired by dark souls and so get ready for a frustrating difficult ride.  I list this on the positive and negative side because it is worth noting that if you like a real challenge than this game is for you. If you like fun casual games steer very far and clear away from this game.
The controls are slightly difficult at first to get used to even if you use an xbox controller (which it was designed for).  I wish there was a way to map what you want for yourself or have more default configurations to choose from.
Since you will die a lot, the story is difficult to get into.  After 10 hours of play, the only thing I understand is to save (I forget what the mouse's name)'s father from somewhere (I forget where because He wasn't in the prison and it took me hours to get through that part).
TLDR:  Get ready to work for it.  This is a rewarding game for those who are wishing a real challenge from their video games.   Steer clear of this game if you are not a hardcore masochist who needs to be punished for even the smallest mistakes.

This game is a hack and slash game set in arenas as opposed to stages like other games such as Ninja Gaiden or Metal Gear Rising. This doesn't mean that the game is worth any less when compared to them, especially considering this is an independent game whose staff consists of three developers, a musician and two voice actresses for its original Japanese release.
You attack by using hand to hand combat for charging the sword gauge, using the sword and a quick draw blade attack. Once enough damage has been dealt to the enemies, they will begin glowing red, which means they're wounded. Unlike other games of this genre, MHK has a move in which the protagonist, Misa, sheathes her sword and all wounded enemies sustain damage as she draws orbs for upgrade points (currency) and for healing herself. Moves like guarding are also available, with the possibility to counter with the sword and a special parry called "Flourish," which deals a large amount of damage.
Upgrade points are, as their name implies, used to strengthen Misa's parameters like health and the sword gauge. Her moves can also be upgraded for dealing more damage, better range and mobility.
The playability of the game compares to the bigger franchises, which is always good. Replayability is key when trying to unlock and upgrade all of Misa's skills and new to the Steam version, unlocking two of her costumes.
While the game is optimally played with a controller, keyboard controls are also available (no mouse support, though). Everything can be mapped to the user's liking.
For the asking price and the amount of hours of fun it represents, this indie game quite a bargain.

I had high hopes going into Alan Wake, it being recommended after completing the Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and now that I’ve finished my first run through I’m a bit disappointed.
In Alan Wake you play as Alan, a writer confronting a “darkness” with your trusty flashlight to guide the way.  It’s an episodic/narrative type game, not to be confused with Telltale games where you barely get to move around – in Alan Wake you do have combat, driving, and most things you’d expect from a normal video game.
My first run through of the story, including the two DLC episodes only took 11 hours.  Each of the main 6 episodes take about 1.5 hours to complete.  While other reviewers are praising the story, I just couldn’t get into it.  The writing and voice acting were excellent, and there were some very good parts, however the story never drew me in, mainly due to Alan Wake’s many faults and the general premise of a writer or artists impact on the supernatural.
To the main drawback - the gameplay itself was frustrating.  The camera view alone, being force on a “over the shoulder” experience didn’t fit with the play style.  Sprint in the game became a joke, forced into a perpetual reminder of how they could have done soooo much better.  If you sprint for too long (5 seconds?) you basically stop in your tracks to catch your breath – terrible for escaping enemies.  The main drawback is the gameplay is extremely repetitive.  Walk, trigger a scene, use flashlight to stop darkness, shoot, and repeat.  It’s the same cycle throughout the entire game.  When a boss fight, or a major skirmish does happen, they all unfold in predictably the same ways, with the same waves of enemies, which you combat in exactly the same method.
As mentioned before, the DLC consists of two episodes which continues the main storyline, but not in any meaningful way, and there is no multiplayer which is a good thing.  Graphically the game is fine, in line with the times, but nothing spectacular.  The graphical rendering between gameplay and cut scenes is obvious and they could have done a better job smoothing it out or rendering the cut scenes with actual gameplay.
With the lack of a gripping story, and lack luster and frustrating mechanics, finally nailed by the repetitiveness, this isn’t going to be a recommendation.  However, just like with books there are some good and some bad, but either way when you’re reading it you enjoy it slightly…. that is kind of how this was.  I still had fun playing it, just didn’t leave a good aftertaste.
4 out of 10. Just can’t recommend it.

DarkMaus is a Dark Souls inspired game about mice in a doomed land. The theme of desperation and futility is very apparent. Unlike Dark Souls, this game presents itself in a shaded black and tan art-style that works very nicely with the light mechanics.
This game is hard, or at least it was for me. Enemies are far more agressive than the hollows of Dark Souls. They'll attempt to swarm you, they'll charge you when you're at your weakest. For example, an early enemy you encounter will dodge back out of your sword swings, then attempt to get behind you in a swarm. Some enemies will charge you if you attempt to turn tail and run away. Because of this, you are forced to play either very defensively OR hyperaggressively with shock-and-awe tactics.
The game gives you a varitey of weapons, including spears, swords, bows, and pyromancy, though, some of them feel like direct upgrades of each other. This is a bit weird, considering DarkMaus has a weapon upgrading system where you invest resources you find in the enviroment to increase your weapon's stats. This can lead you to feel a bit cheated. Depsite this, most weapons have something they excel at, so as long as you like the mechanics of the weapon, it should be viable till the end.
Light seems to have a bit of usefulness in DarkMaus. It isn't very apparent at first, but your torch has a lifespan and must be replenished at a campfire. Light reveals enemies farther away from your character, and I believe it also shows the stamina and health of the enemy (I might be mistaken). When the torch burns out, you won't be able to see enemies until you got close enough to aggro them. The light mechanic doesn't seem to be too much of an issue, as I rarely had a torch burn out on me.
The biggest departure from Dark Souls is it's ghost mechanics. In racing games, a ghost is a copy of yourself that appears when you finish a lap. It is common in racing games to compete against your ghost, as it is a visual representation of your time on the track.
In DarkMaus, after you aquire a certain item, you gain the ability to spawn ghosts. When you die, you respawn with a friendly ghost(s) who will aid you in your battles. I believe the ghosts have a mind of their own and will attempt to relive your death, meaning they will charge at the enemies that slayed you previously. I might be misinturpreting their actions; however, there are additional abilites that make the ghosts follow you more closely with additional health. I found myself with an entourage of mouse ghosts during the more difficult sections. Unfortunatly, these ghosts can not follow you into boss arenas.
At times, you will also have an NPC with you. Their usefulness is questionable. They require a scarce healing item if they become wounded, and they are very suseptible to friendly fire. Their biggest benifit is that they can enter boss arenas, and there is some cool stuff with the story, but I won't get into that.
Overall, I enjoyed this game. It took me about seven hours to beat it once, and there is a New Game Plus that has harder enemies and a few new weapons.
I recommend this game to Dark Souls fans. It also has cute mice in it.

'Alan wake is such an underrated game', is what I heard a lot before I decided to play this game. So is it actually an underrated gem, or simply average at best? After playing through it twice and collecting way too much collectibles (a grant total of 298, not taking the DLC into account), I think I can give you a clear view of what the game is like.
Wether or not it's a hidden gem for you depends on what you are actually looking for in a game. If it's raw action you seek, you will probably be disappointed. If it's a scary horror experience, you'll probably end up with the same experience. Then what is this game? The best description will probably be a story-based thriller, if that's even a genre for a game.
How does it run, you ask? I can't really help you with that. The only thing I can say is that it run well on a pretty slow system (read: my laptop :p). And if it ran smoothly on that old toaster, I'm pretty sure it will run nicely on your *whateveryouhave* aswell.
To be honest I have no idea what the controls with mouse and keyboard are like. I've read somewhere that they are bit clunky, but than can also be said about the way the controls work on a controller, even though it's a xbox port. After a while you'll get used to it though, although I must say that the actually car controls are pretty horrible. Luckily, you don't have to deal with that for an extreme long amount of time.
As I said before, gameplaywise Alan Wake isn't the strongest of games. It's actual description as a horrorgame doesn't fit what it actually is like. Sure, you have some horror-aspects, but does that alone make a horrorgame? No. Especially because those aspects don't evolve during your playthrough. You'll get used to the dark atmosphere of grey fog blowing all over the place. Your first hour, maybe two hours, can be scary because of that, but after that you get used to it.
The actually gunplay feels somewhat unique, since you need to shine your flashlight for a certain amount of time at the enemies before they can be hurt. However, this type of combat becomes very repetitive after a while, which is the biggest problem Alan Wake has from preventing it to be a brilliant game. But what makes it that people think it's still a hidden gem then?
It's very simple: the story of this game. The story of this game is simply brilliant. The big difference between a lot of games nowadays and this game is that most of those have a story that's serving the gameplay. For Alan Wake it's the opposite (although I think the story is exactly long enough to kepp the gameplay somewhat interesting). The story is unique, and not only that, it's also presented in a unique way. Aside from the main character giving you his thoughts about the situation, you also get to collect pages of the story you're experiencing. That way you can sometimes read what will come in your path, which is very unique.
Even though the story does feel a bitlackluster at the beginning of the game, it will be compensated big time when you hit a certain point in the game. It pretty much needs to 'warm-up'.
Since there's is a bundel with DLC along with this game, I figure I'll add a small review about the DLC aswell. Both are short and sweet, giving more of a challenge in the gameplay than the actual game. They add some new features to the gameplay, although the main concept stays the same (of course). The biggest role the DLC plays is extending the story, giving new insights. Both the DLC will take aroung 2-3 hours to complete, depending on how completely you want to scout the areas.
So, is Alan wake a hidden gem? Still depends on what you seek in a game. It has both strenghts and weaknesses. Gameplaywise the game gets repetitive quite quickly, although the story is the thing that keeps the game running. I can't tell you wether or not you'll like this game, since I can't see what type of gamer you are. What I can say is that I, as someone who loves getting into a good story, really enjoyed this game, even to the point where I declared it one of my favorites. To me, it was most definitely a hidden gem.

Let me preface this by saying that I really, really enjoyed Dysfunctional Systems. However, I cannot in good conscience recommend this for many people. Let me explain.
Firstly, what I did like about Dysfunctional Systems. While very short, the story is extremely compelling in terms of the writing, and especially the premise, which is very unique and one of my favorite aspects. The interface is very slick and polished, and the art and character design is fantastic. I absolubtely loved my short romp through the world(s) of Dysfunctional Systems, and I sincerely wish I could spend more time in that world.
Unfortunately, this brings me to why I ultimately cannot recommend Dysfunctional Systems despite its fantastic setting, storywriting, and art direction. Dysfunctional Systems was originally created with the intent of being a 3 episode series, which was funded through kickstarter. However, Dischan, the creators of Dysfunctional Systems have confirmed the cancellation of the release of the next installment of Dysfunctional Systems, and have put the entire series on indefinite hiatus, and most likely permanent cancellation.
I cannot recommend Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos because the entire VN was clearly centered around the notion that it fit into a greater story, and the endings of Learning to Manage Chaos are clearly structered around this assumption. While Learning to Manage Chaos is a great story for what it is, it does not work very well as a standalone story.
If you are willing to play what was suppossed to be the opening for a greater story, then go ahead and get Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos. If you feel like you will be dissapointed by the notion the story is incomplete, then please avoid this title.
It's a pity really because I really did like the premise and setting of Dysfunctional Systems.

Alan Wake is a good test of how important you find gameplay in video games. Essentially, Alan Wake is a cool episodicallly presented story about a man doing everything he can to find his spouse. It's strong narratively, and the presenation of rural northwestern America is pretty spot on. Voice acting is good, and by the end of the story you'll be wanting to jump on the DLC for the next chapter just to see where it goes.
Unfortunately, Alan Wake has serious issues in terms of gameplay. Don't get me wrong; it
, it's just that you essentially do the same sort of survival gameplay (stop the darkness by blinding it with light) through the whole game. The game's combat sequences are almost all the same, with nearly identical enemies defeated in identical ways. It's a solidly long game too; my game time as of this review (~15 hours) is the equivalent of one playthrough.
In other words, Alan Wake is extremely repetitive. This is why it's a good test of how much you really care for a game's narrative. If you love strong stories in video games and are fine with repetitive gameplay, this will be a blast. If you came here looking for invigorating gameplay, it isn't happening.
In short, I can't recommend this game if you can't handle repetitive gameplay. If you can, then buy this game. It's a great story everyone deserves to see.

Once you're in the game itself, the UI is really messy, not clear at all, there's a lot of elements on the screen, and the game never explains what each thing is for. Combat is ok, I guess, being a fan of turn-based strategy games, but for some reason I had 4 healers in my party and no offensive skills and I ended up quitting out of how confusing everything was.
I would not reccomend this game to anybody who hasn't played it before, or anyone who, like me, doesn't have the time to research the game outside of it, but if you do purchase it, I reccomend you do a little bit of external online research before starting to play.

This game is such an excellent example of what can be done with current tech for the timeless point and click genre. The visuals are bold, bright, and colorful, and I love how they achieved an illustrative effect for an interactive game. The voice acting is superb, and I loved hearing actors I love as hilarious characters. The story is so fun, it has funny and heavy moments, and they did a good job of executing a story with complex elements and character development. It was great to have such unique and brave male and female characters, with a story that touched on very 'human' elements.
My only criticisms would be: (1) at times, the puzzles veer into being too simple or too abstract, which can make for a frustrating problem that limits player brainstorming (hate being forced to check online for hints, it suspends the story), and (2) the second part of the game loses a lot of its wonder and becomes a bit monotonous. It's still an excellent and enjoyable story and I have shared it with eager players. Those problems just feel a bit disappointing for an otherwise fantastic game. I would still recommend giving it a try, and the sale price is definitely worth it!

TL;DR: Since the developer has abandoned the project and the remaining episodes will not be made/released in the foreseeable future I wouldn't spend your money on this. Its story is incomplete and will probably never be completed. In the end by paying $5 for this you'll have 1.5 hours of prologue that is, in itself, not nearly enough to leave you satisfied.
Update: As of July 14th, 2015 Dischan Media has officially shut down. Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos will not be reinvigorated.

Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel about, as the title inclines, the managing of chaos. The premise of dysfunctional systems revolves around an organisation in some technological utopia that sends meddlers to other worlds to solve their problems and reclaim order. It's an interesting concept, but it's not too different from what we've seen before. That said, it doesn't mean dysfunctional systems has no potential, in fact it has loads of potential. Too bad none of that really matters.
The story is basically an introduction to the universe and it's characters. We get to see the main characters do their jobs as meddlers in a world that is having diplomatic problems. Things escalate, I won't spoil anything, I'll just say that: it's way too short to develop anything outside of a prologue to the other episodes. Yes, there is a story in it, no you're probably not going to cry over it. It isn't insanely good and it isn't bad. At best this will leave you wanting more, where the problem of an abandoned project reels in again.
Even if an incomplete story wouldn't bother you, this first episode leaves too much to be desired and too many questions to be asked. The game is way too short to accomplish any real world building, something that is so important when your game is literally about travelling and meddling in the affairs of other worlds.
The characters, focusing on the two main ones, consist of your basic grumpy teacher and stubborn student. That's not to say the characters aren't enjoyable or not well written, they share some funny and touching moments. It's just that the game is simply way too short to develop any character properly. Thus we are left with... again, nothing special.
Then there are the choices, which are very important to get right when you make something in this medium. It is unfortunately something dysfunctional functions had a serious lack of. The entire game basically has 1 choice. 1 choice in the entire thing. After this one choice dysfunctional systems might (depending on what you choose) present you 2-or so more rather confusing choices.
The only difference is that you'll be getting a different achievement.
Something I can praise dysfunctional systems about is it's amazing art and music.
The art, although perhaps a bit repetitive at times, looks amazing, there isn't a whole lot of animation but that's alright, in the end I wasn't expecting there to be any. The UI is really good, everything fits together nicely and I actually enjoyed reading the few codex entries there were, as bland as they may be. As for the music, it was very nicely done. You won't have the same track looping every other sequence or anything like that here. Good stuff, Ill probably end up listening to it more in the future.
After all that I do feel the need to honestly say that Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos is not a bad visual novel at all, at least, as a prologue. Sure, it doesn't hit all the good spots and the lack of choices is pretty disappointing. But that doesn't mean it's necessarily bad. It does it's job as a prologue - it gets you excited for more whilst giving a basic introduction of the universe.
The real reason you shouldn't buy this is because the developer abandoned the two sequels that were originally planned. Reason? Financial problems and a lack of motivation. The development team did a poor job of financing the funds received from the kickstarter campaign. People have lost a lot of their trust for the developers, and righteously so, it was one big mistake after another for the dev team and the death of Dysfunctional Systems as a result of that. It's a real shame, I would have liked to see more from this.
So, in the end Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos gives us a 1.5 hour prologue of a story that will probably never be made. Whether you are willing to spend $5 on that is your choice, but I personally wouldn't recommend it.

This is a story game. Like a choose your own adventure, except without the "choose" bit.

Now, on with the review.
Broken Age is a point & click adventure game developed by Double Fine and designed by the now legendary Tim Schafer, known by his previous works such as Grim Fandango, Full Throttle and Psychonauts. The game tells the story of two teenagers, Shay and Vella, both looking to break the monotony and tradition of their lives. The game is split into two acts, which were released a year apart.
The first thing that stands out is the voice acting, which is no surprise. Elijah Wood, Wil Wheaton and Jennifer Hale are among the lead roles so you'd expect a good performance from them. But, it doesn't end there. Each and every single one of the side characters is voiced superbly well which all adds to the immersion and believability of the world.
The art style is  beautiful, having a "children's picture book" look to it. The animations that go along with it are expertly done as well. All of the character movements are fluid and none of them feel awkward or out of place, they all work well with the amazingly drawn and animated backgrounds.
The soundtrack fits the game well, it's a joy to listen to while playing.
Despite puzzles being one of the main complaints people have with the game, I think that they don't bring the game down to the point of not recommending it. The puzzles in Act 1 are a bit too simple but at the same time they are logical and well designed, while the puzzles in Act 2 are more challenging,  they have a glaring, immersion-breaking design flaw and are therefore less logical, which might leave you feeling stumped more often than you should be. Once you get used to it after the first time though, it should be smooth sailing for the most part. The puzzles in Act 1 serve the story more, but managing to beat the puzzles in Act 2 feels more satisfying.
The story is interesting, and I was stunned by how well it was told in Act 1. It is truly perfect in its subtlety and execution. The dialogue is excellently written and it flows really well. There isn't a single bad character in the game, they all feel real and the dialogue makes them even more so. The immersion breaking flaw in Act 2 is what severely damages the subtlety and execution which made Act 1 so great. I'd even say that the finale may seem a bit rushed. There's also a few plot holes, but thankfully these don't ruin the experience nor damage the narrative, they just sour the moment in which they happen.
Broken Age is a very good game. Its production values such as the art style, animation and voice acting are among the best of the genre. The story is interesting, but its execution, subtlety and characters are its true strengths. Unfortunately, the first two suffer greatly during Act 2 due to a design flaw in the puzzles, but in turn the challenge is improved in contrast to the simple puzzles in Act 1. The ending, while good, leaves a bit to be desired and can feel slightly unsatisfying. It leaves some things up to the imagination, but it still menages to provide good closure.
I would recommend this game to all fans of the genre, and especially fans of Tim Schafer's previous works. Even if you don't like simple puzzles, Act 1 is worth going through for the story, while you get the challenge in Act 2 at the story's expense, and vice versa. Since the game is about 12-14 hours long , it might feel that there's not enough content to back up the $25 price tag, but its a steal at $10 or less.

So it took me ages to finally get to Broken Age(DoubleFine has burned me a billion times before, and I wasn't keen on playing through another unfinished hunk of crap) - but I sat down for it and while it admittedly took me a while to get into, it offered a robust and unique point-and-click experience with all the hallmarks that the bygone ages of Tim Schafer promised.  Weird and interesting artwork, wonderful voice acting, cute and childlike(which is different than childish) dialogue that's nice and chuckleworthy - but more than that, dialogue with *heart* - and a cast of weird characters that have no business working together to make an enjoyable experience, but somehow do.
The only gameplay gripe I had were the puzzles, especially in Act 2 - many of them were so arcane that they'd be nearly impossible to suss out without a walkthrough(which I admit being guilty of a few times).  Some of the puzzles are time based, meaning you literally had to sit around and wait for minutes at a time for an effect to occur - which is maddeningly frustrating especially when the rest of the puzzles are offer thing/payoff based.  Without that though, the dual-storyline system and how they interacted back and forth and switched horizons was really interesting and a fun take on a classic adventure system.
...HOWEVER.
No spoilers here, but... is Tim Schafer pathologically averse to writing endings?  Like Brutal Legend and the pantheon of other modern Schafer titles, this game just... ends.  Don't expect anything wrapped up, don't expect any explanations - if you're someone who thinks the gameplay is the point of playing, have at it.  But if you're someone who plays and expects a big payoff when you beat the game, you will almost certainly be sorely disappointed.  The world was so interesting, but there were so many loose ends left untied when it was over that it was almost heartbreaking.  For me, having a story based adventure game simply END is the most cardinal of sins.

I put off doing a review on this title for a long time. Not sure why, but I probably just forgot.
The RTS genre is dieing out, if it hasn't already. So instead of developers cranking out RTS games, we are starting to see a new trend of FPS-RTS hybrids. Nuclear Dawn is an example of this, and TF2 could have been the same way (see developer commentary). I used to be a big fan in many regards, but there just doesn't seem to be any good classics. EA over milking their acquired IP such as C&C has lead to disappointment, and reason as to why they were voted the worst company 3 times in a row.
Many describe Natural Selection 2 to be like Counter-Strike in many regards. It's true for the most part, as realism isn't the focus -- competitive play is. Updates seem regular enough to resolve problems which is nice to see.
While it's unfortunate that the developers scraped using the Source engine, it is certainly nice to see people try and release competing engines. One of the certain draw backs to releasing a custom built engine has to be the increased work of maintaining not only the engine but the game. After I don't know how many updates, the developers continue to ignore the hull sizes of models. Could it be caused by an oversight in development? Certainly, but for how long it's been with the game, it's ridiculous. When I refer to hull sizes, I'm talking about the collision "mesh" which detects where things can fit. The tanky alien unit "Onos" fails in this regard, being able to fit (and let alone jump) to places that don't make any logical sense. The outside parts of the model just pass through solid objects, which can really infuriate marine players.
Part of competitive play has to do with teamwork. While new fronts have been opened in regards to making the first time experience more inviting, some work needs to be done else where. Even with the dynamic loading of textures and models, it just takes way to long to load maps. Servers still seem to be single core based, so GSPs will not be jumping at it because server processors tend to be clocked lower.
While certainly pressing new ideas into the industry that lacks a lot, I wouldn't want to rush at this game.

Despite the fact that I haven't played the first two, this was a Day 1 purchase for me.
The Setting, Music and initial few hours were great. Cutscenes and voice acting were masterfully done and the driving is incredibly satisfying on 'Simluation Mode'. Overall, apart from the 30fps debacle, and glitchy AI aside, I was enjoying myself.
However, after the initial 'ooh new and shiny!' wore off, the cracks began to show.
The missions are painfully repetitive. One particular mission sequence took place in a Slaughterhouse. You visit the location and clear out the bad guys, only to have to return to that exact location later to finally off the boss (and, of course, all the previous bad guys were back) At the end of the mission, you choose whether to kill or recruit the boss.
That's bascially everything the game has to offer. Take the previous couple of sentences and repeat them with different locations and that's what you'll find yourself doing until the story is complete. Every 'kill' or 'recruit' option plays the exact same animation. There's just very little variety.
While I'd like to complete the story and see what happens at the conclusion, Mafia 3 seems too much like a chore right now and there's nothing there that's drawing me back.
Not recommended. At least for now.

This is a great sequel that offers some enjoyable changes and some less enjoyable changes, but the changes in which doesn't effect the game in a way that makes me like it any less so ill start off with my opinionated cons then go into my opinionated pros:
Major Game BREAKER: Game somtimes either perpetually loses its ability to save the game and reloads the same spot, or even worse your save will sometimes be erased for some unknown reason...
Cons:
- Implimented loot cases
- Cannot recruit orcs / warchiefs higher level than yourself
- Remapped some of the original ways you accomplished tasks
- Removed weapon runes system
- Never fixed the targeting to not beat up your own troops during battle
- Inverted button prompt
- added step in promoting a orc to a warchief (them killing the previous warchief isn't enough to promote them they have to do another duel in order to actually be promoted after the other one dies)
Reasoning: Loot cases are mostly always bad when they contain items that can make you stronger not only is it game breaking but it also takes away the point of playing through the game when you can pay for items that would make the rest of the game a breeze, plus i heard of some online elements between seiging other players which that could also be game breaking, i personally dont mess with online other than vandetta also heard they have some that can contain overpowered warchiefs to add to your army for online, not sure if this is rectified at the time of me writing this review or not. if i spend a lot of time or have a struggle battling a higher level orc and finally manage to tag him while nearly escaping death, i should be able to recruit them no matter what i shouldnt have to humilate and weaken them first then have to strengthen them back up thats completely dumb. i personally liked the rune perks. coming from the original shadow of mordor when trying to do things like interrogate or drain a warchief to recruit them you used to have to grab them to do it no exceptions, now you cant grab them and do it you just drain them instead, this got confusing and was a hard habit to break when first playing coming directly from shadow of mordor and being used to all the mechanics taught me on there. i dont like auto targeting my own allies in combat whats the use in having an army if you accidentally target them, beat them up and potentially kill them yourselves because the auto target system deems them as a better target than the enemy next to you. i have my left and right click on my mouse inverted so it gets confusing on a qte where i have to press the opposite mouse click than the one its prompting me to do.
Pros:
- Added cool drakes / dragons to ride on
- Orcs seem more lively and have personality to them
- Mount Stealth when on a carogor
- Leaping off the mount to stab an enemy was changed to L-shift + E
- ElfShot is no longer skill based and number of arrows is dependant on your equipped bow / hammer
- Graugs can climb
- Orc bodyguard system
- orcs have random commentary when traveling around with a bodyguard
- expanded skills further and added a new special wraith ability
- a few new warchief abilities
Theres probably more too that i cant think of comepletely at the moment of writing this and will probably remember at some point after im done writing this but the point being this is another great game in the series nonetheless speaking from a fully singleplayer experience without buying anything and the pros for the most part outweight the cons.

It is rare to see a game like this be this well done. Dust: An Elysian Tail was made by one man, and the game has the quality of that you see with teams of hundreds working passionately on a project.
The game itself is a 2D Sidescroller inspired heavily by games like Metroid and Castlevania. You will find yourself exploring a fairly large open world, looking for items, money, and powers which will allow you to explore areas that were locked to you before. The aesthetic style of this game is truly amazing as well. The use of varied colors really helps the world and its residents come to life in ways rarely seen in games today. I would find myself staying in areas long after I should have left just look at the visuals and marvel at how breathtaking the vistas are. While it is cartoony, it serves the game very well.
I would also travel the long way through areas, ignoring shortcuts I had opened, just to listen to the music. The music in this game is nothing short of spectacular, with each area having its own theme that sets it apart from the others, whether it be a mountain pass that screams for adventure, or the haunted remains of an old estate with creeping terrors around every turn, the music sets the tone and atmosphere for each area very well.
The combat in this game is a blast to play as well. You will find yourself slicing your way through hordes of monsters, with a small but very versatile moveset that never gets old. It is actually possible to have a fight last upwards of a minute, without ever touching the ground.
Another point about the world of this game that I wish more games outside The Elder Scrolls series would use is the use of anthropomorphic animals. All of the characters are some kind of anthro-morph, whether it is a fox, rabbit, mouse, lizard and many others. I really enjoy this kind of thing, and it really helps the game stand out on its own, instead of falling into the tired fantasy traps of the overused elves, dwarves, orcs, and so on, which have been used to the point of being a checkbox for fantasy.
In terms of story, this game is a marvel. The plot is surprisingly mature despite the E10+ rating, and makes a lot of "Mature" rated games look childish and infantile, and should last you around 11 hours depending on how many side-quests you do. This game! What should I say? I don' know.. It's good. Somehow.
But 10€? I'd rather wait till you can get it for 5$/€.
The game itself has some neat graphics, as you can see in the trailer/ screenshots, it has a nice soundtrack, really accurate controls and cool gameplay.
As for:
- the graphic: sure is nice, no doubt - especially for a game with not even 300MB in size. The downside is that, if you want some variety, you'll be disappointed. There are only 4 different enemy models (+4/5 bosses) and 4 arenas. Your attacks look nice, but nothing overwhelming or new. If you watched the trailer you've seen quite everything. Also you cant alternate your character. At all (Okay. There are only 2 costumes you can buy, but that's it)
(also there are no lip-sync in cut scenes)
- the soundtrack: more like the 3 songs. The music fits really good. But: The game contains, as far as i noticed it, like 3 different tracks (normal fight, boss battle and final boss) which will loop endlessly. Again: some more variety sure would have been nice.
- the controls:  simple, yet very effective controls! Your character responds immediately and with a few buttons you can chain your attacks together to devastating combos.
- the gameplay: All in all... Sadly quite repetitive. It IS a fun game, no doubt. But it feels incomplete. It feels more like a tech demo for a fighting system. You simply fight wave after wave of enemies within a circle shaped arena which you can't leave, fall/ throw enemies off or use any objects/ items.
After like 5 waves you fight a boss of this arena. The bosses usually are have easy to memorize and clearly predictable attacks. That's somehow good since it won't get frustrating at all. But on the other hand it sadly makes the boss battles far too easy.
You start with a weak 4 hit combo attack which fills up your "katana gauge". Each attack (you don't even have to land a hit) with your katana drains a bit of it. So you'll have to chain together weaker and stronger attacks to not run out of it completely (side note: there are no other penalties to an empty katana gauge other then not being able to use the katana. Also this system gets completely pointless once you've upgraded your character a bit. I never had the slightest problem with running low on katana energy.)
Every killed opponent drops more or less "SP" which is the 'money' for buying upgrades for your character. You can buy a few attacks, upgrade every attack to deal more damage or have extra effects and upgrade your health (+regeneration) and your katana gauge (+regeneration).
In conclusion I'd really love to see this fighting game, or rather "fighting system", to be developed further and put into an open world, or at least bigger action adventure game with more skills and a bigger variety of attacks/ combos.
If you can live with a bit repetitive, short arena fighting game, you'll sure have fun with this. If you want this game and are patient: wait till it has a bigger discount!
(On a side note: If you're planing to play on "Hard" mode right from the beginning: that's pure suicide. You won't stand any chance. You'll HAVE to do a play through on normal or easy to unlock some power ups so you stand a chance on hard)

I really enjoyed playing through Alan Wake. It has a tremendous, thick atmosphere throughout the entire game. I was always a little un-easy and on my toes while going through the story. I would label this a thriller more than a horror game. I don’t recall any jump scares but was startled numerous times by the environment, sounds or enemies that would sometimes creep up on me.
The game is broken up into different episodes and plays out like a TV show. Each one flowing nicely into another. A recap is given at the start of each episode as well.
The plot is good and kept my interest. It’s paced well, but felt sluggish a small handful of times.
The graphics are really nice. Some textures up close can be a bit dull but as an overall package it is a beautiful game. The devs did a great job in porting this over to the PC. Ran at a stable 60FPS with no crashes.
Sound design is great whether it’s environmental sounds, subtle background music or a sudden crescendo. All of it meshed together well. Voice acting is also well above average.
The mechanics of the game are pretty simple. When fighting enemies, you must shine your flashlight on them until it breaks them from their cover of darkness. Then you can shoot them. Resources like batteries (for your flashlight), guns, flares and ammo were plentiful and I was never stretched too thin.
The “levels” are built in a linear way. However, collectibles and hidden item stashes can be off in a side path, so checking out various areas can be rewarding. There are a good number of collectibles. I decided to focus on the story and not follow a guide to get all the collectibles. I feel it was more enjoyable this way.
There are a few things I didn’t like. The biggest one being how anemic Alan was. He can only run for very short distances before getting winded and forcing you to do a slow jog. The sprint time could have easily been doubled or tripled.
Combat is very repetitive. The same strategy is used throughout the entire game.
There are a few puzzles scattered around. They are way too easy and I would have preferred more, tougher puzzles rather than walking through areas fighting off the Taken.
I almost didn’t notice the 2 extra episodes to complete after finishing the main game. They were good and bad. The very abstract nature of the 2 episodes was really appealing with the strange situations and having to shine your flashlight on actual words to get the items was neat. However, it relies, again, on repetitive combat. This time, with more enemies which was a jump in difficulty from the main game. It also relies on much more jumping, which is poorly handled in the game to begin with. I would rather have had the abstract aspects tied into the main game.
+60FPS
+Amazing, heavy atmosphere
+Scenery and town fleshed out well
+Good story
+Great graphics
+Great sound design
+Voice acting
+Sprint duration too low
+Repetitive combat
+Easy puzzles
+No manual save
+Poor checkpoint system (not the frequency but how it’s handled)
Alan Wake is a mix of really good things and some mediocre things. However, every time I stopped playing for the day, I would always anticipate firing the game back up to continue. To me, that’s one mark of a good game.

The story centers around a mentor and a protégé, and their mission is to go around worlds to prevent catastrophic crisis.  At first, It does sound quite interesting and somewhat unique background setting for a story.  But I was disappointed, nothing seems to get it right in this game.
I have played some visual novels before, and I know it's mostly like reading a book with some interaction.  For this type of visual novel, if it doesn't have a good and interesting story; it is vital that they have at least something that can make us like the game, i.e., likeable characters, nice artwork, or even just decent voice acting.   Unfortunately, it has none of that.  Everything seems so dull, and the game doesn't even have dubbed voices.
Even with just a handful of characters in this story, I find none of them likeable.  Basically we have this clueless protégé and a cynical mentor.  The mentor seems to have a dark past, but lack of proper character development for us to really empathize with him.
This game does give the player choices at different point in the game, so you can get somewhat different endings; that's probably the only good thing about this game.  But to get to those turning point choices, you'd have to do a lot of saving and reloading.  And you probably have to start from the start at least once, and choose skipping text till the point they have those choices.   I just wish they would somehow categorize the whole game chapter by chapter where you can load at certain chapter from the start.
It seems a bit unfair to not recommend a game that is supposedly an episodic game.  But the game just did not have a good start, and I just don't see how much better it can get.

A great simple platform-puzzle game and that's all there is about this game. You navigate the main character towards the blue onion-looking alike house per level. There is a good amount of levels (40) that you can choose to play a few at a time or play it all at once like I did. None of the levels were drastically difficult, but a few will get you excited for sure. I was definitely okay with the pace of the game and didn't feel bored from level 1 to level 40. The game has two types of levels: paced and not paced. In the paced levels, you will need a bit more skill and memory to recall when to flip and when not to flip the character as you progress in the level. In the non-paced levels, you can take all the time you want to map out how you want to progress with the level. Throughout the levels, it was fun and the music kept me entertained. Overall, this is a good game and I don't mind paying $2 for it. Not much replay value unforunately, but worth it. Minor things: 1) once or twice when I clip the corner, the main character gets stuck and can't move left or right; the only way to un-stuck was to flip up and down and 2) sound-effects did get slightly irritable, but you can change that.
Perhaps a time-attack/race 2 players (with up to 4 players - couch) edition can be in the works? Having certain levels and then racing a friend(s) would be nice.
For the value and this type of game, I would say 8.5/10
