Before I got this game I did the usual thing, read the reviews, looked at how negative and unrecommened the game was. I wasnt going to buy the game just on that, but I decided to give it a go as I'd just been paid. Firstly the sound track, WOW I mean its like the equivilent of Gta: Vice City but in the 60's. Yes there is some negative things like how even on a high end rig the game isnt very optimised and how there used to be a 30 fps cap (which is gone now) but if you look past that this is a fairly good game. You mainly spend your time taking over rackets and giving them to 1 of your three lieutenants and getting rewards based on who you give them to this can get repeatative, but in realistically this sort of thing happens in most modern open world games now (I dont condone this Im just saying). One of my favourite things is that I find myself cruising to my next mission and waiting outside the mission just to hear the end of a song that I like, which i havent done since Vice City. The gun combat is very satisfying and you also nearly always have the option of the violent or non violent stealth approach (can switch to non violent takedowns in the options menu). There is quite a few things to do in the game perhaps not as much as games like Gta V and such but I havent found that much of a problem.
I have to say that if you are a fan of all the little things you could do in the other mafia games such as bribe the police, limit your car, grab a cold one from the fridge ect. you cannot do this any more, which is a shame as those sort of things made mafia stand out in my opinion, but i guess the developers decided to leave it out either due to not wanting it or being lazy. The collectibles are back! you can get your hands on all the playboy mags from the months and years around the late 60's which I am glad they kept as it reminds me of the other games. You can now upgrade weapons, your car and Lincoln himself, though some are minor upgrades I think this was a nice feature to add (even if they took away a lot of the features I liked).
I bought this game without any hype, i mean its a different teams behind it (hanger 13) so I know not to get too excited. To me this game is a little bit of several other games (Godfather 2, Gta ect.) with mafia sprinkled on top, it has some really nice references to the last mafia game which a follower of the series will understand. I my self have had a blast on the game, though its not a 10/10 game its certainly no lower than a 7/10 in my opinion.
I recommned the game however, I would advise that if you have the money and wanted to get it then do, if youre still cautious then just wait for a steam sale and get your hands on it, I would say go into it without a Mafia game mindset and you will discover that the game has a very good story and is definitely worth playing.
p.s there is sometimes a stange lighting effect in the game (looks like a bug) but i think its the clouds going infront of the sun, i found putting shadows on high resolved this for me :)

Castle Of Illusion is one of those games you thought would never be remade or even thought of. It's an early nineties video game for the Sega Genesis. Castle Of Illusion Remake is a short sweet game that captures the sprite of the original. In terms of length it should take no more than one hour to complete, again, this hearkens back to the original 8bit/16bit days in terms of completion. The only thing with this port of the game, is that you cannot turn off fxaa, so the game has a slight blur to it, and it's not really optimized, I was getting slight frame drops on a 980ti. I bought this game for $4 bucks, and it was worth every penny. So if you are in the mood for a trip down memory lane, or you just want a cute platformer, I would highly recommend this game.

Overall, I think this was a good game experience. This was my first attempt at a visual novel, and it's definitely not for everybody. This is a short story, and it's obvious that there will be more games out there, as the story line leads to a sequel. Alan Wake is a strange one. It isn't a horror game. Yet I wouldn't really call it a thriller either. I guess it kind of falls into "Forgotten Stephen King TV miniseries" territory with a smack of Twilight Zone's surrealist menace. Often it's slightly creepy, but beyond the very occasional jump scare never really ventures into actually unsettling. And I'm never really sure if it is badly written or not. The writing is hammy, but it is also told through the lens of a fictional author... so how much is intentional (like how 'actors' inside of films are always invariably awful) is beyond me.
Perhaps a layer of genuine twist or subversion somewhere along it would have given the story the substance I felt it needed, but as it is there's not a strong resolution and it doesn't deviate terribly from the initial set up which for something that falls somewhere between "thriller" and "horror" seems like a cardinal sin.
Gameplay wise it is competant, the flashlight mechanic is sometimes more annoying than anything else though, it definitely seems to lean towards a horror game's style of scrambling about low on ammo (or flashlight batteries) while enemies repeatedly bite your backside... but without the sense of genuine threat or terror it can feel a tad more frustrating than it probably should. Guns are satisfying enough when you've eventually burned away your enemy's protective darkness with your very unreliable flashlight, and the flaregun is a quite a fun get-out-of-jail card that nukes most regular enemies even in groups.
Graphically, while it will begin to age as a last-gen game, it looks very good still. The lighting effects are fantastic still, and it applies interesting distortion effects when the supernatural Dark Presence is chasing you which gives a malignant and warped appearance to the enviroment as though the towns and forests around you have come to life.
Sound design is also good, with a very decent soundtrack topped off with some great original songs from Finnish band 'Poets of the Fall'.
Great port. Good gameplay. Story is decent, but could have been twistier and commited stronger to what genre it wanted to be in combination with the gameplay.

Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel that tells of a story about individuals dealing with problems of other worlds. The protagonist, Winter, is one of such individuals - a mediator - who tries to keep a world in proper order. As with most visual novels, you direct Winter to decide on different choices presented throughout the game, ultimately deciding the story's ending.
The story itself is a quick one, and I do wish it was a bit longer (a playthrough can be done within an hour or so, if you read through it quickly), though it's a bit understandable since this is the first episode in the series - there're a couple more episodes after this one, and I believe there's a prequel in the works as well (you can check out their website to find out more about them). Given the short story, there weren't really a lot of choices. I liked the plot and I'm quite eager to know how it turns out.
The artwork and soundtrack are pretty good too - the visuals are drawn beautifully, and the soundtrack complements the various events in the game. Kudos for including the soundtrack along with the game and not as a separate purchase (I have it on my playlist to listen to on the go, loved the title theme song). It'd be a nice touch to have some character voices though, which should make it even more engaging.
Overall, it's a pretty good title - it has an good and interesting storyline, but is rather short that it's like a teaser for the succeeding episodes. A bit pricey for the length of the story, though the inclusion of the soundtrack more or less offsets this point. Everything else is pretty good - 3.5 out of 5 stars for me.
Postscript: Considering the story and all
, they should try producing an animation for this one after all the episodes have been released. It certainly has potential in my opinion - hope you can make it happen Dischan! =)

Keep remastering games like this and we'll keep buying them. When I was a kid I owned and played this game and loved every minute of it, and today that hasn't changed much. This game is still an amazing game but now it looks even better.
The gameplay is the same as it was when it came out on the Genesis/Mega Drive, sometimes punishing, but as fair as all difficult games in the old days.
You begin by running through a level of whackiness until you get to the castle, there you can save and start new levels of whackiness. There is something magical about this game that comes from the nostalgia factor combined with it being a really good platformer. It is a semi 3d/2d experience that reminds me a little of mario 64 at times. (a little I said.)
Pros:
+It may be a shorter game than you are used to, but its quite challenging at times. Because its gameplay comes from a time when games were much more difficult, there are times when you may end up repeating the same thing over and over trying to make a jump or get a crystal or apple or something. It's forgiving but not by much.
+It looks quite good, remembing its based on a game that came out in 1990, that's 25 years ago at the time of writing this. They took all that gameplay and redid all the graphics creating a contemporary platformer that still feels like a classic.
+ It can be hard, but not overly hard. It's not a remake of battletoads or anything, and I imagine compared to games of its time it was not considered hard, however games today are quite easy in comparison so kids playing this today may find it a little difficult.
+The music and sound is really good, and they give you the option to choose the contemporary updated music or the classic stuff from the game, something they didn't have to do but is really appreciated.
Cons:
- The controls may take a few to get used to. Like I missed several jumps because I didn't get the timing correctly, or I thought it didn't jump when I pressed it, however after about 15 minutes it was all good for me and I corrected whatever issue I seemed to be having.
And let me be clear this isn't really a problem, but I thought I'd list it to give warning if someone played and thought "What the heck?"
Originally I thought I'm not sure this game is worth $15 but having tried it I can say they put a lot of work into making this game look like a contemporary game, and its definitely worth the price tag.
For kids who like everything explained or a big sign telling them where to go, they may not like some of this game. At times I wondered if I was going in the right direction, but I realized it doesn't matter, the game won't let you really make a mistake in that way, however you find yourself doing the same thing over and over until you realize, "no I'm supposed to go down here or up there instead."
Final Verdict:
7/10. It's a really nice, relaxing, fun, trip down memory lane, and for kids who have never seen it, it will surely delight. This is for all ages and don't be fooled by having Mickey, even adults will enjoy the challenge.

The game is fairly easy but I find the platforming is enjoyable due to the creative level design. While there is generally only one path, it goes in all directions and never feels like you're just going in a straight path from left to right. I never played the original Genesis version so I don't know how closely it follows it but I understand this is more a reimagining than a remake. I know that I do like the variety of platforming and contrasting styles and designs of each level. The transitions from 2D to 3D gameplay generally flow well and it's easy to re-orient yourself to play the short 3D segments. Missing a jump usually does not lead to instant death but is often just a setback as you land in an earlier part of the level. I personally appreciate this as someone who hates bottomless pits. The bosses are also fairly fun to beat if again a bit easy. There is a bit of a challenge in getting all the gems as some are carefully hidden and require exploring off the obvious path. I generally dislike collect-a-thons but since the game is not too long and there are not too many gems, it was actually interesting to try and get all the gems without looking up a walkthrough.
Graphics and music are very well done. The graphics do not obscure any platforms but give life and personality to each level. I particularly like the overall relaxing tone of the music, which gives a whimsical fairy tale feel while still being interesting to listen to. The occasional narration that occurs due to certain actions is also a nice touch.
As a fan of 2D platformers, I found this to be a very enjoyable and imaginative game. Maybe it could have used another world with a few levels but what we got was high quality where replaying levels is not a chore.

While short, what Dysfunctional Systems brings to the table is excellent artwork, world building, characterization, and music. Taking the role of Winter, a student from a utopian Earth-like world, you shadow a seasoned veteran Mediator as you learn about how to settle problems in worlds and maintain balance. The story itself uses a lot of sci-fi elements, and while their world is hailed as utopian, the setting of this visual novel is very much dystopian.
The premise itself is quite intriguing, and all the world-building (aided by the Codex) is really fascinating to read. Through the dialogue and interactions with key players, you learn a lot about the motivations of each character, and Winter herself learns about the impacts and pivotal role her choices (and sometimes her lack of choices) can have, which does impact her character a lot based on the endings you get. Choice wise, your choices really only branch at one point, however in order to reach a specific outcome you have to maneuver your way through several responses, something that I did not necessarily mind, though you will not have five endings here that are wildly different from one another.
A big issue many have is the length of this game, and how it ends. It's not entirely unfounded; the game is very short for one playthrough depending on the speed you read at, and the endings don't really differ except for how the characters react. This almost makes your choice seem pointless, if this visual novel was going to be the only one from this series. However, with the way it sets itself up with the end, as well as the recent confirmation of more episodes, the story will continue and so one way to think of this is the beginning act of the story, and thus everything would not have reached the climax yet. It sets up the events to get the ball rolling. Whether this makes or breaks your decision to purchase depends entirely on how you feel about that.
Art and music are top notch and excellent. Even the UI is presented in a rather appealing manner, though not quite as unique as, say, the console in Analogue: A Hate Story. The interesting thing that separates art for this VN with others is the painterly style, and it actually blends in well with the background and makes the characters feel very much a part of the world they are in. Writing is also very good, with a lot of good focus on characterization and growth, however the dialogue can feel stilted from Winter. There was also a lack of world building for their world, for the most part, and something I hope will be explored in the future (it would also explain why Winter's dialogue feels a little forced). While not impacting the core of the game, I also felt the fanservice-y pictures of the underage characters really off putting, and I'd rather there be more varied art to unlock since it's feels really exploitive having those pieces take up 50% of the unlockables.
Definitely recommended if it's on sale at all. If you're going to buy it full price, be mindful of the length and endings. The art and music (soundtrack included) does make it a great visual novel to play through, though, and gives us a good idea of what to expect in the future quality-wise.

Fallout 1 and 2 are available on Steam.
Get them if you've never played them.
You'll understand why this game has so many negative reviews.
If you want to drop 40 bucks on a game that doesn't hold a candle to games you can currently get for $5-$10, that hails form a modern era but lacks so much of the depth both in combat and questing systems and dialogue that Fallout has... then buy Wasteland 2.
In Fallout 1, you're pretty much released from the intro mission, and given the ENTIRE game map to roam. You can follow the quests or wander off, and time isn't completely irrelevant either, but it doesn't punish you for exploring and side-questing.
There is very little of either, exploring or side questing, in Wasteland, due to the constrained play areas at each step of the plot. The plot is fairly linear, and often the plot's goals and requirements are not only unintuitive, but completely nonsensical, and not even brought up or highlighted or alluded too in any dialogue with any characters.
(One quest you have to stop a small war from breaking out, the only way to do it is to murder a drug dealer who I'm not sure how he's even related to the damn quest at all... But you HAVE to murder him. Only way to stop it. Both unintuitive and very narrow).
In short. Buy the game on sale. 20 bucks or less.
You'll get LONG play time out of the game, but its really up in the air whether that play time is quality enjoyment, or tedious simplistic combat with a constant feel of nostalgia reminding you... There's more to the Wasteland than what you're doing.

I'd like to recommend this game, I truly would but I cannot do so in good faith. There are a few very key flaws with this game that prevent me from being able to recommend it. I don't regret the purchase and I did enjoy it, for as short as it was but I imagine a lot of people could easily be put off by the experience. In fact I'm probably being very lenient on it myself.
Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos is the first in a series. The following installments have yet to be released but will be longer and also must be purchased individually. It is a visual novel that relies heavily on immersing players with story and characters, with the only gameplay being making choices throughout the story to change how things go. But here comes the biggest issue. Throughout the course of the game, I made one choice. Literally one. In other words, this was a short story, not a game. I cannot call something that had such bare minimum interaction a game. The game itself also only lasted around two hours. The length wouldn't be a big issue, since it is cheap and I got it on sale, but the fact there's only one choice throughout is a damn joke.
However, the appeal in a game like this is that you can go down other paths, see what happens if you choose another option, right? And I'm sure if I picked the other option, I'd have at least one more choice to make, based on what I've seen. I don't know for sure though, since I haven't been able to replay this game. Attempting to reopen the game gets me an error message, one which haunts me no matter how many times I reinstall, verify game cache or restart my computer. The game doesn't even work properly.
The third key issue is one that's going to bring down the wrath of men's right's activists everywhere on me. The extras in this game include artwork. Some of this artwork is fanmade and portrays the (underage) female characters of the game in risque positions. This automatically makes the creator's respect for his characters come across as shallow, as he willingly keeps extras that objectify and sexually exploit his characters in the game. Apparently this is because of a dislike for retroactive censoring. I think a bigger issue is the ominous aura that now surrounds this game and its characters, that no matter how well developed or interesting they may be, ultimately they will be used for shameless fanservice.
I want to end this review with some positives. While it was short, it was still a great story. It centers around two main characters, Winter Harrison and Cyrus Addington. Both these characters are not only entertaining but very interesting, with unique backgrounds and moral beliefs. I don't want to spoil anything so I won't give away the most interesting aspects. I do hope both characters reappear through the series and that both characters are treated with respect. There was some soapboxing from one character in terms of moral values that irritated me but hopefully that was the character talking and not the game trying to force its ethical views.
The art and music are also fantastic. I do want to stress that this is a great visual novel, just not really a game. More than anything, it's the fact that it's not opening for me any more that'd most keep me from recommending it. Otherwise, if you're okay with getting a good story in place of a game, go for it.

Broken Age is a well made adventure with an intriguing story and two likeable protagonists. Its high production value makes for an outstanding game and is thus commendable for players with an affinity for old school point and click puzzles. The lovely graphics, across-the-board superb voice acting and cute animations are a joy to experience, suitable for all ages.
The topic of coming of age may seem stale at first but is presented in a fantasy universe that includes some of the typical teenage issues in a more abstract way. As a result Broken Age's story shines with clever allegories refreshing its theme. The ending however falls flat and leaves the player with a plethora of questions never to be answered.
The puzzles are mostly reasonable in difficulty with a few bumpy parts, notably towards the ending. The solution process takes a lot of creative thinking, pushing the player to discover connections seemingly made up out of thin air. Those particular puzzles appear viable
. They could be made a bit more comprehensible, but that may be an inseparable trait of the genre.
Although flawed, Broken Age is definitely worth playing at the very least because of its audio-visual delight.

So, let me start this obviously super professional review because im pretentious and like to think that my opinion matters by saying that i've never been a fan of the LotR series. i dont hate it, but i just cant sit through hours and hours of a movie that i honestly feel like nothing super actiony and cool happens. from what i saw of the movies, they just like to stroke peoples fantasy boners. so, i was pretty skeptical of how much i would like this game from the get go, i didnt even buy shadow of mordor for the same reason. but, my curiosity peaked (if not entirely for the nemesis system... im a sucker for rng anything) and led to the climax of buying the game during the black friday sale. i will structure this review in a few parts (im writing this review as i go, i like to just improv things as i go when it comes to writing.) and at the end of each topic, i'll rate it and show the average review score after each to show how the final score is affected by it i guess? i dont know, i've never seen people do that before and i think it might be an interesting thing to do. we'll see how it plays out based on the helpful votes i guess?
STORY: man, that word looks strange in caps, doesnt it. anyways, one big thing i was afraid of was not understanding whats going on because of not playing the original, as well as not watching the series it was based off of. im very glad i was wrong. so far, its all very engaging and even though i have some minimal knowledge of the series, i feel like it wouldnt have been necessary. the game does a very good job of explaining whats going on, who you are, who this celebrimbor pleb is, and other key figures. there wasnt a time so far that i was like "what the hell is going on?!". my favourite part is how i actually care about these people. i actually feel dread when i see the witch king or sauron. the story gets an 8/10, only because i havent beaten the game yet. i'll edit it when i get to finish the game.
SCORE: 8/10
FINAL SUBTOTAL: 8/10
GAMEPLAY: Not to be confused with combat, which will be the next topic. i classify gameplay as all of the other stuff. the progression system, loot and the like. anyways, if it isnt apparent by my game time in 2 days of buying the game, it. is. amazing. i've just gotten to act 2, by the way. i spent 6 hours in the very first area, collecting the collectables, killing millions of captains, and just running around. the nemesis system... its the best god damn thing since sliced bread. i personally dont know any game that has a similar system that is nearly as in depth and cool as this. i can imagine that the titles the captains carry are limited, and i've already seen a couple duplicates, but the different names, the way they act, their strengths and weaknesses... everything is seemingly somewhat different every time, and the captains having a chance to come back to life (essentially) and they recognize you is such a good thing. there was this one captain that came back to life 5 FREAKING TIMES, and he always had something different to say. the amount of strategizing that you CAN put into it is amazing, and i imagine that if i was playing on the self titled "nemesis" difficulty, the game really pushes you to do that. im a major sucker for progression, and this game has a lot of it. leveling up for skills feels great. on the other hand, exploring and collecting shiz for more skill points to get even more skills and the incentive to unlock skills feels... good i guess. collecting collectibles always feels somewhat tedious, but the rewards that you can get make it bearable i suppose. the loot system is satisfying, lacking depth though. i have a lot of time in the borderlands games because i really like how you can get 2 pistols, and they'll be entirely different 99.999 percent of the time. so whenever i think of loot in any game, thats what i compare it to. the fact that weapons only change damage, armor only changes health, and robes only change the stealth stat as a number (however the hell that works) is very disappointing. the worlds i've been to are very fun to explore, rather large, and running across them like a badass elf dude is super fun. i think thats all for this section, it got pretty lengthy but there was a lot to cover. im giving the gameplay a 9/10, it would have been a 7, but the nemesis system really carries the game in this department.
SCORE: 9/10
FINAL SUBTOTAL: 8.5/10
COMBAT: my final topic is the combat, and i'll start by saying that it definitely succeeds in making you feel like a badass, but the way it makes you feel like a badass is lackluster. i never liked spam x and occasionally hit y combat. it doesnt carry much weight to it. but once you progress and get the executions, the elven fury, the shadow strikes... it makes up for it a little bit, even though it would be dumb to use it fighting a handful of orcs. the stealth functions the way you expect it to, with stealth kills and brutalizing moves. but these orcs... are they blind, or just immensely dumb. i could be standing in broad daylight on a platform, and see an archer on an opposite platform looking directly at me, and they dont see me. its rather shabby AI work that i'd expect from a ps1 game, but some games on the ps1 even had this down pat. the final score for this is a 6/10, only because the combat against the captains actually has depth to it.
SCORE: 6/10
FINAL TOTAL: 7.6/10
CONCLUSION: overall, this is a very fun game to play. the nemesis system is definitely the biggest drive for this game by a long shot. even though i scored it somewhat roughly, i still have a blast playing it and will play it for a long time to come. would definitely reccomend to anybody that likes rpg-like, open-world games with a twist, hell, anybody that likes video games even. as a reminder, this is more of a mid-game review, so my thoughts and ratings should be taken with a grain of salt. but if you liked this review, please give it a +1 or however the helpful system works. maybe if i get enough i'll consider doing youtube reviews, then you get to hear me and see my ugly mug. that being said, i also wrote a couple of other, less lengthy reviews. check out my profile to see them. until the next game to enter my library, i'll see you guys next time. ta-ta for now.

It's dirt  cheap during any sale and it is as gold as everything else Team Meat has managed to churn out. If you are curious what you are getting into it, it's something strangely familiar and incredibly well made. It is basically a top down shooter reminescent of old Zelda games (my favorite kind) with roguelike elements and some twisted humor.
*On a side note: buy the DLC, I don't need to add why, its everything you love topped with more of what you love.
Roguelikes have been making a resurgence lately as part of the revisionist mantra of "real gamers like hardcore challenges". Which is all well and good, sure I like to be challenged in certain ways, but I definitely like to relax too. More importantly it's not just any challenge that gamers should clamor for, it's the good kind, the fair kind. Team Meat has this down perfectly. When ever you die in one of their games it's not a question of a flaw in the game's design, an enemy that is overpower, or an impossible obstacle, the only the wrong is you. The game has a simple set of mechanics and some secrets in gameplay that you can and should figure out on your own. When you lose in this game you should feel that welcome brand of shame that says "I should've known better". This game isn't trying to fool, you know what you are playing and you know what you should've done.
The real draw from a game that is continously killing you, besides the superb gamplay, is the sense of progress and reward. There is a plethora of secrets to be found in The Binding of Isaac, all unlocked in a variety of ways and adding to the gameplay. The game starts with Isaac, there are more characters to unlock later, shooting tears and running around naked. From defeating bosses, random chests, or treasure rooms, Isaac unlocks various items that alter his abilities. Most of the abilities are passive and stack, and some are useable abilities like cards or a cat's head. These items are all random ( a treasure may net you a spiffy spider upgrade to your tears or just a teleporter) and the levels are procedurally generated. On top of all  the game altering the items can do, they also change your character's appearance into something that is usually atrocious and hilarious.
The Binding of Isaac will kill you a lot (and not in the Dark Souls way where  you can still get something back and respawn from the last campfire), but you will never feel like it was a waste. I've had some two minute sessions of this game that netted me a new secret item, and there is always something to unlock in The Binding of Isaac. After dying so many times you will get better, and then you will still keep dying, but you'll enjoy it.

Ah yes, Dank Souls in 2D with mice. Why mice? No idea.
TL,DR:
Entertaining but short-lived, slow-paced, harsh, top-down sword fighting  with the occasional dash of bullet hell. Wait for a sale or give it a spin if you're craving for a soulslike (because that's apparently a thing now).
Just like in the Souls series, you must keep an eye on your stamina bar more so than your health, proceed carefully or else run into death around the corner, and there's a sense of achievement when you unlock one of the many shortcuts that make your life a whole lot easier.
The difference is obviously that this game is played from a top-down perspective, so arguably it's much easier to know when exactly you will hit the enemy with the tip of your weapon whilst avoiding theirs.
As for weapons, you have a good variety to choose from, but they're not all that different from one another due to the limitations of the game's 2D design. It's just a matter of reach, damage, and speed because there are like 3 different attacks in this game aside from the 2 unlockable moves that all weapons have access to. This is part of the reason why this game has less replay value than the Souls games. At least I didn't feel like replaying the game with a different build because the experience would have been mostly the same, unless I completely forgo archery and pyromancy.
That's another thing. There's quite a lot of cheese in this game, pun intended. You will frequently run into situations where you pop in and out of cover to fight archers because the entire room is filled with them so going the melee route is like a dice roll waiting to fail, or spam pyromancy at a horde of turtles because it ignores their shields. I can see how these situations can be immensely frustrating when you decided not to invest in archery and pyromancy. Is that a flaw? I would say so, yes. It's as if the player is punished for playing how they like to play. In the Souls series, diversifying is a choice driven by comfort, not necessity.
Something else that's uncomfortable are the controls. In the Souls series and in this game, spacing and timing are of utmost importance, so it's rather frustrating to see your little mouse do a heavy attack in a combo even though you could have sworn you tapped that button to perform a light attack or the other way round.
Similarly, the way you turn is clunky. Sometimes it feels as though you turned around and hit the enemy by sheer chance whereas other times you miss an attack that had no business missing, but such is the folly of keyboard + mouse controls in the Souls games it seems. The gamepad controls are hopefully more responsive, but I can't say because I've been playing Souls exclusively on keyboard because I'm crazy.
At least the torch mechanic is suspenseful. Dark Souls 2 promised truly dark areas that pretty much require a torch for traversal. Unfortunately, it didn't deliver and the torch ended up worthless. In this game, you're always carrying a torch. By that I mean you have a ring of light around yourself that gradually becomes smaller until you rest at a campfire. When you have already been somewhere, you can see objects and enemies in the dark. When it's your first time exploring though and your torch is in its weakest state, you struggle to decide whether to turn back or keep pushing forward because you feel like the next campfire is near.
So all in all, this game is not a Souls clone, instead it takes what's good about Souls and presents it in a nice 2D format, but can be annoying more so than genuinely challenging. I would personally wait for a sale because you will be done in 7 hours give or take, unless you're enthralled by the simplicity of the combat, so you just keep restarting or keep going into new game plus. For me, it was a mostly pleasant one-time experience, so at least I don't regret buying this game.

While I can't NOT recommend it, I can't exactly recommend it with flying colors.
It's not a bad game, unless you get stuck encountering bugs that show up due to your hardware configuration (and there are a lot of hardware configurations this game doesn't like, both AMD and Intel, both Radeon (AMD) and Nvidia (Intel) graphics cards), you will probably find this game endearing and a bit nostalgic at first.
Then you'll realize that's just icing, and there is no cake underneath. It's a very thin layer of icing too.
Fallout 1 and 2 are available on Steam.
Get them if you've never played them.
You'll understand why this game has so many negative reviews.
If you want to drop 40 bucks on a game that doesn't hold a candle to games you can currently get for $5-$10, that hails form a modern era but lacks so much of the depth both in combat and questing systems and dialogue that Fallout has... then buy Wasteland 2.
In Fallout 1, you're pretty much released from the intro mission, and given the ENTIRE game map to roam. You can follow the quests or wander off, and time isn't completely irrelevant either, but it doesn't punish you for exploring and side-questing.
There is very little of either, exploring or side questing, in Wasteland, due to the constrained play areas at each step of the plot. The plot is fairly linear, and often the plot's goals and requirements are not only unintuitive, but completely nonsensical, and not even brought up or highlighted or alluded too in any dialogue with any characters.
(One quest you have to stop a small war from breaking out, the only way to do it is to murder a drug dealer who I'm not sure how he's even related to the damn quest at all... But you HAVE to murder him. Only way to stop it. Both unintuitive and very narrow).
In short. Buy the game on sale. 20 bucks or less.
You'll get LONG play time out of the game, but its really up in the air whether that play time is quality enjoyment, or tedious simplistic combat with a constant feel of nostalgia reminding you... There's more to the Wasteland than what you're doing.

Rewiews keep telling that this game is like Fallout, and this is very much untrue.
I remember walking by a small village made of junk and rust, treading heavily in my power armor. Children were playing around, and the wasteland sun was shining. One kid threw a stone at me, it clancked off my shoulder plate. I decided to play along, picked that stone up and threw back at the kid, my hand accelerated with well-oiled X-series power armor motors. The stone went right through kid's body, he screamed and fell into a puddle of his own blood and entrails. Suddenly i became an all-hated child murdering psycho, but what did i care, i had a Bozar on my back, helload of ammo and iguana on a stick. Terrified villagers heard my helmet-muffled whistling as i walked away, towards the white wasteland sun and new exciting adventures.
That's one of my many Fallout memories, and the only memory that Wasteland 2 left is gosh that sucked.
Wasteland 2 is on a level of really good tablet or smartphone game. It's built on awful Unity engine, which screams lazyness, it has a tablet-level dumb combat system, bland graphics with no textures, you name it...
The plot and setting are extremely uninspired, if you are a veteran of Fallout franchise, you will feel a very strong deja vu.
Mutant plants on a food growing facility? Nuclear bomb worshipping fanatics? Robot army? Raiders? Fanatics preserving technology? List could go on but i didn't make it to the end of the game.
Quest system is tedious and lacks logic. I remember doing a lot of quests to make peace between two gangs in some village, even did some not obvious things, like disarming bomb on a bycicle quickly, but in the end they still shot each other, i checked on the internet and realized it's all because i didn't kill(on purpose) some drugs producing guy, who had nothing to do with the rivalry!
Though i liked some non-obvious thing in game, like strange creature in a cell which asks for candy, strange person standing in a pointless location, it's very rare in modern quest markered games with no mystery to them.
Overall, i don't recommend this game to Fallout fans, because it's nothing like it.

The twin destines of two children with overbearing parents overlap into an adventure of epic proportions in Broken Age, a point and click adventure game by Double Fine.
From the very start of the game, you are able to control either of the two main characters (Shay and Vella) and progress their storylines independently up until a certain point. You can switch to the alternate character at any time and this can be helpful later on in the game for when you need to solve puzzles that require information only accessible to the other character.
When this game first came out, there was a lot of controversy regarding delivery of promises and some quantity of millions of dollars for funding. I’d have to argue that the game does indeed deliver when it comes to visual and audio quality. The graphics are quite detailed for such a simplistic style and the animation has a very professional and smooth quality to it. When characters move close to areas the camera moves with them creating very fluid and natural movement. Broken Age also features a captivating soundtrack and a collection of talented voice actors including Wil Wheaton and Jack Black, a big step up from other indie adventure gaming efforts.
Unfortunately, the game does fall a bit flat in one important factor: length. I went back over my catalog of adventure games made by smaller studios and wouldn’t you know that they took about the same amount or longer to beat (10+ hours). Considering how they cost half the price for the same amount of entertainment, I can see how some people might feel a bit disappointed seeing as how this was a high budget epic without the epic-sized story. I suppose it’s also worth mentioning that there are a few re-used puzzles in the second act which further cheapen things by artificially extending the game.
With all that taken into account, it’s pretty obvious that the solution to the puzzle that is Broken Age is simple: wait for a sale. It’s not a bad game per-se, but grabbing it at $5 instead of $25 can be the difference between satisfaction or buyer’s remorse.

Got this product for free via a friend buying the Double Fine humble bundle and giving me his spare code for this game.
Let me start by saying. Full price buy? Hell no. Sale? Yes. For sure yes. Do I recommend? Bottom line, yes. Let me detail why.
Broken Age is split up into 2 acts for 2 individual protagonists you can swap back and forth between. Then a third act they both share and you have to solve a few Bullsh*t puzzles for each of them so the other can move on. Both teenage protagonists you take the role of are both likable and believable characters
Anyways spoiler rant aside, you have to explore the story from both their perspectives. Their stories eventually come together in a big plot twist that surprisingly took me off guard which bridges together Acts 1 and 2 for each of the protagonists and ties their stories together well.
Along the way for each of them you meet interesting and silly characters each more memorable than the last ranging from a cloud living cult, teenage "blind" druids, a talking tree, a lumberjack turned metal smith, a very aggressive yet cuddly snake, talking utensils "DEATH FROM ABOVE", and robots made of yarn. Helping them in their issues to advance your goals.
If you're a fan of point and click story driven games this is a great experience, I felt a lot of old school vibes from old PC point and clicks I played when I was younger which was a very welcome feeling. I iron maned through the game in a bit under 11 hours mostly blind, I looked up some solutions via google and steam guides for some of Act 2's puzzles and Act 3's incredibly vague and randomized "puzzles" if you even want to call those annoying blockades that. So the game is very doable in about a day or two. Great for cheevies too if you're into collecting those as well.
The ending without spoiling, left me wanting more. It is a happy ending, don't get me wrong. But the ending is wrapped up in a blue ball of a cut scene which is tied up with very few sketches to tell a shoddy epilouge during the credits (which is mostly made up of a long list of kickstarter backers, seriously please stop offering to put names in kickstarter games for story driven titles, I'm so tired of sitting through hour long lists of names hoping for a post credits scene only to be kicked in the balls for it).
The game's story is great, get it on sale if you're looking for something different. Every character really stuck with me, I love how Schafer pulled this off. That unpredictable, unstable, funny Alcoholic. :)

OK so I'm about halfway through the game, and it's... all right. I wish I could say more about my feelings on it, but I'm at best indifferent to this game, and am only voting it thumbs up because there's no 'thumbs sideways' and voting thumbs down seems a bit too harsh.
This is a platformer where you flip gravity instead of jumping. That's the entire mechanic you deal with as you avoid traps and enemies while you flip switches to make the exit accessible. The biggest challenge arises out of timing your steering of your character while falling up or down. When you learn that, the map you're working with becomes easier. It has a cutesy graphic style with fun music in the background and isn't something that you play as a serious game, it's a fun thing you play for a few minutes and then walk away from.
One minor gripe and this isn't really a gameplay thing- does there need to be an achievement for literally everything? Congratulations, you actually played the game! That said, considering only 17% of people who own the game have the 'you turned it on' achievement it says a lot about how many people get this because it's cheap and then forget about it.
If you want a light platformer with a fun gimmick, this is something to pick up. If you're a platforming wizard who breezes through a lot of games, then this might be a bit on the easy side.

The AI is some of the worst i've seen in a long time, where enemies will walk 1 by 1 into a death trap and/or barrage of gunfire until an entire area is clear. They also seem to miraculously know your location at all times, so if that pile of bodies is getting a little too big, moving to a different doorway ensures the herd keeps churning. There's maybe 4 different animations that are used, depending on what weapon you're using, and it all gets incredibly old incredibly fast. This turns what should be fun stealth sequences into absolute junk.
It takes hours of this repititive nonsense to get to the 8 or so good parts where you get to take on a boss in a new environment and see some more of the story unfold. These areas are usually challenging, fun, and the payoff is great, but the 40+ hours in between them are both completely unnecessary (they add nothing to the story and taking over rackets is literally pointless) and absolutely terrible at the same time. Buy it, but definitely buy it on sale.

A Dark Souls inspired top-down action RPG.
Simple yet solid and enjoyable combat system which takes a while to get good at. It is complemented by a nice weapon selection; Dexterity weapons, including high attack speed and low damage swords and spears; Strength weapons with heavier swords and twohanders; and Precison weapons with bows and pyromancies.
While fairly basic, they are well implemented and every weapon is unique enough to be interesting, and each weapon type offers its own fighting style. While there is a decent amount of choice, a few more weapons probably wouldn't have hurt.
The areas are pretty varied both in theme and in gameplay, and are all open to exploration, with little nooks and crannies containing goodies that never disapoint. The encounters are all intersting, fun, and creative. Some are fairly frustrating with some types of builds, tho. (Mostly thinking of having to go through an archer heavy area with a two hander focused build that can't block arrows. Pretty painful.)
The bosses are a mixed bag. 4 are just normal enemies, but bigger or in greater number. They are still enjoyable, but kinda disapointing. Of the 2 original ones I fought (I read somewhere that I skipped one), one just felt like a non stop barrage of attacks that seemed to start and stop at random. The other one, which was the final boss, was pretty good however.
The game itself is pretty short. I finished it in 6 hours, but I did skip an area, but I did pretty much all of the other optional stuff and explored the areas fully. It's kinda redeemed by a NG+ mode with exclusive weapons and modified encounters, but it doesn't negate the fact that I finished the game still wanting more of it.
The art style is well used and implemented, and manages to give a good deal of detail and serve the gameplay with a good use of shadows and line of sights, while still remaining simple.
The narrative is pretty simple and cliché, but the story that unfolds still has its little moments.
Overall, it's pretty good. An enjoyable and challenging, if short experience well worth its price. And who knows, maybe there is gonna be more content to come in the future.

The Witcher series is a fantasic RPG series with a gritty story based around the player's choices in the story.  Similar games like the Dragon Age series or Mass Effect allow player choices that are more or less black and white, whereas with this series, the choices presented are very grey and what your choices are will have meaningful consequences throughout the game. Like Mass Effect, some decisions you made in the first game will rollover as story items in this game, but they will not greatly affect the story, so you are not required to own the Witcher 1 (but I recommend it). This results in a game where your decisions will have meaningful consequences as you decide how your story will unfold.
Downsides:
- Combat can be awkward at times. It's almost like playing Dark Souls.
- Crafting system items may be unobtainable for long stretches of time, even if it's a "lower" level item or may require MMO-esque farming.

I'm still not sure what to think of this game. Visually it's absolutely beautiful. The story and the lore are great, there's a branching path which makes the game play differently, there's no "right" and "wrong"... But the actual game itself, as a game with its technicalities and mechanics, falls short of my expectations.
The user interface is confusing, and not only because there are no tooltips:
The only witcher sign whose purpose I could remember was Igni, because it burned things.
Inventory management is a mess; they have tried simplifying it compared to the first game, but again, without any tooltips, the only sorting options I figured out were "by newest obtained" and "by most weight". The others... I have no idea what they're about.
The character skill tree won't list where mutagen slots are located. I've talked to a couple of people who played the game, and they all mutated their first ability with something stupid. You can't remove the mutagen, so you're stuck with that choice until the end of the game. If you're reading this, don't do it until you're absolutely sure that you chose correctly, because it won't be surprising if you used a lesser mutagen and got a greater mutagen five minutes later.
You have to decide early on which path to take: magic, alchemy, swords. Not enough talents to push all three branches.
Looting is a problem, as there is no "highlight loot" key, and there are no labels. If a corpse leaves more than 4 things to be looted, you won't see them until you enter the loot window. Positioning the character to loot items and rotating the camera is too hard.
The map is confusing, especially if you're outside a city. Sometimes it seems you can go a certain way to get somewhere, but it's blocked by some bushes and you have to go back and find an alternate route. You can't leave markers, nor is everything on the map marked: for example, in Flotsam I found a book merchant in a random house.
Buying weapons/armor from merchants doesn't let you compare stats to items you own.
You can get good items by crafting diagrams, but you have to find someone to craft; Geralt can't do it. He can just make potions. I actually had to use pen and paper to write down what I want and what I need to craft it.
Speaking of potions - you can't drink them during a battle. You have to do it before, but... How are you supposed to know you'll be in battle? Some people like it, some don't, but for most, if they desire challenging combat, it'll be a case of "save often, reload often".
Eventually I dropped down to easy difficulty, stopped caring about my inventory, looting, oils, potions, bombs and all of that, and just concentrated on the story and the quests. Before that, I was fighting the game itself, instead of monsters.
And the game became fun.
If you want a deep story - go for it. If you want perfect and streamlined game mechanics, go for it still, but you might want to do what I did.
Recommended anyway. Looking forward to the third game!

Act I is delightful, charming, fun. Act II tries too hard to please the Point'n'click core audience and their incomprehensible, unshakable love for the tenets of traditional point and clicks, including terrible puzzles that are at odds with the development, and telling, of the story.
Though I'm not quite as
, I wouldn't go as far as to say the story of Act II is 'an awful mess', for an instance, Act II is indeed a disappointment given the accomplishments of Act I, and while I think he is spot on about so many things, and that that's worth a read even if you disagree, ultimately Act II elicited more of an "oh." from me - expectations probably play a role here, as I tend generally to try and play games as a blank slate, and often manage to come in with close to none.
So, thumbs up or down? tough one: there's so much to like; the art is absolutely amazing, the music is good, and the voice-overs are both well made and a breath of fresh air from the usual TTG voice set, as fantastic as that is. Act I does work very well, with fun writing too, but the second part of the game ultimately breaks the promise of being something more than a very traditional PnC. I could have lived with the almost complete asset reuse, but the underwhelming development and focus on obtuse puzzles spoiled my enjoyment. The UI is pretty clumsy for today's adventure games standards, as well, too much of a concession to mobile platforms, with frequent loading screens that are never seen in native adventures.
All in all, if you can put up with Act II, and the good things I mentioned sound like enough for you, then by all means get it: just don't let Act I push your hopes up too much. If you're more the type who would love to see narrative-driven games move past tradition and on to something better, and more accomplished, there are better games to play.

Alright, I got a lot to say about this one because it really just baffles me.
I don't understand how people forgive Alan Wake for all the glaring issues it has. I guess I can give it credit for trying to be unique, but underneath that... it tries to do a lot of things but fails to do them well. The only redeeming qualities for me are the visuals, sound and atmosphere. The facial animations really haven't aged well though; too often descending into uncanny valley territory.
The combat is just frustrating and tedious. Most of the difficulty seems to be movement, positioning, timing, and to a lesser extent resource management based. It isn't really that hard, just strict when it comes to mistakes. Most importantly though, it just never feels fun, satisfying, or engaging.
The light mechanic only serves to take control of the pace of battle away from the player, meaning most of the time you're just sitting around waiting for things to be vulnerable so you can shoot them. Everything has to be time consuming.
Speaking of pace, almost every time enemies spawn the game goes into a slow-motion cutscene. This really takes away from the horror aspect of the game (if you can even call it a horror game, or a game at all) when you know nothing can ever really get the drop on you.
And speaking of enemies, there are only about three or four of them. The way the game amps up the challenge is by just throwing larger amounts of them at you as you progress. There are no real boss fights either, unless you count utility vehicles and inanimate objects coming to life or "defend this position" segments.
When you do have to run, Alan can only sprint for a measly few seconds before he has an asthma attack. There's also a dodge mechanic that's tied to your sprint key, which is unreliable and only works half of the time.
Nothing about the story or characters intrigues me. I really don't see it as the massive step in video game narrative that everyone else does, it just takes itself too seriously and comes across as campy and pretentious. I'm sick of games trying to prove themeselves as a relevant artform when they don't need to, they always have been. Stop trying to make them like TV shows or movies, let them be their own thing.
The plot is that you're a best-selling novel writer whose cliché horror story is becoming true, yet it takes the majority of the game to establish this point even though it's obvious from the very start. Also, your wife is missing, because of course she is.
Alan narrates everything you do, and his voice is just... weird. Awkward. I don't think it's so much an issue with the voice acting as it is the audio equipment used, it really doesn't sound right.
Characters constantly reference other, better horror stories and authors that remind me that I could be doing something better with my time.
There are long segments where you just follow someone around while they repeatedly tell Alan he's crazy. When I'm playing these segments I just want to get to the game segments. When I'm playing the game segments I just want the level to be over. It's a cycle of constant boredom.
The game is structured like an episodic miniseries. I really don't get why some games do this whole "Previously, on >insert show here<" rubbish, it's just really tacky to me. I don't even like it when TV shows do it so why the hell would it work in a game?
The only thing to keep you going is the hope that there's some sort of payoff or revelation at the end.
*Yawn*
Oh yeah, and there's product placement. Yup. Buy Energizer! Their batteries last for a staggering five seconds!
The irony is Alan Wake would probably make a better TV show, or hell, even a novel. But the way I see it there is just no sense slogging your way through this game for what it offers. It doesn't hold my attention at all. Then again, I'm of a small minority, and many people will just downvote me. So who knows, maybe everyone played a different game to me. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Dysfunctional Systems: Learning to Manage Chaos is a 2014 Visual Novel developed by Dischan Media, the creators of Juniper's Knot. Learning to Manage Chaos is the first game in the Dysfunctional Systems series and acts more as a sneak peak for the rest of the series.
Learning to Manage Chaos follows the journey of Winter Harrison, a 14 year old Mediator who has traveled to the world of Sule to control said world's chaos with her mentor Cyrus Addington. Dysfunctional systems blends politics and sci-fi elements to create a very interesting world (or worlds) which is genuinely intriguing to read about. There is a good deal of world building through not only the dialogue but also the Codex which acts as a portable encyclopedia with information on the world. Learning to Manage Chaos does a good job of exploring philosophies such as Utilitarianism and their effects, both posotive and negative. Despite having very few choices to does a great job of adding weight and immersion to the story through the writing. The biggest flaw of Learning to Manage Chaos is undoubtedly the length which clocks in at less than 2 hours. There are reasons to play through such as the getting all the achievements and different dialogue but even with this you won't be spending any more than a few hours on Learning to Manage Chaos.
The majority of Learning to Manage Chaos has you playing as Winter Harrison. Although Winter is naive she has a strong sense of justice and is pretty cute. On the other side of the spectrum Cyrus Addington, her mentor, is a more mature and experienced Mediator whose opinions often clash with Winter's. The interactions' between both characters are at times funny and cute and at others' thought provoking as much of the subject matter is war and nuclear weapons. The characters add a lot of substance to the game and make the tense moments of the story more gripping. There are few other characters introduced that I won't go into because they only play a small part in episode 1 but they are all fairly likeable so far.
One of the games strongest points is it's visuals and music. The character designs are very well drawn and nice to look at and the backgrounds are some of the best I've seen in this genre. They are all very detailed and unique. The music is very atmosphere as it contains some great Ambient and Electronica tracks which heavily lend to the dystopian-esque atmosphere that the VN is going for. All of which can be accessed from the main menu.
While the length of Learning to Manage Chaos and the miniscule amount of choices hinder the overall quality of the game, Episode 1 of Dysfunction Systems has a great story, characters, visuals, and soundtrack. Although this is only a review of the first episode and shouldn't be applied to later episodes in the series.

I can't recommend this game highly enough to anybody interested in a branching-linear story-based adventure game.
The gameplay is solid for a "walking simulator" experience (and the rewind mechanic is mostly handled well), and the art style prevents the graphics from looking noticeably outdated, but where Life Is Strange truly excels is in its characters, story, and soundtrack. I won't say much for fear of spoiling any of the experience, but suffice it to say that LiS does a truly wonderful job of capturing the atmosphere and character growth is strives for, despite occasionally weak voice acting and sometimes-laughable dialogue.
With the first episode being indefinitely free, I can't think of anyreason not to give it a try. Be warned, however, that if you get caught up in this work, it will absorb you completely. At $20 and frequently to be found on sale, I strongly advise you to pick up Life Is Strange and try it out. When you finish it, you will regret it all, but wouldn't take it back for anything.
Recommended for: fans of choice-based linear games such as The Walking Dead; everyone.
Not recommended for: people who dislike emotional impact or prefer action-oriented or more open games (caveat: try it anyway, since Ep.1 is free).
Be warned: you will cry.

Mafia 3 - It's year 1968 in the city of New Orleans, where a Vietnam soldier Lincoln Clay finally comes back home from the bloody war. Being an orphan, streets and the mob was the only true family he's ever known. But little did he know the only thing he's changing is the battlefield, and it's going to get more bloody than the war he just came from.
Same as in first two games, you play as male protagonist though this time around the story is more twisted around the racial hate towards African Americans. So in the old games you played as Americans or Italian Americans, you mixed up with Italian Mafia, you started working for them, etc. This time around you pretty much go against a Italian American Mafia, because of what they did to your surrogate family aka black mob.
But even though you are technically not part of the "real" Italian Mafia, you befriend 3 other "misfortunate" gang leaders in town, who also want to get back in business and get Don out of the picture. By helping them with various tasks you get them on your side (for as long as it lasts), and in return they help you finance the whole "revenge" thing.
Many may dislike that you're not part of Mafia this time, but as time moves on even the simple criminal gangs were considered Mafias, no matter if the origin wasn't originally Italian. Even though you're in a "self made gang", you will meet the main protagonist of Mafia 2, Vito Scaletta. He has his own gang even though he's a bit aged and roughed up by the time.
Gameplay wise it's your standard 3rd person shooter, with some variety of WW2 / Vietnam weaponry. You can use hand to hand takedowns to disable enemies, be it lethal or non-lethal. Stealth is also part of the game now, so you can sneak around and eliminate enemies silently. Game has decent variety of ground and water vehicles, though they are not as detailed as for example the GTA5 ones. Driving itself is responsive and it is easy to handle car drifting through corners, but make sure it's set on simulation in settings. Character movement is fluid, though you get a feeling like you're stuck to cover once in a while.
You mostly help the gangs get on their feet, increase their money income by doing cargo retrieval missions, be it collecting weed drops on boat, stealing trucks full of liquor or weapons and deliver to warehouse or simply help out with killing, sabotaging rival businesses and squeezing info from enemies.
Helping your new "friends" also rewards you with more money, as well as some perks you can use while in the city. For example call in a ammunition van, to refill ammo or buy new weapons. Or contact a mechanic to get you wheels when you need to without stealing vehicles on street. Depending on how deep you are in the story, you will unlock total of 9 unique vehicles that you can also pimp out with parts you unlock by supporting your gang. And the last thing you can call off the police if you ever get in trouble, or call for a currier to get the money you "earned" to the safehouse, so you don't loose it if you get killed.
Talking about the police in game, the AI is not very smart and unless you drive someone over, shoot or take someone down in public, they won't care. Even if you're speeding, going on red light unless some pedestrian runs to the phone and calls them. Sometimes NPC controlled vehicles have weird looping steering, meaning they oversteer and the wheel flips on the opposite side, resulting on amusing donuts for no reason and sometimes vehicles crash, glitch together while passing through eachother thus explode offscreen for o_O moments, when a burning semi falls from sky right in front of you and explodes everything in fiery blaze.
City map is decent size, with many areas from down town, residential, suburbs and farm/swamp country zones. A lot more places you can enter compared to first two games, though mainly stores, gas stations and diners will have something of use inside, as well as locked places with collectibles that you will have to break open to get. City itself is detailed, with a lot of pedestrians going around, doing their things, but I like it mostly at night when all the lights are on. By day it looks washed out, with weird reflection and lighting system that makes the whole world have a strange shine, almost gloss effect.
Characters have great texture and animation as well as lipsync, but only in cutscenes. Out of the cutscenes they all look pretty generic. Texture quality in game is horrible, with low textures on everything. Cars look more or less decent, but the lighting and reflections don't add to the charm. Every gang boss has a bit of their own story to tell whenever you do a mission for them, but nothing big just bits and pieces.
Overall game has great story, satisfying takedowns, good gunplay. The only things that are a letdown for me are: poor vehicle sounds, low texture quality, weird reflection and lighting by day, not that great optimization and no ability to simply jump when you want to. Collectibles are neat if you like pinups and nude ladies, other than that they are mostly to waste time.
If you like Mafia in general, buy this just to experience the story, it's what I did even though I expected a bit more from the game. As always research before you buy if you're not sure if you're going to like the game, check YouTube, streams and other reviews, I just tried writing what was on my mind.
Thanks for reading. ;)

I'm just shy of 70 hours in game and I've made it to chapter 4 where I will probably spend several more hours, this is what  I make of things. I'll be breaking things down point by point.
Gameplay;
Overall pretty dull, arkam/assassins creed style of gameplay with a bit of spice, the resorce mangement involving what skills you use with your might, arrows and when you use elven fury makes things interesting and keeps you invested on a tactical level. The mounts are fun and unique as are the various elemental effects. There's a wide varity of builds and playstyles based on the skills and armor loadouts chosen and you can change things around on the fly easily enough.
Which brings me to the nemesis system which takes a well made but ultimately tired style of game with a few gimmicks and makes it horrendously addictive. Uruk and Olog captains are your main foes, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, you sucessfully defeat a captain you need to change your tactics accordingly to suit each one. Chapter two onwards you can recruit your own uruks to build a army and it is really addictive to scoure the maps for strong uruks who will serve you well. I'd rather leave you to discover the depths of thye nemesis system for yourself however as that is what most the fun is.
Now I meantions maps, there are five in total, each with their own theme of sorts and each can be tailored to suit a theme of a tribe based on the local Overlord who rules the fortress that enhabits each map. While the maps are great and have actual charm and varity, the fortresses are pretty much the same layout squashed onto the different maps, always pushed up against a cliff of some kind and always with two walls and a central keep.
All in all, aside from some lag when commiting stealth kills every now and then the game plays great.
Narrative;
No spoilers but the game's protaganist and the characters he encounters are pretty standard for a open world action adventure, the general tone is edgy and brooding contrasted with a huge helping of comic relief from the uruks. Honestly I don't feel much about the characters but there are a number of moments that are particularly charming or suitably dramatic enough that I feel invested in the events of the story.
Unfortunately this cuts counter to what middle earth and the LOTRs is known for, it doesn't really fit in the universe and if your a fan of tolkens work then you will definately find the plot in this game Jarring. It is best played while keeping in mind that this is not cannon and exists mostly for the gameplay rather than to tie into the greater universe of middle earth.
Aecetics;
The music and visuals are top notch. The game is pretty much always looking good. The only issue is that some of the lighting settings can leave things a bit confusing. Camera angles are also painful at times blinding you to your surroundings by either focusing of Talions back or him stood in a corner while enemys off screen whollop you.
Character design with the uruks is simply fun and lively, while talions different armor sets are suited to various tastes. You only really feel that there is repeated material when it comes to the fortresses, the observation towers (3 in each map) and some of the ruins, namely the elevated one story building with a C shape wall wrapping around it, usually with a archer patrolling the walltop and often with a campfire and uruks on the floor with one of them standing close to a ledge on a regular basis, this seems to be repeated on at least 4 of the maps several times and while they may have changed some of the details around each time, after a few hours on each of the maps you'll notice it.
There are alot of great veiws and the world does tend to feel pretty lively and imaginative when you're not in a fortress or ledge stealth killing a archer off that one building though.
Final note on loot boxes;
You dont need them, don't waste your time or money on them except to burn in game currency on silver chests for two useless captains and a training order which might allow to teach a existing captain something useful or more likely will go on the pile of caragor rider and warrior gang traits you'll never use. You can kill the captains you get for loot without even putting them in the world but the whole process is slow, boring and unrewarding, it would be nice if you could organize your 'garrisoned' captains by marking favorites and then dumping the rest enmass but as it is using the loot boxes is a thoroughly unenjoyable and unhelpful experience because most of the captains you get will be weak. You can get the premium currency by doing daily quests and get boxes with legendary uruks from doing community events but all legenday captainss are is a captain with two epic traits which are hit and miss and even then if they are dazed by combat finishers they are pretty much trash so its just a good way to get legendary gear.
I have seen outlets suggest you need legendary captains in your entire army to beat the game but really you just need captains with good skills and the time invested in them to level up which is easy enough, you just have them fight in the pits or go on missions and they will gain levels relative to the difficulty. So no, at this stage although I haven't completed the game, I have yet to see anything that sugests a legendary captain is actually game changing unless he cannot be dazed or terified by anything and has some of the good epic traits but a epic or even common captain can be just as good if they have good traits. Note, I have been playing on the hard difficulty the whole way and this is my conclusion.
Conclusion;
The game isn't purfect, its ideal if you want to invest large amounts of time raising captains and trying to find ways to exploit their weaknesses. Its nice if your a fan of open world action rpgs, gameplay is a bit basic with QTE style counters and a smooth learning curve. Once you level up and get a few choice skills you should be able to play smart and pretty much never die, although when you do die it won't feel cheap.
If your not interested with it to that extent I would still recomend getting it when its on sale at a comfortable price, even if you dont particularly care for the idea of the nemesis system or another open world action rpg you can still have fun with the game for more than a few hours before you'd likely get bored of it.

Mafia 3, as much as I want to love the game for my admiration of the previous installments... I can't.
In my humble opinion, if this game wasn't set in the pre-established 'Mafia' universe and managed to avoid the on release PC cockups this game would of been a real win as it tackles a really interesting premise which does sadly end up falling off and becoming a plain old revenge story where Lincoln's character seems to end up taking a back seat and the age old gaming trope of nothing getting done without you doing it occurs. For example, the Black Mob at the start of the game are really struggling, until Lincoln comes home and makes everything nice and dandy again, which was a real problem for me as Lincoln basically becomes a one man army with only him being capable of taking down an entire crime family singlehandedly, which although they tried to justify how this is possibly by him being a highly trained black ops esque macho man from 'Nam with government connections just doesn't feel right to me, and isn't really what myself (and various other people, from what i've seen) wanted from an installment in the Mafia franchise.
When you partake in a game set in a time and setting where you're involved with organised crime, you want to feel a part of something whereas it seems like Lincoln's associates are merely pawns and are always bickering like children with one another (which I suppose was done to reiterate the harsh reality that the devs created that not everyone gets a happy life) and you never feel like they are truly involved in anything you are doing and are just doing you favours so you dont turn your Terminator-esque rampage on them, which isn't what people want to feel from a Mafia experience. People associate Mafia with family and a code of honor, which isn't prevailant here at all.
People consuming media related to the Mafia are generally hungry for feeling the power and respect of rising through the ranks of the Mafia with the hope of every game finishing with you ending up as the Don of your own crime family (usually the ultimate goal of any Mafia related media), but you don't get this here, you get an empty feeling of being an outsider who just happens to be in a position where 3 mobsters kick up to him because only he alone can accomplish what droves of men with better guns and equipment than him can't (plot armor?).
To me, this game just seemed to get lost in not knowing what it wanted to be, a story driven game with a deep commentary about racial oppression in 60's heavily right wing America, an open world gameplay driven experience with lots of mindless shooting people and taking over the various areas offered (which was done better in Godfather 2, IMO), or a game about organised crime where, in the name of revenge you take out the traditional sicilian mafia and become the don of a new era of criminal via unconditional means and try to do things differently. This is probably the games most glaring issue (although, not forgetting about the lack of character customisation, which is a really important part of making you feel connected to a character, IMO...) as the previous installments knew what they wanted to be, sticking to the more popular and sought after world of italian organised crime families and allowing people to live out their fantasies of becoming a made man and living in the dangerous world of a criminal.
Although, It's not all bad though, I found the gunplay in this game to actually be pretty fun, I wouldn't say it feels realistic at all, however, it does feel really satisfying to play as the gun sounds for the most part are decent and aside from the odd issues here and there the gameplay is pretty solid, however after the first few 'takeovers' you quickly realise that it's just basically a rinse and repeat to advance the story to completion which is kinda dissapointing.
Anyway, if this game would have been a new IP about the ethnic minority protagonist Lincoln Clay battling the mob and fighting racial oppression in the 60's, I feel it would of left less of a bad taste in my mouth as this didn't really feel like a true Mafia experience, aside from the returning characters from previous installments being in this game. That being said, I think this game should be used as a learning experience for the game devs and should there be a Mafia 4, if they listen to peoples opinions on their shortcomings and really polish what they did well (which is a fair bit, for all my dissapointments I still dont regret purchasing the game or spending my time playing it, I should add. And by no means is this a 'bad' game like some people are making out) I feel confident that they will be able to make something truly great.
Also, what we see of the prevailant characters are really interesting and make you want more - which sadly never seems to come into fruition. As much as you want to, it's hard to end up truly caring for any of the characters despite their initial interesting back stories and motivations as it all takes the back seat for the revenge. For example, your accomplice John Donnivan is clearly a shady CIA type and you want to know more, but nothing is really explored (suppose they are holding out for the 'Nam based DLC they announced, *sigh...)
All that said,im still giving the game a positive review as i'd still reccomend buying it as it offers a somewhat unique experience, fun gun battles and when the story comes into play it is actually enjoyable to follow, but with my experience from the previous games I found it hard to get past the shortcomings that were present. (No Customisation or Suits available on release? C'mon. Atleast let me wear a nice three piece suit so I can look good whilst fixing the entire Mafia problem in NB...)
