This is a relatively short platformer with high production value.
The art is beautiful, and the level design is excellent, with 5 differently themed areas and their corresponding enemies, and a linear progression that still feels exploratory. There is a good variety in the boss fights, with each of them feeling truly different from the others. The difficulty peaks for boss fights feel quite appropriate, too.
In terms of gameplay, the 2.5D platforming is largely smooth, but the 3D platforming parts can be a bit of a pain - as is usually the case. Thankfully, the latter is not overused, and transition between the two always feels natural.
The story is about as original and enthralling as you'd expect, but at least the narration is well written and well performed. Through narration, the game continually gives an impression of progress, as well as an idea of how far into the game you've made it.
Overall, I'd say that this is a good, entertaining platformer.

Darkmaus is a heavily inspired tribute to Dark Souls, play as a mouse as he journeys through the scourge of Hazarth in this fantastic little action RPG.
+weighty combat
+smart AI
+good soundtrack
+unique aesthetic
+mice eat cheese to heal
– NG+ balancing could use work
DarkMaus is the first entry of hopefully many games for indie developer Daniel Wright. It is no secret that DarkMaus is heavily inspired by Dark Souls, with the developer openly talking about his love for the series itself and how there was nothing quite like its combat which led to him making DarkMaus. While DarkMaus is clearly inspired by it, it has developed an identity of it’s own with it’s minimalistic artstyle and 2D top down combat. You find yourself adrift on a shoreline with a broken raft nearby, dialogue prompts show up along the way explaining the mechanics of the game.
If you’re a Dark Souls player like I am, most of the mechanics will feel very familiar. If you’re not acquainted with the series then there are a couple key points you should know before diving in. DarkMaus has slow, weighty combat, it rewards patience and well planned combat initiations. You cannot button mash or rashly run through a mob of enemies, they will punish you thoroughly and make quick work of you. Healing items come in the form of cheese and are especially scarce so you cannot waste them on the simplest of battles. You want to avoid death at all costs, the reason being is that you lose all your bone marrow upon death. Bone Marrow is used at bonfires which are basically check points that save your progress and allow you to recover all your health and upgrade your stats. DarkMaus is an RPG at it’s core, and while you could finish the game at level 1 with enough skill and patience, levelling up is usually the recommended route for newbies.
You have a level up menu that shows all your weapon skills and attributes. Health affects how much damage you can take, Stamina determines how many attacks or dodges you can do before getting tired, Capacity reduces movement penalty on heavy armour, resilience affects how easily you get stunlocked by attacks and Dexterity affects attack speed. You gain 1 point per level to put in any of those, the only downside is that it requires more bone marrow from enemies the higher the level you are.
Each weapon type has their own moveset, and damage types. You can specialize in many different types of weapons but it’s usually best to specialize in 1 or 2 weapons that cover your weaknesses. There are clones of yourself that you find scattered around the world who have your exact loadout so it’s doubly important to cover your own bases and have a backup weapon that can counter your moveset. All weapons have a minimum spec requirement in their respected skill type with most basic weapons having an average requirement of 2 points, giving you an opportunity to try out most of the weapons and see which playstyle you’re most comfortable with. On my first run I championed a Katana and shield which allowed for a very agile moveset, where I mainly concentrated on flowing in and out of battle with short quick attacks which gave me ample time to dodge out of harm’s way at any given moment.
Like the Souls games, it tends to rely on showing rather than telling. It relies on visual storytelling rather than narrative, allowing the player to interpret what has happened and decide what you should do about it. There are rare moments when you will come across other sane mice in DarkMaus, most of them friendly in nature. If you decide to help them, only then will you learn what exactly is happening in the world of Hazath. An ancient Necromancer named Zarristar has returned, his army of hunters prey on the living, feeding on them for power so in turn he can feed on them and regain the power he has once lost. His constant revival of his enemies for feeding has caused them to go feral, becoming the vicious monsters they are now. Lord Victor went to face Zarristar before the scourge occurred but he has yet to return…Your task, if you choose to accept, is to find him and creating a plan to break Zarristar’s curse once and for all. The beauty of DarkMaus is that you don’t have to play nice, you can kill everyone and the game will play along. It’s up to you whether or not you want to restore peace to the world or become a vessel of Zarristar himself.
DarkMaus has a beautiful, dark minimalist art style that perfectly embodies the cruel reality of the world you’re exploring. The world surrounding you is bleak, covered in shadows. You can barely see anything past the light of your torch which slowly diminishes the longer you go without finding a bonfire. Every step into the unknown is filled with uncertainty and dread, knowing that your next step could lead to your inevitable demise. You will die, a lot. Levels are filled with all sorts of traps, that will corner you and force you to fight enemies while heavily disadvantaged. Darkmaus introduces a mechanic called Death Echoes to overcome these odds, if you find these trinkets everytime you die, a little ghost ally will follow you around and fight with you for a fraction of your strength. Find enough trinkets and die enough in a specific area and you’ll be roaming around with your own little mouse army. If you’re a roguelike fan, death and repeated frustration is probably your idea of a great time, otherwise stay far, far away.
The soundtrack supplements the atmosphere of the game with slow moving synth pieces, that are ambient and droning, shifting in nature giving the player subtle clues of what’s to come next. This is most apparent when the music becomes clashing and cataclysmic, with only one message warning you “You are Being Hunted.” Every once in a while, you will be invaded by Hunters whose soul purpose is to kill you and feed on your corpse for your bone marrow. The hunters are fast, they are fierce and they are merciless. If you get caught by a hunter while in the middle of clearing other enemies, chances are you will not survive. Your best course of attack is to run far, far way until you can fight him solo and even then it’s still quite the challenge. If you lose and they feed on you, you will respawn with only half your health which slowly goes back to normal over time, while victory rewards you with a massive amount of experience.
My biggest critique of DarkMaus if I were to choose would be the balancing of NG+ and beyond. The combat went from unforgiving to absolutely brutal in the later sections. I believe this is due to the randomized curse you are given which can range from, harder to stun opponents to your dead corpses are reanimated and become enemies. I received the latter curse and I absolutely dreaded the thought of dying at any moment due to how strong my build was, making it impossibly hard to face not only myself in combat but avoiding other enemies and traps at the same time as well. Other than that, I have very few minor qualms about DarkMaus except possibly adding a strafe mode outside of combat to avoid traps adeptly.
Darkmaus is a rare gem that captivated me for hours on end, only breaking the spell once I actually finished the game in a single 6+ hour session. And once I did, the very next day I went straight back to marathoning it until completion in NG+ mode. It’s that good. DarkMaus emulates and captures the atmosphere and gameplay that I loved so much from Dark Souls 1, bringing it's own well done minimalistic approach with adorable mice characters that can go feral at the drop of a hat. I
recommend this game to anyone who wants to scratch that Souls itch or to new players who want a unique experience of patient and rewarding combat that will keep you enthralled for days to come.

Darkmaus is a pleasantly surprising start to the indie year, the game draws heavily from the Dark Souls games and has the difficulty of one to boot. There is a good amount of content and replayability, especially for the £6.99 price tag. Not to mention the game is still being worked on to squash out a few bugs other people (Not me.) have been experiencing.
You are a maus (German for mouse, credit goes to Othrandur for pointing that one out.) who wakes up on a shore next to a boat armed with a toothpick and a shield. Your first move is to explore the surrounding area and try to find some purpose whilst learning the basics and fending off bugs, arachnids, other maus and various other eldritch horrors.
As somewhat of a Dark Souls veteran, I personally feel that the game does a good job of maintaining the atmosphere of the source material while still presenting new and often challenging elements throughout the experience. The game is not exceptionally long, however there is plenty of content that will have you hugging every wall looking for secrets. Being heavily exploration based you may find the world to be a bit overwhelming early on, but just keep checking that map and you're bound to discover a route you previously missed.
The combat is weighty and fairly simple once you get used to it, there are a few imbalances here and there (Almost exclusively in the player's arsenal.) but it's easy enough to learn with a little patience. The biggest change in the Dark Souls formula to me is the frequency of bonfires and the scarcity of healing items. Often each area will serve as a test to your abilities, pushing you to do better in order to succeed. Healing items are extremely sparse and should be used accordingly as a result, always try to keep a couple handy for reviving friends.
The selection of weapons is widely varied and most weapons offer something unique to them. This serves to add variety to the combat and differentiate weapons in the same classification from one another. My favourite example is the scimitar, which swings faster after each successive hit. The Katana has more base damage, but I really enjoyed getting behind some bosses and comboing their butts to death.
The most recent patch at the time of writing this added a quick heal feature which was highly requested from fans (Myself included.) which is a welcome change. Healing items are still rare, however you no longer have to access the inventory mid battle to use them. This small change shows that Daniel (The bloke who made the game) listens to his feedback, something many AAA developers could stand to learn from.
TL;DR
It's like Dark Souls with mice and simpler two-dimensional combat, if you like the Souls series or just challenging games in general then I highly suggest checking this game out.

Castle of Illusion is a remake of the 1990 Sega Genesis classic, which was considered one of the better Mickey Mouse games in the 16-bit era. I've played the original before, but far later in life, so I probably do not have the same level of nostalgia others may have with the game. Still, seeing as there was a remake out, I was curious on how the game would be reimagined to today's standards, and tried the new one out.
Story:
It's a very basic "rescue the damsel-in-distress" kind of story, with the damsel being Minnie Mouse, and the protagonist being Mickey. The main villain is a witch named Mizrabel, who looks like the evil queen from Snow White, and who is trying to steal Minnie's beauty. So, the game's story won't blow your mind, but given that it's a remake of an old Genesis platformer, it's passable.
Gameplay:
Castle of Illusion plays as you'd expect a traditional 2D platformer to play, for the most part. You try to reach the end of the stage, hopping on different platforms, and defeating your enemies by jumping on or throwing projectiles at them. Mickey controls really well, and despite the simple platforming mechanics, there is enough variety in the level design to definitely keep you interested in progressing from level to level. They did remove the butt-stomp from the original game, though, which is odd to me (why make the game even simpler?).
In addition to the 2D platforming from the original game are the 3D platforming sections. This is mostly seen in the hub world of the game, and in some of the boss battles. Unfortunately, the 3D platforming in this game are the parts I dislike the most, as jumps to platforms away and towards the screen are far to imprecise for me to judge. As a result, I found levels like the Dessert Factory to be far more cumbersome to play through than the rest of the game (which, admittedly, was quite easy). This game definitely could have gone without these 3D platforming sequences, as much of the game was already a 2D platformer, anyway.
Music:
This game, being a remake, borrows a lot of music from the original classic. The main difference in the score, however, is that it was now composed by Grant Kirkhope of Banjo-Kazooie fame. Thus, the songs from the original now have a different feel to them, being more whimsical, and more fairy-tale like (in other words, they now sound kind of like they came from Banjo Kazooie). Given that this game's story is the typical damsel-in-distress flavor, I felt this was a very fitting change. As usual, Kirkhope's compositions were very fun to listen to while playing this game, and was probably the biggest thing keeping my interest in this game.
Presentation:
Graphics-wise, this game does its job in showing off its colorful worlds, and definitely looks like a typical Mickey Mouse CGI cartoon would look like. Often, you'll see background events as you're playing (like an upcoming boss moving catching up to you from the background), making the game's environment look much livelier than the original game. I thought was a nice touch.
In addition to all this, this game has some pretty good voice-acting. There is a narrator who will give the player some insight to the story during the beginning of levels as the game progresses, giving the game more of the storybook feel. Mickey and Minnie, as far as I know, have their original voice actors acting as them, as well.
Conclusion:
At its core, I only thought this game was just good, but not great. The 2D platforming was very fun, but the 3D platforming segments really miffed me. I would say this is one of the games where the the soundtrack was the best aspects of the game, so I'd say definitely give it a listen. If you do find this game on sale, though, I'd say give it a shot, especially if you were a fan of the original game.

TL;DR If you are new to point and click games, this one is a good starting point for you to feel and enjoy the game type.
If not, however, then at least the art style and music is pretty welcoming.
Review:
I am honestly new to the point and click genre, I bought this game to try and dip my feet on these type of games and see how clod the water is. While I cannon comment on the genre itself, I can confidently say that this game is worth your time. It starts off elegantly and peacefully, and slowly builds up its momentum later in the story in a way that is very appreciating.
It took me around 16 hours to finish the game, But that is only because I was scratching my head over a few puzzles here and there and sometimes would go AFK. I believe it should take a regular player around 10 hours to finish the game (Even though there is an achievement to finish the game under 1 hour).
Story:
It fits the theme at least. Lighthearted, mysterious, wondrous, social, and overall family friendly.
While this game could have had a much more mature theme especially since a few mature elements were hinted around. Yet, the choice of crafting it in this direction fits perfectly with the aesthetics. it is passable when taking everything else into a count, not it alone however. If you were just to read the story alone you would feel very... childish, I guess?
Aesthetics and world design:
The art style combined with the mysterious unusual (not so magical) world of Broken Age is very beautiful. Everything feels in place in my opinion. A much more realistic or edgy art style would throw everything apart, likewise with the world and characters. It also accommodates well the story as well so all is well.
Characters:
Side characters first: They might not have much screen time, they mostly are just there to help you progress in the next act. Yet, some good amount of work was done on them. To have them fit the world they resign in, To have their characteristics be fitting to the environment, Their design and voice acting was superb as well. Hell, There is a talking tree that constantly insults you for being part of a race that cuts down trees, That was pretty clever in my book.
As for the main characters, Shay (The male) and Vella (The female). Honestly, I didn't like shay very much. Maybe because he doesn't have that much of an interesting story line. Maybe because I felt he was overshadowed by Vella. Or maybe just because I prefer female protagonists (Not a feminist, That is just an opinion of mine). in any case, while I find him lacking in some areas, He does provide with really hard puzzles.
As for Vella. She is by far the best character I see. She has conflict, motivation, reason, wits, and opportunity. her way of converting with others is damn humorous as well. I like everything about her. Nothing much about cons regarding her I can say.
Music:
Every song in every location is played out well and corresponds well with the theme of the areas. from soft strings to long pipes every instrument was used well and with care here. They are pretty catchy as well. It is not repetitive as well. Some areas use the same tone but different play-styles to mix up a bit and not have the same theme playing over and over. I wouldn't buy the music as a standalone. But it was nice overall.
Gameplay/Puzzles:
Easy to access, everything from the starter levels acts as a hidden tutorial. and most of what you have learned you will need to reuse time and time again to progress. Puzzles are not that hard, But sometimes you will be scratching your head, mostly because of how unusual the world in this game acts out. But over all, I would say it is pretty enjoyable and has a few good headscratchers here and there.
Rating: 7.5/10

Two things!
As I was much younger I loved the book "The Warlock of Firetop Mountain" and the many books that came after this, it started my year long affection to roleplaying games and adventures. You try to affect the game with your decissions, the newes fad in this category are "Visual Novels" - some of them are quite blatantly Dating Sims. Luckily this game doesn't fall into this category of "Visual Novel" or "Romantic Readalong". It has a dystopian backdrop, and some, well you can say demands. During the past months I developed a healthy - avoidance syndrome - towards this relatively new genre of games, but since so many of them landed now in my backlist, I'll play them. Some of them are good and interesting, the most are not. This game is no exception to the later group.
Second, the game was praised for the different and variable outcomes of the game. Ok, there are some choices, but the choices are leading to the same end result (not the epilogue - that isn't even a funny little thing with the room-mate, dear developers). I played it several times only to gain the achievements - but alone on the end result of this first part, I wouldn't buy the second part. You are very limited in the choices, and the outcome is with just little variations the same.
To a fan of this genre it might be a godsend, to all others it can become a burden and bore to play, it's winded up in it's own verbosity, it lacks a lot of humor (naivity of the protagonist isn't really funny) and the really good artworks are like a dull firework in a even duller story.
I'd vote for more ingenuity.
Postscriptum after some months: Yes, some people didn't found this review helpful - I can tell you why, because no one remembers nowadays the really good start of interactive novels. Read some Steve Jackson and Ian Livingston. Take up some dice and play Wizard of Firetop Mountain, Forest of Doom and others - and learn that there were good one, and bad ones - learn the difference why FF and Lone Wolf, maybe even Grailquest were good and while some of the "CYOA" and "Give yourself Goosebumps" Stuff alongside with "Endless Quest" from TSR were bad.
A cheesy story won't get better by fancy graphics. Period.

I love this game, when I was first looking at it I saw a lot of reviews complaining about act 2 and the story within. I picked this up during the summer sale and decided to give it a go a couple of days ago. I was completely hooked. It has a really interesting story and delightful visuals, it is super well crafted.
The negative reviews about the story in act two (such as "anything you make up will be better") are completely inaccurate for me. The story followed a pattern that I started to understand when I was swapping between characters and I thought the game followed a logical path.
The reviews about walkthroughs in the second half are quite true. The puzzles aren't completely unrelated and I think sometimes I was actually so focused on something that I had gleaned from a brief look at the walkthrough that I missed an obvious solution to the problem I was having. The game does a good job at hinting at what the characters need if you get it wrong, but it can be entirely frustrating when you just can't see the answer, particularly like in the second half where sometimes you need something from the person you are not playing as to help the one you are playing as (but now that you know that you'll know to look for it so you might be better off already).
Overall I got a little frustrated at times but I loved the clever quirks put into all of the characters and the silly outcomes of the puzzles (silly as in fun not as not matching to the rest of the story). I loved this game I would recommend it happily.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is an action side-scrolling platformer game with a very fluid combo system and well animated attacks, giving the player a sense of simply being awesome in combat.
I've played a lot of games, but nothing is quite as unique as Dust. The game gives the player the ability to move freely throughout the world, going to whichever areas they so desire to rack-up XP, explore or find hidden secrets in past levels.
The story in Dust is one surrounded by mystery, the protagonist, Dust, starts off with amnesia and cannot recollect a damn thing about his past, which I know is very cliche but it suits Dust's story just fine. The protagonist is alway accompanied by a cat-ferret-bat creature by the name of Fidget (who is also the cutest damn thing I've seen since Tali in Mass Effect), who offers humorous dialogue and grants the player a ranged attack. To clarify: I f*cking love Fidget.
Dust's combat system flows beautifully, utilizing a mere three buttons for attacks, the combat is simple but at the same time awe inspiring, easy to pick up on and very well made, when the player whipes out his/her first batch of enemies you immediately feel like an incredible badass and leaves you itching for more. As the game proceeds you acquire new abilities that complement your already formidible attack options and keep the game from getting stale, all the while maintaining a steady difficulty curve alongside an easy to understand XP and level-up system.
Graphics-wise: It's an indy game, you don't come into it expecting mind-blowing graphics. Dust uses a simple but lovable anthropomorphic cartoon art-style that is both charming and outright adorable, but also dark and serious when it needs to be. All perfected with an amazing musical score and top quality voice acting. As well, Dust makes numerous quips at the expense of the fourth wall and makes references to other games, like Resident Evil 4 and Castlevania.
The one flaw I've seen thus far is a somewhat finicky platform system. Sometimes if you don't land on a platform at exactly the right angle you're going through, which in a platformer game is a real kick to the groin.
In conclusion: Dust: An Elysian Tail is fun, fluid, and highly addictive. I definitely recommend anyone reading this to pick it up immediately.

Not worth the time to play let alone spend money on.  It's designed to completely trash your vault.  You can have one invader that will obliterate your entire structure.  If you happen to get very lucky and get a rare weapon you can survive for a bit, but they continue to send foes that can enter your vault with impunity.  The only invaders that are usually okay are the raiders because they are about equivalent in strength.  The mole rats and radroaches are very inconsistent in their strengths, sometimes they can be dispatched relatively easily, but other times they just mow down your entire fortress.  Deathclaws and Radscorpions almost always leave my vault with numerous dead dwellers.  I can't see a significant difference in dwellers that are level 25 and those that are level 1.  The main thing is the weapon they weild and the armor they wear and those aren't easy to obtain, especially the really good ones.  As a result, you can play along and think you're doing well when one invasion will literally decimate your forces and you'll struggle just to keep vault resources coming in enough just to let it survive, let alone prosper.  It's too random and you are too vulnerable to attack to make the game worthwhile, of course, this is what they want... they want you to spend money to get out of jams (and there are plenty of jams).  It is fun for awhile, but very disheartening to spend a few hours getting your vault established then to have one event destroy everything.  At least, I didn't spend any money on it (which is probably one reason game is so difficult, they almost make it that you have to spend money.)

Mafia 3, as much as I want to love the game for my admiration of the previous installments... I can't.
In my humble opinion, if this game wasn't set in the pre-established 'Mafia' universe and managed to avoid the on release PC cockups this game would of been a real win as it tackles a really interesting premise which does sadly end up falling off and becoming a plain old revenge story where Lincoln's character seems to end up taking a back seat and the age old gaming trope of nothing getting done without you doing it occurs. For example, the Black Mob at the start of the game are really struggling, until Lincoln comes home and makes everything nice and dandy again, which was a real problem for me as Lincoln basically becomes a one man army with only him being capable of taking down an entire crime family singlehandedly, which although they tried to justify how this is possibly by him being a highly trained black ops esque macho man from 'Nam with government connections just doesn't feel right to me, and isn't really what myself (and various other people, from what i've seen) wanted from an installment in the Mafia franchise.
When you partake in a game set in a time and setting where you're involved with organised crime, you want to feel a part of something whereas it seems like Lincoln's associates are merely pawns and are always bickering like children with one another (which I suppose was done to reiterate the harsh reality that the devs created that not everyone gets a happy life) and you never feel like they are truly involved in anything you are doing and are just doing you favours so you dont turn your Terminator-esque rampage on them, which isn't what people want to feel from a Mafia experience. People associate Mafia with family and a code of honor, which isn't prevailant here at all.
People consuming media related to the Mafia are generally hungry for feeling the power and respect of rising through the ranks of the Mafia with the hope of every game finishing with you ending up as the Don of your own crime family (usually the ultimate goal of any Mafia related media), but you don't get this here, you get an empty feeling of being an outsider who just happens to be in a position where 3 mobsters kick up to him because only he alone can accomplish what droves of men with better guns and equipment than him can't (plot armor?).
To me, this game just seemed to get lost in not knowing what it wanted to be, a story driven game with a deep commentary about racial oppression in 60's heavily right wing America, an open world gameplay driven experience with lots of mindless shooting people and taking over the various areas offered (which was done better in Godfather 2, IMO), or a game about organised crime where, in the name of revenge you take out the traditional sicilian mafia and become the don of a new era of criminal via unconditional means and try to do things differently. This is probably the games most glaring issue (although, not forgetting about the lack of character customisation, which is a really important part of making you feel connected to a character, IMO...) as the previous installments knew what they wanted to be, sticking to the more popular and sought after world of italian organised crime families and allowing people to live out their fantasies of becoming a made man and living in the dangerous world of a criminal.
Although, It's not all bad though, I found the gunplay in this game to actually be pretty fun, I wouldn't say it feels realistic at all, however, it does feel really satisfying to play as the gun sounds for the most part are decent and aside from the odd issues here and there the gameplay is pretty solid, however after the first few 'takeovers' you quickly realise that it's just basically a rinse and repeat to advance the story to completion which is kinda dissapointing.
Anyway, if this game would have been a new IP about the ethnic minority protagonist Lincoln Clay battling the mob and fighting racial oppression in the 60's, I feel it would of left less of a bad taste in my mouth as this didn't really feel like a true Mafia experience, aside from the returning characters from previous installments being in this game. That being said, I think this game should be used as a learning experience for the game devs and should there be a Mafia 4, if they listen to peoples opinions on their shortcomings and really polish what they did well (which is a fair bit, for all my dissapointments I still dont regret purchasing the game or spending my time playing it, I should add. And by no means is this a 'bad' game like some people are making out) I feel confident that they will be able to make something truly great.
Also, what we see of the prevailant characters are really interesting and make you want more - which sadly never seems to come into fruition. As much as you want to, it's hard to end up truly caring for any of the characters despite their initial interesting back stories and motivations as it all takes the back seat for the revenge. For example, your accomplice John Donnivan is clearly a shady CIA type and you want to know more, but nothing is really explored (suppose they are holding out for the 'Nam based DLC they announced, *sigh...)
All that said,im still giving the game a positive review as i'd still reccomend buying it as it offers a somewhat unique experience, fun gun battles and when the story comes into play it is actually enjoyable to follow, but with my experience from the previous games I found it hard to get past the shortcomings that were present. (No Customisation or Suits available on release? C'mon. Atleast let me wear a nice three piece suit so I can look good whilst fixing the entire Mafia problem in NB...)

What can I say about The Binding of Isaac. Well, first it's both addictive and infuriating. The premise is brilliant...it blends the controversy of religious nutbaggery with hardcore old school gaming....it may be a first and I say 'bravo'.
The mechanics are simple, you go from room to room, dungeon to dungeon, fighting deadly mobs with powers that increase as you down more bosses and collect more items. Should you die (and you will, many many many times) you lose everything and start over. Dark Souls anyone? Also, if you die it's by your own mistake, the game isn't cheap in that regard. The dungeons are also randomly generated, so it's a different experience every time which is also really cool.
This is by the same fella that helmed Super Meat Boy, so you should know what to expect. This is indie gaming at it's finest. Support it folks. You get the same rehashed AAA nonsense every year, different names, same packages, and you shell out big bucks for it. How about celebrating some real innovation? Spend the 4.99 and dive into your new addiction. Indie gaming...we need more of it!

Alright, I got a lot to say about this one because it really just baffles me.
I don't understand how people forgive Alan Wake for all the glaring issues it has. I guess I can give it credit for trying to be unique, but underneath that... it tries to do a lot of things but fails to do them well. The only redeeming qualities for me are the visuals, sound and atmosphere. The facial animations really haven't aged well though; too often descending into uncanny valley territory.
The combat is just frustrating and tedious. Most of the difficulty seems to be movement, positioning, timing, and to a lesser extent resource management based. It isn't really that hard, just strict when it comes to mistakes. Most importantly though, it just never feels fun, satisfying, or engaging.
The light mechanic only serves to take control of the pace of battle away from the player, meaning most of the time you're just sitting around waiting for things to be vulnerable so you can shoot them. Everything has to be time consuming.
Speaking of pace, almost every time enemies spawn the game goes into a slow-motion cutscene. This really takes away from the horror aspect of the game (if you can even call it a horror game, or a game at all) when you know nothing can ever really get the drop on you.
And speaking of enemies, there are only about three or four of them. The way the game amps up the challenge is by just throwing larger amounts of them at you as you progress. There are no real boss fights either, unless you count utility vehicles and inanimate objects coming to life or "defend this position" segments.
When you do have to run, Alan can only sprint for a measly few seconds before he has an asthma attack. There's also a dodge mechanic that's tied to your sprint key, which is unreliable and only works half of the time.
Nothing about the story or characters intrigues me. I really don't see it as the massive step in video game narrative that everyone else does, it just takes itself too seriously and comes across as campy and pretentious. I'm sick of games trying to prove themeselves as a relevant artform when they don't need to, they always have been. Stop trying to make them like TV shows or movies, let them be their own thing.
The plot is that you're a best-selling novel writer whose cliché horror story is becoming true, yet it takes the majority of the game to establish this point even though it's obvious from the very start. Also, your wife is missing, because of course she is.
Alan narrates everything you do, and his voice is just... weird. Awkward. I don't think it's so much an issue with the voice acting as it is the audio equipment used, it really doesn't sound right.
Characters constantly reference other, better horror stories and authors that remind me that I could be doing something better with my time.
There are long segments where you just follow someone around while they repeatedly tell Alan he's crazy. When I'm playing these segments I just want to get to the game segments. When I'm playing the game segments I just want the level to be over. It's a cycle of constant boredom.
The game is structured like an episodic miniseries. I really don't get why some games do this whole "Previously, on >insert show here<" rubbish, it's just really tacky to me. I don't even like it when TV shows do it so why the hell would it work in a game?
The only thing to keep you going is the hope that there's some sort of payoff or revelation at the end.
*Yawn*
Oh yeah, and there's product placement. Yup. Buy Energizer! Their batteries last for a staggering five seconds!
The irony is Alan Wake would probably make a better TV show, or hell, even a novel. But the way I see it there is just no sense slogging your way through this game for what it offers. It doesn't hold my attention at all. Then again, I'm of a small minority, and many people will just downvote me. So who knows, maybe everyone played a different game to me. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Castle of Illusion is a remake of the 1990 Sega Genesis classic, which was considered one of the better Mickey Mouse games in the 16-bit era. I've played the original before, but far later in life, so I probably do not have the same level of nostalgia others may have with the game. Still, seeing as there was a remake out, I was curious on how the game would be reimagined to today's standards, and tried the new one out.
Story:
It's a very basic "rescue the damsel-in-distress" kind of story, with the damsel being Minnie Mouse, and the protagonist being Mickey. The main villain is a witch named Mizrabel, who looks like the evil queen from Snow White, and who is trying to steal Minnie's beauty. So, the game's story won't blow your mind, but given that it's a remake of an old Genesis platformer, it's passable.
Gameplay:
Castle of Illusion plays as you'd expect a traditional 2D platformer to play, for the most part. You try to reach the end of the stage, hopping on different platforms, and defeating your enemies by jumping on or throwing projectiles at them. Mickey controls really well, and despite the simple platforming mechanics, there is enough variety in the level design to definitely keep you interested in progressing from level to level. They did remove the butt-stomp from the original game, though, which is odd to me (why make the game even simpler?).
In addition to the 2D platforming from the original game are the 3D platforming sections. This is mostly seen in the hub world of the game, and in some of the boss battles. Unfortunately, the 3D platforming in this game are the parts I dislike the most, as jumps to platforms away and towards the screen are far to imprecise for me to judge. As a result, I found levels like the Dessert Factory to be far more cumbersome to play through than the rest of the game (which, admittedly, was quite easy). This game definitely could have gone without these 3D platforming sequences, as much of the game was already a 2D platformer, anyway.
Music:
This game, being a remake, borrows a lot of music from the original classic. The main difference in the score, however, is that it was now composed by Grant Kirkhope of Banjo-Kazooie fame. Thus, the songs from the original now have a different feel to them, being more whimsical, and more fairy-tale like (in other words, they now sound kind of like they came from Banjo Kazooie). Given that this game's story is the typical damsel-in-distress flavor, I felt this was a very fitting change. As usual, Kirkhope's compositions were very fun to listen to while playing this game, and was probably the biggest thing keeping my interest in this game.
Presentation:
Graphics-wise, this game does its job in showing off its colorful worlds, and definitely looks like a typical Mickey Mouse CGI cartoon would look like. Often, you'll see background events as you're playing (like an upcoming boss moving catching up to you from the background), making the game's environment look much livelier than the original game. I thought was a nice touch.
In addition to all this, this game has some pretty good voice-acting. There is a narrator who will give the player some insight to the story during the beginning of levels as the game progresses, giving the game more of the storybook feel. Mickey and Minnie, as far as I know, have their original voice actors acting as them, as well.
Conclusion:
At its core, I only thought this game was just good, but not great. The 2D platforming was very fun, but the 3D platforming segments really miffed me. I would say this is one of the games where the the soundtrack was the best aspects of the game, so I'd say definitely give it a listen. If you do find this game on sale, though, I'd say give it a shot, especially if you were a fan of the original game.

I'm not one to enjoy using the term "souls-like" because of the endless abuse the term's received. People seem to relate any third-person RPG (or just any RPG) with Dark Souls because DARK SOULS DA BEST GAME EVER, ALL GAMES AR JUS BADER DARK SOULS. However, this game is quite honestly a major take from Dark Souls. It takes a similar approach to lore and a similar approach to gameplay.
It's very punishing. It starts off with no explanation, just "run around, hit things, get hit, die and kill," which must be quite frustrating for players not familiar with a Souls game. Inventory system is like Dark Souls and not Demon's Souls in that it only tracks the gear that is "equipped" as far as weight. Otherwise, you can carry five tons of gear. This gets really annoying as nothing is sorted really well. Inventory screen's a 3 block tall grid with about 5 or less blocks horizontal with little arrows you have to click to sort through. It's clunky to go through the inventory screen like this, and it's horrible if you've moved the bottom most part of the inventory screen rightwards and need a healing item, as the healing items are all the way leftwards. The game does not pause whilst managing the inventory, like the Souls games. You can, however, pause the game and get the typical "Unpause, Load, Settings, Exit" screen by pressing Escape.
It starts off fine enough with a handful of enemies that will hurt you and punish you if you don't play careful. Later, it becomes mired in overabundance of enemies more akin to DS2. Instead of giving you more reasonable challenge, it desires you to attempt to "pull" a single enemy's attention like the less-polished parts of Dark Souls and the general makeup of DS2.
Now, reading that, I'd like to make a clear statement. I define two things when playing a game, or at least try to: There is difficulty, where you are presented with a challenge that you must struggle and learn to overcome by means of understanding the obstacle or enemy and proceeding with tact to surmount whatever is the challenge; Then there is tedium, where you are presented with an abundance of obstacles by various forms (i.e. overabundance of health in place of movesets and AI that require stratagem, overabundance of enemies in place of well-defined AI, etc. more in the way of quantity over quality) more often in a repetitive manner (i.e. fight one million annoying swarming enemies to get to the big bad and then get screwed up by him). I feel the game is rushed in the way of the end. In place of large, drawn out locations with traps and perhaps even puzzles, you are instead greeted with a ridiculous amount of aggressive enemies that seem to desire to make Shrine of Amana look like a kiddy pool
.
There's absolutely nil on the lore. Dark Souls gave you insight into the lore not just from cutscenes, but as through the character maker. Preset faces were common looks of people of different lands. Then of course were item descriptions which've become so infamous with the Souls series. This has next to nothing. Names are thrown around as well as places, but there's no substance or characterization worth nothing for to add character to any location or person. In Dark Souls, you could summise that people from Carim were shifty, keen, and ultimately mysterious from interactions with characters Lautrec and Oswald, and from description of the preset face in character creation. You have nothing here. This person is from here. That person did that. The game's world in the way of gameplay is already rather small and uncomfortable in its design (another note taken from Dark Souls 2's poor design?) to the point where this poor lore removes even more substance from the game.
There's very little in the way of content. Very few weapons in each category of Short Swords, Long Swords, Curved Swords, Greatswords, Pointy Sticks, Smashy Things, and Crispy-Critter-Cookers; very few pieces of armor; very few shields; very few accessories. Yes, $10 game, I know. I'm still going to complain because I spent money on it and I'm thinking you're thinking of doing the same. Don't expect to get much out of the game in the way of playtime. It's a shortened Dark Souls/Dark Souls 2 with budget cuts on everything.
Gameplay's annoying half the time. Birds have a tendency to twirl around you violently instead of doing "dive bombs" you'd expect a bird to do. Bulls really hug onto you with their heads and their charges are anywhere from useless-stupid-flailing to ow-ow-ow. It's not fun to fight them, even though it's definitely not difficult to beat them. The varieties of rats are rather intelligent. They won't let you get away unless you absolutely exit their "leash" area. They block often and attack viciously as often. It's an active effort for the most part to fight them, at least in my time as a Spear and Shield user. Solid AI on the enemies, but this becomes frustrating as I've said earlier where enemies become numerous and globbed. It's not impossible to do, it's just not fun, at least for me.
Now, the final boss has rubbed me the wrong way. I've yet to beat him, and I'm sure I will eventually, but I really dislike this kind of thing. The boss has a very simple moveset of "stand idle and get destroyed." This is aided by his ability to call in very aggressive and horrid creatures that have served as a verifiable nightmare through my playtime. Stamina consumption is so great I'm left breathless in between dodging the boss' attacks and the attacks of his little pets. I've discovered, however,
.
I'm really interested in seeing what the dev does in the future, as this game simply reeks of amateur design and lack of thorough polish which is easily resolved by constant effort and a desire to improve. I'm not expecting any changes to the game in any major way to cure my ills with it since it's not one of those horrid Early-Access titles, so I'm afraid I'll have to settle for negative on it. However, I hope the dev takes well the criticism and improves. My main problems stems from later level design, truly, where there stands tedium in place of challenge. Consider drawing out the map with a variety and combination of traps and enemies that require tact to get past in a way different from "juggle 3 giant rats that really don't like you at the same time".

That evil, no-good hag of a witch Mizrabel (HA, Miserable...get it?) is at it again—no longer content with attempting to murder Snow White for being prettier, she's kidnapped Mickey Mouse's main squeeze Minnie in an attempt to steal her youth. Armed only with his plucky attitude, dogged determination and a mean throwing arm, Mickey immediately sets out to rescue the love of his life from Mizrabel's lair, the titular Castle of Illusion.
Castle of Illusion takes the 1990 Sega Genesis title and spiffs it up with some voice-acting and sharp graphics, but at its core it remains a side-scrolling, two-dimensional platformer.
It looks like Sega Studios Australia enjoyed twisting the concept of "side-scrolling", though. The linear stages mix up the traditional "go right" design by taking advantage of the new three-dimensional engine. Paths weave into the background or curve along cylindrical towers in twisting, circuitous routes that double back on each other at unexpected moments. Some stages even shift to a top-down perspective, allowing Mickey free, unfettered access to all three dimensions of movement.
Also new in this remake is a hub area where Mickey can roam around, viewing anything he's unlocked and can select levels to journey to, provided he has enough gems to unlock them.
The levels are whimsical affairs - Mickey travels through exotic locales like haunted forests, undersea ruins, and a world of sugar and candy found within a cup of tea. Accompanied by the ever-present narrator, Mickey navigates these fantastical lands in pursuit of Mizrabel's henchmen and the seven rainbow gems they carry. These gems will open a path to the boss witch herself at the top of the Castle.
Of course, with new dimensions comes a change in controls. Mickey's jumping skills are serviceable, but feel weightless. This shift makes leaping difficult to control, and the top-down segments can aggravate the problem with the lack of depth perception—it's sometimes hard to know if Mickey has jumped high enough to clear his jump.
Swimming segments are where the controls suffer the most. Mickey has all the maneuverability of a steamboat, and requires constant buttonmashing to travel with any speed. Mercifully, these swimming sections are both infrequent and brief.
Other than the somewhat floaty controls, there are no real flaws in Castle of Illusion. It's a short game that's easy to complete in a night or two, and it offers collectibles for those who want some replay. It's charming and well-polished, but players craving challenge might be disappointed. On the other hand, people wanting to relax with something that doesn't require a huge investment of time or effort should consider joining Mickey on his newest mousecapade.

I think this game deserves credit for making some ballsy decisions in terms of puzzle design.
For my experience it meant that there were a lot of interesting puzzles, but at times it also seemed very unintuitive to a point, where I wasn't able to tell, if I was going in the right direction or not.
I got through this game in 10 hours, which seems to be the average for the main story of the game according to
At times I felt I must've been moving very slowly through the game for the exact reasons mentioned above. I would spend a lot of time walking back and forth at certain points, because I was missing some or clue or at times disagreed completely with the intended solution(
).
That's about it for the negatives, which most of the time was a positive.
Another particularly great thing about the game was the story - especially the first half. It fooled me on several occasions. I'm only sad that the end of the story wasn't elaborated a bit further. Might've been due to a lack of exploration on my part, but I think that just signifies the story was interesting enough to want to know more.
I also really liked how well the game played with a controller. I didn't realise this until halfway into the game, but the game has implemented a really nice selection mechanism in the right analog stick. The left analog stick works like a regular cursor, while the right analog stick drags the cursor to interactable elements on the screen.  Other controls in terms of selecting and using items etc.
Finally, I really enjoyed the art style too. I'm quite surprised at how well they managed to make important elements stand out in this style, where colours sort of blend together a lot. Voice acting was top notch too, but even more I liked the script, which was executed excellent by the voice actors. There was a lot of humor in the game of all sorts that made the game a lot more enjoyable; especially while trying different item combinations that were commented upon by the characters in the game.
To summarize: It's a quality production with fun puzzles and an interesting story that is supported by good writing, good voice acting and beautiful art.

Learning to Manage Chaos is Part 1 of the Dysfunctional Systems visual novel series. It follows the story of Winter Harrison, a student at some kind of... orginization? It's never too clear. Regardless, you follow the story of Winter and help to make choices that lead to multiple endings, each with varying differences.
The story is amazing. It takes place during a futuristic, post-apocalypse setting, where technology to travel between planets in an instant is available. The characters are all unique and very engaging, making you take sides very often in the story. (Go, Winter!~) For someone like me who likes to escape reality (assignments most of all) it is amazing. The artwork is goregeous. An almost rustic, stylized and crisp style brings alive, simple yet powerful character designs and image stills for the story events. If you're someone like me who loves a good browse through artwork, the images are available after a certain point.
Finally, the music. What's better than a soundtrack that caresses your ears like a silk glove on your bare bre- arms. I mean arms. What can be better than that? If said soundtrack comes with the game once you purchase it. Done and done.
In short, this game is a must-have for your steam library this Chirstmas, with a soundtrack to keep your ears warm by the fire.

Man, I really wanted to like this game... but I just didn't.
This game almost feels like two separate entities put together which doesn't feel coherent.
You have the main story missions and its proper quality cutscenes which advances the plot on the one hand, and the bland, optional mission-filled open world on the other that feels like a chore to get through in order to get to the next actual interesting main story mission.
The gameplay loop is something like this: Speak to boss, speak to underboss, kill/interrogate a POI 4-5 times, speak to underboss, kill/interrogate a bigger POI (main mission), speak to boss, assign racket. That's just for one district and there are like 9 of them or so. THIS IS ALL YOU'RE DOING IN THIS GAME. Get's boring real god damn quick even though the shooting mechanics are solid. Also, there's no fast travel, so you're gonna do a lot of driving!
This game has some of the most uninspiring open world activies. It's like the developers were held at gunpoint being specifically told not to be creative at all when it comes to that. Or maybe they spent all the budget on the soundtrack.
The open world feels so tacked on and unneccessary. If you could just skip all that and only do the main mission, it'd be a lot shorter game but ultimately a lot better game.
Pros:
- Solid shooting/cover mechanics on foot, feels meaty
- Decent animations (some very brutal)
- Fantastic soundtrack
- Overall nicely directed cutscenes and voice acting
- The main story plotline is engaging enough, but is hindered by the awful pacing of having to do grindy missions to get the next interesting one
- Interior lighting looks good
- Driving mechanics (if you're inclined to like the style of GTA IV driving)
Cons:
- Bad shooting mechanics in vehicles
- The jarring and random shifts in in-game cutscenes to prerendered cutscenes
- Very inconsistent graphics, it's only interior/indoors that it looks consistenly decent, outside is just a mess, some nightscenes can look good with the rain and all, but more often than not it looks bad, which ties in to the next point:
- Very bad textures, low resolution upscaled, horrific skybox
- Bad, uninspired mission design, which results in the game feeling like a chore or a grind
- Bad pacing
-♥♥♥♥♥♥poor optimization. I run a Strix 1070 OC with i5 6600k and I couldn't even get consistent 60 FPS in 1080p.
- Not the best AI
- Driving mechanics (if you're inclined to like the style of GTA V's more arcady driving)
I paid 30€ for my copy which is a lot lower than what Steam sells it for, but I still feel ripped off. I'd definitely not pay more than 15€ for this at its current state.
If you really must have this game wait until it's on sale or something, and then ONLY do the main missions and the absolute minimum of "side" missions required to progress further in the main story, because that's the only redeeming factor as the main missions are the most varied and comes with quite decent cutscenes.
At the current pricepoint: Ultimately cannot recommend.

I went into this with very low expectations, looking for something casual but with enough gameplay to keep me interested.
I should note I'm a fairly big fallout fan, played it since Fallout 1 back in them there 90's, and almost every game since. The use of fallouts music, sound effects and pipboy cartoon style graphics are almost enough to garner my interest from the start, but the game has enough merit to keep me going for at least a few days.
The game is essentially a real time anthill strategy game, with about the same level of depth as a reasonable board game. You construct a vault from small number of settlers, add various rooms, and assign your settlers to work in the rooms, do quests outside the vault, and then theres the breeding... which is highly amusing.  you put a couple in a room together and if/when they hit it off, they disappear into the back of the room and the lady comes out pregnant. There is a degree of entertainment here just in making sure you don't breed out the genetic diversity from your settlers. Not too difficult but but novel nonetheless.
Earlier I mentioned realtime. When I say realtime there is a lot of waiting around... the idea (from the publisher) being that you get sick enough of waiting and start paying to win (in the form of nuka cola quantum bottles which speed up various tasks). I should note that 'pay to win' type games are something I normally run a mile from, but Its buried enough that It doesn't interfere with the gameplay for me.  In regards to waiting around this is (primarily though many things take time) for your teams to go on quests and for the babies to gestate, and then grow up (about 4 hours each in real time). One nice thing is that the game time keeps running (for about four hours max I think) whenever you shut it down, so ideal if you have a real life as well. You can come back and spin the plates, match up some new couples, set off on a new mission etc, and then step away again.
Quick summary.
Great if you like casual wee strategy games with about a board game level of depth, and indeed being a fallout fan will help keep you interested.
It is addictive, and really quite fun, great for hourly doses a few times a day.
Biggest negative is that this was a mobile game ported to PC, and the interface is a little clumsy as a result, but still bearable. Pay to win not an issue if you are fairly patient and don't need to binge this game.

What can I say about The Binding of Isaac. Well, first it's both addictive and infuriating. The premise is brilliant...it blends the controversy of religious nutbaggery with hardcore old school gaming....it may be a first and I say 'bravo'.
The mechanics are simple, you go from room to room, dungeon to dungeon, fighting deadly mobs with powers that increase as you down more bosses and collect more items. Should you die (and you will, many many many times) you lose everything and start over. Dark Souls anyone? Also, if you die it's by your own mistake, the game isn't cheap in that regard. The dungeons are also randomly generated, so it's a different experience every time which is also really cool.
This is by the same fella that helmed Super Meat Boy, so you should know what to expect. This is indie gaming at it's finest. Support it folks. You get the same rehashed AAA nonsense every year, different names, same packages, and you shell out big bucks for it. How about celebrating some real innovation? Spend the 4.99 and dive into your new addiction. Indie gaming...we need more of it!

Introduction
What do Duran Duran, toaster repairing and a post nuclear wasteland all have in common?
Around 1988 I played Wasteland 1 on a C64. It was a cross between Bards Tale 1 type combat with Ultima IV type world movement. It was one of the first games to include a persistent world. The manual asked you to create a copy of the game disks so that choices and consequences you experienced during the game were saved. If you suspected your entire party was going to be wiped out or a gaming catastrophe was imminent and tried pulling out the floppy – it failed.
You were prompted to read chapters of text from a booklet at key points in the game to further the storyline. Wasteland 1 was released in a world without many hard drives so computer memory was restricted. The story booklet also provided a form of copy protection. The developers included fake text to give cheaters a hard time and prevent players from reading ahead and discovering the plot.
Time passes and its now 2015. It fascinates me that I have read reviews about Wasteland 2 from RPG “experts” who were not even alive in 1988. It’s been a long time. Reading these thoughts from youngsters about a sequel to a game they have never played was slightly interesting and mostly offensive. Saying that, I know nostalgia can be a powerful thing. I am glad that the passage of time has faded my memory. Some days I believe any old game released in the 1985-1995 period was a great game as there wasn’t many around. Or more accurately I could not afford that many – heck I was in school. Just look at me now with Steam or GOG – I don’t even have to leave my mother’s basement :)
WL2 is set in Arizona after a nuclear event destroyed much of civilisation. It is a RPG where you can control a party of four rookie desert rangers that have been asked to investigate the murder of a veteran named Ace. As your progress through the game you can recruit NPCs that join your party who bring along their own skillsets. Lacking a medic in your party? Recruit a Doctor. 15 long years have passed since WL1.
Character design
When you begin a new game you can create a party from scratch or import and amend existing rangers. In an attempt to show traditional RPG credentials – the developers have given each character seven attributes using the CLASSIC method (never heard of it either – hardly classic). These include Strength, Intelligence and Awareness.
Interestingly Luck and Charisma also appear. These two seem to be a throwback to D&D and live gaming with a Dungeon Master. Developers seem to struggle finding a real use for them and most players will therefore roll a low score in these to obtain higher scores in Strength, Endurance etc. I would have preferred a more balanced approach regards the attributes so that they were all equally important depending on the build or concept for that character.
It’s almost become fact now that Intelligence is the most important attribute in WL2 as that determines the ability to learn skills. Pretty soon it becomes apparent that unlike many RPGs your attributes do not always link with or enhance your skills. For example a character with 1 ST can be highly skilled and effective in a skill called Brute Force. This disparity is not quite fatal but a poor show nevertheless.
The skillset of your characters are the key factor in determining on whether you will be successful – at anything. The skills are divided into three groups, general, weapon and knowledge and each has ten levels of expertise. There are far too many for any one character or party of four to excel at everything. You need a plan.
If you want to recruit other party members beyond your base four – learn the Leadership skill as that improves their combat abilities and keeps them in check.
If you prefer to shoot first and chat later – you may want to ditch the three conversation skills.
Over my 100 hours of game time – I found that levelling is quite generous and any reasonable INT team member would gain sufficient skill points over the game. I also found that combat skills and ‘how to open stuff’ skills were used 95% of the time.
Skills such as Animal Whisperer, Alarm Disarming and Surgeon were hardly required. The Toaster Repair skill just seemed to be included without much thought and relied heavily on pre-game knowledge. For example, if you fixed a toaster in day 5 of gaming and subsequently acquired an item, that same item would only be of value if you happen to have it in your inventory on day 55. Items from toasters are not marked as quest items. Poor show.
Game Engine
The game engine has a two-fold approach. Movement across the world map is a 2D affair – think Indiana Jones in his airplane. 95% of the game is top down, 2.5D isometric movement with a camera that can zoom out and turn left or right. Graphics were sufficient and I cannot remember any bugs or glitches. Sometimes the game would slow down a trifle in heavy combat or densely populated areas.
The local map representation of towns and places you visit is just diabolical. I struggled to find any use for it apart from seeing where your party is in relation to your entry point. For some reason the developers camouflaged the entries/exits to buildings and other locations on the local map so it takes the gamer about 50 hours to even realise they are there. Not fantastic. I thought we were going back to Wasteland of 1987 – not some crappy game from 1957. Ask the developers when Ultima Underworld was released – for goodness sake!
Summary
There are a lot of things wrong with this game. I would really like to know if players spent more time on opening things or in the dialogue system. I would like to know why in the Rail Nomad area I had to criss-cross the various maps about 100 times.
I want to know why the local map is crap.
Looking back to all the press about it, I wonder about the ‘choice’ you are given at the beginning of the game and why so many journalists sang its praises from high.
I couldn’t remember which items emerged from toasters.
Then I met Simon Le Bon in a random encounter that was Hungry Like a Wolf and then Frankie told me to Relax. Then my heart just melted away and this somewhat not that bad game became something special.
I really enjoyed storytelling for once even though some of it was boring and mundane.
I really enjoyed building up my team of four and wanted them to do well. I watched over them, groomed them and bent them to my will. I was proud each time the radio sent me a message back promoting them in the field of operations.
I spent 100 hours on this game to completion and the only reason I didn’t do another playthrough was because I have some urgent business working through a list of 71 other decent games.

***THIS IS A VERY LONG REVIEW/THERE WILL BE A TL;DR AT THE BOTTOM***
After a much longer length of gameplay than expected, I'd finally completed Dark Maus, albeit with a sour taste in my mouth. Before you read, please know I am a veteran Souls player. I've spent, literally, thousands of hours in these games, collectively. Also know, that I don't see any of those four titles as perfect. Each one has some pretty strong weaknesses, but generally these are overlooked because the games are so well crafted. I strongly urge everyone AGAINST using this in reference to, or as part of the Souls series style of games. This game differs heavily and it's most prominent features make it more akin to a horror game with action/rpg elements.
Dark Maus left a very sour taste in my mouth. The game started out great. A simple, yet elegant aesthetic, relatively tight gameplay, and it seemingly functioned well. I guess it was all there right? Absolutely not. The first few hours of this game are a sickening ruse.
In my opinion, this game embodies what an outside perspective of all Souls titles is; no story, extraordinarily brutal gameplay, and absolutely no explanation of anything. These are the negative tropes that really drive people away, and yet they account for most of the game.
Towards the end, the game's progression started scaling a wall and never stopped. Dark Maus went from reasonable to insane over the course of one level and never dropped difficulty. Packs of enemies fill rooms, TRAPS EVERYWHERE, tight spaces and terrifyingly aggressive, intelligent enemies. The second half of the game is a veritable gauntlet until the very last boss. The way these were combined made the game feel needlessly difficult. My only drive to finish was that I wouldn't let a cheap imitation beat me.
Dark Maus feels like someone glossed over a list of items to cook a dish with, crossed off one line, and added a few odds and ends that were thought to liven up a dish;
You. Can't. Do. That.
There's a reason why Souls games work. Specifically because there are so many titles on that list and have only improved because of the design progression. For the most part, every subsequent title was an improvement in a core area of the game (I have slight hang-ups with saying that about Dark Souls 2. However, the DLC and SOTFS redeemed the game, albeit at the cost of almost two and a half games worth of purchases and another year's wait to get a functioning product, but I digress).
^ ***To counter my above statement, in favor of the lone developer of Dark Maus, it is just one dude working here, I believe. Not a whole studio. So, he deserves some credit for making a pretty functional game solo, even if it did rehash most of it's substance from another game series.***
Surely, you must be wondering how a game tanks so shortly into it's livelyhood. To give an abreviated list:
-A lack of ways to counter obstacles (I.E. No backstabs or parries. Staggering is wonky and unpredictable outside exploits.)
-A learning curve that evolves into a 90 degree angle at the drop of a dime
-A poor iteration of existing mechanics from Souls games
-What I can only assume to be less than thought out enemy progression/level design
-Literally, no lore
-An even worse direction than people perceive of Souls games
-Generic and unrewarding boss style encounters (Only one boss was difficult. Artificially at that.)
But it does things differently, and different isn't always bad, right? Perhaps some of the new iterations are positive? So, as an homage that chose to be brave and stray from the fundamental design, how does it differ? Well;
-No on-demand healing. That's right. There is no one button command for healing. As far as I can tell, this was a purposeful feature. Dark Maus' lack of reliable healing was set in place to really instill dread in the heart of the player in combination with another mechanic I'll address shortly. This made each camp fire feel miles apart; contributing to a rather soul-crushing journey. Now, this would be great if tuned PROPERLY, as this became ferociously annoying. Dark Maus felt as though an estus flask system was intended and I believe would have enriched the game; creating a much more fair environment for new and veteran players alike.
^ ***To amend the above, there are actually healing items in the game. However, they are VERY few and far between and only usable from the inventory menu which you cannot physically move while inside of. Also, the menus are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to navigate quickly, as they feel very flimsy and disorganized.***
-Dark Maus features a semi-unique torch system. This torch provides light in the darker, and most dangerous, areas of the game. It functions on a timer; really reinforcing that dread, as you never know where the next fire to refresh your light, health, and spells will be. This is actually the strongest feature of the game. Souls could never pry that terror out of me. Dark Maus is ♥♥♥♥ing scary.
-The Abilities system. Entertaining at first, grown stale by the end. Sadly, most of these are rendered useless. Only a few really matter and you get enough points to use all of them by the end. So, really they're kind of arbitrary. Honestly, these should have been trimmed down to a smaller list and incorporated as part of the base game design, rather than locking them away and saving them for later. For example: your standard dodge/dash action, which is your best buffer versus damage, has ZERO invincibility frames, as opposed to the natural I-frames given to you in Souls games. While this is quickly remedied through the abilities function, this shouldn't even be considered in the formula, especially when the entirety of the game is a more claustrophobic and hazardous version of another game that's already considered very challenging; favoring my above statement of the abilities being a poor system.
-The world as a whole wants you to die. Seriously, Daniel, who hurt you, dude? I jest, but I've never felt more singled out and targeted before. The land will surround and wash over you with waves of unforgiving natives of a feral mindset. There is no reason, only death. So, this sounds a lot like Dark Souls, right? Wrong. The core difference is that the Souls games are designed with perception in mind. The top down style in combination with the torch system doesn't bode well for being alert to dangers. Most of my early game deaths were because I couldn't appropriately account for what was out of my vision. The game punishes you just for existing, where as Souls only punishes you for mistakes. The Souls series shows you everything, and allows you to react to it. That's a world of a difference.
^ ***It should be noted that this is more of a design limitation. I could not expect the same level of detail from Dark Maus. However, it does show how taking 3/4 of a forumla and swapping it in where it might not belong inhibits a game.***
So, there lie the key differences. Overall, not terrible iterations. In fact, this game could have been truly unique if Daniel had more time to polish it. Personally, I'm overjoyed to see large studios and indie developers alike take a crack at the Souls formula. It means I get to play more of these awesome games that I love. Especially, filling that void after Bloodborne: The Old Hunters and before Dark Souls 3.
***TL;DR/FINAL VERDICT***
6/10
Dark Maus was a decent attempt at recreating the Souls style gameplay. However, ultimately it failed, in my eyes, due to being too quick to change certain things in the formula. I would only recommend this game to those who are truly curious and content to get a cheap Souls thrill. I don't recommend this game to anyone who hasn't been exposed to the Souls genre, because there is very little chance you'll reap any enjoyment out of this.

Dead TrailZ:
~~~~~~~~~
Armed with a machine gun, EMP shotgun, mines and smoke grenades, you are a spotter / sniper. You have to protect your runner - make sure his runs are successful by picking up all supply boxes and return to the train without being torn apart by your friendly Zombies!
Dead Trailz is a First Person Shooter/Tower Defence game which offers 2 types of modes in this current version (early access). You will be able to play either runner or strategy modes.
In the runner mode, you will have to protect your faithful friend as long as you can, so he can pick up as many supply boxes as possible without being eaten by despicable zombies. In this mode, you will have tasks to achieve so you can earn extra coins which you can dispatch at the shop to add ammunition to your weaponry, especially the mine and EMP bullets.  Essentially, you will be able to move yourself to several vantage points on the map so you can effectively protect your runner by shooting at the upcoming wave of zombies. Your runner will have a limited amount of ammunition and he will be able to take care of himself until he runs out of bullets. If he is caught by Zombies, well, it will be game over. Also, within the action, choppers will come regularly and will drop crates and barrels. Shoot all crates before they hit the ground and you will receive extra mines or coins. Barrels are like bombs - shoot them when zombies approach them and you will probably hit a strike! If you reach a certain score, you will unlock an additional difficulty level.
In strategy mode, you have to make sure all survivors reach the train station and jump up onto the wagon to score 3 stars. The further you go, the harder it will become to save them all.
Dead TrailZ has cartoon–style graphics which add to the fun component of the game. The controls are fine and the game runs very well.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun and addictive gameplay
-	In game tasks to achieve
-	Cartoon style of graphics
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
-	I’ll like to see more maps

Dead TrailZ is a Tower Defence game where you’re the towers, you zip-line between multiple advantage points and rain fire on your foes. Missions revolve around killing zombies while protecting survivors as they either evacuate areas or collect resources. Your weapons include an Assault Rifle, Mines, EMP Bazooka and Smoke Grenades to guide your allies.
The game contains a’ Skirmish’ mode were you protect a single survivor as they collect resources, it’s a bit like your classic ‘Horde’ mode. ‘Strategy’ mode pits you in multiple predefined situations by limiting the enemy spawns, setting certain spawn locations, limited shooting locations and limited access to equipment, think of it as a ‘Trial’ mode. These two game modes take place over two separate maps, one centred around a set of buildings, while the over in an open country/rural town.
It has a cool feature where you can link your Twitch profile to your account, allowing people in your chat to appear above the heads of the Zombies, but being a nobody and this game not being fully released yet I was unable to test this feature, seems really cool though.
Currently the game is in Early Access so we have to view it for what it is currently + future promise. As it stands the game is quite basic, I did a majority of the Strategy missions within an hour (they’re all very similar atm), and got to a point in the Skirmish mode where I felt I had enough. The Zombies have limited movement and maybe even missing animations, while the gun play feels a little floaty, I can’t quite put my finger on it but if you watch the gameplay you’ll see the camera continue to move even though I’ve stopped moving my mouse. In saying that I think it’s an interesting pick-up if you’re into Early Access, there seems to be some promise with the amounts of Zombies and Survivors on screen at once and wacky elements such as the Mines and EMP Bazooka, which is where I hope they take the game. Currently it’s only single player, but I think it’d do wonders if you could add a friend to join in on the fun, you would be able to get further + it gets very chaotic which are always great moments with friends.
Atm I’m going to have it as a recommendation due to it being Early Access & future potential. It’s over the top with its look and weapons, and that’s exactly what I’m looking for. The promise of more levels and possibly more objective types also is something the game needs to stop it from being stale. If you’re looking for gameplay of both Skirmish and Strategy I have that in the video above and several over on the community hub & my YouTube channel. If you’re not a fan of unfinished games I’d skip it for now, just keep it on your follow list and follow the game through its Early Access cycle.
