Do you give a game a thumbs down for being thoroughly competent but utterly unremarkable in every single way? I don't know. I'd rather not.
and games like it are really the reason that Steam needs a 'Meh' button or at least that sideways thumb that Roman emperors used to make while they were deciding whether a gladiator deserved to suffer their opponent's gruesome fatality move or not.
It's a sniper game. With zombies. And not a lot else. You can either choose to partake in Runner Mode (protect a luminously dressed imbecile from afar as he scuttles around the town for supplies) or the slightly more engaging Strategy Mode (aid groups of survivors in escaping the map via missions with various special conditions).
Although still in Early Access, the first issue you'll come across is that the tangle of alleys in the centre of the game's first map are practically impossible to see into from any vantage point. If your runner or your survivors wind up in there, you'd better hope the dead haven't gotten there first or you'll be treated to an elaborate camera pan of your ward being messily devoured. And I do mean messily. I don't want to lower the tone here but many of the undead in this game seem to be drawn to eating the, uh... the inner buttocks of their victims. Whether that's because it's the centre of the character model or not, I don't know. It started to make me feel sick after a while.
On the plus side, Dead TrailZ tries its hardest to escape its budget trappings and oversaturated genre with at least a basic stab at replayability; there's random bonus jobs to fulfill and the strategy missions do a fair job at keeping you engaged with inventive objectives and the challenge of pulling off a perfect run. It's fine. It works. But it does belong in Early Access while it discovers some sort of individuality.

I remember when this was first released, and I enjoyed it, although it being only on my mobile was frustrating, particularly the wonky screen attention movement and the really bad zooming and focusing.  ultimately gave it up and uninstalled.
Now, I see they have somewhat improved it and released it on steam. Great!   that wonkyness with zoom and focus is still there, but much better on a larger screen, and the pc  mouse control is way superior to the tiny touchscreen interface.  I like the additions of the pets and workshops, and the quests!
HOWEVER, and that is a big however, the RNG event generator is broken.. I mean really, frustratingly *ing broken.  I think I understand how the algo is supposed to work, and it IS effective. however is there a better algo rng than "whatever will * over the player repeatedly, and make the experience less enjoyable"?  come on.at first it was multiple deathclaw attacks in a row laying waste to multiple layers of dwellers.  ok. some levelling, and it's down to one, maybe 2 vault layers.  so now it's  10 unkillable radscorpions in a row?  Seriously? I can see if it's only 2 or maybe 3 dwellers in an attack, and it gets bored and runs off, but laying waste to at least 3 full rooms of decently armed dwellers before running away.. seriously? oh, and spawing other unkillable rs's to do the same simultaneously? seriously?
another item that needs be addressed  is the scaling.  on the quests, you have the three dwellers that can take on a full structure of radscorpions, or irradiated ferals, or what have you, and  while they take damage, it's not the insta-drain it is when the same # attack the vault.  if there is a weird scaling, where on the quest,  one is one, but at the vault one is 5, I could see that, but not the one is apparently 10...
Because it is initially enjoyable,  I am giving it a recommendation. it IS at it's core a good  work.. it just REALLY needs to have better clarifications and some tuning to make it more about difficulty than just being mind-numbingly frustrating.

I would like to start by saying the game does have a good overall concept, and I believe that the issues here can be fixed.
The biggest reason I find the game unplayable is that combat is very confusing. Frequently, you will get raids by sword weilding samurai. They don't come for resources, they just come to kill your survivors, and suck their soul into a pokeb- sorry, wrong game.
If an attack does happen, your characters just kind of stand around and do nothing. You can equip weapons and all that, but the effectiveness varies. You also have to manually move either the weapons around between characters, or move your characters to the room under attack.
This could be improved if the survivor AI is updated to automatically seek out and destroy threats, and to automatically move to rooms under siege.
It would also be kind of nice to have more mechanics in the underground. In XCOM, you build chambers very similar to the game here. In XCOM, geothermal caves will spawn underground which provide extra electricity if you build a power plant on it. It's little things like that which could really add to the game's playability.
So summing up, I ask that Bethesda makes combat more fun, and less confusing, as well as adding a few mechanics to give the player a reason to keep coming back. It's that thought of, "gee, I can't wait until I can build my base up to reach this cool looking location."

Castle of Illusion is one of the most nostalgic platformers I have ever played. I never played the original Castle of Illusion, so my nostalgia doesn't come from that. It does come from being a fan of Disney and their cartoons for many years. I had not seen Mickey in a entertainment medium since Kingdom Hearts so it hit me in a good way. It also made me feel old. Now technically, the game has pretty good controls for a platformer. The jump is solid if a tad bit floaty. The game is kind of simple and easy, but it definetly is fun. The game is two hours long and is rife with critical flaws. Returning to this page, it's evident to me that Dischan Media put more effort into their Teaser video than the actual video game.
The artwork, while very good - is far too sparse to express the story in any meaningful way.

Dysfunctional Systems follows a fourteen-year-old mediator-in-training named Winter. A mediator's job is to travel to other planets and to balance the scale of order and chaos by whatever means necessary. Winter is shadowing a mediator, Cyrus, known for being cold and willing to kill in the blink of an eye. Assigned to the planet of Sule, their mission is to balance the scale.
The game's art, from the start, is beautiful (I could stare at the menu for a long time). The characters are all well drawn and expressive. The story is written well and the characters' personalities really seal the deal and just pull you in. You can tell how Cyrus is from the art and his lines; he's cold, but also has a side that you don't hear being talked about. Winter is very expressive and idealistic, and it is easily conveyed to the reader. She's not just some random protag-kun, but she has her own personality, and it shows. The music fits perfectly with the setting, and the setting further immerses you and you can quickly get a good idea as to how everything is. The detail in your character's actions and movements has plenty of detail; it gives you enough to where you can picture exactly what's happening.
By the end, I was dying for more. Sadly, I finished it in around three hours, give or take a few minutes depending on your choice. There is one choice you can make, but from my experience through the second playthrough, it changes the story line in many ways. Reading after the choice was completely different between option A and option B. It wasn't worlds-apart different, but you could definitely see the changes; I found this highly fascinating.
I'm not a major reviewer, so I'd say the only con I could find was it's three-hour playtime, but I'd also say it's a pro because it readies you for more episodes and leaves you wanting more. This game was right up my alley, and I'm utterly excited for the rest of the episodes.

After playing this game for 100s of hours, I can say that I both love and hate this game.
Pros:
Very fun and varied; There are two sides and each side is unique and interesting.  Most other shooters I have ever played is little more than identical teams against one another.
Well made; The game has enough polish to it to please myself and others.
Deep and interesting; This game has a lot going on and has a lot to take in.  This can be a challenge, but it's also allowing for a less than boring game.
Cons:
After writing for a few days on this matter and re-editing several times, I've come to realize there really is only one note worth issue with this game.
Lack of player balance; Halo 2 had it going on back in the day with it's amazing ranked matchmaking system.  It wasn't likely that a rank 45 player wasn't going to face a rank 5 player in halo 2.  But in natural selection 2, this is and has been really rampant, lots of newbies facing against seriously seasoned players.  This might not sound like an issue to some, but I think this is a devastating flaw to this game.
The skill ceiling doesn't exist in this game, it's incredible how good a player can be in this game, but this means the learning curve is nearly a straight up wall in which many players simply can't climb when facing 100+ hour players as newbies themselves.  I love how deep and skillful this game can be, but the lack of forced ranked matchmaking may have been it's greatest weakness as a game because of how extremely skilled a player can be within this game.
To add to the player balance issue, I have encountered many matches where a small number of friends played together on the same team.  This is great in many ways, I love the idea of teamwork amongst friends, but the problem was their enhanced synergy and usually higher combined skilled level was compounding.  I might go so far as to argue that two friends that played well together were worth 3 strangers even if all involved were of similar skill level and experience.  So if a group of 5 friends joined a 16 player server, the results were often horrific for player balance.  If I could, I would develop a game similar to natural selection 2 but include solutions to this problem relating to player balance which I imagine might solve a lot of other issues.  Basically, forced ranked matchmaking is likely the only way to manage a game such as this and I'd adore to see it done well in any game, but especially one such as natural selection 2.
Overall this game is incredible as far as shooters go, but the vertical learning curve, lack of matchmaking and seemingly tenaciously negative player base (likely heavily bittered by the games lack of matchmaking, awareness of this or otherwise) really ruins this game for myself.  As I am sure you can see, I've played this game a lot and purchased it before it was even released (played natural selection 1 100s of hours as well), while I think that even today this game would be worth a $60 buy in many respects, the other lacking issues make the game, in my opinion, a frustrating mess that is nigh unplayable.  You can certainly enjoy the game and playing it plenty, but most of the time most players probably won't have a great time playing it.
Online multiplayer shooters haven't existed for very long (compared to human history or the total time the universe has existed), but ranked matchmaking has been the best experience in terms of gaming I have ever encountered and without it many games end up being less than viable.  Sadly, this idea seems to go wildly ignored for reasons that elude myself.  Many newbies, people who I have given this game away to for free, absolutely refused to play this game after a short period of time due to this reason.  Being obliterated in a game by extremely skilled players isn't something many enjoy and when trying to introduce someone to this game they become soured towards the idea if while just trying to gain some understanding they get torn to shreds non-stop.
To add to my anecdotal tale that I am sure nobody will ever read, I have spent some time playing with a small number of random players of NS2, talking with and playing beside, some lesser skilled, a few wildly too good at this game.  For some reason, every player that I played (on a deeper sort of friendship level) with saw zero value in the notion of ranked matchmaking, but became infuriated and hateful towards newer or lesser skilled players on their team if they didn't live up to their own expectations.  Naturally, I stopped associating myself with these types of individuals, but it did an excellent job of reinforcing my opinion that a game like NS2 without ranked matchmaking is no game at all.  A game like NS2 is about competition (like many multiplayer shooters), there isn't much competition to be had when one of the competing sides is obscenely superior to the other.
In summation, this game is phenominal, but it's death(at least in my opinion, and certainly for myself) was spawned by a lack of ranked matchmaking.  I am sure ranked matchmaking sounds complicated and difficult to impliment, but without it this game seems like it wasn't worth the time, sad as it is to admit.  You might argue that I got my moneys worth, but truthfully I wasn't eager to continue to play this game after less than a lengthy period of time because of the flaw, I only hoped things would change.

Broken Age is a nice nod back to the classic point-and-click adventure games of yore, when 16-color monitors were all the rage and your mouse had one button.  Time has granted a few key improvements to the genre, and especially Broken Age.  This game's graphics are stunningly gorgeous, with a unique and sweet storybook style.  The voice acting is excellent and the music lovely without being overblown.  The story brings nothing innovative to the genre, but there is a nice attempt to mix things up with the split storyline between the two main characters.  Many of the secondary characters are amusing and their comments and stories drew a few chuckles from me.
Sadly, the game does fall short in a few departments.  Act 1 is well-paced, but Act 2 involves a lot of backtracking and the puzzles becoming far less intuitive and more frustrating. The final motivations for the villains sadly aren't much better than "We're superior evil smug people;" there could have been a far more interesting story there, but it's rushed through and glossed over.  The main characters also don't get as much development in Act 2, and do little more than act as avatars for solving puzzles.
Like many Double Fine games, Broken Age is great for kids and the young at heart, but be warned Act 2 is going to involve a lot of help from parents and/or walkthroughs and story-wise isn't as strong as Act 1.  I still enjoyed the game enough to recommend it to those who like games strong on charm and quirk, not to mention those fantastic graphics, but players looking for more depth in an adventure game are going to be disappointed.

I can't even begin to express my love (and emotional attatchment lol) to this game. I could hit the "Yes" button 10000 times if I could.
I first started this game on my other Steam account 3-4 years ago, and since then I've played this game (all episodes) more times than I can count on both my hands, and watched others play countless times.
This is a beautiful, tragic game.
The way this game is built with the Buttergly Affect really pulls you in, so you're forced to emotionally invest in each charater this game presents. You're forced to really think about your actions before you make decisions, as what you decide affects the rest of the game, including the past. The storyline is truly execptional, unique, and memorable. Every character gives you reasons to love and hate them as you figure out their past. It's a gam you can't forget once you finish it, and it'll have you coming back to play it again and again. On to the tech stuff...The graphics are pretty great, despite how long it's been since the first episode was released. Move with your usual controls- WASD, or arrows if you're like me and prefer to move that way. I believe you can also use a controller, which makes things easier. You click to make choices, take pictures...etc.... It's built so you can play with ease, and its not complicated to the point where you'll quit.  THE SOUNDTRACK is on point with the game, quite beutiful and fitting. I could go on and on about it all.
Overall, PLEASE, PLEASE, PLEASE give this game a try, I can assure you that you won't regret it. And, best of all, it's FREE. An even better reason to try it. You'll laugh, you'll cry, and you'll be thrown on to a rollercoaster of events and  mysteries in Arcadia Bay. (:

DarkMaus unappologetically tries to emulate the Dark Souls series in a top-down format. It doesn't even try to hide the fact that it's a blatant ripoff of the style and genre, and frankly, that's perfectly okay with me, because the game is a lot of fun.
If you've played Dark Souls (and if you haven't, stop reading this and go do so, then come back when you're done and keep reading), you'll be immediately familiar with the formula - you have a stamina and health pool, a light and heavy attack, you can sprint, dodge and block, and all of these consume stamina. Run out of stamina, and you're stuck waiting for it to regenerate. Combat is largely based around timing your blocks, dodges and attacks to avoid attacks while getting your own hits in. Killing enemies often earns you Souls - uh, sorry, 'Marrow', which can also be found occasionally on corpses pre-populating the world. Dying causes you to drop your marrow where you died. You can return to the spot to reclaim your lost Marrow, but if you die again before you do, it's gone forever. You rest at bonfires - excuse me, 'campfires', which heals you and lets you spend your Marrow to level up, but also respawns all non-boss enemies in the world. There's a variety of weapon options, each of which have different advantages and disadvantages as well as differing attack patterns, in addition to being able to learn magic in the form of pyromancy.
Sound familiar? It should.
One difference really stood out, though - you have weapon skills that you must invest levels into to use weapons of that type. While this isn't a problem per se, it forces you to choose a weapon type and specialize in it, rather than being able to try out each new weapon you find as you can in the Souls series. I found some interesting looking weapons later in the playthrough that I would have liked to try, but investing 10+ levels into a skill only to potentially find out that I didn't like the weapon was not something I was willing to do. (To illustrate how much 10 levels is, I finished the game at level 68.) Further, weapons can be upgraded using a limited availability upgrade material (similar to Dark Souls), but each new weapon in a weapon class is more or less an upgrade over the previous one, so I felt compelled to wait until I had all of the weapons in my chosen weapon type before starting to upgrade anything, because I didn't want to waste the materials on a "sub-par" option. As such, even though the upgrades became available early in the game, I wasn't able to really leverage it until more than half way through, so it felt like a bit of a wasted mechanic, on me, at least. Your mileage may vary depending on your playstyle.
The combat is very tight, and the controls feel responsive. Some aspects of movement, though, take a little getting used to - for example, you can't turn in place easily. This is the product of the game having only a single control for movement (the left stick on the controller you should be using to play this), which controls both facing and movement. The right stick is used for locking onto enemies (though if there are no enemies around, it can be used to adjust facing, as well). This makes negotiating some environmental hazards a bit frustrating, particularly if you're forced to do so quickly, and you'll likely endure a number of frustratingly "unfair" deaths because of this.
One particularly trap-filled area was frustrating me endlessly, and I was prepared to come and complain about it in this review, but then after banging my head against it for some time, I realized that there are a number of alternate paths to take through the area (apart from the 'direct' route), and that completing these alternate paths would in turn make the 'direct route' more manageable. Upon discovering this, the area became much more fun, and despite the initial frustration, I'm inclined to applaud the designer for this particular facet of the game. In Dark Souls style, it rewards exploration, which I love.
The bosses weren't as difficult as I would have liked - nor are they too numerous. Most are easily defeatable in 1 or 2 tries (the first time to see the attack patterns, the second time to win the fight if you didn't on the first try), and even the final encounter is very strait-forward once you identify the gimmick and realize how to deal with it, but that isn't much of a detractor - the game itself is delightfully difficult at times.
The music is simple but fits well, and the art aesthetic works very well.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game for fans of top-down action games, or fans of Dark Souls. It's not too long (5ish hours for my first playthrough; I expect a NG+ playthrough would be closer to 2 hours, though I've yet to attempt this), but for a $10 game, that's good value for the money, in my opinion.

This game is astonishingly polished considering some of the Early Access crap that's floating around. As near as I can tell, this was a one-man effort. There are no bugs that I could identify and the sound, visuals and music are all very professionally done.
I sucked badly at the combat, and there were footprints and blood spatter everywhere in the one room I was stuck in. But for all that, the game only took me about 11 hours.
There are some very minor nitpicky issues.
There isn't a way to rebind your keys.
And because I can't rebind my keys, there's no way for me to look up the lock-on button for the keyboard-mouse.
Finally, this game works best with an X-Box controller. It's rather hard to move diagonally using classic WASD. This isn't really any fault with the design of the game itself, since the top-down movement really does require that you have a joystick.
All told, a very good bargain for 10 dollars.

DarkMaus, it wears its inspiration on its sleeve (Dark Souls) and does so proudly, with a comfortable, easy to learn and deep identity of its own. Broadly speaking, should you play this game? Yes, yes you should. Even if you're someone who's not interested in Dark Souls and its ilk, this is an amazing top down 2d rpg, well worth the asking price.
It's bleak and dark aesthetics suit well with the atmosphere its developer tried to create. You're instantly put into a strange world with realistic rules. It's free flowing tutorial allows a new player to easily flow into the gameplay, while challenging them. Even as a Dark Souls veteran (Over a thousand hours of gaming in the games respectively.) I felt that there was challenge, fair challenge.
The map allows and encourages exploration at the risk of losing your EXP (Marrow), with interesting enemies all teaching you something new in how you should approach combat. Even if you start hitting a wall of difficulty, the ghost mechanic, whereby you get the aid of a ghost NPC that lowers the difficulty by attacking the enemies, something that is entirely optional and modifiable if you so choose to use this mechanic to aid you, allowing great difficulty tweaking for the player themselves. Something that even Dark Souls would be proud of.
The characters you meet along the way exploring this desolate world are engaging, I cannot tell you much more without spoiling, so you'd have to experience it for yourself.
There are some areas where you're left wanting however. Take for example the clumsy inventory, which can make it somewhat uncomfortable to traverse. Another one of these places is the sound design, while the game is very minimalistic in its color and assets, which helps the mood of the game, there are some areas where the lack of background noise makes it seem much too quiet and not in an eerie sense. At least, that is my subjective viewpoint of the sound design.
+ Deep combat mechanics
+ Welcoming to veterans and new players alike
+ Branching weapon/skill/custimization early on
+ Exploration is rewarded
+ Interesting NPC's
+ Ease of entry
+ Fair Challenge
- Clumsy Inventory
-/+ Minimalist Sound Design
9/10

This game is a good example of something that truely tested time and aged well. I played this game back when it first came out on the Xbox 360, and playing it again on PC not only brought back good memories, but also showed me that this game to this day is still fantastic.
Graphically for the most part it is beautiful especially when it comes to the game's lighting, but there were some low res texture, some of the screens from TVs are a bit hard to see, foliage popped in at ridiculously low ranges when driving in some areas, and in one section there were some funky shadow problems even though I had the graphics settings set to as high as they will go.
Technically, the game does run fine for the most part. I did encounter some slow down and very minor stutters, but only when it was very busy on screen with flare and flashbang effects, but other than outside of that it ran fine.
The story will keep you on edge of what is happening with the mystery of the setting of the game, Bright Falls, and the curse that is on it and what is all happening with the character waking up from a car crash a week later after he tries to save his wife and not knowing what is going on.
Gameplay is very innovative where you have to use lights to defeat your enemies. Flashlights and lanterns only get rid of the darkness that shields enemies so that you can kill them with guns, flares ward enemies off while getting rid of the darkness on them in a wider area, and flare guns, flashbangs, and giant lights will outright defeat enemies. There are a few variety of enemies, although not many. I really only count about 6 different enemies, normal enemies, tougher enemies, much tougher enemies, fast enemies, crows, and poltergeists, and while they do vary a bit like the tougher enemies can shrug off you using the light boost and fast enemies easily dart around an area and much harder to concentrate your flashlight on, they all pretty much require the same way to defeat them; get rid of the darkness in them with your flashlight or any sort of light source and then shoot them, unless you defeated them with a flaregun or flashbang or it is a crow or poltergeist to which they'll just immediately die after the darkness is gone from them. I honestly think that is this game's biggest fault, the combat, because it will get very repetitive very fast especially since each level lasts quite a while. The game does present itself as pretty challenging at times, while being as fair as possible. I do think that the way that some enemies can easily gang up and almost immediately drain your health bar without any kind of recovery was a bit cheap, but you are given resources to help keep this from happening.
Speaking of difficulty, and this is just a small note on something for anyone who wants to play the game, I have not done any kind of searching about this nor do I remember if this was part of the original Xbox 360 release, but it does seem that the difficulties are a bit misleading in the game. The game has 3 total difficulties, Easy, Normal, and Nightmare. Now I played the game through Normal, but when I beat the game it says that I completed it on both Normal and Hard even though a Hard difficulty option is not showing up at all. I have a feeling that there is no Easy difficulty and Easy is actually Normal difficulty, Normal is Hard, and Nightmare is Nightmare.
As mentioned earlier, levels do last quite a while, and even though the game is mostly linear, there is a great deal of exploration that can be done in each level, and you are rewarded for exploring the levels to find each of the game's hidden secrets rather it be hidden chests which you can find by shining your flast light on certain areas that will reveal yellow paint that show you where to go, manuscript pages which tie into the game's story, TVs that will broadcast a TV show called Night Springs which is sorta like The Twilight Zone or will show Alan thinking about the situation he is in, Radios that will give a bit of behind the scenes of what is happening at the time of the level, or give a bit of history to the game's town. The game also encourages a 2nd playthrough where some manuscript pages can only be found on Nightmare difficulty. There is however 2 other collectibles that are in the game for seemingly no reason other than achievement purposes, the coffee thermoses and can pyramids, which to my knowledge don't seem to unlock or do anything, they're just there.
There is a good amount in the game that will be worth the purchase. There is a total of 6 levels in the game that make up the core main game, and it'll take about 8-10 hours if you decide to go off the beaten path a bit to find some of the secrets in the game, maybe around 6 hours if you decide to rush through and skip over the secret stuff. There is also 2 bonus levels which will give you around 2-4 extra hours.
My main complaints about the game is that it seemed to drag on with how fast the gameplay becomes repetitive and the levels while explorable to extent, go on for a while.
I can easily recommend this game if you're looking for a horror game that has a great story and will give you plenty to do. The gameplay will get old fast, but if you do not mind it, then this game is easy enough for me to say that I recommend a buy.

tl;dr: 6/10 - Pretty good but really short.
As a rather critical visual novel fan, I can't say I'm easily pleased. A visual novel being sold on Steam does raise some eyebrows, but nonetheless I decided to give it a go, and I was pleasantly surprised after reading the disappointing World End Economica a while back.
Although Dysfunctional Systems is an original English language (OEL) visual novel, which is generally a good indicator of poor quality, my past experience with another OEL VN (Katawa Shoujo) was actually rather good, so I wasn't deterred from the beginning. Overall, the visual novel was quite good, all things considered, but we can take a bit of a deeper look into things.
First thing's first: the writing. I can't vouch for the story being fresh and original, but it was well executed regardless. The characters' personalities were generally consistent and the story developed in a logical order. However, the visual novel was painstakingly short. I felt like I was just thrown into the middle of things, and even though the story wasn't too complex to figure out what was going on, a longer introduction would've been welcomed with open arms. There's also the issue of how easy it is to get to the bad end. After several playthroughs of making and recording different decisions, in desperate search of the good end,
. As it stands, the story is
, but much too short for my liking, and a lot more content is due. The ratio of number of choices to length of story was horribly skewed in the wrong direction, but I can respect the amount of tedious coding it would've taken to link everything together the way it was done.
Technically, the English was rather good. It was by no means perfect, but it made good use of stylistic devices and all of the other things English professors like to rant on about for an easy-to-read experience. There were a few mistakes that the more pedantic of us (such as myself) may wince at, and the word choice was often pretentious, to say the least, but otherwise, Dysfunctional Systems was well written. If anything, it was better than the disgrace World End Economica was, which I can only imagine was a machine translation done by an IBM 5200.
On to the art and sound - long story short, they were also quite good. While the drawing didn't exactly fit the conventional visual novel clique, there was something about the brushed watercolour style art that appealed to me. All the ren'py animations (yeah, I actually bothered to look through the game files to confirm it was a ren'py game) were used well and surprisingly weren't skimped on - this kind of production quality I can appreciate. I'm not much of an audiophile, but I can also vouch for the soundtrack being great on its own. In the game, it can be a bit overpowering at times, but the volume controls presumably exist solely for that purpose. If only they had some voice acting to go with it - in Japanese, of course, since I'm a filthy weeaboo and English sucks - but alas, one can only dream.
It might seem like I'm bashing the game pretty harshly here - and that's probably true - but I actually did enjoy the game. Although it was
short (short enough for me to get 100% completion after only 3 hours), and there were the other issues I'd mentioned previously, it was an interesting story and fun to read. Even though I'm bringing it up again - the sheer lack of content was detrimental to the score I gave - we mustn't forget to interpret the ten point scale correctly. 5/10 is
, and not garbage by any means. Going from there, 6/10 isn't a bad score, despite what IGN and whatnot want you to believe - but that's a story for another time. I know episodes 2 and 3 of this series are due to come soon, though, so hopefully they can make up for where this episode fell short and salvage the trilogy as a whole.

Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel that attempts to portray the idea of a utopian society using their advanced magic dimension-tripping technology and superior history and intellect to help guide other planets in subtle ways -- managing their "chaos". However, Episode 1 presents itself as more of a teaser than an actual iteration in a series due to its short length (two hours is more than enough time to rinse this out), lack of choices and minimal explanation of who or what is really happening in the utopian society.
Given that the start of the game (and store page) makes a point to mention how "Your choices affect the story" theres a distinct lack of any choices to be made. Which is doubly odd as the game takes care to give you a codex with which to keep you up to speed with the world and current trends or plot devices. This may be a personal qualm but I expected it to come in to some use when it came to "managing the chaos" of the world, such as reading it granting an insight into how to take action, but instead the sole decision you get to make in this title has but four resolutions resulting in two endings that you make through a series of choices that are mostly red herrings. This makes the codex feel rather unwarranted as everyone always explains themselves in enough detail such that reading it is a waste of effort.
The writing itself feels quite contrived: characters and, in this episode, countries presented are almost painting-by-numbers in their given role. I mean, who hasnt heard the one about the gruff, old mentor with a plucky, slightly rebellious voice-of-reason apprentice. Or the one about the two large nations stuck in a [cold] war over a third, smaller independence.
That being said, credit where credit is due, the game does look lovely. The UI is clean and distinct, backgrounds are nicely detailed and the character portraits display many emotions in a variety of poses. Most of all it feels consistent -- portraits dont just sit on top of the background but instead fit in, general colours and tone do well to make this.
I can only really hope that future episodes really expand on what I would only really call an extended teaser here.

Wasteland 2 throws you into post-apocalyptic turn-based combat.

The story isn't anything new; a land being ravaged, once again, by a robot army. The story flows nicely, being held up by interesting characters and a variety of environments which you explore. As the setting begins to become stale, you are thrown into a new part of post-apocalyptic America to continue your journey.

Leading a squad you have created through each new location of the game, the areas and enemies change frequently enough that it all feels new. With the different combinations of weapons and skills for your characters moving you forward to the next slew of combat.

Combat is strong in this game. The variety in your strategy is determined by the development of your characters and the new enemies thrown your way. Whether keeping a sniper in cover on a hilltop or rushing forward a bruiser with a crowbar, there is plenty of variety inbetween. Any combat scenario you encounter can be approached in a number of different ways.

If you enjoy post-apocalyptic landscapes and turn-based RPG's, buy this game.

This is a very fun free game, but not without it's share of faults that need to be addressed
Pros
- Gameplay is pretty fun and varied. From vault building to quests to exploration, there's a lot to do.
- Quite a bit to the strategy of this game. It looks simple on the surface, but it's quite complex, with it's SPECIAL stat system, which determines how dwellers perform in different situations. A lot of trial and error is needed to master this game.
- A bunch of different rooms, allowing you to craft your own gear, train your people to your liking, as well as producing the basics to keep everyone alive
- You can earn all the pay shop items through regular play, which is always a plus to me.
Cons
- I saw another review use the word "chaotic", and that is a perfect word for the game as you progress. You very quickly  jump from simple to challenging to completely insane as you're bombarded with things like Radscorpion invasions, which will not only beat you senseless, but deplete your resources as they do it. It can be very hard to just tread water once the difficulty ramps up. I like a challenge but I'm finding this to be a bit over the top and the level of micromanaging is also a bit much.
- The programming is on the poor side in some areas. You can tell it's a port. There's a mystery man that pops up every once in a while, and you've got about 10 seconds to locate him. There's nothing like hearing his music, being right in the middle of looking for him when you have a raider attack, which centers the camera on them, hearing the music of the mystery man disappearing, then killing the raiders only to watch one spend 10 or 15 seconds limping across the screen as he drains your resources in the process, and you're helpless to do anything until he finally collapses. It can also be painfully difficult to click on things such as the mystery man, finding that the game thinks you intend to click on the room itself, and you may lose him in the process. Hopefully things like this are addressed because they seem like unnecessary punishment for doing nothing wrong.
- Not impressed by some of the cash items. Mr Handy, for instance, moves painfully slow when he's on resource gathering mode. I find it much quicker and more efficient to just manually collect, as you lose resource production time when he's dragging himself all the way across the floor to collect. In my opinion, if it's a cash item, it should be instantaneous. Also, not much to say for his cap collecting ability on exploration. Even though he can't take damage, it's much more lucrative to send a regular dweller exploring. He seems like a jack of all trades, master of none. I found mine through the course of the game, but if I had spent money on this thing, I would feel ripped off.
- There seems to be one gamebreaking issue where save files become corrupt, and if that happens, support will not help you. That.. in a word, sucks. In fact, I might be tempted to spend money on this game, but after hearing that, I will not. Not if that's the level of support they provide.
So in closing, it's a perfect free game. That's the right pricetag in it's current state. It's fun and worth your time to try it out. Enough to earn a thumbs up, but not a glowing endorsement. If they address some of the issues, it would raise it above that level.

At first glance, it's easy to miss this gem under the massive amounts of flashy games out in the market now. But, as soon as you let go of the visuals, you get something even better: An actual good game.
Just like any Dark Souls title, this game pretty much follows the working formula to the T. You got your weapon system pretty well done. And finally, you have those impossibly hard as balls challenges that make you wanna break your controller, unistall, and git gud.
There are some draw backs in my book though and theya ren't enough to actually deter me from recommending this game to anyone else. Some of the drawbacks would be the lack of a dedicated slot for healing items or a resuable healing item like in many other DS games. The map disappears in different areas, obviously to make newer areas stand out, but this also makes knowing where you went and what you did much harder
. Finally, not sure if it's just me or not, but whenever attacking once or twice, the game picks up a second hit for no reason. Normally, that isn't a problem unless you're low on HP and desperately trying to dodge instead.
All in all, this game is simply amazing. It does justice to the DS franchise and I'm very happy to have spent my money, time, tears, and frustration all on it.

In terms of the translation itself, you need some background knowledge about Chinese and also the history of China to really understand that phrase “不到Mun非好汉”.
The word "好汉" doesn't mean 'male' specifically. It means HERO. In ancient Chinese, there is a phrase “英雄 好汉”, it's a technique in Chinese that you put two words of the same meaning together to emphasize it. And here is the example.
So my point is, the previous translation “不到Mun非好汉” means that you can not claim to be a hero before you have reached the Mun.
HOWEVER, it's just a sentence! Most people don't really notice it on the splash screen. There is NO POINT to spam negative reviews for a single sentence.

An unexpected gem that was well thought out and given praisworthy amount of attention to detail by the creator.
As for the Dark Souls influence, yes, it's pretty obvious. But this is quite a different experience that goes beyond it being top-down 2D. The game plays out in much shorter bursts. Rather than having relatively wide open areas and lots of ground to cover between enemies and bonfires, DarkMaus has incredibly small, but well detailed areas with a handful of enemies and well placed environment set pieces, that challenge the player into making every single move correct. The combat is the same risk/reward style as in Dark Souls, with each enemy given neat little traits that make them all different.
My main gripe is pretty obvious - the lack of deeper characterization and RPG mechanics. Leveling up is quite shallow and rather linear, with only a handful of each weapon types. You don't really 'build' much of a character outside of a couple of obvious choices, and given the length of the game that's obvious why.
Otherwise, this is such a neat game to pick up while waiting for Salt and Sanctuary to one day finally get a release date.

Does it have the best graphics? No. Does it have steller animations? No. Is it without bugs? No.
Is it fun?
...
ABSOLUTELY YES.
How fun? Lemme put it this way: It's my new Halo.
While it may not be as polished a product one might expect, it does one thing very right: IT'S FUN.
As someone looking for a game to replace Halo after the letdown of Halo 4, this game has filled that void.
It doesn't play EXACTLY like Halo, but it has just as big a skill gap. Natural old-school talent will transfer well.
My suggestion for best experience: Play single-player survival first. If you can complete an entire map by yourself (it will take several tries, and several hours if you take your time to purchase things to make your character OP during the match), you'll beast at the game forever (for me the support class is best). Figure out how matches play out, and you'll be victorious in survival mode. PVP is as core as it can get on the few times I've tried it, and you really have to outthink your opponent. No killstreaks. No perks. No unlocks. Just you and your skill.
There IS an unlock system, but as far as I know it only works for co-op survival games. It also takes a LONG time to unlock anything (one single-player three-hour game WITH VICTORY=one revolver). It doesn't really matter much though. Anything can be bought for the match so long as you kill enough dinos and earn enough credits. The unlock system is only helpful for not having to buy certain things during the match that you would have anyway. For example, I used to always have to buy the revolver near the beginning of the match, but now I start with it (which is the only thing I've unlocked as of now).
To sum the game up, it's like Left 4 Dead, TF2, Borderlands, COD Zombies, and Halo all tied in with dinosaurs. It borrows mechanics from many games, but does so flawlessly. The only thing it doesn't have is COD mechanics, other than the survival aspect of zombies mode. Even though there are vehicles, they're far less effective than one might think. If any get pinned by a large dino, they're pretty much toast. This keeps the survival aspect going despite having tanks, mechs, and jeeps. The only vehicle that's over-powered is the helicopter-thingy that functions like a Halo Hornet on steroroids. However, it is the last vehicle that's unlocked during the match and serves as a finally where the tables turn on the dinos. But even those get plagued by flying dinos, and have to be repaired from time to time.
If you just want a game to be fun and nothing else, this is it. (Warning: sometimes you can get stuck in cracks of rocks on the map. It's my only real complaint. But either by patiently wiggling free, or waiting for a helpful flying dino to pick you can get you out. This may be only troublesome for the support class, because assault has a jet pack and the stealth class can roll. I play as support, so it's probably why I have the biggest issue with it.)
Now, "Somebody bring me a pizza!" (lol biggest kill chain in game. Has announcer that stats multi-kills like in Halo.)
BTW, I will admit I got it on sale for 99 cents. Best dollar ever spent. Actually, I got the four pack which was $2.99. Don't even buy the game just ask me for a copy if I still have one! I assume this sale was to help get rid of the bad rep its former title 'Dino Beatdown' had. They really updated this game so it does not deserve the poor metascore it has anymore. I had not originally planned on getting this game, but the sale was tempting. Glad I helped give it the second chance it deserved.

Hotline Miami is a fast-paced, top-down retro game in which you punch, stab, bash, and shoot your way across ever increasingly complex floor-plans, while wearing your choice of animal-themed mask. I won't spoil any of the story, but I will talk about the gameplay.
In Hotline Miami, you start each level with nothing, and as you violently massacre people, bashing their heads against the floor until they pop, you pick up their weapons, slowly upgrading what you use like Bruce Lee in Enter the Dragon. The game is not easy, as your character will die after a very small number of hits, but enemies can't take hits either, and the game becomes almost instinctive on later levels as you rush into a room with four people in it, kill all of them, and then die as you realise one of the walls was glass and you were seen by a machine gun wielding bad guy. In some stages there are bosses, too and while some people may find that these stick out a bit compared to the rest of the game, I enjoyed panickedly trying to dodge a biker's razor blade or rushing to get a shotgun to try and take down an unflinching giant of a man, and feel that these actualy add to the game, though they can be a little more frustrating than the other levels.
In short, Hotline Miami is an incredibly well designed game, and one that (if you can stomach it), you should play, and obsessively murder your way through its blood spattered levels.

It's an humble game but it's surpringly good for what it is.
Combats are challenging, most of the enemies are tough and require you to take real care at their patterns in order to be defeated without harm. The level design will usually place you in really tense situations where you'll most likely die and learn from your mistakes. In fact, most of the progression in the game will come from you, learning of the enemy and their placement, along with a few, really handy perks that will allow you to have ghosts like minions or better dodging (which is crucial if you want to survive).
Though leveling your character can feel a bit weird and even frustrating early on, for you really don't know what to upgrade at first. Most of the weapons dps or efficiency will be based on skills relative to specific weapons types, which makes you really hesitant in what to specialise because the game doesn't really give you clue of what will be best at use. For example i started by really focusing on spears and some mobility until i realised that most boss fights were better handled with long or great swords. Also i felt like the bow was really unworthy other than in locations that you already known, unless you spam randomly at the distance hoping to hit something that won't punish you after that.
But in overall the game feels decently balanced. Weapons brings their own playstyle, some being safer than others.
The game have some good ideas too, especially the ghosts followers and the way it tackles story and quests. Loved the pacing and attention to details, from the light radius effect tied to your torch to the small foot prints displaying where you already go and stuff like that.
But to be fair, what really makes the game is the atmosphere, which is gorgeous ! It's dark, mysterious and have moments of thrill that will make you shiver and progress with caution. I especially love how you go from an underdark cave that feel claustrophobic to a suddenly wide plain with a strong breeze. Makes you really paranoid to what you might encounter from any direction.
My only few complaints would be that, well i found myself getting disoriented quite often and had to rely heavily on the in-game map due to the art-style of the game. I mean, i don't blame the artistic direction that i find really good, to be honnest. Just that even if there's attention to details that helps bring some personnality to a few places, the black and white look get a bit unclear at some points.
The Maniability can be really abrupt sometimes too, stuff like dodges or attacks that doesn't always work in close combat even with a good stamina on, or even occurs twices when you didn't meant to. It usually happens when launching an attack, while the character was preparing to swing, if you happen to hit the trigger again.
Also i admit that sometimes i just killed my character so i could proc the two ghosts follower to make the playthrough a little easier, for there's some really unfair moments here and there. It's also sad that the huge amount of campfire feels a bit like a way to compensate the low amount of healing items, and that using inventory in combat is just impossible.
Lastly, there's a lot of details that will look like a Darksouls copy paste. Which i don't really complain since i like that game a lot. But still, you got bonfire and pyromancie and undeads and the UI and buttons placement... i can't help but feel a bit sad that it reproduces a concept without really improving on it or go a little ahead.
I always felt that most of the souls serie gameplay mecanic were strongly tied to the lore of the game, from pyromancie being an art of using the flame within mankind and getting more powerful by feeding it or, the fact that you loose souls when you die because there's a thematic of going hollow and stuff like that. Dark Maus doesn't really seem to think or get that deep into that, even if the gameplay works fine.

Also the music, while being well composed, can be a bit off sometimes.
Besides, i really enjoy the game and will probably play it through NG+, just so i can see how the game react if i kill everyone (especially Anna, for she really kicker my♥♥♥♥♥in my first try because i friendly fired her a little too much >.<).
It's pretty good, and since i always felt that there was too little RPGs with mices (being a fan of Mouse guard, Mice and mystics and Redwall) i'm just more than happy to have sweet title like these coming into the market place, and will gladly recommend it.

Spintires is without doubt the best offroad driving game on the market since Cabela's Off Road Adventure. It was conceived in Russia like another relatively recent off-road game UAZ 4x4 (never published internationally as far as I know). However, UAZ 4x4 was about racing to the prejudice of realism, so I lost interest to it fairly quickly and had no desire to complete campaign. Spintires is different because it is all about real off-road challenges. It is mostly slow and often boring driving with rewarding sense of achievement at the end of your trip.
Spintires is definitely a niche game far from mainstream. It is not about speed and reflexes. It is about knowledge and experience. It is about accurate planning and careful execution. It is an open-world game, so you can find your own way to complete objectives. During my first try, I lost both available trucks - one was stuck and damaged in deep water, another ran out of fuel - so I was forced to explore the world using remaining operational Type-A 469 and was able to locate and unlock two new trucks which saved my day. Joyful moments.
In general, for any unknown map it is advisable to explore entire area and remove cloaking before making decision about your way to complete objective. Removing cloaking also reveals locked vehicles on the map, so it is easier to locate them. Use entire fleet of vehicles with many suitable attachments and trailers to ensure successful and timely fulfillment of the objectives. If your planned route from lumber to objective is far from garages and fuel stations, make sure to position other trucks alongs the route to provide repair points and fuel if needed.
Although multiplayer is not as good as it could be, it offers a sense of collaboration with other drivers when they actually feel like collaborating and working together. Playing with your friends, knowing what you are going to do and doing it together by supporting each other is a great way to play this game. Personally, I think multiplayer would be much more interesting if players had to share trucks available on the map rather than having all trucks available to every player like doing single player mode simultaneously.
Another great thing about this game is that the developers keep updating and improving it. It is already the greatest off-road simulator, and it is going to be even better.

I got this game in early access. I tried to play and like it but was frustrated at the learning curve and didn't really have the time to invest in it. This winter/spring I finally had the time and was rewarded with a terrific experience. Like every game I have played, it has a few warts. That's expected and if they are warts you can live with you will absolutely love this game. So let's talk warts first.
Very convoluted plot lines for a few important quests. I didn't find the solutions intuitive and resorted to a walkthrough because while I had extra time, I didn't have THAT much time to constantly reload and try all of the different permutations.
I did not like the mechanics of weapon stripping. Could just be my luck but when it said I have a 20% chance at a tactical scope...it never worked out that way. But honestly, the system could be better. Realistically, a weaponsmith takes a gun or whatever and removes the non damaged parts...right? At level 10 weaponsmithing I expect to be able to choose what to take and, assuming it's viable, I should have a 100% chance of removing it. I own firearms in RL, have stripped them and cleaned them too many times. A better approach would be a predetermined roll on what attachement(s) is/are undamaged and then based on your WS skill make the roll. Frankly, a Tactical scope is still a scope, and if undamaged, would be just as easy to remove as my old scope I had on my .22.
I started recording my skill checks and at the end of the game, for those checks of 65% or less, I averaged half that. One time it took me 23 tries on a 28% lock. So, my point is, I wasted a lot of time reloading instead of playing. Accuse me of OCD? You'd be right but it still interfered with the game to a level that I thought, disturbed the immersion.
So, the good stuff? EVERYTHING else is fantastic. The combat tactics are brilliant. The skill and attribute systems perfect for this game. The atmosphere, the music, the diverse characters you meet and sometimes recruit...love you Scotchmo. Story, excellent, gear, terrain and graphics very good. Voice actors, 9/10.
All the little bits. IE: finding caches and shrines. Having a goat or a dog or a puppy (careful with that btw) or a robot or a terror hang with ya and love you....priceless.
Finally, if you want and old style isometric game that is very challenging to learn, then provides a great story and combat tactics......this is for you.

Unfortunately, though, the game does feel like it drags on a bit longer than it should.
This is a good game, but not a great one; it may be worth your while, but you have to know what you're getting into.

I can only praise Natural Selection 2.
It's very rare to see such a successful, well-balanced and engaging mix of RTS and FPS, but it really delivers.
The maps are well-designed; the weapons of choice for each faction are diverse to the point where they're completely different playstyles - and yet, they even out very nicely, with marines that use rifles, shotguns, grenade launchers, jetpacks and exosuits (mechs), and aliens that rely on biological evolution to grant them different abilities.
As a marine, apart from the exosuit, a purchase might just change your playstyle, though usually for the better. As an alien, an evolution changes what you are and how you interact with the world in all cases, so alien upgrades, costing the resources over which the two factions battle, make them stronger than individual marines usually, but are harder to earn.
The RTS part involves a commander for each side giving individuals orders and placing buildings to help their faction's growth. It's also pleasantly diverse in how it works; marines rely on power nodes that also provide lighting for the sectors they're in and buildings that are linked to those nodes, while aliens rely on infestation spreading and use certain upgraded units to provide frontline defense in a way that regular marines cannot.
As a final perk, this game has a somewhat small playerbase (the price tag makes for a very small influx of new players given its niche genre, though it does go on sale from time to time and I personally got it from a Humble Bundle), but it's generally mature and friendly. You'll find that on almost every server players use mics, and people generally do their best to win.
I heartily recommend this game to anyone looking for a unique multiplayer FPS experience.

Oh man, there are so many good things about this game, and I really want to recommend it. :( The art is colorful, the settings are interesting, and the story is really cool. The character design is splendid. Actually the overall design of everything is splendid. The female protagonist is pretty awesome, and I think the story has some good messages. Some of the dialogue is really witty too, and all in all the game seems really well thought out. I like the story, too -- lots of good plot twists, interesting, unique.
But... maybe it was too well thought out. It started out fun enough, though at times I had to wonder to myself "I feel like this game is meant for an age range of about 8 to 13???" (But it is marketed as "family friendly," so I shouldn't complain now.) By the second act, everything starts to feel extremely tedious. It took me forever just to get through the puzzles. It felt like I'd have to walk through a million rooms and do things *just right* just to get things to work. Whereas I didn't have to use any walkthroughs in the first half of the game, I kept getting so frustated at how slow things were in the second half that I resorted to them multiple times near the end. By the end of the game, I just wanted to be done.
In addition, despite having a really cool story to begin with... the tedium somehow ruined it for me. I felt completey unattached to the characters. I liked the female protagonist well enough, she seemed really strong and daring and at least that gave her some kind of characterization. The other protagonist, well... if he'd fallen into a pit and died at some point I really couldn't have cared less. Which is sad, because his backstory is interesting enough and I feel like there could have been more... introspection there? Even a little?
In all fairness, point-and-click adventures aren't really my thing, I guess. I hadn't played one in a long time and I wanted to try this game because of all the good reviews. But... I WAS SO BORED. I want to give other point-and-click games the benefit of the doubt, because I'm certain I've played some that aren't quite so tedious. If you're into this type of game, maybe you'll like Broken Age anyway -- after all, it does have a lot of cool elements in it. I just feel like they missed some things in the execution.
Saving grace: It has tree jokes. And makes fun of hipsters, whom we all love to hate. Feels like there's some of that classic Monkey Island humor in there, too.
So... time to make like a leaf and... no, never mind.

This is a short (A little over an hour for one run, though you might do more than that to follow alternate paths) but high quality visual novel. If you like VNs, then this is definitely worth looking into. Keep in mind that, if you are expecting lots of dialogue options or more traditional "gameplay," then you won't get that here. The story is largely linear with one really major choice followed by some shorter dialogue that you can select. If you want to get a good idea of how DysSys will play out, check out Dischan's other work, Juniper's Knot. It's short and, most importantly, free, so you can get a good idea of how Dischan does things. Though it has absolutely 0 player involvement, unlike DysSys. JK is a great story worth looking at for its own merit, honestly, so even if you don't want to buy DS then still consider JK if you like visual novels.
So, if you mostly want to invest in a brief but engaging story, then DysSys is pretty great. The characters are well-written with good dialogue and the worlds are pretty immersive, though we don't get to explore them in great detail in Episode 1. Episode 2 is reportedly going to be much longer, clocking in at rougly 12 (!) hours according to the developers, if memory serves. Accordingly, it will also involve more choices and more exploration of the intriguing world introduced in Ep1. Of course, that's all yet to be seen.
Final conclusion: Won't appeal to anyone expecting much player agency or a "real" game in the traditional sense, but definitely worth it if you want a great story. I certainly enjoyed my time with it, no matter how brief.
I'm also going to add that, if there's one thing that Dischan has down to a T, it's music. The soundtracks to both this and Juniper's Knot are phenomenal.  Do yourself a favor and listen for a few.

The brilliant trailer and soundtrack are worth more than the rest of the game, which is complete くそゲー and worthless even as fanfiction.
The concept is fascinating, and brutalized by a substandard script. The storyline is paced badly, and there is never a proper sense of characterization developed through the text. Ellipses are overused for dramatic pause. Winter's narrative monologues are tediously long, and the profanity is gratuitious while failing to generate dramatic tension.
After the decision point leading to a drastic scene shift and the introduction of additional characters, the creative team behind this game decides to lose their minds. Characters such as Henry Pen are text only. A massive wall of text is a placeholder for character interaction. The shallow script essentially craters, lost in marooned plot devices like hints of a lesbian romance which inexplicably awards an achievement.
There is minimal backstory to speak of. The Codex, an interesting plot device, is grossly underutilized. The origins of Winter's homeworld and how they developed Mediators are neglected. Some brilliant, evocative art direction could have filled in, but what we get are anime watercolors and bad writing that demands mashing the space bar to banish from screen.
Visual Novels require superlative scriptwriting and engrossing characterization. This game provides neither, unless the tastes of the reader are just as shallow as the gameplay and satisfaction comes easy. Future episodes in this series are not worth consideration, the dismal writing and the plot structure would require vast improvement beyond the hack writing in place.
However, the soundtrack is lovely as background music, which is why I have so many hours logged.

Broken Age is really like two games, one of them great, the other not that good at all.
First, on the surface layer:
BEAUTIFUL presentation, lovely (in act 1) charming characters, great voices, sfx, animations etc, all around, presentation wise it's great.
At first glance and initial play, there is a lot to literally love there.
So then, going deeper, the two games in gameplay and story:
One, the first act, is a quite good classic (if by itself a bit short) adventure game modernized in some nice ways.
It came off a bit easy in some aspects and only had two puzzles where i wasn't sure what to do next.
(which is a good thing in my book regarding the not getting completely stuck/lost aspect)
The puzzles in act 1 were overall for the most part easy and logical to grasp (again, besides two exceptions for me) and most of them were fun or lead to fun/nice/memorable story outcomes.
The second act/later part of the game (which was initially also released way later) sadly is way worse though.
In the second act the puzzles were changed to a completely "requires walkthrough constantly for sure" level and even with a walkthrough they didn't seem logical nor fun.
It's like the game was suddenly made massively more "difficult" in all the wrong ways.
Like "how many most not logical at all/most not intuitively discoverable things can we stuff in there at every corner?"
That would still be much more tolerable to me if the story went on as great as in Act 1.
Sadly it didn't =(
Sadly, also the story aspect fell apart completely for me in the second act.
There were way less fun and charming moments with characters there and the whole plot turned from could totally happen/ realistic/believable and very charming scenario to totally cheese and totally not relate-able to rage causing levels regarding how/why they let it sink there.
I read some reviews stating one should best not play the second act and imagine for oneself how the story from the first act could end, well, obviously i didn't go with that recommendation since i wanted to play onwards after the great act 1 part and see where the story goes, but post playing act 2 i can see where they are coming from with those recommendations.
I really liked the story and enjoyed the gameplay a good bit during act 1 and i feel like act 2 really tarnished that.
If i wouldn't remind myself of Act 1 i would have to give this a way more negative review overall.
So, overall i have a bit mixed feelings about it.
On the up side, there are extremely charming, really lovely characters, art style, music and sound effects presented in the first act, the whole outset of the story is beautiful and i loved being in that world with those characters (and so charming presentation).
I most loved the aspects that one could play the girl or the boy both with their different (seeming) eras, environments, back story etc. and playing through that portion was overall largely a joy.
_______________
SPOILERS FROM HERE ON
_______________
Sadly the second act completely trashes that all.
Basically initially it seems like storywise a few possible scenarios could have been the case. Like the boy or girl could be time traveling to meet the girl.
The boy's Mom could be a computer only for real and not his actual Mom so it would pose the question if his parents long died or what. And the question why she/it imprisons him, why he was put on that mission alone. There was also the question (even touched upon briefly) whether the second "astronaut" could be an older version of the boy or a younger version of his father, again implying quite interesting story twists.
Sadly, none of that all, what was unveiled with Act 2 storywise was basically a way worse and way less plausible and less interesting and less appealing turn of events /plot twists for pretty much every major character that really ruined any connection with the storyline to me completely.
All aspects of how the two "eras"/worlds/characters were brought together felt forced, unrealistic and like complete nonsense. Hey, hooray, it was fake, more fake and most fake and what really went down was the least plausible way more idiotic setup.
It went from some masterfully done great story portions in Act 1 to some super sloppy and bad plot overall in Act 2.
The whole plotline of the boy was basically turned into complete made up nonsense in multiple ways, and each "unveil" making the plot worse than the previous.
_______________
Major Spoilers below
_______________
Hey, his "Mom" and "Dad" whom he only saw on the computer screens initially and who there came off as both very computery and also totally not trustworth at all, as if they were imprisoning him with some dark motives, were then unveiled to actually be his real parents, just for some reason had not been around him in person for so long that he didn't remember them even being his parents or real humans at all.
Ok, i get it, it plays on the point that many parents work so much that their kids don't see them much for a while, but it is just the lamest story twist option in this setup, where the initially presented setup was so much more interesting with so many more interesting possible outcomes.
Then another plot twist, that the spaceships are not actually space ships and have never left earth.
Downgrades the whole setup and story potential so much.
Then with that also the unveil that they are all in the same era/planet/place.
Another big story downgrade.
Then that the "spaceships" from the outer shell look like monsters and are what's picking up the maidens.
Then the twist who let's those monsters do that etc.
With each plot twist, one by one, it got worse and worse and less and less plausible/likeable/connect-able.
Like really, why did the story have to get worse by every 10 minutes in Act 2 until it was a complete dumpster fire? =(
And as i said before, many of the puzzles in act 2 seemed so random, too that i feel like the chances for solving them without constant walkthrough usage are very low to non existent to most players, they were for me despite i played many adventures in my days.
Some puzzles are also made in a way where they can't even be solved easily with a walthrough since some aspects are randomized, which is extra enraging when an annoying non onbvious, non logical and not fun puzzle after the other already forces one to play through with a walkthrough and then on top even with that one in between gets stuck at some points.
Some of the puzzles in act 2 made me really really not enjoy playing the game at all anymore for a while and i only went on since i wanted to see the end of the story.
Sadly, the ending, like most of the entire second act was not satisfying at all.
I so wish the whole second act could be rewrittten completely, because i would so love to play through it in a version where the story could have progressed in a  form where it hadn't been turned to this trash later on.
So, where does that leave us?
Still a bit sad/upset about what happened there with act 2 and i wish it had storywise gone and played completely different.
It's a rare case where i wish there could be a director's cut/revisit/remake of a game later on where the first part would be left mostly as it is and the second half completely redone with major changes in plot and gameplay.
Still, i think after a while, i will play the act 1 parts again some time, because within those, there is some awesome stuff there.
The first portion of the storyline was downright excellent in my eyes, there was so much wit and self and medium aware joy in those aspects making fun of games, hero and decision making or how they are presented as such in games or in the world and how we choose our own paths or not etc, some great stuff there.
And for that all in Act 1 i give it a thumbs up =)
I just have to get rid of the sour taste of act 2 and play act 1 again some time later to refresh those good memories of Act 1 =)

Dark Maus is an top-down action game with a lot in common with dark souls. It has plenty of things that make it unique, however, such as the Death Echo and ability systems, the fighting style, and the art.
Pros:
-Fighting is fun and varies greatly from enemy to enemy
-The Ai is intelligent for what it is, and forces players to try different items and strategies. I often found that the harder enemies were more sneaky and skilled than I was, and had to return later when I'd gotten better.
-Level design and enemy placement is very well done, and captures the feeling of relief/surprise when finding a shortcut in the original Dark souls. There are also some enemies that, when defeaten, change the dungeon in some way, which is neat.
-When the player is killed, they are ressurected along with a "Death Echo", a ghost of your former self that retraces its steps and battles enemies along the way. It's a nice way of making sure players don't get stuck in hard areas, as you can make sure your ghost hoard is carrying the weapons that will benefit you the most (by dying while wielding them) and power through tough spots.
-The dev (yep, singular) is very helpful and dedicated to his game, and is trying to work out any problems players report
Cons
-It's a bit rough around the edges. Music will cut out and restart randomly, there's no real title screen,  and there are a number of bugs (most of them harmless, but some frustrating) that I've run into. After the most recent patch there have been a fair bit of crashes as well, although I feel that those will be solved relatively quickly.
-The game seems pretty heavy on CPU usage and could use some optimisation.
Overall, it's a challenging, fun game that's experiencing the few hiccups that follow any game release. I wholeheartedly recommend it, but if you don't want to deal with these early bugs I'd put it on your wishlist and check back in a few weeks.

Games that play off more famous games names usually send a big red flag for me, but Dark Maus and its similarities to Dark Souls feels justified here, and reasonable. The combat does a great job of providing a challenge for the player, and the gameplay is precise enough to reward smart and tactical movement by the player. The level design helps in providing wide open spaces when you need it (when facing enemies that charge you like bulls), but shrinks it down to small corridors to cause some claustrophobia as the traps and enemies surround you at every turn. The difficulty is high: and yet fair: not relying on tricks, but forces you to adapt to your environment. While some of the sound design needs a bit more impact and there's some goofy menu implementation, the game's weaknesses don't overshadow the core combat in any way. If you're looking for a 2D combat fix, you could do a LOT worse then Dark Maus, because it's got the combat down.

I wasn't going to write a review because, to be honest, I'm biased. Life is Strange has been my favorite game for years.
