I can admit that it's a far cry from the best game ever made. The graphics are very stylised and gorgeous for what they are but it can stumble into the uncanny valley at times. The dialogue is... uh, well, I'll just say that the word "Wowser!" is used more than once and leave it at that. And there isn't a lot of "game play" in the traditional sense. It's very story oriented. If you're looking for an action-packed romp, this probably isn't the game to play for that.
That being said; for all its faults, I still found myself deeply immersed in the odd parallel dimension that is Arcadia Bay, Oregon, I still fell in love with nearly every character, and it's still my favorite game. if you're willing to take a chance on a story that has an 85% chance of messing you up, I
recommend Life is Strange.

I admit, I was skeptical at whether or not this game was worth it. Now, I see I have been completely missing out on a face-paced, indie game of insanely joyful proportions! The controls are easy to catch onto after only a few minutes, and the game flows easily. In the beginning, expect to fail several times, but it you remain persistent then you will find yourself spending a couple hours fly by with ease. The dungeons are randomly generated each time as well as the items and enemies you face each time, so expect a different and refreshingly new playthrough everytime you start a new game :) One big feature about this game is that once or if you die, you must restart all over again from the beginning. Why this may seem malproductive to gameplay, it is rather quite ingenious and works well for this style of games. it allows you to start fresh as every gameplay, all the strategies you use, and tactics you incorporate are constantly changing as you adapt to new scenarios the game dishes out at you. I highly suggest buying this game--it is cheap and you can find it for one key on tf2op most days. I hear the dlc content adds so much more to the game as well and based on my first impressions (a.k.a. 20 hours spent playing the game over 3 days time), I am anticipating myself purchasing the dlc in the near future. Don't miss out on this amazing, albeit somewhat gruesome/dark, game.

Would I recommend this game to everyone? No. But I would recommend it to those who can either ignore or enjoy the core gameplay loop.
First off, the story is good. The cutscenes and facial animations are great. But the core gameplay boils down to going into a district, which there are 9 of them. You talk to two informants in the area. Each informant then tells you about a set of activies which basically boils down to 4 activies. Kill enforcers, interrogate gang members to get access to more activies, go break stuff, and steal money from the gang. There are also "Targets of opportunity" where you either kill a group of enemies in a vehicle, blow of a vehicle, or follow them back to a stash house and steal some cash.
Thats it, the core gameplay loop, you do like 4-10 of these activies till you go after the racket boss which always ends with the same exact "execution" style moves where you either add them to your racket or kill them. Though sometimes you dont get a choice. Once you get both rackets you go after the district boss and enjoy a unique mission for most of them and you get to watch some sweet cutscenes.
If you have ever played GTA or Saints row the shooting and driving will be fine for you and you should have the ins and outs of those covered by the time you have your first or second districts covered.
There are some extra things involved like assign district ownership between your underbosses and so forth. But the overall enjoyment of the game will come from that core gameplay loop. I found myself towards the end just really playing to see the next cutscene instead of actually enjoying the game for what it is.

A well executed metroidvania with addictive mechanics and a nice story, Dust got me hooked very quickly.
All dialogues are voice acted (and rather well at that) and the cartoon style graphics are well done (but not really my cup of tea). Pretty much everything apart from the voice acting and the soundtrack has been done by ONE guy, and that guy used to do artwork for Jazz Jackrabit- which clearly shows in Dust.
The sound design is superb, and the background music helps develop and keep the atmosphere.
Combat is dynamic and fast paced, with 200+ hit chains being commonplace, and there is enough variation and different skills to make every fight an unique experience (although I find myself using the projectile+dust storm combo a LOT). The controls are fluid and responsive which helps the pacing of the combat.
I liked the few puzzles I encountered, and I hope there's more, as they serve to break the frenzied combat instances with some basic adventure-style quests.
Your character gains experience and can level up, which enables you to enhance one of his several skills (attack, defense etc). There are shops strewn across the game's rather large world map, where you can buy and sell various items that contribute to your character actively or passively.
I like the fact that there are quite a few references to other well known games, such as the mysterious wall chicken you can find inside walls- a clear shout out/stab at Castlevania 1 ;)
I can definitely see why this game got so many positive reviews on teh internets!

For one, you cannot warp out of zones and need to walk to the exit each and every time. It makes completing quests and doing side battles a chore, since you always have 30 seconds of running to the exit after you do anything. End of the day, Wasteland 2 is a good game, but not a great one. Still worth it if you are a fan of the genre.

So what is this game about?  In a nut-shell this is a game that gives you the amazing chance to play as either a Marine, or an Alien in a struggle to take over a station.  As a marine this means building and protecting a defense grid that allows you to exterminate the alien menace and their queen, securing the station for humanity.  OR as the aliens, you get a chance to spread your hive across the station, spawning alien minions, and protecting your Queen.
Great game!  Take your time.  Learn the game.  Be a teamplayer.

is a (planned) series of interactive visual novels, where decisions in previous novels are planned to reflect in future episodes. The episode, and perhaps the series from what I've read, focus on the character of Winter, a sort of student or trainee paired with a mentor to learn how to do their job, which is...manage chaos and bring forth stability. Cryptic, I know, but considering how the episode plays out even explaining the basic premise of the plot could be considered giving spoilers, which I shall not do. :P Episode 1, which is what I'm reviewing here, was released last year, while Episode 2 is in the process of being developed after a successful Kickstarter campaign raised $67,000. As with most visual novels, there is very little opportunity for user input in this "game", so it lives and dies by the setting, plot, story, as well as the art and music to a lesser extent.
Speaking of the art, it's obvious that a lot of time and effort went into it...yes, they're static graphics that change as the scenes or situation changes, but there are a number of scenes drawn for any particular part of the game. For example, one may have one of the characters looking a different way or with a different emotion on their face, so they can change the scene graphic when something particular is said to show the character responding to it. Also a neat little thing I noticed is that there is a particular scene where our character is walking and the camera moves with it to simulate movement...buildings move in and out of range, which I thought was a nice little touch. The music was overall pleasant and seemed appropriate to the situations and settings that arise in the game, but weren't horribly memorable.
Not like they had
's budget for music though, I'm sure. :P
As for the story, I like the premise a lot...without saying what it is, it makes for a lot of potential variety in the game as other episodes are made, and I thought the characters were well-written as well, with unique personalities. My problem here is that much of the game comes off as feeling static, like it's a teaser or tutorial level instead of a paid game. It's not the lack of interactivity that bothers me, it's the lack of variety. Most of the game is spent having discussions between the same two characters, and there's precious little breaking all that dialogue up. It also made the story feel like it was proceeding slowly, even when urgent events were building up...a very odd feeling in those instances.
Also, I know this was an introductory episode and they wanted to focus on the two main characters, but it's disappointing that there wasn't much interaction with the actual game world, especially given the game's main premise of dealing with worlds and systems. I think two birds could have been killed with one stone by having more scenes that focused on the world they were in, such as the bar scene where Winter meets David and a game event happens. To me that was a standout part of the game that temporarily broke the monotony. Another standout part of the game was during the epilogues, because the character interaction between Winter and her roommate was just so damn good, and it was nice to get a taste of Winter's life and the people she's around. In fact, I wish the game had started out this way...I think being able to be introduced to Winter and her friends before the events of the story start would have been a nice touch, too.
I want to stress, it's not that I found the story
...quite the contrary, I thought it was quite good. It just would have been even better with more variety of things interlaced within it. There's only so much you can do in a visual novel that mostly involves the same two people talking with each other. :P
Overall, I suppose I find the implementation lacking, but the concept promising. From what I've read, the developer is improving on many of the issues I'm pointing out here for Episode 2, and it already sounds like it's going to host a much more vibrant world than this episode did.
My recommendation? If you like visual novels, go ahead and get it! $5 isn't a lot of money, it's hardly a bad game, and I have enough faith that Episode 2 is going to be so great you're going to be glad you already know the basic premise of the series. Otherwise, wait for Episode 2 to come out...Episode 1 at least is definitely not for people who don't like the genre, so it may be worthwhile to see exactly what Episode 2 has to offer before putting down money.
If I were to give a rating, it'd be 6/10, a rating that I'm almost certain will go up when Episode 2 comes out, which I am looking forward to. :)

Would I recommend this game to everyone? No. But I would recommend it to those who can either ignore or enjoy the core gameplay loop.
First off, the story is good. The cutscenes and facial animations are great. But the core gameplay boils down to going into a district, which there are 9 of them. You talk to two informants in the area. Each informant then tells you about a set of activies which basically boils down to 4 activies. Kill enforcers, interrogate gang members to get access to more activies, go break stuff, and steal money from the gang. There are also "Targets of opportunity" where you either kill a group of enemies in a vehicle, blow of a vehicle, or follow them back to a stash house and steal some cash.
Thats it, the core gameplay loop, you do like 4-10 of these activies till you go after the racket boss which always ends with the same exact "execution" style moves where you either add them to your racket or kill them. Though sometimes you dont get a choice. Once you get both rackets you go after the district boss and enjoy a unique mission for most of them and you get to watch some sweet cutscenes.
If you have ever played GTA or Saints row the shooting and driving will be fine for you and you should have the ins and outs of those covered by the time you have your first or second districts covered.
There are some extra things involved like assign district ownership between your underbosses and so forth. But the overall enjoyment of the game will come from that core gameplay loop. I found myself towards the end just really playing to see the next cutscene instead of actually enjoying the game for what it is.

Long story short, Mafia III will be divisive. If you hated Mafia II, Mafia III will not change your mind on the franchise. If you loved Mafia II, Mafia III is definitely worth a buy.
The biggest issue with the game is repetition. The critics hit that hard, but that's because it's true. You'll have to kill someone or destroy something a few times before you can target an underboss. You'll be doing this a lot. As a way of alleviating it from being quite so bad, the game can be played in stealth or as a third person shooter. The stealth is incredibly simplistic, but it's functional. The guns feel powerful and there are quite a few to play with.
Mafia III's biggest triumphs are in atmosphere and story. The rendition of a 1968 New Orleans is incredibly detailed and pulls no punches. The racially charged atmosphere is a huge portion of that. Police will have a slow response or maybe not even respond at all to crimes if they're in a black neighborhood. Some stores that can be visited will still be marked as 'whites only' and going inside will get you a call to the police. The soundtrack is one of the best ever put together in a game. The Animals, CCR, and Jefferson Airplane are some highlights.
As for the story, the premise is an original one. Black Vietnam vet Lincoln Clay comes home and loses everything after the betrayal of the Italian mob. What follows is a bloody quest for revenge where interesting, well-written characters will help or hinder the journey. Dialogue feels authentic and raw and your allies have real motivations that can elicit sympathy or disdain from the player.
I love Mafia III, but it's not for everyone. For fans of Mafia II, it's a must-buy. For those who didn't like Mafia II, consider holding off for a sale.

Let's get it clear, first of all: THIS IS NOT A GAME. Anyone who reviews Mountain as if it is your traditional game needs to reevaluate it under a different perspective.
Mountain can be seen as a screensaver, visual entertainment, aesthetically appealing content--anything along these categories. If all you do from morning to night is play mainstream high-action games (i.e. Dota 2, CS:GO, etc.), you probably will not immediately be able to enjoy the abstract simplicity that this game offers.
Let's get down straight to the meat of this. The only user interaction that you have at your disposal is using your mouse to move the mountain three-dimensionally, your keyboard to play music notes (which can be used to unlock easter eggs), picking up and organising "artefacts" that drop on your mountain overtime, and the almighty eye of the beholder to watch the mountain collect random objects and pile up on the mountain. The biggest input the player has to the game is three questions asked in the beginning, prompting the user to draw three images to represent three different things (i.e. mother).
The only spontaneous events to occur are a meteor that may destroy your mountain and changing weathers/seasons. Ocasionally your mountain will "think" and provide some interesting, philosophical annotations about its existence. If you leave the game open for a few minutes, your camera eventually will zoom out into an outer-space view of the mountain.
I would recommend it buying it especially for how cheap it is (kudos to the developers for not overrating their game). I really just leave the game open and use it to take a break from my studying to look up at the screen and just relax a bit.

I admit, I was skeptical at whether or not this game was worth it. Now, I see I have been completely missing out on a face-paced, indie game of insanely joyful proportions! The controls are easy to catch onto after only a few minutes, and the game flows easily. In the beginning, expect to fail several times, but it you remain persistent then you will find yourself spending a couple hours fly by with ease. The dungeons are randomly generated each time as well as the items and enemies you face each time, so expect a different and refreshingly new playthrough everytime you start a new game :) One big feature about this game is that once or if you die, you must restart all over again from the beginning. Why this may seem malproductive to gameplay, it is rather quite ingenious and works well for this style of games. it allows you to start fresh as every gameplay, all the strategies you use, and tactics you incorporate are constantly changing as you adapt to new scenarios the game dishes out at you. I highly suggest buying this game--it is cheap and you can find it for one key on tf2op most days. I hear the dlc content adds so much more to the game as well and based on my first impressions (a.k.a. 20 hours spent playing the game over 3 days time), I am anticipating myself purchasing the dlc in the near future. Don't miss out on this amazing, albeit somewhat gruesome/dark, game.

Wondering if this is a top down Dark Souls like game?
The answer is a resounding YES
Soul System? Check
Level Up System? Check
Vancian Magic System? Check
Multiple Weapons and Builds? Check
Red Eyed Mini Bosses? Check
Bonfire Save System? Check
Weapon Upgrade System? Check
Drop Souls on Death? Check
Keep Items on Death? Check
Hidden Secrets and Traps? Check
NPC Allies? Check
NPCs You Can Accidently kill? Check
Dark Desolate World? Check
Exact Same Combat System? Check
Even the same combat buttons? Check
Same HUD/UI? Check
Plays Better With Controller? Check
Invasions By NPCs? Check
Lose Max HP After Invasion Loss? Check
And those are just the Dark Souls influences. The game also goes a further step and adds in an Ability system, which are essentially Active and Passive Perks you can add together to create many different builds. Also unique to this game is the Death Ghost system. Anytime you die you will create a ghost of your mouse that will travel in the same direction using the weapon you died with. You can use 2 of them to help farm harder areas or bosses as well as help you easily get back to your dropped "souls". In other words, nowhere near as much punishment for death as in the souls games.
Just pretend this is the untold Dark Souls Spin-off story of the Undead Rats from the Dark Souls Games and you will be having a great time in no time!

Spintires aka ,Getting stuck in the mud in the Russian tundra simulator 2014, is well a game where you deliver Logs from Point A or B to Point C, and sometimes to Point D too.
Point A is a Lumber loading zone, where an infinite amount of Logs, in the length they are needed in, are supplied to you.
Point B are Logs that have to be picked up by a crane and loaded on to you.
Point C/D are the locations where the Logs are to be delivered to.
For this mission you have a collection of Trucks, from an UAZ to an MAZ-7310, and a collection of attachment for these trucks to help you in your mission, log trailer, a crane, fuel canister, repair attachment etc.
This missions sounds simple right? WRONG. Because there is an enemy working against you... the Ground itself.
The Engine of Spintires allows the ground to deform and change it's condition, so that getting stuck in it gets very easy.
But luckily there is a winch that can help you to get out of the mud, most times.
But before you deliver the logs, it would be wise to uncover the map as it is cloaked at the beginning of a map and certain areas must be explored to uncloak it, And Garages must be unlocked with a Garage attachment or Trailer, so you can repair your truck there and recover a lost trucks to this location.
And now the real challenge starts delivering the logs to the objective, what will set a challenge since your truck is heavier now.
But enough of the Objective.
The Game supports Keyboard+mouse,controller and steering wheels as input.
The Gearbox is nicely different in here, it has 4 gears, Revers, Forward, Forward in high gear, and full automatic.
Also All wheel drive and Differential Lock helps you with rather tricky areas in game.
And if you ever get lonely in the mud, call in your friends in the multiplayer mode.
Luckily the modding community starts putting out more and more content for it, sadly Multiplayer and Achievements will be disabled if mods are installed, but that is hopefully a subject to change in the future with the hopefully soon upcoming Workshop support.
Since just the objectives are a can get a bit boring, the Achievements are the thing that can give the Game more challenge and keep if fun.
Another downside is that there is at this moment only an external view available for the trucks.
All in all it provides fun on the long run and stays challenging.

When I first started playing this game, I was very excited. I thought that it would be a very promising VN. The artwork was beautiful and the soundtrack was great. In fact, it has some of the best music for a VN (in my opinion).
Unfortunately, those were the only good parts. The entire game only has one major decision. They don't even give you the illusion of autonomy by giving you useless choices that lead to the same path. For example, the game could have asked you whether you wanted to drink the beer or not, a pretty arbitrary choice. Instead, pretty much every choice is made for you. In addition, I didn't find the story to be very moving and the dialogue just seemed off. It's all just worded in a way that doesn't sound natural. To add insult to injury, there's only two endings, despite all of the branches in the one major decision.
If you want a good VN, look elsewhere. Don't waste your cash to buy a few hours of poorly worded dialogue.

I did find this game to be fun for a while, despite constantly dieing. I was intrigued about its unique gameplay style and its focus on resources and upgrades. But as I played I always felt that the sides weren't properly balanced. After bouncing from one explanation to the next I've finnally decided that the biggest problem this game has (despite the lack of commanders that people won't kick out) is the skill cap imbalances between the sides. First there is an initial skill wall that players need to get used to, so they can kill anything on the other team; but worst of all is that the best players can do so spectacularly well that the entire other team can deprive these "pros" of their teams recourses and still be out matched. In fact they can do so well with basic equipment and aliens that they won't need any or many other upgrades.
In short Natural selection hasn't removed enough of the skill disparity between players to keep induvidual skill from surpasing and making team collaboration, and the need to control resources.
Its like the sniper in team fortress 2, Valve made it so you can't crit unless scoped for a headshot, and the damge delt is also proportionate to the time the sniper has spent scoped. Valve went to great lengths to keep induvidual skill from surpassing team collaboration. Something Natural Selection 2 needs to improve on.

The gameplay isn't much: you spend most of the game clicking through dialogue, with only a few decisions (can be as few as one depending on your first choice), and one instance of accessing the codex.
The music, for me at least, was forgettable.
The art I liked. Nice character designs, some great compositions, digging the style. Higher quality than most indie VNs I've seen.
The writing is what makes or breaks a VN, and it's my main reason for recommending this game. The story was well-written, with no big plot holes that I noticed. The universe seems interesting. The characters are the game's biggest strength: Winter was annoying at first, but she grew on me, and I'm interested in how her character will develop in the sequels. I found Cyrus the more interesting of the two, and I hope I'll get to see him again as well. Waverly came as a welcome surprise--I did not expect the game to continue for so long after the big climax, but I liked that it did (my only complaint is that the atmosphere got weirdly jovial in one ending, but the other one was much better). The quality is just as high as in the art: I noticed no typos or grammatical errors, and that alone makes this better than many indie games I've played.
TL;DR:
Negatives:
- short
- pretty linear with only 2 main branches
- not much gameplay
Positives:
- good story
- great characters
- high quality for indie

UPDATE: Decided to write an actual review instead of leaving it as a complaint
Kerbal Space Program (KSP) is a sandbox space & rocket enginerring simulator. In the game, you are working in the space program on a planet called Kerbin, where you can build rockets to explore, research or even colonise your solar system. If you are uninterested int the stars, you may also build airplanes to fly around the planet (although your space centre is probably the last place with life activity....)
The game used simple classic orbital mechanics that is easy enough for everyone to understand while keeping the some of the most essential real-life mechanics. This can also be very educational and gives the player a sense of satisfactory when they learned something new.
Most of the fun in KSP came from building and flying your ship, which KSP does very well. The controlls are smooth and simple, and the game features time warp which kills off unnecessary idle times so piloting would almost never fell boring. The game  came with hundreds of basic rocket parts you can use. Aside from the basic rocket engines and fuel tanks, theres also unecessarily expansive experiment gear, off-planet hotels, superpowerful nuclear engines etc. The base game have enough content to build the most creative fireworks that always explodes when you launch them, but if you are unsatisfied, the game also have a very active modding community. Here you can find all sorts of mods can turn your game into NASA simulator, Star Trek (game ver.), or even War Thunder ripoff.
The game suffers a little bit from its somewhat low quality graphics (mods: *cough * cough) and the occasional bugs in its physics simulation, but these serves litle distraction to gameplay
The largest problem I had with KSP is its mediocre performance. KSP have physics simulation for every parts on a ship separately, so eventhough you can probably fly something into orbit with a WinXP PC, once the part count gets higher (especially large station/bases) the frame drop became more and more apparent, and eventually unplayable..
Overall the game itself is quiet enjoyable since we can strap more and more boosters on our rockets. so... why do I give it a thumb down?

Don't let the amount of hours I have in the game fool you. I completed this game offline so there is roughly 8 more hours for the main story and 10 for the achievements.
This game exemplifies what a "realistic" action game should be. Many contemporary games have you hiding behind cover and peeking out at other people doing just enough damage that they can recover it all in a course of seconds. This game takes that and removes the part where you regenerate health. They also remove the part where you can take damage. The every one is mortal philosophy means that you will die a lot. Imagine the game to be a blending of super meat boy and binding of isaac.
The music in the game blends with the art style, setting, and gameplay seemlessly. It is best exmplified in the level Push It where you kill Russian Mafia in a night club. The music in that level is a blend of rave music and your standard 8bit stuff.
The story to me is fantastic. I know some other people think it is boring/dissapointing. However when looking back on it it provides an accurate deconstruction of video game violence. That is hard to do when you are a violent video game but the game manages it.
However the flaws of the game do exist. I know that some people get motion sickness from the swaying of the screen. Additionally there is one level that destroys the pacing before what is arguably the hardest level of the game. This was the only level I looked up a guide for and I feel that if it had been left out the game would have been better. It goes against the entire thesis of the game and while arguments could be made about how it fits in thematically it frustrated me more than any number of deaths in any other level.
There is also a problem with the boss battles. While the climactic Showdown does get better upon replaying it at first it is one surprise kill after another. Similarly the boss battle after Neighbors is entirely pointless and takes the games good idea of instant death and merges it with its lackluster movement.
Finally there are a few quality of life issues. Many times there are clusters of weapons that you have to switch through to find the right one. Also when trying to get an A+ on a leve they don't include your final score (with your time bonus or boldness bonus) you also don't freeze time at mask selection making your first run on some levels a suicide run.
In spite of these flaws I found the gameplay compelling enough to get every achievement in this game and I found the story compelling enough that I have beaten it more times than I can count.
If you enjoy stories this is a must play.

Duck Game is a 2D  fast paced multiplayer shooter that faces up to four ducks in a head-to-head tournament to reach the score limit, which is achieved by winning each round.
Duck Game has combat that results in a fast paced round almost every time you play. It features one-hit weapons that will surely finish your opponents with ease, while also leaving you to play tactically so that you dont end up victim of those who face you.
There is a vast array of weaponry to take out your foes with, such as the devastating minigun, land mines, revolvers, and even bananas to make your opponents slip. Every weapon will kill you instantly if hit, unless you happen to find armor sprawled around the map.
One of the most talked about features in the game is the dedicated button for quaking, which is great for many things such as taunting your opponents or breaking the silence in an awkward situation. Another great feature is the ability to ragdoll your character, which when used at the right moment may lead others to believe you are dead, giving you an advantage
leaving you vulnerable to be picked up and possibly thrown off the map or into a trap.
Duck game is well worth it's price in my opinion. Playing with friends will lead to a great time, and quite possibly an ended friendship. Overall, the game is well done and it may be one of my favorite games of this year.

Story
Wasteland starts in the year 2087 following the devastation of global nuclear war of 1998, a far remnant force of the United States Army calling themselves the Desert Rangers is based in the Southwestern United States. A team of Desert Rangers is assigned to investigate a series of disturbances in the nearby areas and, throughout the game, explores the remaining enclaves of human civilization, including a post-apocalyptic Las Vegas. Over the course of the game, the player's party discovers evidence of a larger menace that threatens to exterminate what is left of the human kind in the game's region and eventually the world. It is a pre-war AI computer that is operating from a surviving military facility Base Cochise, where it is constructing armies of killer machines and cybernetically modified humans with which it is attacking settlements; its goal is to replace the current 'flawed' population with genetically pure specimens. With the help from a pre-war android named Max, the player recovers the necessary technology and weapons in order to confront the computer at its base and stop it by making the base's nuclear reactor melt down. Wasteland 2 goes by the same scenaristic choices and happens in the same environment.
Gameplay
Wasteland 2 is an RPG in isometric view from above in 3D. At the beginning of the game, youmake a squad of 4 desert rangers, you can chose from a set of existing rangers or chose to make your own desert rangers with a custom set of skills and so on. The game features turn based combat where each desert ranger has an amount of action points to use each turn. The game features over 150 weapons, dozens of skills and all of that with an RPG style character evolution. It also promotes exploration of the areas as it will allow the player to gather more weapons and bullets. It also features, decision making with consequences with both short and long term reactivity to the player's choices, every decision matters in the outcome of the story because every NPC in the game is killable but will bear consequences. There is also a 'discover what happened here' aspect to the game based on the examination of clues and information instead of being read, or shown, appear as a scrolling text at the bottom of the screen giving the game a refreshing old school aspect.
Graphics
Wasteland 2 is in isometric view and in 3D. The amount of detail is not spectacular but is enough to convey the post-apocalytpic landscape with an impression of permenant "dust". The dark atmosphere reminds me particularly at fallout which was inspired by wasteland. The whole game is tainted by that old school 90s CRPG style which makes it refreshing and maybe nostalgic for  those that lived in these years.
Audio
Aside from the regular visual effects, what plunged me really into the game was the soundtrack all the noises in the game contribute to making it a really immersive experience for the player. I feel like the audio expresses more the post-apocalytpic atmosphere than the graphics actually do. Also, most of the characters in the game are voice acted, however I have run into some glitches where the voice acting just stops in the middle of a sentence. But since it is only in beta version, I hope that it will be corrected for the final release.
Conclusion:
Pros
- If you liked the Fallout series, you will love this game
- Backed by over 70 000 kickstarter backers, so already existing community
- Tactical decision are required to be made during combat and there definitely is a learning curve so it makes it very gratifying
Cons
- Sometimes voice acting stops randomly
- No multiplayer mode, but probably due to their limited budget
- Can take a while to get used to the mechanics of the game
Opinion
Wasteland 2 is an amazing game, that will probably only appeal to some kind of gamers, but its defined genre brings a refreshing gameplay when most games of today rely on overly used game mechanics. However, if gamers make the effort of getting to know the game, there is a big chance they will quickly get addicted to the game's refreshing gameplay. In the end, I give this game 8 out of 10.

Never played the original NS1, but one day, i've decided to just buy NS2. Don't know what made me buy it, i just sort of felt the need to do it. And man i'm glad i did it. There is so much stuff going on in this game it's just not possible to write it down in a reasonably short review.
It's a blend of FPS and strategy game with great emphasis on team work. Because on your own, you're are a dead man/dead alien. Granted, hours and hours of training will give you a huge edge over new players, but doing it as a team helps even more.
There are so many upgrades, different weapons, vehicles, tactics, methods of attacking, methods of coordinating attacks, exploiting environment and different paths, abilities. It's just insane and awesome!
One thing that i recommend is that you get yourself a decent headphones with mic. Because the only way to play this game is to hear the team and communicate in real-time. Typing stuff is just too time consuming and clumsy. Keeping team up to date with combat status can often be a matter of win or lose. And don't even think of commanding without a headset. You just need it to do the job right.
There is one special thing about this game, while it was made by indie developer, the game apart from occasional balance issues feels like a proper high profile AAA multiplayer game. It just all feels really professional, well executed and polished.
Did i mention the graphics look absolutely amazing? It's incredible what kind of graphics engine they developed themselves for this game. I wish they'd sell it to other developers, because the worlds, models, effects and the lighting and shading itself is sometimes so realistic you could almost mistaken it for a photo. I'm not kidding!

After several new updates to NS2, I'm afraid to say that it's only gotten better.
No longer do I feel like the steep learning curve is thrown at new players, or that the community is negative about them. In fact, I've come to see only incredible improvement to the community since my arrival to it.
With the addition of the BootCamp update, servers are now dedicated to allow new players to learn without the advanced players. This allows all new players a chance to get their feet on solid ground before someone sets you off on a sixty meter dash.
In total, I recommend this game wholly. As an RTS, the game is well balanced and challenging, leaving multiple paths to victory and few 'meta' tactics. (There are indeed still meta tactics, but they are not required in order to win.)
As an FPS, this game is fantastically diverse; Not only do you get guns, but you get to learn how to bite people as a Skulk, slice people as a Fade, or gore people as an Onos.
If you're interested in a challenge, buy this game.

Got to be honest here - I've only played a couple of visual novels, so I can't attest to how well-written this game is compared to the majority of them. I can, however, state that it does not live up to my expectations or the standards my previous experiences have set.
First, terms. A visual novel is just what it sounds like: a game in which the gameplay is principally reading lines of text, and watching character portraits and backgrounds. Most visual novels allow the player to make choices that will change the outcome of different situations, and this game has those choices as well.
In order to write a fair review, I played all routes of this game. The game's main problem is that it feels like it was written by either two people and only one of them knew how to write, or the one person who wrote it was a schizophrenic. Parts of the game are moderately well-written and feel natural when read, but other parts delve far enough into purple prose that it was a physical chore to sit through them. This trend continues in every route, and when the story/dialogue stops being melodramatic, it is boring.
My advice is, don't buy this game if you're looking to try out a visual novel - it may turn you off of the genre completely.

Kerbal Space Program (KSP) is a sandbox space & rocket enginerring simulator. In the game, you are working in the space program on a planet called Kerbin, where you can build rockets to explore, research or even colonise your solar system. If you are uninterested int the stars, you may also build airplanes to fly around the planet (although your space centre is probably the last place with life activity....)
The game used simple classic orbital mechanics that is easy enough for everyone to understand while keeping the some of the most essential real-life mechanics. This can also be very educational and gives the player a sense of satisfactory when they learned something new.
Most of the fun in KSP came from building and flying your ship, which KSP does very well. The controlls are smooth and simple, and the game features time warp which kills off unnecessary idle times so piloting would almost never fell boring. The game  came with hundreds of basic rocket parts you can use. Aside from the basic rocket engines and fuel tanks, theres also unecessarily expansive experiment gear, off-planet hotels, superpowerful nuclear engines etc. The base game have enough content to build the most creative fireworks that always explodes when you launch them, but if you are unsatisfied, the game also have a very active modding community. Here you can find all sorts of mods can turn your game into NASA simulator, Star Trek (game ver.), or even War Thunder ripoff.
The game suffers a little bit from its somewhat low quality graphics (mods: *cough * cough) and the occasional bugs in its physics simulation, but these serves litle distraction to gameplay
The largest problem I had with KSP is its mediocre performance. KSP have physics simulation for every parts on a ship separately, so eventhough you can probably fly something into orbit with a WinXP PC, once the part count gets higher (especially large station/bases) the frame drop became more and more apparent, and eventually unplayable..
Overall the game itself is quiet enjoyable since we can strap more and more boosters on our rockets. so... why do I give it a thumb down?

Woo! another round of writing reviews. Lets get to it? Binding of isaac for the most part, draws from roguelike elements, namely permadeath and randomized environments. Each 'run' through binding of isaac is very quick, if you're new. This quad-directional shooter is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥you. I mean you have NO chance at the start, but then you start getting better and better, learning when to take an item, and when not to, how to deal with certain mobs/bosses etc. The levels in binding of isaac consist of usually 8-10 small rooms, each of which are randomized with different mobs, types and loot. For example, you have the arcade, stuffed with gambles for your hard earned pennies, you have the 'Deal with the Devil' room where you can trade off health for high risk/reward items. The art style is very much appreciated, some runs I end up with cross-dresser Isaac, some I end up with Demon Isaac, all of them look awesome. The storyline is insignificant, but cheesy and hilarious, namely a 1 minute video at the start explaining the situation that the game starts you off in, on every run, though if you are thinking of buying this for the story-line alone, don't. Protip edit- Download Binding of Isaac Spidermod. For arachnophobes; there is no spiders added in the mod, but there are already plenty in the game itself. Spidermod simply adds 1080p, fixes help strings and other good things. Fully recommend it.

DarkMaus takes the top down combat formula and turns it into a brutal, deliberate and challenging format that really gets under your skin.
I would highly recommend using a controller with DarkMaus, you'll still die but you'll die with more dignity.
DarkMaus is, well, dark. It brilliantly uses high, sharp contrast with light and dark (think top-down Limbo) and a limited field of vision to set a great mood and give combat a bit of panache as it helps hide enemies which leads to exciting surprise attacks.
What at face value looked like a simple game of generic hack n' slash dodge/block/stab is a fairly complex and engaging system of meaningful stats and inventory building.  There are a variety of fire magic attacks and weapons to use with different damage ratings, ranges and attack speeds to help you survive.
You won't survive but that's neither here nor there. I found that once I realized death was a part of the game I had a LOT more fun with that knowledge.  When you die a ghost(s) will spawn and fight along side you and help you get back to your body to re-collect your marrow. Marrow is the currency you need to level skills and is vital.
Combat is intense. Whether fighting one foe or 40 baby spiders every battle is life & death and you have to be very focused and deliberate to win.  Quick/strong attacks, blocking, backing off to regain stamina is like a compelling dance and really gets me into the combat in a unique way.
The story is spread out sparsely and the one NPC I found to fight with me and share some of the in-game history ended up aggroing me HARD when they kept getting in my way when fighting and getting spanked. This was irreconcilable. I felt crappy and will have to restart my game but it was a tough lesson to learn.
The campfire system is interesting and I did have issues with it.  When you use a campfire you safe, get your health back, and level skills. Also every enemy you've faced respawns.  This is good as you can grind a bit without dying but you end up having to face the same group of mobs and it gets a little repetitive and annoying.  You want to get through without damage to get farther the next run, and that can be easier said than done.
DarkMaus is a game that I hope does very well as it really surprised me and I think it'll surprised other gamers, too. Plus, combat mouse. Come on. That's friggin' awesome. :3
Disclaimer: I was provided a copy of DarkMaus for review purposes. My thoughts and opinions are my own, as always.

A top-down, stylized game that borrows quite a lot from Dark Souls.
The game has quite an in-depth combat system that makes it fun. You've got a quick, weak attack, and a stronger one that drains more stamina. You can also block enemy attacks, at the cost of losing stamina.
As you play through the game, killing enemies and looting their bodies will allow you to enable new abilities. These add further variety to the combat. One ability allows you to dash forward and attack quickly, while another allows you to continuously swing your sword heavily. Although it leaves you vulnerable, each consecutive attack deals more damage. It's a great trade-off situation.
Enemies occasionally drop marrow. This works like souls in the Dark Souls series. You can use these to increase your stats at campfires, Stats such as health, how much weight you can carry, or attack speed. Depending on what type of weapon you want to wield, you'll also need to put points into that weapon class. My favourite being magic :)
Resting at a campfire will heal you, but also respawn all enemies.
If you're killed, you will drop all the marrow you currently have, and respawn at the last campfire. You have a chance to fight back to where you died, and pick it all back up. If you die again though, your previous marrow drop is gone. I personally love this kind of punishment, as it allows you to possibly redeem yourself.
There are a lot of paths and secrets you can find, which makes exploring rewarding, despite it being dangerous.
There's an absence of music, but I love the ambiance and world sounds. They really add to the creepy atmosphere, along with the awesome visuals.
Overall, it's a really fun game. Hardcore, unforgiving, but it never got frustrating.
Recommended!

I found it to work well combined with charming graphics and fun but simple platforming.  The boss fights are interesting and unique, and the final boss fight is a satisfying challenge.  Throw unlockable costumes to the mix for collecting hidden secrets and you've got a great game.

Few games draw me back to them like Alan Wake. Few games can boast an atmosphere that feels like an American fever dream brought to life. Equal parts Stephen King thriller and Twilight Zone episode, you take the role of a big-city writer caught up in the ancient horrors that refuse to stay asleep at the bottom of a lake.
The soundtrack alone is chill-inducing. Despite some dated facial animations that can feel a bit dated or puppet like in mouth movement, you'll be a bit too busy dealing with the Taken to worry yourself about that too much.
With surprises hidden around every corner and startling revelations to be made, Alan Wake takes the crown as one of my favorite games Remedy has produced so far.
If you're a fan of their work, this is an absolute must. If you're looking for a spooky but less gorey equivalent to survival horror, this is also perfect for you. Less jumpscares and more tension, sure, but this game stands the test of time.

I've never laughed so much at unintentional humor while playing a game. It feels like a mix of Blackthorne and smash brothers. I first heard about it from TotalBiscuit , and have been in love with it ever since.
The multiplayer is where the real fun is at, where up to four people play either free-for-all or on teams until they're the last duck(s) standing. It only takes one hit to kill another duck, so there's a lot of strategy involved in trying to kill other ducks while keeping yourself alive. The weapons are quite varied, but far from useless. A dueling pistol only able to fire a single shot a few feet against a chain gun sounds like a bad matchup, but you'd be surprise what you can accomplish with some quick moves and a little bit of mind games thrown in.
The single player is also very well done. While it's just a set of levels with goals and timers, it becomes addicting to try to get the best medal on all of them, and unlock as many hats and game modifiers as possible. It's also a great way to learn all the ins and outs of the gameplay so you're better prepared for the chaos that ensues in multiplayer.
For a $1 you can't go wrong, lots of fun.

Wasteland 2 is best described in the terms of it taking place in a freshly founded roleplay group's basement.
The DM's got their nose pressed up against the book, and insists that the group's main campaign should follow the pre-fab, since that's the right and proper way of doing things.
The group begrudgingly goes along with this, and creates an oddball cast of characters. They manage to entertain themselves for the first dry sessions, goofing around with some dumb gimmick character based around the inexplicable Toaster Repair skill. All good fun.
After a couple of rough dungeons - quite insistent about it being
- the DM looks up from their book, and see the others goofing off. They put the book down, and decide to move the campaign over to LA instead of boring Arizona and instantly everything becomes more fun and interactive. They still wants it to be tacticool though, and kills off the gimmick character. But it's alright, she was one-note anyway.
Basically: It's awkward and janky and plays by the book but gets better eventually. You're gonna have to bear some of the weight of entertaining yourself until that happens, though. Also it's not Fallout, in that any build is viable, and it will kill off your gimpy characters without remorse.
All in all, it's alright. No revolution or anything, but pretty fun.

This game teaches you the valuable lesson that world is made of mud, not dirt.
If you're one of those types who enjoys being in a sandbox game and making really challenging things to try and solve and get out of, Spintires is very much like that.  A major spontaneous problem solving game.  You may think the main objective of hauling lumber is very simple.  Well, it is, in concept.  The thing is, when your log truck rolls, then your winch truck runs out of gas, then your gas truck breaks down, you'll understand how it's so much deeper than just 'hauling lumber'.
It's like a mini-version of life in general...  You have your main goals, but yet on your way you're faced with many obstacles, some of which are created by the things you yourself have done.  That same sense of accomplishment is in this game, not only when you -finally- deliver the lumber, but every time you right a tipped truck, pack some wood using the crane, or unlock a new garage by delivering the garage trailer to a location.
Not only is the concept simple but satisfying, the physics are top notch.  The mud physics are the main brunt of frustration in this game, as they are quite punishing and sometimes random as mother nature can be.  Aside from the couple glitches I've encountered [which both involved my truck being tossed into the air and spinning at an extreme velocity for no reason whatsoever], it plays like you'd expect a big lug of a truck to drive.  The one vehicle that is very strange to drive [as well as quite useless, in my opinion] is the regular 4x4 jeep.  It doesn't drive down the road, it bounces down the road, and will then sink when it hits mud faster than any of the other larger vehicles.
Other than these few peeves, I fully enjoy playing this game for large portions of time.  It's very ambient.  No music, unless you include the insane and random guitar bit that will blow your eardrums out of your head every time you get an achievement.  Sometimes, I'll put on my own tunes on the computer and play.  It's as if you have the radio on.
Multiplayer is, as you'd imagine, even more fun than single player.  Plan your routes/plans/truck builds with your friends or stranger fellow-loggers.  Tow each other out of a bind, or follow your friend as a backup repair vehicle.  Accidental crashes into your fellows are often quite detrimental, and thus also fun and exciting.
I know it sounds like a foolish and random concept.  Maybe it is, 'Russian logging game' didn't seem to appealing to me when I bought it and I had my doubts.  But now, I'm very glad I bought it, and I play it often.

Good old-school RPG and a perfectly faithful sequel. Best post-apocalyptic setting since Fallout 2; superbly reactive world, great story, and plenty of interesting locations, characters, and quests. Eerie radio broadcasts and Mark Morgan’s music sound great, but there are disappointingly few music tracks. The sporadic voice acting is decent and the writing (text descriptions and dialogue) is mostly enthralling. The dialogue “keyword” system was refreshing to use. Graphics get the job done… character models and portraits specifically could use more variety and polish. Good selection of items and weapons, though weapon balance seemed a tad off… Certain weapon types seemed obviously superior to others; shotguns and brawling weapons seemed particularly underperforming. Furthermore, often the most powerful weapons were too quickly and easily obtainable leaving tons of weapons underused and long stretches between upgrades. Skills were an interesting lot, but generally I felt they could have had more varied uses throughout the game, more skill checks, and more unlockable perks. No sneak skill was a bit of a bummer. Gameplay is a tad slow, but in a relaxing way not boring. Not perfect (no doubt due to budget constraints), but Wasteland 2 is a fun, atmospheric, adventure with an impressive amount of content and surprisingly few bugs for a Kickstarted game; it is completely faithful to the original Wasteland, clearly made with love, and easily more satisfying than the recent Fallout games in my opinion. I recommend this game for anyone who enjoys classic isometric RPGs and post-apocalyptic settings. Crossing fingers for Wasteland 3!

-I was intrigued by the story and was really guessing most of my playtime where story could've lead to, but after more and more things became revealed, it statrted to get bland to me.

Can't believe how very positive this game has been rated, I don't understand how the majority can like this game. Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game that, when the conditions of its creation are put on paper and read, simply should not exist. One man over the course of four years with the desire to create the game of his dreams learned everything he knows about game creation from step one through the creation of this game.
Impressive as that story may be, Dust isn't a great game because it's such a labor of love. Dust is a great game that gets by on its own merits with fantastic and engaging combat, some of the most beautiful 2D sprite and background art you'll ever see, a huge world to explore with lots of secrets to find, and a wonderfully acted story and world full of adventure and endless intrigue.
Though Dust began its life as an XBox 360 exclusive, "PC Master Race" nerds (I mean that in the most insulting way possible) shouldn't feel put off by the prospect of this being a lazy port. Dust has been optimized in a great number of ways for its PC showing, including full 1080 support, uncompressed visuals, a new UI specifically tailored to keyboard and mouse controls, and a set of keyboard and mouse controls that make sense. As someone who originally played the game on a gamepad, I had no problem adapting to the mouse and keyboard controls offered here, and they're as configurable as you'd want them to be for your own ideal setup.
Dust's only real shortcoming is that it can be a tad on the easy side, but it's nothing that can't be somewhat remedied by cranking the difficulty up to Tough or Hardcore to provide a bit more of an adequate challenge.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is a no-brainer, really. It's fun, it's charming, and it's one of the best damn PC ports ever. Get it now!

The review will be constructed into 5 parts:
1. Game description (from what i've seen in the time i've played).
2. Did i finish the game (YES/NO/Maybe in the future) and why.
3. Pros/Cons.
4. Final thoughts.
5. Rating
So let's beggin...
1. Game description:
A point and click adventure game with a small twist. You play as 2 different characters and cand switch between them whenever you want. At first it is very simple but after a while it gets a little bit complicated and a little bit counterintuitive, but nothing  too complicated. Astonishing visuals, and although I am not a big fan of hand drawn games, this one did it beautifully.
The environments and atmosphere are totally gorgeous , the music fits perfectly in, and the voice acting is beautiful. Thought I recognized some voices but only at the end credits did I realize that that was because  some major Hollywood actors voiced the characters.
The story unfolds before you and is very well done.
2. Did i finish the game? YES
Once in a while H.B. manages to surprise me. This game is one of those games. It caught me completlly offguard and I finished it all in one sitting. It has been a while since a game got me pinned to my screen for so long. I was not expecting this.
3. Pros/Cons.
PROS:
- Nice visuals
- Funny
- Great voice acting
- Good story
CONS:
- A few puzzles are counterintuitive
4. Final thoughts:
I cannot recommend this game enough. Just  get it and buy it! You will be pleasantly surprised even if you are not a big fan of point and click adventure games.

I went to McDonald's today and got a Filet-O-Fish combo with a bacon cheeseburger on the side. I was eating it in my vehicle in the parking lot and listening to an audiobook when I glanced up and saw the McDonald's worker I ordered outside having a cigarette.
She waved at me and I nodded and had to wait 7 minutes before she went back inside and I could eat in comfort again. I don't think that employees should be bothering or even trying to socialize with customers outside of the McDonald's restaurant or drive through, but that is another story.

I've never laughed so much at unintentional humor while playing a game. It feels like a mix of Blackthorne and smash brothers. I first heard about it from TotalBiscuit , and have been in love with it ever since.
The multiplayer is where the real fun is at, where up to four people play either free-for-all or on teams until they're the last duck(s) standing. It only takes one hit to kill another duck, so there's a lot of strategy involved in trying to kill other ducks while keeping yourself alive. The weapons are quite varied, but far from useless. A dueling pistol only able to fire a single shot a few feet against a chain gun sounds like a bad matchup, but you'd be surprise what you can accomplish with some quick moves and a little bit of mind games thrown in.
The single player is also very well done. While it's just a set of levels with goals and timers, it becomes addicting to try to get the best medal on all of them, and unlock as many hats and game modifiers as possible. It's also a great way to learn all the ins and outs of the gameplay so you're better prepared for the chaos that ensues in multiplayer.

A solid game if you are already a fan of old school RPGs. Anyone else should approach with caution, there are certainly better entrypoints into the world of deeper RPGs. I backed this on Kickstarter, quickly tried the original release but never got very far. Finally got around to playing the Director's Cut and finished it on Ranger difficulty.
The good:
- The actual RPG part is quite good, with decent amount of choices and consequences
- Lots of the individual locations have interesting stories. Too bad the main storyline isn't nearly as compelling
The bad:
- Game mechanics are badly balanced, some stats, skills and weapon types are simply much more important than others
- Combat is passable but lacks any real tactical depth. There's lots of it too, and it gets quite repetitive by the end of the game
- Graphics are passable but certainly one of the weak points of the game, even after they were redone for the Director's Cut
The ugly:
- Lots of scripting bugs with the quests. A couple of the side quests were completely broken
- Stats have minimal effect on most non-combat skills, which leads to some extremely silly builds

Even before actually playing the game, I was already hating Sega with my guts for this piece of crap.
- "Best played with gamepad" shown (actually "Am besten mit Gamepad gespielt." - see below), and this is apparently just advertising for Microsoft input devices. It's also helped along by only giving you three keyboard control presets (and they're all sub-optimum, and it's incredibly lazy considering you have two actions plus direction keys). Yeah, you won't need analog movement controls for this game either, so the controller advertising is complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. (At least the few movement tests I did with keyboard felt like giving me enough control. Analog controller movement results in either run or stroll.)
- Said message is part of the ♥♥♥♥ing 25 seconds of unskippable game launch intro! (More if you don't press Enter and then Esc at the right times.) And even returning from in-game to the main menu (e.g. for quitting) wastes several seconds with unnecessary transitions. You're better off just pressing Alt+F4, but hell, who knows whether that might screw up your probably only savestate in this autosaving piece of console crap.
- Menu navigation is slooooow. You cannot press an arrow key and expect the menu to switch to the next point with that. No, you have to do things slowly, the way the game wants you to do it. It wants to complete its fancy text animation first before going to the next point.
- Game disregards Windows version locale, general Steam language setting and game-individual Steam language setting and runs in the location set in Windows system config, which is idiotic, because what's relevant is the language the user understands, not where he is located. I tried finding config files and couldn't, except one with two useless entries. I searched the Windows registry and couldn't find settings there either. Command line parameters? Who knows? Very likely not, since this is just another piece of crap carryover from consoles. I eventually, using a frickin hex editor like a code hacker, found all the available variables and the registry key for the config, which is "SSA\COI", which explains why my keyword search earlier remained unsuccessful. And, well, ... there is no language setting at all in this game. It is hardcoded to take the Windows locale setting, so you'd have to change that every time you play the game if it's not the desired language. And as you can derive from the game forums on Steam (which you should always consult before buying a game, after you've read some of the negative reviews), some people have no choice, their game being in Japanese.

Achievements are either damn easy or too difficult to be motivating, since getting 100% of some items can mean searching for hidden stuff, and in some levels you might skip items because there are multiple paths and once you take one, the other one is locked. So some achievements would require tedious repetition of content. The same type of 100%-completion-achievements in Giana Sisters - Twisted Dreams were much more motivating and fun.
Difficulty is not trivial. It provides some challenge. Bosses for example might need one failed run in order to learn how the fight works. Level design is done in an interesting way, with lots of variety and intermission scenes and such. Game also has a narrator.

This game is a lot of dark fun. In dark forests, fighting against dark people imbued with dark power on a dark night. Fighting with light is quite original. Aiming with a flashlight is done very well, though one could be bothered by the lack of a crosshair. Its absence adds to the great immersion this game allows. What I hated though was the terribly weak sprint capability of the player character. It would be nice to add a sprint bar to the HUD. The story events are comprised of narration by Alan Wake and unchronologically placed manuscript pages (meaning we know what will happen in a few moments), that detail actions by the many characters of this game. I liked Barry, Sheriff Sarah and Dr Hartman the most. The ensemble of voice actors did a great job though many people don't like it. Alan Wake's model did a great job as a live-action actor as well. The story is very mysterious and leaves you in the dark most of the time, though it has a satisfying pace and finale. Some people say the game is too easy. Well, I would definitely tell them to try the game's Nightmare Mode or the significantly harder DLCs. The soundtrack has some great tunes, mostly rock songs (like Space Oddity) and the industrial score for the game is nice. The story is not pure gold, it's pretty B-movie, which isn't a bad thing, but I didn't pay much attention to it during my second playthrough. The first one was indeed very satisfying (even with hundreds of collectables).

I am writing this review about 6 hours into the game, and I'm out. I can't finish it. I've been enjoying the story. Visually, it's very well done. The gameplay is just monotonous and awful.
You run through the woods at night with a gun (if you're lucky) and a flashlight. You face one enemy over and over again. They only make it harder by making it unfair. They just throw more of that one enemy at you at a time. I finally gave up on the game when two of them materialized 6" away from me and killed me before I knew what was happening. The basic combat mechanic is that you use the flashlight to burn the evil off the enemies and then you can shoot them. This leads to "holy crap... aim the flashlight... WAIT A WHILE... shoot," which really creates a weird rhythm when you're trying not to be killed by ghosts with axes. The flashlight has a button, that I've never seen on a flashlight before, that makes it way brighter, but kills the ENERGIZER batteries in seconds. In fact, you spend so much time in this game replacing dead batteries, I don't understand how Energizer thought this particular product placement deal was going to help them. It makes me want to buy Duracell.
For those who really like collecting things, there are also thermoses you can pick up throughout the game, but I have no idea why. They are not discussed.
So, as I said, I'm out. I hope Alan finds his wife, but I can't be the one to help him do it. I simply cannot bear another 7+ hours of this repetitive combat. What I really want is just a video of someone playing the game, with all the combat edited out. That wouldn't suck.

Hard West is a good game that is mired by a few poor design decisions but stands strong on what it does have in the end. The game isn't very big, and you'll repeat combat encounters on many of the maps that are there. The tactical options are limited, which is the biggest problem in this game, there is no real character progression and the 'between battle' portions are woefully inconsistent and need to be redone in there entirety. That being said, they aren't boring or bad. They just add very little.
Despite these failings, the game delivers in spades to a theme(The Weird West, think fantasy in a Western setting) that is woefully lacking in video games. The dialoge is strong, the voice acting is astounding and the whole sound design is much stronger than expected. Even the game play, with its lack of tactical options(no over watch, like XCOM. And it is sorely needed), Hard West is a solid tactical isometric strategy game, even if it only feeds you in small bites.

Hot damn. This visual novel is awesome.
Other reviews have already mentioned the nice art and the exceptional music, but to me the most interesting aspect was the way it made me think about the issues at hand.
DS:LTMC will interest you if you're into moral choices (and dilemmas), problem-solving and/or a heated discussion. Although there aren't many dialog options, the words, art and music work together to create a thrilling scenario that had me sitting in front of my computer pondering each option carefully for sometimes up to half an hour.
The characters are very believably written, meaning you can relate to most of them. Though that doesn't necessarily mean that you'll like them. In addition to that, the VN gives you some minute background information on its inhabitants and inner workings that introduces what could become an amazingly detailed story world. There are lots of hints that leave me hoping they will be explored in the episodes to come.
And aside from the intellectual points of interest and the detail of the story world, the emotional impact this VN has had on me was one of the greatest among everything I have bought on Steam so far.
I heartily recommend buying this. Five bucks is somewhat steep for the amount of time you'll spend with it (up to 3 hours max for the first playthrough), but the sheer quality of this production damn well justifies the price.
Also, their Kickstarter was a success, so Dischan will release the remaining two chapters as well! Hooray!

: Due to the developers not being able to make a sequel right now, and this game being what is essentially the first chapter of a book, I can't recommend this game if that's not your thing. It's still an excellent experience, however, and is worth it's small price.
I notice people complain both about the length of the story and the small number of choices. However, the story is rather deep with a good sense of innocence that really drives the character development. Equally so, the choices carry with them some fairly large ramifications. For example,
.
Yes, the story may be rather short, but I still feel it has a good amount of content; considering it's only $4.99, you can't really turn it down.
There are many a debate in the discussions area for this game, about world economics, strife, turmoil, and the other various topics this game gives you thought to. If anything, if you're the debating type, you could get a lot of brain candy out of playing this and mulling it over with others.
Obviously, the length and the content are the main factors to gripe about, but like I said, it's worth it taking the price into consideration. Another reason you might not want the game is the fact that though the choice trees give a different emotional outcome, the story is largely "on-rails" and the physical, general outcome of the story is the same no matter what choices you choose. Of course, this allows the story to follow the path the developers want and to allow them to craft a truly excellent story, but veteran VN players may find issue in this.
As an up-side to the short length of the story, each choice tree provides almost completely different dialogue than their comparatives, filled with witty, humorous writing. It'll be the same general story no matter what you choose, but you'll get a totally different emotional side of it. I think this really helps define the characters, as well, giving much more depth in the span of time the game allows.
The art is really quite excellent. I love the sharp facial features and the muted colors. However, the "painted" style of the background is somewhat iffy at times; it isn't to my tastes. It would look much nicer if it was a bit sharper to match the foreground, though it does allow the characters a better contrast to their surroundings, causing you to focus on them and their expressions more.
It would have been neat if the 3D designs featured in the AV sequence were extended and put to use as background material or similar.
The UI is gloriously developed and a joy to both look at and navigate. All of it animates smoothly and completely and fits the psuedo-futuristic feel of the game. It's a little visually busy, but I like that.
The characters all feel like they have established roles, identities, and personalities, but the story is too short to really get to know them as much as I'm sure the average VN player would like. If you're the kind of person to play VNs for the character development, Dysfunctional Systems is rather good at that in the small time it plays for.
There are a lot of different sounds in Dysfunctional Systems, all of them atmospheric, quality, and unique. They put a lot of work into the sound design of the game. I will most certainly be putting the complete FLAC OST, which is included with the game files for free, into my music library. If anything, get it for the kickass music. It's incredibly high fidelity and plays like a professionally released album.
I would recommend this to any VN player that doesn't mind a shorter experience. Despite its length, the story is hard-hitting and is both relevant to the issues of today's world and challenging to the mind.
Unfortunately, the developers went essentially bankrupt and have shelved any and all future projects indefinitely, so we won't be able to see any more of this universe for a while, if ever. It's a shame, really. You can check our their blog to see what happened and to browse their other works (including more awesome music).

It's a visual novel, through and through. Though some people may argue that visual novels aren't games because they don't contain actual gameplay, it's certainly not a bad thing to have them around as people such as myself certainly enjoy them. Besides, if you choose to get this game you should be well aware of what it entails. That said, I'll try to briefly highlight the pros and cons without spoiling the story.
If you're expecting a story which is tailored to the choices you make as you try to alter the outcome of your journey, then it might disappoint you when I say there isn't much of that to be found (yet). Sure you will get a chance to choose on how the story continues but that opportunity will occur once and can only go in either of two directions. Both having a different kind of ending but aside from the words you choose to get there are pretty much identical. Now I included the word "yet" in brackets because this is just the first episode out of a three in total.. and from the looks of it, episode two seems like a more branched out story.
Being a visual novel, that's about the only possible con I can think of because the story in itself is really intriguing and takes place in a quite captivating era. Everything else from sound to music and artwork is well done and really sets the mood for the events that are to come. Even the characters look very promising with their different personalities. It's a great and elaborate premise to what just may turn out to become a marvelous series.
Like almost every other visual novel, the game features a quick load & save system allowing you to save your progress before you make a choice and go back if you're not pleased with it's outcome. This is partially in vain because you can just use the regular save and load system at any given time during the story or choices. It only saves a bit of time and perhaps a save slot. Also, with only one set of choices and two outcomes, one may question the use of choosing a different road other than fully exploring the available dialogues. In the end it does ask if you want to save your profile, which basically means your choices may affect what is to come in the next episode.. but other than having two profiles for both endings, I wouldn't expect any major changes.
In conclusion, it's a great prelude to what promises to be a great series albeit a bit short in length. It is in no way to be considered a full story in and all by itself.. whether that's worth the price comes down to how much you're willing to pay for an opening introduction. My opinion: other than fancying a well-told story; if it develops a bit more and becomes more subject to the player's choices.. I'd say it's definitely worth it.

Let me first say that I never played the original Castle of Illusion, so I'm judging this game by what it is on it's own.
And what it is is a rather short but all right platformer with excellent presentation.  The storytelling aspect, narrator and all, is pretty good.  The level and enemy visuals are appropriately creative and "magical", evoking that early "Harry Potter" feeling of wonder.  But the gameplay itself is "merely ok".
Castle of Illusion is pretty easy for the most part, though the difficulty does ramp up toward the end.  I died a few times to almost every boss while figuring out the patterns (I'm a bit slow when it comes to this), and had to use a continue on the final boss.
I had some strange drops in performance in most levels - strange because while my system doesn't quality as a "modern gaming rig", an i7-920 w/HD4850 shouldn't have had any trouble running a game with these graphics - which while rather nice looking, aren't exactly complex.   And this was with Anti-Aliasing disabled.
It should also be noted that this really is a very short game - it took me just under 3 hours to beat.   It would obviously take longer to 100% it (get all the gems and other collectibles in each level) but if you're like me, you don't care about that kind of stuff.
As such, I'd recommend waiting for at least a 75% off sale.  I think I got my $3.74 playfire reward's worth out of CoL, but I'm glad I didn't pay any more than that.

Overall, Alan Wake is very well made when it comes to storytelling. As you play, you get to collect manuscripts which contain your story - its past, present and future. It is an interesting way to provide some insight into the background of what is happening somewhere else at the same time, or what will happen to our protagonist in a moment - very unique. The combat is very simple but nevertheless, still fun as you gain access to a variety of weapons such as flashbangs or flares which enhance the experience rather than just simply making it shooter game. I also enjoyed the characters, there were not too many but each of them was memorable and had impact on the story. What I'd like to bring up was the animation of characters' mouths during cinematic cutscenes. Most of the time it looked poorly made but let's keep in mind the game's 7 years old now so for that matter, it's as good as it could be - but then I'd just be trying really hard to find mistakes in the game. Developer's commentary brings something really new to the game. You can turn this feature on in the settings which I suggest to do on your second playthrough. You will get some really interesting info from the developers about the game and the story, it's sometimes played over the game's dialogues and contains spoilers often so make sure you don't turn it on during your first playthrough.
If you're really into games that focus on story with horror atmosphere, Alan Wake is the way to go, surely enjoyable experience that I haven't had perhaps in good 2 years.
