Spintires can simply be described as an off-roading simulator. You're driving Russian trucks in varied landscapes to achieve objectives. Simple enough, right? So what's included?
The vehicles, all of which have their unique feel to them, actually fight the terrain. If you're going up a hill and you get stuck in the mud with 2 wheel drive, you can bet your two pennies that your rear end is going to be sliding. If you're going over some rocks and you high center the truck, better hope to have a winch or the ability to reverse out. There are so many things to think about from watching how deep the river is that you're about to cross, to things like if the truck weighs too much for the questionable bridge you may be crossing. You really have to know how to manage your resources, and make the best with what you've got.
The game supports a Logitech G27 which made me feel like a kid at Christmas! With the G27 racing wheel, it feels realistic. When you go up a hill or hit a bump and the truck wants to steer one way, you will feel the wheel move in that direction, which is very cool. Of course you can adjust the wheel to your settings. You can use it with a manual shifting setup, or if you're a novice, you can still use it with the automatic shifting. Absolutely wonderful to have that option!
So what are the downsides? Well there's not a lot to do in this game. You explore to reveal the map, deliver some logs or other supplies, repair or refuel other trucks you might find, and that's basically it. Fortunately the maps are large, and there are a good handful of them to keep you busy, with some maps being much more difficult than others. Additionally there are difficulty settings which will change how your trucks get damaged via your driving.
There's no multiplayer. You cannot go out with your buddies off roading, or have your friend winch you out of that mud hole that you're stuck in. It's solely single player.
Lastly, the camera. There's no interior view, as the kick-starter for this game didn't make enough for it to be an included feature. The camera you have is very awkward and I've found myself stopping my truck just to reach over for the mouse and adjust the camera angle. It doesn't automatically move, at all. Additionally you only have two camera-settings to keybind. A Front/Back on/off toggle, and Trailer. That's literally it! The camera has been a real pet-peeve of mine. You might get around it but others, not so much.
However, there is mod support for this game, and some mods might fix this camera issue, but I haven't found any success with that yet. You can modify this game with new maps, sounds, vehicles, textures, and other odds and ends. I haven't modded this game at all, so I can't confirm if modding this game is difficult or not.
This is a very promising and satisfying game. If you can get past the camera, you can sink a lot of your time into this. The biggest thing that makes me happy about the game (Other than the G27 support) is that it made you think. I have little to no off-roading experience, so it is very fun to figure out how a certain situation was going to turn out. Buy this game and give it a go, you won't be disappointed.

Broken Age is a story driven point-and-click 'adventure' game in the vain of the old classics such as Grim Fandango.
When I bought this game, both acts were already available to play back-to-back. Apparently though, when Broken Age was just released, act II was unavailable for quite a while. That's pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥to begin with, because act I is about 2-3 hours long, even while exploring and trying everything there is to see.
Though Act I was pretty short, it was easily the best part of the game. You choose between 2 protagonists in vastly different settings, and can switch between them freely to progress their stories. All of the puzzles and riddles and what not are pretty logical, and as mentioned, the fact that you can switch between 2 different characters means even if you're stuck, you can always try something else for a while.
The only negative thing here would be that the game could be too easy for you if you're a seasoned Point and Click player.
Still, there are some stupid puzzles in the latter half of Act I, but all in all, act I was pretty good.
Act II is where the ♥♥♥♥♥torm starts.
I don't want to spoil anything, even though the game is pretty old by now, but there is not much new stuff to see in the second act. The plot gets pretty ridiculous pretty fast, and the puzzles get a lot less fun. Most puzzles in act II required me to have a walkthrough open in another window just to progress. Maybe that's just because I'm a bit stupid, but I think most people would agree that act II was a serious downgrade from act I.
In the end, the story has a pretty mediocre ending, and the game isn't really memorable at all.
The voice acting and art-style are pretty amazing though, a lot of celebritys lended their voice to this project, but ultimately, in my opinion, I wouldn't recognize this game, as it's a bit short and a bit mediocre to really buy it for 23€

Hard West is an interesting game but it is not the game for me.
The game is broken up into Scenarios which consists of small, bite-sized bits of content and a few combat encounters. Very little of your progress from these Scenarios carries through the game; the primary exception being any "rewards" you get. These rewards come in the form of unique weapons and talisman items. I completed 2 scenarios, and from my experience there is nothing else that follows through. Your characters do not gain Experience or Levels, nor do they gain new abilities. The upgrade system in Hard West comes in the form of poker cards, 9 through Ace and Jokers. These cards provide stats based on the face and on the suit, and also provide unique abilities. Abilities have wildly ranging usefulness; some are game-breaking and some are completely useless.
For combat, the game is tactical turn-based, very much in the vein of the new XCOM games. Your character has 2 Action Points - 1 typically spent moving, and the other to attack, reload, etc. As with every tactical game, using cover is absolutely vital to your survival. Hard West is otherwise no different. The main problem is that "cover" and "line of sight" mean literally nothing here. Enemies will take shots at you from positions that they could not possibly have line of sight on you. In the first scenario, after killing the local crime boss, the town ends up being overrun by criminal scum that you get the opportunity to clean up. During this battle, there is an enemy on a building rooftop. There is no physical way to get up there, and the only way to win the fight was to slug it out with him from inside the building that he was on top of.
Just to clarify: I exchanged shots with a man by shooting him through the ceiling. When neither of us could have possibly been able to see the other. Most of the combat in Hard West follows a similar formula.
I will say that the first scenario had me very hopeful for what the remainder campaign would be. You and your family are trying to establish yourself as prospectors. The game had a distinct boardgame / choose your own adventure feel with some tactical combat thrown in. It was interesting and then I realized it wasn't going to get any better. If nothing else, the combat really drags the game down with its shoddy mechanics.

Imagine XCOM with a weird west theme and you've got the basic idea.  You play as a variety of characters over the course of 8 scenarios, seeking lost treasure, seeking revenge from beyond the grave, and a variety of other things, too.  There are some supernatural elements to the plot (mostly demons), but in my opinion they're subtle enough that the game doesn't fall astray into fantasy/horror territory.  It's a western adventure, through and through.
I love the tactical combat in games like this.  Also, each scenario has its own unique rules in the "world map" layer, which keeps things interesting as you try to complete your varied objectives from one to the next.
The combat mechanics are also highly thematic for western shootouts.  You have HP and Luck.  If a shot hits, you lose HP (and you can only take one or two hits if you aren't in cover, so you need to be careful.)  If a shot
, you lose Luck equal to the percentage of success on the shot.  (When you get hit you also regain some Luck as compensation.)  The overall effect is that, even when you're doing remarkably well, you're constantly aware that
The game is fantastic, but it also has some flaws - all very minor though.  The ability to zoom in and out during missions to get an overview of the area is sorely lacking, for example.
On the plus side, the devs seem to be pretty responsive - other issues I've seen reviewers point out seem to have been addressed with new settings options in updates.  For example, the inability to save in the middle of a mission was addressed with an "experimental" quick-save/quick-load feature (that seems to work just fine for me.)  Also, there's an option to alter the speed at which text is drawn, so if it's too slow you can now make it faster (or even instant.)
If you like XCOM and other isometric tactical combat games, you'll feel right at home here.  If you like westerns, I think this game does a great job of evoking that atmosphere.  You can practically taste the dust in the air.
Because you like the idea of a western XCOM.  I know I've already made that comparison, but it really is the easiest criterion by which to decide if you're wasting your money or investing it.

I really wanted to like this game. My two favourite games are Planescape Torment and Fallout 2. I’ve completed both numerous times, however I gave up on Wasteland 2 halfway through due to a combination of boredom and frustration. Let me try to explain why.
Before the final release of the game, I was pumped. I read the whole manual, then sat down and wrote lore friendly bios for my four rookie rangers and distributed all the stats according to their role in my team. In the end I found this whole process more fun and engrossing than the actual game.
Basically the game is boring. These were the main things that I found dull:
•It’s filled with loot which is pretty much junk and doesn’t give you a proper reason or options to customise your character load outs.
• Drawn out, repetitive, dumb combat. They could have learnt some lessons from X-Com here. Basically there are no tactics, there’s no cover, no use of the terrain. I ended up maxing out the Outdoorsman skill and skipping Outdoor encounters to avoid the snoozy combat and the same tiny maps I’d seen so many times before. The combat boils down to a battle of attrition. I hurt you a little, you hurt me a little. Repeat.
• Poor level design combined with a plethora of boring fetch quests which force you to run from one end of a massive map to another.
• Finally the choices you make don’t impact the world in a way which made me care. The only noticeable impact was that in the main base everyone was like “Why are you so big and strong and everybody likes you!” Which I generally liked. But it does feel shallow after a while. I hadn’t really appreciated how immersive and good the quests were in Fallout 3 until I played this game.
In the end I hit a bug where one of my party members got stuck in a quest and I couldn’t get him back or replace him. I think that bug has gone now, but I still feel no inclination to go back to the game.
Basically I can’t recommend this game even a little. If it was free, I’d suggest that your time is too valuable to spend on it.
Also I forgot to mention. At one point you have the opportunity to free a bunch of female sex slaves from the Red Scorpion Militia and one of them is called Schnitz, which I found to be poor taste and it’s the kind of joke a kid might make. This gives you an idea of the maturity of the people that put this game together and the kind of story telling you’ll be exposed to playing it.

I have played many many hours with Natural Selection 2 and for the most part, I have greatly enjoyed my experience. My feelings about it are very complex, as it's a bold and innovative step in FPS multiplayer, has excellent developer support, and a pretty good community to boot. There are frequent updates and gameplay balances, and a new map is released roughly every six months or so. The two opposing factions are assymetrically balanced and gameplay is varied and interesting. So much so that you don't mind playing the same few maps over and over again countless times. In some respects, this game has pretty much everything going for it.
Sadly, I simply cannot recommend Natural Selection 2 for one very specific reason. The game's greatest strength is its ability to seamlessly blend the RTS experience with the FPS experience, and when you have a team that works well together, under a commander who knows the ropes, this game offers one of the most fun multiplayer experiences available.
It is this same strength which is also the game's greatest flaw. Very often - almost always - your experience is entirely dependant on the person in the command chair. To begin with, no one ever wants to be commander. You will sometimes spend as much as 10 minutes waiting for someone's patience to wear thin enough that they finally get into the command chair, at which point you are at their mercy. Sometimes you will even spend longer waiting for the commander than the actual game lasts.
If this person happens to be you, your command experience will go one of three ways: 1) You will do an excellent job and everyone will love you for it, in which case your game will likely be over very quickly. 2) You will do an excellent job and everyone will hate you for it anyway, because you didn't build X thing at Y time. They will complain at you for arbitrary reasons, even though you are winning the game. 3)You will do a bad job and everyone will hate you for it, likely resulting in you being kicked from the command position, ostricized, and ruining everyone's fun.
Additionally, while the game is quite expertly balanced, it takes very little to upset that balance. A bad or good commander can mean everything in a game, and very often the fun and enjoyment of as many as 24 people hinges on that commander's ability to play the game. It's not uncommon to spend hours going from stacked game to stacked game because teams just can't seem to turn out right. And then, when that magical golden ratio finally occurs, and the game looks like it's going to be a long, bloody, brutal fight to the death, someone rushes your base and the game is over before you have time to check the map.
So, while I have had some real fun with Natural Selection 2, at the end of the day I just can't recommend a game with such a massive, fundamental, and irreversible flaw. The average player just has to put in way too much effort and patience to squeeze the fun out of this game. But I do admit that if you manage to do so, you will be in for quite a treat.

"If god spoke to us, what would he say?" - Bill Cosby, I'm pretty sure.
I've always pondered this question, being the good Christian boy I am, but never thought I'd discover it in a game worth less then a frozen Hot Pocket I haggled off of a LA street vender.
Mountain, to simply put it, is a game where you are God. You create this mountain purely off of representations of your feelings, or just out randomly moving your mouse like an epileptic monkey on LSD.
Once you have created you master piece you can slam random objects that fall from the heavens (repeatedly until you get Achievements). Many of these objects are truly metaphorical and mean more than meets the eye, for example:
*The Satellite: this shows that the NSA is even spying on God
*The Unopennable Message in a Bottle: this represents the money that you will never get back
*The Trashcan: the reflective surface shows you where the real trash is
*The Baseball: this shows us crying is useless
Another cool feature is just watching. Random events can happen where sometimes it becomes foggy, seasons change or, if you look hard enough, the grass grows! This spices up the gameplay alot, and gives the game a lot of replayability.
You can also express you creativity in this game through the language of music, by rolling your head across the keyboard. (Post Edit Note: I would recommend attaching tacks to each key as you do this to get more "enjoyment" out of the game)
I have so far created master pieces like Mary Has a Little Lamb, Ode to Joy, or even Let's Randomly Spam Key Until Something Happens With My Life.
Just like every God, you can also completely obiliterate your creation by pressing as,zb. So far I have died to The Eye of Love Unrequited, The Sun of Infinite Darkness, and the 2 hour mark.
In conclusion, this game is a masterpiece hidden deep within Steam, one that truly you can only discover for yourself by buying.

When I first tried out this game, I was overwhelmed by the combat mechanics and UI. I had a bad first impression and didn't try it out again for a long time. Having read some great reviews by others, I decided it was worth giving a second chance. I cranked up the difficulty to hard (now I want to try Dark) and finished my first playthrough yesterday. It was a lot of fun! I misjudged the game and found that while there are some learning curves to become good at group combat, this is a game that can stand out next to other RPG series like The Elder Scrolls, Fable, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.
I can't and won't directly compare this game to Skyrim, because I feel they inhabit different subgenres. Skyrim is more about the open world, exploration, and freedom of action, while The Witcher 2 excels at storytelling, well-scripted combat encounters, boss fights, and living the life of a monster-hunter.
The only thing I wish was different about The Witcher 2 is even more monster contracts. There is just something exciting about fighting with silver sword and using alchemy to brew the right potions and oils for the task at hand. I can't wait until The Witcher 3!
If you enjoy games like Skyrim, Fable, or KOTOR, give this game a try!

As a longtime fan of platformers, 2D and 3D, this was an obvious purchase.
I love what they managed to do with this game. It blends 2D sidescrolling platformer, and 3D platforming into a near seamless experience that manages to incorporate elements of old and new into a wonderful experience.
Now, it might seem "easy" at first, but let me tell you, that like any 2D platformer of the time, this is quickly thwarted once you get to the later levels. If you want to get EVERYTHING, it's going to cost you. Some of the later levels, like the library and the castle, are most definitley a test of what you've learned throughout this adventure.
The boss fights are mostly just pattern memorization, as there is no randomness that would otherwise make it harder, and they're all on set patterns. As long as you memorize what order a boss does something, you should be fine.
Overall, if you want a fun platforming experience, and want to just have a quick romp, give this a spin.

Building a minimalist puzzle game must be equal parts satisfying and immensely frustrating.  I think it takes a very keen sense of logical mechanic design and an understanding of what is visually and aurally appealing.  The developer of Hex seems to grasp these concepts well, but does miss the mark in a few areas that affected me personally and perhaps some others with the same limitations.
Hex is a puzzle game that has you moving a dot between hexes directly away from each face of the shape to another (much like a hex-based board game) with the effort to clear the board of the required hexes.  There are a variety of hexes with different properties, for instance, the black hexes only need landed upon once to remove them, but grey ones twice.  It doesn’t take long for the types and colors of the hexes to grow and this presents a diverse set of rules that must be followed to complete each level successfully.  Moving your little eraser dot is reminiscent of Chinese Checkers in that you can either move one space to a hex or two spaces – potentially jumping over another hex.  This is of course much more complicated as you reach hexes that can’t be jumped over, or hexes that can only be accessed by a double jump or single jump.  However, the entire process of playing this game is simple to pick up and certainly accessible for a lot of people, including those with limited motor skills.
There is one particular issue that I found in Hex that made it particularly difficult for me - as the hexes grow in color, my color blindness starts to be a significant issue in solving puzzles.  The biggest issue I came across so far is that using pink and purple – with each shade changing subtly as you approach them and they are highlighted for moves – created an effect that made the colors very similar in my eyes.  I’m not sure if there’s a simple resolution in color changing as I don’t know what other colors may be used in the many levels of the game, but perhaps some sort of icon or symbol would be a possibility for use in a “colorblind mode” that would make the game more reasonable for people that have difficulty discerning colors.
My history with puzzle games hasn’t been a particularly strong one.  I’ve really enjoyed only a handful and played them through to completion – and of those, most are more mainstream titles like Portal.  However, I do see the merit in puzzle games, especially for those people that want something that keeps their brain working while not requiring a significant time investment or featuring a steep learning curve.  I found the minimalist design, soothing music and sounds, and general low energy of the game to be very relaxing and it actually almost put me to sleep while playing during the evening.  That’s not something I’d normally express as a positive, but when a game seems to strive toward a tranquil experience, I would definitely say the developer has succeeded.  Hex is a game that I recommend primarily to fans of puzzle games, but it may find some more appeal to a slightly broader audience with discounts in the various Steam sales of the future.

Overall, Alan Wake is very well made when it comes to storytelling. As you play, you get to collect manuscripts which contain your story - its past, present and future. It is an interesting way to provide some insight into the background of what is happening somewhere else at the same time, or what will happen to our protagonist in a moment - very unique. The combat is very simple but nevertheless, still fun as you gain access to a variety of weapons such as flashbangs or flares which enhance the experience rather than just simply making it shooter game. I also enjoyed the characters, there were not too many but each of them was memorable and had impact on the story. What I'd like to bring up was the animation of characters' mouths during cinematic cutscenes. Most of the time it looked poorly made but let's keep in mind the game's 7 years old now so for that matter, it's as good as it could be - but then I'd just be trying really hard to find mistakes in the game. Developer's commentary brings something really new to the game. You can turn this feature on in the settings which I suggest to do on your second playthrough. You will get some really interesting info from the developers about the game and the story, it's sometimes played over the game's dialogues and contains spoilers often so make sure you don't turn it on during your first playthrough.
If you're really into games that focus on story with horror atmosphere, Alan Wake is the way to go, surely enjoyable experience that I haven't had perhaps in good 2 years.

So the last few patches have included a repair for my initial complaint.  That being, the game no longer exits when you loose your connection to Steam.  So why am I still downvoting this?  Simple, it still REQUIRES a connection to Steam in order to even start the game.  If your internet is down, or you simply don't have internet access available, you can't even start the game.
This is an absolutely HORRIBLE choice for copyright protection and, as I stated in my origional review, it hasn't even stopped this game from entering the pirate community.  Now they're talking about making another Spintires?  This one isn't even finished!  Good luck team...
Seriously though, this is a pretty fun game.  What got me to purchase it was playing the free demo and deciding that, with the understanding that the game wasn't finished, I liked what I saw.  That said, many months later (has it been a year yet?) the game still has a lot of flaws.
The worst offender is the camera.  It's absolutely horrible, and the "hood camera" hasn't changed that at all.  The main camera is like they took a 3rd person camera and only gave it the option to zoom out 5% of what you actually need for it to be useful.  The roof, I mean hood camera, is only usable when you want to look directly ahead or directly down at the tires and don't care about your actual surroundings.  They're both very jumpy and hard to get at an angle that is actually useful.  When you do get a good angle all it takes is a turn of the wheel to loose it and be stuck in camera adjusting hell again.  About the only good thing is that it's tied to the mouse, which means you can move the camera around without actually stopping.
Another flaw to the game is that it gets repeative and looses it's "challenge" fairly quickly.  Even switching to harcore mode doesn't make much difference.  They seriously need to consider adding more options than just driving from point A to point B and wondering if you have enough fuel to do it.  It would be nice, for example, if you actually had to load and unload the logs yourself instead of it all magically happening.  At this point the lumber "crane" is kind of a pointless vehicle addon, although some community mods are trying to change that a little.
Finally, I have to say that I'm really kind of annoyed with the "cloaking" fields on the map.  Seriously, we live in a day and age where Google can provide us with any overhead view of anywhere we want to go.  No bush driver (I know many) would go into a bush without a map of the area.  It's absolute stupidity to do otherwise.  Why these maps have a "fog of war" is beyond me.  You get to see the uncovered map on the select screen, and it's zero challenge to remove the cloaking fields (just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥.  It almost seems like the designers wanted to throw in a mini-challenge to make you feel like you're doing more than just driving from point A to point B and wondering if you have enough fuel to make it.
At any rate, even though this is a fun game, I'm still giving it a downvote.  The internet requirement is the biggest reason for that, but the repeativeness and annoyances (hello camera!) make the game a chore to play.  Unless you ABSOLUTELY LOVE big trucks and constantly fighting through unpassable trails, skip this title.
Even then, try before you buy!

☻Pecetowego Alana Wake'a ocenić jest bardzo ciężko. Ma swoje atuty (związane zwłaszcza ze sposobem wydania), ale są i wady w rozgrywce. Tym niemniej, dobrze się stało, że pisarz wreszcie na blaszaki przybył.
™W maju 2010 roku Alan Wake zadebiutował na Xboksie 360. Remedy Entertainment nad swoim survival horrorem pracowało przez kilka lat, a przez niemal cały ten okres gra była zapowiadana w dwóch wersjach: na wspomnianą konsolę Microsoftu i komputery osobiste. Kilka miesięcy przed premierą okazało się jednak, że do sklepów trafi wyłącznie ta pierwsza. Trudno zapomnieć rozczarowanie, jakie wśród pecetowców wywołała ta decyzja. Po dwóch latach wreszcie doczekali się jednak opowieści o pisarzu nękanym koszmarami na swojej platformie. Czy warto było przez cały ten czas zaprzątać sobie głowę tym tytułem? Odpowiedź brzmi: tak, chociaż ma on swoje przyległości.
✯Alan Wake to przede wszystkim historia opowiedziana w grze, dlatego trudno ten element pominąć - nawet jeśli został już zanalizowany na wszystkie strony przed dwoma laty. Tytułowy bohater przybywa wraz z żoną Alice do Bright Falls, by oderwać się od rzeczywistości. Owo oderwanie wypada nader okazale, choć zapewne nie tak wzięty pisarz je sobie wyobrażał. Już pierwszego dnia Alice ginie w niewyjaśnionych okolicznościach, a Alan, próbując ją uratować, wskakuje do pobliskiego jeziora i... budzi się ni z tego, ni z owego w rozbitym samochodzie. Na to wszystko zwalają się jeszcze czające się w ciemnościach kreatury, które źle reagują jedynie na światło. Nie jest więc dobrze, zwłaszcza, że Alan musi przebijać się nocą przez ciemny las.
🔫Alan Wake to, jak zaznaczyłem już we wstępie, gra, na którą warto było czekać. Mimo braku szczególnej różnorodności rozgrywki, dostarcza, razem z obydwoma dodatkami, ponad 10 godzin przedniej zabawy. Straszy kiedy trzeba, niekiedy śmieszy, umiejętnie podsuwa użytkownikowi pytania. Dzieło Remedy świetnie dozuje też emocje - mamy tu długie wprowadzenia, chwile napięcia i wreszcie akcję dokładnie wymieszaną z narastającą grozą; to survival w pełnym tego słowa znaczeniu i pod tym względem, podobnie jak w przypadku świetnie poprowadzonej fabuły (za wyjątkiem jej zakończenia), gra przez te dwa lata nic nie straciła. Cieszy obecność obu rozszerzeń, Sygnał i Pisarz - dzięki ich obecności produkt jest tak naprawdę kompletny. Rozszerzenia oferują nie tylko kolejną możliwość wypadu do Bright Falls, ale też odmienną stylistykę i sposób przedstawienia opowieści.
👌Minus należy się za to producentom za kwestie techniczne. Pecetowy Alan Wake nie daje po sobie specjalnie odczuć, że najpierw dostępny był na konsoli - sterowanie, razem z wszystkimi grafikami interfejsu, dostosowane jest do potrzeb użytkowników komputerów, poprawiono także jakość wizualizacji. Jeśli macie więc ochotę na solidną porcję strachu podaną na telerzu wykwintnej fabuły, nie zastanawiajcie się - inwestycja w ten tytuł to pewniak, nawet mimo doskwierających mu niedoskonałości.

If Steam had an "indifferent" classification, I would go with it here, but there isn't and I liked this game more than I didn't so I'll go with a recommendation.
For me, this game was merely alright. It gets bonus points for being a truly cinematic game (not just a game with a lot of cutscenes and then calls itself cinematic to absolve any blame) and the gameplay is really unique. However, it becomes very repetitive quickly and there's not much to change up the formula until the DLC's. The story is...it's mostly well-written. It uses a lot of cliches, Alan has the temper of a four year old which is used multiple times as an excuse to move the plot forward, and has a generic light .vs. dark plot, but the actual dialogue and lines are really, really good.
It felt like this game was taking one step forward, one step back the whole entire time. It gets a lot of points for it's pure creativity and Remedy's willingness to make a somewhat risky venture, as well as it's very good graphics for a 2010 game. However the lip synching is absolutely inexcusably bad, which is more noticable than the excellent graphics. It's especially intriguing about how this game used to be open-world early in development, and the final two episodes are very open ended in nature, but the linear nature of the first four levels feel like they didn't change anything and just dropped barriers down to keep you from going off course.
Did I enjoy Alan Wake? I guess so. I really wanted to love this game going into it and even though it was disappointing and IMO isn't worthy of all the praise it gets, it's not a bad game.

The back-story itself is good too, if you can wrap your head around different planes of existence (with rigid (real) to loose (fantasy/magic) physics). People from Winter's dimension (where violence hardly exists) go to different worlds in different dimensions, and indirectly (or if needed, directly) help solve their problems to "reduce chaos." These problems range from economical woes to the destruction of soloar systems, and everything in between. The smallest decisions can alter the greatest of events. Sometimes, the greatest of decisions can't change the outcome.
Main character, Winter, is considerably witty and self aware while conflicted with her 14 year old naivety, rebeliousness, and need to be autonomous. I get a kick out of reading her internal dialogues.
Things will get sad. Things will get depressing. Things will feels. Things will get intense. Things will escalate quickly.

Alan Wake is a beautifully balanced fusion of movie and game. It's one of the most polished games I've ever played, boasting excellent graphics, sound design, cinematics and, above all, a story that is truly Hollywood quality.
The game is in the main a survival horror, and as is required of the genre, sustains an unsettling, supernatural atmosphere for the most part. My only criticism is that the game isn't able to maintain the atmosphere all the way to the end: in particular, when the game should have been most terrifying, the climax, it felt rather too "comfortable". I think this might be because the game had shown all of its tricks before the end was reached, so there was nothing new to keep up the psychological pressure. Thankfully, the story was closed with such skill this shortcoming did not feel too prominent.
Combat is a lot of fun: It is very exciting when hoards of enemies come at you relentlessly, your limited ammo is running out, and you are desperately reaching to your safe point. My criticism here is by the end of the game, the difficulty doesn't ramp up sufficiently, and battles feel easier and less frantic than they should.
Most of all, I LOVE the story, which is a wonderfully crafted, original and  disorienting affair. The writing  is tight and polished, with great pacing, great dialogue and very little redundancy,. If I were to be picky, the biggest weakness is that Alan Wake himself is not particularly likeable. I was never really rooting for him as I played though: just too self-absorbed and angsty.  As a comparison, Deadly Premonition's story felt more enjoyable because Francis York Morgan was such a cool protaganist. That's despite Alan Wake's writing being superior in almost every other way. Likeable protagonists matter!  Small beans though, because the overall story is masterfully told.
To conclude, this is an awesome port, of an awesome game, done by a clearly awesome team. I recommend this to anyone who likes a game with a great story.

This is a classic, a truly enjoyable game. It returns to the old school fallout scheme centered on impactful decision making freedom and character development centered on alternative ways to approach objectives. It is openworld in the way that the old fallout games felt openworld, but not so much in the way the new ones do. It is more linear in the sense that it is event driven, the locations tend to tie into the main story in some way, and the main questline ends the game.
Notes - mostly the cons you should be aware of:
1. They've created great characters, but they still don't feel "alive." There is no day/night cycle, characters simply sit in their placed spots on the map and you interact with them via admittedly well done dialogue options. This is helpful at times, like when you want to find someone. That said, the lack of movement and life in the characters themselves could've been handled better. Games like Arcanum managed to do this to perfection years ago.
2. The wasteland environment doesn't feel dull (a problem I had with F3 and beyond); the environments feel varied, pretty much all the groups and locations feel unique.
3. Not a great deal of weapon/item variation - You just slowly progress up the pricepoint chain as the game goes on. Would've liked sidequests or encounters that wouldve opened up more unique options in this regard. Also, other than for reasons of bullet scarcity, the game doesn't give you a compelling reason to ever use smgs, pistols, or even melee characters to a certain extent. There is no need to mod weapons to get through the game, and weapon mods are also pretty standard.
4. Main story is solid, but the side quests are really where the game shines. The decision-making freedoms are absolutely excellent and consequences change the game in real ways. Lots of text, but not problematically so.
This game had me all sorts of confused, sad, happy, astonished, and more.  It's worth playing, definitely.

Good game but still feels as though we're being guided along the rails. This feels like a step back from Mafia 2. No clothes shops, no car workshops, no gas stations. Graphics were pretty blah out of the box, but after the patch that unlocked FPS and a ReShade preset, the game looks pretty good on a 1070 GTX. It ran consistently, based on the Steam overlay, at 56-57 FPS.
Pros:
-Little details - reactions to PC, witnesses calling in crimes, etc. The city feels alive.
-Environmental/Weather system (people use umbrellas when it's raining, streets get wet when it rains, and they gradually dry after rains)
-Story is very good
-Voice acting is exceptional
Cons:
-Weather system - sometimes it rained for days at a time, and weather changed far too abruptly at times.
-Side missions to increase racket income are repetitive and tedious. This is where a lot of time in the game will be spent as objectives are clear on the other side of the map from you.
-Enemy and Police AI needs some serious attention. Enemies were completely inept unless it was a scripted event. As far as police: No speeding tickets, I could ram into cars all day in front of police but if I accidentally bumped a civilian a 5 state all points bulletin happened.
-Motorist AI is horrendous. I experienced huge traffic jams in some areas of the city which made some missions impossible to complete.
-Buggy:  Had dual Cassandras and Burkes when I did the last of their personal missions, boats spawing on land, cars I needed to steal blowing up for no apparent reason before I could get to them. Disappearing icons - being told to go talk to so and so (while doing racket earning missions) and not being able to as the icons didn't appear on the map. My "GPS" path displayed would bug out occasionally turning into some super wide path that was impossible to follow, and many more.
-Unless you're a completionist, there's zero replay value. As stated above, racket earnings missions are extremely tedious and that alone is reason for me not to want to touch this game again.
-Locations get reused. "Hey kill a pimp here.." 30 minutes later, hey the boss is so dumb he went back to the same location the pimp was at. Kill him there." With so many locations possible, this is just pure laziness.
-Different endings but really doesn't feel like it means much, because there's nothing after the little ending spiels. What happened to "open world games" letting the player continue playing after the main story is finished? This game could be so much more..
-DLC: First DLC, through free, offered outfits that should have shipped with the game.
tl;dr Good game if you're a "one and done" player. If you're looking for replay value I'd wait and see what future patches and/or DLC offer. As of now I can't recommend the game. It's buggy, should have never shipped with a 30 fps lock for PC players, and feels more hollow than it's predecessor.

Hard West is an OK game.
It's not bad, it's not as great as it could have - it's just OK.
I initially gave it a thumbs down but then I stuck with it for a few more hours and I admit I've enjoyed a good part of it so here I'm correcting my initial review for a more accurate opinion.
The setting of the Weird West is grim, violent and full of ambiguous characters and steampunk-y surprises.
If the developers had access to a higher budget they could have probably made it more interesting in some areas, for example making the endless walls of text more digestable with more comic book sequences or something else. What they didn't need more money for however are a list of obnoxious details that make the gaming experience needlessly grating.
For example, at higher resolutions text is very small and hard to read, and often it's hard to tell if stats are positive or negative (minuses and pluses all look the same) when they could have just easily made the lettering bigger and distinguished values with different colours (the classic green and red).
Sometimes messages appear in the middle of the screen sometimes appear in the lower right corner imitating the style of Steam achievements, needlessly requiring the viewer to move the eyes across the screen and squint at something written even smaller and even faded darker.
The game is always set on permadeath, and if you want to correct a choice you need to restart one of the many campaigns the game is divided into. This means that even correcting the assigned equipment to each cowboy before one of the combat sessions is impossible. Forget to assign that rifle, HP potion or card and you must forget about it for that mission. The combat also gets very same-y after a while: despite the XCOM and RPG facade, the game doesn't really offer much progression and variety - enemies are more or less all the same and weapons too.
The combat however worked well enough and the narrative of some campaigns is rather well thought out, so much so it wouldn't look out of place in a fantasy-Western TV series.
I'm hoping this is the precursor of a much bigger and better game because the ideas aren't bad at all - just the implementations of them a bit simple and mediocre.

Hard West is an isometric grid-based shooter with many mechanics in common with the recent XCOM games.  Deadlands RPG fans (pencil & paper game from the 90s) will be instantly familiar with the genre.  It features characters with 2 AP per turn, 1/2 cover and full cover, flanking and an optional Ironman mode.  In two full playthroughs I found the game stable (non-crashing) but prone to a slow memory leak that occasionally slowed down menu transitions but otherwise did not affect play.
The pace of the game varies between tactical shootouts (the meat of the game) and text-based exploration of the weird West in a landscape format, where your characters make decisions, gain gear and resources, and generally get to know the lay of the land.  There is a lot of text to read!  This may be a plus or minus, depending on your personal preferences as a gamer.  Not all the text is voiced over -- but when he talks, the narrator Death is a major plus.
Hard West consists of eight short campaigns, each of which are self-contained.  Gear, skills and characters don't carry over much from one campaign scenario to the next.  Every five or six tactical missions, you'll be given a new posse of colorful characters and start from scratch in a new campaign with some new, unique associated mechanic (such as precognition, scientific discoveries/tech tree, provisions & passage of time, or simply building the ultimate posse to take down your arch-nemesis).  Unlike XCOM you don't play one squad for the whole game -- you're definitely jumping around to experience different vignettes in the weird West.
Tactically, the game is fair and unforgiving of unforced errors.  Cover is enormously important, as is the counting of "Luck" which decreases on a character when a shot misses them, and increases when a shot hits them.  It models the inevitablily of being shot in an Old West gunfight and eases the sting of missed shots, because misses at least peel Luck stat off the target.  There is also a stealth element to certain missions with the "setup stage," where you can stage holdups and use your team to set up brutal ambushes.
If you can afford to pay full price for this game I feel it is worth it.  You are supporting a small Indie development house who clearly love the weird West genre.  On sale, it is a bargain and a very easy recommendation.  The game features no microtransactions or cash shop, and its DLC is a perfect add-on giving a whole new & challenging independent campaign/storyline and about 20% more playtime for a single, small fee.
It has good replayability if you're going for achievements, because many of the rarer ones require a second playthrough to complete.  The game is full of dark, adult themes and is not suitable for unattended minors.  For a thoughtful tactical gamer, Hard West is a hidden gem. All fans of both Deadlands and XCOM will enjoy their time spent.
Overall 8.6 out of 10 -- could have been longer and featured more enemy variety and sharper AI; occasional hiccups in menus due to memory leak.

When I first tried out this game, I was overwhelmed by the combat mechanics and UI. I had a bad first impression and didn't try it out again for a long time. I can't and won't directly compare this game to Skyrim, because I feel they inhabit different subgenres. Skyrim is more about the open world, exploration, and freedom of action, while The Witcher 2 excels at storytelling, well-scripted combat encounters, boss fights, and living the life of a monster-hunter.
The only thing I wish was different about The Witcher 2 is even more monster contracts. There is just something exciting about fighting with silver sword and using alchemy to brew the right potions and oils for the task at hand. I can't wait until The Witcher 3!
If you enjoy games like Skyrim, Fable, or KOTOR, give this game a try!

A soundtrack to die for, ultra-violent executions, and a difficulty level that will make you scream at your computer, Hotline Miami is one of my favorite games ever. It's a breath of fresh air from your typical "tactical" FPS shooters and the effort Dennaton put into making Hotline Miami really shows. The top-down view lets you plan your attacks out, while the stealth aspect makes it incredibly challenging to blast that mobster behind that window without the other one shooting your face in.
The game has an interesting narrative. You take the role of an un-named man, known to the fans as Jacket. You receive a mysterious phone call as well as a mask and a note telling you to get a briefcase and stick it in a dumpster somewhere. Every once in a while you'll wind up in a room with three masked people, with a horse mask, a rooster, and an owl. They'll ask you strange questions.
I feel as though the game's narrative is well-made because it uses lack of explanation to further the plot, the "Hitchcock Effect".
Overall, I give this game a 10/10. It's a great buy, but only if you're the kind of person that doesn't get mad easily, as it's not an easy game at all.

An intense top down action game set in late 80's miami. very simple objective. kill everyone. occasionally even a boss. of course there's still a twist or two beyond just that. You can kill most enemies on one hit with melee weapons or just gun down everyone you see. I like the realistic aspect added into the gameplay. While it's easy to kill enemies in this game, it's just as easy for them to kill you with a single bullet or blow to the head being able to end your run. With that being said, youre going to die a lot. The game gets incredibly intense and fast paced at certain points with the player needing to make quick decisions based upon the layout of the room. However if you do get killed (which you will) youre able to retry whatever room youre on pretty much instantanously with the press of a button, meaning that it doesnt disrupt the flow of gameplay. Even then, most of the characters deaths dont really feel like the fault of game but rather the player themself.
This game has an asortment of weapons to unlock. You can easily use a gun that an enemy could have been using, but this comes with a risk. Using guns tend to create noise which gets the attention of almost everyone in the room, resulting in death if youre not careful enough. While its not really reccomended to bring a knife to a gunfight for obvious reasons, melee weapons tend to be more quit and make stealth easier. knowing when to use a gun or melee weapon helps. There are also a series of masks you unlock over time, each adding their own little perk to the gameplay such as having your fist do insta kills, starting off with a drill, homicidal door powers and many more. There's also a story somewhere in here I guess. It's pretty vague and it likely means something.
Overall its kind of short but still really entertaining and definatley replayable.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Hex by Studio Goya.
Hex is a meditative puzzle game where your goal is to clear all of the colored hexes from the game board. The game starts off with some pretty simple puzzles to solve but as you complete each world the puzzles will get more advanced.
There are 7 worlds in total for you to play through with 70 levels to complete. There are also challenge levels which increase the difficulty by quite a bit. Each world introduces new mechanics such as Portals, White Tiles and Wall Tiles. There are 12 unique tile types in all and they each change up the gameplay a little bit.
One thing that I really enjoy about this game is the music. It’s really relaxing to listen to and it adds to the overall experience.
Overall, Hex is a fun puzzle game with a simple objective to achieve. It likely won’t be a game that everyone is going to enjoy but if you’re looking for a new puzzle game to play with a great soundtrack then I recommend giving Hex a try. I will also say that the game is great for escaping. It’s meditative music and entertaining puzzles make for a very enjoyable experience.

Hex is, on the surface, a simple hex-based puzzle game where you move your piece around 1 or 2 spaces, trying to clear all the tiles on a screen. Simple enough right...? No, not really. As soon as you get complacent it makes a point to throw new tiles with new rules at you, scaling the maps up and making sure nothing is too easy. Puzzle games are a hard thing for me to put into words what makes them great or not, but I'm gonna try because I had a lot of fun with this game.
Just to touch on some pros. Because of the nature of this game I never really felt helplessly stuck on a single puzzle. When you lose you know exactly where you lost and exactly what tiles you missed. I think everyone's had that game where a puzzle was beyond you and because you either "get it or you don't" you just felt stupid and frustrated and things ended there... oh I spent longer on some stages than any competent person should've, but I was always building off of my mistakes and learning from them. This is also in part to the strong level design, which kept me feeling challenged rather than overwhelmed.
Really the biggest con for some will be the price point. I think it's completely fair for those looking for a quality puzzle game, but people looking for a casual time waster may be put off a bit given the playtime it offers and want to look out for a sale. (The description time is pretty accurate; expect 4-6 hours of playtime.)

This is my first review ever on a game, but here it goes.
I'm going to start off with a list of the upsides of the game followed by the things that really bothered me about it.
Upsides
- Beautiful graphics
- The missions are very simple which isn't much of an upside, as they are the same on every map. But once you get into the map and uncover the cloaking points, it makes it very hard to walk away.
- Very realistic mud physics, haven't seen any other game come close.
- Provides multiplayer support.
Now for the downsides
-Camera view could have been done waaay better, it is a serious pain.
-The multiplayer support could've been done better also. The lobby starter/owner basically serves as the server host, meaning everyone's ping is sh!t. I literally had a friend playing on my lobby using my internet (fiber optic, mind you) and his ping was still over 100.
-The devs have seriously dropped the ball on what could be a seriously amazing game if they would put forth the effort and make more content for the paying customers.
- I believe it comes in overpriced at $30.00, for the fact that you only recieve 5 maps and 7 trucks.
In my personal opinion, I love this game. It has a lot of downsides, but if you're an offroad enthusiast like myself then I think you will enjoy it as well. I would wait until you find it on sale though as I do not agree with it being $30, unless the devs get off their butts and make a dlc pack of some sort.

Middle-earth™: Shadow of War™
This game is of God-Tier level. I love this game, I love the way that it improves from Shadow of Mordor. I just love this game.
Pros -
1. This game looks amazing. It looks fantastic, and I just love looking at the scenery. The 4k Cinematic addon makes it look even better.
2. The fluency of the game is fantastic. You don't feel like you're rushed to do anything, or like you are pushed in the middle of some crazy catastrophe. (Although we really are). The game gives a splendid tutorial, it paces itself very well to those who are new - and those who are coming from Shadow of Mordor can really find themselves getting used to the controls agai.
3. Skill tree - I think the skill tree is something that should be talked about, considering how well thought out it was in comparison to a linear lackluster skill tree like SoM. You can branch out into different options in the skill tree, and can only select one at a time. I think this was a smart move, it allows you to adapt to a certain style. (e.g, preferring Extra Crit strikes, more radius damage, explosions are triggered easier etc.)
4. Story - This works so well in conjunction with my 2nd point. I think the fact that we jump in and continue off exactly where we left in SoM is fantastic. Rather than changing directions entirely, they follow a plot to the end. This makes the game so much better to listen to, and follow the cutscenes. Seeing references to the previous games allow us to have memories about it, or be reminded about and thus leads to the current scene.
Cons -
1. Nemesis difficulty feels like a joke. It's supposed to be the hardest difficulty, yet you can easily wipe it over like it isn't a problem? Nemesis difficulty should be very difficult, not adding one extra hit to every enemy required.
2. I don't think the story was long enough, although this took years to produce, and yes is very good, I would have loved to see more acts, even if it was just filler for the main plot. I like the idea of the DLC coming out, but I feel like it won't be very long to finish those, and may just feel like another side mission. (Quoted 11/26)
I Highly recommend this game to anyone.

It's okay, but not great.  Its clear a huge amount of effort went into the artwork and world creation, so kudos to the developers for that.  But for all that work, the truth is the gameplay doesn't feel all that compelling and quickly devolves into a tedius slog.  Despite the size of the world, you really don't feel "free to explore" it, because the area you are allowed to explore is artifically constrained depending on where you are in the plot.  Once you finally gain access to a new area, there is no reason to go back to the old ones.  It all results in highly linear gameplay, rather than world exploration.  There are other ways to control the plot development, rather than walling-off the player.
Adding to the tedium, about halfway through the game it gets really preach-ey.  And I mean really.   It's clear the developers have a social message they are trying to send, but it's so relentlessly beaten over the player's head that it comes off with a very self-righteous air.  I just wanted to play a game, but I felt like I was reading a never-ending steam of someone's angry Facebook rants.
Lots of potential, and it looks like a lot of work went into it...but I regret purchasing the game.

tl;dr: A promising game ruined by unforgivable design mistakes.
I could tell you how much promise I saw in this game.
Nice and fresh setting, good narrator, interesting enough story, good combat mechanics.
But it doesn't matter because this game features three (!!!) unforgivable game design sins:
In a turn-based game, animations must be entirely skippable or at least allow to fast-forward them.
They are not. This game has missions that will make you painfully watch 2-3 minutes long of enemy movement.
I'd estimate that you spend about 30% of your time actually playing the game and the rest watching it.
Repeatedly, of course, as the game is also rather hard and you will die. Which leads to the next point.
Forcing ironman missions upon players is already a bad idea (let people play how THEY want), but this game goes one step further and does not even allow a save-and-quit during mission. That's right, in a game that is pretty damn slow, you have to play each mission in its entirety and cannot quit. Quite the horrible thing for people with a life.
There are unskippable sequences in this game. I'm not talking about the story videos, but turn-based sequences during missions that are not part of combat and where you have no influence on their outcome. And yet, you will have to do them again and again as you repeat missions.
I am simply baffled as to why any developer would willingly ruin what would otherwise be a good game with easily solvable nonsense like that...

Ah yes, Kerbal Space Program. One my favorite games that i still enjoy playing to this day.
In this review i will tell you why i think Kerbal Space Program is a game that you should pickup if you find it's on sale or if you're feeling smart.
Kerbal Space Program is a space exploration sandbox game that allows you to build your own space- and aircrafts that you can then fly around on a planet similar to Earth called Kerbin.
In Sandbox mode, it's basically up to you to build the crafts of your wildest imagination.
You can create giant Jetplanes that look like they could move the entire population of Kerbin or you could create a huge metal squid to send into space, or maybe a mixture of both :D.
The only thing limiting your creations is your imagination...
It should also be noted that everything is unlocked as soon as you load the save and that no parts or crafts cost anything to produce in Sandbox mode.
In Science mode, you build space- and aircrafts and fly them to different locations and planets to try and collect as much science before either transmitting it back to the KSC
or flying back to kerbin and recovering the vessel through the Tracking station
. You will also need to research tech nodes in order to unlock new parts to use in your Space Program.
In Career mode, you have to manage every single aspect of your Space program, from funding to reputation.
You also have to invest Science similar to Science mode to get new parts, but if you have the "No entry purchase required on research tab" turned off, It adds even more challenge to your career as you not only have to research the parts, but pay an entry purchase to use them in your Space Program
and even then, you still need to pay for the entire cost of your Space- or Aircraft.
The modding community for this game is amazing, they are almost always updating their mods, and if someone decides that they don't want to work on updating mods or that they simply wanna move on, someone else can revive the project and continue on where the old modder left off.
I sincerely recommend that you visit some sort of Mod website such as Forge or Spacedock as the mods for this game are fantastic. Some mods i recommend are: BDarmory, which adds weapons, bombs and missiles that you can attach to your ships, Mechjeb, for newcomers who are just starting to learn how to fly Spacecrafts and B9 Aerospace pack+Extras, which adds a ton of parts that can help you further design the space- or aircraft of your dreams.
To summarise why i recommend this game: It's fun and let's you use your creativity to create awesome Crafts, The modding community is amazing, Hardware optimization is actually pretty good compared to older versions and you can even play multiplayer using a mod called DPM.
If you have the chance to find this game on sale, if you're looking for a fun game where you can use mods to build giant airships with a ton of bombs or have an online spacerace, if you're looking for a game to teach you about how the smarts over at NASA plan and execute their missions or if you are just interested in Space travel in general, i URGE you to give this game a try.

Remember when your parents told you as a child, that 'Patience is a virtue'? (followed by a series of brutal beatings and repeated lashings with a lead-tipped whip?) With Wasteland 2, patience most certainly does pay off. I say this because the game does take a while to get going – from the outset, you’ll find yourself wandering the wastelands with your selected squadron, like a pack of ill-prepared hobos, with access to limited armaments and scarce supplies. But like all good RPG’s, once your characters begin to become more powerful and greater weaponry becomes available, you won’t be able to tear yourself away from it.

The dialogue in Wasteland 2 is kept to a bare minimum and you won’t ever find yourself drowning in an overwhelming deluge of lore, banter or character back stories. Instead, the focus is firmly on combat. Those familiar with turn-based RPG’s will be right at home with Wasteland’s turn-based combat system, with two of the most critical player combat stats being Action Points (AP) and Combat Initiative. A higher number of AP allows your character to perform more actions per given turn, such as firing a weapon, reloading, moving, etc, while Combat Initiative determines how soon your character will have their turn once a battle has commenced and how often they will have their turn throughout the course of the fight.
One of the things I found quite surprising, was how quickly characters tended to level up throughout the game. Even with high level characters, you’ll find that your squadron will still continue to level up in no time at all. This is markedly different to most RPG’s, where it typically takes exponentially more time.
Although not absolutely necessary, previous experience with similar turn-based strategy games such as the original Fallout games (of which Wasteland 2 is undeniably similar to), the XCOM series and so on, is desirable. For those who haven’t played such a title before, I’d suggest accessing the no-doubt numerous online guides to provide you with a comprehensive understanding of Wasteland’s gameplay and help you avoid the frustrations that you’d otherwise encounter as a newbie to the genre.
Along with Pillars of Eternity, Wasteland 2 represents one of the finest gaming experiences I’ve had in recent memory. Veterans of the genre will be immediately reminded of old-school classics such as Fallout 1 & 2, The Jagged Alliance series and the XCOM games, while users who are new to the genre entirely, will discover the true wonders of turn-based RPG’s.

Starting as a mod for HL1 that I have played for hundreds of hours, this has evolved into a terrific game. A team of aliens plays versus marines, each having a commander that controls their team from above in a RTS style gameplay making this team-shooter a unique game with a unique gameplay.
The gameplay is very quick, especially when playing on the alien side due to the high movement speeds, but still strategy is paramount to win in this game.
Some points I especially like:
+ Completely different gamplay, based on which side you are on
+ Offers possibilities for slower/more relaxed players (Use the Gorge form as alien - building structures, supporting your team; Welder as marine - repairing structures/armor of players)
+ Succesively unlocking new items in the tech tree diversifies games
+ Having a commander gives the game a special "feel"
+ Teamplay is encouraged
+ Huge choice of upgrades/weapons
+ Playing as commander is absolutely huge and an excellent experience
There are also some things I don't like but they are negligible towards the positive points:
- Finding someone to play commander on your team is often difficult on public servers
- The success of a game depends heavily/ultimately on the skills of your commander
- Overwhelming the marine team after a long game as aliens can be very tedious and lengthy, even after the whole map apart from one base is under alien control. Marines are able to easily defend a single base.
I think this game is a worthy purchase and I can only recommend playing it. Thank you, Unknown Worlds.

Dysfunctional Systems:Learning to Manage Chaos, is not a game, but rather a visual novel. If you judge it under the umbrella of games it doesn't fair well but under the latter it is a very high quality piece of work. It is an enjoyable read from start to finish, this is the first episode in the series and introduces the characters and the concept of the world. I will say that it does start slowly for the first 10 minutes of dialogue and environmental setup, but as it progresses you will get entralled in the world they have created. It discusses some difficult issues of morality and without going into spoilers has school/adventure elements. It has   a relatively good soundtrack, clean interface and offers a few dialogue options (although very minor and few and far between). On the downside it has no voiceacting (but decent sound effects, just shocking no VA given how polished everything else is), and it is quite short, capable of completing within about 1.5-2h. Lastly its second episode is on hault for whatever reason and although at the time of writing this it is underway, the story leaves you desperately wanting to know more. Do I recommend this, yes, however if cost is a major factor I'd likely wait until it goes on sale to see if it is something for you, plus as it is presently an unfinished series you will be left waiting for more.

I really had no idea what to expect going into The Witcher 2, but I everyone seemed to praise it, so I checked it out. I've now played through the game three times and enjoyed it more each run.
The story and writing is definitely a strong point. The characters are memorable and the plot keeps you interested all the way through. The branching storyline also offers high replayability.
The combat is good overall, though I find the trees to be a little imbalanced, and it often turns into roll-fest 2011. I recommend pumping up the difficulty to dark or insane. It will seem pretty hard at first, but once you get a hang of the combat and utilizing all your abilities things will go smoothly.
I hope that in the next game they will increase incentives for going deep into alchemy. While certainly not a useless skill tree, it isn't as inately effective as the others and even when used well, it isn't necessarily extremely strong.
The game has a good amount of interesting sidequests to extend your playthrough and grab interesting gear. Additionally, there are some minigames to be played (arm wrestling, dice poker, and brawling).
Overall the game is fun and challenging at the right difficulty. It's definitely one of the best games of the last few years.

Wow. What a game. Ive heard about this one for a while, but I was never really intrested. Thankfully, I bought this game for a very small price during the summer sale. I ominously opens with a homeless man directly teaching you how to kill people. I was instanly addiccted and played through the levels showing no signs of stopping. Unfortunatly, I was forced to stop after I realized the game crashed very frequently on windows 10, which is my main and only proplem with this FANTASTic game. What else is there to say? The gameplay is satisfying and brutal, which makes hitting a faceless enemy with a door, then chopping into his face with a katana, then struggling to pull it out as the room is painted red with pieces of the guy's face even more brutal and sadistic. It is extremely hard, but not unfare. I have died at least 2,000 times, but I never thought it was the games fault. While games like dark souls create difficulty by making the game basically unfair, this game presents a realistic challenge. What REALLy makes this game one of the most brilliant games in recent years is the range of emotions it inspires among the player. For the first time in a while, I have felt genuinly disturbed and scared even after I turned off the game. This is a game you play alone, at night, with the light off, and the volume turned up high. The chilling and repetitive soudtrack will put you in a trance, and the surreal graphics and visual design makes playing this game the closest youll ever get to doing hardcore drugs without any illegal hardcore drugs. It actually feels like I snorted some cocaine and went on a killing spree, making this game one of the most immersive and disturbing games ive ever played. Also, the story is personally my favorite video game story ever. I have went on a few killing sprees wearing a pig mask and using a pool cue just to learn the origins of a convenince store employee, and it presented new questions and moral dilemmas up until the very end. I give this game a 10/10

This is a weird game at first. I remember first buying it after looking at the polished-looking screenshots (polished, with a lot of grit, if that makes sense), but it sat on the shelf for a while before I actually decided to boot it up. Once I did, I was dropped behind the wheel of a pair of trucks and decided to just roll with it. I got stuck, instantly, and couldn't get myself out. I closed the game in frustration.
For some reason, I couldn't let the game go, and I felt compelled to try again the day after. I discovered that there was an "all wheel drive" function. I got slightly less stuck. I played a little longer, got a little farther, and wasn't nearly as frustrated.
Again, the next day, I was compelled to boot the game up. I then noticed the differential lock button and how to change options on trucks at the garage. See, this story progresses as a linear experience of learning new tricks and tehcniques when it comes to trucking offroad. There's a true sense of power and satisfaction when you drive through places you'd have surely been trapped in due to your own experience and careful wisdom learned through pervious playthroughs. I am now thoroughly addicted to this game and I am learning new tricks every new session. I haven't even tried the co-op mode yet, and I have a feeling that it's amazing. I highly recommend this game for its unique nature, its advanced physics engine, and its palpable sense of achievement which is attained if you just stick with it for a couple of gaming sessions. This game does far more than simply spin its wheels.

Overall, I like the game. It's a fun addictive interactive open-world game which expands upon the previous game's mechanics. I'll give a short pros-neutrals-cons list because you should be pretty busy running your Uruk armies.
Pros:
-Larger world (Something about 4x as large) Total of 5 areas w/ standard game (Galadriel is supposed to add another)
-Olog-hai War Trolls.
-Nemesis System heavily expanded to include more classes of Uruks and more flavors
-More intricate item system involving 6 wearable item slots and 6 gem slots for gems you get from battle/quests
-Siege Attack/Defense battles
-More types of Nemesis Quests
-Ambushes and Betrayals
-Faster movement around the maps
-You get to fight a Balrog
-More skills and a new upgrade system that lets you tailor to your combat preferences
-I don't remember having any great stories from Shadow of Mordor. This game gave me a good story already and I'm sure there'll be more.
Neutral:
-Higher difficulty. (You should die a lot to get the full gameplay experience)
-Collection system is better than before. You get better rewards for running around like a Gofer
-Leveling up is pretty grindy and everything in the game is based on how high level you are
-Combat is pretty similar to the previous game. (Probably a good thing to be honest. Easy to ruin something great if you try to change too much)
-Might/Wrath system.
Cons:
-Hunters are laser accurate spear throwing killers.
-Endgame Grind to finish the game. (Unless you pay money.)
-Repetitive Dialogues
-Derpy movement makes it easy to jump when you don't mean to or just get stuck and die somewhere.
-Derpy combat system makes it easy to sneak attack the wrong Uruk even though you have the captain you want to sneak attack highlighted

[/h1] HERES MY REVIEW FOR BROKEN AGE! [/h1]
I found Broken age when randomly scrollign through the adventure game section of steam, and I LOVE it.
The first thing I will say about this game is that it's not for everyone. It's only for those who are willing to face challenge to get good gameplay, and story.
The puzzles are complicated, and often times can be slightly tedious, but even though that is true to me, Broken age is one of my favorite games of all time, and without a doubt deserved its nomination for a Steam Award.
[/h1] Here's a brief overview of the story: [/h1]
- Broken Age takes place in a kind of two story plot. Which (Through multiple fourth wall breaks, and complex puzzles) Meld together into one. The two main characters, Shay, Vella, and Spoon (Just kidding, spoon is a side character) appear in two different scenarios. Shay lives in the far future, on a starship that patrols the deep abyss of space, but frankly, is treated like a toddler. And Vella lives in a scenario of medieval/fantasy times.\, and is selected to be a sacrifice to the anchient beast known as Mog Chothra. (That is all for this brief overview, I don't wanna spoil stuff)
[/h1] The Pros [/h1]
- First of all, I don't think it's possible to go through this game without acknowleging how beautiful the visuals are. Everything is hand crafted, and I couldn't love it more.
- The puzzles are complicated, which is a con to some, but in my opinion a pro.
- The story is fun, and engaging. The fourth wall rbeaks jsut make it even better.
- The game isn't afraid to have both funny, and dark moments. Which I absolutely love.
- All the characters are cool, and fun. Even if at times they don't feel very... Real.
[/h1] The cons [/h1]
- Some of the more childish moments can be slightly annoying, and make the story less intense.
- I found some parts of the story I would crash, but that ay jsut be my computer.
[/h1] THE VERDICT [/h1]
I absolutely love this game! If you're a lover of puzzle games I would say it is an absolute must play!
But still, it does fall short for soem more casual players, or players who don't have much time.
Overall, I would give Broken Age an 8.5/10, and I highly reccommend it.

has a few minor flaws, but the game as a whole is so amazing and heartbreakingly beautiful that those flaws are easily forgiven. Ah, this is the good stuff right here: "Castle of Illusion".  Yeah, baby.
Hey, look buddy: I'm a grown-up.  I like bourbon after work, fixing motorcycles on the weekend, and watching my wife cook me breakfast in her bathrobe.  But dang it if I don't love me some "Castle of Illusion".  Nothin wrong with that.
Almost every one I know who owned a Sega Genesis back in the day played this game.  Today, I have kids myself but you better believe I'm going to play this game first before I let them get their hands on it.
This is a remake done right.  Not only will you enjoy this game for the nostalgia factor if you played the original back in 1990, but it's a solid "collect-the-items platformer" as well.  Short, yes, and nothing "rogue-like" about it (and that's a good thing, just like the original!),  but absolutely charming and entertaining, improving upon all the reasons why the original game was so great: pleasing soundtrack (same tunes-- thankfully, nicely re-arranged and re-done), surreal graphics, solid character control, and the newly-added option of being able to return to any level to grab up those items you might have missed on your first (or fifth) run.
Bottom line: only the most jaded hipster rogue-lover would not find this game fun.  Do yourself a favor and pick this game up before you buy "Super Indie Hamster Runner" or "Sandwich Simulator 2014".  You'll be glad you did.  And tell 'em Okihara Jones sent ya!

Is the game recommendable? Yes, if you enjoy platformers and a Disney storyline. The actual story was a bit corny, but the game itself was pretty entertaining and well-made, with half a dozen semi-interesting boss-fights. The game is however only a few hours worth of gameplay (to 100% it even), so it serves as a nice game to play when you feel like playing something casual.
Castle of Illusion is first and foremost a remake of the old SEGA Genesis game by the same title. The game is in essence the exact same as the original, in the sense that it features the same maps, the same boss-fights, the same enemies (mostly), but it does so in what is literally a future version of the game.
Back in 1990 when the original was made, the majority of the mechanics they made use of in the remake (2013) were simply impossible to achieve, such as making use of 3D gameplay. While the 2013 remake is mostly a 2D sidescroller (staying true to the original), it does on occassion let you run freely in a 3D space, and it does so very seamlessly while entering and leaving those spaces.
The remake's art is basically based on the same art that the original had, but with a major overhaul in actual graphics and style, as in, you will find the same type of forest, the same kind of castle, the same kind of various areas throughout the remake that you found in the original, just with a modernized style (aka the remake is not a 16-bit game :p)

Title : Hotline Miami
Developer : Dennaton Games
Publisher : Devolver Digital
Genre : Action
Hotline Miami is a 2D top-down action video game. Set in 1989 Miami, the plot consists of two protagonists, Jacket and Biker, who have been receiving phone calls instructing them to commit massacres against the local Russian Mafia. The game blends top down perspective with stealth, extreme violence and surreal storytelling, along with a soundtrack and visuals influenced by 1980s culture.
Hotline Miami is divided into several chapters, each of which is further broken down into several stages. At the start of most chapters, the unnamed protagonist wakes up in his apartment and listens to cryptic messages on his answering machine. These messages tell him to perform an arbitrary task at a certain location, which in each case is inferred as a metaphor for killing every person at that location, such as giving VIPs at a hotel a 'great stay', or taking care of a 'pest infestation'. Prior to commencing a mission, the player is asked to select an animal mask to wear, each of which provides unique advantages or handicaps.
