Decent, if you're into turn based tactical games.
The campaign is broken up into several scenarios, each one is worth a few hours playtime. Your progress and character development do not carry over to the next, so you tend to not care very much about the items and upgrades you obtain.
The gameplay is mostly in an overworld map, dialogue is entirely text based, except for Death narrarating your story as you proceed. Build your party, obtain weapons and supplies, complete quests, enter combat mode, repeat.
The plot is based around a supernatural wild west theme. You fight demons, corrupt lawmen, cult members, talk to magic indian shaman, make deals with the devil, etc. Interesting story progressions, if you like reading.
Combat is like a simplified XCOM, or Fallout Tactics (old reference.) The attack is a hit chance percentage based on the weapon, your aim skill, the enemy's cover, etc. It's all about staying in cover, and out flanking. Your defense is dependent on your luck points. They will deplete as the enemy misses you. Run out of luck and get shot.
Before each fight you will be able to change the loadout of your party. As you progress through each scenario, you obtain special abilities in the form of playing cards, which can be assigned to different party members to form hands which give bonus abilities. Certain abilities require using luck points, such as chain kill, ricochet shots, demonic power buffs, etc.
Overall I would recommend picking it up when it's on sale. It's a good game to kill time with if you are a fan of the genre.

This is a nice, addictive game with a lot more depth than most matching types of games.  It took me a few times playing it to really understand what is happening, but once I understood what I was doing, I found the puzzles to be quite challenging, yet achievable.  Unlike most games like this, if you just randomly start matching items, while you can complete a level, you won't be able to hit the target score.  It takes more strategy to understand where to start and where to focus to hit the high scores.  So if you enjoy a matching type game, but want one with more strategy and planning, you should try Fourtex Jugo.
As I said, it took me a few plays to understand what I was really trying to do.  Here's what I found out.
The goal of the game is to get to a target score for a puzzle.  To do this, you'll need to score as many points as you can.  You get the most points by making Voids.  However, once you make one Void, basically the final stage of the game starts - so you want to hold off making Voids until you are just about ready to finish.  You end a game by using all 16 squares of the 4x4 grid.  Voids are made by combining oms of different colors.  Oms are created by combining pis.  Pis are made by combining two numbers that add to 15 or combining two 14's.  Numbers are created by combining like numbers (so combining two 5's will make a 6.)
So basically you combine numbers, building them up to 14's, or combine two that add to 15.  Make as many different types of pis as you can.  There's a pattern to how to make different pis.  Combine the pis make oms.  Try and get a good collection of black and white oms ready to combine (ideally you get a 4x4 grid with 8 black and 8 white oms), while not closing out the 4x4 grid.  Then combine the oms and quickly close out the grid.  It is more complicated that other games like this, but that's what I liked about it.  You need to study how the board is repopulated from the sides and determine how to attack the board to get the pi then om then void states.
The variety of puzzles they include require different strategies, so you're not just playing the same strategy over and over.
Again, if you're looking for a casual game with some depth to it, give Fourtex Jugo a try.   It's a casual game for the strategist in you.

This review will be in more detail than is probably wanted for potential customers because I want to actually try to help the developer understand why I didn't like it. I would also like to throw ideas on the table with regards to possible improvement.
The mantra any puzzle game should adhere to is
. Incredibly, somehow
actually mangages to do the exact
. What we have here is a puzzle mechanic that is based on crafting/building higher-tier icons using more basic elements. There are several tiers of complexity and each has its own rule set. All that is good and fine, but the rules are 1) fairly arbitrary, and 2) don't actually respect other rules. For example, 8+8=9, yet 8+7=pi. And not the mathematical pi that everyone knows; in this universe, pi = 15. Why? No idea. There is also an ohm, but not the physics unit. To complicate things further, the spelling of each of these units is all over the place.
I also said the rules are fairly arbitrary. What I mean is that they don't follow any kind of logic pattern that makes them easily remembered. You would do well to actually print out a chart of the rules, otherwise your brain is always working hard to remember these goofy rules. Here is an example of how wonky things get:
Quick! How to make a red pi? To me there is nothing for my brain to grasp onto logically to remember these in any fun way. Like maybe if it was red+pi=red pi. Now that makes sense. You couple this with the fact that there are a metric ton of variables, and its just all very confusing. I'm a smart guy, so it's not that I can't wrap my brain around it - it's just complicated in a way that is not fun to untangle. Here is a brief list of variables: numbers, red pi, blue pi, black ohm, white ohm, vortex, devil hand, tile color, background color, tile shape. Woof.
The design decisions for the UI aren't great either. The puzzle is not centered on the screen. There is unnecessary clutter all over. Just look at the screenshots on the store page. Why do I need all that other stuff? I don't. That top left logo and everything other than the puzzle at hand, and perhaps the score. Check out
for good UI design.
Another thing - for being Early Access, the developers aren't all that active on the forums. Let me be clear - they are there, though. Really, at the time of writing this (11/2016), there is only one other active person on the forums other than myself. I've posted about a bug that the developer did address and acknowledge. I've also posted thoughts and, for the most part, have been ignored. Thats fine, but this is Early Access. I guess I just put it in my review.
How does this title manage to be 'impossible to learn, yet easy to master'? Winning a level is absurdly simple. In fact, I've *almost* never lost. There are about ?four tiers to winning. See the store page for details on that. There is no satisfaction, really, when you clear a level because of this. Mind you - I've only 'beaten' a level by the most simple of winning conditions. For the majority of my playtime, we focused on trying to beat the 2000k score for the
level. We never were able to do it.
The game has a math 'skin' to it, yet really has no math in it. No logic either, other than the obscure ruleset. As I have voiced on the forums to a silent crowd, I think the game would do much better if it were skinned differently. I mean idk, off the top of my head here, how about a fantasy setting where knight+knight=blue army; blue army+white army=civilization. Boom. Solved. It makes *logical* sense, and ends up being more fun at the same time.
What I did like about the game was that it had good controller support, and good music. The music has little variaty, though. I think there could be a gem here, but it needs an overhaul. I congratulate the developers on the Steam release, which is a major accomplishment in itself. Again, thank you for the free key.

Alan Wake could be the perfect example of a psychological thriller where the main protagonist meets the arts of writing and gets traped in a story (much more like a nightmare). Everything works with this game from point A to point B. It gets you hooked from the start into the story, creating questions that you need to seek the answer by embarking onto this incredible realised narative.
''Alan Wake'' as the title says, suggests the center of the game, which is also the protagonist and by ''center'', yes he is the key to all of it. I haven't found any plot-holes at all and the story seemd so satisfying to go through, which made me curious about every detail of it, indeed it could work aswell as a TV show, a great one to be honest, and I'm really happy that Remedy had the great idea to encapsulate it all as a TV show, every chapter as an episode and at the very first of every the chapter, a rewind from the previous chapter. There are a variety of characters which are also very well written and you can easliy get attached to any of it. The main villain is none but the darkness following your every step you do in the beautiful realised mountain landscape with huge forests that makes you feel very lost. The game is linear but it doesn't feel like that at all, it didn't bugged me off and I think it won't do it to you.
It's incredible simple and all you have to do is to weakean the darkness by pointing a flashlight towards it and then shoot ! Sounds fun right ? It sure did for me at first, but it can get repetitive overtime if you play on the easiest difficult. The game is not a difficult one, but you have to preserve some of batteries and bullets if you want to survive, so my tip is to not waste them and collect everything that game offers you, in fact the gameplay is all about surviving.
The experience isn't as horror if you are into horror games, although it is scarry for a new comer to this genre and it really feels like you are always followed, combined with the uncertainity it gets you to feel like you are trapped.
It looks pretty good, the setting looks amazing, and it's really well optimized, this showing that developers cared about almost everything that ''Alan Wake'' meant.
I cannot but to recommend to you this game as it has a brilliant story, great protagonist, great atmosphere and all feels really polished and well done. I loved this game at it's time and even right now it's an incredible game. Playing this pays off, at the end it feels like a rewarding experince and I really needed to tell you this. I enjoyed every minute of it's atmosphere and I hope you will too.

Okay, this might come off as a tad hypocritical seeing as I do put time into this game and I do enjoy it despite what it is. But the thing is, what it is, is a skinner box game. Seeing as it is a mobile port this is hardly surprising as the majority of such games fall into that category, in fact I even used to play it on my pad before it came to pc up until the glasses patch where 90% of all dwellers were stupidly given glasses for some reason.
For what it's worth its not among the worst of such kinds of games, the replacement currency of nuka cola bottles aren't super rare or anything and lunch boxes, pet boxes and Mr. Handy boxes are all available as drops, nothing is really behind a pay wall so with patience it is very much a free to play game if you want it to be and have the willpower and patience required. But having said that, that's like saying it's a mild form of cancer. These types of games really shouldn't exist in their current form, and while I'm aware that having that opinion and still playing the game isn't very conducive, I can only shrug at that. I care, but I don't care enough to meaninglessly boycott and trying to drum up support for the cause, that's just the sad truth of it.
But I cannot in good conscience give this game a thumbs up, even if I can enjoy it, because I'm as far away from the target audience of these kinds of games as humanly possible, heck I even have it as an ironclad principle to never pay a single dime for something I can get for free (within legal limitations ofc). But the target audience for games like these, are gambling addicts, people who chase endorphines by clicking buttons and seeing flashing lights, dinging sounds and seeing bars slowly fill up, the proverbial Pavlovian dogs of humanity, the weak and vulnerable. The cynical mobile developers even call these people whales, and they are the small percentage of f2p players which keep monsterous games like these afloat. Because they actually pay for these games, and they pay ALOT. Much more than what is advisable and sane, because they're addicts, because they can't help it.
It's especially disgusting for a well established developer who are already making tons of money on actual games to dive into this cesspool side of mobile gaming. And I am a bit ashamed of being passively an accomplice in this but at least I'm not paying for it and never will, so there's that.
-
As for game mechanics, there are some ways you're getting screwed. One of which is the UI and the Rush mechanic. While it may say that it's 30% chance for an incident to happen, it's probably more accurate to say that you have about a 30% chance for an incident NOT to happen. I'm in no way exaggerating this, if it says 30% or higher, you're almost guaranteed for it to fail. I've even had it say 18% and it still failed twice in a row. Statistics-wise this may be possible, but it is in no way probable and I've had it happen with such consistency that I can guarantee that the UI is lying to you and like with all skinner box games/badly weighted RNG in general similar to one armed bandits, the odds are weighted against you.
Another failing of the UI is not giving you the information you require. There's no hard data being displayed on how much of a resource you are currently using, there's only a little line on a bar giving a weak indication. The further to the right the line is on the bar, the more of the resource you're using. But there's no compilation info available on how much you're producing in total, at what rate you're earning versus losing resources, so you're constantly either overproducing or struggling.
The available in game help is extremely lackluster and doesn't go into detail regarding anything either. Like how anything actually works. Is it better to have one power station with a full staff or two with half staff in each? Is it better to have two unupgraded power stations versus a single upgraded one? Is it better to have a few fully trained workers and are there any stats besides the primary room one and luck that matters at all? Does having low luck affect the rush mechanics somehow without it showing in the UI? What's the difference (if any) between the different types of weapons? Is it like in Fallout that they simply use different S.P.E.C.I.A.L stats (which is bound to become pointless once you've maxed all stats) or is all combat dependant on the same stats no matter the weapon? Does the DPS rate differ? Is there any reason whatsoever not to always use the weapon with the strongest attack available?
None of this is mentioned or explained.
And while some of these questions could no doubt be answered using spreadsheets and careful monitoring, why should the player need to put that much effort in? Having crossed the boundary from mobile to pc, I see no reasons why this game shouldn't be held to the same standards as normal games, at least when it comes to things like clarity in UI and explanations available. Mobile games look and function the way they do because of the limitations of the medium, these same limitations disappear when we play it on PC, so there's really no valid excuse for it, especially when they hope to monetize it the same way on here.
Another way a mobile game just isn't fit for pc consumption is the way you're intended to play. Mobile games are meant to be played a few minutes at a time, and this game even goes as far as to punish you for actually actively playing it. It does so in the form of incidents, which range from fires to various raiders.
Now, one could argue that without these events, it would get kind of boring with nothing happening and there are some events which even have some inherent reward to them, for instance defeating the raiders gives you caps as well as some random drops and even recipes, which is great.
But there are also events which give no rewards and are only there to punish you/discourage you from playing at any length of time and waste your resources, and sadly every single other event except the raiders are just that. Feral ghouls, mole rats and death claws definitely belong to this category. You get no reward for killing them and you're usually forced to waste rad aways and stim paks when they appear. On top of that, you can't build anything as everything goes into lockdown mode when an incident occurs.
The longer you play for, the more incidents occur. The severity of the incidents also goes up as you upgrade rooms and build up your base. So it's not a good idea to upgrade too many rooms too early.
I would also wager that the risk of some incidents occuring increase when you have an empty room, and some rooms are always bound to be empty so that could definitely pose a problem depending on how you build your base, as if an incident goes unchecked it will spread to adjacent rooms. You can get around this problem by building rooms like the storage bays and bunk rooms (which are likely to be empty most of the time) separated with one empty level with nothing but 2 elevators on it, but doing so is expensive, requires planning ahead and will only be possible during late game. There's also the possibillity that some of the late game incidents can bypass this, as I haven't really gotten to the very end yet in this version, but I know that so far it works for fires, rad roaches and mole rats at the very least.
But that's only helpful for the empty rooms, incidents can and will still occur in occupied rooms as well and failing a rush (which is bound to happen often seeing as the RNG is heavily weighted against you and the UI is lying to you) results in an incident as well.
-
Anyways, tl:dr; if you know you lack patience, have a disposition towards addiction and/or is just under the age of 18, I would strongly advise you to stay far away from this game. I  gain some enjoyment out of this game despite it being what it is, not because of what it is and only because I'm not its intended target audience.

This is a bit of a spoiler, but I met a weird guy out in the wastelands who professed his love of vintage video games. Dude's place was stacked, every wall covered with game posters, every shelf packed full of memorabilia--dude even had a collection of vintage arcade cabinets. We had a fun little conversation and after I left that town I didn't think of it again.
A few weeks later I'm out dicking off in some obscure corner of the in-game map, wandering around looking for an oasis to refill my canteens when I stumble upon a little easter egg: the buried literal truckloads of unsold 1980s ET atari cartidges. There were a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of them, way more than we could carry in our packs. Then it ocurred to me: you know who I bet would be into all of these cartridges? Video game collector guy.
So we load up with as many cartridges we can carry and backtrack all the way to that town. Now, we exhausted all the quests in that town, met with all the dudes and solved all their weird problems; we had no real reason to return. The game gave me no indication that this dude would be interested in these ET cartridges. No quest compasses, no journal entries, nothing. But lo and behold collector dude loses his♥♥♥♥♥♥with excitement over the ET cartridges. It was like we brought him the holy grail. We got experience and rewards for doing it. The Witcher 2 is one of the best fantasy epics I've played for a while. Dark writing that will compel you to push forth and delve into the story; going so far as to consume your days! And then, in the final moments of the game, the narrative will have you begging for more, making you wish the game was longer--or that Witcher 3 would come sooner! (P.S. The game is over 20 hours long, yet I wanted more. Yes, the story is that gripping) The game also treats you with some god-damned maturity, CDProjekt Red doesn't ♥♥♥♥♥ out here, the game contains a lot of sex--and it's magnificent; especially when other game developers don't have the balls to go there, or when they do, they often don't have the balls to see it through to the end.
Sufficed to say, all those who haven't played the previous game (of which I am one) will,  at-first, find themselves lost. The game will try to get you up to speed, however you'll feel very lost at the beginning of the game. But soon you'll be caught up in a web of conspiricy and intrigue that, when the jarring moments of exposition pretaining to the first game come, it will do little to sour your mood, and soon, you'll be back into the fray of the story.
Also, choices, choices that bloody matter! Do you know how refreshing that is? Yes? Then jump on in!
The gameplay is burtal and unforgiving if you are unready--plus the saving system isn't very... lenient with you. So if you screw  up and you haven't saved, oh boy you're in hot water! Enemies will challenge you, hoards of them can be just as effective as a boss. Which, to mention the bosses, yeah, they're hard too! Especially the last. However, I'm just speaking from my own experience here, it will greatly vary by user ability and game difficulty. (I can imagine that, after playing this bloody romp on normal and dying a couple of times, that on hard it's a bloody nightmare.)
The presentation of the game isn't too shabby either, bearing in mind it's been 2 years from release, it couldn't look any better; sure in some areas texture can appear flat or certain other graphical annoyances may appear, however it will do little to deter you from playing! Character models are detailed to the level that you would expect. Glitches are minimal--although some may make themselves apparent. The game has a highly fine level of polish that will be apparent as you play through the wonderful game; the craftmanship that has gone into this game is insane, CDProjektRed are masters of making video games, so you're in safe hands.
Convinced yet? I should bloody hope so. If this game is on sale and you're reading this, I can only ask why? Why are you wasting you time? This is such a great game that any [reasonable] cost is well worth it! Especially on your nice fancy PC rig. So, stop reading and add this game to your collection now! You won't regret a single moment, a single dime, that you'll have poured into this game.

I just want to start this off by saying that Wasteland 2 is not a game I'd usually associate with. I don't generally play a lot of top-down turn-based tactical RPGs. (That's a mouthful...) Even ones I enjoy don't get much of my time.
That being said, I would highly recommend Wasteland 2. I've been playing through it on the normal difficulty before the Director's Cut upgrade, and I have to say it's difficult. But it's fair, too. Play your cards right, make the right moves, and every battle is perfectly winable. Every encounter is fair. There are some sections where you can usually see right away: "I'm gonna have trouble with this." But that's usually your hint to turn around and come back later.
I've spent most of my time in Wasteland 2's classic version, due to the Director's Cut coming out after my 4-5 day binge on the game. I finally sat down to try out the Director's Cut, and I have to say... I'm impressed. The UI is improved, the graphics are sharper, the game is more responsive. Everything feels so much smoother. Class and character building at the beginning of the game has been improved ten-fold, with perks, and a new, MUCH cleaner system for allocating points (Which I have to say, I've fallen in love with. No more confusing menus with 30 unrelated options)
In the end, all I have to say is this. If you like the more classic games like Fallout 1 and 2, or you enjoy the combat systems from games like XCOM. Or even if you're a fan of newer Fallout's and think a change back from first person to top down would be nice, I could not recommend this game to you enough. And even if that doesn't sound appealing, if you ever see this game go on sale, give it a shot. Hell, look around the internet, you can find this game cheaper in a few places.
I'll leave it there. This game is well worth your time and money. There are problems with the game that I've found, and ones I haven't, but so far they're all so minor that I don't feel like they're worth mentioning. I'll update this at a later time if I fend anything worth mentioning.

NS2 is an amazing fusion of FPS and RTS elements where communication actually matters.  This isn't CoD or Battlefield where talking and communicating doesn't matter, it is integral to the game.
The premise is simple: destroy the other team's bases and you win.  How you do it is up to you.
Given equal skill on both sides, the game is pretty well balanced and everything can have a counter.  Games can range from 2 minute base rushes to 60 minute grindfests; from 6v6 competitive style play, to 12v12 chaos.
THIS GAME HAS AN INCREDIBLY STEEP LEARNING CURVE.  DO NOT COME INTO THIS GAME THINKING YOU WILL STOMP PEOPLE BECAUSE YOU WON'T.  Most rookies tend to be next to useless without a LOT of practice.  Aiming and tracking in this game is incredibly different from other FPSs.  For example, not every game has targets on the ceiling, most games tend to be left to right tracking and strafing.  This game has up, down, left, right, and do a spin move, shooting mechanics.
It is incredibly fun, but doesn't come from without its issues:
Team balance can become an issue at times.
Requires a strong processor / GPU to play.
Being able to see improper team balance is important for your NS2 experience.  As you play more and more, you'll recognise when the teams are unbalanced and it's time to find a new server.  Most servers have a randomize or a team balance option to be voted on as well.  It happens, it's just something you need to deal with.
If you can master the art of tracking, if you can master the art of 2 bite parasite, you will have a load of fun playing this game.
I really wish UWE would permanently drop the price of this game because for 25 dollars is a lot to ask for most people.  I'm willing to bet a ton of people play this game, get stomped and think it's bad.  If it was cheaper, more people will be willing to try (although the game did go on sale during the winter sale which brought a surge of new rookies, which is another issue altogether).  If you can find this game on sale, most likely for $6.24, consider picking it up.  If it's on sale for $2.50, there's no reason not to try it, provided you have a computer that can support it.

Perhaps I'm just a cynical bigot blinded by nostalgia, but in my eyes Disney has lost quite a bit of its magic in recent years. Instead of the delightfully imaginative works of their glory years, we've been "treated" to an abundance of derivative shovel-ware and cash grabs, all relying on their branding and marketing instead of actual quality to make them a success. A remake of the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive classic, Castle of Illusion could have very well been just another mediocre licensed game, but to my absolute surprise and delight it is anything but; a whimsical joy of a platformer that pays homage to Mickey's past, while bringing him into the modern day just as enjoyable as we remember him.
Opening like the typical fairy tale it is, Mickey and Minnie are just setting out for a picnic when the witch Mizrabel spies the pair and gets jealous, swooping in and kidnapping Minnie, with the goal of using the damsel's youth and beauty to rejuvenate herself from the old hag she is. Mickey will have none of this however, and thus enters the titular Castle of Illusion to obtain the seven magic gems, cross the rainbow bridge, and get his girl back!
Like the 1990 original, CoI is a basic platformer whose strength lies in its imaginative levels and environments. Each stage is unique and bustling with creativity, from a giant library full of bouncing letters and slinking bookworms, to a world made entirely out of sweets that has you swimming through jello and bouncing on cookies floating in a milkshake river. There are so many charming little touches in every location you traverse that I couldn't begin to name them all (and doubt I saw even half of them). Sega perfectly captured the happy-go-lucky mannerisms of Mickey, right down to the trademark hop in his step and chip of his voice, an attention to detail which extends to every secret area and extra path, and makes for an immensely enjoyable game. I gleefully made my way through every level never once tiring of the seemingly endless stream of fantastical places I was sent to, but alas every good thing must come to an end and CoI does so all too soon.
For all its wonder and the many things it gets so very right, CoI is over in a heartbeat (around 2-3 hours to be exact). This short-live adventure seems to end even more abruptly, do to how easy it is to jump from one level to the next and how quickly and seamlessly they flow together. In a sense it's about as long as the average animated movie (which almost seems intentional, opening and ending with the camera panning out to a theater), but for a $15 game it had me wanting more.
I say that however with the caveat of wanting more because I loved my brief time with Mickey so much. Castle of Illusion is a pleasure and has given me hope that Disney is still capable of creating something with as much heart and wonder as what made them a household name in the first place. If Mickey Mouse has ever meant anything to you, you owe it to yourself to play this lively tribute that does as much for giving the icon a proper video game outing, as it does a starting point for what could (and hopefully does) come out in the near future. It's pure childish fun that capitalizes on its goal of being a lighthearted game that almost anyone can enjoy, recapturing the magic of yesteryear for the new and old generation alike.

In theory, Avoid is a pretty straightforward game. In practice,
it's a mad and magnificent dash with a heavy dose of difficulty and a nice dash of variety.
The difficulty ramps up nicely - for the first set of levels or so, you have the leisure to worry about collecting every multiplier powerup to finish the level with a perfect score. Gradually, that ideal fades into unfeasibility, and you're left with the simple goal of getting slightly farther on each attempt. It's plenty hard but far from impossible - in 7 hours I was able to complete everything through Hard and one set of Extreme levels (though I decided the rest were probably beyond my skill level). The ability to 'learn' each level over the course of many (many) tries is nice as it makes it rare to feel cheated - and if you'd rather focus on snap reaction than, uh, lethal reconaissance, there's an endless survival mode as well.
The levels are divided into four different themes (scroll through those pictures at the top for a sense), each with its own set of level features and powerups. This does a nice job of keeping things fresh - the levels in each theme have a fairly well defined mechanical identity to go along with the visuals, keeping them distinct enough that it doesn't get boring over 128 levels despite the minimal nature of the game.
One point worth mentioning is the controls - some other reviews have complained that you should be able to move exactly one square at a time. There's some merit to that - digital movement on an analog grid can feel pretty awkward at times - but this scheme is so much smoother than the alternative (especially on the synthrock levels with diagonal blocks) that it's absolutely the right decision for the game.
Avoid takes a simple concept and executes it well - if you're up for some frenzied arcade action, give it a shot.

Broken Age is a 2D Point & Click Adventure by Double Fine, the same crew who brought you Grim Fandango Remastered, another P&C game which I also happened to review recently.
The game is broken into two distinct 'acts' (I think this may be the reason for the title, I'm not sure) that were originally released a week apart. There are also two protagonists, Shay (boy) and Vella (girl). It runs as two separate threads that you can switch between whenever you fancy a change. It's rather ingenious.
Shay is in a spaceship, bored with life and sent on missions (more like errands) by his mothering over-protective ship's computer, involving ice cream mountains and cute knitted aliens with squeaky voices.
Vella lives in a little village during the Mog Chothra festival. This is a many-eyed monster that looks like a huge brain with tentacles which comes to claim a few lucky young ladies from the village once every 14 years, and Vella has been chosen for this privilege but decides to kill Mog Chothra instead.
What I've described covers the first part of the game, which seems to be two entirely separate stories. At the end of Part 1 the connection is revealed, at which point the whole thing gets much more interesting, so I would encourage you to stick with what is essentially the set-up for the proper story in Part 2, which again has separate threads for Shay and Vella. So in all the game has 4 distinct chunks to it.
Coming from Grim Fandango, the orchestral music (featuring a lot of oboe) was familiar to me and gives the game a feel of quality and class. The hand drawn artwork is very nice and there's an endless stream of long cutscenes which overshadow the gameplay, especially in Part 1.
They hired a bevy of A-list celebrities to do the voice acting. It is very good indeed, as you'd expect from some of the best professional actors in the world, but in my opinion they could have saved themselves a fortune by hiring cheaper talent because none of them have distinct voices that immediately stand out. I just about managed to identify Jack Black one time, but the rest could have been anyone. Ask yourself if you would recognise the voice of Elijah Wood in a crowd for example.
Grim Fandango had extremely hard gameplay, I had to consult a walkthrough for the whole thing more or less. Broken Age is the complete opposite. Part 1 is very easy indeed, there is no challenge at all, it's like all you're doing is clicking to progress the cutscenes. Part 2 does become more tricky, although still nowhere near has hard as Grim Fandango and I'd say a bit easier than your average Daedalic title too. The dialog is done in such a way to give you very clear directions on what your objectives are so if you are stuck on a task at least you know in general what that task is.
Some P&C games can become too sprawling and cause you to become lost and confused. This is tightly woven and your mind will be on the storyline and puzzle rather than "where the heck am I?". Another welcome feature is the generous click areas and the way they light up on mouseover. Impossible to miss.
Absolutely rock solid (played on Windows and Linux). Full 1920x1200 resolution available and not one single glitch, spelling error or so much as a flicker out of place throughout.
It has trading cards, cloud support and also achievements (which is not stated on the store page). The achievements are well thought out. You get a decent number of them during normal gameplay but there are also enough others to encourage a 2nd playthrough to nab the extra ones.
It's priced slightly higher than other quality games in this genre, perhaps due to the celebrity wages bill, but worth the price I think.
The storyline is a slow starter but comes to life in Part 2. I've only managed to complete about 75% of it so far but I'm hooked and looking forward to the culmination. A lot of care has been taken to define the limits of the game locations (rooms etc) to avoid any frustration or confusion, which are often symptoms in games of this genre. Hand drawn artwork is quite nice and has a distinctive style. The only negative criticism is that Part 1 is perhaps just a little bit too easy. If I'd been an original customer at the launch of the game I would not have been impressed during the wait for Part 2 to arrive.
If you're shopping for a good P&C game and wondering how this compares to others, this is family-friendly and has a particularly easy-to-navigate structure to it. There is good challenge to the gameplay in Part 2 but not to the point of frustration.

You'll inevitably run headfirst into a brick wall sometimes (actually, might as well make that "many times"), but at the end of the day, when you get your first Mom kill (did I mention how twisted this game was?), the game just gets so much better. I had seen mixed reviews for Hard West but picked it up in a Steam Sale anyway. I liked the concept of the Wild West but was unsure about the supernatural elements. As I got through the first few senarios I found that it really fit and added depth and atmosphere to the game. The sound track also fits and is very atmospheric with a particularly twangy western guitar riff which will rattle around my head for a few more weeks im sure.
The story was really engaging and follows a meta plot supported by mini chapters, I found that only one of the chapters seemed a little tenious within this meta plot but the rest fit together really well. Some people have complained that the game lacks character development, I would argue against this as the same people pop up here and there and can be allies or enemies depending on what your up to.
The combat was very Xcom like and i found it quite a challenge as enemies would dig in for the most part and really give you a fire fight. I had to look for new ways to flank and get behind them for maximum accuracy and damage. This was also backed up by a neat target range meaning if my guy had been spotted I couldnt simply cheese by closing to point blank range. When people complain that they lose too many men or the game is unforgiving I can only assume they dont understand the concept of "flanking" or "cover" having played XCOM on the hardest setting would really assist your initial skill level on Hard west as well.
There were a couple of bugs I have to mention, the first being with flanking. Sometimes I would be facing a guys back or side and they would get maximum defence adjustments despite me being in the perfect position, but this happened so rarely it did not really hinder over all game play. The second major bug seems to be a frame rate spike on the world map. For some reason this worked my graphics card out and fired up my fans, all a bit confusing as I run a top end machine, a bit of research told me that a lot of people had this and there was not really a fix, pretty lazy on the developers part I felt. However this did not damage my experience and just irritated me rather than anything serious.
The only real issues I had with this game were the luck / ability system. The characters have a rating called luck which depletes when an enemy fires and misses and rises when you take damage. Luck was also the pool that fires off your special abilities. It was all rather anoying to want to use a special ability but have no luck left as some muppet had been firing at my guy and missing, i found myself in certain situations allowing a guy to take an open hit to simply regen some luck. Not sure if this was planned or an over sight. Again it can be worked around by having one pawn as a tank and another guy at the back stacked up with skills and luck enhancing objects, but this verges on cheesing. The special skills in the end became more of a luxuary for me than a go to.
Another main whine of mine in many games is too many obsolete weapons. Hard West suffers from this as well, there must be at least 30-40 different weapon types which at first is cool, then over whelming and then obsolete. You find the guns you like "cough" cannon cavelera"cough" and just equip those ignoring everything else meaning new guns are just sold or ignored rather than utilised. I know this is however a major selling point for some people.
Having finished Hard West I have to say I really enjoyed it and would love to see a sequal or more DLC campaigns, over all not sure why people have put hate on this as its a really solid little tactical with a great storyline!

Hard West lacks complexity and replayability of genre icons, but definitely has its own style and charm. I wasn't expecting much looking at all the reviews, but it surpassed my initial scepticism.
Yes, it will never be called truly great. Yes, its batlle mechanics is simpler in comparison to mighty XCOM. Yes, battle interface wouldn't mind a slight polish. And it's rather unlikely that you would want to play campaign more than a couple of times (but since it is story-driven, I don't consider this a problem).
But, it is still quite a decent and refreshing attempt. Its plot about Wild West with a demonic twist is quite engaging. Campaign consists of several different scenarios, each telling their part of the story from different characters's perspective. Besides several fights, each scenario has a strategic layer, where you advance the story through moving your party from place to place and solving text-based quests. They won't change the final outcome, but might reward or punish you in different ways.
Battle system lack variety a bit, but I still find it decent. On one hand, the Luck system they introduced often encourages you for  risky moves. On another hand, such behaviour might be (you knew, you knew!) fatal. An interesting combination, in my view.
Just do yourself a favor and start playing on Hard difficulty right from the start, because that's  the only way it can shine. Characters are pretty fragile in each difficulty (which complements to  atmosphere, in my view). Still, difficulties below favor player too much and might ruin the impression: Easy is a kindergarten and Normal is often as challenging as dishwashing. On Hard (especially with Combat wounds/Ironman options), things get much more entertaining: AI becomes much more brazen; enemies get more HP so you can't one-shot left and right no more; your party members have, at best, a slight HP advantage over a generic cowboy. Adding the fact that you're always outnumbered, it feels much more tense.
Overall: has its flaws but has its moments. Very pretty looking. Won't be the thing for which you miss your sleep time, but definitely above mediocrity and nice to spent some evenings with.

Hard West is Turn-Based Strategy game with some RPG elements sprinkled on top. The game is set in two different instances, the world map where you guide your group of adventurers through a variety of locations where you can make decisions, barter for items, heal, and bet for body parts over a game of dice, and the combat gameplay, where you guide your group through individual locations to face off against your enemies in a turn-based combat styled gameplay that will remind most people of XCOM with a twist.
So far so good, I'll admit I was pleasantly surprised by the world map and how the game handled the whole subject, you get to play around on a more personal level in a way that makes more sense for the setting. However the game's flaws quickly spoiled any pleasant feelings I had for the game.
-There are several scenarios in the game, each very short in time, meaning the process of building up your force, the potential consequences for your actions, and the development of your characters is all made mute once you get to the next scenario
-Each scenario has its own gameplay "quirk", some of which are executed horribly, I can name two mechanics (future sight and the workshop) that were interesting due to risk/reward and the planning envolved in them, but the gameplay mechanics in all of the other scenarios bottled down to clicking through the same menus over and over again until you had enough people/gold or had fed your group enough times to carry on. These quirks are also inconsistent, why do I have to feed my group  in one scenario but not in the others? Why is gathering a group in the final scenario considered the scenario's gameplay "quirk" when in the other scenarios it's just a run of the mill action that you're expected to do?
-The constant hopping around from scenario to scenario makes the player stop caring about the game's characters. I was invested in the game's story to some extent, but I wasn't invested in my characters as party members since I constantly had to swap them around and reset their state.
-The AI straight up refuses to move quite often, in situations where flanking is the ideal approach to a situation, combat can become really static due to this.
-The Luck based system simply does not work, a status bar that nulifies the change of you being hit sounds cool and all, until you realize it forces every showdown to bottle down to who can spend the most time shooting each other to lower a character's Luck. A system that nulifies multiple ~85% shots is simply not a fun system.
-Abilities use luck, luck depletes when enemies shoot at you and miss (and they always do as long as you have Luck), Abilities require you to be positioned in certain ways, but to be positioned in those ways you have to expose yourself to being shot. Meaning you will rarely, if ever, use abilities during most scenarios, with the exception of Golden Bullet which ignores everything I just stated by allowing you to shoot from just about anywhere in the map.
-The voice acting in Scars of Freedom is depressing.
Now onto the good stuff
-Game looks great, I like the graphics and the art direction made the game both immersive and a blast to look at.
-The music is great, it might get a bit repetetive if you spend too much time in the same combat session though.
-Large variety of items and weapons allow for different playstyles for members of your group without having to adhere to a "class" system.
-Instead of leveling and perks you have a deck of cards with abilities that can be matched for extra bonuses, I found it to be really fun to manage my cards and see what worked with what.
-The story is rather simplistic in a good way, it doesn't overcomplicate its subjects nor does it explain too much, it has the simplicity of westerners with the mystery of the supernatural.
-Each scenario has a bunch of optional content which helps breathing in life to world.
Overall, I don't believe the XCOM comparisons are fair at all, the game does more with the story, visuals and certain aspects of gameplay, it's also a lot more experimental in some ways. However the reason why I'm leaving a thumbs down for now is because of how messy the gameplay is due to the Luck based shooting mechanic (which ironically enough ignores the real shooting percentages) and due to the way the scenario quirks were handled. If you indeed are a fan of XCOM, this isn't exactly for you, if you're into turn based strategy, like the theme, and don't mind being forced into reset states halfway through a game, then sure give this game a shot, you might just like it despite its flaws.

One of my favorite games of all time. It's like a Stephen King book come to life. It manages to be very scary by preying on your fear of the dark without resorting to cheap jumpscares. I definitely recommend you play it.
The story is filled with suspense and mystery, it's super engaging. It's heavily inspired by Twin Peaks, so fans of the show take the time to spot some easter eggs and find some thermoses filled with some damn good coffee. The soundtrack is awesome too. The "light" combat system this game utilizes is pretty neat, and although people say it can get repetitive, I think it's fun enough that it doesn't detract from the game. This is also one of the few games where playing on a harder difficulty can make the game harder without making it needlessly frustrating.
I will list a few cons, however. This version is a console port, and this really really shows on older end machines. Luckily, most PCs today should be able to play it no problem. I can run it on highest settings at 60FPS on my GTX670 no problem, but the game doesn't visually seem like it would require as advanced a GPU as it actually does. The aiming and walking may also seem a bit wonky, but that's also a consequence of it being a console port.
Overall rating: 9.5/10. I absolutely love everything about this game, but I gotta take half a point off for the issues stemming from it being a console port.

I played this game on PS4 from start to finish. I bought it again for PC because I love this game so much. This game is easily one of the best game I have ever played in my life. If you like these sort of adventure games - then I highly recommend picking this one up. It's a great expirience from start to finish. If you don't like adventure games - then I don't think this one will change your mind.
Pros:
1. Wrting is top notch. Each character is well written and as a result they all feel alive and like real people.
2. Art direction is amazing. The world of Arcadia Bay feels real, and a large part of that is the excellent art design.
3. Voice acting is very well done. Adventure games heavily rely on their storytelling, but even a great story can be soiled by bad voice acting. You wont find any bad voice acting in this game, it's all every well done here. Especially coming from the voice actresses for Max and Chloe.
4. Interesting time manipulation gameplay makes this a bit different than other titles in the genre, and makes for a great storytelling element.
5. Music. Both licensed and original works are all amazing. I love the soundtrack to this game. If you love indie music - then you'll like the soundtrack to this game.
6. Easy to run. This game can run at 60fps on my budget gaming laptop which has a GT 940MX GPU on mostly max settings at 1080p.
Cons:
1. Keyboard and mounse controls are mostly good, however, using the mouse to select things can sometimes be slightly furstrating. The developers suggest using a controller, and I can see why. However, don't be afraid - this game is still enjoyble if you hate using gamepads.
2. Lip sync is very basic. The characters move their moves when they're supposed to, but that's about it. I wish they emoted more - but overall it works. It's not game breaking, but it's something you'll notice when you first start playing.
3. Texture work is not as high resolution as I would like. While the art style saves this game, and is one of its strong points, I do wish the textures were higher resolution. Again, not a big deal and it's easy to not notice it - but it's worth mentioning.

I was surprised to find myself instantly engaged by the story of Winter as she follows her mentor, Cyrus, on a mission to lower tensions between countries on an alien world. Winter's lawfulness, idealism, and inexperience creates a strong contrast with Cyrus, who seems so accustomed to work as a mediator his practical and detached approach and cynical attitude to his work comes off to Winter as heartless and unprincipled. Your major choice in the story is how you choose for Winter to respond to this in the midst of a political crisis that transpires on this world.
The quality of writing in LTMC is its primary strength, bringing Winter and Cyrus's thoughts and feelings to life in a way that is touching, humorous, and fun. The background music is very complimentary and sometimes just stand-alone good. I really enjoyed my first playthrough, and at the real critical junction in the story I took a full day to mull it over before proceeding because it felt important enough.
While I enjoyed it, it isn't without some fairly significant weaknesses. Most notably, this episode in the planned three-part series is VERY short. There is really just the one really important decision in the game, although there are differences in the details of how you end up on the two different paths. You'll need to enjoy it for the different stories that are already written if you are to enjoy it because you just aren't going to decide much for yourself. When it comes to actually approaching the politics of the world, you have almost nothing to go on. The stubs of histories of the relevant countries you get in your data book make next to no sense at all. In most cases I had to just see what played out from choices because there just wasn't enough consistent information to make choices from, so that the data book basically fails in its one purpose. The contrived histories mirrors the contrived political crisis. It feels like a kid came up with it. It's only other information in it is a poorly written article about how nuclear bombs work, the shortcomings of which are also mirrored in the storyline.
Finally, the episode ends on a particularly weak note, where you switch to someone else's experience, and have their experience of hallway conversations that are just tedious and meaningless. I suppose this is supposed to be a lead-in to the next episode, but what a horribly dry lead in, as though switching to another character weren't already disruptive, and, frankly, a little more than what the story length qualifies it for. So, in the end, Learning to Manage Chaos comes off as a sort of disjointed combination of ideas and directions and input from people with varying talent that seems more like a demo than a finished work. Nevertheless, I enjoyed it, and don't think of it as a bad experience for $5.
The ending left me wanted more from this game, but it was honestly a fun time while it lasted.

The people do level up and you can give them items and send them into the wasteland to explore / do quests. Each person also has different attributes making them work better in a given area of the vault. Drag and drop them into a room and that's it. You can also get them to breed to make more people. That's basically the whole game play for 10% of the time, the other 90% of the time is basically waiting for something to do.
You do get rooms come under attack at random and your people deal with this themselfs but you can also micro manage your people to stop them from being hurt to much.
I can see that after a lot of time and effort spent this could eventually become a semi decent micro management game, however getting to that point is itself a challenge with basically nothing to do but wait or pay real money to speed things along.
It is worth stating that the game continues to run in real time (1 minute of real life time = 1 minute of game time and each day in game takes 24 hours) even if you are not playing. So if you want a game that you log in for a couple of minutes click a few things and then leave alone while you play something else until the next day you can do that but it's not the sort of game your going to want to boot your computer up to rush back to. It's clearly aimed at mobile user where this sort of short term play works best. As a PC game...

The Witcher 2 is one of the best fantasy epics I've played for a while. Dark writing that will compel you to push forth and delve into the story; going so far as to consume your days! And then, in the final moments of the game, the narrative will have you begging for more, making you wish the game was longer--or that Witcher 3 would come sooner! (P.S. The game is over 20 hours long, yet I wanted more. Yes, the story is that gripping) The game also treats you with some god-damned maturity, CDProjekt Red doesn't ♥♥♥♥♥ out here, the game contains a lot of sex--and it's magnificent; especially when other game developers don't have the balls to go there, or when they do, they often don't have the balls to see it through to the end.
Sufficed to say, all those who haven't played the previous game (of which I am one) will,  at-first, find themselves lost. The game will try to get you up to speed, however you'll feel very lost at the beginning of the game. But soon you'll be caught up in a web of conspiricy and intrigue that, when the jarring moments of exposition pretaining to the first game come, it will do little to sour your mood, and soon, you'll be back into the fray of the story.
Also, choices, choices that bloody matter! Do you know how refreshing that is? Yes? Then jump on in!
The gameplay is burtal and unforgiving if you are unready--plus the saving system isn't very... lenient with you. So if you screw  up and you haven't saved, oh boy you're in hot water! Enemies will challenge you, hoards of them can be just as effective as a boss. Which, to mention the bosses, yeah, they're hard too! Especially the last. However, I'm just speaking from my own experience here, it will greatly vary by user ability and game difficulty. (I can imagine that, after playing this bloody romp on normal and dying a couple of times, that on hard it's a bloody nightmare.)
The presentation of the game isn't too shabby either, bearing in mind it's been 2 years from release, it couldn't look any better; sure in some areas texture can appear flat or certain other graphical annoyances may appear, however it will do little to deter you from playing! Character models are detailed to the level that you would expect. Glitches are minimal--although some may make themselves apparent. The game has a highly fine level of polish that will be apparent as you play through the wonderful game; the craftmanship that has gone into this game is insane, CDProjektRed are masters of making video games, so you're in safe hands.
Convinced yet? I should bloody hope so. If this game is on sale and you're reading this, I can only ask why? Why are you wasting you time? This is such a great game that any [reasonable] cost is well worth it! Especially on your nice fancy PC rig. So, stop reading and add this game to your collection now! You won't regret a single moment, a single dime, that you'll have poured into this game.

I played adventure games mostly as a child during late 90s and early 2000s. Even though they were my favourite genre back then I often felt the puzzles are forced and too cryptic and the good writing wasn't rewarding enough - I either had to use walktroughs or keep clicking everything aroun for half an hour and get extremely frustrating. Now, as an adult, I find these puzzles way easier, however I still get annoyed by those lazy "challanges".
The first half of Broken Age is almost free of this kind of obstacles. The second half is from the gameplay perspective is significantly worse (someone could say "more challanging", but I think "ridiculous" would be more in place), but it doesn't spoil the overall extremely rewarding experience Broken Age was for me. The graphics and animations are just beatiful, voice acting top notch, music either amazing or decent - never bad.
I like the story a lot and I was laughing pretty hard at times. The worst part is the ending, which left a lot to player's imagination. The problem isn't the quality of ideas shown to us, but more the lack of the last swing of a pen - something is missing and I've already seen that a lot of people would like just a bit more. 5-10 more minutes of content would make this game very close to perfect.
Still - I think this game does what older point & clock adventure games wanted to be, but were unable to succeed. I am so happy I could return to this genre in such a tasty way.

Firstly I don't know why the record says 6.5 hours. I've easily hit 20+ since I bought it. I have gotten more than my money's worth for this title.
I think how much you're into the 'navigate obstacles at high speeds' genre will largely determine whether you'll find this game worth your time and money. It's far from the best on offer, but it's solid in most respects and can make for many hours of weirld relaxing-yet-hectic fun provided you're willing to look over some issues.
Firstly, the difficulty. It's unbalanced, and quite noticably so. These are the 4 difficulty settings, with what they actually feel like:
Easy = Very Easy
Medium = Very Hard
Hard = Extreme
Extreme = Muscle Memory Master from Hell
You will have quite a difficult time navigating the narrow pathways of the harder settings while also managing to avoid projectiles, gather multipliers and avoiding dying. It is a mess, in an overall good way.  It's well conceived, but doesn't have enough middle ground in terms of difficulty for more casual players. It'll either put you to sleep or make you want to punch your monitor. Not much in between.
Gameplay is your standard stuff. Avoid walls and holes while grabbing multipliers which increase the rate at which your score counts up per amount of time, along with powerups of various kinds which are level-dependant. nothing new or exciting, but still solid and fun for short spans of time.
Controls are solid and seem to fit the level design as they should. At no point have I felt a death was unfair due to shoddy controls. It's tight and handles well, to an extent that all the dying you'll be doing (a lot), madding as it is, is not likely to feel overtly cheap.
Aesthetic is kinda basic with no surprises. Strictly 'arcade' with a few different techno Tron-inspired layouts and color schemes, with a lightshow in the background which keeps a beat to the music.  Nothing spectacular, but I can't complain.
Music is hit and miss. Each difficulty setting per layout has it's own track, with some having two tracks each which alternate. I found about 65% of the music to range from boring to annoying as hell, while the other 35% was decent and kinda catch and enjoyable. YMMV on this. Rather standard techo/electronica with scarce variety. Not in my opinion noteworthy.
Overall I would fully recommend this game when it's on sale to people who already at least somewhat like the genre. They won't be disappointed in having another game for their collection to load up here and there for some casual fun. Nothing new here really, but nothing really bad either. You'll likely come away satisfied for at least a good 6-8 hours spread out over a few weeks.

Look, I wanted to like Mafia III. I enjoyed 2, but sadly 3 feels empty. The story is alright, the soundtrack is great, but the gameplay is extremely repetitive, even for an open world game.
The game looks nice, and the voice acting and lip syncing is superb. All of the story cutscenes are done fantastically.
However, that doesn't make a game worth buying. The city feels empty. You can only do story missions and a small amount of extremely repetitive side missions. Sometimes day becomes night, somethings the opposite happens -but there's hardly a transition. Every racket boss is the same, every mission is the same.
There's a limited selection of guns and items you can buy which is OK, but you'll rarely ever buy them. You can only carry 3/4 magazines for most of the weapons and at times this makes carrying an SMG almost useless.
There are no clothing options, car customizations, and the police system is busted. No fines, no pursuit without firearms. They instantly open fire on you.
All in all I can't recommend this, and I honestly don't see it getting much better. I'll play it to completion but I'll probably never touch it again.
I'd give it a 6.5 / 10 . Maybe pick it up at $15 .

Let me start with the fact that I love games/movies that involve manipulation of time.  They can even be kind of crappy and I'll still at the very least enjoy the experience they give me. Who hasn't thought about time manipulation?
Life Is Strange was a visceral story that I couldn't complete in just one go.  I had to take breaks after each chapter because of how each of them ended...especially episode 3.  Though I suppose I sort of knew how the game would end before it did (as the story itself hints towards it), the experience was well worth it.
If you're all about action and quick plot progression, this game isn't really for you.  I think you'd like this game if you ever played Dear Esther or the 1990s game Loom, as I would probably call this game somewhat of a blend between the two.
I'm not quite sure how replayable Life Is Strange is, as much as the developers probably wanted it to be, but I'll definitely be seeing what other choices I could have made every now and then.

A more interactive twist on an existing genre of decision-driven story games, with pleasant results to boot. While certainly better than something like Telltale's brand of narrative story-style gameplay, the game is still very much a hit-or-miss depending on one's tastes.
Life is Strange takes the walking simulator style of narrative gameplay and adds on a nice layer of interactivity that makes it stand out amongst the crowd. However, the devil is in the details and this game is chock full of them. The writing is, overall, well done; each character has a personality that makes them feel rounded, even if their purpose is to simply fill the usual archetypes in any high school drama.
However, the game is not without flaws. From a gameplay perspective, it's still a very linear, hard-scripted, storyline with the only varience being the many
decisions you make that drives the story. This in and of itself is not an issue. The main gripe I have with the game is that not all choices feel very important or well thought out. You have instances where seemingly huge decisions result in just one extra line of dialogue later in the game. Furthermore, the game tends to muddy the water a lot by introducing these B and C storylines in between the A (primary) narrative. Unfortunately, pursuing many of these leads to unrewarding results, often times the difference between one inconsequential additional line of dialogue.
This isn't to say there aren't many other very well done bits throughout the game. The optional scavenger hunt for achievement photos was definitely a highlight of this. Certainly for me, I thought the game to be worthwhile in my time spent, though I do not think I enjoyed it enough to come back for the sequel. And, while I can't ensure you'll enjoy the game, I do believe it is worth experiencing.

I think my only complaint would be how short the game is. The entire game hinges on a VERY small set of decisions, and should be almost entirely viewed as a visual novel, more than an interactive one.
That said, the story is wonderful. It quickly pulled me in, and easily kept my attention. And while the entire story, if I'd played out my first set of choices without any rethinking at all would have been short, it was definitely interesting to go back and see all of the consequeces for alternate paths, and look at the other courses that were available. The characters, though only allowing for a small amount of exposition in the space given, seemed very fully developed, and were consistent to their apparent personalities, without any seemingly random mood swings with no explanation.
The plotline and setting itself were both very interesting, but there is definitely room to grow. For the amount of information that is presented, it could easily be expanded upon, even if only through secondary, non-essential entries in the game's codex, or information accessible through the main menu, but what is shown through the story is very entertaining. A powerful climax of the story, and... realistic, if not entirely satisfying ending following, result in a story that definitely makes me want to read further.
The setting is really interesting and because there are not many good round based strategy games out there, this is a must buy for fans of the genre. It is also quite challenging.

Having very little experience with VNs (visual novels) I picked this game up on a whim. And what a good choice that was. I found the story very compelling and the music is phenomenal (After hearing the soundtrack I found the music alone to be worth the price of the VN).
The game does restrict viewer choice, so don't expect to be making a lot of descisions. However, the few choices it does force you to make are very well thought out and genuinely difficult to make in a great way that gets you thinking. They also appear to be adding a lot more choice in the future episodes (currently on kickstarter till march 24th of 2014, so go back it if you have the disposable income as it is deserving of the support).
The only major complaint is that the game is relatively short (roughly 2-3 hours long depending on how fast you go through things) and the ending isn't fully complete (the ending is not bad but it was still designed to be continued), however with the recent addition of the future episodes being added to kickstarter it seems that the story will get the continuation it deserved.
If you aren't sure or are fairly new to visual novels I'd recommend checking out the developers free VN from their website (the VN is called Juniper's Knot) which should help you find out if the writing is something you like.
Overall a great buy for the price if you're looking for a good story with good art and music supporting it. And while the descisions may be few, they are extremely good at making you think about them and second guessing yourself on what the best choice should be.

As a big fan of Fallout 1 and 2, I had hoped Wasteland 2 would be their legitimate successor. Unfortunately, it is more an XCOM-like RPG than a Fallout-like one.
Unlike the Fallout series, the game does not allow you to play whith just 1 character. Instead, it forces you to manage a group. You manage their skills, perks, levelling. In every phase of the game, you have to think in term of group. For some people, I guess it is alright; to me, it was a deal breaker, for two reasons.
The first one is that I felt no connection at all, with any characters; not the four I created at the begining of the game, nor with the NPC ones who joined the group.
What I loved in the Fallout 1 and 2 games was that you played as yourself. You controlled 1 character, companions had their own AI. Because you played just one character, you felt really involved in your quests, your skills and perks. You, alone, made decisions, joined factions, helped or killed whoever. The NPC followed you and you just had to watch out for their weapons, ammo and stimpaks, as you were the one looting.
In Wasteland 2, I felt like a manager, who had to form an heterogeneous group with all skills present and spread to all your characters. But I felt no connection with any of them, I didn't feel involved in the quests: it wasn't ME playing (1 character) but THEM (the group). I just felt overwatching rather than roleplaying.
The second one, is that the game is just not made to play as 1 player. Even if you start the game with 1 character instead of 4, the game mechanics are not made to let you play alone. The fights are group vs. group, and there is just no way to survive those encounters if you fight alone. And as soon as you take a companion with you, you have full control on that character and have to play it, even if you don't want to.
I think I would have enjoyed the game if i could play 1 character, and NPC joined me with their own AI, like the first Fallout games.
All in all, it's not good enough to be a Fallout successor; and the combat system is just not good enough if you compare it to XCOM. The game might be best enjoyed by XCOM fans, but I cannot recommend the game for those like me who expected Wasteland 2 to have the same mechanics as Fallout 1 and 2.

the witcher was a global phenom that apparently the US wasnt ready for during its original debut in 2007.  having read 5.5 of the original 7 novels i have a better understanding of the story to date, especially having played the first game.  but none of that matters as, introduced in the first game, our hero geralt, has no memory of his past, ie the novels.  either way, the witcher series is about the story of geralt of rivia, a witcher or professional monster hunter, who is dragged into a twisting and turning story of political bull.sh.it that he wants nothing to do with, but unfortunitly cant escape.
Unlike the first game of the series, the graphics are far more refined, the story is much more cohesive, complex and inline with what original stories would lead to, and is exactly what CDProjekt were hoping to create with the first game.  not only does choice matter, it is essential to the very core of the game.  every decision has a consequence, whether you see it now or at the end of your journey.  this is the type of game that bioware has wet dreams about but instead sells you a half♥♥♥♥♥copy of.  litteraly the 2nd half of the game takes completely different paths depending on a not so simple choice in the 1st chapter.
one of my personal favorite features is "survivor mode"...dont be fooled, combat can be extremely difficult in this game, but entering the arena is a nice change of pace that will give you some, albiet, over exaggerated practice, but it is a great time killer that will keep you going in the hopes taht you can get your name of the leader board.  highly addictive and extremely punishing to the say the least, especially at higher difficulty levels.
sure theres flaws, very few games are without but this is a game, that even if you didnt play the first, will have you from beginning to end leaving you begging for more, and unlike most games that claim to be of the same ilk....*cough* mass effect, there actually is more to do that you can not do because of the decisions that you made the first time around.
Buy this game now, especially being 5$ as it will give you some back info to Witcher 3.
p.s. if you can get your hands on teh novels, they are fantastic and really give a detailed backstory on most characters, especially geralt and his close companions.  trust me you wont regret this purchase <3

Virtually unrivaled among modern games in terms of quality and depth of its story, The Witcher 2 is a visually stunning RPG in which the player's choices really and truly have a meaningful effect on the way the game unfolds. The world in which the stoic and cynical Geralt of Rivia inhabits is so detailed and rich in lore and history it can sometimes be difficult to keep the political maneuverings and geographic regions straight, but as so many games make compromises for the sake of wider mass appeal, it is refreshing to get lost in the in-game glossary of people and places to sort it all out.
The story is dark and violent, and the areas the player visits are designed perfectly for such themes. Corpses hang from gallows in a village square, minority races suffer prejudices, and unlucky victims dot the environments where they met their doom at the hands of men or beasts. The combat, while not groundbreaking, is quick and competant, with many skills and options for customization in the player's hands. Equipment upgrades take place fairly regularly, with many weapons and armor pieces to be discovered by diligent explorers. A straightforward crafting system also keeps players invested in scrounging up materials from slain enemies and the environment.
All told, The Witcher 2 is a beautiful game with a complex and mature narrative devoid of unrealistic black and white morality distinctions imposed on the player. It is a game in which you are required to think about and invest yourself in the troubled world presented. To me, Geralt is a fascinating and likeable character with a still developing story and clearly defined personality. I cannot wait to see what is in store for him in the upcoming Witcher 3.

Played 5 hours on normal difficulty so far. I think I'm half way through the campaign and honestly feel I've experienced everything the game has to offer.... which is limited.
Pros:
- X-COM in the wild west.
- Although not exceptional, the graphics are nice (especially playing at 4k).
- Nice voice acting. Well, the narrator at least. Actual missions seem devoid of all but "arrgh" when someone gets shot.
- Audio in general is good. I like the music. It does the wild west theme justice and adds sufficient atmosphere to the game.
- Engaging story line. Cowboys, demons, death, revenge.
- Good and evil choices affect the game (in a small way). It's fun being able to choose to let people go or lock them in a house and burn it to the ground... and then those choices affecting future actions.
Cons:
- After the first tutorial mission you're dumped into map mode with no hint as to what do do next. I'd have preferred the tutorial to at least give some guidance about moving around the map and interacting with points of interest etc.
- I don't understand why the game is broken into scenarios. After a small number of combat missions (like 3) your party members and items reset. This makes it utterly pointless in caring who is in your party, and what items you give them.
- Far too many 'perks' to give to your characters. What I mean by this is if you assign the *must survive* party members with playing cards, a healing item, and use their default skills (like turning into a demon) they're so tough I just didn't care that they were a *must survive* character. Your characters basically become terminators in stetson hats.
- When the 'fires twice in one turn' weapons come into play the 'fires once per turn' weapons become obsolete. This is really early on in the game too. There's no reason to use them after. "Hmm... should I fire once and cause 4 damage, or fire twice and cause 6 damage...". Especially when a lot of enemies have 3 hit points. Why kill one per turn when you can kill two?
- Weapon damage. What you see is what you get. If it says it does 4 damage, it does 4 damage (unless they're in cover). It'd be nice to have a '4 damage within x range, 3 damage within xx range' etc. Critical hits would be nice as well.
- Weapon damage. There's very little difference between shooting someone with a pistol from 30 yards away, and shooting someone point blank in the back with a quad-barrelled shotgun. It still only does like 1 extra damage.
- No melee weapons (that I've found). The story makes a point of saying you slit people's throats, yet there are no knives, axes, etc in the game. I'd love to be able to give a character playing cards that boost movement and defense, a knife, and go charging in to good old melee combat.
Overall it's an okay game, but if you are expecting a game as good or as satisfying as X-COM then you will be disappointed. I can't say I like it enough, in its current state, to give it a thumbs up.
