Make deals with the devil and get your just desserts in Hard West, a turn based squad strategy game featuring demons and cowboys alike.
Gameplay in Hard West is often likened to XCom due to its turn based nature and percentage-to-hit with an interesting spin added: luck. The luck system serves both as a character’s “magic points” pool as well as their evasion modifier. As fire is exchanged, you (or your enemy) lose luck according to the estimated percentage to hit until damage is received. Being damaged will restore a significant amount of luck and the process starts over again. To use luck abilities, you will need to collect and combine various playing cards which give additional bonuses if you form specific poker hands with them. Similar to Xcom, this game features a half and full cover system which is often the focus of combat for good and bad reasons. Interestingly enough, you can also manipulate your environment via lifting well covers or flipping tables to create your own cover when needed. Hard West also utilizes an overworld system where you move a cow skull token representing yourself from location to location processing text prompts backed by randomly generated chances to succeed or fail, the latter often resulting in injury or a party member’s death.
Once the wonder of demonic dealings and spaghetti western wear off, Hard West’s flaws become almost impossible to ignore. Combat is often a tedious chore of taking extra turns to flank enemies or spam card abilities to get it over with as fast as possible. Overworld missions are coded in a way that makes it too easy to accidentally put yourself in an unwinnable situation, forcing a complete restart of the scenario if you want to proceed. Weapon variety is so-so and many times I found only the luck and health boosting items to be worth carrying into battle. Characters come and go and there’s no real attachment to any of the people you find along the way, making them more like cannon fodder than interesting sidekicks. Finally, the game is poorly optimized and suffers from a lot of performance issues even with lower resolutions and reduced graphical quality settings.
To me, the overall gameplay served more as an obstacle to the story than the vehicle it should have been. This is unfortunate as the story and additional gameplay systems were at least interesting conceptually, albeit poorly executed. Thus, the only thing I can recommend at this point is giving Hard West a hard pass.

I really want to like this game, I love the setting and atmosphere, but the combat is frankly extremely frustrating. Routinely enemies have random angles to hit and wound/kill you through walls, cover isnt exactly obvious if it is working or not as enemies can see the very tip top of your shoulder through a window and will have no penalty for shooting you, and most of the special abilities are pretty useless or require a ridiculous confluence of events to be used that rarely happen. This may be because the game doesn't explain jack♥♥♥♥♥♥to you, such as the overwatch mechanic enemies have, and if you are even able to do that overwatch ability yourself. I got through half the scenarios before just giving up on the game, as the stealth bits seem interesting but ultimately half baked and dependent on you having a full party to do anything interesting, which if you are playing on higher difficulties is not always a guaranteed thing.
The largest probblem, is the Luck mechanic is incredibly poorly thought out, and is a prime example of trying to reinvent the wheel just to break it. Luck is basically your ability to not get shot, and your action points for abilities at the same time. The only way to regen is to get shot and not die from the shot. The problem is you are always outnumbered 5-1, and on higher difficulties you get shot you die. So, in essence, you never get to use those cool abilities cause it just means you get murdered the next enemy turn because it took most of your Luck, and the 5-12 enemies you are facing can now proceed to shoot you to death because you are defenseless and cover is pretty useless.
The effective ranges of various weapons seems a little wonky and inconsistent too, as shotguns are worse than pistols up close, unless you expose yourself to get a good shot to then get picked off by the 7 enemy riflemen that will then immediately blow your man away. Basically, you will end up using a volcano or special pistol for about everything, and a rifle for the enemies that are too far away cause a specific character has crap movement.
But again, the scenarios wipe every item and weapon from your previous scenario, so it really doesnt matter anyway. The lack of ability and item progression cripples the game, as I finally found an item and card combo I enjoyed playing, had built a fun team, just for it to be wiped every hour or so for a new scenario and story time jump. Lots of potential here, but I mostly found myself constantly annoyed and frustrated due to poor basic design choices.

Standard style visual novel with lovely art and music. Your character is a mediator in training (shadowing a mentor). Mediators travel to "chaotic worlds" and attempt to fix problems. I really like the premise, but the game only focuses on one world's situation, and is fairly short at about 3 hours. The backdrops and character animations/expressions are fairly basic and there isn't a lot of variety, but the game is still pleasing to look at.
The first third of the game is fairly long and sets up the story and characters. There are no choices to be made during this time, so you really just watch it play out. The second third of the game is where all of the dialogue branches are made, but they really only unlock variations of dialogue. The last choice you make during that section determines which ending you get. The last third of the game is much like the first, just seeing it play out.
Aside from the lack of impactful choices, my only other gripe is that much of the dialogue is simply bickering back and forth. Some of the choices seem slightly out of character, but they offer the sense of you being able to change someone else's mind via dialogue in order to open up a different viewpoint.
Overall, I enjoyed this game but would have liked it to be much longer, with more characters and more impactful choices. This is supposed to only be "Episode 1" and is priced appropriately for its length; however, the developers are unable to make a sequel unless they find funding via their Kickstarter (Found here
)
I'd love to see a sequel that expands upon what they've created here, as it has a lot of potential to fully explore the plot and characters in much more detail.

I really wanted to like this game, and I tried really hard to do so. But in the end its numerous flaws were too pungent to ignore:
1) A really dumb combat system. Now don't get me wrong, there are tactics involved, mainly dealing with the positioning of your characters in such a way as to avoid friendly fire. But that's about it. The rest of it is just standing in open ground, and plugging and/or slashing away at the nearest target.
Yes there is a smattering of "cover" here and there you can shield yourself from fire with, but animals and melee units are able to pretty much run up to you in one turn with impunity, and attack you regardless. And they always seem to run up to you in such a way as to place your other characters in the line of fire, necessitating you to move away to avoid friendly fire.
So yeah, there are "tactics" here, an elaborate dance where you move your guys around the map in such a way as to shoot the enemy without shooting your teammates in the back. Ie, tactics that bear no resemblance to combat tactics in real life.
2) The artwork is just cheap, horrible and amateurish. And some of the portraits don't match the character descriptions, and many are reused for other characters, just simply destroying game immersion. For a $40 buck game, the consumer deserves better.
3) The number of times you have to go back to a previous save because you accidentally triggered combat with friendly NPCs is utterly frustrating, and just indicative of a terrible design.

Broken Age is an old-school point-and-click adventure game. You play as two characters – Shay and Vella – and can switch between them at any point during the story.
This sounds neat, but unfortunately, while this sounds neat, for the vast majority of the story – indeed, up until the very, very end of the game – it is almost completely irrelevant. And unfortunately, in the bit where it IS relevant, it actually makes no sense. But I am getting ahead of myself.
Broken Age is an old-school adventure game. You have a (very small) inventory, though unlike some old games you can’t create unwinnable situations or nonsense like that. There are puzzles you have to solve in the world, primarily by taking inventory items, combining inventory items, and delivering inventory items to people/locations to solve problems. Some of the items have to be manipulated within your inventory – in particular, you get a robot later on in the game which you repeatedly have to rewire to perform various tasks on your behalf.
The actual story is split into two parts – Shay’s story is about him trying to escape from his rather controlling ship, where “Mom” (a woman’s face in a glowing orb) is rather controlling and has him do ridiculous “missions” which are all just fake adventures. Robots serve the roles of NPCs in these adventures, and it is only when Shay deliberately breaks one of the adventures that his story really begins, as a stowaway wolf (or, more accurately, man in a wolf costume) offers to help him find some REAL adventure – saving some innocent creatures. But he has to go around the ship and bypass various security and safety mechanisms in order to do it.
Meanwhile, Vella’s half of the story is that her people periodically sacrifice maidens to Mog Chothra, a tentacled flying monster. She has been chosen as one of this year’s sacrifices for her hometown, but she isn’t going to go down without a fight – this whole thing is stupid, and Vella believes they should fight the monster rather than appease it. This leads to her doing exactly that, and her going on an adventure which eventually results in her battling the thing.
The second half of the game has the characters switch places – Vella has to go through Shay’s ship, while Shay has to deal with Vella’s world. Both realize that not everything was as it seemed, as does the player.
Unfortunately, this reveals one of the three major flaws of the game – you basically spend almost the entire game backtracking back and forth across two fairly limited areas. The ship is smaller and quicker to go through than Vella’s area, which requires significant backtracking. Thus, even though there’s not that many areas in the game, the game as a whole takes nearly ten hours to complete. This can make the game feel a bit tedious at times, doubly so because there just aren’t many new areas to explore after the first half of the game.
The second problem arises from the fact that Vella’s part of the game is just generally more interesting than Shay’s ship. Shay’s ship has basically one joke, and it is repeated over and over again, while Vella’s area is more varied and has more interesting people to interact with. Vella herself is a kind of bland character; Shay is somewhat better, and his companion, a spoon in his inventory, is more interesting to drag around. It also is with him longer; Vella acquires a fork and knife, but they are less interesting NPCs and have fewer interesting things to say (though they, too, are amusing).
Alas, by the end of the game, the whole thing has worn a bit thin, and it felt like the central villains in the story don’t have a major role at all for a large portion of the gameplay due to Vella’s world being larger and longer than Shay’s. And honestly, the ending felt a bit rushed, with the bad guys apparently being thwarted, but half by accident, with everyone coming together to sing Kumbaya at the end in a kind of dubious way.
The third problem comes from the gameplay itself. It has some of the flaws of the old-school games, most notably the “Try to combine everything with everything and everyone” problem. There was at least one puzzle in the game that I only solved by trying to combine an inventory item with everyone in the game until it finally worked, as the vague hints were… well, vague. I knew I had to get an item from a “chain of deals” type thing, but I was missing an intermediate step and it took a bit to figure it out.
While it all made sense in the end, it still ended up involving a lot of backtracking.
A larger issue, however, lies in the endgame – there are some puzzles which are pretty obscure and require you to notice some symbols in the background of a photograph. Worse, this is not really called out in any major way, and it is extremely easy to miss.
However, the largest problem lies in the fact that this puzzle – along with a puzzle that Vella has to solve – require the characters to get knowledge from the other character’s section. BUT THERE IS LITERALLY NO COMMUNICATION BETWEEN THEM. It is purely meta – the player learns the solution in one half of the game, and then applies it to the other half. It makes no sense, and in the finale, this is even more blatant, as you constantly have to switch back and forth and use things learned from one half to apply to the other half. It is not at all obvious and it is, frankly, nonsensical, as the characters aren’t actually in active communication with each other. Once you realize that you have to use things from one half in the other, it does sort of come together, but while the idea of the two halves coming together was literally the only application of the “switch between characters” mechanic which was otherwise pointless, the fact that there was no in-character communication between them in order to do this is kind of annoying and feels very “gamey”.
Ultimately, I don’t think that this game quite came together for me. The endgame crossover puzzles aren’t the best thing in the world, and the story sort of felt like it never really came together as an exciting whole. There was a fair bit of humor, but the more serious side of the story felt kind of wonky, and Shay’s ship relied far too heavily on a single sort of joke and added essentially no fresh humor in the second half of the game.
There are better adventure games out there in the world, and while the humor in this is kind of cute, I’m not sure if it is worth 8-10 hours of your time.

Broken Age is a traditional point-and-click adventure with beautiful 2D art. I kickstarted this game back in 2012 back during the early Kickstarter craze.
The game starts out quite strong. The 2D art is gorgeous and the voiceacting is absolutely superb. The first act also has some decent puzzles and Vella's story is pretty interesting too.
Unfortunately the game kinda falls apart in the second act. The biggest problem is the gameplay itself, as for some reason there's suddenly a huge jump in difficulty and many of the puzzles are rather obtuse and tedious. Additionally, you are just revisiting the exact same locations from the first act. Even the story and the writing felt much weaker in the second act and the ending in particular is extremely lackluster.
The game doesn't really take proper advantage of the two protagonists either. For starters there's minimal interaction between Vella and Shay. Furthermore, Shay's role in the overall story feels rather limited and he often feels like a fairly useless character.
The game also makes the highly dubious design choice of forcing you to use player knowledge gained with one character while playing with the other one. This feels extremely artificial, as often the other character would have no in-game way of having the knowledge.
My first impressions of Broken Age were very positive and after finishing the first act I would have recommended the game to any fans of classic adventure games. Unfortunately the second act is much, much weaker and I can't really recommend this as a complete experience.
The good:
- Great visual style
- Superb voiceacting
- Nice soundtrack
The bad:
- Overall the story is pretty bad
- Shay is fairly useless as a protagonist
- Limited interaction between the two main characters
- Lots of obtuse and tedious puzzles in act 2
- Heavy reuse of locations and other assets in act 2

Broken Age is a pretty classic style point and click adventure game, for lovers of this nearly exctinct genre. It is, however, also made by people with a great deal of experience in making such games. It's not annoyingly difficult, and even the few real challenging puzzles are not unfairly difficult. In the old games of this type, you'd end up frantically trying all your items on everything and exhausting everyone's dialogue; in Broken Age, you'll get the hints you need to piece together solutions by just going around talking to characters and showing them the handful of items you carry around. I found this made playing the game pretty smooth.
Much like in Day of the Tentacle, you can switch between two characters in different locations, and the narrative flows together interestingly. The game has a gorgeous hand-painted cartoon style with beautiful, soaring music that feels like you're in a Miyazaki movie at times. The game's writing is great, funny and the voice acting is excellent. Really an all round classic. If I have to complain about anything, it's that I wanted the game to last longer, but that's because I wanted to spend more time with the world and its characters. I also had rather heavy load times inbetween every game screen that got on my nerves more the longer the game went on, but I'm still trying to figure out if that's a problem on my end or not.
If you're looking for an classic gripping adventure game, Broken Age is it.
It's still a blast!

Virtually unrivaled among modern games in terms of quality and depth of its story, The Witcher 2 is a visually stunning RPG in which the player's choices really and truly have a meaningful effect on the way the game unfolds. The world in which the stoic and cynical Geralt of Rivia inhabits is so detailed and rich in lore and history it can sometimes be difficult to keep the political maneuverings and geographic regions straight, but as so many games make compromises for the sake of wider mass appeal, it is refreshing to get lost in the in-game glossary of people and places to sort it all out.
The story is dark and violent, and the areas the player visits are designed perfectly for such themes. Corpses hang from gallows in a village square, minority races suffer prejudices, and unlucky victims dot the environments where they met their doom at the hands of men or beasts. The combat, while not groundbreaking, is quick and competant, with many skills and options for customization in the player's hands. Equipment upgrades take place fairly regularly, with many weapons and armor pieces to be discovered by diligent explorers. A straightforward crafting system also keeps players invested in scrounging up materials from slain enemies and the environment.
All told, The Witcher 2 is a beautiful game with a complex and mature narrative devoid of unrealistic black and white morality distinctions imposed on the player. It is a game in which you are required to think about and invest yourself in the troubled world presented. To me, Geralt is a fascinating and likeable character with a still developing story and clearly defined personality. I cannot wait to see what is in store for him in the upcoming Witcher 3.

Being a true fan of point 'n' click adventure games since...well... forever, and Tim Schafer being about the closest thing to a god in the game developing world for me, it is almost unbelievable that I haven't played this game before now. I can promise that I was totally hyped about this game ever since I first heard about it when it launched on Kickstarter. Even more hyped when it broke records with funding and seemed to be an extended experience. I truly expected an epic masterpiece. A true adventure of old in new packing.
Somehow I lost the hype over time, and after reading mixed reviews and critics about the business practice of Double Fine, I ended up just postponing playing the game at all. Finally I got around to it and have just played through it, and now I'm just...well... slightly disappointed.
Don't get me wrong. There is lots of things to like in this game. The initial setup is creative and intriguing. From the very start I found myself asking questions about how these seperated stories were connected, and how they would conclude in the end. There were surprises and creative ways the story twisted itself throughout the game. But in the end it just felt that it was cut short. Many questions left unanswered and unsatisfying "conclusion".
The art style was fully ok, but in my opinion it was not that great. Yet, I respect developers that dare creating something new and different approaches. Some might appreciate the art style much more than me.
The dialogue and voice acting can only be praised. Tim Schafer never fails in his clever and humoristic approach to dialogue. It fits my humor to a tee, and is easily comparable to previous games he has been involved in. With actors like Elijah Wood, Jack Black, Jennifer Hale and Wil Wheaton and a team of very talented voice actors it does not fail to impress. Especially Wil Wheaton should consider to do this more often as he has a very good voice for this sort of thing.
The gameplay itself varies. It has its remarkable puzzles with some mindbending solutions mixed in with some rather strange approaches to puzzle solving. Everything from the traditional backtracking to progress, typical inventory puzzles to some new odd, and mostly unexplained or poorly introduced puzzles. A rather mixed bowl of rice in other words.
All in all I don't feel that it amounted to anything but a mediocre game, especially considering the track record of the brain behind this. The game has been on some great sales, in bundles and even came free with Playstation Plus, so I assume most people fans of the genre has already picked it up, but if you haven't you can be assured that you can great deals on this game in the future as well, so wait to get it until then at least. I do not feel that it is worth a full price.
I just barely recommend this game, as it is recommended for fans of point 'n' click and traditional adventure games. It is likely that you would enjoy enough of this game for it to be worth your while.
I give it a 6/10 rating
Remember that this review is my personal opinion and yours might vary from that. I know many that adores this game. Check out several reviews if you are in doubt of playing it.

Warning: rage quit ahead!
Avoid - Sensory Overload is a simple game that is strangely addictive. Controlling a small racing hovercraft ship thingy, you fly into the screen on a series of obstacle-course-like tracks, which become faster and more evil as you progress.
The game has four level 'styles': Electronic, Minimal, Laserdance and Sythrock. As you may have guessed from the names, each of these level styles has its own musical style to go with it. Each is also unique in terms of graphical and obstacle style, too. For example, Electronic sees you speeding across bright, colourful stages to electronic music, dodging occasional glowing orbs, whereas Minimal levels have a march darker and minimalist theme (and are, I find, the most distracting, graphically speaking).
After choosing a level style you are then able to choose from defined levels or 'endless' mode, which sees you endlessly racing across a randomly generated track in your chosen style until you crash or fall off the track. If you choose the levels option, then you'll find that your chosen level style has four difficulty groups of eight individual levels each, ranging from Easy, through Medium, Hard and Extreme. These are pre-defined tracks, each of which always plays the same, so beating the levels is a matter of skill and memory, especially as you progress through the harder stages.
Playing through the pre-defined levels, you are graded on how well you do collecting bonuses and not dying. Each track gives you two extra lives to begin with, so you can crash or fall off the track twice; on the third such event, you lose the level and must start again.
At this point I have completed all 32 Easy levels with full points (collecting all bonuses and not crashing or falling off the track) and all 32 Medium levels with varying degrees of success. I now find the difficulty is about at my limit: I've only completed two or three Hard levels, and only one of them with full points. I now usually find myself playing a level or two and rage quitting.
The controls are very simple -- just move left or right -- but they feel a bit slow. And when you're on the edges of the track, especially, it can be hard to gauge where your ship thingy is; I've crashed or fallen off the track numerous times when I thought I was correctly in position. I think a higher and further-back camera angle would have been a better choice for the game.
Graphics are simple, but do the job. Music is pretty good; I think I even recognised an instrumental version of a popular song or two in there, but I may have been mistaken.
So, do i recommend this game? Yes, if you can pick it up on sale or in a bundle for the right price. It should keep you entertained for a couple of hours, at least.

Castle of Illusion is a really fun platform game. It's all out running, jumping, stomping your enemies, swinging, swimming, the usual. You collect diamonds along the way to unlock the subsequent levels. You don't need anywhere near the 800 possible diamonds to proceed, however. More diamonds, chili peppers, statues, and playing cards unlock costumes and really bland concept art as paintings in the castle.
The story is a traditional Disney fairy tale. Mickey and Minnie are in love. The witch captures Minnie. Mickey goes to save the day. The narration reads like it's from a child's storybook. It's nothing that will blow your mind, but if you love Disney, you'll enjoy the story. Mickey and the other characters sound great, exactly like you'd expect them to, though their dialogue is limited.
The graphics update for this game is phenomenal. It's gorgeous artwork in the traditional Disney style.
Level design is exceptional, reminding me of the charm of games on the original Nintendo and Genesis systems. Each level has a theme and all the obstacles fit well within the theme.
At times the game makes you move quickly as platformers traditionally do and you need to make quick reactions as the floors fall out from under you. It does feel like a bit of a memorize and repeat formula at times and can be a bit frustrating if the checkpoint is a bit further back.
Boss battles are unique each time, as the various monsters have different themed attack patterns. The forest tree boss rolls like a log, the toy world boss is a jack in the box that jumps around and tosses a spring-loaded boxing glove your way, etc.
The controls are very simple and worked perfectly on the XBOX controller for Windows. I would have liked an option to pan the camera to look around the immediate area for hidden collectables (as that is a significant part of the game), but it's not that big of a deal. Sometimes I would just make a jump to see what I could find. A few times it paid off. Other times, I fell into the abyss. Once I couldn't see what was on a platform I needed to jump to and a bookworm bit me. I think that was just a random glitch though because that area didn't have the same problem again. I never had any other technical concerns about the game. It's a rock-solid game.
Sometimes, the game switches to more of a 3D perspective instead of side-scrolling. It's rarely used. You can play an entire level with one camera style and suddenly the boss is in 3D mode, so that can be a bit counter-intuitive. It's slightly challenging to judge the depth of your jumps in this mode, but it's not that big of a deal.
I would recommend this game, but not at the $15 price point. It only takes about 2 hours to complete the story. Then you can repeat the levels of your choosing any time you want as time trials. Combined with a small system of collectibles, the game does present some replay value, though the collectible rewards aren't really that exciting.

I loved this game on the Mega Drive when I was young and still play it today. If you've never played it before it's a linear 2.5D platformer with some 3D sections, starring Mickey Mouse in all his cartoon glory. This update sticks fairly faithfully to the original, there are a few minor additions and re-imaginings of sections which make use of the 3D environment (the final boss is a good example of this). The controls are smooth, the music is great and the graphics are beautiful - the levels look like scenes painted in a particularly well-illustrated storybook, which is very much what the game is. It's not a long or particularly difficult game, bear in mind the original can be completed in about 20 minutes and I played this to 100% completion in a few hours. The replay value is the same as the original, this is the sort of game you pull off the shelf from time to time to while away an hour or two. Definitely worth snapping up when on sale.

I just can't recommend this. I really, really wanted to like it. I love the wild west, I love supernatural, and I love tactical, but this game is just too confused for its own good.
As others have said, everything is divided in scenarios. Unfortunately, the scenarios are short (1-2 hours), so just as you really get rolling and interested in it, it ends. Then nothing you did in the previous ones carry over. The cool guns? The characters? The snazzy equipment? Were you buying and using alcohol to raise your characters Max HP? None of that matters. 1-2 hours and you start from scratch.
The other problem with starting from scratch is by Scenario 3, I just didn't care anymore. The characters disappear, the plot is jumbled and confusing (scenario 1 is you as a miner fighting cowboys, scenario 2 is you as ghost rider fighting demons - I'm not joking), and it just takes away all enjoyment when you know none of it matters.
The luck system is also a pretty huge failure, as it makes it nearly impossible to figure out when you can hit. It might say you have a 60% chance, but I tested this 10 times against one enemy, and I missed every time. Luck will ultimately decide whether or not you hit.
You also can't take back moves, so you if you accidentally click a space, there goes your character, walking to their death.    As a huge fan of tactical games, they really took out a lot of the tactical things and strategy. They could have done a lot with medium, short, and long range guns and party members that excel at them and making you fight a variety of enemies with specialities. Ultimately, nearly everyone gets a six-shooter and a longer range gun and it doesn't matter. Why is my shotgun better at hitting a guy 12 spaces away than my pistol? I have no idea. The game said so.
The final nail in the coffin is that each scenario has its own gimmick, but those gimmicks are the ENTIRE scenario. So scenario 1 is all about gold mining (which is pointless, you discover. I had 1300 gold at the end of it with nothing to spend it on and none of it transferred). Scenario 2 is just about ruthlessly murdering people, and Scenario 3 is... a trading game. Yes. It's a trading game. You need to buy goods from one store at a low price and sell them at a higher price later. Also the game suddenly introduces a hunger mechanic for no reason.
I can't emphasize enough how confusing and frustrating this is for a player. I liked being a miner - I really did - and just as I got used to it, it changed. Then I was a spirit of vengeance - okay, complete 180, but I went with it. Then a trading sim? That isn't what I signed up for, and it not only wasn't what I wanted, it was really poorly done. It wasn't intuitive how to figure out prices, who to sell them to, or when.
A great idea gone completely to waste.

The game tells a decent story, but its core mechanic (manipulating time) is bugged to♥♥♥♥♥♥ and it doesn't seem like the devs have done much to try to fix it. I've had to replay large chunks of boring repeated dialogue because the thing that is supposed to make this an innovative game broke the game and forced me to reload to the checkpoint.
Given how easy it is for the game to lock up in a rewind like that. I eventually started wincing my way through dialogue heavy sections, hoping every rewind or skip wouldn't suddenly force me to restart what I was doing.
Outside of that, well, the story is really well done, except this rather nagging undertone of misandry. Now, don't get me wrong, turnabout is fairplay, and if it were just a matter of having male characters relegated to the background while female characters played a more complex role in the storytelling, I'd be all for it. It's not like women haven't played second stringers in well-made games for long enough.
[Warning: Potential Spoilers]
Hell, most of the male characters were even given complex reasons for what they did (except maybe the primary villain, which is fine, villainous villains are good). I almost forgave it until a nightmare sequence at the end in which pretty much the entire male cast is turned into a evil caricature, hunting down Max in a bit of annoying stealth segment. This might have been fine, except not even the ♥♥♥♥♥y, prep girl is included as one of these taunting, villainous threateners, eschewed instead for male characters who were not nearly as antagonistic. This whole section just seems to solidify this message that ultimately, no matter how redeemable, women should embrace their trust issues because all men are potential threats. That's just not conducive to the message that much of the rest of the game seems to want to send, which is that even truly horrible people probably have a reason for being that way, and communication and empathy are the way to deal with them.
[Potential Spoilers Ended.]
On top of that, the game plays all around these progressive themes, but it feels like it just won't commit to letting the main heroines do anything more than play at romantic feelings, even when it's clear there's more there (and the metaphors about how the closet used to be their favourite hiding spot as kids... seems that hasn't really changed...) It feels like they were either afraid to commit or so afraid of fanservice that they allowed the audience's presence dictate whether the heroines could actually have a relationship or not. Ultimately, given it means another piece of media dancing around having openly gay characters, I'd say it was a poor choice on the dev's part.
Still, I honestly want to recommend the game, because other than a few sticking points, it has a great story, and Max's choices really do seem to matter. That said, if there was a 'Mixed Review' option, I'd give it that, but since I have to go thumbs up or thumbs down, I have to instead err on the side of thumbs down due in large part to the glaring technical flaws that 2 years later have not been addressed. I would still recommend watching a Let's Play or longplay of the game, or a trying it out if you have the patience for some rather irritating bugs.

From the music to the artwork, the story to the characters, Dischan released one hell of a VN. Although short, this game was very immersive and felt quite polished for an episodic work.
The story lasted only about an hour and a half on fast text speed (it would take a bit longer if you read at a slower pace), but it was a compelling and interesting idea about a futuristic society. What really caught me was the parallels between this game and Steins;Gate about the idea of time and space.
The music was composed impeccably and every use of each song fit well with the events of the story. It's a great soundtrack to listen to as a standalone as well, and it is provided free, absolutely free, with the game in the game folder. Big props to CombatPlayer for their quality work.
The artwork had a lot of detail and depicted each scene exquisitely, which really helped with putting yourself into the setting of the story. It also looks very cleanly and neatly done, with a nice mix of colors to please the eyes. Some quality VNs don't have the most impressive of artwork; however, this one won't let you down.
Character development, although it throws you in somewhat quickly, is done rather well. You will get to know mainly three characters with the focus being on two of the tree - Winter and Cyrus. This episode follows them through a good 90% of the game, with Waverly (Winter's roommate) being introduced near the end, where episode 2 is supposed to begin. However, you get a good sense of Waverly at this point before episode 2. Other characters get introduced, but they only appear with very minor roles and nearly no detail about them - yet.
I'd love to see the next episode of this series be released, and it was definitely worth the few bucks spent to enjoy the few hours of story and many hours of OST listening.

I really wanted to like this game, and I tried really hard to do so. But in the end its numerous flaws were too pungent to ignore:
1) A really dumb combat system. Now don't get me wrong, there are tactics involved, mainly dealing with the positioning of your characters in such a way as to avoid friendly fire. But that's about it. The rest of it is just standing in open ground, and plugging and/or slashing away at the nearest target.
Yes there is a smattering of "cover" here and there you can shield yourself from fire with, but animals and melee units are able to pretty much run up to you in one turn with impunity, and attack you regardless. And they always seem to run up to you in such a way as to place your other characters in the line of fire, necessitating you to move away to avoid friendly fire.
So yeah, there are "tactics" here, an elaborate dance where you move your guys around the map in such a way as to shoot the enemy without shooting your teammates in the back. Ie, tactics that bear no resemblance to combat tactics in real life.
2) The artwork is just cheap, horrible and amateurish. And some of the portraits don't match the character descriptions, and many are reused for other characters, just simply destroying game immersion. For a $40 buck game, the consumer deserves better.
3) The number of times you have to go back to a previous save because you accidentally triggered combat with friendly NPCs is utterly frustrating, and just indicative of a terrible design.

I really want to recommend this game - the first couple of hours were very enjoyable, the Director's Cut improvements actually seem to have fixed many of the original issues...but it's STILL an unfinished game, even after forever in Kickstarter and a 'final' edition. It's basically a game where the developers got most of the way through, then just thought 'sod it, that'll do'. It's effectively broken in most of the sidequests, and unbelievably frustrating for the rest. Buy it in a sale for a fiver - don't spend any more on it.
Pretty much every sidequest is bugged so you can't complete fully. The interface means you'll frequently be unable to target enemies, even when in open ground. Dialouge is more often than not nonsensical. There's what initally seem trivial but turn into mindbending frustrating issues with the inventory - basic stuff like being unable to sort by weight or value, or sell all items in a stack, or other basic things that were sorted in RPGs decades ago. The map and journal are aggressively unhelpful. You'll be forced into quicksaving every couple of minutes as the companion AI is so bad, and you can so easily unintentionally ruin a quest due to the terrible dialogue options. Tedious and repetitve 'random encounters' (which are anything but) on the world map make travelling a chore. There's a total lack of polish throughout (for example, every hat, say a 'metal helmet', has a stetson model. None of the clothing options display on your character model. Your guns don't line up properly. Item descriptions are frequently missing or half finished).
Most of these complaints may sound trivial, and I have never played the original so may be missing any familiary or tolerance for the interface others may have, but the irritaions quickly add up and end up destroying any form of immersion. There's the core of a very good game in here, but it's just too frustratingly unfinished to recommend, sadly.

This is how you kill a franchise.
[Edit]
To clarify, my biggest complaint(s) with regards to this game is not so much the pay to 'succeed system' that monolith has implemented. No, my largest criticisms are resereved for monolith's lack of thorough playtesting that has resulted in an unpolished and hardly functional combat system that shouldn't have made it past early acces before being released for public sale.  Of the many problems that need to be addressed, here are a few that require immediate attention;
- Input command lag
Judging by the volume of users with high end gaming platforms that are complaining of the same thing, it seems that this is independant of hardware inadequacies.  This problem is inherantly game breaking as much of the story missions require players to repond to precision combat prompts to defeat enemies.  Naturally, this is one of the most frusterating as the lag between pushing the button and the response often means that the window for the desired effect has long since passed often resulting in death/last stand.
- Geographical features and environmental obstacles
If there was ever any evidence that monolith didn't playtest SoW enough it would be this.  Much of the extra 'things' (tables, broken barrels, corpses, boxes. rubble, stumps, forges, etc.) that serve no other function than aesthetics (that I'll hereby refer to as 'flair') will get your character stalled, staggered, or completely stuck thus interupting the flow of combat and outright getting oneself killed or discovered if in stealth.  This is especially annoying if grinding through a story mission or trying desperately to recruit/kill a hard-won enemy captain.  But what's even more annoying is that these nonfunctional environmental objects are EVERYWHERE.  I can only assume that the developers wanted to make the geographical locations in mordor all the more immersive by adding such flair.  Unfortunately, these all seem to provide a direct hindrance to the playability of the game.  Indeed, the very way these unintentional obstacles are littered haphazardly across the whole damn world makes me think that they were all added in as a sort of after thought.  It doesnt work.  In a game where the environment is to be utilized to achieve victory over the enemy, the extra flair is simply intolerable and should't be implemented. Period.  The reason for this is that this game is inherantly imprecise due to the constraints of the controller, volume/space of immediate environment, number of enemies, and input lag.  By comparison, the developers of the first game seemed to understand this all too well.  Seriously, if you reading this and own both of these titles, do a side by side comparison.  Shadow of mordor is virtually barebones and because of this is much easier to navigate through- even when surrounded by a large volume of enemies.
- Physical space constraints are a bigger problem than most realize.
Not surprisingly, the constraints of physical space for the character to operate in and interact with drastically limit the player's potential and flow when navigating through fortresses or outposts.  Readers who have have had the unfortunate experience of sprinting through/down narrow corridors only to have Talion spontaneously leap into a wall or proceed to parkour over an entire building know what I'm talking about.  It's time consuming and difficult to correct if being pursued by an angry mob of enemies- doubly so if on a mount.  Again, compared to SoM, this wasn't a very large problem- mostly due to the fact that not a lot of the missions were dependant on Talion lurking in areas with so many walls.  This problem really f*cks with the camera in SoW
- Bugs.
The online pitfights and sieges are understandably wonky considering how long this game has been on the market.  The biggest complaint from the community seems to be that the algorithm for pitfights will often pair orcs who aren't anywhere near comparable in stats and level which results in a one sided victory.  Another is that some orcs won't even attack and only taunt until they are killed. The list is long.
The most noticiable and common bugs include; spontaneously teleporting to other parts of the map when branding caragors in battle, warchiefs not displaying rank (common/epic/legendary), attacking different targets than the one that is highlighted when doing ariel stealth attacks (this happens way too much to even attempt ariel stealth with any expected outcome), the game completely ignoring or not registering input commands, etc.
- Story, tutorial, & word puzzles.
If not everything else, this is what I have the least tolerance for in this game.  As others have said, the story is not engaging and the tutorial is far too long.  Solving Ithildin poems?  What the hell are you thinking, Monolith? Did you forget what kind of game you were making?
- Ethics & integrity
Shady and twisted, Monolith.  Doubly so for Time Warner (albeit, expected).  Every other complaint I have can be corrected and has the potential to improve the game.  This one, however, is irredeemable.  For shame.

Have you ever imagined, what lies above us, far in the stars? Have you ever imagined how it is like to pilot a rocket, conquer and colonize new worlds and moons? Have you ever dreamed of being in control of a great city-station on orbit of a gas giant? Have you ever thought of murdering every single one of the colonist on said city-station by re-directing them into the gas giant?
Kerbal Space Program does all that. Seriously. Never have I seen such a deep developed game, even in it's alpha-stage (!)
First and foremost, you get a new Kerbol-system, being about 6x times smaller version of our own Solar system. The pilots, your astronauts are little, cute green aliens named Kerbals. Some of them are badass, like Jebediah, and some are not. All they strive for is a great adventure - and it's your job to provide them that, either by leaving them stranded on the orbit or crash-landing them on Eve (Venus in-game), or anything else your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mass-murdering mind can come up with.
As the time of writing i spent 180 hours in the game and I still haven't found my way outside Kerbin and it's moons - The learning curve is rather high, but fortunately there are so many cool people on the Kerbal forums who are more than happy to help you.
Another thing to note is that this game has such a great modding potential - tracks, weapons, new engines, interstellar-♥♥♥♥ery, Alcubierre drives, FTL drives, new star systems. The list goes on and on.
This game actually inspired me to get interested in astrophysics. God i love this game. 10/10. It's lovely.

I found the public consensus to be spot on with this one, in regards to the drastic differences in quality between both halves. The first act is a total tour-de-force, with puzzles that made sense and served the plot, compelling characterizations, and an intriguing plot that successfully mashes up beautiful sci-fi and fantasy worlds. The second act comes across as rushed by comparison, re-using the first act's areas and assets almost the whole way through, with puzzles that grow increasingly more frustrating as an interesting plot becomes suddenly incoherent.
So, first act is great - a high-production masterpiece of the form that truly encapsulates everything great about the genre. Second act by comparison feels lazy and falls short, with illogical "try combining everything with everything" puzzles throughout that exemplify everything that turns people off from the genre. Ignoring kickstarter scandals and all that and just looking at the game as a whole, I think it can be said that by the start of the game's standards, the back half is objectively mediocre.
But, that first Act is a truly great piece of adventure gaming, so I have to recommend this. Know that the game doesn't maintain it's quality throughout, but the things that work here really work, and I'll definitely remember the best setpieces of this game for a long time to come. Imagine if Grim Fandango progressed in reverse - starting with the End Of The World and Rubacava, and ending in the comparatively tiny Petrified Forest with all it's cryptic puzzles. It would still be an extremely memorable game, just one with pacing problems and a bad ending - which is exactly what Broken Age is.

In this game, you move a spaceship left and right as it automatically scrolls forward, avoiding obstacles as you progress. It's a simple premise, and Avoid: Sensory Overload really isn't breaking any new ground. But what begins as a rather mediocre addition to the pile of retro-inspired games available on Steam quite rapidly develops into one of the toughest games in your library, and what's more, it's addictive. At advanced levels, the game's pace is breakneck, and the course is littered with pitfalls and obstacles. Leagues harder than comparable titles like Audiosurf, Avoid: Sensory Overload is a no B.S. test of skill and reaction time. Your average gamer probably won't make it through the Medium levels, and most of us probably won't make it through the Hard levels. Even if you're the kind of Ulillillia tier savant it takes to make it through Extreme difficulty, you can pile on a fresh challenge by playing the Endless mode for a randomly-generated infinite run. At the fair price of $5, Avoid: Sensory Overload scratches the itch for a simple game at both extremes: It's fun enough to pick up and play for a quick session, and difficult enough to provide a challenge in the long term.

Basically, if you want a platformer that's made the way that platformers USED to be, go for this.

There's very little to do rather than move a left analog stick and press a button or two. Yet, the "Disney-ness" of Disney's graphics - especially Mickey Mouse himself, who has lost none of his charm over the years - as well as the story of the game told through a magical bodiless narrator really add to the whole storybook feel of this game. And it truly does feel like a storybook at times. The voice actor for Mizrabel definitely played her part very well. I do wish there was a tad bit more replayability rather than having the existing levels simply timed, or collecting all of the gems. Additionally, I dislike how third parties have to solve the game's issues concerning 30fps and failure to fully support high resolutions, but these are more minor complaints that far too many people have brought up.  All in all, Castle of Illusion was a nice return to classical gameplay of olden years that I never enjoyed as a kid. I would suggest this to any child gamer, as well as any adult who enjoys games with charm like this every once in a while.

Dysfunctional Systems is a visual novel with dialogue choices that affect your ending.  There is one ending to the first episode but your choice(s) during the half-way point affects all the dialogue in the entire second half
.  There's also no voices, which can be bad for people like me who have poor reading comprehension.  That's all the negative aspects out of the way.
In DS, you will enjoy an extremely well-written script.  With a great deal of backstory and detail, the universe is very believable and makes it a pleasure to immerse yourself within the world and its inhabitants.  Even with my reading comprehension issues, I found myself focusing all my attention to understand the remarkably deep story.  The characters are interesting and complex to the point where you won't find any stereotypes that you may have grown accustomed to.  The art in its own merit may not stand out, but when coupled with many others of the same genre, it definitely rises up and stands out from the common crowd.  A lot of the music is forgettable, and you may not want to listen to it in your car or on an iPod.  But every track seems to harmonize with the story and situations on-screen.  The music is immensely atmospheric and envelops the reader in the narrative.
The greatest strength in this story is the setting.  It is so very interesting that you will eat it up and ask for more.  I can only hope that development for the second episode will eventually begin so that this story can continue.

This game is one of THE best visual novels I've ever played/read. It features decisions you have to make, even when you don't want to do them at all. As like other visual novels, the choices affect your character in different ways. Having slugged it out for a while with this game, I can safely say that it was a massive disappointment and in no way, shape, or form that it is a true Mafia game. The fact that it tries to ride the coattails of what a Mafia game is...is really disheartening.
The gunplay is decent but it lacks any form of kick, so most of the time you will just breeze through enemies like they are made of paper.
This could have been counteracted by actually intelligent enemy AI, but they might be dumbest in a game I have ever seen. Too many times have I seen them walk into traps too easily, or not see their dead friend's body as I was sneaking around, only to notice the body as they're about to step on it. The simple idea of them throwing grenades is too much for them as they have to announce they're throwing a frag and take three seconds to expose themselves and pull the pin in front of you. Then there are the times when they just rush you in hopes of actually doing anything to you but end up getting mowed down by your weaponry, and much to my surprise they will all do this in spite of losing lots of men this way.
The story reminds me of Mafia 2 in the sense of a bland premise but kept up with a few interesting set pieces and a few good missions. Granted it tries REALLY HARD at making everyone you go up against as racist as they can be, which in my opinion is forcing it just a little too much, even though this is a city based in the South. Every build up to a district's takeover is done the exact same way, with very little in terms of variety and it ends up getting boring well before you get halfway through. The actual confrontations with the lieutenants and capos are decent but they're bogged down with all the boring stuff beforehand and are over way too quickly. All of that leads up to a rather lackluster finale in which you feel empty as you realize you played through all of that just to share a bottle of scotch and hold a single key/button.
The game isn't all bad, though. I found the motion capture and facial expressions (MOST of them, anyway...) to be fine. Voice acting is above average; I think it could have been done better, but it was fine for the most part.  The setting was nicely set up despite how empty it really felt. As always this review is just my own opinion and what I think about this game. If you notice any mistakes I made (apart from grammar mistakes) feel free to report them in the comments.
Did you ever read a Stephen King novel in your life? No? Then you should. Yes? Then some aspects of this games story may remind you of his works. The story focuses on writer and husband Alan Wake, who after a severe writer's block decided to leave the bustling city for a long holiday with his wife Alice. Together they visit the small town of Bright Falls, with its old and rural look, including odd townfolk. Telling any more about the story would (in my mind) spoil it for you, just know that things soon take a dark and mysterious turn, all the while letting the player guess about what is really happening until the end. This and the plot twists throughout the game, combined with a storytelling like you would read a good book make for one of the best stories I've ever encountered.
Again, actually telling you about the gameplay would spoil some of the story for you, so this will be rather short. The combat system and view is third-person. You get various weapons, like a revolver or a hunting rifle, which you will need to combine with the light of your flashlight to fight off your enemies and make it through each chapter. Darkness and light also play an important role, both story and gameplay wise, since light serves as protection from the dark and even heal Alan. While this system is pretty fun at first, it might get rather boring for you after some time, even though the game gives you new stuff if you progress. For the collectors among you, there are different things to collect, like Coffee Thermoses (ever writers friend) and manuscript pages, which tell part of the story. The levels might sometimes feel repetetive (lots of forests) and linear, but deliver a creepy and rustic atmosphere.
Alan Wake was made in 2010, but even then the graphics seemed a bit outdated. Some of the textures seem a bit unsharp or muddy. The faces could be a bit more detailed. But what is really impressive is the way the game plays with light effects combined with darkness. Your flashlight, a small light pole in the distance, or even light from a window feel somehow alive and give the player a feeling of safety. The game also runs smoothly and without problems, at least in my experience.
Never in my life would I have thought that a video game would introduce me to a band that I would listen to even years after. Alan Wake did exactly that. The "Poets of the Fall", or "Old Gods of Asgard" as they are called in-game, are a great and underappreciated Alternative Rock band with a charm like no other. Working together closely with Remedy (Alan Wakes developer), they brought forth songs like "Children of the Elder God" or "The Poet and the Muse, which fit great into the setting and story. On the other hand and more on the soundtrack side is composer Petri Alanko, who captures the atmosphere and feeling of Alan Wake perfectly with his genius tracks.
Depending on how much you explore and how fast and skilled you are, the game may take about 10-20 hours, 25-30 for completionists. The two DLCs offer about 2 extra hours each. The game also leaves some manuscript pages unobtainable while playing for the first time, these can only be collected in Nightmare mode. Since the game itsself is rather linear, the time won't strech too far. (I've played through it multiple times though, since its one of my favourites.
None.
Alan Wake is a third-person mystery thriller that scores with an incredible story and soundtrack, that captures the hearts of those who play it. Even if some of the graphic features lack in looks and the gameplay is not too special, these things are not what make Alan Wake one of my all-time favourites. A greatly underestimated and overlooked game, which rewards anyone who loves a good story, well written characters and coffee thermoses.

TL;DR - Don't spend money on this game, especially if you play on multiple devices, or care about your save data syncing correctly.
Fallout Shelter is worth checking out for the first time, or returning to if you haven't played since it initially launched on mobile (lots of interesting new depth with crafting and quests).
The fun just ended for me, though. Lost a week's worth of progress due to Steam Cloud Save shenanigans (booted up a laptop I'd left the game running on over a week ago). The game generates 1 backup save that I found after digging for a while, but it was overwritten before I realized what had happened. Lost over a week's worth of progress.
Syncing is destructive with no regard for time spent in game. There's no confirmation/indication that you're stomping local saves with cloud saves.
I've written cloud save integration, for Unity games even. I know the Steam Cloud API is garbage, but you work around it by building redundancy into your local saves, then sync the whole lot of those, and implement your own UI to guide users through reconciling cloud vs. local data.
I'm flabbergasted that you're taking money from people with such a terrible cloud save solution in the game. Especially where redeemed purchases can be affected.

I can't recommend this game, it's a big let down from InXile, I backed both Wasteland 2 and Numenera and it's clearly the last time they'll get my money.
I don't understand the hype behind this game, it represents a lot of things that are wrong in this industry, it was marketed as a Fallout 1/2 revival, but it's as close from these games as Call of Duty would be from Super Mario.
Everything seems shallow and poorly executed, and more importantly far from Fargo's flamboyant speeches about the virtues of old school games. Come on man, really? I won't blame him, many amazing things happened because of him during his time at Interplay. But his crew at InXile is definitely not of the same caliber as the one from Interplay/Black Isle.
What bugs me the most are these people comparing this game to Fallout 1 & 2, I played them both hundreds of hours and I keep re-installing them every year or so. People making the comparison clearly have no idea what they're talking about. No, it's absolutely not the same team responsible for these games who's behind the development of Wasteland 2 (Jason Anderson has left InXile before the start of the development, Tim Cain and Leonard Boyarsky aren't InXile employees). Wasteland 2 should be compared with Neverwinter Nights (which I hate for the same reasons - except Neverwinter Nights came with a top-notch editor).
Here's the short version:
- Attributes, skills and mechanics are broken (wtf is "toaster"?). Where Fallout allowed so many ways to solve a problem and literally "roleplay" through the game, Wasteland is just a linear succession of areas with dull fights against weirdly scripted enemies. My favourite part is this "out of control" mechanic, when your allies start moving around on their own during a fight and do the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ moves possible (most of the time it ends in them getting killed). Apparently it can be fixed with "leadership". Why bother upgrading this skill just so your allies stop acting stupidly? Game design is lacking and not up to its predecessors (a shame).
- Very low production value, I won't talk about the graphics, it would be like making fun of a disabled kid. Heard they bought many 3D assets from the unity store, 5$ for a set of rocks, is that how you built your game?
- In Fallout, dialogs and actions could change the course of the game. In wasteland 2, there's barely any choice to make and they have little to no impact onto the game. There's a lot of text, great. I won't say it's pointless, but it's uninspired. Cliche post-apo. By the way, did they have to copy Fallout Tactics story arc?
- Even Mark Morgan's music sounds like it got bored.
- No immersion. Okay it's a post-apo setting, but why does it all feel generic, lifeless and dead? Polishing such a large and complex world requires time and talent, clearly InXile had none of these.
My review sounds bitter, but the game isn't totally bland and pointless, I guess some people might enjoy it
Had a lot of expectations about it, I just feel they didn't take it seriously, or just the development team didn't have the right amount of time and talent for such an ambitious project.
Good bye and good luck InXile.

TL;DR : Game can be fun at times and if you are not bothered by grindy activities. Lots of improvements in several game systems compared to Shadow of Mordor, but still lacks polish in some areas. Recommended, but do not buy at full price, wait for a sale.
The story isn't excellent though there are some interesting moments and a few surprises here and there, the combat system is adequate without bringing anything of note although the mounted combat has been improved since the first game and is now a viable choice, the soundtrack hasn't much changed since the first game but remains enjoyable - though  the game could have profited from more tracks similar to the main menu theme -, and you'll spend a lot of time looking for, and slaying, Uruks and Ologs in order to get the one Follower that'll help you progress through the game. All-in-all, the game is fun and enjoyable for a few dozen hours if you really want to see all the Nemesis system has to offer.
Obviously, the lootboxes system was a mistake. Rather than using a pseudo-random system to get loot and followers, a crafting system in which the player has at least a minimum of influence on the potential outcome would have been a much fairer choice. On the subject of crafting, the game immensely lacks a full-fledged "Orc creator" allowing the player to choose the various traits, the appearance and defining characteristics of an Uruk in order to truly create the perfect Orc. This kind of system could be one worth spending huge swathes of mirian for.
End disclaimer : This review has been rushed in order for me to get my Autumn 2017 SASC badge.

Quite a fun game. I offers 2 gameplay modes, one is a standard FPS like mode where you play as one of the human squad members, and the other as one of th ealines. Each one of the factions (human/alien) has its own different unit types, and heavy units. The second mode is the commander mode in which only one player plays the game in a top down view, simmilar to Real Time Strategies. The commander can place "building blueprints", which then the team can construct, in order to gain additional upgrades (ammo/armor and so forth), There are additional upgrades/buildings that let the teams build/construct their ultimate units - a big mech, and a huge rhino like alien. The commander can also drop ammo and health packs for his troops (if he has enough resources), that aer gained by expansing the team's control over the map and building harvesters. The play style of both aliens and humans are bit diffrent. While the humans favor conventional guns and stationary projectile turrets, the aliens usually domiinate in up close meely combat...and flying units.
Overall this game is rather enjoyable, and offers a nice change of pace. If you get bored of the FPS portion, you can play as a commander, and get into the strategic view. The community seems to work rather well together, reminiscent of the old days BF2 (real team play) gameplay, where people support one another, and have helpful roles.

Actual Review:
The Music
wear on you.
There are 4 different Tracks to progress down, each with their own visual and musical themes.
Each of those Tracks has 4 different Tiers (difficulties), each with 8 Levels;
Each subsequent Level in a Tier adds to how far through the musical track you get through -
Each Level within the Tiers is different from the last, though they appear to be static (i.e. you can memorize the layout).
The different Tiers within the same Track have different Music to accompany them.
Tracks:
===Electronic: The advertised image is the Electronic track; the cylinder you're shooting through appears to surround a visualizer, reacting to the Music. Avoid sets of Orbs bouncing between two points.
===Minimal: The obstacles pulse to the Music. Avoid Rival Ships that fly down the Track with you.
===Laserdance: A pulsating corona within the center of the Track responds to the Music. The obstacles are the same color as the collectibles. Therefore, the only thing to (")avoid(") is Sliding Platforms.
===Synthrock: Another pulsating corona (though to a lesser extent). The Tracks are much more, er, angular (diagonally inclined). Avoid Spike Traps.
Mind that these summaries are only from the first (and sometimes second) Tiers; I've no doubt that with each subsequent Tier, more obstacles and features will be implemented.
You can customize the color scheme of your ship.
You can play with keyboard, controller and even the mouse - the only controls are "Move Left; Move Right."
Keyboard, of course, offers better responsiveness.
Mouse seems to allow your ship to move slightly faster, at the loss of some precision.
Have yet to try controller.
There are different (")power-ups(") to collect, such as a Shield that allows you to survive one collision, a "Drop" that lowers all obstacles in your line of sight, a [unknown] that fills the gaps in your path for a(n extremely) short period of time. These power-ups are Track specific.
If you wish to chill while being stressed: Avoid Sensory Overload.
The overall feel of the game is the most relaxing (rave-induced) trip you'll ever experience; the (")checkpoints(") - which aren't really, as any time you crash, you'll respawn a little ways before then, invincible for a few moments - are points at which the speed of things is increased. Break out in a stress-induced sweat while calm. How strange.
I was torn between this and Race the Sun.
I don't regret my decision.
(I got Race the Sun in a Bundle soon after; it is amazing too, in its own right - hardly comparable to Avoid, except in that you're flying down a track.)
*EDIT*: Were it not for the (almost) assaulting visuals, I would argue that this game should've been called "Muscle Memory Trainer." It claims reflexes are necessary; I claimed "you can memorize the layout [of the tracks]."
False; your first several runs will be to get a feel for the tracks; your golden runs will be to put that muscle memory (which I guess could be called "reflexes," at first) to use.
This is not necessarily a criticism, I will keep coming back to the game when I'm pondering what other game to play.
Just. Fair warning.
Muscle Memory Trainer WHILE Avoid(ing) Sensory Overload.
Also: There is an Endless Mode on each of the Tracks with different difficulty levels; Leaderboards. I'm fairly certain that the Endless Mode is randomly generated; it is here that reflexes are actually necessary, *nodnod*.
Also: I think the music is not necessarily bound to a certain Level/Track/whatever; it might be random what music plays when. Maybe.

Ok, so I'm usually a criticize first and compliment by omission kind of guy. In other words, if I never shut up about how the wallpaper in your house makes me want to stab my eyes out lest they see it again, you can assume the plumbing was functional. But "Hard West" breaks my line of thinking. There are a few criticisms, but all of that pales in comparison to the great quality of the game. I was hoping for wild west XCOM. And I certainly got that, but it was jumbled in the middle of a genuinely unique and great RPG in the exact style of "Deadlands" an RPG in the savage worlds system. The Story Elements genuinely make this game fun. Maybe not an original world since it's on the coattails of the Savage worlds game. But so what? Game of Thrones ripped of Tolkien, and they're taking that copy/paste to the bank. The game is enjoyable, and full of heart. People put art and inspiration into this game. And that goes a long way. If there was any complaint (which with me, there must) it'd be that the UI could use a few missing features like a "next character" button. Or a better scroll wheel on the shopping menu. But that's like complaining about the flavor soup served in the white house kitchen. Surely if that matters, you've missed the point.

Mafia III was my most anticipated game in 2016, I've played both Mafia I and II and enjoyed them so much that the Mafia franchise became my most favorite franchise to date. However I do feel like this installment of the series is the one that I enjoyed the least, it doesn't mean that I thought it was bad, not at all, but it didn't click with me as much as the previous two games did, let me mark some points.
The game starts of fantastically, throwing you right into the story and putting you on the edge of your seat. The cutscenes, lip syncing and voice acting is through the roof, along with the old fashioned documentary style kind of tell telling. It makes the story so incredibly exciting and grasping. However I do feel like the developers really wanted to focus more on the cutscenes and story telling than the actual gameplay.
Don't get wrong, the gameplay has great elements, the shooting is satisfying, the driving is fantastic (it even has two styles of driving which you can select in the options menu) and the executions are exhilarating. The combat in general is great in this game, no doubt about it.
Thing is, the gameplay is EXTREMELY repetitive, and why is that? Well, your main mission is to try and take over the city of New Bordeaux (fictional New Orleans) district by district. There are nine districts which you take over. Each district has two rackets that you need to take over first in order to get in control of the whole district. How you can take over a racket is simple, you do a certain amount of damage to that racket, so that the income decreases. When the income reaches $0, the boss of that racket comes out, which you have to kill in order to take over the racket. You can decrease the income by destroying objects, interrogating people and killing prime members in the racket.
This is where it gets repetitive, because there is no variation at all when it comes to taking over the district, it follows the same damn pallet everytime, which eventually makes it a chore to continue the story. At one point it was so bad that I had to take a break for a few days to continue, since it really became a chore which I didn't enjoy anymore.
When you killed both bosses in the rackets, you unlock a story mission, which are amazingly good. It's such a shame that the side activities and overtaking rackets are so repetitive and boring, since it completely overshadows the awesome story missions this game has. It's almost if the game lets you grind just so you get rewarded with a story mission.
I also want to bring up the soundtrack, which is fantastic! It was so great to listen to CCR, Johnny Cash, Steppenwolf etc etc. It was so good that sometimes when I arrived at my destination, I just waited in my car until the song was over, something I haven't done in a long time in a game. The game also has an original game score which suits every situation perfectly, may it be a stealthy or hectic situation. The game really scores points with the soundtrack for me.
The collectibles are also great in this game: Playboys, Vargas pinup paintings, communist propaganda posters, hot rod magazines and so on. They're really fun to collect.
One last complaint I have of this game is that it lacks so many great things that Mafia II had, like interactions with the environment, realistic police (other than the fact that police treats you different in certain districts, they don't do all that much) and mechanics with cars, like bringing them to a car mechanic, customizing them (which will get added later but it's something I would've liked in my first playthough) and fueling your car.
One last praise I want to give to this game, is that it emphasizes a lot on racism, which was very normal and common in the 60's. It really makes for an immersive experience and makes you feel what racism actually is, how it feels to be treated unfairly and differently, it's a nice touch to this game which I really appreciated.
Even with the repetitiveness of overtaking districts, I'm still recommending this game, it unfortunately didn't strike me as much as Mafia I and II, but it was still a great experience overall. The soundtrack, driving, shooting, dialogue and story are amazing. Hell, I even got to see some old familiar faces in this game, which was a great experience. Buy the game in a sale, then you'll get the most out of your money.

First of all, the metacritic review is off, yes. But the real score is not that high after adjusting it either.
First off, the problems I encountered right off the bat:
- Connecting to a game is hard, most lobbies are either full, or always stay in lobby mode. (On a side note, why do people make lobbies and never start a game is beyond me).
-More than half the time you do try to connect to a game, its a time out error.
Other issues:
-Collision detection is akin to  early 2000-era fps games. You know, when you'd hit a couple of pixels and the target gets a a set amount of damage?
-Small targets near impossible to hit, even when point blank. I'm not talking pin point accuracy, I'm talking a full shotgun blast at point blank range, the crosshair is on top of a compy, you fire... and no damage registers. The compy has no problems biting you all the while this happens.
- You steer with the mouse. Very un ergonomic, and not very useful when you need to do some maneuvering and ensure your vehicle gives a proper firing angle while avoiding running into the big dinosaurs (which will essentially chain combo your vehicles into oblivion).
- On a related note: if your vehicle is trapped against a wall (or any structure) and you need to get out, you better hope your exit point is not against it... as you'll see the getting out animation, the character hits the object, and you're magically in the seat you were again. Granted, this doesn"t happen often... no wait it does! It happens every time a dino hits your vehicle and you are sent flying to a place the developers never designed a vehicle to be positioned (hint: any place a dino can bump your vehicle to, that is not the ground).
- Annoying slow down every time the game considers a "great kill" has been made. Useless, and more often than not throw off your timing when fighting as a team.
When it works, it can be a rewarding experience. The problem is getting it to work.
On a side note, I have played the original, and other than a graphical overhaul, I see no difference, heck the other version let me connect at least.

A well-written visual novel which manages to (mostly) break away from all the tired romantic tropes and panty-shot fetishism which stereotype the genre; the setting is unique and compelling and the groundwork is laid for some interesting development in later chapters, it looks (or looked) like setting up to be a somewhat similar in structure to a Telltale style experience where the choices made branch out progressively as chapters progress; in this episode however the choices are few are far between, and heavily biased towards the earliest decision point in terms of quantity.
That said, there’s a lot to enjoy about the writing and the characters here; and if you don’t mind more reading than interacting then you’ll probably enjoy watching the well told story progress at a good pace. As a side note, the soundtrack (which can be all be streamed on Youtube) really is well above par, and honestly I would have been happy to pay $5 just for the mp3s alone. The same can be said for that ‘animated opening video’ that the blurb talks about which is a really well put together piece of art by itself and makes me think that the developers should be pitching their concept art and story as the basis of an anime series.
Unfortunately the audience hasn’t flocked to this title and harsh commercial realities have led to many of the team leaving Dyschan (including the chief Art director), so this is one story that you’ll probably have to generate an ending for in your own mind (or read fanfic). It’d be nice to see this find some success though; and it’s a great price for what it is.
