Update: I changed my review to not recommend in order to purposefully lower the rating of this game on Steam. Quite simply when I kickstarted this game, Brian Fargo liked to go on and on about how they wanted to get away from big Publisher models, always being on the hook to publishers just seeking profit. But then they have been going out and trying to force developers with complete success so far, to change the names of their games if it contains the word Wasteland.
You know its funny, because thats exactly something a publisher would do, they would throw money away pursuing these things instead of making games like Brian Fargo claimed thats what he wanted to do. Its understandable to engage in these legal matters when a game is intentionally trying to ape your stuff, but in every case the only similarity between titles, was the word Wasteland.
Have the courage to stand for something InXile, no one is going to try and USURP the Wasteland IP by making ♥♥♥♥♥♥ little indie games. I won't be sending you anymore of my money(unless you get the Fallout IP back and make Fallout games). So yeah, Never again.
Original, still true review below:
I have about 110 combined hours between Wasteland 2 Classic and the Director's Cut.
I backed this game on kickstarter and was pleased with Wasteland 2, to get the Director's Cut after for free was a huge bonus for me.
The game itself plays like a squad-based Fallout 1 and 2, but in its own 1980s style post-nuclear setting. The RPG elements are solid but the game is combat focused which I am happy for. You get a number of useable skills to to do quests with, find hidden objects and loot. There is a ton of flavor text everywhere you go which help adds to the immersion and feeling of the game which I love. The music is a perfect ambient style soundtrack which hits all the right notes and there is an ambient soundtrack for areas aswell to help add to that immersion.
There are tons of things to do in the wasteland and plenty to shoot aswell. Lots of weapons to choose from and different types of armors to wear. You can find clothing to dress your rangers up if you want, or will need to find clothing if you get it burnt off in combat!
I think if you enjoy squad based turn based combat, you'll like this game. If you enjoy post-apocalypse settings, you'll enjoy this game. If you like to read and use your imagination, you'll like this game.
If you liked Fallout 1 and 2, you will like this game.

As much as I played this game and reasonably enjoyed it, I have to give it a thumbs down for the following reasons:
- Absolutely NOT worth $30. I bought it on a 40%-off discount and still feel like I overpaid. The game is incredibly simple and there's not much in it.
- The mud is ridiculous. I guess the game is called "SPINTIRES", so it is honest at least. 90% of what you do in this game is drive slowly through unrealistically soggy mud. It is NOT a "offroad logging" simulator as the screenshots and videos try to imply. It is a "driving through mud during Noah's flood" simulator. There is no rainfall, yet most of the ground is soaked and never dries. There are no other drivers, yet most of the roads look like 50 trucks drove over them in the past 6 hours. Your trucks all must have sprinkler systems attached to the wheel wells, because even apparently-dry ground will quickly begin to deform if you drive on it too much. When you make a game that is 90% centered around mud physics, you could at least try to make it believable. People seem to like to claim that it's realistic, but no, sorry, it's not. Saying that the terrain deformation in this game is realistic is like saying that DayZ was realistic when it made you starve to death unless you ate something every hour. Because people get hungry in real life, right?! Realism!
- Camera controls are embarrassing. There is not even a first-person-view mode. All you get is some extremely cumbersome "over the shoulder" camera that awkwardly swaps shoulders and zooms itself in/out as you try to rotate it. They literally had to go out of their way to make the camera that bad. Making the gameplay as tedious as humanly possible just for the sake of it is one thing, but basic user interface features like camera control must make sense in order for your game to be good.
- No way to get out of your truck and examine the immediate area. This might seem like an odd request if you haven't played the game, but you'd be surprised how often you will desperately want to see the terrain/obstructions around you without having to actually drive your truck onto them. Even a limited-range free-flying camera would get the job done. Although, not if it spins around and does back-flips every time you try to move it, which is a legitimate concern when you consider their current camera implementation.
- The drama behind the developer/publisher that you can find in news posts about this game. Apparently, the publisher ousted the developer after he did all the work, so any purchases will go to line the publisher's pockets while the guy who actually made the game doesn't get jack. Who knows what the future of development for this game will be in light of all that drama.
My enjoyment of the game stemmed from the fact that I sometimes just like to torture myself with gritty games just to teach them a lesson. I beat every map in the game on hardcore and got most of the achievements. However, while writing this review, I tried to go back and play it some more just to make sure I wanted to give the thumbs down, and I am sure. Replay value is nonexistent. Once you slog through the mess of each map once, there is absolutely no reason to do it again.
So, the only circumstance that I would recommend that a friend get this game is if it was at LEAST 60%-off, and that friend loves really slow and gritty games that involve trucks and pretty scenery. Keep in mind that I am someone who absolutely loves cooperative games, and I generally try to get all of my friends to play every cooperative game that I own. Not so much this one. I feel bad for the couple friends I convinced to buy this game with me before I knew what we were getting into.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

If you like XCom, you will probably like this.  It is XCom in a western setting, sort of.  The campaign is split into several chapters, each isolated from each other, and each plays a little differently with altered mechanics from the main map.  The battle events are the core xcom like turn-based mechanics.  On medium, it is easy enough that you'll probably win without dying quite a bit if you are a little careful, and it is easy to restart a level anytime.  Between battles you spend time on the map going between different locations, buying, occasionally selling stuff, upgrading weapons, items, & perks, finding & adding someone to your crew, etc.  The map portion can take a while if you try to do everything carefully.
The game only has an auto-save, which happens every time you start or finish a battle, or quit to menu or exit game properly (not if you just kill it).  If you prefer to save-spam (save a lot and try every option), then you can just copy the single save from the Documents/HardWest/nnnn... folder and paste it back whenever you want to go back.  The devs are trying to discourage save spamming, but not outright preventing it.  Load times are excellent too.

As a fanatic of the sega genesis version, I was hesitating  at getting this game, bc I read bad reviews since it was released , but  nostalgia beat me and I had to put my hands on it and here's my humble review.

To start off, this game has "+" and "-" and sadly more " - " than "+":
cons:
- The control  of mickey is different, but ackward different, it doesn't feel like in the classic version.
- The game is is TOO short! you can easily beat it off in a couple of hours if you rush it up.I managed to beat it off (full achievments complete) in just  a few hours, and I'm not even a hardcore player!
- The plot, as usual it's a Disney story, very plain and simple, but they could take advantage of it to create  some kind of plot twist to make the game last longer.
- Too damn easy!!! Ok, this could be more a bit of subjetive opinion, but I really found harder the classic version, maybe bc I was a kid back in the 90's and found some parts of the game really frustrating  to go through, even though it had the right amount of difficulty to get back at it and make you want to play all over and over again. Although with this one, well is easy, I admit that a the candy dragon boss and mizrabel gave me some tough time but once I figured out their pattern attack, it was easier. Aside from that, there's no real challenge, I think they set the difficulty of this game for nowadays kids as they use to complain for high difficulty in games. This one is a very big con bc I excepted more challenge.
pros:
+ AWESOME music! the BGM and SE of this game are very very good,  the old songs are all remasterized  and recomposed and they did a good work at updating them with digital music and sounds, this was a bull's eye!
+ Graphics: what can I say? just stunning! they're beautiful, If the original japanese sega crew could have access to nowadays technology to create such graphics back in the 90's , they surely could had came up with something similar to this. The redesign of the levels are very well excecuted as well, they keep the spirit of the original version. Just Bravo!
As a conclusion, I might say that I'm aware that the studio that did this game wanted to keep the spirit of the orinigal COI, and didn't want to change much elements in order to do so, but really, this game could have been a bit longer, with more levels (and bosses). A true shame! but it's still enjoyable and fun to play. If you didn't play the sega genesis version, then go ahead and play! but if you're a fanatic of the classic version  like me, you' ll be dessapointing of it when you'll beat it as there's no real challenge.
If you want a real challenge, then you can download a sega genesis emulator along with the COI rom or undust your old sega genesis and original COI and beat it! bc with this one, you won't get any.

Hard West combines XCOM-esque gameplay with a rather fresh Wild West setting, but wait, there's more.
The story comprises 8 scenarios, which are more or less tied together, but the story arc splits up after the first scenario. You can either continue to follow the "main protagonist" or play through a side arc or play a prologue mission after you have completed the second "main" scenario. It's not hard to imagine that the story feels...disjointed, but it's excellently narrated and the scenarios themselves all present different challenges.
The game basically has 2 different layers: the overworld and the actual combat. Most combat missions are not optional, though some are. Depending on your options these can be really tough. I played on easy, because I just don't have so much time anymore and still it took me about 14 hours (including DLC), but you can roughly estimate 1.5 hours per scenario if you don't need to restart battle after battle. In these battles you will play in typical XCOM fashion with a twist: There is no real "hit chance", instead your characters have "luck". Luck diminishes after every attack against a character. Unfortunately you can't see how much luck your enemies have and I'm still not totally sure how the system works myself, but basically, when you run out of luck you get hit. Range, weapons, cover and special attributes all factor into the actual hit chance. Say a character has 100 luck and you have a 75% chance of hitting him...then that character loses 75 luck and I believe your next attack will hit, instead of then having a 50% chance of hitting, but like I said, not sure. The system is very obscure. After you get hit, you get some luck back. Obviously very important, since skills also require luck.
The game sports a plethora of different weapons and also has a "card system" that is based on poker hands. The better your "hand" the bigger the bonus you get, although you have to balance what individual card bonuses you actually want for each character, as well as which special ability. Factor in consumable items as well and you have yourself a tactically deep combat game.
To that comes the strategy layer of the overworld. In each scenario there are different gimmicks to observe and various goals to achieve. You do that by visiting points of interest and making choices, spending money, buying items, etc. These are really what keep the game interesting, because as fun as the combat can be, it's often too samey to motivate for long.
The Scars of Freedom DLC adds another, longer scenario, which can be quite frustrating and which mixes up the card system. Quite interesting and totally ok for the price.
Now to the bad parts of the game:
- Performance in the overworld and in menus in general is atrocious. It often takes 5-10 seconds for a menu screen to open, which only gets worse the longer you play. Maybe there is a memory leak or sth...not sure, but it doesn't take long, until you have to wait for almost every action, be it visiting a shop, opening the inventory, etc. Very annoying.
- Game crashes frequently on startup if you try and skip the intro...or maybe you just need to let it "crash" for 5 minutes...even when you let all videos play, the game seems to crash, only to recover. Not sure who programmed that, but it's utter crap and it's far from an isolated issue. I would have expected a patch by now.
- The AI is...dumb as ♥♥♥♥ or broken sometimes. I've had one mission in which a guy was just constantly running back and forth. I was supposed to defend for 8 rounds and wasn't even attacked....sometimes enemies just run past you to flank you, but by doing so leave themselves open to death from all sides.
- Speaking of flanking: There is no overwatch in this game, which is a shame in itself, because it would prevent stupid bumrushes. The AI does have a sort of OW feature on the other hand. It will automatically shoot anything in a certain radius, when you're in line of sight.
- Typical XCOM issue: You're often not sure if moving to a certain position will enable you to hit or even flank an enemy. At some points enemies shot me through walls, while I was not able to target the guy right next to me. A visual indicator, which enemies can target you and can be targeted by you before moving a character would be great, especially since the game doesn't allow many mistakes aaaaaand which brings me to the last point:
- There is no save feature during fights. Nor are there auto saves. Since combat can take quite long and make up the majority of your time spent in this game, that is quite inexcusable. Having to restart a 20 minute mission from the beginning, because you've made one mistake or because real life called, is not fun at all. It's frustrating.
Despite these shortcomings I've had fun and I hope there will be a sequel that improves upon this interesting concept.

This is a game that is, without a doubt, mediocre. Not simply because it was bad but because we have to currently view this game in isolation to the rest of the series. Dysfunctional Systems looks from the outset to be an ambitious project from a group that although experience have yet to release a full fledged commercial game. Dischan as a group has its potential but that potential was not fully realised here. the limited space here certainly contributed to that feeling of mediocrity. Taken part by part, the game excells, the writing was fluent and natural as well as good artwork and a suitable soundtrack. However due to its relatively short play time (2 hours in my case) it lacks a natural conclusion that would make this game excellent. This game can only be considered good when the sequel/ subsequent episodes come out and true judgement can only be made then on the series itself.Then again, if you are a fan of visual novels and have enjoyed Dischan's previous game Juniper's Knot this game is for you.
TLDR: Not for everyone. Needs episode 2 to be better. Otherwise solid overall.

To start, if anyone is having crashing problems on WIN 10, type -force-d3d9 into launch options on Steam. Haven't had a single crash after that.
About the game, Wasteland 2 is not for everyone. Not by a long shot. It requires patience, thinking and in some cases, nerves of steel. The top-down view and turn-based combat may turn some people off. It's a hardcore RPG where your choices, starting from the very beginning at character creation, have lasting consequences throughout the game. If you're looking for an experience similar to the more recent Fallout games, you won't find it here.
The character creation is intimidating at first, especially for newcomers to these types of games. There are tons of skills and you have no way to know in advance which are useful and which are more situational. I suggest consulting a character creation guide, but if you want to do everything on your own, one tip: make a team of specialists. After character creation, it's good to keep in mind these three things: Talk to EVERYONE, LOOT everything that isn't bolted down (or if it is, Brute Force can help with that ;)) and do EVERYTHING you can before moving to the next area. If you miss something, it might mean missing out on quests, companions or loot.
The combat is tactical and turn-based. Director's Cut added precision strikes, which are not too useful at the beginning but can be lifesavers late in the game. It also brough some flavor to the combat system, which can be somewhat tedious at times. I found most of the quirks to be quite useless; their downsides were either too bad or they were too situational.
Same goes for perks, they were a nice addition, but when selecting perks I had difficulty finding ones that were actually useful. Overall, precision strikes, quirks and perks feel somewhat like an aftertought; they're there and they're nice to have every once in a while, but they aren't really crucial to completing the game.
The weapon rebalancing of DC was a welcome addition. Assault rifles and Snipers are still king, but Shotguns, for example, now actually have some use. SMG's and Handguns still suck, though.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game to everyone. While it can be somewhat tedious and difficult at times, it's still a whole lot of fun. The world is huge and there's plenty to do, like blowing off the heads of raiders or solving feuds peacefully. BUT DON'T PRESS THE BUTTON AT RANGER CITADEL!

Went into this blindly, definately not disappointed.

Although there is not much gameplay beyond selecting dialogue choices the game does hint at potential future gameplay aspect, such as a mini-personal-space dimension named "inventory", and the ICD that tells time, logs information, and does "pretty much everything" I'm really hoping the utilize these features in future episodes.
The soundtrack is professional pitch-perfect music, very fitting for the enviroment and sounds as needed (footstep, door knocking and such) although there was no voice acting.
The art style is definitely something worth commending over as it's really innocent and easily attaches to that soft side in us, as well as giving intresting feel to the enviroments without going overbored..
The story should be the main reason for buying this, and so it should! lasted me well over 4 hours in my first playthrough but I did find myself playing it again in the same day for a total of 6+hours of absolute entertainment! no petty inventory management, no repetitive grinding and mindless restarting. Pure. Entertainment.
As of now I could think of no drawbacks or negative sides to this game, it does what it aims to do very very well and my only complaint is the lack of content, as different splits in the story branch will eventually lead to the same areas and enviroments.
Definitely worth giving a shot although you're not likely to be replaying this many times, should you chose to go that route though, the differences in outcomes are very impressive and serious, a change in the tree will have very little to no similarities with the other branches (maybe a line of dialogue or two).

I think as most people who played Mafia II before (which is definetly one of my most favorite games), I came with high expectations to Mafia III. After roughly 20 hours in the game I am coming to a close with the story and I have to say im not impressed..story wise. It does start out interesting and gets you hooked on the life of Lincoln Clay, sadly the missions do get repetetive quite fast. Every district has the same scheme of destroying businesses and then taking down the boss and assigning it to one of your 3 associates.
One major turn off is also the lack of customization, for 20 hours I am wearing the same clothes and cant modify my cars (at least not visually, yes you can tune all cars over you associates). But I really hoped some sort of freedom in choosing your Outfit and Ride would be implemented since it surely cant be that much of time in development compared to the building of the huge city and you had in already back in Mafia II.
Driving with 60's Rock on the Radio is still a lot of fun, I do enjoy the game but I wish there would be more ways to discover parts of the actually very well designed depiction of New Orleans. I liked the collecting of Playboys and Wanted Posters in the previous title and I liked the fact it is back, just with adding 4 more collectibles I feel they kinda try to keep completionists as long in the game as possible which makes the actual search somewhat quickly boring.
I was a bit worried from the start when the game was locked to 30FPS but I have to say 2K resolved this quite quickly. The map itself and its content makes ground for a great game, just the really most important part, the story was left behind in the production in my opinon. Which however doesnt mean you cant enjoy the game, it just doesnt reach to the level of Mafia II, which I really looked for. I do consider getting the Season Pass actually, in hope for some more interesting content.
After all I would rate the game a 7/10 and recommend it.

Wasteland 2 is both fun and challenging while having it's nice funny moments while you're paving your road with blood and corpses. You start with 4 cool blokes who you can modify yourself or just go with... premade characters if you're into that. You can even do anything you please in their customization up to their biography if you are so inclined and since it is RNG based you can have your own little stories about your guys like my sniper "Dead End" ambush sniping everyone into their own little dead end... in a bloody explosion that involves their head.
With the pros there's a solid combat system, lovely music score, solid story and properly fleshed out characters out there. Some love you on sight while others hate you, and of course there are some that just don't really care about you until you do something.
Most of all your decisions make an impact on the world while some not being obvious. Do you help this faction or that other one? Can one of your decisions is to do nothing and hope it solves itself? Yeah, you can choose to do nothing. And then you get to deal with all the consequences of those decisions.
Oh, and if you feel like it you can kill everyone you meet. Is this a good idea? Probably not... but this kind of thing is what I'm going to judge other RPGs on. Such as you don't like how someone looked at you? You can kill them. You don't like goats? You can shoot them. Don't like Mr. Boss Man telling you what to do? Yeah, you can shoot him to. Probably won't end well though.
Sadly with all games there are cons. Such as random encounters using the same map repeatedly. Slow on response, especially on the world map.
So yeah, if you like cRPGs that use Action Points and where character stats matter you'll like this game.

I've been a player since OB44 and have watched the game grow in a lot of aspects. Introducing heroes with unique and cool kits, making the game less grindy for free players as well as squashing bugs. Hirez has done a lot to try to sell their game. However, the only thing that is holding me back from recommending this game is the current direction the game is heading.
Since a couple patches ago, Hirez nerfed hyper mobility and started to increase damage and to lower Time To Kill (TTK). There are only 2 things that separate this game from Overwatch: Higher TTK and customization. As compared to OB44 when I first joined, killing something now takes really quicky. Get ready to die in 2s to any damage/flank hero. The high TTK was something that I really enjoyed in this game but now that TTK has been greatly lowered, the game feels like a chore to play. If you are a player who does not mind lower TTK, then give this game a shot. You'll like it. But as a player who preferred the higher TTK, the changes felt like Hirez is trying to make this game faster paced and less strategic.
What this game offers is customization. You can make a deck that enchances certain aspects of the hero you are playing. This is something rather unique and it was the main thing that drew me away from Overwatch. Balance wise, a lot of heroes are actually in a good spot. There are only 3-4 heroes that are in needed of dire tweaking. Hirez has been rather slow to buff these heroes, but they have proven themselves to be capable of that. BUT, note that Hirez has a knack to rework heroes unnessasarily.
Servers are one of the things that make me hate playing this game. If you happen to be from SEA, don't bother playing this game. Its the same thing as playing russian roulette on whether you will get 15 ping, 50 ping or 200 ping. The thing with SEA server is that once you are put into the game with a certain ping, that is your baseline ping throughout the game. Play a carry role and pray to RNGesus you dont get 200 ping. Also ping fluctuates A LOT. This has been a problem persisting since the start of open beta and Hirez has not taken measures to rectify the issue. Way to go killing your own playerbase because you do not care about SEA.
With all that being said, I have a love/hate relationship with this game. It's a pity that its not what it used to be.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Alan Wake is a model for story driven immersive gameplay. Everything about this game is great, the setting, the gameplay, the characters... everything.

All in all I recommend this game. It's a mixture of XCOM and Expeditions: Conquistador. BUT there are a few things that XCOM lovers might dislike.
- Too much focus on the story: you don't fight as much as in XCOM. You rather run around the world map, clicking through some story events and from time to time you have to fight (this part of the game is like Expeditions: Conquistador). Don't get me wrong, the athmosphere is great, the story also not bad, but I caught myself several times in just clicking away the text boxes because I wanted to start the battles.
- Fights are too easy: even on the hardest game mode the KI is not very challenging and once you know you to beat it, the game gets really easy. The fact that some of the cards (and combinations) are a bit OP doesn't help either.
All in all I had fun playing the game and deeply hope there will be a second one. If so, I'd prefer less text events and more turn based fighting with a more challenging KI.

First off: it's hard to not recommend you at least try something that is free. Go out there and see if you like it. The game is definitely better than it was on launch. There are quest lines, silly "dialogues", random locations when exploring the wasteland, and more.
That aside, there are some major issues with the design of this game. Or, rather, lack of its re-design for PC. And I am not talking about the timers present everywhere. The game was originally designed for tablets, where one "button" and dragging can do everything. This doesn't exactly translate well to PC though.
Steering. Both left and right mouse buttons can be used to move your view around the vault. They are also used to move dwellers around. Both done in a click and drag fashion. As the time goes, you will have your entire screen consisting of rooms filled with dwellers. Guess how many times you will drag the wrong thing around. Spoiler: quite often. At least you can also pan the view via edges of the screen. Then there's the problem that when you drag the dwellers around. The active zones for each rooms are probably their back walls, because the further away from the centre of the screen you are, the less sense it makes as to where you need to drag a person to drop them in a target room. Far enough up or down that zone is literally outside the room you are aiming at. Which brings us the a vide spread problem with this game...
Precision. Precision is something that this game does not require, but sadly also does not exactly let us participate in either. Rooms are three dimensional, with sprites of our dwellers and the enemies moving between front and back. This helps the immersion, but also causes a lot of problems of clicking on the correct thing. If there's a lootable object or corpse behind your characters, you will have to play around with the camera to hopefully see it, and only then click it. Health bars of the enemies also love to be layered one on top of another, so that you can't see the effect of your shots unless you are attacking the enemy most towards the foreground. Targeting specific enemies can also be a nightmare.
Same precision issues go for automatic prompts for using stimpacks and radaways. Radiation damage can reduce your dweller's healthbar down to 50% at most. Stimpacks heal 50% health. It would be logical to remove radiation before applying healing if you have full radiation poisoning. Prompts will usually have you heal dwellers first, then use radaway. It takes them quite some time to realize that it's time for a radaway before stims. "Well let's do it manually", you'd say. Great idea! Except you need to select your dwellers by sniping their legs, because clicking too high will apply the prompt above their heads. Guess hitting that prompt was too precise for tablets, so its hitbox is massive to compensate.
Then there are some utterly weird design choices like doing a critical hit automatically applying all stimpak and radaway prompts. Why? I couldn't tell you if my life depended on it. To hell with efficiency. Applying a stimpak on a fully irradiated person before radaway so that it heals maybe 2/3 of what it could is a great idea! The game knows better, shut up.
Then there are minor things like the mysterious stranger mechanic. He will randomly appear around the vault along with a sound que. You then have a limited time to find and click him for caps reward. Except the game just loves to drown that que sound with other sounds (so that you don't even know it's happening) or, better yet, give you the que and then immediately proceed to start a random event (e.g. raider attack) and take over your camera to shove said event in your face. Have fun having only half of the very short time to find the mysterious stranger. That is, after you use half of that to get the camera back to where it was.
This game has issues that could've been easily avoided. It's still playable though. And free. So give it a shot and decide for yourselves.

[This review is NOT for Director's Cut, it is for Standard Edition - Director's cut only adds to this]
If you like post-apoc games, this might be for you - especially the very patient, more old-skool users who have LOTS of time on their hands...
No really, I mean lots of time, sometimes, a bit too much honestly.  In-case you don't get it PATIENCE MUST BE ONE OF YOUR VIRTUES, otherwise completing this game WONT be.
Load times are quick [1-6 seconds on SSDs], gfx are okay (for this year, could be better...) sound is appropriate including periodic voiceovers that are well done and music that is quite fitting and will make FO 1&2 players feel right at home (Mark Morgan).  Good job getting the Fallout music man to come back.
Went through and got the repeaters, and then had to go to the Ag center, to do the next mission, and the whole while I'm doing this, another outpost is claiming it's getting clobbered, and now I'm poisoned, and don't have a clue what to do.  You feel a bit helpless, and at fault, and not entirely in a good way, but that may have been just me.  There is entirely too much going on at once and I'm unable to concentrate on this mission enough to solve it, while still having to go to another place after this is done.   First hour or two went pretty smoothly, hours three and four I'm out of ammo, there's entirely too much ammo management for me to put any more effort into it so in most of the battles half my guys were without ammo and getting massacred by rabbits on easy (well almost).
May want to invest in some unarmed skills at some point, just keep in mind to save enough skill points to get your gun skills up too or you won't hit ANYTHING.
Will eagerly be waiting for Fallout 4 as this definitely is not Fallout... not 1 not 2 not any of them.  Too much inventory juggling - that was the icing on the cake and I'd have rather eaten the plate whilst I tried to figure out what to do!  A shared inventory screen would have been a wonderful invention with individual character inventories being limited to slots guns, armor, trinkets, etc.
Pass this one up until you've exhausted the fallout series as of late.  It can be a good game, but you will struggle to afford enough ammo unless you loot everything and take every last bit of junk you can scrounge.  There is a barter perk but it brings at most 10% discount/10% bonus on bought/sold items.  It's not that this game is bad, it can be very unforgiving and hard to keep your guns loaded let alone hit the target until your gun skill is maxed.
For those playing on a RADEON video card, I can attest that there isn't much gfx issue at all sans the water-building interior in Domonta - a little bit of flickering, but can still play fine.  You're only in there for the duration of one battle anyways so regardless, it won't be too much issue.
I have updated my review a bit, after playing 30+ hours (it is a long game, I'd say im half-way through it), and it feels like a touch of fallout tactics along with fallout 2.  I'd have to say that players who enjoyed the late-90s playthrough of Fallout 1 and 2 will feel at home here in the setting - all the way down to accidently nuking some religious cult - oops... heh.  Though I will say you can with assuredness tell that this is the first-go-round for some of the people creating the game, it is NOT shoddy work by any means.  There is much fun to be had here, and much humour to snicker at if you have the patience.   This isn't DooM, this isn't run-and-gun and blast through everything with reckless abandon...this is it's own game.  A 25-40$ USD price-tag seems appropriate here, and I think most people would be satisfied with the game for this.  That being said, it isn't nearly as crashey as Fallout 3 and New Vegas were out of the box (or possibly even now years after release), so don't let me sell it short.  Watch some videos, read the reviews and decide for yourself.  Try not to get discouraged before getting to level 15-20 or so with your characters, as it gets much more rewarding when you can actually afford ammo AND hit the target in battle.  I would also mention on this last note that the age-rating for this game applies to both the violence and the difficulty mentally that you may have if you lack extremely good problem solving skills (teenagers barring some ingeniously crafty ones may have trouble).  Good luck.
Recommended to take a field medic-surgeon, weaponsmith, locksmith/safecracker, and someone with keen perception and good with knocking down obstacles with you on your first try, you'll get more characters in your party at a later date if you so choose.  You still won't be able to do everything your first time.  This game for most will be good for more than one play-through.
Just buy up all the ammo & health-items you can afford, seriously.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

I have played both Wasteland 2 and Wasteland 2: Director's Cut. I *really* wanted to like this game, and there are things I do like about this game, but unfortunately they are overshadowed by several design decisiosn that I feel are completely game breaking, decisions that ultimately left me feeling nothing but disappointment.
To get this out of the way first, yes, there were a *lot* of bugs, from graphics not lining up properly, to strange problems with the names of clothing, to crashes to desktop on load, to a horrific problem in Ranger Citadel where attempts to load the game in Ranger Citadel would leave me with a completely crippled interface and the feeling that I had somehow broken the game so much that it would never recover. To be clear, while these were annoyances (yes, even the Ranger Citadel bug for which I eventually found a work-around), none of them were bad enough to actually make me dislike the game.
Also, to get THIS out of the way, I agree that the visual style could have used some work, and the audio definitely left something to be desired, especially the background noises which, in the Ag Center, nearly had me tearing my hair out at one point. But, again, none of this actually made me dislike the game.
Instead, up to a point I liked the game *in spite* of these problems. I liked the combat system. Sure it was relatively light on tactics if I wanted to just plough through encounters, but if I was smart, I could end encounters in one or two rounds. I liked the weapon and armor system well enough. They were definitely servicable, and modding weapons was kind of fun. I liked character customization well enough. The perks and quirks were a nice addition. I also liked some of the rebalancing, and felt like my characters in the DC were better able to handle themselves in a variety of situations than my original Wasteland 2 characters. I liked the plot for a while. I saved Highpool on my original Wasteland 2 playthrough, I saved Ag Center on my DC playthrough, and I liked them both. I liked the Rail Nomads, and the little hidden surprises scattered around the wasteland, including the random encounters. I especially felt good about the number of options I seemed to have for resolving a number of the situations I ran across. It felt good. It felt right. I was pretty happy.
Then I went to prison, and everything went to hell. Suddenly all my options went away. Without spoiling anything, the prison area presents you with little in terms of choices, and it is frustrating. Especially in the DC, I got to the prison with characters that had a lot of options available to them, and yet at the prison they were largely unusable. Further, the logic that the game presented behind *why* I had no options just did not follow. What's worse, the outcome at the prison seems to be the same no matter what you do there. I've searched for an explanation online, only to discover various apologists saying that the development team was trying to hammer home the idea that the wasteland is really terrible. The problem with this argument, of course, is that you do not have to take away player agency to get this point across, and yet this is what we are left with. Confusingly, in earlier versions of this game those choices did exist at the prison, and there seems to be no good explanation as to why they were taken out.
And, unfortunately this is where I had to stop playing both versions of this game. This is when it stopped feeling like a role playing game, and started feeling like a visual novel with some cosmetic combat, and not a particularly interesting or engagine one at that. Is it unfair to judge the entire game based on my experience? Maybe. But I have tried to get back the feeling I had of playing a role playing game, the one that the game still managed to engender early on in my playthroughs, but the immersion has apparently been broken irreparably.
Maybe if I hadn't seen the setting half a dozen times in other games, or if the plot were more unique and engaging, or the gameplay more interesting, or the game less frustratingly buggy, or the graphics more beautiful or the audio less . . . horrific . . . Maybe if these things had been the case it would have carried me through this immersion-breaking area and onward towards the end of the game. And maybe I will still be inspired to play through the rest of the game, experiencing it in its entirety and I will change my tune. But every time I try to play again, I am presented with the fact that my choices in the Prison area will have no impact on the game, not even any HOPE of impact, and then despair sets in and I cannot continue. Not despair over the setting or the plot. Not despair over the fates of the individuals in the Prison area who are doomed because the wasteland is a horrible place. No, my despair is over the poor design decision. I *know* that it could have been a better game, that they could have confronted us with an unforgiving area that showed us how brutal the wasteland can be without taking away our options/choices/agency. But they did not, and so I cannot recommend this game.

This is quite a gentle, slow-paced game for the most part. While there are some timing puzzles that require you to be quick, overall everything takes a leisurely pace. This didn't bother me but some may find it too slow.
Act 1 of the game is the only part of the game worth playing. You play as either Shay or Vella up to a certain point, and then switch to the character you didn't choose at the start to play through their story until the two stories align with each other. While Vella's story is more interesting, there are moments in Shay's that genuinely made me laugh. The NPCs are interesting and have some well-written dialogue and the environments are rich and colourful.
Act 2 is very confined to the areas you can explore and doesn't tread much new ground. I was disappointed by this as I'd hoped that it would add more new areas or expand old ones - you barely get a glimpse of the final area which ws built up to be this large and menacing place. The puzzles spike in difficulty, with some being made artifically difficult and frustrating. The second part of the story is also rushed through at a tremendous pace and almost entirely through dialogue with the antagonist. It was interesting that the tone of the game became a lot darker,  but it was never fully realised. The execution is clunky.
Overall this game was a big disappointment. If you want to play I would advise keeping a walkthrough handy and having a phone nearby to take photos of some puzzle elements that need to be memorised, but even then you're going to be frustrated.

This game isn't perfect. In fact, it's a long way from. In fact, if there was any real competition--any at all--in terms of a Space Program Simulator, I could even say it wasn't very good. What this game IS, is one of a kind.
Buggy, simple, almost barren, pretty much all this game has you do is fly around a scaled-down solar system with graphics almsot as dated as those of Frontier: Elite 2 (and bearing a remarkable resemblance to that game in some ways), do "science", and earn "funds". There's very little lore, no plot at all, no characters you don't control, and all you have to compete against is your own mistakes. Most of what you'll find yourself doing is designing and building your own ships, which is one of the few things that feels very nearly complete; once you actually start flying... and Oh my God the CAMERA ANGLES! One minute you have the camera right where you want it, you're flying your ship, everything's doing fine... THEN IT SWINGS AROUND ON ITS OWN AND ALL OF A SUDDEN YOU CAN'T SEE WHAT YOU'RE DOING. So you try to put it back... Nope, not gonna. The game, for some reason, thinks you absolutely don't need to see from the ONE angle you actually want to see from...
And of course there are endlessly more problems. Squad's attempts to make the game user friendly are clumsy, ill-coordinated and more often than not counterproductive. If you could hear me playing, every so often you'd be deafened by "I CLICKED ON YOU, YOU STUPID THING!" "What the F___ are you DOING?!" And, more frequently than anything else, "Now Cut That Out!!!!" as I encountered one idiotic or poorly implemented feature after another, usually involving navigation. Just for one example, their idea of an SAS system is something that overcorrects like a rookie driver that refuses to moderate his reflexes. I was one. We all were. If this is the best autopilots can do, no WAY we should ever have self-driving cars, much less let computers fly a space ship. And then the map system--even when you have a dialog box open, all the hotspots from the map itself are still active, so as you click your way through a menu, you are forever opening MORE dialog boxes to "warp here" or "add maneuver". And when you actually try to click on something IN the map, it CAN NOT figure out what you're trying to click on; even when other orbits are nowhere near it, you get the "warp here, add maneuver" dialog box. Repeatedly.
I know there are mods out there to fix these things and even add features the developers didn't bother to... but I am NOT rating the MODS.
Without actually rating the mods however, I can say that one thing that this game does right is in fact allow--even encourage--modding. This could be an even better thing, unfortunately as in too many cases these days the game designers seem to have relied on it too much. The game feels as though they thought modders meant that leaving features out of the game wouldn't affect its quality; that the existence of the modding community meant they could charge the same thing for an inferior product. That getting lazy would cost them nothing. So they gave us a bare-minimum, "we'll do as little as we can possibly get away with and then slap a big price tag on it and the modders will make us look good" game. I don't appreciate that. I don't like it at all.
Steam doesn't have a rating system. If it did, I'd give it one star. If it had even the slightest competition, I'd hate it. But like I said, it's really the ONLY modern game that gives you a taste of real space flight. That I know of anyway. Buggy, irritating, obnoxious, stubborn, cantankerous, user-unfriendly, clumsy, poorly-programmed, lazily-implemented, glorious spaceflight. So I'm giving it a thumbs up regardless. But come ON Squad! You can do better than *that*. And you'd better, because I'll already never buy another game from you. If you want to keep the rest of your audience, Shape The Heck Up.

Overview: Avoid Sensory Overload is a really fun arcade dodging game, slightly reminiscent of titles like Race the Sun. You're speeding forwards at an ever-increasing rate, and you control your little ship and steer it around to collect score multipliers and powerups while avoiding walls and holes in the track.
Accessibility: The easiest mode is very accessible to casual players, while the harder modes require lightning reflexes. There are a lot of flashing lights, so if you're sensitive to that then you might not want to pick it up. The controls are keyboard or gamepad, which is a bit of a shame as I'd love to play this with the mouse. They are rebindable though.
Game modes: There are fixed levels, where you replay them to try and get perfect runs, but to me the real appeal of the game is the randomly-generated Endless Mode. Naturally for a game like this, there are leaderboards for all difficulty levels. There are also currently 3 "themes" as the devs put it, which play slightly differently and have different aesthetics.
Graphics/Sound: The visuals are bright, bold, and striking. It's also got a lovely electronic soundtrack.
Price: It's 4.99 right now, and it's got trading cards that are fairly high-valued at the moment if that makes a difference to you.
All in all, a really nice little indie game that I think deserves a bit more exposure.

If you expect something like a 4X or combat-heavy strategy game, you'll be disappointed. This is quite an interesting simulation where you set trends for the populations in a cluster of star systems. I would personally have preferred that your actions were even more subtle and long-term oriented, instead of being somewhere in the middle. Overall, I think it's a good game that I do recommend if you are looking for a strategy simulation. It feels very much like an indie game, and it is a bit rough around the edges, but I've enjoyed it so far.
What could have been better:
- The UI. This is the biggest problem I have with the game. No hotkeys, no way to scroll between planets/systems, no filtering system to find your industrial districts and so on. There's a lot of clicks in just one territory, and a lot of searching for that district that had X.
- Combat. They way it is, I'd actually prefer a full simulation. The way it works now, you need to have ~4:1 advantage to be fairly certain you'll win, and a ~6:1 advantage to be fairly certain to not suffer any casualties. And you can do it manually, which lets you set up your forces and see them scatter and die alone. Pitched to me as a strategy heavy economics game and I thought this would be right up my ally. Instead what I get is a clunky simulation that bottle-necks early game play into a similar vane then offers a rinse-and-repeat mechanic as replay value. I found this more like a complicated game of solitare rather than a really intricate space economy.
You're a Viceroy of a small cluster of stars and planets. The game presents a little micro-economy within each new play and a series of semi-random issues particular to the cluster. The replay value drops quick after about 5 or 6 plays as a lot of the same mechanics pop up. "Influence" is a thematic rebrand of experience that carries over from cluster to cluster. After you've wrecked two economies and had one cluster invaded by rebels you're promoted somehow and get access to more bonuses that can be carried over to make the game a bit easier or more fluid.
The real issue is that you're bottle necked into raising the army, not touching certain mechanics like mortality or spamming the happiness tech tree in order to rust into stability. Each round starts off a lot in the same way. Then you're mindlessly growing your safe cluster until... not sure. Its good enough or the place has stagnated to the point of worthlessness. Back out. Get promotion. Get new cluster.
I say its like solitare because the replay value kind of reminds me of a toddler yelling "AGAIN." Start new cluster. Get a bad hand? Stagnate. Play new cluster. Make bad moves or not good enough. Ditch it and find another. Kind of... win? I guess? Win enough? Ok, watch the cards bounce around in victory. Start again. Just isn't a very rewarding game.
My suggestion, without saying to rehash the whole capitol system dynamic, is to create more thematic objectives. You only get barely usable turn based build objectives and they're monotinous to keep up with if not completely ignorable. A better guiding hand with influence bonuses would really turn the game into a more rewarding feeling.
Again, not a terrible game. Just lacks a real sense of accomplishment.

TL;DR: If you're looking to satisfy your XCOM needs, look no further than Hard West.
All in all, I really enjoyed my time with Hard West. If I had played it before the game introduced the quick-save mechanism, I might have hesitate to recommend the game, but right now? I would gladly recommend it, provided you're fine encountering a few bugs here and there.
A more detailed look:
+ Intense, tactical combat.
This game really nails the tactical part of a combat. Most of the time, your shot is deadly enough to kill an enemy in 1 hit, but this goes for enemies' attacks too. So the combat turns into a game of positioning and flanking where any mistake could result in your character killed.
+ Strategical stealth section.
I didn't realize there's a stealth part in the game, so I was quite happy when I found it. It was less "stealth" and more "choose an advantageous position to start" though. Nonetheless, I really like it.
+ Story-rich exploration
There's an open world exploration between each combat, and oh boy, the game really delivers on this part. The world doesn't only hides many interesting stories and event, it's also full of decision-making moments. Do you choose to get a buff, or do you rather have an extra companion? Etc.
= Okay-ish RPG aspect.
The game has plenty of RPG aspect, and it ties in really well with both exploration and combat gameplay. But overall it felt kinda shallow. The card-based element is pretty limited too, where a low-level buff feels stronger than higher level buffs.
- Not western enough
Despite the game taking place in saloons, bars, as well as having skill like fanning, I never felt like a cowboy in the wildwest while playing the game. I'm not sure why, but I guess its because the mystical aspect of the game overshadows the western aspect.
- Bugs galore
During my playthrough, I encountered multiple bugs. One of them is severe enough that made a particular mission unfinishable. Fortunately the game is fun enough to make up for it.

OK, I just finished the Castle of Illusion remake: it's a firm 10/10. I've got a little more to do before it's 100% clear, but it's yet another candidate for my Game of the Year.
Castle of Illusion (the Master System version) is a game I counted as my favourite since I was around five or six years old until recently when The Binding of Isaac challenged it, but Castle of Illusion is rock-solid and Binding is buggy as heck; it's still great, but Castle pips it by virtue of being faultless, basically.
So this remake was a long time coming and something I had a lot of nostalgic and, frankly, emotional stake in. The remake is actually of the Mega Drive version of the game (which I don't like as much but is still a good crack), but the principle is thus; the "...of Illusion" series is very dear to me, and this remake is more than worthy. It take the basic elements of both versions of the original game and expands upon them sensibly and non-intrusively. The spirit, the feel of the game is bang on. It's incredible just how charming this remake is, and how perfectly it nails the Illusion magic. It makes the recent 3DS Epic Mickey: The Power of Illusion look even more like the insult it was. Screw Dreamrift for daring to put the word "Illusion" on their piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥game.
This remake is perfect. Sure, it's taken me just shy of two hours to finish it, but those were two hours where at no point did I say "for ♥♥♥♥'s sake", two hours I spent grinning like a loon, completely enraptured by the sheer friendliness of the game. Ten out of ten, everyone should play this. The studio have disbanded so there will not be a sequel and if there is it's a risky proposition. This was a once-in-a-lifetime thing and Sega Studios Australia pulled it off with incredible ♥♥♥♥ing skill. Props to them and I hope their staff all find success at whatever they do.

Tomb Raider: Chronicles is linear and quite short. It took me roughly 5-6hrs. The level environments are small in scale compared to Tomb Raider 1-4 and feel more compact. Honestly, this made it harder to maneuver Lara through tight corridors, or perhaps the game responded awkwardly to my Xbox controller. However, my Xbox controller works fine with Tomb Raider 2-4 (the original game requires Xpadder).
The game is presented decently, but there is no story in Chronicles. Instead, the game is divided into four sections that recount some of Lara’s past adventures.
The first section are the Rome levels that provide throwbacks to the original Tomb Raider and some Tomb Raider 2 Venice vibes (without the speed boat). These levels focus on exploration and puzzles mostly.
The second section is Russia and these levels pronounce all the action elements from the series. The Russia portion reminded me of the offshore rig and diving levels from Tomb Raider 2.
The fourth section takes a younger Lara introduced at the beginning of Tomb Raider: The Last Revelation and strands her on a haunted Irish isle without weapons. These sections are very survival horror based with lots of puzzle solving. This portion of the game was my favorite as the levels were atmospheric and did something different for the series.
The last section takes place in a high-tech skyscraper in New York City. These levels resembled the Area-51 levels from Tomb Raider 3 and focus more on stealth sequences. These levels are the most challenging in the game. Also, the last level “Red Alert” is very buggy. Certain bugs can prevent the player from finishing the level, so it’s a good idea to have multiple saves. And save frequently!
While the Russia and VCI skyscraper sections are slight improvements from the contemporary levels from Tomb Raider 2 and 3, neither live up to the franchise name. Still, these levels are straight forward enough and presented better via the in-game cutscenes and Hollywood inspired approach. The game design in Chronicles is never intelligent like it was in The Last Revelation, nor does it ever feel as challenging like Tomb Raider 3.
Overall, Tomb Raider Chronicles is rather average. The first section is too linear and easy. It’s a far cry to what Tomb Raider 1-4 are. The environments are dense and lack the scale as big of previous installments. For that reason alone, makes Chronicles a tad lackluster, but there are still a slew of entertaining gimmicks and challenges in Chronicles.
PROS:
+The Ireland levels remain the best section in the game
+Decent presentation
CONS:
-Last level (Red Alert) very buggy
-Rome levels are too linear and easy
-Environments lack the scale of the previous games

I bought this game because I like the art and had heard some good comments but I didn't know much about it actually. I didn't have many expectations besides it being visually enjoyable. To my surprise I liked this game a lot! I love adventure games and stories and found this story to be very interesting from the beginning on. The voice acting was great! It really gave more depth to the story, IMO. The writing and some situations presented were actually funny, which I liked, and the game still managed to keep a balance between serious and funny. I enjoyed the art and colors very much! The music was also nice. Puzzles were mostly entertaining, there is only one part in which I had to go read online because I was too frustrated. But the game was mostly enjoyable, nonfrustrating, entertaining, and intriguing. Great game! It was a great dventure! Definitely exceeded my expectations. Would absolutely recommend it to any adventure seeker who's into stories and thinking.
SPOILERS AHEAD:
.
.
.
Now being more specific, I really liked the story being about two different people and happening at the same time. To actually play both stories at the same time was something refreshing. I really liked to be able to switch when I got stuck. I liked to be able to play two very different characters who at the same time were living a similar frustrating situation. I loved how both stories started to relate to one another as the game developed and how one thing done in one was of help in the other one. Although I would have liked for the dialogs to integrate to the story the fact that what Vella does helps Shay and viceversa and not it just happening like magically. When it happens without it being it integrated to the story, it kind of cuts the flow of everything and makes you feel again like a simple external player and not as the character in the story. But overall, I really liked the dynamic of the relationship between the two stories.
I also liked the twists of things being different from what you think. But I think that the game should dedicate more time and depth to explaining the whole deal with de Dandelion mission and why things happened like they did, since it was a bit vague at times. This leads me to talk about the ending. I found it very abrupt. It's not exactly clear to me what happens with the Loruna people nor why you had to melt the ships. Some more story was needed towards the secod part of the game when you are really waiting to get a deeper understading of the characters and events.
Now about the puzzles, the robot wiring doesn't have enough clues to figure it out in a challenging yet attainable way. I got impatient and had to go look online and that ruins the puzzle experience. Also the part where you convince Hope that you are Shay was hard since there weren't enough hints and I had to go look for info again. Same problem as before. Bringing the hexigal to open the door for the central control room sounds like a very fun idea but it got hindered by there not being a clear logic of how things needed to be done for her to move. It was mostly trial and error. The other puzzles were fun and very original and creative.
Another thing I disliked is how slow charachters walk. You have to walk a lot in the game and it's annoying to walk so slow. There should be some button to make it quicker of you want to.
This is just a personal issue. I would have liked the game better if it wasn't "point and click". I would have loved to be able to walk around normally and just approach stuff and hit a button to interact with them.
On the whole I really liked this game! It felt different, creative, intriguing and engaging and also looked beautiful and different! I would give it like an 8.5 out of 10. The idea of making the documentary was alos great! I've watching it and have found it very interesting. I didn't know the adventure genre was kind of problematic with publishers. It's a shame since it's my favorite genre. I hope more game studios start bringing it back like Double Fine did! Thanks for a great game!

I was a backer on Kickstarter for this game and I'm also a huge fan of Tim Schafer and his Double Fine Productions. That's why I backed this in the first place, but also because I'm a fan of the adventure game genre, of course. Nevertheless Broken Age is the first game which I've played on Steam which I can't right out of my heart recommend, but why is that?
The game is split into two acts and while the first act is just brilliant not only because of it's warmth, colorful visuals, lovely soundtrack or its charming characters, but also because of its well designed and thus entertaining puzzles. So everything's fine up until the end of act 1. It's ending will eventually already make your eyebrowes raising, but since everything is still open you may advance to act 2 to see how it's going on only to discover that starting from there everything is getting really worse just in every aspect.

First off, I'm not going to go into the micropayments because I have given them no attention whatsoever. I played the first game (in case you don't know 'shadow of mordor') and I had lots of fun with it. It was an open world sandbox with very fun combat, some dynamic enemy captains, some interesting backstory, ect. It is a very fun game to me. By the end nothing could kill me no matter how ridiculous it's bonuses were.
Starting in this game you do have some of your abilities from the end of the previous game taken away. This is fair because you can't be OP murderous ghost batman at the beginning of the game. Still, the combat style works in almost the same way as the first game and I cannot criticize because the first game had the combat style refined and balanced to the point where I do not think it could be improved any further.
However I did start noticing some minor snags. First, there is a levelling system. This levelling system gives you a skill point but does not increase your stats. Your health is already at the max. Second, they replaced the killstreak executions with 'might' generated by doing, and sometimes taking, damage in combat. This seems to work out ok for me so I wouldn't call it a point against it. Third, there is now equipment leveling. My complaint is this: the concept of unlocking new equipment per level, and rarity and the like do not belong anywhere near this game. Shadow of mordor's upgrades for the weapon are acquired by doing side quests to 'forge the legend' of that weapon, thus improving it. This was a unique and functional style that gives you an actual reason to do the side quests, and they are usually quite fun. Shadow of war however seems to be angling towards the MMO upgrade style, which again, has no business being in a single player game and does not appeal to many single player preferred people.
Here are the major snags, the captains. This was my experience on normal difficulty. While the grunts do next to no damage to you, the captains do a stupid amount of damage, even at the beginning of the game. The average captain can kill you in three to four hits. This wouldn't be an issue if they all did not have much more health than you, requiring significantly more force to take down. This is not difficult, it is tedious. It means I have to spend five minutes hacking away at his health while avoiding every attack or die. This does not count in some of the captains that have grabbing abilities which will drain almost all of your health in one hit, the captains whose primary method of attack consists of 'spam heavy attack in succession', or the captains that blow a horn and cause everything around them to do just that.
The game had some good things going for it, but the gameplay so far just isn't fun. This isn't hard, it's tedious. It's boring. I keep reminescing about the previous game when I am playing, thinking of how much fun I would have walking into an orc stronghold, and challenging myself to survive the onslaught, meanwhile in this game I have to spend what feels like forever to kill one captain.
Final verdict: This game had too many elements that just kill the experience for me. I got all the way through Act I collecting all the collectables and generally trying to enjoy the game, and I'm not having fun. I'm just not enjoying the experience.
Edit: The constant betrayals that seem to happen for no reason, out of nowhere, really isn't helping this game's case. If the betrayals made sense (blood brothers) thats one thing, but most of these are so abritrarily contrived. It really feels that the game is just spinning a random number generator on whether or not this will happen.
Also, your practically crippled from the previous game by limiting your focus, elf-shot, and most of your abilities are based on your equipment, most of them provide 5 arrows, and they can only be replenished by finding the floating arrow marks in the world, not by draining, or fighting, or any other mechanic that existed previously.
The fact that they decided to replace the runes, which were very functional upgrades that could very well change your gameplay style, are replaced with the weapon rarity system specified above, essentially removing them entirely. The game tries to replace this by increasing the amount of base abilities you can have, but most of them are only useful in extremely specific instances, and if your might is not up and your out of elf-shot, your out of luck.
The game also makes a pathetic attempt to replace the 5 runes you could get with ONE gem, that provides pathetically little bonus, such as 2% damage increase. Oh, but if you get three of them you can combine them to get the next level of gem with gives a 4% damage increase! So staggering! The max level for these gems is 5 btw, and it takes way too much effort to get those.
Again, I must ask, why are all these MMO gameplay mechanics that would enhance a bunch of people cooperating to overcome groups of enemies they cannot take on alone, doing in a singleplayer game that relies on ONE character being powerful enough to take on a small army? For the microtransactions of course. DO NOT BUY ANYTHING FROM THE MARKETPLACE!!! By doing so you are enabling this company to pull scummy tactics like having the balls to put microtransactions, which the game mechanics were crippled to hinge upon, in a full payed 60$ game! The people screwed up what this game could have been, all for the sake of their greed!
Avoid at all cost, story might be interesting, but combat is full of bad development decision, and it boils down to flanking enemies one by one and a lot of waiting.

First of:
I played this game for 50 hours now and it did not crash a single time. It tolerated me accidentally shuting down the computer while having the game running without corrupting the save. I'd consider it as stable as current software gets. The negative reviews in that regard seem to be outdated.
The good:
If you like turn-based economic management games, sicfi settings and rewarding micro-management, you will very likely enjoy this game. The hardware requirements are pretty low, so a lot of dated systems will be able to run this game. Combat is usually a whack-a-mole style sending around of a sufficiently staffed fleet. Don't be afraid about it and read more about that in the following section.
The bad:
There is a lot of room to improve the ingame explanation of the game mechanics and accessibility by more information on how an improvement plays out. For example, the help tells you that one level of happiness increases the percentage of revenue that you receive from a territory. But how much? (5 percentage points) - Why do I have to build a happiness improvement to find out? A lot of issues like this could be covered if the game would give you a better estimate of how the improvement would play out.
The territory map is quite large for smaller screens (sub 1920x1080) so there is a lot of scrolling around. It makes sending the fleet around unnecessarily painful.
And why has there been investment in combat animation? You can place your ships and then watch. Auto-resolve works as well. The effort put into that could have been placed elsewhere.
Micro-management afficionados like me would love to have more table overview options to look for districts/planets where you get the most for your buck investing in infrastruture. Considering the amount of investment options you have, there would have to be quite a lot of them ;)
The ugly (nitpicking):
While the animations of the economic activity in your sector look rather fancy, the mouse cursor should not (very, very slighlty) stutter on a Radeon 5770 considering the graphics level. The animations could be a little slower to my taste so this might be a way to fix this for the developer.
