It's fun for the first few hours hours, but it's not worth twenty bucks
In the game, you rule over a territory that has recently had a disaster befall it. You win by maxing out your people's wealth and removing "mortality" (death rate), ignorance (having a negative balance of the game's research points), and misery (have too few "hapiness" points in your systems), then leaving your territory to do the same thing in another one.
The entire game is based around building "upgrades" in your planets to increase your people's  stats, and the "challenges" in the game function exactly the same as the upgrades, but they give a detremental effect rather than a positive one
For example, one upgrade gives +1% population growth. ALL OTHER population growth upgrades increase pop growth at the exact same rate, and all "challenges" that have to do with population growth decrease it by 1%.
How do you get rid of the "challenges"? You research a tech to nullify them, then you have to pay to remove the challenge- in the exact same manner you build the upgrades.
All techs give you acess to one new upgrade (none of which do anything unique), the ability to nullify one challenge, and a 1% increase in productivity in one area of your economy. You get more tech points by building upgrades and changing your policies (they are functionally just sliders)
Your early game territories have 3-4 solar systems in them, each with 2-5 planets, each planet with 1-11 districts. Upgrades and challenges exist in each "layer" of a solar system- they effect the whole system, a whole planet, or a single district.
To build an upgrade, you go into the desired level you wish to build it on, then you click and drag the upgrade onto the center of the screen. So if I wanted to increase my pop growth by 1%+ in a solar system, but I only have tech that lets me build on a disctrict scale, I have to click and drag up to 50 times! Roughly 1/3 of the upgrades exist on the district scale, so most of the time you play will be taken up by clicking and dragging. In the late game, expect to start your turn, click and drag for 5 minutes, get tired, save, come back, and then click and drag for another five minutes before you can end turn. Unless the devs add a way to "mass upgrade" several district at once, don't play this if you would rather not develop complications in your wrists.
EDIT: Since writing this review, the UI has been upgraded to include a "mass build" funciton. It is still, however, clunky and irritating to use, and the game gets stale just as fast as before.
Every new territory you rule over has its own unique challenges. However, these are all solved in the exact same way: research tech, then click and drag to nullify it. After you figure out how to "max out" a territory, you realize that the solutions for each set of challenges are almost exactly the same. Focus on maxing out a single planet's money-making stats, set your policies to get max income, and then proceed to max out the rest of your territory.
Once you 'solve' the game and 'beat' one territory, it becomes a horrible grind with NO replay value. You can get 'promoted', but all that does is increase the size of the territories you rule over. Which means you have to click and drag EVEN MORE to win!
It proports to have a sophisticated econ system, but it's incredibly simple. There are three types of goods- biological, industrial, and cultural. The people of your planets make money directly proportional to how many goods they produce- this money is then divided between taxes, support for rebels, and consumption (which increases your people's wealth stat). How good a solar system is at producing each one depends entirely on the upgrades you have built in it. Because upgrades exist for productivity on each 'level'- solar system, planetary, and district, the only course of action is to max out productivity of one type of good for the entire solar system, and let it import the other two. There is a cost to import goods, but it can be completely nullified by- suprise suprise- clicking and dragging upgrades onto the district, planetary, and solar system levels.
To fight rebels, you click and drag ships onto your fleets, then click and drag the weapons you want on your ships onto your fleet, then click and drag your fleets onto the rebels. There is a combat system, but you have so little input that you'll end up auto-resolving every battle ( all you can do is click and drag your ships into different starting positions on the map)
If the UI was less atrocious, this game might be fun in short bursts. But as it stands, I don't reccomend it.

I'm doing a
and have now completed my first territory successfully. For reference, it took about 2hr30min to beat that territory, the smallest in the game, though I can easily see it being completed more quickly or lasting much, much longer depending on how you want to play the game. The game is very complex and has a steep learning curve, but a lot of the fun in playing it comes from trying to figure out how everything works together and then making things more efficient.
CONS
The biggest problem with the game is the lack of any sort of real tutorialization, meaning you will probably struggle until you understand the basic gameplay mechanics through trial and error. There is a manual and an extensive in-game encyclopedia, but these don't really explain how to play the game so much as they hint at the actual purpose behind game mechanics. Combat is not very fleshed out, not that this game is meant to be about combat, but you have the option to auto-resolve or command your ships in a fight, the latter choice allowing you to position them before a battle. The audio is entirely forgettable, which is unfortunate in a game where you spend large amounts of time contemplating options on single screens. The graphics are competent but definitely not the focus.
PROS
On the positive side, the game features a very deep and interesting lore, mostly delivered through the tech system (which is also high unique and is implemented very well). It gives a lot of ACTUAL depth to the administrative process (more than any other game I've seen) and provides you with all the information you could want to govern in the way you like. If you like the Democracy series, some of the older political sims like Shadow President, or grand strategy in the vein of Victoria 2, this game will be perfect for you. Even city-builder fans (especially of the older Sim City games) should be able to enjoy this game, as it is fundamentally a game about managing people and a government from the desk of an administrator. If you've never played any of those games before, I can say that if you enjoy economics or puzzling out the best, most efficient way to do something, you will really like this game.

Many says that Paladins is a clone of Overwatch. Well, when you actually play the game it's totally different. It's a shooter game with cards system and in-game items where 2 5-players teams fight for a sweet victory.
Four modes actually exists:
- Siege - one capture point, almost symetrical map. Being played until either team reach 4 points. First objective is to capture the point (NOTE: number of players from one team standing on point doesn't make capturing faster). Team which will do it, earn 1 point. After capturing, during the same round, the same team has to push spawned payload to the checkpoint (which is close to enemy spawn point), they have about ~2:30 to do this. If succeded, team earns another point, when failed - enemy team earns 1 point (until they have 3 points already, then they earn nothing). It's possible to run into overtime during a round: in capture phase - by standing on point with opposing team, when any of team bars shows 99%; in pushing phase - by pushing/standing near payload when timer reaches 0.
- Payload - One team is Defenders, while other is Pushers. Pushers have to push the payload all the way from starting point (near their spawn point) to capture point (near Defenders spawn point). Their progress is shown by a % of distance that payload was pushed. They have 8 minutes to do it. Round ends when Pushers will make it to the end or timer reaches 0. Then second round begins, and teams sides are switched (Defenders are now Pushers, and vice versa). Winner is determined, who did pushed payload to the end faster (when both teams had 100%) or further (beating other team by 1% during 2nd round ends the match automaticly). No overtimes.
- Survival - just team deathmatch with no respawns during the rounds. Like in Siege mode: first to 5 points wins.
- Coop vs AI - Special mode where "rules" are being changed every few weeks.
There is also another queue, but dedicated for testers who would like to test upcomming maps to the game.
Champions are categorized in: Front line, Support, Damage, Flank. Each has unique playstyle and different role.
Every champion can be customised (from sprays, through MVP Poses and Voices to outfit).
Each champion has 3 legendary cards (1 is available by default, other 2 can be bought by Essences) and a basic loadout called: Basic [insert champion name here] which is pretty good and universal. You can have in total 6 loadouts, each contains 5 cards (selected from 20-cards deck) where each card can have different levels (from 1 to 4). Each card has rarity which determines its price in Essences. You have to buy a card before you can use it in your loadouts. NOTE: each loadout has to have exactly 12 loadout points (these are being calculated by summing up used cards levels, f.e.: 1+4+3+2+2).
Before every match in any game mode you have to make a selection, which legendary card and loadout you would like to use. As soon as match didn't started, you can change your selection by pressing U.
In-game shop offers 16 items in total in 4 categories: Defence, Utility, Healing, Offense. These items can be bought using Credits that you earn during the match passively, eliminating enemies, capturing objectives and by doing your champions role specific things (f.e. when playing as Damage you will be rewarded for doing high amount of damage in short period of time). You can only buy 4 items max, but every item has to be from different category, so you can't have f.e. 2 Defense items. Each item can be upgraded to max 3rd level.
Overall, it's a great game where shooting is important, but not the most one. If you ever played a FPS game, and MOBA one, you will definitly love it as i do <3

I enjoyed most of my time with this game but would recommend getting it wihle it's on sale.

They've recently had to put a hiatus on making the other episodes, and I can understand their decision. Visual novels aren't all that common, with the most promenant ones I can think of being Telltale's Wolf Amongst Us and The Walking Dead seasons, so it's not that difficult to realise that they didn't make enough money from their game sales. Japanese dating sims (being almost identical in structure, albeit not gameplay) have huge markets in their native country, and whilst fanbases for these games grow, there's still not a guarantee that the games will sell, and are left untranslated.
They've said that when they get the funds they'll restart. Who knows when that will be is a valid question, but showing support by buying the first episode will at least make a start. Neither money nor time was wasted playing this game, and I hope that this announcement doesn't put other people off at least trying it.

The first chapter of Dysfunctional Systems, Learning to Manage Chaos is a visual novel. If you like a more relaxed experience, then certainly look into this genre more, but otherwise gamers with trigger fingers will find nothing for them here.
The story itself is well-written and I feel the universe created by Dischan can be expanded upon in a variety of ways for future installments. The music is great, and I was pleased to discover the soundtrack is included with the game in its directory.
Length is a real problem though - the episode is only an hour long, and I feel it could have been expanded upon exponentially. More than half of the characters are introduced in the epilogue.
The achievement system in the game is also significantly flawed. Like most visual novels, you can make choices along the way to alter the story. The catch is, this only occurs at one point during the game. Most of the achievements are gained at this point by selecting different combinations of responses within five minutes of each other. Therefore, it is easy to collect most of the achievements in only thirty minutes by saving right before this point. These are not the most straightforward, and you'll either need a guide or a lot of repitition - not what I think an achievement system should be. The rest are collected by completing the game's two major endings, which are both only a half an hour after the decision point. I got a 100% in this game in a mere two hours.
I also found out that Episode 2 won't be coming anytime soon. First, Dischan said they were in trouble, then they ran a Kickstarter, which succeeded! Yay! But then it didn't work out and they've been (partially) refunding people, saying that the series will not continue after all. Boo! With that in mind, I can't really say I recommend this unless you're a fan of the genre.

Billed as the spiritual successor to the original isometric
games, the Wasteland 2 that we have today is the result of 3 years and 3 million dollars' worth of work. And it
The new graphics are based on an innovative new rendering system that builds characters and environments using nothing but jaggies, bringing to life a rich and vibrant world of faded browns and greens. Despite the 3D graphics, the bold choice of camera angle in the game restricts your view to only a tiny rectangular area of the game world at a time, at times feeling like the top-down perspective of the 1988 release - something that should go quite well with inXile's nostalgia-based marketing. In essence, they've managed the herculean feat of combining unattractive low-budget 3D graphics with a visually uninformative, claustrophobic old-school style, and the results speak for themselves.
Which brings me to the next point I wanted to discuss: the interface. Now, I love games like
and
not because of the sheer breadth of possibilities and amount/variety of content that they offer, but because I'm a masochistic chump who enjoys the feeling of eyestrain, befuddlement and constant annoyance. In that sense, Wasteland 2 was perfect for me as a game in that regard - as it's managed to combine the obtuse, archaic interface design of those aforesaid games with the gameplay of a straightforward and mediocre RPG. I was worried that the Director's Cut might excise this feature from the re-release, so imagine my relief when I started the game and found it nearly impossible to buy or sell items! Folks, this wasn't even something that was a problem in the original release - you can tell that they really went the distance here.
But, when you get down to it, all of that stuff is just window dressing when it comes to an RPG. The two things that really matter are the gameplay and the story. Where's Wasteland 2 stand on that? Well, the gameplay's your standard fare - you click on guys that you want your guys to shoot. There's also enemies that explode on death so that four guys with clubs isn't the most optimal party. That's the extent of the tactical gameplay.
Roleplaying-wise, Wasteland 2 is very limited. Your party members are all interchangeable, and your communicative options are extremely limited as a consequence. For the most part, skills don't really factor into things beyond being used on objects to get extra loot. Your party does go around resolving conflicts and righting wrongs, and there's even a handful of world-affecting decisions you can make. It's got some interesting bits of world-building and story elements, and I feel that the story is genuinely interesting, if unexceptional - after all, as my friend Manco says, fight one megalomaniac with a messiah complex and you've fought 'em all. As an aside, you can tell how unimportant the characters are by the fact that there are only about four portraits per gender by default (and only two genders? inXile could stand to learn a thing or two about cis privilege I think) but I'm willing to excuse this because you can play as the Madoka Magica crew if you import your own portraits.
All in all, Wasteland 2 is extremely disappointing. For all the hype it's gotten, it is ugly, limp and flaccid. Out of all the more recent RPG releases,
has funner tactical combat and
has a much better story. That said, I kind of liked it - I don't really regret backing this game, despite my disappointment, and I enjoyed the time I spent playing it. However, I still wouldn't recommend it to another human being, unless they're also the kind of weirdo that feels the need to play every isometric cRPG in existence, in which case they probably wouldn't even listen to me if I told them not to play this game.
Also, the music's pretty decent.
Overall, I'd give this release an outrageously disgraceful 7/10

TL;DR: The mood is good and I mostly enjoyed playing, but it's short and simple. There are a few nice elements in it, so if you see it on sale and understand that it'll take you 15 hours to finish, pick it up. Other than that, move on.
THINGS I LIKED:
Turn based action with character development? Count me in! Wild West? Aaaah yeah! But with a supernatural twist? The game is all these, in that you won't be disappointed. The low growl of the narrator walks you through a bizarre and dark storyline, with more than a few enjoyable moments. I played the game in several sessions, and overall was looking forward to each session.
THINGS I DIDN'T LIKE:
It's short. 8 scenarios, which roll out some story to fill in the gaps between shootouts, but much of the scenarios seem like there just there to take up some time before the game nudges forward through a shootout. You have to get X amount of gold by doing one of the gold mining actions at different locations until you have it. You need to collect Y pieces of McGuffin so better start visiting all those random locations, hoping it's a piece is in there and that the "but first, you must do something for me" doesn't take forever or is at least interesting (it won't be, all the action you came for is in the main storyline).
Combat mechanic is that you'll either flank your opponents, or spend the whole day shooting at them (which does push the game north of 15 hours, the same if you re-do some of the shootouts). The "hand-crafted" combat scenes means that you won't find decent cover when you're doing that, but the enemy is entrenched. This doesn't make the shootout harder, just annoying. The action itself is not fast paced, you're watching animations play all the way through and people walking from place to place, taking incredibly long to execute the shot.
Character development is through equipment and poker cards which give you special abilities.
I'm a much bigger fan of action point turns than "You get to move and shoot. Or just shoot. Cool actions take the whole turn."
Final piece of advice if you've read this far: For once, choosing Iron Man mode on the first play through is something you should consider: the scenarios are short so replaying them might not be too much of a hassle, plus you're really not all that likely to die anyway.

Decent game for fans of XCOM.  It keeps the basic mechanics -- high/low cover, two moves that end when you shoot -- but tweaks them in interesting ways.  For example, cover reduces damage as well as hit chances, increasing the importance of it and the value of flanking shots.
The most interesting difference is the use of a deterministic "luck" factor to decide whether or not a shot hits, removing the RNG from the game.  It makes for some interesting moments.  Using luck to power special abilities works as a mechanic in some ways but not others.  On the one hand, it makes the special abilities risky, because draining your luck increases the chances that the next shot will hit.  On the other hand, other than one single-use item, the only way to recharge luck to a moderate level is to get shot and then not get shot at again for the rest of the enemy turn.  The more expensive abilities are thus hard to use after the first few turns, so with a few exceptions the "active" abilities go unused.
The "setup stage" is often tedious, as is some of the "strategic map" action (like feeding every member of your party one ... at ... a ... time).  There are occasionally long pauses when opening inventory or a shop.
I enjoyed the story, which gives you various perspectives into a demonic struggle.
NOTE: I first played this after the 1.5 update, which added mid-fight save/restore.  I probably would have rage-quit somewhere along the way without that.

I would love to recommend this game, but in its current state of development at a $20 price tag – I cannot.
Despite being called a full release, it is very much on par for a late early access title. Let me break it down:
The Good:
-	Interesting and novel approach to an economic management game.
-	A plethora of strategic and engaging choices on how to develop your territory. A Steady learning curve – though a primer on early rebel management would be nice (lost my first two territories to rebels).
-	Decent graphics, varied and appealing art/icon style.
-	Active Developer. Browse the Community page, and you will see several replies by the Dev. May he can redeem this title.
The Bad:
-	Oh. God. The crashes. In the 20 or so hours I have put in already, I have had 10-12 crashes and lost 4 different saves. BACK UP YOUR SAVES!
-	The Balance, once you master some of the more advanced mechanics, the underlying mathematical model goes crazy. With a little ingenuity, you can get 6-800 Levels of Influence from the TUTORIAL mission, which immediately skews the game into even crazier imbalances.
-	Very shallow combat system (though I suspect it’s not a core feature).
-	Get an autoclicker, and save yourself the Carpal Tunnel diagnosis. This game needs a serious UI/X rework. Expect to spend most of your play time mindlessly clicking through badly optimized interfaces.
I’ll check back in after a few weeks, maybe I’ll be able to swap this review to a positive.

Very unique take on the "decadent empire" narrative that underpins a lot of the best Sci-Fi epics like Asimov's Foundation and settings like WH40K..The game seems daunting at first due to the complexity, but if you dive in and just mess around for a while, it's pretty easy to pick up as long as you're willing to fail and restart a few times, and experiment with the mechanics. The manual is there if you need details, but the early game is very forgiving and the time investment is low enough that it's fine if you mess up and learn by failing.
The persistent "Viceroy" RPG-ish element is one of the things that sets the game apart, and sometimes the best way to "win" is to not actually go straight for promotion, but to collect influence points to "level up" your Viceroy so that when you finally do go for the promotion, you have the skills and bonuses that will let you take on the extreme difficulty of the larger territories. It forces you to think more broadly about your overall playstyle/strategy as opposed to just fixing one territory's problems.
This game takes 4x strategy games where they need to go, someplace different that isn't just MOO2 all over again. The non-sale price is very reasonable considering the amount of entertainment I've gotten out of it so far, so if you see it go on sale, don't hesitate to snap this one up, because you're guaranteed to get your money's worth. Thumbs way up for this one!

This is NOT a review of the Director's Cut. I'll get to the "why?" later on.
Let's start by saying that I bought WL2 not long after release without looking into it too much... Everyone was praising this game, reviews were all positive...
At the time it suffered some (*A LOT OF) bugs, some of them gamebreaking. So I had to put it aside for some time. When I took it back, the bugs had been fixed (at least the ones that plagued my playthrough), so I went on...
The game wasn't as good as I expected it to be, but at the time I needed something to relax after more action-oriented games, and this one, for some time, suited my needs.
It quickly bored me though. It was super repetitive and combat was so boring... but I wanted to see if, progressing through the game, things would have changed.
I had to stop again when I read about the upcoming Director's Cut: better graphics (wow that was needed!), reworked gameplay, perks, quirks, body parts aiming à la fallout... oh and CONTROLLER SUPPORT!!! That's what I needed! A relaxing game that could be played on my big tv while lying on the couch!
So I waited. And waited. And finally it came out.
So going back to the opening of my review, why isn't this a review of the long awaited DC? That's quite simple... because I didn't had the chance to try it yet.
CONTROLLER SUPPORT (my top feature): moving my guys is impossible.
They do half a step at a time. Animation is broken and movement is slow and clunky as hell. I google for a few seconds and see that I'm not the only one experiencing this.
They say that turning the graphics to minimum settings resolves the issue.
IT'S TRUE! IT WORKS NOW!
Just, the game, which already didn't look good, looks even worse now.
Ok, nevermind, let's ignore graphics and let's enjoy all the amazing improvements this version introduces...
CRASH TO DESKTOP.
Ok, nevermind, let's reload and try again.
10 minutes in, CRASH TO DESKTOP!
AGAIN AND AGAIN!
And googling around I see that I'm not the only one. And it's not the only bug. for example, a known issue concerns dismissed followers who, instead of going back to base waiting to be recruited again, just disappear...
At the moment I don't even want to try any workaround as I personally think such release status is unacceptable even for an indie/small team game.
I'll sure wait for some updates (they already had one out, but it did just address the zoom level of the camera as far as I understand...)

Beware: This is essentially an economic management game with light combat. If this is not your thing, do not buy.
Other than that, I recommend the product. It reminds me highly if a more strategy based version of The Last Federation.
The graphics aren't exactly nextgen, but they work for what they are meant for, the music is a bit repetitive but not obnoxiously so. You don't play these games for visual and audio input though.
The management aspect is very complicated and indepth, with quite a few things constantly affecting one another, and sometimes it becomes a bit difficult to track. Especially since it doesn't show you the effects of most changes you do until the next turn. I would like to know if, for example, moving a citizen from unspecced production to specced production will help the district/planet or not. Some more feedback before passing a turn would be helpful. I've had multiple times where I've had 6-7 districts drop a wealth level from merely moving 2 citizens in the districts.
Also, one minor thing: the citizen allocation. A feature I wouldn't mind is some sort of auto-optimization.
As for the GUI, it could use a few tweaks and new features. Right clicking in the district list to go to planet list, right click again for system. Maybe click the money up top for quick policy access (in addition to the already existing policy button.) Also: Buttons. Nothing fancy needed. Simply having the 5 menus up top actually have a little border and maybe some subtle graphics would look alot better.
Finally, the voiceover is a tad on the quiet side and could really benefit from subtitles.
In summary: a quite decent management game that have some nitpicky problems.

I talked a friend in to buying this for me, and now I feel bad about that.  I guess I owe him another game!  At least we might have some multiplayer fun with it ...
Why don't I recommend this game?
Artificial difficulty.
It seems there's nothing but marsh land everywhere, so virtually wherever you drive, the truck sinks deep in to the terrain, cutting huge grooves and getting stuck.  Sure, it's fun for a little while, but it gets old pretty quick.
Apparently, you're supposed to move heavy loads across this marsh land.  Good luck doing it.  What you spend most of the time doing is trying to move from winch point to winch point, because that's how you're going to be doing it.  The slightest little miss step, and that aforementioned marshiness everywhere is going to see you sinking like a rock!
If that's not all, trying to avoid the marsh lands by, say, driving somewhere else (they are off-road vehicles, after all, so the marshy roads aren't the only option, right?) you end up running in to trees left and right because, frankly, you can't see where you're going.
This last point is called "artificial difficulty."  Instead of letting you see what you're doing out of the cab, they make you look over the top of the truck, so the truck blocks most of your view.  Worse, the camera controls are clunky, and you have to turn the camera as the truck turns.  Finally, even though being out of the cab can be useful, they keep you so close to the truck it's difficult to see what exactly you're trying to do even when you need to use the out-of-cab!
For driving, you should be in the cab.  For hooking up the winch, you should have a more "free range" camera.  If they must include a third-person view, then at least give us the ability to, you know, see better around the truck.
I don't mind the lack of variety in trucks.  I'd actually prefer fewer vehicles, if the rest of the game was "done right."
But the rest of the game isn't "done right."  And so I can not recommend this game.
(I have only had a small amount of time in this game.  Maybe it just has a steep learning curve.  If that's the case, and I later find the game is quite enjoyable, I will come back and change this review.)

•	Artwork: The feeling of the old-school hand painted Kings Quest style artwork was very nice.
•	Soundtrack.  It was pleasant and not overwhelming. This was one of the select few games that I didn’t turn the music down on.

One year later, in 2000, Core Design released Tomb Raider: Chronicles, the 5th installment in the series. Now this was probably an unexpected entry in the series, after the events in The Last Revelation. But in comparison to past games...it's a good entry in the series, but not really an improvement. I'm not saying the game is bad, though.
But let's start with the story. Now for those of you who don't know the story, SPOILER ALERT!
Now for gameplay, there isn't anything new, really. It's more of the same from The Last Revelation, only with very few new things. One of the new features and probably the most known one is the tightrope walking, which has the player controlling Lara moving forward on a tightrope while they try to have Lara maintaining her balance on the tightrope. If they fail to keep Lara balanced, she will fall and possibly to her instant death. You can also now roll out of crawlspaces, which saves a lot of time and effort when leaving crawlspaces.
New and old weapons have also returned, aside from the good old pistols. Oldies like the shotgun, uzis, the revolver and the desert eagle return. As for the new weapons, they're the HK Gun (pssssssst it's pretty much the MP5 from Tomb Raider III but with different fire modes) and the Grappling Gun.
Chronicles this time has a total of 36 secrets, which are all golden roses. Although unlike The Last Revelation, these will unlock in-game content. Get all 36 golden roses and unlock concept art and storyboards, which you can access from the Options menu.
The four adventures in this game, since they aren't really that long as each only has like 3-4 levels, the game can be completed in like 7-8 hours. It's not bad, but it's a bit of a disappointment in my opinion, compared to games like TR III or The Last Revelation which take a lot longer to beat.
As for graphics, there aren't any improvements, really. The graphics didn't really improve from The Last Revelation. So I can't really talk much about these.
And with all that out of the way, it's time for the final score. Tomb Raider: Chronicles gets a 6/10. It's an average game. It is kinda fun. Its stories within the narrative are interesting, alright. But the game sort of lacks the tomb raiding, past the first chapter. Although it's nice to see some weapons returning, particulary the fan favorite Desert Eagle.
I kinda recommend this game, though. I have to admit that I had trouble reviewing this one, cuz I really love this game. This was the first Tomb Raider game I ever played. But I tried my best to give an honest opinion. Aside from that, if you're able to, buy this game. c:
Horror games done right. Thrilling story, scary environments, interesting characters. Combat is a little wonky at times but has a very interesting style. 9/10.

Having 30 hours into this game, I can say that I really enjoy it.
Though the game had some problems during release (and still do), the game is still really fun.
Sure, the game gets repetitive, like you do the same thing over and over again. But it pays off as the story unfolds.
You meet a lot of interesting characters, including Vito Scaletta from Mafia 2. You learn of Joe's fate if you play your cards right.
The 30 fps issue at launch has been fixed, and I think It's really unfair that the game got a lot of negative reviews because of that. The devs fixed the issue 2 days after launch, so they listened to us, unlike many other devs.
Now I'm not saying that we should look past this. I saw a review that said that we shouldn't let developers release a game with such major issues, because the devs will take notice and continue releasing broken games, and still earn money doing so. That is true. But Hangar 13 took notice to our frustration and fixed the issue right away.
They have a lot of plans for this game, including 3 major expansion which I am really looking forward to.
The game has a lot of graphical bugs. Blurry and washed out textures. It feels really weird at the start of the game, but you will adjust quickly. The game is not very well optimized. I run 58 fps on a GTX 960 on the lowest quality, which is a shame. Comparing that to GTA V for example, which I can run at max with around the same fps.
But in the end, I recommend this game for the story. It's quite the journey, and I will promise you if you look past doing the same stuff over and over again, you will enjoy this game to the full.
